The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele



The point
Here’s the whole thing before any of the careful parts. I’m going to start with one
small picture, take it apart, and keep asking what each piece means, as far down as I
can get before I hit something that holds or something I can’t get under. I’ll tell you
which. Then I’ll put it back together at the end and you can check whether it still
stands.

One warning about how this went, because it explains the shape of everything after
it. Most of the time I had the hunch first and found the names later. Over and over,
somebody had been here before me. Sometimes that made my day. Sometimes it
pissed me off. You’ll see both.

Two computers that end up the same
Put two computers on a table. Hand each of them the same list of a thousand numbers.

The first one sorts it. It compares, swaps, walks the list again and again until nothing
is out of order. Then it does one more thing: it walks the whole list front to back and
checks that every number is no bigger than the one after it. That check could have
failed. It passes. Then it tidies up after itself, wipes its scratch work, and leaves the
sorted list in memory.

The second one never looks at your list. Somebody typed the sorted version into it
earlier, same thousand numbers, same order, and it puts them in memory.

Now wait until both are done and look inside. Same bits in memory. Same bits on
the screen. Set it up right, and you can, and it’s the same everything, down to the last
bit. One of them found something out about your list and stood behind it. The other
one is holding identical bits and found out nothing. Wheel them out on a cart, swap
them, wheel them back, and ask me which is which. I can’t tell you. You can’t tell me.
And the part that bugs me most: built the ordinary way, neither machine can tell you
either.

Sure, while they ran they were different. One did thousands of comparisons, the other
did a copy. But the runs are over and the runs are gone, and nobody was being sloppy.
Ordinary computers are built to forget how their bits got there, on purpose. Later in
this chapter there’s the sentence where a physicist said so in 1961, and why he said it
costs heat.

Who cares? Anybody who’s been handed a sheet that says “all tests passed.” Anybody
who’s looked at an inspection sticker on a windshield: the sticker looks the same
whether somebody checked the brakes or somebody sold the sticker. An audit, a
proof, a ledger, an AI that sounds very sure of itself: every one of them is a pile of
bits that could have come out of either computer, and the question that matters is the
one the bits can’t answer. Did something establish this, or did it just print it? I’ll come
back to every one of those at the end of this chapter and say which of them this book


                                            10
The Thiele Machine                                                              Devon Thiele


actually helps with. Fair warning: fewer than you’d hope.

I’m going to call the difference established. The first machine established that your list
is sorted. The second has the same answer and established nothing. The rest of this
chapter is me taking that one word apart.

Look harder
The obvious answer is: just look harder. Don’t look at the end, look at everything.
So make the computers as lookable as computers get. Scale them up to the size of a
warehouse, every wire a lamp that’s lit or dark, every switch something you can walk
up to and touch. Nothing hidden in a chip too small to see. Put both of them side by
side and walk the floor.

While they run, sure, you’d see the difference. One has a whole wing lighting up,
comparing and swapping, and the other just copies. But they finish. The comparing
wing goes dark. Now walk the floor and look at every single lamp. The sorted list is
spelled out in lit and dark lamps in both, the same pattern, and everything else is dark
in both, because both cleaned up.

There is no lamp anywhere that says “a check ran here and passed.” Not hidden. Not
encrypted. Just not there. You can see everything there is, and the thing I’m after isn’t
one of the things there is. Looking harder doesn’t help, because the problem isn’t that
you can’t see enough. It’s that nothing was kept.

That’s the shape I want you to carry through the rest: it’s not a visibility problem, it’s
a keeping problem.

So keep the trace
Then the fix is obvious, isn’t it? Don’t let the run go. Keep the trace: every comparison,
every swap, the check and its answer, written down as it happens. Wheel the com-
puters out on the cart and back, read the traces, and you’ll know which one sorted.
Problem solved?

It’s the right instinct, and it gets most of the way to this book. But take it apart, because
“just keep the trace” has three things wrong with it, and each one turns out to be a
piece of what comes later.

First, a trace is bits, and bits can be typed in. Whoever typed the sorted list into the
second machine can type a trace in too: “compared, swapped, checked, passed,” a
few thousand lines of it, every one of them plausible. A trace written by a program is
something the program produced, and the machine running the program doesn’t care
whether it’s true. So keeping the trace doesn’t answer the question. It moves it. Did
something establish this trace, or did it just print it?

Second, the way out of that is to take the pen away from the program. Don’t let
the program write its own trace. Have something underneath it write the trace, one


                                             11
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


step at a time, as the steps actually happen, so nothing a program does can add a
line that didn’t happen or erase one that did. Airplanes do a version of this. Flight
recorders, which go back to a prototype David Warren built in Melbourne in the 1950s,
are fed by the aircraft’s own instruments rather than by anybody’s account of events,
and they’re built to survive the crash, so the investigators don’t have to depend on
anyone’s memory of what happened. That’s the right shape, and it isn’t mine. Later
in this chapter it gets its name from computer security, a reference monitor, and I’ll
say outright that a machine built that way would be doing what this book describes.
What the book adds is narrower than a rulebook for everything underneath. It’s about
the records that go up and never come back down: what that something has to keep
for good, and what keeping it costs.

Third, you can’t keep all of it. A full trace grows with every step and never stops
growing, and a machine with finite memory runs out. Even the flight recorder doesn’t
keep everything. The cockpit voice recorder is a loop: for decades it held the last thirty
minutes, now it holds at least two hours, and everything older gets recorded over.
Every real machine that keeps a trace keeps a window of it, or a fingerprint of it, and
forgets the content.

The fingerprint is the sharpest reply, so take it seriously. Fold every new line of the
trace into a fixed-size scramble of everything before it, and you’ve got a hash chain.
Haber and Stornetta’s timestamps, later in this chapter, work that way; so do the audit
logs Bruce Schneier and John Kelsey designed in 1999; and so do the measurement
registers in the security chip a lot of computers carry, the TPM, which a running
program can only extend, never set, until the next reboot. That really does keep
something about the whole trace in a few dozen bytes. But look at what it keeps. It
keeps a binding, not the content: to read the history you still need the trace stored
somewhere, and the fingerprint only tells you whether a copy somebody hands you
is the one that went in. The binding holds only because nobody knows how to find
two traces with the same fingerprint, which is a bet on how hard a search is, not a law.
And squeezing traces that keep growing into a fixed number of bits has to land many
traces on one fingerprint. That’s a merge, the same merge as the chairs further down,
hidden behind how hard it is to find which traces share a seat. Fingerprints are great.
They’re not a way out of forgetting. They’re a very clever way of forgetting.

So the real question was never “save everything.” It’s this: what’s the smallest thing
worth keeping for good, and what does keeping it cost? The answer this book ends up
with is not the trace but the commitment (in the database’s sense, a question closed,
not the cryptographer’s sealed envelope; both come up later). Not every comparison
the sort made, just the one fact that a check of this very claim passed and the question
got closed. And here’s the part that matters most: on a finite machine, keeping even
that one fact for good forces the machine to forget something somewhere else. That’s
the chairs, further down. And keeping things for good fills up, which Part II turns
into a count.


                                           12
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


So the premise was never that computers can’t keep records. They keep records all
day. It’s that nothing in the rules of an ordinary computer makes the record paid for,
permanent, or earned, and those three come in at different places, so here’s where.
Paid for is the model’s one rule: in the Thiele Machine, the step that raises the record
has to cost something. Permanent is a premise, the one the chairs need, and one of
the conditions Part III puts on a record. Earned, meaning a check of this very claim
passed first, isn’t in the model’s core at all; it’s what the step of the small machine in
Part IV enforces, proved for that machine and every program on it. A machine that
charges one mark for every step it takes meets the first rule and none of the others,
and I’ll keep pointing that out.

Computed, stored, established
Three words that get used like they’re one.

Computed is about the steps. The first machine computed the sorted list. The second
didn’t.

Stored is about the bits. Both machines stored it.

Established is neither, and that’s the whole problem. It isn’t the steps, because they’re
gone. It isn’t the bits, because they’re identical. It’s something like this: the first
machine has a right to lean on “this list is sorted,” because it ran a test that could
have failed, the test passed, the test was about this very list, and then the question got
closed. The second machine has the same sentence and no right to it. That’s a true fact
about the two of them, and it’s written down nowhere, in either one. (Whose right,
strictly? A machine doesn’t lean on anything, any more than a filing cabinet does. It’s
the right of whoever reads the first machine to lean on what it says, and the machine
is where the grounds for that right would have to be kept. “The machine has a right”
is shorter, so I’ll keep saying it, and now you know what it’s short for.)

Four words I’ll hold still from here on. A check is the test, the thing that could say no.
A commit is the closing, the question shut for good, about that edition of that thing.
The record is whatever stays behind to say so. And established is all three, about one
thing. That’s the working sense. The book cashes it at three depths, a paid closing in
the bare model, an object with a checked relation and a paid event in Part III, and the
whole chain on the small machine in Part IV, and each place says which one it means.

Which raises a fair question. What if the second machine, handed the typed-in list,
runs the check on it? Then it has established that the list is sorted. Full stop. It didn’t
do the sorting and it doesn’t need to. The line I’m drawing is between checked and
unchecked, not between computed and copied, and “found out nothing” up there was
about the copier that never looked. So whatever this book ends up counting, it isn’t
how hard anybody worked.

People say “a right to lean on it” about a lot of things that turn out to be vibes, so I



                                            13
The Thiele Machine                                                          Devon Thiele


had to find out whether this one was anything. So I went looking. Here’s what I ran
into.

The clerk who forgets everything
The picture everybody passes around is a person with a pencil, a strip of paper and a
short list of rules, and that’s what a computer is. It’s worth going back to the source,
Alan Turing’s 1936 paper, and seeing how far he actually takes it.

He takes it a long way. Back then a “computer” was a job, a human doing sums by
hand, and Turing modelled that person. He’s careful with the person’s mind: whatever
the clerk knows, beyond a handful of states, has to go down on the paper. Then he
goes all the way. He imagines the clerk getting up, walking off, forgetting everything,
and coming back later. To pick up where he left off, the clerk leaves himself “a note
of instructions,” and Turing says that note is the clerk’s state of mind, as far as the
computation is concerned. Marks on paper and a note. That’s the whole state.

My two computers are sitting right inside that. Suppose the clerk didn’t write the note.
Somebody slipped it under the door, in the right form, with the right instructions. He
comes back, reads it, carries on, and every mark he makes from then on is exactly
what he’d have made if he’d written it himself. Turing’s model can’t tell the clerk who
did the work from the clerk who was handed a note saying he did. It was never asked
to. Turing wanted something you could check without crawling into anybody’s head,
and a note on a desk is about as checkable as it gets. That’s why the paper still works
ninety years later. It’s also why there’s no place in it for the thing I’m after.

So the founding picture of computing is a man who leaves his desk, forgets everything
he was doing, and trusts a sticky note. I relate to him deeply.

And now the question nobody needs answered to follow the argument, which is
exactly the kind I can’t leave alone: who were those clerks? Real people. Before
machines took the word, a “computer” was a job title. In the late 1800s the Harvard
Observatory hired rooms full of women to do the arithmetic of the sky, cataloguing
stars by hand for a fraction of a man’s wage, and some of them found things the
astronomers who hired them had missed. Rooms like that ran artillery tables in both
world wars. So when Turing modelled “the computer,” he was modelling somebody’s
actual afternoon. Does that change the argument? Not a bit. But it changes the picture,
for me anyway: the sticky note was always a person trusting another person’s work,
and the question of whether the work behind it was really done is older than any
machine.

Information doesn’t have it either
My next guess was information: one machine got some, the other didn’t. That one
died fast. Claude Shannon, who turned information into a number in 1948, says on
his first page that the meaning of a message is “irrelevant to the engineering problem.”
His number measures how many messages you could have sent, not what the one you


                                          14
The Thiele Machine                                                               Devon Thiele


sent did, which is exactly right for building telephone lines and exactly no help to me.
Same message out of the same set, same number, for both computers. He’d give them
the same number if one of them got hit by lightning and came out right by luck.

Fine, look at the one message instead of the set. In the 1960s some people (Ray
Solomonoff, Andrei Kolmogorov, Gregory Chaitin, separately) worked out how to
measure the information in one string: the length of the shortest program that prints
it. Same two computers, same string, same number. And then there’s the thing in that
theory I keep going back to and standing on, to see if it creaks. Running a program
can’t add this kind of information. What comes out can’t hold more than what went in
plus the program, give or take a little. Leonid Levin, who proved a general version of
this, has a one-liner for it that’s too good not to repeat: you can torture an uninformed
witness all you want, you won’t get information about the crime.

Which means, as far as information goes, sorting your list told you nothing. The sorted
list holds nothing that “your list, plus the word sort” didn’t already hold.

And it turns out logic says the same thing in a different coat. The standard logic of
knowing, the one Jaakko Hintikka worked out in 1962, has a property people call
logical omniscience: if you know some facts, you automatically know everything that
follows from them. So by that logic, once you knew every number on your list, you
already knew whether it was sorted. Hintikka flagged the problem himself, in the
same book, and people have been trying to fix it since. The fix that comes closest to me
is Sergei Artemov’s, from 1995: you only get to know a thing if you’ve built an actual
justification for it, and the justification rides along with the claim. That’s a reason
traveling with the claim, which is almost a record. But it’s a way of writing things
down and reasoning about them. People have taught it to count, too: Ho Ngoc Duc,
in 1997, made knowing take reasoning steps, and Artemov and Roman Kuznets, in
2014, asked how big a justification can get before knowing by it stops being feasible.
What none of it has is the closing of a question as a step with a price.

So the two most careful accounts I could find, one about bits and one about knowing,
say the same thing: the sort added nothing.

And yet you know something after the sort that you didn’t before. You can read the
smallest number off the first slot. You can stop worrying. Something happened. That’s
the clue, and it’s the first solid thing I’ve got: whatever established is, it isn’t new bits.
It’s the same bits, settled.

The guy who got closest
Somebody had that clue before me, and he’s the closest neighbour I’ve found, so he
gets the most room and the hardest push.

Charles Bennett, a physicist at IBM, wrote a paper in 1988 that starts where I just ended
up: information isn’t the same as value. His example is an almanac of where the moon



                                             15
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


and planets will be every day for a hundred years. It has no more information than
the equations it was calculated from, but it saves you doing the calculating. So the
value is the work. He called the amount of work a thing carries its depth.

Was this my idea, already done, by a guy at IBM? The only way to find out was to find
where it parts from mine, because if I couldn’t find that place I’d just be renaming his
idea. And it’s one word: plausibly. Depth is the amount of work a thing was plausibly
made with. Bennett says straight out that you can’t know how a message actually
came to be; for all you know it came from flipping coins. Depth is read off the finished
thing, the way a fossil’s age is read off the fossil.

Bring the two computers back. The sorted list in the first one has some depth. The
identical list in the second has exactly the same depth, because depth looks at the list
and nothing else. A photocopy of a deep thing is just as deep. Depth tells you some
work was done, somewhere, by someone. It’s not a record that this machine did it,
and it’s not a receipt for what doing it cost.

So Bennett’s standing right next to the line, on the other side of it, and as far as I can
tell he got his own question right. He asked how much work a thing embodies. I’m
asking who has the right to lean on it and what they paid to get there. His answer
lives in the object. Mine, if I’ve got one, has to live in the machine.

Statues that walk off
If it isn’t in the information, maybe it’s in the knowing, so I went and read the philoso-
phers. And there it was again: people had been arguing about the difference between
having the right answer and knowing it for a couple thousand years.

Plato’s version is a joke about statues. There was a story that the sculptor Daedalus
made statues so lifelike they’d walk off if you didn’t tie them down. Plato says true
opinions are like that: they wander off, and they’re not worth much until you tie them
down with the reason why. Once they’re tied down, they’re knowledge, and they stay
put. Knowledge tied to a reason, and knowledge that stays. Of everybody I’d have
bet on to hand me that shape, Plato wasn’t on the list.

Then in 1963 a philosopher named Edmund Gettier broke the tidy version in three
pages. Smith and Jones are up for the same job. Smith has good reason to think Jones
will get it, and he’s counted the coins in Jones’s pocket: ten. So Smith figures, fairly,
that the man who’ll get the job has ten coins in his pocket. Then Smith gets the job,
and, unknown to him, Smith also has ten coins in his pocket. True, believed, backed
by a reason. Not knowledge. He was right by luck, because his reason was about the
wrong pocket.

That’s the push that matters for a machine. Checking one pocket and committing to
a claim about another is right by luck. So whatever a machine commits to, the check
underneath has to be about this very claim, and I’d better say exactly what that means,



                                           16
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


because it carries a lot of weight later.

A check is about this very claim when four things hold. It tests the same property the
commit names, not a cousin of it. It tests that property on the same thing the commit
names, not the thing next to it. Nothing has written to that thing between the check
and the commit, so it’s still the same edition the check looked at. And the check is
honest: it says yes when the property is true and no when it isn’t, on every value it
could ever be handed, not just this one. Break the first three and you’re Smith with
his ten coins. Break the fourth and the check is just a rubber stamp. Later in the book
I build a machine whose step won’t let a commit through unless the first three hold,
and whose checks come with a proof of the fourth.

Two notes on those four, because they matter later. The fourth asks for more than
it needs. To rule out luck, a check only has to never say yes when the property is
false; saying yes every time it’s true is a bonus. And the third is a very old bug in
computing wearing Gettier’s coat. Security people call it time-of-check-to-time-of-use:
check a file, use it, and something swaps the file in between (Matt Bishop and Michael
Dilger wrote up how to hunt for it in 1996). Databases guard against the same thing
by making sure, just before a commit, that nothing they read has been written since;
H. T. Kung and John Robinson called that optimistic concurrency control in 1981. A
philosopher’s pocket and a sysadmin’s race condition, same bug. One limit, said now:
a machine can only promise “nothing has written to that thing” about its own memory;
for brake pads or a voter roll the third condition becomes a premise about whoever
measured (Section 12).

And here’s where I went further than this chapter needs, because the obvious next
question is: does anything fix Gettier? People tried for years. The first patch is “no
false steps in the reasoning”: Smith’s mistake was believing Jones would get the job,
so rule that out. Then a philosopher named Alvin Goldman, crediting Carl Ginet,
came back with barns. You’re driving through a county that, unknown to you, is full
of fake barns, just painted fronts propped up to look like the real thing. You look
at the one real barn in the county and think “that’s a barn.” True. Believed. Good
reason, your own eyes, and no false step anywhere. And still you were lucky: if you’d
glanced at the next one over you’d have believed the same thing and been wrong.
Every patch gets a new barn, and as far as I can tell the arguing hasn’t stopped. Which
tells me something I’ll keep: whether a check was good isn’t only about this one case.
It’s about what the check would have done on the cases next door. Hold on to that,
because it’s the next section.

What “could have failed” means
I keep saying the first machine’s test could have failed. Take that apart, because it’s the
piece everything else hangs off.

The machine is deterministic. Given your list, the check was always going to pass. So
in what sense could it have failed? In this sense: if your list had been out of order,

                                            17
The Thiele Machine                                                              Devon Thiele


the check would have said no. That’s a claim about a different list, not about chance.
Run the second machine on a scrambled list and it prints the same sorted list anyway,
because it never looked. Run the first on a scrambled list and its check catches it. The
first machine’s answer follows the truth about your list; the second machine’s would
be the same either way.

Here’s the shape. A check is a question asked of every possible input, and it splits
them into two piles: the ones it says yes to and the ones it says no to. “Could have
failed” just means the no pile isn’t empty. A check that says yes to everything has an
empty no pile, and it establishes nothing, however long it runs and however official it
looks. A philosopher, Robert Nozick, made a version of this a condition for knowing,
in 1981: you know a thing only if, had it been false, you wouldn’t believe it.

Push on it once more, because this is where it really gives. “Could have failed” is a fact
about the procedure, about what the check would have done on other lists. It isn’t a fact
about the end state at all. Look at the first machine’s memory when it’s done: a sorted
list. Nothing in those bits says “and whatever made me would have caught a mistake.”
That’s the warehouse again, every lamp visible and none of them saying it. The one
thing that makes the first machine’s answer worth more is exactly the kind of thing an
end state can’t hold. The only way a machine can own it is to write something down
at the moment the check passes, and to have that something mean what it says. More
than anything else in this chapter, that’s why I ended up needing a record and not just
a better answer. Even then the record only carries half of it. It can say this check ran
on this edition and passed. That the check would have said no on a bad list is a fact
about the checker, and that half rides on a proof about the checker, which somebody
outside the machine has to read and accept. Where that kind of chain of reasons stops
is Popper’s swamp, a little further down.

One more thing that tripped me up and then didn’t. Rig a check to pass only on your
one list. Is that cheating? No. It’s a perfectly honest check of a different claim, “this is
that exact list,” and it has a big no pile: every other list. It establishes exactly that and
nothing more. What a check establishes is whatever it’s honest about.

Put that next to the empty no pile and the two fit together: a check establishes what
it’s honest about, and a check whose no pile is empty is honest about nothing, so it
establishes nothing. One thing I’ll say plainly now, so it doesn’t ambush you in Part
IV: the small machine I build there doesn’t police this. Its step makes sure a commit
was checked first, about the same thing, by a checker proved honest. It doesn’t stop
you asking a question that can’t come out no, like “is this number at least zero.” Ask
one and the whole chain runs, three marks paid, and nothing is established but the
chain. The certificate I show off there asks one that can fail.

Settled, whether it’s true or not
Then I ran into Charles Sanders Peirce, writing in 1877, and he said the thing I’d been
running together without noticing. The point of inquiry, he says, is to get out of doubt

                                             18
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


and settle on a belief. And when someone objects that surely what people want is a
true belief, he answers like a guy who’s watched a lot of arguments end: “as soon as a
firm belief is reached we are entirely satisfied, whether the belief be true or false.”

That’s funny, and then it isn’t, because he’s right. Settling and being right are two
different events. A question can be closed on a wrong answer, and once it’s closed it
acts closed. Peirce cares a lot about which ways of settling hold up (science wins, for
him, because it has to answer to something outside any one person), but the settling
itself, the question snapping shut, is there every time, and it never comes with a
guarantee.

Karl Popper said it from the other side. Every test, he says, has to stop somewhere, at
some statement somebody decides to accept, and nothing in the evidence forces you
to stop there instead of one step further. You stop when you’re satisfied. His picture is
a jury: the verdict is a decision about what happened, and the jury deciding it doesn’t
make it true. Science, for him, is a building on piles driven into a swamp, and the piles
stop where somebody’s satisfied they’ll hold, not where the ground gets firm.

That swamp sent me further down, because it’s the oldest problem in the book and
it doesn’t have a bottom. Ask why you believe something and you get a reason. Ask
why you believe the reason and you get another one. Sextus Empiricus wrote down
the ancient version, credited to someone called Agrippa, and in the 1960s a follower
of Popper’s, Hans Albert, gave it a name with a joke in it: the Münchhausen trilemma,
after the baron who claimed he pulled himself out of a swamp by his own hair. Every
chain of reasons does one of three things. It goes on forever. It loops back on itself.
Or it stops somewhere, because somebody decided it stops. People have argued for
a very long time about which of the three to live with. So “when do I actually know,
and when am I done checking?” doesn’t get a clean answer from anybody. What you
can do is be honest about where you stopped and why. That’s a lot of what the rest
of this book is: every place it stops is written down, with its name on it, so you can
decide whether you’d have stopped there too.

Lay those two on top of each other and here’s what shows through. The check is one
act. The stopping is another. The check can run as long as you like and it never makes
you stop; at some point something decides, and the deciding is its own event. That’s
the second machine’s whole trick: it skipped the check and kept the answer.

And a logician said the part I didn’t expect a logician to say. Per Martin-Löf, whose
ideas sit underneath the kind of proof checker that checks this book, says a proof isn’t
an object, it’s an act, and once it’s done it’s done, irrevocably. You could say that’s true
of everything that ever happened. Fine. But it’s the two computers again: the first
machine’s check happened, irrevocably, and the machine right now carries no trace of
it. The past can’t be undone. The record of it can be lost, unless something keeps one.
That gap is where this book lives.



                                            19
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


Turns out computing already had a word for it
Here’s the slightly embarrassing part. Computing already has a word for this and
uses it every day. Anyone who’s used a database has seen it: COMMIT.

A database does a pile of tentative work, and then there’s one moment, the commit,
written to a log, after which the change counts. Jim Gray, who more or less built the
theory behind that, opens his 1981 paper on it by saying the idea comes from contract
law, and his example is a wedding. People negotiate, somebody asks, two people say
“I do,” and from then on it’s binding. If it was a mistake you don’t erase it; you do
another transaction to fix it, the way a bad contract gets a second contract and not a
time machine.

The wedding was a philosopher’s example first. J. L. Austin, lecturing in 1955, said “I
do” doesn’t describe a marriage, it makes one, and sayings like that aren’t true or false.
They can misfire (the wrong person says it, a step gets skipped) but they can’t be false.
That’s a commit exactly. Writing the commit record doesn’t report that a question got
closed. Writing it is the closing. And a commit can’t be false, only misfire: committed
without the check, committed about the wrong pocket. Gettier and Peirce again, from
a third direction. Then somebody else reads the record, and for them it stops being a
performance and turns into a report: “this was checked and closed.” A report can be
false. On the small machine in Part IV it can’t be, about the machine’s own history: if
its flag is up from a clean start, some claim was checked and closed, and that claim
held of that edition when it was checked. That’s the one place in the book where a
commit and the truth get tied together, and it took a proof to do it.

Robin Milner, building a proof checker in the 1970s, ran out of memory, so he decided
to keep only the finished theorems and throw the proofs away, like a teacher rubbing
out the blackboard to make room. The obvious worry is forgery: if the proofs are
gone, what stops someone just writing a theorem down? His answer was beautiful.
Theorems got their own type in the programming language, and the only way to
make one was through the rules of logic. You couldn’t forge one because the language
wouldn’t let you build it any other way. He named that language ML, for Meta
Language. I wanted to call my machine the meta machine. I’m choosing to treat that
as a coincidence and not a sign, which is more restraint than I usually manage.

Bitcoin is the loud modern version. Its records can’t be changed without redoing all
the work that came after them, and a computer that drops off the network and comes
back trusts the longest chain as the story of what happened while it was gone. That’s
Turing’s clerk again, coming back to a note. The difference is that the clerk’s note costs
nothing to forge and Bitcoin’s costs a mountain of work. It’s the clearest case I know
of somebody making a settled fact expensive to fake, and they got there by paying for
a search, not by putting a price on the settling.

That’s a different job from the one the toll does, and it’s worth saying before you read
the toll as a deterrent. One mark deters nobody. Bitcoin’s work is tied to something

                                           20
The Thiele Machine                                                              Devon Thiele


scarce, electricity and hardware; a mark in this book is tied to nothing. What makes a
raised record mean something, on the machine where it means anything, is an order
rule: check, then commit, then certify. That rule would work just as well at a price of
zero. The price is there because, on the premises of the chairs a little further on, a finite
machine that prices its merges can’t avoid it, not because it scares anybody off. The
machines I actually build don’t meet those premises, so on them the price is a choice
made to match (Section 14 says why).

And Bitcoin wasn’t first. Pull on its footnotes: three of the eight references in the paper
that started it point to Stuart Haber and Scott Stornetta, who in 1991 worked out how
to stamp a document with a time nobody could fake later, by chaining each stamp to
the ones before it. A company built on their idea has been printing a short fingerprint
of its chain in the classified ads of the New York Times, once a week, since 1995. Think
about that for a second. To make a record nobody could quietly rewrite, they put it
somewhere a million people would keep a copy of without even meaning to. That’s
the same move Zurek describes the world making with a measurement, and I’ll get to
him at the end.

There are more fences like these: logs that can’t quietly change, certificates you can
check. Later in the book I take five of them apart. I lean on all of them. They work. I
want that said plainly, because the next thing isn’t “they’re broken.”

The next thing is where they sit. The database’s commit is bits in a log, kept by
a database program, on a machine whose own step will overwrite those bits the
moment some instruction says to. Milner’s guarantee is a type checker; it holds inside
programs written in his language and nowhere else. Bitcoin is a protocol on ordinary
computers that will do whatever they’re told. Every one of them is a program or a rule,
on top of a machine that can’t tell my two computers apart. The machine underneath
keeps nothing and charges nothing for what got settled.

The obvious comeback: so put the rule one level lower, in the operating system, or
what security people call a reference monitor, the small always-on piece everything
has to pass through. Yes. Exactly that. A monitor that wouldn’t let any program raise
its record without paying would be doing the thing I’m talking about. In this book’s
words it would be implementing the model, and I’d count that as agreement. What I
care about isn’t who builds the fence. It’s what the fence has to obey, wherever it’s
built, and whether that’s forced or just a good idea.

That comeback has a history, and it’s older than me by a lot. In 1972 James P. Ander-
son’s planning study for the US Air Force described a reference monitor: a piece every
access has to pass through, that can’t be tampered with, and small enough to check.
In 2000 Fred Schneider worked out exactly which rules a monitor that only watches a
run as it goes can enforce: the ones whose breaking shows up at some finite point, the
kind computer scientists call safety rules. “No certificate without an earlier passing
check and a commit” is one of those. And in 2015 Arthur Azevedo de Amorim and six


                                             21
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


coauthors built monitors that check a rule at every single instruction, and proved them
correct in Coq, the same proof checker this book uses. So putting a rule under every
program, so nothing can get around it, is their move, not mine. What I’m putting
under that move is narrower: a record that has to be paid for, on the small machine
one that has to be earned, and a reason, from counting, why a finite machine that
prices its merges can’t make that price zero.

What settling looks like
The chapter on what structure is (Section 2) ends with a pile of things sorted into
buckets. Settling a question is that, plus one more thing.

Picture every state the machine could be in as a field of dots. A yes-or-no question
about the state splits the field into two rooms: yes and no. That’s a sorting, the smallest
one there is. And remember the no pile: if one of the rooms is empty, there’s no sorting
at all, just a field. Now the extra thing that makes it a settlement: once the machine is
in the yes room, no step it can take leads back out. The door opens one way. A settled
question is a sorting plus a door that only swings in.

At its best, what goes through the door is a relation: these numbers are in this order,
these two things belong together. There’s a chimpanzee named Sultan, later in the
book, who fitted two short sticks into one long one and reached the food. Nothing
new got added to the cage. Two sticks became one tool. That’s what I’d want the door
to be for.

But the door doesn’t care, and this is the honest edge of the whole picture. Hook the
door to a check that says yes to everything and the machine walks through, settled,
and wrong. Settled whether true or false, like Peirce said. A door that only swings
one way tells you a question was closed. It doesn’t tell you it was closed right. Price
and correctness are two different books, and I keep both, separately.

One more edge, the one Gray’s wedding already hinted at. What stays shut for good
is that the question got closed, about that edition of that thing. Whether the claim is
still true is another matter. Change the list after the commit and the record still says,
truthfully, that the old edition was checked and closed. And if the claim turns out bad,
the fix is another act on top, a second record that says “withdrawn,” never the first
one quietly coming back down. So “entitled to lean on it right now” is three things at
once: closed, not withdrawn since, and the thing unchanged.

Why it has to cost
This is the part I’m proudest of, because once you’ve picked a record that stays, the
choosing stops and the counting takes over. And the counting is chairs.

Take any machine with a finite number of states. Its step is a function: give it a state
and a move, it gives you back one state. Pick a yes-or-no reading of the state and make
it permanent: no step ever turns a yes back into a no. Now suppose some step takes a


                                            22
The Thiele Machine                                                              Devon Thiele


state that reads no and lands it on one that reads yes. Then that step has to land two
different states on one. It merges.

Do it with chairs. Draw a box on the floor, three chairs inside, one chair outside by the
door. Four people, one per chair: the four states the machine could be in. The three
inside already read yes. One step moves everybody at once, each to the chair the rule
sends them to. Nobody inside may leave, because yes is permanent. The person by
the door has to come in, because this is the step that flips them to yes. Now finish the
move, one person per chair. You can’t. Four people, three inside chairs: somebody
shares. Maybe the newcomer ends up on a lap, maybe two insiders squeeze onto one
chair; either way, two people end on one chair, and from where everyone’s sitting you
can’t tell which two. That’s the pigeonhole principle, which is old and not mine, and
the checked version, with exactly those three conditions (finite, permanent, one flip),
is in the chapter “Why the toll isn’t arbitrary.” No physics in it anywhere. Counting.

(How old is it? Older than you’d guess. A French Jesuit, Jean Leurechon, used it in
1622 to argue that two people somewhere must have exactly the same number of hairs
on their heads, which is the kind of thing you can be completely sure of and never
check. Its first proper name came two centuries later, from Dirichlet, who called it
the drawer principle; the pigeons came later still. Is 1622 the bottom? I can’t tell you.
History is like that: it’s where you start digging, not where you stop.)

Turn it around and it gets better. A reversible computer, one where every step can be
run backwards, never merges anything, because a step you can undo never puts two
people on one chair. Bennett, the same Bennett, showed in 1973 that any computation
can be done reversibly if you give it room to keep its history while it works. But give
a reversible computer a finite memory and, however much it computes, it can never
raise a flag that stays up. It can always back up to before the flag. Settling needs
exactly the kind of step a reversible computer refuses to take. (Where does the merged
state go, physically? Out of the machine and into the room, as heat; the machine and
the room together never merge. Section 4 comes back to that.)

Now the physics, as an assumption with its name on it. Rolf Landauer, at IBM, 1961,
said that a step that can’t be run backwards, that merges, “requires a minimal heat
generation.” That’s the rule people call Landauer’s principle. On a finite machine,
settling something for good takes a merge, and if Landauer’s right, a merge costs heat
whenever the machine doesn’t already know which of the merged states it was in. So
on that assumption, a device that has to settle things correctly without knowing its
own state ahead of time can’t do it for free.

And here’s the rest of his sentence, the one I promised at the start. That heat, he wrote,
“serves the purpose of standardizing signals and making them independent of their
exact logical history.” That’s my two computers, in 1961. Ordinary machines spend
their merges, and their heat, on forgetting how the bits got there, on purpose, so a 1 is a 1
no matter what path made it. That’s why the sorter and the copier end up identical,


                                             23
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


and why the comparing wing goes dark. And the very same kind of step, a merge, is
what it takes to close a door for good.

So here’s the deepest thing I can say about settling, and I’ll say it carefully, because
it’s easy to say it bigger than it is. Not every forgetting settles anything: wiping a
scratch pad closes no question. But on a finite machine, every settling forgets. The
step that closes a question for good lands two states on one, somewhere, maybe not
where you happen to be standing, and afterward nothing can tell which one it was.
A verdict keeps the decision and lets go of the arguing. An ordinary computer pays
for the forgetting and keeps nothing to show for it. What I want to know is what a
machine looks like that pays for the same forgetting and keeps the receipt.

Every assumption in that is a way out, and you should know where they are. Give the
machine unlimited memory and it never has to merge; it can write its history down
forever, and the chapter on the toll builds exactly that machine. Let the flag come back
down and the chairs lose their grip. And the heat isn’t owed by every run. Landauer’s
principle, in the general form Part II adopts, charges for what you didn’t know, so one
run from a known start owes no heat at all; the floor bites for a device that has to cope
with states it can’t tell apart, which is how devices get built (Theorem 4.12). The toll
still charges its mark on that run, because the toll is a rule about the move, and the
move doesn’t know who’s watching. And Landauer’s principle is physics, not math.
A group in Lyon measured the heat of erasing one bit in a tiny bead held by a laser,
in 2012, and it has serious critics too, the philosopher John Norton among them. So
the counting is proved and the price is an assumption, and I never let those two swap
places.

Somebody got there first, goddamn it
Bennett also says looking can be free. His famous move with Maxwell’s demon (the
whole story’s later in the book) is that you can write down which side of a box a
molecule is on without paying anything, as long as you write on a blank page. What
costs is wiping the page to make room for the next one.

I’d been sitting on this idea that committing is what costs, not learning, and I thought:
this one’s mine, I finally had an original thought. Then I found Carlo Rovelli’s 2024
paper, “The Thermodynamic Cost of Choosing.” Nope. Somebody got there first,
goddamn it. A real physicist, with a real paper, saying that making a choice that sticks
costs at least the same heat Landauer charges for erasing a bit. He even quotes a
German saying, Wahl ist Leiden, to choose is to suffer, and at that point what are you
going to do but laugh.

And then, taking him apart properly, it got good, because he seems to contradict
Bennett. Bennett says measuring can be free; Rovelli says any measurement costs.
So which is it? Look at what Rovelli calls a choice. A coin in the air hasn’t chosen
anything; it has to hit the ground and stop. And then the sentence I’d put on my
wall: “stabilization must be irreversible, otherwise it is not stabilization.” Bennett’s

                                           24
The Thiele Machine                                                               Devon Thiele


free measurement is one that could still be undone; that’s why it’s free. Rovelli’s choice
is one that’s been made to stay; that’s why it costs. The way I read them, they’re
standing on opposite sides of the same door: learning on Bennett’s side, committing
on Rovelli’s. (Bennett’s demon still pays in the end, when it wipes the page.) Neither
of them puts it that way, so push on it. But if it holds, it’s the best sign I’ve got that the
line I keep drawing between knowing and settling isn’t something I made up.

Push on it, then, with his paper open, and it gives in four places: his choice is unpre-
dictable, it’s a branching where mine is a merge, it’s stable only for a while, and he
stands against Bennett’s free measurement, not beside it (Section 5 goes through all
four). So the two-sides-of-one-door picture is my reading, not his, and the piece of it
that’s really his is the one sentence about stabilizing. That sentence I’ll still put on my
wall.

So he’s my closest neighbour, and here’s the difference, exactly. His is physics: a
price in heat, at a temperature, for a choice that sticks. Mine is a rule in a model of
computation: a charge in the machine’s own count, on the step that flips a permanent
reading on, with no temperature anywhere in it. Same instinct, different place. I’ll
take it. It’s annoying to be second. It’s worse to be alone and wrong.

What the Thiele Machine is
So here’s what I built, and which parts I was pushed into and which parts I chose,
because you should know which is which.

The Thiele Machine is a model of computation, the way Turing’s machine is: math you
can reason about, not a box you can buy. It has a few parts. A state. A step that moves
the state. A record: a yes-or-no reading of the state that says whether something’s
been established. A charge on each kind of move, added up on a counter that only
climbs. One rule, which I call the toll: the step that flips the record from no to yes has
to cost at least one mark on that counter. And a window, what an outside observer gets
to see, which is there because the two computers already showed you the problem:
the usual window, the bits, can’t see the record. The toll’s first name, the one I gave it
before I understood it, is No Free Insight.

One what, and why one? One mark, in the model’s own count. One because it’s
the least a whole-number count can charge and still not be free, and the toll only
says not free. The model doesn’t say a mark is worth a joule or a dollar; whether it’s
worth anything physical is Landauer’s assumption, named, and nowhere else. And
one is just the floor: Part II shows that if you charge one mark per halving, a step
that squeezes a lot together pays at least the logarithm of the squeeze, roughly how
many times it halves the number of states it can tell apart. Don’t read that backwards,
though. One mark isn’t one halving. A single state flipping into a big room of states
that already read yes squeezes things together very little, much less than a halving,
and the whole-number count rounds that up to one.



                                             25
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


What was I pushed into? That on a finite machine, a record that never comes down
can only be raised by a merge: counting, proved. That merges cost: physics, assumed.
What did I choose? To put the count inside the step, as part of what a step is, instead
of in a log off to the side. Nothing forces that. It’s my claim about where the account
belongs, and the rest of the book is the case for it.

About the name. I named it after myself, on purpose. Half of that is a joke and half
of it is a stake in the ground. Turing got a machine, so here’s mine. The longer story,
meta machines and all, is in “How I got here” (Section 1).

The names work the way Turing’s do, and I’m going to be a little annoying about them.
The Thiele Machine, capital letters, is the model and nothing else. A Thiele machine, lower
case, is any particular system proved to fit the model, the way one rule table is a Turing
machine; a two-box toy on a sheet of paper counts. A Thiele machine is Thiele-complete
when the machine under the record can compute anything a Turing machine can while
still keeping the record and paying the toll. And a universal Thiele machine is one
fixed machine that runs other machines as guests, with each guest’s record kept and
its toll collected by the host’s own step, not by the guest’s good manners.

Those bars are lower than they sound, and I’d rather you hear it from me. A machine
that charges one mark for every step it takes, whatever the step does, obeys the toll
for any record you like; a clock is enough to make something a Thiele machine. Thiele-
complete is Turing-complete with a record and a counter that obey that. The content
isn’t in the names. It’s in what a particular build proves on top of them: on the small
machine, that a raised record was earned; and, in Part III, a price that charges exactly
the certifying steps and nothing else, which no clock manages (Section 7).

The two computers, put back together
Here’s the two-computer story again, rebuilt as Thiele machines, with the record and
the counter written out, so you can watch it instead of taking my word. The prices
are the ones on the smallest machine I build later: one mark each to check, to commit,
and to certify (raise the record), and nothing for ordinary work like moving numbers
around.

At the end, the bits on both machines are still the same sorted list. Everything else
differs. The sorter’s record is up and its counter reads 3. The copier’s record is down,
and it’s paid 2 for two refusals, because on that machine a refused attempt still costs
what it costs. (Read those as two separate attempts. Written as one stored program,
the copier would stop at its first refusal and pay 1.) Nothing the copier can do raises
its record without first running a check of that very claim that passes. And no outside
window that only shows the list can tell you which is which; the difference is all in the
part the window doesn’t show. Walk that warehouse now and there’s finally a lamp
that’s lit in one and dark in the other.

Now how literally to take that table. It’s a picture of the chain, and the chain is what’s
proved. The small machine’s own checks are three questions about one counter: is
it zero, is it even, is it at least some number. What its proofs need from a question
is only a checker proved to say yes exactly when the answer is yes. That’s enough
for “sorted”: a version of the machine that takes any questions with checkers like that
proves the same chain once for all of them, and with a list packed into one counter it
certifies a sorted list for three marks and refuses an unsorted one forever (Section 14).
Without a proved checker for “sorted,” the chain would be honest about a counter and
only by convention about your list, which is Gettier’s pocket again, one level down.

And a lamp for whom? The record is bits too. It’s a lamp on the machine, for anybody
walking that warehouse. Hand somebody a printout of it across a desk and you’re
back at the sticker on the windshield: they have to trust whoever hands it over, or

                                            27
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


have some way to check the box that says it ran. That crossing is a different problem
with its own tools, signatures, attestation and proofs a stranger can check, and this
book doesn’t solve it. Section 7 says what those tools rest on, and the chip in Part V
reports its record down a wire with nobody’s signature on it (Section 27). What the
step changes is the question, from “did it run?” to “do I trust the box that says it ran?”
That’s a smaller question. It isn’t no question.

Now the honest half. Take away the small machine’s rules and keep only the bare toll,
and the copier has an easier move: pay one mark, flip the record to yes, done. The
toll is satisfied. The receipt is real. It’s a receipt for nothing. The bare toll prices the
closing of the door, not the check behind it.

What putting it in the step buys
So here’s the hardest objection, and I’d rather make it myself. You defined a flag
and a charge, then proved the charge gets paid when the flag goes up. That’s your
definitions agreeing with each other.

On the bare model, that’s fair, and the copier’s receipt for nothing is the proof. What
makes the record mean established is the small machine’s step, which won’t let a
commit through unless a check of that very claim passed, in the four-part sense from
Gettier’s pocket. And what it proves isn’t about one program. It’s this: on every list
of instructions anybody can write, starting clean, if the record is up, then somewhere
earlier a check of exactly that claim, about exactly that edition, passed; then a commit
of the same claim; then the certificate; with nothing touching the thing between the
check and the commit.

That “every” is the whole answer to what the step buys. A log kept by a program gives
you a fact about that program: if the program’s right, the log’s right. The database’s
guarantee holds for work that goes through the database. A rule in the step gives
you a fact about every program the machine can run, the buggy ones and the hostile
ones too, because there’s no way to run anything on it that isn’t a string of its steps.
That’s what moving the rule down a level changes. Not what can be computed. Which
programs the guarantee covers: this one becomes every one. Most of the rest of the
book is how far that “every” goes and where it stops.

Two limits on that “every,” said now rather than found later. First, it’s every program,
not every everything. The guarantee covers any list of instructions, run from a clean
start, one step at a time, on a step that does what its definition says. Hostile programs,
yes. A hostile start (a table of facts nobody checked, a reset), hostile hardware (a
soldering iron on the flag’s bit, a second writer the step can’t see) or a hostile reader,
no; Section 31 lists the whole fence. That’s the same shape as the database’s guarantee,
true if the layer underneath is faithful, with a much bigger class of programs inside it.

Second, the flag and the counter on their own are what people who verify programs
call ghost state: erase them and every program computes exactly what it did before


                                            28
The Thiele Machine                                                              Devon Thiele


(Section 6 has where that idea comes from). What isn’t ghost on the small machine is
the table of checked facts, which the step reads and refuses on, at run time, for every
program. And the move of putting a rule under every program isn’t mine either; it’s
the reference monitor’s, and its history is a few sections back.

What it isn’t
It isn’t more computing power. Anything a Thiele machine computes, an ordinary
computer computes too. The book proves that over any machine at all, an honest
record is a switch the machine’s own events flip once and nothing flips back; it watches
the computing, it doesn’t add to it. It isn’t faster. It isn’t quantum. It says nothing
about which problems are hard.

And an ordinary computer can keep a record like this. Give a Turing machine a spot
for the record and a track for the counter, write its rules so it never sets the spot without
bumping the counter, prove that, and it is a Thiele machine, not a counterexample.
What an ordinary programmable computer, as built, doesn’t do is make its own step
enforce a record for the programs it runs. When it runs another program, that program’s
record is just data in memory the program can write, and a buggy program can flip it
for free, because the host’s step has no opinion about it. Could it be built otherwise?
Sure. A universal machine with one fixed table, the kind Turing built, could have that
table written so it mirrors each guest’s record and charges for the raise, and it would
qualify. Nothing about ordinary computers stops that. They just aren’t built that way.
That gap, between the machine doing the stepping and the program it runs, is where
the databases and the proof checkers and Bitcoin built their fences, and it’s the gap
the universal Thiele machine later in the book closes, for the programs of the small
machine it’s built on.

Be clear about how much that host’s universality is worth on its own. It runs a guest’s
step as one of its own moves, so “it runs any guest” is true by construction, and I
won’t pretend that part is deep. The theorems with teeth are the others: the host’s
copy of the guest’s record always equals the guest’s own; no sequence of host moves
raises the copy for free; the host’s own instructions can’t touch the guest at all; and if
the copy is up, the guest’s own run went through a passing check, then a commit of
the same claim, then a certificate (Section 14.12).

What’s proved, what’s argued, and what I just believe
Every claim in this book has a status and I’ll tell you which, every time. Here’s the
whole list at once, so you know what I’m on the hook for.

Checked by a proof assistant, with every assumption printed, for any system with
the named parts: anything that obeys the toll pays at least one mark to get from
not-established to established (short enough that you’ll prove it yourself on paper in
Part II). On a finite machine whose record never comes down, the step that raises it
merges, which is the chairs; with merging priced, the toll follows, and the price is an


                                             29
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


assumption with a name. Finding out can be free: you can learn something from a step
that merged nothing and cost nothing, so the toll lands on committing, not learning.
A window that shows a paid state and an unpaid one as the same can’t price the step
between them exactly, however clever it is. And over any machine, an honest record
is a one-way switch on an event, with two choices left free: the price list and which
event.

On the smallest machine I could build, six instructions on two counters: the chain in
the table above (check, commit, certify, same claim, same edition), for every program,
not just that one, with claims about any property that comes with a checker proved
to mean it, “sorted” included (Section 14). A raised record always went through a
passing check, then a commit, then a certificate, of exactly the same claim about exactly
the same edition. Nothing gets into its list of checked facts without a check writing it.
Every certificate costs at least three marks, and three is enough: check “this counter
is zero,” commit to it, certify, and when the counter is zero that pays exactly three;
when it isn’t, the check traps with the flag down and nothing after that ever raises it.
The machine doesn’t stop you asking a question that can’t come out no, and I say so
where it matters. It’s Thiele-complete, because it does everything Marvin Minsky’s
two-counter machines do, and Minsky proved those can compute anything a Turing
machine can. And a host built on it is a universal Thiele machine for its programs:
it runs any of them as a guest by construction, and what’s proved about it is the
copy, the isolation and the earned chain from “What it isn’t” above. A machine from
somewhere else gets in only by being encoded into the small machine, which keeps
its computation; that its own record and its own prices carry over isn’t proved.

Argued, not proved: that an account of computation should carry what was established,
and what it cost, in how it steps. The proofs show that it hangs together, what it follows
from, and what it costs (six instructions and three marks, on the small machine);
whether it ought to be adopted is argued, and it’s a claim about what matters, which
no proof checker can check.

Guessed at, with the ways to kill it written down: that the event worth recording is
certification, because its records are the ones that get copied and relied on all over the
place (the pointer conjecture, Part III).

Not proved, and I’ll say so every time it’s tempting: any physical price for one mark,
anything about real hardware that was ever switched on, or anything about which
problems are hard.

Which of the proved part is new? Not one big thing, and I’d be suspicious of me
if I said otherwise. By my own sorting at the back (Appendix C) it’s four smaller
ones, each with its neighbours standing right there. The toll derived from finiteness,
permanence and a price on merging: the pigeonhole principle, Landauer and Bennett
on merging, and the finite heart of Zermelo’s 1896 recurrence argument are all next
to it. A window that shows a paid state and an unpaid one alike can’t price the step


                                           30
The Thiele Machine                                                              Devon Thiele


between them exactly: an old fact about functions, Moore’s 1956 experiments and
Kalman’s observability, with a price put in. An honest permanent record, over any
machine, is a latch on one event: the 1918 flip-flop and write-once memory are its
neighbours. And the small machine and its host: a record that’s priced, and on the
small machine earned, under the reference monitor’s every-program move (Anderson
in 1972, Schneider in 2000, Coq-checked monitors from Azevedo de Amorim and
coauthors in 2015), built and checked rather than new in idea. The first three are small
exact statements I didn’t find stated before, where I looked. The two-player game
check later in the book is careful engineering, not a fifth, and nothing it passes feeds a
record.

At the bottom: what I suspect and can’t prove
This is underneath the proofs, so read it with the lights on. None of it is a theorem,
and I’m not going to dress it up as one. It’s why I care, and I’d rather you know that
going in than catch me sneaking it in later.

Physics has a word for the moment a question closes: measurement. And the people
who thought hardest about it keep describing it in this chapter’s shape. Before a
measurement, it could go either way. After, it’s settled, and the result gets copied out
into the world, the light and the air, so many times that it can’t be taken back and
everybody who looks agrees. Wojciech Zurek has spent decades on how that copying
works. Rovelli’s coin has to hit the ground.

Niels Bohr said seeing anything at that scale depends on an apparatus that works
irreversibly, like permanent marks on a photographic plate: a door that swings one
way. John Wheeler went further and said every physical thing gets its existence from
yes-or-no questions answered and registered, and boiled it down to “it from bit.” And
Peirce, way before any of them, said the kind of settling worth trusting is the kind that
has to answer to everybody.

Lay that next to everything above and the parts line up: a check that could have come
out either way, a result that’s now settled, a price paid in forgetting, a record that stays.
I suspect that isn’t a coincidence. I suspect the event this book prices on a machine is
the same kind of event physics calls a measurement, showing up in a different place.
One piece already sticks out, and I’ll leave it sticking out: in Zurek’s picture the world
settles a result by copying it, and copying merges nothing (Section 13 pushes on that).
Which picture a settling on a machine matches is part of the suspicion, not settled by
it. That’s as far as I’ll take it here, and it’s a suspicion, not a finding.

Now let me point the biggest gun I can find at it, and that’s John Bell. In 1990 Bell
wrote a short, furious essay against the word “measurement,” with a list of words he
said have no place in a physics that wants to be precise. On the list: system, apparatus,
environment, irreversible, information, and measurement, which he called the worst
of all. I used half of them in the last few paragraphs without even trying. Bell would
have taken my suspicion apart in an afternoon, and he’d have been right to, because

                                             31
The Thiele Machine                                                          Devon Thiele


every piece of it leans on words physics hasn’t pinned down. Nothing in this book
proves any of it. The proofs are about models and machines, and whenever physics
shows up in them it shows up as an assumption with a name on it. The suspicion is
why I went looking. It isn’t what I found.

Where this goes
So here’s the picture, put back together. Two machines can hold the same bits and
differ in what they’ve established, and you can’t see it even walking the floor between
them, because it was never kept. The difference isn’t information; information theory
says the sort added nothing new. It isn’t depth; depth belongs to the bits, and a copy
has just as much. It’s an event: a check that could have said no, about this very claim,
then a question closed for good, with no promise the answer’s true. The could-have-
said-no part lives in the procedure, not in the end state, so only a record can carry it.
On a finite machine, a record that never comes down can only be raised by a merge, a
kind of forgetting, the same kind ordinary computers pay heat for so their bits forget
where they came from. If Landauer’s right, that costs, for any device that has to settle
things without already knowing which state it’s in. The Thiele Machine puts the
record and the charge in the step itself, and what that buys isn’t more computing. It’s
a guarantee about every program instead of one.

Every time I thought I’d found something new on the way down, somebody had a
name for part of it already, and that last sentence is no exception: a rule under every
program is the reference monitor’s move, from 1972. Fine. What I think is put together
here is smaller, and more than one thing: the four I listed under what’s proved, several
small things, each with its neighbours named, not one big one.

And the stuff from the start, the test sheet, the sticker, the confident AI? Here’s the
straight answer on which of those this helps. The sticker is a question of whether a
piece of paper is genuine, and nothing here touches it. The “all tests passed” sheet
fits only if the test is a checker proved to mean what it says, in the machine’s own
language; a test suite that can miss a bug certifies “this procedure said yes,” which
is true and smaller. The AI that sounds sure of itself isn’t addressed at all. What the
book gives you is a record on the machine itself, with a proof of what a raised one
means. Getting that record to somebody across the room who has to believe it is a
separate job, and Section 31, under “Outward consequences,” says how little of the
outside world I’ve reached. If you came for a tool, that’s a short list. If you came for
the question, this is where it starts.

The rest of the book is me trying to break all of it. First where I came from, then the
word I couldn’t define when I started, structure. Then the smallest thing that could
carry the bill, on a sheet of paper, with one rule I’ll hand you without a reason, and
then the chapter where I find out whether I had to pick it. If it breaks there, the book
ends there. I’d rather know.
