The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele



Before the book: the short version
The book in one paragraph. The Thiele Machine is an abstract model of computation: a
state, a step rule, a counter that only climbs, a rule that the step turning a certification
reading from no to yes costs at least one unit on that counter (I call that rule the toll,
and its first name, the one I gave it before I understood it, is No Free Insight; Part II
builds it), and a window that says what an observer sees. Here’s what’s proved, in
Coq (a proof assistant: software that checks every step of a proof), with every premise
printed. Any system that follows the toll pays something to get from uncertified to
certified. On a finite machine whose certificate is never taken back, the certifying
step merges states, so the toll follows from pricing merges, with Landauer’s principle
(the physicist’s rule that forgetting costs heat) as a named premise. A measurement
that forgets nothing can be priced at zero. A window that shows a certifying step
and a quiet one as the same can’t price certification exactly. Over any base machine,
an honest permanent record is a latch on an event (a switch the event flips once
and nothing flips back). And no procedure a substrate can represent decides which
programs admit a shortcut, given a recursion theorem (the fact that a program can
act as though it held its own code). A substrate is the model’s bare shape, a kind of
state and a rule for stepping, with whatever extra pieces a given theorem asks for;
here the extra pieces are programs written as states and that recursion theorem. All
of that is about the model: any system with the named pieces. Two builds carry the
model, and both are Thiele machines in the sense a few pages on pins down. The
small one, six instructions on two counters, is where commitments are earned and
universality is proved. The big one is what I mean every time I say “my machine”:
a fifty-one-instruction machine in Coq, a runner extracted from it as ordinary code,
and hardware in Kami (a Coq library for describing circuits) refined instruction by
instruction. On it, under the hypotheses of one representation theorem, a run that
paid at least as many floor steps as a covering tree is deep has paid for the index bits it
commits to (roughly, how many times it halves its list of possibilities); no run is shown
to have to pay them, and a checked bit search is an instance where the hypotheses hold;
the recursion theorem is proved for its twelve-instruction guest (a small fragment it
runs as data), as it is for the lambda calculus L, and on the full machine it is a premise
about a chosen class of program transformations (asked of every transformation it is
false there, and that is proved too); and an integer check on eight counters implies that
a fixed moment matrix is positive semidefinite, and so Tsirelson’s bound, the ceiling
quantum mechanics puts on the score of a two-player game (Part IV builds the game,
the matrix and the check from zero; it’s there as a check with a striking result packed
into one instruction, to show the toll charges the same however deep the check is, not
as a physics tool, and passing it feeds no record). Not proved: a physical price for
one mark, any separation of complexity classes, that certification is the event worth
recording (that’s a conjecture), or anything about a powered-on board, since none was.
Of all that, what I’d call new is several small things, not one: the toll derived from
finiteness, permanence and a price on merging; a window that can’t price it exactly;


                                            33
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


the latch shape of a permanent record; and, built and checked rather than new in
idea, a priced record, earned on the small machine, under the reference monitor’s
every-program move. Appendix C puts each beside the work it leans on.

I didn’t invent a machine. I found one. That’s how I see this work, and I’ll be straight
about the difference between that conviction and a theorem before I do anything else.

That sentence walks straight into one of the oldest fights in mathematics, so here’s a
short trip into it first. G. H. Hardy, in A Mathematician’s Apology in 1940, came down
on the found side about as hard as anyone ever has: mathematical reality, he wrote,
lies outside the people who study it, and the theorems they like to call their creations
are really just notes on what they saw there. Leopold Kronecker supposedly split the
difference: God made the whole numbers, and everything else is the work of people.
Supposedly, because push on that line and it gets thin fast. It comes down through
Heinrich Weber, in a memorial piece written after Kronecker died, pointing back to
a lecture from 1886, and that’s the only source anybody cites. A great line with one
witness. (The first chapter of Part II stops early on to ask how many witnesses a claim
ought to need. The answer is more than one.) So does any of this settle whether I
found the Thiele Machine or made it up? No. A proof checker doesn’t settle it either;
Coq checks a proof the same whether you think the theorem was out there waiting
or you think you built it. That’s why it’s labelled a conviction. What it changes is
how I hold the thing: like something that was already there, which means I can be
wrong about its shape and the shape won’t care. And to be exact about what “found”
covers: the parts the counting forces on you, the latch shape and the merge. The event
to record, the price list, and putting the count inside the step are choices, mine, and
the first chapter said so where it sorted what I was pushed into from what I chose.

What the Thiele Machine is. An abstract model of computation. A machine the way
Turing’s machine is a machine: mathematics you can reason about, not a device. It
isn’t a CPU, an instruction set, a graph, or category theory; those are things I built
with it, or things it can carry. The model is small. A state. A step rule. A counter that
only climbs. A rule for which steps have to pay. And a window: what an observer is
allowed to see. Like a Turing machine, it’s a precise way to say what a computation
is. Unlike a Turing machine, it computes nothing new. It adds what a computation
establishes, and what establishing it cost. The event it accounts for happens on any
computer, whether anybody keeps track of it or not. What Turing’s model doesn’t
have is a place for the record of that event, or anything that enforces one. A Turing
machine can be programmed to keep the record, and then it obeys the toll and it’s a
Thiele machine in its own right. But when it runs some other program’s record as data
on its tape, nothing in its own step enforces it (Section 20.7). The event’s physical cost
comes in only under Landauer’s premise, with its name on it. The record exists only
if something keeps it, and keeping it, priced, is what the model adds.

What this book is. An argument, made with that model, about what an account of


                                           34
The Thiele Machine                                                              Devon Thiele


computation should preserve. The usual account describes a computation by what
it reads and writes. I think that account is a shadow, and that there’s another axis,
holding what the computation established and what that cost. Here’s the argument in
five steps, each with where it stands.

Holding a sorting costs something; standing behind one might. That’s Part I: one word,
structure, pushed on with you through as many of the people who wrestled it before
me as I could reach. It finds three different acts that people run together. Building and
storing a sorting you can read back costs work and space. Forgetting where things
came from costs heat, if Landauer is right. And standing behind a sorting, vouching
for it, is a third act that nobody I read had put a price on. Whether it has one is the
question the rest of the book takes up.

Establishing is not free. If the step that turns uncertified into certified has to pay, every
run from uncertified to certified has paid. Proved, for any system that follows that
rule, whatever its states and steps. And the rule isn’t arbitrary: on any system with
finitely many states, a certificate nothing takes back can only be switched on by a step
that merges two states. That part is pure counting, proved. If merging is charged for,
the way Landauer’s principle charges for it in its worst case, the rule follows. That part
is proved with the charge as a named premise, its critics named, and every premise
refusable with a counterexample built. Learning isn’t what costs: a measurement that
forgets nothing can be priced at zero by an honest price list, and an observer still
learns from it. Proved. What can’t be free, on those premises, is committing to what
you learned in a record the machine can’t take back.

Two more things belong to that step. First, which steps a price on merging has to
charge: exactly the ones that merge. Every step that writes a record nothing takes back
is one of them, and on a finite machine a step that switches a certificate on escapes
the price only when the same step switches one off somewhere else. The tidier guess,
that the priced steps are exactly the permanent records, is false, and three states show
it. No theorem picks out a wider class of events every account must price. With one
mark per halving, the step that writes a permanent record costs at least the base-two
logarithm of how much it squeezes together (how many times it halves the number
of states it can tell apart), and the same bound holds in bits of Shannon entropy, the
standard measure of information. Proved, with the price as a premise. Second, where
the machine I built stands, which is a Part IV fact and not a Part II one. A small finite
piece of it, eight states seen through a narrow window, is such a machine, and the
machine runs it paying exactly what that finite machine charges; one of those charges,
two for a jump, is the program’s own choice, which the machine’s price list allows
and doesn’t force. The full machine isn’t one: every step that raises its certified flag
merges states and costs at least one, but an ordinary jump can merge states too and
cost nothing. So the full machine doesn’t price every merge, and that’s a theorem too
(Section 23). The small machine of Part IV isn’t one either: its counters have no top, so
it isn’t finite, and some of its free steps merge states too. On both builds the toll is a


                                             35
The Thiele Machine                                                               Devon Thiele


design choice the chairs don’t force.

A window can hide what was paid. Two runs can look identical through the usual window
and differ in what they established and paid, and nothing reading only the window
gets the difference back, so no price read off the window charges the certifying step
exactly. Proved, for any window with such a pair; and the machine I built has such a
pair for both windows you’d point at it.

Leaning on a fact takes a paid history. A computation is entitled to lean on a structural fact
when it holds the object, a checked relation, and a paid event on its record. Defined,
for the model, with a counting fact beside it: narrowing a list of rivals down takes at
least the yes-or-no questions that name the survivors. The cost floor that ties those
questions to steps a run actually paid for is proved on my machine (Part IV), for
shortcuts that hand over their receipts (the record of what they paid), under a list of
hypotheses printed in full: if a run paid at least as many floor steps as a covering tree
is deep, those payments cover the index bits. No run is shown to have to pay them.
Entitlement is a license to lean on a claim, not a proof that the claim is true.

So the axis belongs in the step. An account of computation should carry what was
established and what it cost as part of how it steps, not as something bolted on after.
Proposed. The proofs around it show it hangs together and what it costs; whether
it should be adopted is argued, not tested. What’s proved around it: over any base
machine, an honest record is a latch on an event, with two free choices, the price list
and the event; no procedure a substrate can itself represent decides which programs
admit a shortcut, given a recursion theorem, by the same self-referring trick, the
diagonal, that put a hole in Gottlob Frege’s foundations for arithmetic (Part I tells that
story); and which event deserves the record is a conjecture, with its refutations listed.

Certification is one point I could pin down. It gave me a law I could state, a machine
I could build and run, and proofs I could put in front of someone who didn’t share
my intuition. It’s one witness in a larger argument about structure and observation. It
isn’t the argument.

How the book is laid out. Part I is the picture: how I got here, and what structure is.
Part II is the axiom: the smallest thing that could carry a bill, and why its one rule isn’t
arbitrary. Part III is the logic: the counter, the windows, entitlement, insight, the latch,
the diagonal, five real systems, and a conjecture. Parts I to III never use my machine;
every claim in them is about any system with the pieces it names, and the pictures
are toys. Part IV builds twice. First the smallest honest machine I could make: two
counters, six instructions, a table of checked facts, a ledger and a flag. On it a raised
flag provably went through a passing check, a commitment and a certification of the
same claim, in that order, and it computes everything Minsky’s two-counter machines
can, so whether it halts is undecidable. Then the big build, one try, in three materials,
as the witness for everything before it: its state and fifty-one instructions, the claims a
module of it can carry, what insight and entitlement look like on it, and where each


                                             36
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


Part III result has a machine instance. The big build prices every commitment and
doesn’t enforce that one was earned; the small one is where earned commitments and
universality are proved. Part V is the chain from the proof to a chip, with each link
labelled proved, tested, or trusted, and the sentence that no board was ever powered
on. The chip implements the big build, so no circuit in this book enforces that a
commitment was earned: the hardware was built for the big build first, the small
machine came last, and a chip for it is still open. Part VI is how to check all of it and
how to break it. The vocabulary I had to learn is at the back.

If you want the argument and not the whole tour, read “The point” and this short
version, then Section 3, Section 4, Section 10, Section 14 and Section 32. If physics is
your thing, add Section 5 and Section 26. If you mean to check me, add Section 29 and
Section 30. The big build of Part IV and the chip of Part V are reference: everything in
them is there to be looked up when a claim points at it. Nothing gets cut for that. It’s
a map, not a diet.

One more thing before the book starts, because people get it backwards. I used
language models to write the code and the proofs in this project, and I trust language
models about as far as I can throw them, which is exactly why every formal declaration
is checked by a proof assistant that doesn’t care who or what wrote it. Coq rejects a
wrong proof the same whether a tenured professor or a model hands it over, and it
accepted these, with none of my own axioms anywhere in them, re-checkable by the
procedure in Part VI. Being self-taught and using modern tools didn’t make this looser.
It’s the reason I made a machine check the formal corpus, and then built an auditor to
read over the checker’s shoulder for every way I might have cheated, on purpose or
by accident (Part VI says what it looks for). It doesn’t trust me either. Good.

I think there’s something foundational here. The results in this book have statements,
premises, and proof terms. The larger claim is a conjecture, not a theorem. I built
the machine so that the work could be done in public, with something firmer than
my confidence to argue over. If you’re the skeptical sort, and I hope you are, the two
places to aim are the appendix that sorts what’s mine from what isn’t (Appendix C)
and the chapter of ways to break it (Section 29).

Let me be straight with you
What this project is. An argument about what an account of computation should pre-
serve, made with an abstract model built to carry it. Its central proposal is that what
a computation established, and what establishing it cost, belong in how it steps. The
working form of that proposal is structural entitlement: a computation is entitled to
lean on a structural fact when it holds the object, a checked relation, and a history
that earned it. The model, its laws, and the instructions of any one build are different
things, and I keep them apart. The generic flag-raising step pays to set a flag; it checks
nothing. A claim that something is actually true needs explicit witnesses and a checker
proved sound, and some results here are of that kind; the generic accounting law isn’t

                                           37
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


one of them. It’s a law about marks.

The proved core, in three steps. Anything that follows the toll pays something to get
from uncertified to certified. A window that shows two states as the same, when they
disagree on the counter or on some other question, can’t answer that question on every
state. Those two are about any system with the named pieces. The third is checked on
my machine, in Part IV: a checker that only sees the bare window, where a named pair
of the machine’s states collides, can’t be both sound and complete about the claim that
separates them. All three are statements about named laws and named windows. An
ordinary machine can keep a richer encoding, or enforce the same invariant through
its own transition table. What I’m proposing is about why the extra distinctions matter.
It isn’t a theorem that every Turing-equivalent system lacks them. And if you want
the list of what I think is new, it’s the short one at the end of “What’s proved, what’s
argued, and what I just believe” in the first chapter, the same four things the short
version names, and nothing bigger.

Substrate versus scaffolding. Two layers run through the book, and confusing them
makes the theorems quietly stop meaning what they say. The substrate is the shape: a
kind of state and a rule for stepping. Different theorems ask that shape for different
extra pieces, and the pieces aren’t the same. The universal floor (the “pays something”
result above) asks for a certification reading and the toll on it. The counter’s unique-
ness (only one count fits a chosen start and price list) asks for a starting value and a
schedule of increments; Part III gives the argument, a short induction that works for
any system with those two pieces, and the checked theorem is stated for my machine
and sits in Part IV (Section 23). The diagonal asks for a way to write programs as
states and a recursion theorem for the transformations the substrate can express, and
needs no toll at all. “Substrate-level” doesn’t mean one fixed plug that every theorem
shares. A theorem only gets to use the parts it asks for. Ask it what it needs and it’ll
tell you, and whatever else is lying around the workshop isn’t the theorem’s. So each
result is stated over exactly the extension it uses. The substrate with the extension a
theorem names is what I mean by the model, and the name Thiele Machine belongs
to the model. The scaffolding is everything that holds the shape up so you can touch
it, and when I say my machine, the machine I build or the build, this is what I mean: its
state record (registers, memory, a program counter, a graph of groups and arrows, the
certification readings, the counters), fifty-one instructions and their prices, a reference
kernel (the machine’s definition in Coq), the guest it runs as data, an extracted run-
time, the Kami hardware, a simulator harness. The build fills in several extensions at
once and borrows, for any one theorem, only the extension that theorem names. Let
that line blur and a theorem stated over one extension starts reading as if it carried
premises it never uses. “Substrate” never means the build, and it never means the side
of a simulation doing the stepping; for that I say “the machine doing the stepping,” as
against “the program it runs.”

So here’s how the book keeps the two apart. Parts I to III are about any system with


                                            38
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


the pieces each result names, and their pictures are toys you can hold (two boxes on
a sheet of paper, chairs in a room, a row of dots), not my machine. My machine first
appears in Part IV. Every Part III claim that has a machine instance gets that instance
in Part IV or V, with its own checked name, and Part III says so in one sentence at
most. When the origin story, a few pages on, says the shape “was the substrate the
entire time,” it means this layer, the model’s shape, and not any piece of the build.
Same story with two more of its words. When it says “the machine” about the thing
it named the Thiele Machine, or calls that thing a meta machine, it means the model;
“my machine” is the build, and the build doesn’t show up until Part IV. And when it
lists what the model asks for (a state, a step, a ledger, a window), read the ledger and
the window as two of the extra pieces: a result asks for them only if it uses them.

Part IV has two pieces of scaffolding, not one, and I’d rather you know that up front.
Section 14 builds the smallest honest machine I could: two counters, six instructions,
a table of checked facts, a ledger and a flag. Earned commitments are proved there
(a raised flag was checked, then committed, then certified, on the same edition, with
nothing in between), and so is universality, through Minsky’s two-counter machines
and a halting result borrowed from the Coq undecidability library. Then comes the
big build of fifty-one instructions, which is what “my machine” and “the build” mean
everywhere else in this book. It prices commitments without enforcing them: its check
commits to nothing and its commit doesn’t look for a check (Section 22 shows where).
Neither one is the model. The small one shows the model fits in six instructions; the
big one shows how much a single build can carry while the toll holds.

The names again, this time with every part pinned down, because I’ll hold to them
for the rest of the book. The Thiele Machine, with capitals, is the model and nothing
else. A Thiele machine, lower case, is any particular system proved to be an instance
of the model’s core definition, a certification system with its five parts and its toll
(Definition 3.1), the way one rule table is a Turing machine. The toys on paper in
Part II count, the same way trivial Turing machines do. Both of my builds count
too, each with its toll proved, and Part IV names the theorems. A Thiele machine is
Thiele-complete when its base is Turing-universal, so it carries the record and pays the
toll while computing anything a Turing machine can. That bar is low on purpose, and
so is the one under it: a machine that charges one for every step is a Thiele machine
for any record, so Thiele-complete amounts to Turing-complete with a latch and a
counter that obey the toll. What a particular build proves on top is where the content
is. The small machine is proved Thiele-complete. Whether the big build is, I haven’t
proved, and nothing in this book depends on it. A universal Thiele machine is one
fixed machine that runs any machine of a stated class as a guest, with the guest’s
record kept and its toll collected by its own step. Part IV builds one: its guests are the
small machine’s programs, so every computation runs on it. Running a guest’s step is
one of the host’s own moves, so that part holds by construction; what’s proved with
content is the copy of the guest’s record, the isolation of the host’s own instructions, no



                                            39
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


free host certification, and that a raised copy means an earned guest run. A machine
from elsewhere comes in through the two-counter encoding with its computation kept;
that its own record and prices carry over isn’t proved. And the chip of Part V isn’t a
Thiele machine at all. It’s hardware that implements one, the big build, inside bounds
Part V states, the way a laptop implements a Turing machine, and like the big build it
doesn’t enforce that a commitment was earned. Push on that last comparison, because
it’s looser than it sounds, and the looseness is the point. Does a laptop implement a
Turing machine? Not exactly. Turing’s tape never runs out, and a laptop’s memory
does; strictly, a laptop is a very large machine with finitely many states, and it behaves
like a Turing machine only on computations that fit. Nobody minds, because the
bound is known and most computations people care about fit inside it. That’s the
same deal the chip gets. The words “inside bounds Part V states” aren’t fine print.
They’re the whole difference between implementing a model and being one.

What “new model of computation” means here. It adds something to how a machine
runs: structure it keeps, and an account of what that structure cost. It doesn’t add
computable functions. It’s an abstract model the way the Turing machine is, but it
doesn’t hand you a new primitive to compute with; whatever base machine sits under
it still does all the computing. When I say “shadow” I mean the particular window I
name, not every way a conventional machine could store things. Enforcing the law,
storing it, and letting an observer see it are three separate questions, and the book
keeps them separate.

Which leaves a fair question hanging: if it computes nothing new, does it even get to
call itself a model of computation? I think so, and not only on my say-so. Computer
science has long kept models that compute exactly what Turing’s does and differ only
in what they count, how long a step takes, what reaching into memory costs, because
the counting is the reason to have them. Part III lays the toll over a register machine
of that kind, and over a Turing machine and a lambda calculus, and none of them
computes one function more afterward (Section 10). What each of them gains is a
record and a bill.

What this project is not. Not a solution to P versus NP, and not a complexity-class
separation of any other kind. Not a theory of everything. Not a claim that computation
is physics, or that physics is computation. Not a physics result: the game result (the
integer check and Tsirelson’s bound from the short version) is pure mathematics, and
Landauer’s principle enters only as a premise with its name on it, never as something
derived. Not a quantum computer or a claim about quantum behaviour. Not a verified
chip; a verified model with a chain of trusted and tested links below it. Not a claim to
priority on any idea in it. Not finished; the open questions are listed at the end.

What I do and don’t know about prior work. I came to this with no formal training in
the fields it turned out to need, and I’ve read what I could reach, with every tool I
had. The prior-work map below is orientation, not scholarship: for each piece of this


                                           40
The Thiele Machine                                                                 Devon Thiele


book, who did the thing it leans on, and what, if anything, this development adds. I’d
welcome correction on any row.

There’s a law about rows like these, and it’s a joke that keeps turning out true. In
1980 the statistician Stephen Stigler proposed that no scientific discovery is named
after the person who first found it, and then credited the idea to the sociologist Robert
K. Merton, who had been writing about fights over scientific priority since 1957. So
Stigler’s law is an example of itself, which is either the best joke in the history of
science or a very tidy accident. Is it a law? No. It’s a pattern, not a theorem. But this
book has already tripped over it once, in the opening chapter: the pigeonhole principle
wears Dirichlet’s name, not Leurechon’s. And I put my own name on a machine. By
Stigler’s law, that makes it somebody else’s. The table below is my best attempt at
finding out whose.

What I compare each time is what a result is about. Landauer’s bound is about heat, a
physical cost under a thermodynamic model. No Free Lunch (an optimisation result,
in the list below the table) is about averages over a whole spread of problems. The
toll is a floor on one kind of step, the step that turns a certification reading on. Exact
pricing adds a second rule on top: never charge more. So the comparisons are about
the shape of each result. They aren’t claims about who got somewhere first, and they
don’t show that certification is the only event worth pricing.

The right-hand column uses words the book only builds later (the latch, the fibre,
the guest, the integer gate, the matrix test), so read it as a list of places to go, not as
something you’re meant to follow yet.

Everything in the right column is stated with its premises in the body of the book, and
everything in the middle column is cited where it’s used. The table is the short form.
The long form is Appendix C, which takes each row, says what was already known
with sources, and sorts what’s added into new result, new proof, mechanization,
implementation, synthesis, or conjecture. Most of the right column is mechanization,
implementation, and synthesis.

A few more labels I went and looked up don’t get a row, because nothing in the book
leans on them. They’re neighbours, and I list them so you can see why I don’t think
the toll is one of them in a hat. Each is a claim inviting correction.

   • Linear logic (Girard 1987) treats an assumption as a resource that gets used up.

                                               43
The Thiele Machine                                                          Devon Thiele


      It constrains what a program, or a proof, may consume. The toll constrains the
      model’s step function instead. Same instinct, different layer.
   • Foundational proof-carrying code (Appel 2001) checks safety proofs against the
     smallest trusted base it can: a logic plus the machine’s semantics. Here no proof
     rides along with the program. The step rule writes the receipts as the run goes.
   • Session types (Honda 1993) constrain how programs talk to each other so the
     conversation can’t go off script. The toll is about what one computation has paid
     to establish. Different problem.
   • No Free Lunch (Wolpert and Macready 1997): averaged over every problem,
     whatever an optimiser gains on some problems it gives back on others. That’s
     an average over a whole problem space, and the edge is paid for elsewhere. The
     toll charges one step in one run, with no refund anywhere.
   • Kolmogorov complexity (Kolmogorov 1965): the structure in an object is the
     length of the shortest program that prints it. That’s a property of a finished
     string, with no steps and no moment of paying. The toll is a law about a step.
   • Cook and Levin (Cook 1971; Levin 1973): checking can be cheap while finding
     looks expensive, and whether finding is really harder is the open P-versus-NP
     question, a gap in how difficulty grows with size. The toll puts a fixed floor
     under the one step that commits, however easy or hard the finding was.
   • The thermodynamic cost of choosing (Rovelli 2024): settling a binary choice at
     temperature T gives off at least kT ln 2. That’s the closest thing to the toll I’ve
     found, because it charges a commitment rather than an object or an average.
     But it’s physics, indexed to a temperature, and its choice is unpredictable, a
     branching, and stable only for a while, where the toll’s commit is a deterministic
     merge that stays. The toll charges the commitment in a model of computation,
     with no temperature in it. Closest neighbour, not the same chair.
   • CerCo, the Certified Complexity project of Amadio and coauthors, builds a
     verified C compiler that carries the object code’s execution cost back up to an-
     notations on the source. There the cost decorates the program and survives
     compilation. Here it lives in the model’s step rule.
   • Reference monitors and execution monitors (Anderson 1972; Schneider 2000;
     Azevedo de Amorim and coauthors 2015). A small piece every action passes
     through, enforcing a rule on every program. Schneider showed that a monitor
     watching a run enforces exactly the rules whose breaking shows up at a finite
     point, and “no certificate without an earlier passing check and commit” is one
     of those; the micro-policies check a tag rule at every instruction, proved in Coq.
     That’s the move the small machine’s step makes, so this one isn’t a neighbour,
     it’s the house. What’s added is the edition-bound check-then-commit with a
     paid, permanent record on top, and the derivation of why the payment can’t be
     zero.


                                          44
The Thiele Machine                                                          Devon Thiele


   • Ghost state (Owicki and Gries 1976; Filliâtre, Gondelman and Paskevich 2014):
     variables added for a proof that can be erased without changing what the pro-
     gram computes. The flag and the counter are ghost in that sense. The small
     machine’s table of checked facts isn’t, because the step reads it and refuses on it,
     for every program.
   • Verifiable computation and proof-carrying data (Parno, Howell, Gentry and
     Raykova 2013; Chiesa and Tromer 2010): a short proof, checkable by a stranger,
     that a computation’s output is right. That establishes the claim for the stranger,
     and anyone with the inputs can make one, the copier included. The record here
     is about one machine’s own history. A proof like that is one way to carry the
     local record out of the box.
   • Commitments and entitlements (Brandom 1994): talk as score-keeping, tracking
     who is committed to what and who is entitled to it. Brandom’s entitlements can
     be defeated and can be passed on by testimony. Here entitlement is priced, step
     by step, and a copy carries it only as far as the copy is genuine. Same words,
     different machinery.

And then the silly question that list raises, which I’m going to chase anyway: why
is an optimisation theorem named after lunch? Wolpert and Macready borrowed an
old saying, “there ain’t no such thing as a free lunch,” and the saying is older than
almost everyone who gets credit for it. American saloons in the 1800s put out a free
lunch for anyone who bought a drink, and the drink paid for the lunch. A Washington
newspaper was already saying in 1909 that somebody has to pay for a free lunch;
a newspaper fable by Walter Morrow had the whole line in 1938; Robert Heinlein’s
1966 novel The Moon Is a Harsh Mistress squeezed it into TANSTAAFL; and Milton
Friedman put it on the cover of a book in 1975. People usually credit Heinlein or
Friedman. Neither coined it. Stigler’s law again, at lunch. Here’s what it changes. No
Free Insight sounds like a cousin of the saying, and the sound misleads in one way.
The saloon’s lunch was paid for somewhere else, in the price of the beer, and that’s
Wolpert and Macready’s shape: a gain here, handed back over there. The toll isn’t that.
Nothing gets paid somewhere else. The step that raises the flag pays, on the spot.



Part I

The picture

1 How I got here
What I am is curious, past the point of good sense.

I pick a thing up and cannot set it down until I have turned it over enough times to


                                           45
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


see how it holds together, and this time it did not let go.

I am not a programmer and I was never formally taught any of this.

I was not trying to build a formally verified CPU.

I would not have known what one was if it bit me.

I was trying to build a 3D renderer.

There was no plan behind it.

Just a pull to make something real with my own hands, and the kind of stubbornness
that will not let a thing go until it stands up on its own.

I have worked on it in off hours every day since.

Once I started digging in, two things came clear fast. I knew nothing about computers,
and the field was already saturated, every obvious road paved and crowded. So I
needed an angle nobody else was standing on, and the angle I had was not a strategy,
it was just the only way my head works. I did not know what compositional meant.
I had never heard of category theory. I called the thing I was building digital DNA,
because that is what it felt like in my hands, and I thought about it in the only language
I had: gravity pipes and directions and vectors, things that were linear and somehow
not linear at the same time, structure that flowed and joined and came apart without
my owning one proper word for any of it. I built a custom rendering pipeline out of
those intuitions, by feel, throwing out pieces that did not sit right even when I could
not have told you the rule they were breaking. And then, the way I always do, I went
looking for what I was actually doing, and found out it already had a name. An old
one. A deep one. What I had been reaching for in the dark was composition. It was
category theory, a whole field I had never once heard of, sitting there describing the
exact shapes I had been shoving around. The moment that landed, the rendering
pipeline stopped being a rendering pipeline and started turning into a categorical
engine, and I started swallowing the real theory as fast as I could find the words for
things I had already built.

The method underneath was crude and it held. I wrote a long structured spec in JSON
(a plain-text format for describing data) as a context document, fed it to Copilot, and
had it build one Python file per concept, one at a time, each with its own tests, and I
would not move to the next until I could watch the current one actually run. Category.
Object. Morphism. Functor. Monoidal product. It came together in pieces and never
in chapters, the way a picture resolves out of static instead of getting drawn in left
to right. The Yoneda lemma (a result buried deep in category theory) was the piece
that made the rest snap into place, the night I quit borrowing other people’s runtimes
and started writing my own around it, with Z3 (a constraint solver out of Microsoft
Research) wired into the middle.



                                           46
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


Then within weeks I found out the engine I had built to draw pictures was general
enough to run a physics simulation on the exact same primitives, without my rewriting
any of it. I wrote Newton’s laws as a program in it, half expecting nothing, and it
ran. I want to be careful about what that was and what it was not, because this is
exactly the kind of thing that gets misread. It was not me deriving physics, and I
am not claiming the machine explains gravity. It was the compositional structure
being general enough to express a physics simulation the same way it had expressed
a renderer, and that generality is what told me the structure was the point and the
pixels never were. Somewhere in those weeks I crossed from debugging why one pixel
would not show up to understanding that I had quietly built a categorical computing
engine, and that the rendering had only ever been the first thing I aimed it at. The
pixel did eventually show up, for what it is worth.

I kept going, because by then I could not not keep going. I built a small custom
language for describing scenes (the name for that is a domain-specific language, a
DSL), then a program that read the language and caught my mistakes in it (a linter),
then a way to type commands at the whole thing from a terminal (a command-line
interface, a CLI). The night the engine first ran a program declaratively, meaning I told
it what should happen and let it work out the how instead of my spelling out every
step, I told my wife, Julie, I thought I was onto something. She said okay.

Then I hit a wall, and it is the wall this whole document is about. Z3 could settle
the small questions and fell over on the exact ones I needed answered, which left me
staring down an infinite hallway of guess-and-test with no proof waiting at the end of
it, ever. One night, not even working, I was watching a video about Flatland, the old
story about a creature living in two dimensions who cannot so much as picture a third.
And it landed on me sideways, all at once, the way the real ones always do. I said
it out loud: I get it now. There is another axis. Classical computation only ever sees
what it can read and write off its own surface, and there is a whole direction it is blind
to, not because it is broken but because it was never built with an eye that points that
way. I opened a new repo that same night and called the thing in it the Thiele Machine.
The name began as a working title and became the name of the model. It carries the
larger claim plainly: the machine treats structural state as part of computation.

What survived the whole trip from there to here is not the code. Not one line of it.
By the time the Coq proofs finally landed, every line of that first renderer had been
thrown out and rewritten at least twice, probably more, and good riddance to all of it.
What survived was a single architectural commitment I made early and never once let
anyone talk me out of: structure is the state itself, the actual thing the machine runs on,
not a metaphor laid over some realer state underneath. Category theory was the first
language I found for that structure. It is not what the model is. The model asks for a
state, a step, a ledger, and a window, and category theory appears nowhere in that list.
It lives on in the build. The Category structure that came together in that first week
and first ran morphisms correctly at two in the morning is, in different words and


                                            47
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


different syntax, the same object the partition graph is in the machine I ended up with
(the graph of groups, and arrows between them, that Part IV builds). I did not write
that code, not then and not now. I directed the models and refused everything they
handed me until the morphisms composed the way the shape said they had to. The
morphisms in that early code were objects that remembered where they came from;
the morphisms in the machine I ended up with are objects that remember where they
came from and that you can walk up to and challenge. The receipt grew teeth. But the
shape itself never moved. The shape was the substrate the entire time, and everything
else, every renderer and language and proof, was me slowly learning to see what I
had already built. By the shape I mean structure held as state. Not category theory.
Category theory was just the first language I had for it.

Formal verification was a graveyard of dead ends further on. The hardware came after
that. Every step pulled back to show another layer underneath that I had not known
was there, and I mean that as plainly as it sounds: I did not know what a Turing
machine was when I started, I did not know what Coq was, I did not know most of
the words in this document existed. I learned each one the same way, by walking
face-first into a wall that needed it and not being let past until I had it. The needing
always came first. The learning came after, dragged along behind the needing because
it had no say in the matter.

Large language models were my hands the whole way through, and I want the divi-
sion of labor exact, because it is the thing people most want to get wrong about work
like this. The hands had nothing like this to draw on: no reference implementation, no
prior project to point at. The ideas, the architecture, the direction, the demand that the
thing be true: those are mine, all of them, no asterisk. The symbol-pushing, the actual
Coq and the actual math, the models produced and the proof checker judged. The
proofs compile or they do not. I refused every one that did not. Coq is an obedient
idiot. It checks the proof matches the statement. It does not check that the statement
means what you think it means. A theorem can claim “every cat that is also a prime
number has whiskers” and the proof can be three characters long and Coq will nod
and stamp it. So I read every statement. The proofs you can’t fake. The statements
you can fake by accident, which is the more dangerous failure mode. I refused both
kinds. However the symbols got onto the page, the argument on it is checkable by
reading, and it would be exactly as right or as wrong if a million monkeys had typed
it. The monkeys could not have refused.

A word on what I actually do, because it is stranger than the usual split and it runs
under everything after it. I do not write code or math by hand. I do not pick constants.
I do not grind through derivations. I have never written a line of code on paper or in
a notepad in my life. What I do is see, and direct, and refuse. When I take hold of an
idea it does not stay a point. It opens up. It becomes a shape I can blow up and turn
over and take apart, lay across another shape to find where the two of them touch,
run forward and then back to where it started, zoom into until it is the only thing in


                                           48
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


the world and pull back until it is one dot in a field of other dots, and the whole time
it stays wired to everything I have ever connected it to, the right connections and the
wrong ones both, all of them live at once. I am not reading that field neutrally, the way
a search would. The thing doing the looking is me, the whole of me, my gut and my
mood and my stubbornness picking what lights up and which way I move through it,
and that is the part you cannot lift out without turning me back into a search engine.
So I see where a thing has to fit, the shape it is obligated to have, usually well before
I could write it down in a single symbol. Then the model gives me the symbols, the
proof checker takes them or throws them back, and I refuse anything that will not
compile or does not match the shape I am holding. That refusal is the one thing in
this entire document that is mine and only mine: the demand that it be true, and the
throwing-out of everything that wasn’t.

I am telling you all of this because it is not background color, it is the engine. I did
not come up through anywhere that hands you a foundation and says trust us, this
part is settled. No professors, no colleagues, no field full of authority to lean back on
when a claim got heavy. From the outside that is a deficit. From the inside it is the
whole reason any of this is solid: when I meet a claim I either find the proof or I do
not believe it, and that goes double for my own, because my own are the ones I most
want to wave through. It is how I am built. It is the only way I know to hold a thing
and actually trust that I am holding it.

So everything in here gets built from the ground up, and not as a courtesy to you. I
build it because I do not believe I understand a thing until I have built it with my
own hands, watched it stand up on its own, and tried to knock it over. I built this
document the exact way I built the machine, brick by brick, refusing each brick until
it held weight. That includes the parts you already knew cold before you opened this.
I did not skip them for you, and I could not skip them for me.

The vocabulary I had to go look up to do any of this sits at the back of the book, so
the argument comes first. If a word stops you, it is there. If you already know this
material, you never have to open it. But if you catch something in the basics that is
wrong, I want to know, and I mean that as a real ask and not a polite one. Nothing in
here is correct just because I wrote it. Especially the parts I wrote.

On the name. I wanted to call it the meta machine. Then Facebook bought the word
“meta”: a company renaming itself after a term for self-reference and draining it of any
in the same motion. So I went one level up, where this machine already lives. The
most meta move available, for a machine that runs on meta-level reasoning, was to
put my own name on the cover and take the word back. That’s the whole of it, a meta
move on a meta machine. It happens to be my dad’s name too, and my wife’s now. So
I asked them before I did it. They said go ahead.
