2 What structure is
One word. That’s this whole section, and I’m aware of how that sounds, so here’s the
word and you can decide whether to stay. Structure.

I used that word for most of my life without once looking at it, which I suspect is
true of most people and most words, and it’s fine, right up until you do something
stupid. The stupid thing I did was build a machine that keeps a running bill, and the
bill has one rule I couldn’t talk it out of. You can arrange things however you like
for whatever price you name, including free. But the moment you ask the machine to
vouch for an arrangement, to put its own name on the claim that these things belong
together, there’s a charge, and it isn’t zero. How much, charged in what, why I picked
that and not something else, and whether I had any business picking it at all: that’s all
later, and some of it I’m still not sure of. What I was sure of, standing there with the
thing built, was that I’d made something that charges for standing behind structure
and I could not have told you what structure was. It didn’t care. It can’t nod along
the way a person does. It needed the word to hold still, and the word had never held
still for anyone, least of all me. (The machine itself stays off the page until Part IV, on
purpose. Until then, the one rule is all of it that matters, and I’d rather you met the
rule in a toy you can hold than in a machine you’d have to take on trust.)

So I went looking at the people who’d wrestled it before me. Some of them have
been dead two thousand years and are still, I’d bet money, better at this than I am.
I used everything I had: language models, more than one, books, libraries, my own
gut, anything in reach. I don’t know if I found enough. I never do. There’s always
another shelf behind the one I was reading. And being dead and famous is not the
same as being right, so I pushed on each of them, and what follows is what I could
reach, pushed on as hard as I know how. The one thing I’m asking is that you push on
it with me, out loud, at your own kitchen table, because the first time through I was
the only one checking, and that’s not enough people.

The order I ran into them was a mess. Category theory came first, because I’d built
one by feel before I knew it had a name, and everything else came in whatever order
the next question dragged it in. I’m going to put them in the order they happened
instead, because that’s the order where each one leans on the last. And none of it is
an oracle. History is where I start, not where I stop. It gets retold, smoothed over, and
now and then made up outright (there’s a drowning coming up that never happened),
so every piece of it is a lead to check, and I check the parts I lean on.

2.1 A string, a square, and a drowning that didn’t happen
Start with the oldest one, and start by doing it. Take a string. A guitar string, a rubber
band over an open box, anything that twangs. Pluck it. Now press it down exactly at
the middle and pluck half. That’s the same note, an octave up, the one that makes a
round sound like a round. Press at a third of the way along and pluck the long side:
that’s the fifth, the second note of every bugle call you’ve ever heard. Half. Two thirds.

                                            50
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


Small whole numbers, and your ear says yes before your brain does. About twenty-
five hundred years ago, in the south of Italy, the followers of a man named Pythagoras
are credited with finding exactly that, and it’s as true in your kitchen tonight as it was
on their hillside.

Here’s what they did with it, as best anyone can tell. Nothing survives that’s surely
from Pythagoras’s own hand. The earliest fragments are from a later member, Philo-
laus, and scholars argue over those. Mostly what’s left is Aristotle, one to two centuries
later, writing in his Metaphysics about them the way you’d write about the neighbours’
religion, and he says they took the elements of numbers to be the elements of all things:
everything is number. Not that everything can be counted. That the parts of numbers
are the parts of all things.

Stop and ask what I asked. What does that even mean? Is a chair a number? Does
a chair have a number tucked inside it somewhere? Aristotle doesn’t say, and he’s
reporting a belief he doesn’t hold. So don’t take it on his word, or theirs, or mine.
But before you push on it, know what it was holding up, because you can’t test a
load-bearing wall without knowing what sits on it. These weren’t people doing math
for fun on weekends. They were a brotherhood, with rules about what you could eat
and when you had to keep quiet, and that plucked string was their scripture. Halve
the string, hear the octave: to them that was proof that under the mess of the world
there were whole numbers in clean ratios, that the cosmos was a chord and they’d
heard it. “Everything is number” wasn’t a slogan. It was what they’d organized their
lives around. Which is exactly the kind of sentence you should be suspicious of, mine
included.

Now push, and push where they loved most: the square. Draw one, with a side
one unit long, any unit you like, and draw the line from one corner to the opposite
corner. Call that the diagonal. If everything is number, then the diagonal is some
whole number of parts long when the side is some whole number of parts, so the
diagonal divided by the side is a fraction, a whole number over a whole number.
Cancel anything the top and bottom share, the way four-sixths becomes two-thirds,
until they have no common factor left. I’ll call the top p and the bottom q, and the
letters are purely so I don’t have to keep writing “the top” and “the bottom.”

You need one fact about squares, and it’s the one Pythagoras is famous for. The square
built on the diagonal has exactly twice the area of the square built on the side. If
you want to see it rather than believe it, cut a square along both diagonals into four
triangles and arrange them around; it’s a five-minute job with scissors. So p times p
is twice q times q. People write “times itself” as a small raised two, so that’s p2 = 2q2 ,
and that is the only piece of notation in this argument.

Twice anything is even. So p times p is even. An odd number times itself is always
odd (three times three, five times five, try a couple), so p itself must be even: it’s two
times something, and I’ll call that something r. Put it back in. Two r times two r is four


                                            51
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


times r times r, and that equals twice q times q. Halve both sides: two times r times r
equals q times q. So q times q is even, so q is even too, by the same step as before. But
you already cancelled everything the top and bottom had in common, so they can’t
both be even. The argument has eaten itself, and when an argument eats itself the
thing you supposed at the start is false. There is no such fraction. The diagonal of a
square can’t be named by any ratio of whole numbers, ever. Aristotle reaches for this
very argument in his Prior Analytics as his example of proof by contradiction (suppose
the diagonal can be measured, and odd numbers come out equal to even ones), and
you just did it with a pencil.

There’s a story that’s been told for two thousand years: that a member of the broth-
erhood named Hippasus let this secret out, and his brothers took him to sea and
drowned him for it. I went and checked, because it’s a good story and good stories
are the ones to check. The Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy’s entry on Pythagore-
anism finds no ancient writer who connects Hippasus to this discovery at all. It’s a
legend. But notice that the legend exists. Somebody, long after, felt that a man should
have been drowned for this. That’s how much was riding on it. To them, the diagonal
wasn’t a math problem. It was the end of the world.

So the claim is dead, and you killed it, not me. Now the question that matters: what’s
left? Look at your square again. The diagonal is still there. It still stands in a perfectly
definite relation to the side; you drew it, and nobody drowned. That relation was real
before anyone tried to put a number on it, and it stayed real after the number failed.
The relation came first. The number, when there is one, is a name for the relation, and
sometimes there isn’t a name. I’m going to keep that, and I want you to keep it too,
because you’re going to watch the same move get made again and again as this book
goes on: somebody says “everything is X,” and it’s true enough to do real work with,
and it sounds right when you pluck it, and then somebody draws the diagonal. I don’t
know yet whether the thing I built survives its own diagonal. That’s a real question,
and I’ll get to it.

2.2 Shapes poured into nothing
About a century and a half after the brotherhood, Plato, in a dialogue called the
Timaeus, tried to build the whole physical world out of geometry. Fire, air, water and
earth were four regular solids (the pyramid, the eight-faced one, the twenty-faced one,
and the cube), and the faces of those solids were built from exactly two kinds of right
triangle. You can make one of each in a minute: cut a square from corner to corner for
the first, and cut an equilateral triangle from a corner to the middle of the opposite
side for the second. Everything else, in Plato’s story, was a receptacle, a featureless
medium that takes on shape the way wax takes a seal. Structure, for Plato, is shape
laid into something that has no shape of its own.

Why did he care? He wanted a world made on purpose, by a craftsman working from
a plan, and triangles were the plan. Is it true? No, but not for the cheap reason. You


                                            52
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


can’t refute a claim about what things are made of at the smallest scale by picking
one up; the smallest scale is exactly where your hands don’t reach, and Plato knew
that. What sank it is that it made no prediction anyone could check and the people
who eventually did reach that scale, two thousand years on, found atoms, and atoms
aren’t triangles. The idea was a guess with no way to lose, until it lost. But push on
it and two things survive. One: structure is something laid in, and the stuff it’s laid
into doesn’t carry it by itself. That’s a real idea, and I’d ask you to keep it loosely for
now, because later I’ll have to ask whether the state a machine holds is the wax or the
seal. Two: Plato broke his own claim, in a later dialogue called the Parmenides, with an
objection that Aristotle later nicknamed the third man, and it’s the most useful mistake
in this section. Take all the large things. Plato says they share one thing, Largeness.
But Largeness is itself large, so now there’s a further thing that all the large things and
Largeness share, and that one is large too, and it never stops. Try it with any property
you like; it runs away every time. The lesson, and I think it’s right though Plato never
quite accepted it himself: the structure of a collection is not one more member of the
collection. The plan isn’t a brick. Hold on to that one. It’ll come back in a place you
won’t expect.

2.3 Prove it from what you and I both accept
Around 300 BC, in Alexandria, Euclid wrote the Elements, and the thing to take from
it is not the geometry. It’s the method, and the method is the whole reason I trust
anything in this book, so give me a paragraph on it. He starts with definitions (“a point
is that which has no part”), five postulates (things he asks you to grant, like “a straight
line can be drawn from any point to any point”), and five common notions (things
nobody argues with, like “things equal to the same thing are equal to each other”).
Then he derives everything else, four hundred and sixty-five propositions, from only
those, in order, each meant to use nothing but what came before (he sometimes leans
on things he never stated, and later geometers filled those in). Not “trust me.” Not
“it’s well known.” Here are the rules you and I both accept; now watch. If you’ve ever
been in an argument that ended with “well, that’s just your opinion,” Euclid is the
man who found a way out of that room, and I’m not embarrassed to say I learned the
way out from someone dead for two thousand three hundred years. Four hundred
and sixty-five times he does the same trick, and the trick is everything.

And then there’s the one rule Euclid seems almost embarrassed by, and it’s a hole
worth falling into. His fifth postulate, the one about parallel lines, is long and awkward
next to the others, and for two thousand years people tried to prove it from the rest
so it wouldn’t have to be assumed. Proclus tried. Mathematicians in Persia and the
Arab world tried. In 1733 an Italian priest named Girolamo Saccheri spent a whole
book assuming it was false so he could watch the contradiction arrive, and he got
pages deep into what is now a perfectly good geometry before declaring that it was
repugnant and stopping. A century later three people, separately, took the step he
wouldn’t: drop the postulate, and you don’t get nonsense, you get other geometries


                                            53
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


that hold up just as well. Farkas Bolyai begged his son János to stay away from
the problem, warning that it had swallowed years of his own life; the son went in
anyway and came out with one of those geometries. Here’s the part I keep: they found
something real by refusing to believe one of the rules everyone accepted, and checking
what happened without it. That’s the push, two thousand years long.

What is structure, to Euclid? Whatever the starting rules force. And when are two
shapes the same? Here’s the one you can do: cut out two paper triangles and lay one
on the other. If they coincide, they’re equal. That’s his fourth common notion, and it’s
how he proves his fourth proposition, by picking up one triangle and setting it down
on another. Sameness is coinciding under a move. Keep that; it’s about to get very
general, and I didn’t see that coming either.

2.4 The statue and the bronze
Aristotle, Plato’s student, pulled the forms down out of heaven and put them inside
things, which was a bit rude to his teacher and also, I think, correct. His example, from
the Metaphysics: a bronze statue is bronze plus a shape, and being made of bronze is
no part of what it is to be a statue. The same shape in marble makes a different statue
with the same form. Matter and form, and form is what the thing is.

Push on it. Is that true? Take anything on your desk. Could the same thing be made
of something else? A coffee cup, sure. A sandwich, no; a sandwich made of wood is a
sculpture of a sandwich, and if you’ve ever tried to eat one you know the difference
matters. So the claim doesn’t hold everywhere. It holds exactly where the material
was never doing the work, and that’s a sharper thing than Aristotle said: structure
is what survives a change of material, in the places where the material didn’t matter.
Why do I care? Because the machine I keep mentioning and not describing gets built
more than once, in more than one material, and I’d like it to be the same machine every
time, and I don’t get to just say it is. That’s a promise I make in Part IV (Section 15)
and have to keep in Part V (Section 27), and Aristotle is the one who told me what the
promise means.

2.5 Where things are, without numbers
In 1679 Gottfried Leibniz, who co-invented calculus and had opinions about every-
thing, wrote to the physicist Christiaan Huygens asking for something that didn’t
exist: a way to reason about where things are directly, the way algebra reasons about
how much, without ever laying down coordinates. He called it the analysis of situation.
Try it yourself. Describe where the furniture is in the room you’re sitting in without
using a single number. “The couch is against the wall. The table is between the couch
and the window. The lamp is next to the chair.” You just did it, and what you used was
relations between places and nothing else. Huygens wrote back that November and
was not impressed. It took roughly two hundred years for Leibniz’s idea to become a
field, and the field is called topology, and Huygens is remembered for other things.



                                           54
The Thiele Machine                                                                  Devon Thiele


What survives the push is the same thing that survived the square, coming at you
from the other side. Position is a relation among places. The numbers you lay on top
are a convenience, and they’re a convenience you can take away and still have the
room. I’ll be honest about why this one landed for me: the thing I built keeps track
of which things belong together, and I spent a long time thinking that was a list of
numbers before I understood it was a relation that the numbers were merely naming.
Leibniz had that in 1679. Huygens told him no. I’d like to think I’d have sided with
Leibniz. I probably would have sided with the famous guy.

2.6 Naming a thing by saying when two are the same
In 1884, in a short book called The Foundations of Arithmetic, Gottlob Frege noticed
something you can check in your head right now. “Line a is parallel to line b” and “the
direction of a is the direction of b” say exactly the same thing. There is no fact in one
that isn’t in the other. But the second sentence has a new object in it, a direction, that
the first one doesn’t. Where did it come from? From the sameness. Once you can say
when two things count as the same, you’ve earned the right to name the thing they
share. Frege used exactly this move to say what a number is: the number of things
in a pile is whatever every pile you can match up with it, one to one, has in common.
That’s a residue with teeth: a sameness relation lets you name a new object.

Now push, because Frege pushed too hard, and it cost him. In his big system he
also assumed that any condition you can state picks out a collection, the collection of
everything that satisfies it. In June of 1902, a young Bertrand Russell wrote him a short
letter. Consider the collection of all collections that are not members of themselves. Is
it a member of itself? If it is, then by its own rule it isn’t. If it isn’t, then it qualifies, so
it is. Do it in your head; it flips every time you look at it, like one of those drawings
that’s a vase and then two faces and then a vase. Frege’s floor had a hole in it, and he
knew it the day he opened the letter, and his second volume was already at the printer.
The repair came from Ernst Zermelo in 1908 and it’s the one mathematics still stands
on: you may only cut a collection out of a collection you were already given. You don’t
get to sort “everything.” You sort a pile. I’ll tell you now that this rule shows up again,
later, in a place where I had to obey it or fall through the same hole, and I’ll point at it
when the book gets there.

Frege’s reply is worth hearing, because it’s the best example I know of how to lose.
He wrote back within days. He didn’t hide it or argue around it. He said, more or
less, that arithmetic was tottering, and in an appendix to the volume that was about to
come out he wrote that hardly anything worse can happen to a scientific writer than
having a foundation give way right after the work is finished. Then he tried to fix it.
If I’m wrong about something in this book, and I’d bet I am somewhere, that’s how
I’d like to take it.




                                               55
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


2.7 Choose the changes, keep what survives
By 1872 there were too many geometries. Euclid’s, and ones where parallel lines meet,
and ones with no such thing as distance, and nobody could say what made them all
geometry rather than a pile of unrelated hobbies. Felix Klein, twenty-three years old
and taking up a professorship at Erlangen, published an answer in a program paper
that people still call the Erlangen program. Pick a set of allowed changes: rotations,
stretches, whatever you decide. Then a geometry is the study of the properties that stay
the same under those changes. Pick a different set of changes and you get a different
geometry on the very same page. Euclid’s is the one where you may slide and turn a
shape but not stretch it. And here’s the part I’d underline if this were my book, which
it is: in Klein’s scheme any group of changes can define a geometry. The choice is free.
Nobody tells you which changes to allow.

You can do this one at your desk. Take any drawing and ask what’s still true after you
turn it upside down (lengths, angles), after you stretch it (not lengths anymore, but
which lines cross which), after you crumple it (almost nothing but what touches what).
Three answers, three structures, one drawing. The residue: structure is what survives
a chosen set of changes, and “chosen” is doing real work in that sentence. There’s no
structure of a thing from nowhere. You have to say what you’re allowed to do to it
first. I didn’t know that when I started, and I’d been saying “the structure of” things
for years.

2.8 An invariance comes with a bill
In 1918 Emmy Noether, who wasn’t allowed to hold a professorship because she was
a woman and for a while lectured under a male colleague’s name, proved something
that physicists still treat as close to holy. Take a physical system whose laws can be
written the way most of physics is written, as “of all the paths the system could take,
it takes the one that makes a certain total smallest” (the total is called the action, and
that’s all I’ll say about it here). For such a system, every continuous symmetry of the
laws comes with a quantity that is conserved. If the laws don’t care where you are,
momentum is conserved. If they don’t care when it is, energy is. A symmetry isn’t
decoration. It has a consequence downstream that you can measure with instruments.
I can’t hand you this one to do at the table; the proof needs calculus I’d have to build
first and I’d lose you and probably me, and the “written as an action” condition is
doing real work that I’m not going to unpack here. What I can hand you is the shape.
Structure, once it’s really there and the setting is the right kind, has consequences you
can measure. I’ll admit that’s the sentence that made me think a machine could carry
a bill for structure in the first place, and I’ll also admit I don’t yet know whether that
hope was reasonable. Noether makes it reasonable to ask. She doesn’t make it true,
and nothing I build in this book is a system with an action.




                                           56
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


2.9 All of mathematics as structures
Starting in the 1930s, a group of young French mathematicians began publishing a
vast treatise under one made-up name, Nicolas Bourbaki, as if he were a single person.
He wasn’t. He also applied for membership in the American Mathematical Society
and was turned down, which I find comforting. Their goal was to rebuild all of
mathematics on one idea: a structure is a set of elements “whose nature has not been
specified,” together with one or more relations on them that satisfy stated axioms.
They believed three kinds of structure were the mothers of all the rest: algebraic, order,
and topological.

Push on it, and here’s what the historian Leo Corry found when he went through the
entire treatise looking for the place where this formal definition of structure actually
does any work: it “plays no actual role in the presentation of theories within the trea-
tise.” Outside the chapter that defines it, almost nowhere. And I found no argument
in their writing for why the mother structures number three. And the chapter on
category theory, which they announced, never appeared. Why? The thing their defi-
nition left out was the maps, the ways of carrying a structure from one set to another,
and it turned out the maps were where the weight was. So I keep two things from
Bourbaki. The right thing: relations on elements whose nature doesn’t matter, which
is Aristotle’s bronze in different words. And the warning: a structure stated without
its maps won’t carry the work. I learned that one the slow way, and the origin story
you just read tells it.

2.10 A set with some named relations
What mathematical logic eventually settled on, with Alfred Tarski giving the field its
name, “the theory of models,” in 1954, is almost boring, and the boring ones are the
ones that last. A structure is a set, called the domain, plus whatever relations and
functions a chosen vocabulary names on it. Pick the vocabulary (Klein again: you
choose), and a structure is anything that gives those names a meaning. Now I want to
say “the smallest one,” and the word “smallest” has no meaning until I say what I’m
measuring, so here is the ruler: count the vocabulary. One name, taking one thing at a
time, with two possible answers. That’s a domain with one yes-or-no property named
on it. One question, put to each thing. Two honest limits, and I’d rather give them
to you than have you find them. A vocabulary with one named constant (“this one,
here”) is exactly as small by my ruler and it doesn’t sort anything, so “smallest that
sorts” is the claim, not “smallest.” And one question only splits the domain into two
groups when some things answer yes and some answer no; if they all agree there’s one
group and nothing was sorted. With those limits said, and with the ruler said: by the
count of names, the smallest structure that sorts anything is one question. Someone
with a different ruler (fewest symbols to write down, say, or least information) might
land somewhere else, and I’d want to see where. Keep it. It’s about to turn into the
whole section.



                                           57
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


2.11 The structure is in the arrows
This is the one I met first, backwards. I’d built it by feel, in a rendering engine, as
“digital DNA,” and only went looking for its name after the thing already ran. In 1945
Samuel Eilenberg and Saunders Mac Lane published a paper that founded a field now
called category theory, and they said in plain words that it was a continuation of Klein,
which I’d have loved to know at the time. The move: stop asking what a thing is,
and ask how it’s carried. A category is some objects and some arrows between them,
where arrows can be followed one after another and every object has a do-nothing
arrow to itself, plus two rules that make the following dependable: following three
arrows in a row gives the same result whether you pair up the first two or the last two,
and the do-nothing arrow really does nothing when you tack it onto either end. That’s
the whole definition, and I know it sounds like nothing. The two rules are the part
people skip, and they’re the part you’ll watch me have to prove later. What a thing is
is how it maps. For now the residue is the one Bourbaki missed: structure lives in the
maps. Whether the thing I built honours that, you’ll be able to judge when I build the
category in front of you, from scratch, later in this book.

2.12 Structure is the part that compresses
Play this one with me. I write “th” and you guess the next letter. You said “e,” and
you were right. Now “the q”: you said “u.” Congratulations, you just measured
the structure of English. In 1948 Claude Shannon measured it properly, in a paper
that founded information theory, and found that about half of written English is
“determined by the structure of the language.” It’s the reason a zip file of a long letter
is so much smaller than the letter. Be careful what that says. It does not say that
every other letter is fixed by the ones before it; you just guessed “e” after “th” and you
could have been wrong (think “than”). It says that, on average and over long stretches,
about half of what’s written could be rebuilt from the rest: the text is roughly twice as
long as the choices in it. And he said why that matters in one line that I’d frame if I
framed things: the structure “allows one to make a saving in time.” The more you can
predict, the less you have to read.

Thirty years later Jorma Rissanen turned that saving into a price. His idea is called
the minimum description length principle, and it says: the best model of some data is
the one that makes the total description shortest, where the total is the length of the
model plus the length of the data once the model has explained what it can. A model
is paid for in bits. It’s worth stating only if it saves more than it costs. Peter Grünwald,
in a tutorial you can find online, adds the footnote that keeps this honest: the price
of a model depends on the code you chose to write it in, so the price itself needs a
principle behind it, and nobody hands you that principle for free.

That’s a lot of “length of” to swallow in one paragraph, so do one with me, with
numbers small enough to check on the back of an envelope. Every number in it comes
from a code I’m about to make up on the spot, and I’ll say every rule of the code out



                                            58
The Thiele Machine                                                              Devon Thiele


loud, because Grünwald’s footnote is the whole point: change the rules and every
number moves.

Here’s the data. A row of thirty-two digits, each a 0 or a 1, and you and I agree in
advance that the row is thirty-two long, so nobody has to spend anything saying so:


                     0101010101010101 0101010101010101

(The space is only there to rest your eyes.) Now the code. Every description starts
with one digit that says which kind of description follows: 0 means “here’s the row,
written out,” 1 means “here’s a pattern, then the exceptions to it.” Each digit is one
yes-or-no answer, one bit, which is what Shannon’s unit is. Written out, the row costs
that first digit plus the thirty-two digits themselves: thirty-three bits, and there’s no
model in it at all. A pattern description goes like this. First five digits giving the length
of a little block, anything from 1 to 32, because five yes-or-no answers can pick out
one of thirty-two lengths. Then the block itself. The rule is “repeat the block until you
have thirty-two digits.” Then five digits for how many places the row disagrees with
the pattern (up to thirty-one, which is plenty here), and five more digits for each of
those places, saying which of the thirty-two it is.

Do it for the row above. The block is 01, two digits long. So the model costs 1 (which
kind) plus 5 (the block’s length) plus 2 (the block): eight bits. Then what’s left to say
about the data once the model has said its piece: the row disagrees with “repeat 01”
nowhere, so that’s five digits saying “zero exceptions” and nothing else. Five bits.
Total, thirteen, against thirty-three for writing it out. The pattern pays for itself, with
twenty bits to spare. That’s Rissanen’s sentence happening on paper: a model is worth
stating when it saves more than it costs.

Now spoil the row. Flip two of its digits anywhere you like. The model doesn’t change,
eight bits, but now the leftover says “two exceptions, here and here”: five plus five
plus five, fifteen. Total twenty-three. Still cheaper than thirty-three; the pattern still
pays, it just pays less, because the data has more to say that the model can’t. Flip
four, and the total is 8 + 5 + 4 × 5 = 33, a dead tie. Flip five and it’s thirty-eight, and
now writing the row out is cheaper than explaining it, and by Rissanen’s rule you
shouldn’t state the pattern at all, even though it’s still sort of there if you squint. So
“is there structure here?” has turned into a question with a number on each side, and
a break-even point you can find yourself: somewhere between four and five spoiled
digits, in this code.

And now change the code, because I promised you’d see the numbers move. Say I’d
used six digits for each exception’s place instead of five (wasteful, but nobody stopped
me). Then four spoiled digits cost 8 + 5 + 4 × 6 = 37, and the tie is gone; the pattern
stopped paying one spoiled digit sooner. Same row, same pattern, different verdict,
and the only thing that changed was a convention I chose. That’s Grünwald’s footnote,


                                             59
The Thiele Machine                                                              Devon Thiele


and it’s why I won’t let you take any of those numbers anywhere else. They’re the
price of a description in one made-up code, a length of a written-down message, and
nothing more. They are not the charge I opened this book with. That charge, when
the book finally states it, is on one step a machine takes, not on how long anybody’s
description is, and if the two ever turn out to be related, that has to be shown, not
assumed from both of them being counted in whole numbers.

Now push, because this is where “structure means information” gets born, and it’s
wrong, and it’s an easy thing to believe. Flip a fair coin two hundred times and write
down the string. Almost always, there’s no shorter way to say that string than to
say the whole thing. You can watch it happen in the little code above, cut to thirty-
two digits: a coin-flip row disagrees with “repeat 01” in about sixteen places, which
would cost eighty-odd bits to list, and even the one block guaranteed to fit with no
exceptions, the whole row used as its own block, costs 1 + 5 + 32 + 5 = 43. The written-
out row at thirty-three wins, and no pattern earns its keep. Nikolai Vereshchagin
and Paul Vitányi, in a 2004 paper on exactly this question, put it without mercy:
every bit of a string like that is “meaningless information, random noise.” Maximum
information. Zero structure. So in this sense structure is the part that compresses, the
part where the “th” tells you about the “e,” and most information and most structure
are different things. Hold that one tightly, because if you built something that charged
for information, you’d be charging for the wrong thing, and for a while I wasn’t sure
which one I’d built.

And now notice that the word just changed meaning on you, and on me, and I’d rather
point at it than let it slide. Shannon and Rissanen and Vereshchagin mean regularity:
a pattern that lets you say something shorter. Tarski, a few pages back, and Halmos,
coming up, mean a set with named relations on it, and those two are not the same
thing. Here’s the test, and you can run it: number a thousand objects, flip a coin for
each, heads goes in group one, tails in group two. That’s a perfectly good sorting in the
set theorist’s sense, every object in exactly one group. And the list of who went where
is a thousand coin flips, which is to say it compresses about as well as a thousand
coin flips, which is to say not at all. Feed it to a code built like the little one, with the
fields widened to fit a thousand, and you get the coin-flip row again, only longer: no
block earns its keep, the written-out list wins, and by Rissanen’s rule there’s no pattern
worth stating. By the set theorist’s rule, the sorting is the structure, and it’s every bit
as much a sorting as “evens in one group, odds in the other,” which compresses to
almost nothing. Same kind of object, wildly different description lengths. So the two
meanings don’t even rank things the same way: one asks “is there a sorting?” and
the answer is yes for both; the other asks “does a short rule say who went where?”
and the answer is yes for evens and odds and no for the coins. Structure in the set
theorist’s sense, none in Rissanen’s. I’ll keep both meanings, and I’ll try to say which
one I’m using, and when I slip you’ll know what to look for.




                                             60
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


2.13 The four parts of every computer
In 1936 Alan Turing described the machine that every computer you’ve ever touched
is a version of, and he did it before any of them existed. It’s the clerk with the pencil
from the opening chapter, written down as a machine. Write down its parts; there are
four. A tape, divided into squares. A head that reads one square at a time and can
write on it and move left or right. A finite list of states the head can be in. A table of
rules: in this state, reading this symbol, do this. That’s all, and two different things
are true about it that get run together. Every other formal recipe for “a procedure”
that anyone has written down since computes exactly what this one does; those are
theorems, proved one pairing at a time, and Turing proved the first of them himself.
That it also captures everything a person could ever carry out by rote, everything
“computable” in the plain-English sense, is a claim, called the Church-Turing thesis,
and nobody has proved it, because the plain-English side isn’t a mathematical object.
Turing himself kept those two apart in the 1936 paper, and so will I. There’s a third
claim that gets stacked on top, and it’s a different kind again: the physical Church-
Turing thesis, that every device you could build out of real stuff computes no more
than this machine does. That one is a claim about physics, not mathematics. Nobody
has built a device that breaks it. Your laptop, your phone, every server in every data
center compute nothing a Turing machine can’t; what differs between them is speed,
space, energy, and cost. Hold on to that last word. Cost is where this book lives.

Now do the thing I did, and do it honestly. Look through those four parts for a place
that says “these squares belong together.” I couldn’t find one. Any grouping has to
live in the table, as a rule, or on the tape, as marks, which is to say as bytes like any
other bytes. Maybe you can find a slot I missed. I’d want to know. I looked for a long
time and I kept not finding it, and not finding something is weaker than proving it
isn’t there, so I’ll be careful about what I claim from that.

In 1972 David Parnas, a software engineer, wrote a short paper that every programmer
should be made to read and most haven’t, on how to cut a program into modules.
He took one small program and cut it two ways. Both worked. But one was easy
to change later and the other wasn’t, and the easy one could be “much less efficient”
if talking between modules cost anything. His point: a module is “a responsibility
assignment,” a decision about who answers for what, and how you cut decides what
every later change costs. If you’ve ever maintained someone else’s code, you’ve paid
Parnas’s bill, probably at two in the morning. What survives the push: a division is
a commitment, not a caption. It changes what the work costs. It is not a label stuck
on afterwards. I’d like to say the thing I built understood that from the beginning. It
didn’t. I did, eventually.

2.14 Laying them all down
Now lay every one of those on top of the others and see what shows through. Here
are the seven things I think I see. Be clear about what this is: it’s my overlay, the



                                           61
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


places where I see the sources agreeing, and not a thing the sources proved together.
They didn’t; some of them never met, and some of them disagree (Bourbaki left out
the maps that Eilenberg and Mac Lane built everything on; Shannon’s structure and
Tarski’s are two different words, as I just showed you). You’ve pushed on each source
yourself by now, so you’re in a position to tell me if I’m seeing things.

A list of seven slogans would be easy to nod at and impossible to check, so I’m going
to carry one thing through all seven and let you watch each one add to the one before
it. The thing is the square you drew for the Pythagoreans, side, diagonal and all. Draw
a few more on the same sheet: one small, one big, the small one again but tilted, and
one stretched out into a long rectangle. You’ll want a pile.

Structure is about relations among things, not the things. The diagonal, the bronze,
Leibniz’s room, Bourbaki’s unspecified elements, Tarski’s named relations, the arrows.
On your sheet, what makes a square a square was never the ink. It’s that the four sides
match and the corners are square, and that the diagonal stands to the side the way
it does whether or not any number names it. Every one of those is a relation among
parts. But on its own this first thing is too loose to use, because a sheet of paper is
drowning in relations: this square is left of that one, this one is nearer the coffee ring.
Which relations count?

Structure is what stays the same under a chosen set of changes. Euclid’s triangles laid
together, Klein’s allowed moves, Noether’s symmetry, Frege’s direction that every
parallel line shares. That’s the answer the first thing was missing. The relations that
count are the ones that survive the moves you’ve decided to allow. Slide the small
square across the sheet, turn it, and the diagonal still stands to the side exactly as
before; “left of the coffee ring” doesn’t make it across. The second thing is a filter on
the first.

The same structure can be carried by different stuff. The statue in marble. Two sets
that answer the same vocabulary the same way. This is the second thing again with
one more change allowed: swap the material. Cut the square out of cardboard, or lay
it out in string on the table, and if the relations survive, it’s the same square in every
way you agreed to care about. Aristotle’s bronze turns out to be one more thing you
agreed not to look at, and the wooden sandwich is what happens when the material
was never on that list.

The first act of structure is a sameness that sorts a pile you were already given. Euclid’s
first common notion, Frege’s direction, Tarski’s one question, and Russell’s letter
saying you must start from a pile. This is where the overlay stopped being a list for me
and turned into a shape, so slow down here with me. Look at your pile of drawings
and say: two of them count as the same when an allowed move carries one exactly
onto the other. Watch what happens to the pile. It falls into groups. The small square
and its tilted twin go together; the big one sits on its own; the rectangle sits on its own.
And it falls cleanly, nothing half in one group and half in another, for a reason you


                                            62
The Thiele Machine                                                              Devon Thiele


can check. Klein’s allowed moves always come with three guarantees: doing nothing
counts as a move, every move can be undone, and two moves in a row is again a
move. Those three are, word for word in different clothes, “everything is the same as
itself,” “if this matches that, then that matches this,” and Euclid’s first common notion,
“things equal to the same thing are equal to each other.” So the second thing, sameness
under chosen moves, is a sorting of the pile the moment you ask which drawings it
calls the same. Frege did it with lines and parallels. Tarski’s one question does it in
the crudest way there is, by cutting the pile in two. And the pile has to be there first,
because a sameness has to be a sameness among something; that’s Russell’s letter, and
Zermelo’s repair.

Adding structure rules possibilities out. Every one of Euclid’s postulates is a door
closed. Half of English is already decided. A conserved quantity limits where a
system can go. On your sheet: once the small square and its tilted twin are in one
group, you’ve given up the right to answer any question the moves respect differently
for the two of them. Tell me the side of one and the diagonal of the other isn’t an open
question any more. A sorting is a bundle of doors closed at once.

Held structure gets used without re-deriving it. Shannon’s saving in time. Rissanen’s
compression. Parnas’s one-module-at-a-time. Leibniz, who hoped his algebra of
position would spare people a great many fruitless tries. This is the fifth thing paying
out. The doors you closed are doors you never have to check again: know which
group a drawing is in and you know everything the group shares without getting the
ruler out, the same way the row of 01 never needed writing out. With one catch that
I’ll need a whole section for: it only pays if you kept the sorting somewhere you can
read it back.

And structure is always relative to a chosen frame. Klein’s group. The vocabulary. The
code you compress against. Parnas’s criteria. Nobody gets to say “the” structure of a
thing without saying from where, and I do it constantly, so watch me for it. On your
sheet: allow stretching as one of the moves and the rectangle walks over and joins
the squares; allow only slides and turns and it doesn’t. Same pile, same ink, different
groups, because I chose different moves. The groups were never in the paper. They
were in the paper and the choice, together.

So here’s how I think they hang together. Relations are what structure is made of. The
chosen moves pick which relations count, and a change of material is just one more
move. Asking which things the moves call the same sorts the pile. The sorting closes
doors, and closed doors are what you get to skip later. And because the moves were
chosen, all of it is relative. Read that way, the fourth thing sits in the middle: it’s where
the first three turn into something you can write down, and where the last three get
their start.

That’s my reason for starting the next section with a sorting, and I want to be exact
about what kind of reason it is, because it’s mine and not theirs. None of these people


                                             63
The Thiele Machine                                                                Devon Thiele


said “start with a partition.” Klein would tell you to start with the moves, Eilenberg
and Mac Lane with the arrows, Shannon with the probabilities. What I can actually
point at is narrower. In the framings about when two things are the same shape or the
same kind (Euclid laying one triangle on another, Klein’s moves, Frege’s directions,
Tarski’s question) there’s a moment where somebody decides what counts as the
same, and that decision, written down, is a sorting of a pile. In Shannon, Rissanen
and Noether I can’t find that moment as cleanly, and I’m not going to bend them until
I do. So the overlay doesn’t prove that a sorting comes first. It shows me where the
framings I trust most keep putting their first foot down, and I’m putting mine there
too.

I looked for a framing that denies any of the seven and didn’t find one, which could
mean there isn’t one or could mean I didn’t look where it lives. If you know of one,
I’d like to see it.

2.15 The smallest piece
Now the sentence I wanted to say at the top and had no right to until here, and even
here I have to split it in two, because half of it is a textbook fact and the other half is
me. The piece of structure I’m going to start from is a partition.

The textbook half: a partition and an equivalence relation are the same object. That’s
Paul Halmos, Naive Set Theory, 1960, section seven, and you could read that section
before dinner. Here it is in words. Take any pile of things. An equivalence relation on
it is a way of saying “these two count as the same” that behaves the way sameness
should: everything is the same as itself; if a is the same as b then b is the same as
a; and if a is the same as b and b the same as c, then a is the same as c. Every such
relation sorts the pile into groups, the things that count as the same go together, and
every sorting into groups hands you back a relation, “same group.” Do one and then
the other and you land where you started, in both directions. So a partition and an
equivalence relation are one object seen from two sides, and that’s the fourth thing on
the overlay, the sorting of a given pile, now with a name and a page number.

Here it is in the exact form, since this is the first place the book uses one. A set is a pile,
x ∈ X means “x is in the pile X,” and a relation on X is any rule ∼ that, for each pair
of things, says whether x ∼ y holds. A few more marks show up below, and each is
a word in disguise. S1 , . . . , Sk are the buckets, numbered one to k. A cap, S j ∩ Sl , is
“what the two buckets share,” a cup, S1 ∪ · · · ∪ Sk , is “everything in any bucket,” and
∅ is the empty pile. And curly braces with a colon, { y ∈ X : y ∼ x }, mean “the pile
of every y in X for which y ∼ x holds”; the theorem writes that pile [ x ], the things that
count as the same as x.


Definition 2.1 (Equivalence relation, partition). A relation ∼ on a set X is an equiv-
alence relation when it is reflexive (x ∼ x), symmetric (x ∼ y implies y ∼ x), and
transitive (x ∼ y and y ∼ z imply x ∼ z). A partition of X is a collection of non-empty


                                              64
The Thiele Machine                                                                Devon Thiele


subsets of X, the blocks, such that every member of X lies in exactly one block. Spelled
out for blocks S1 , . . . , Sk : each S j is non-empty, no two share a member (S j ∩ Sl = ∅
when j ̸= l), and together they cover everything (S1 ∪ · · · ∪ Sk = X).


Theorem 2.1 (Sameness and sorting are one object). Every equivalence relation on X
determines a partition, whose blocks are the classes [ x ] = { y ∈ X : y ∼ x }; every partition
determines an equivalence relation, “x and y lie in the same block”; and the two constructions
undo each other.

Proof. The classes are non-empty (x ∈ [ x ] by reflexivity) and cover X. If z lies in [ x ]
and in [y], then z ∼ x and z ∼ y, so x ∼ y by symmetry and transitivity, and then
[ x ] = [y] by transitivity again; so the blocks don’t overlap. “Same block” is plainly
reflexive, symmetric, and transitive. Going relation to partition to relation returns
x ∼ y exactly when x and y share a class, which is the original relation; going partition
to relation to partition returns the original blocks.

This is textbook mathematics (Halmos, section 7), and the book uses it as a foundation,
not as a contribution.

And the smallest structure that sorts, by my ruler in Tarski’s setup, the one question,
is the same object a third time. Put a yes-or-no question to every thing in the pile. The
ones that say yes are one group and the ones that say no are the other. Going the other
way, a two-group partition becomes a question the moment you point at one group
and call it “yes.” The only thing a question has that the partition doesn’t is which
group got the label. So the set theorist’s first step and the logician’s first step are the
same step, and nobody has to pick a side, which is a relief, because it’s an argument
you can lose with yourself for a long time.

That’s the textbook half. Now mine, and hold it looser, because Halmos says nothing
about “smallest” or “first” and I’d be lying if I let his page number carry my sentence.
In what I’m going to build, the order goes: a pile, then groups in the pile, then
whatever connects one group to another, and the groups come first because a question
needs something to be about and a connection needs somewhere to land. That’s an
order for my construction. It is not a law that every account of structure has to start by
sorting. You could start with an ordering instead (“this one comes before that one”),
or with arrows between the things themselves and no groups at all, and people do,
and nothing I’ve shown you rules that out. So the honest sentence is: a partition is
where I chose to start, it is the smallest start by the ruler I gave you, and I chose it
because it’s the first thing that can be right or wrong about a pile and the last thing I
could take away without everything I build on it coming down. If you have a smaller
start by a ruler you can state, I want to see it. It would change this book.




                                              65
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


2.16 Buckets
So here’s the smallest piece, done once, for real. Take everything in front of you
and sort it into buckets: nothing in two buckets, nothing left on the floor. That’s the
whole of the definition. It’s the thing you do with a kindergartner and a pile of blocks,
and I am aware that I’ve just marched you past Pythagoras, Plato, Euclid, Frege and
Noether to arrive at a pile of blocks. Keep the blocks anyway. They’re about to cost
you something.

Ten blocks. Red ones in one bucket, square ones in another, everything else in a third.
Now a red square turns up, as they do, and you’ve got your first crisis: it belongs
in two buckets and the rule says one. So this isn’t a partition yet, and you have to
decide which bucket wins. That decision is the whole thing. A partition is a pile of
small rulings like that one, and once you’ve made them all, the pile is holding a fact
it wasn’t holding a minute ago. The formal version says the same thing with fewer
words and more squiggles, and you’ve already seen it: it’s the definition of a partition
a few pages back (Definition 2.1). Non-empty buckets, nothing in two, nothing on the
floor.

Here’s the part that isn’t kindergarten. Why would that fact cost anything? Watch
what it does to one question. Before the buckets, “are these two in the same group?”
means working it out: go find the first one, go find the second one, apply the rule to
each, compare. After the buckets, it’s a glance: read the first one’s bucket, read the
second one’s bucket, done. And the glance costs the same when the pile goes from ten
blocks to a billion. That’s Shannon’s saving in time and Parnas’s one-module-at-a-time,
the sixth thing on the overlay, showing up in a kindergarten.

Now push on it, because that paragraph sells more than it should, and I want you to
see where. The partition didn’t give you the glance. A table gave you the glance: a
written-down line for each block saying which bucket it went in. The partition is the
fact; the table is one way of holding the fact so it can be read back fast, and you had to
build the table, and you have to store it, and it has to be the kind of thing you can read
in one look (a bucket number, say, and not a list of every block in the bucket that you’d
have to search through again). Anybody who’s used a database has met this table;
it’s what an index is, and an index is a thing you build, store, and keep up to date,
not a thing you get for free. Take the table away and keep the partition and you’re
back to working it out. And sometimes there was never a search to save: if the rule is
“evens here, odds there,” you can answer “same group?” by looking at the last digit of
each, no buckets needed. So the honest residue is smaller than the sentence I wanted:
holding a sorting in a form you can read back is worth something, and building that
form cost something, and those are already two different events. Building the table,
storing it, checking that it’s right, and deciding to rely on it are four different things.
The question this book is about lives in the gap between the third and the fourth, and
nothing in the kindergarten has shown you yet that there’s a charge in that gap. It’s
shown you there might be a place for one.

                                            66
The Thiele Machine                                                          Devon Thiele


So who, in everything I read, says what the bill is? I found three answers that come
close, and I’ll be exact about how close, because this is the edge of what I know.
Rolf Landauer, in 1961, and Charles Bennett after him, say that any step which takes
two possible situations and makes them one, erasing a bit or merging two paths a
computation could have taken, has to push some disorder out into the world, which
in a real machine means heat. That’s not a metaphor; it’s the one place where a fact
about information turns into a fact about your electricity bill, and it’s been measured.
Is sending blocks to buckets a step of that kind? Push, because it depends on what
you keep. If you keep each block and write its bucket next to it, you’ve lost nothing;
you can read the block right back off the pair, and Bennett’s whole point in his 1973
paper was that a computation which keeps its inputs can be run without any such step
at all. If instead you throw the block away and keep only the bucket label, then two
different blocks can leave the same label behind, and that is a many-to-one step, the
kind Landauer charges for. Both are things people call “sorting into buckets.” Only
the second loses a distinction. So the bucket by itself doesn’t hand you a Landauer bill;
the forgetting does, when there is forgetting, and whether a given machine forgets is a
question about that machine, which has to be answered on the page and not waved
at here. Rissanen says a model is paid for in the bits it takes to state, and Grünwald
says the price depends on the code. Parnas says a bad cut is paid for later, at two
in the morning. And that’s where it stops. I couldn’t find anyone who says that
the moment you vouch for a grouping, the moment you stand behind “these belong
together” instead of just arranging them that way, has a price of its own. That could
mean nobody says it. It could mean I didn’t find the person who does. I honestly can’t
tell you which.

So that’s where I am at the end of one word. Holding a sorting in readable form is
worth something and cost something, forgetting where things came from costs heat,
and standing behind a sorting is a different act from either, and nobody I found has
priced it. You can walk back through all of that and tell me where it breaks. Maybe
there’s no such bill. Maybe I’m about to spend a book chasing a charge that nobody
owes, which would be an extremely me thing to do. The next section is me trying to
find out whether that charge is real on any machine at all, not mine, any machine, and
if the answer comes back no, you should stop reading there. I would have stopped
writing there too.

The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


Part II

The axiom
3 A record and a toll
I left you with a question I couldn’t answer: something pays for the glance, and I
couldn’t find anyone who says the moment of vouching for a grouping has a price of
its own. Before I go looking for that price in anything complicated, I want to try the
opposite. Build the smallest thing that could possibly carry such a bill, on paper, with
a pencil, write the bill into its rules, and see what follows from it. If nothing follows in
something with five parts, nothing is going to follow in something with five thousand,
and I’d rather find that out on page one than on page four hundred.

One thing about where the buckets went, because you’ll notice they vanish for a while.
Part I ended on vouching for a grouping, and what I’m about to build prices vouching
for anything at all: a flag goes up, and the rule doesn’t ask what the flag is standing
behind. A sorting is the first kind of claim I care about, not the only kind, and the
buckets come back when the book finally asks what a flag stands behind (Section 19).
Until then nothing leans on them. The floor in this section, the reason for it in the next,
and the latch in Part III all work for any yes-or-no reading whatsoever, partition or no
partition.

But first the word, because I’ve got a new one and I don’t trust it either. Record.
Receipt. Certificate. Vouch. People have been making marks that other people are
supposed to rely on for a very long time, and I wanted to know what they thought
they were doing, and what it cost them, and whether any of them ever said the thing
I need said. So, same deal as before: here’s what I could reach, pushed on with you,
and I’ll tell you where the search ran out.

3.1 Clay, seals, and seven witnesses
Start about five thousand years ago, in the Near East, with people who counted sheep
with little clay tokens. To send a count across a distance without the courier changing
it, they put the tokens inside a hollow clay ball, pressed the shapes of the tokens onto
the outside while the clay was soft, and sealed it. The archaeologist Denise Schmandt-
Besserat has spent a career on these; the ball is called a bulla. Here’s the push, and
you can do it with a cookie tin: the thing that makes it a record isn’t the tokens, it’s
that the outside shows what’s inside and you have to break it to get in. Opening it
destroys it. Tampering shows. That’s a real idea and it will show up again in a form
you won’t expect: a record is worth something only if it can’t be silently undone.

Now law, which is where people get serious about who’s allowed to say what hap-
pened. The book of Deuteronomy, chapter nineteen: nobody is convicted on the word
of one witness; it takes “two or three.” The Roman jurist Gaius, writing in the second


                                            68
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


century, says a will the praetor will honour is one sealed by seven witnesses. Seven.
Why did they care that much? Because one person can lie, and a will moves a fortune,
and the dead man can’t object. So the record isn’t the paper. It’s the number of inde-
pendent people who have put their own seal, their own name, their own risk, next
to the claim. Try it: write “paid five dollars, signed A” on a napkin and ask a friend
to forge it. Takes them ten seconds. Now require two other people to initial it at the
moment of payment and each keep a copy. Your forger needs two accomplices or has
to match two copies held in two other pockets. The claim didn’t change. What stands
behind it did.

Which brings me to seals, and the medieval historian Michael Clanchy, whose book is
called From Memory to Written Record. England between the Norman Conquest and the
early 1300s was learning to trust writing instead of trusting people who remembered,
and the lesson was painful: seals were forged, charters were forged, and historians
today have a whole craft of telling real charters from fake ones because the fakes are so
many. A seal is only as good as whoever holds the stamp. Keep that one too, because
in 2011 a certificate authority called DigiNotar found out, at the cost of its existence,
that a mathematically perfect signature is worth exactly what the custody of the key
is worth, and intruders had taken control of the machines that signed. Nine hundred
years, same failure. I find that oddly comforting.

And then the obvious next question: if seals could be forged, what caught the forgeries?
Not the seals. The most famous forged record in European history is the Donation
of Constantine, a document in which the emperor Constantine supposedly handed
rule over Rome and the western empire to the Pope. It was most likely written in the
eighth century, some four hundred years after Constantine died, and it was leaned on
for centuries. Around 1440 a scholar named Lorenzo Valla took it apart by its Latin:
the language belonged to a much later age, and it used words, “satraps” among them,
that no Roman of Constantine’s day would have used for his officials. (Valla wasn’t
even first; Nicholas of Cusa had already called it a forgery. Valla’s is the version people
remember, which is a pattern that keeps turning up.) Look at what kind of check that
was. Not “is the stamp real” but “could these words have been written when they say
they were.” A record can pass the first and fail the second, which is a hint that what I
keep calling one thing, a record, is doing more than one job.

3.2 Two columns and a stamp
Here’s the one I’d never have guessed mattered. Bookkeeping. Around 1300, the
ledger of a Florentine company called Farolfi, kept at its branch in Provence, shows
the earliest complete example anyone has found of a trick merchants were working
out: write every transaction twice, once where the money came from and once where
it went, and the two columns have to balance. Genoa’s public accounts of 1340 do it.
And in 1494 a friar named Luca Pacioli printed the method in a mathematics book,
and it spread. That’s double-entry bookkeeping, and it’s easy to take it for just a tidy
habit.

                                            69
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


Do it for one day. Keep two columns of every dollar that moves, and total them at
night. Now have a friend secretly change one entry in one column. The totals disagree;
you catch it. Now have them change the matching entry in both columns. The totals
agree. You’ve caught nothing. Push on that and you’ve found what double entry
actually is: a trap for slips, not for careful liars. Pacioli knew. The scholar Forrester
reads him as reporting that in many places the books were taken to the local consul
to be authenticated before a single entry went in. The stamp is a witness again, from
outside. The two columns are the discipline; the stamp is the claim that someone
other than you will stand behind the fact that these books, and not some others, are
the books. Keep both halves separate in your head. One is a method. The other is a
commitment.

And then I found the place where this got turned into a motto. The Royal Society,
founded in London in 1660 and still running, picked as its motto Nullius in verba: take
nobody’s word for it. (Where did they get it? From somebody’s words, naturally. It’s
half a line of the Roman poet Horace, from a verse letter to his patron, saying he isn’t
bound to swear by the words of any master. So the society that takes nobody’s word
for it took its motto from a poet and cut the line to fit. That’s not a contradiction, and
it’s a nice picture of the method: borrow what’s useful, say whose it was, and don’t
swear by it.) The historian Steven Shapin wrote a paper about what that meant in
practice, and the answer is more interesting than the slogan. Robert Boyle, pumping
the air out of a glass globe to see what happens to a candle or a bird, had three
problems: the machine, the report, and the witnesses. He solved the third by having
gentlemen present who’d sign their names, and the second by writing the report so
richly that a reader who wasn’t there could picture the scene and count as a witness
anyway. Shapin calls that virtual witnessing, and he notes, dryly, that the air pump
was very expensive, seventeenth-century big science. So there was a cost. It just wasn’t
a cost of declaring the fact. It was the cost of the instrument and of getting enough
people into the room. Hold on to that distinction. It’s going to turn out to be the whole
question.

3.3 A demon, and the step that pays
Now the strangest entry, and the one that gets closest. In 1867 the physicist James
Clerk Maxwell, in a letter to a friend, imagined a “very observant and neat-fingered
being” sitting at a tiny door between two halves of a box of gas, letting fast molecules
through one way and slow ones the other, so that one side heats up and the other
cools with no work done, which is supposed to be impossible. The being got called
Maxwell’s demon, and physicists have been arguing about it for a hundred and fifty
years, which should tell you something.

Szilard’s one-molecule engine, in 1929, made information part of the accounting. The
tempting move is to put the whole bill on finding out which side the molecule is on.
Bennett pulled that apart from restoring the memory for another round: measuring
onto a blank record can, in principle, be thermodynamically reversible, and resetting

                                           70
The Thiele Machine                                                          Devon Thiele


an unknown record is a different operation. That does not make a real measuring
device free to build or run. It says that learning and resetting do not carry the same
unavoidable entropy cost, and I’m about to pick a step to charge, so I need that
distinction before I do.

Bennett’s version of the rule, in a 2003 paper you can read, is that what must cost is
“the erasure of a bit or the merging of two computation paths.” Erasing, or taking two
possible situations and making them one. And in the same paper he lists copying
something onto a blank place to write as an operation that can be thermodynamically
reversible. So, in the one place in all of this where a record is priced by physics, the
unavoidable erasure charge belongs to forgetting the unknown record, rather than to
every act of making a record. Read that twice. It’s not what I expected either.

I’ll put the rest of the lineage quickly, because it all points the same way. Regulators
who make brokers keep records on media that can’t be rewritten (a rule the SEC had
for decades) are pricing the hardware, not the act. Haber and Stornetta in 1991, the
timestamping that Bitcoin’s footnotes lead back to in the opening chapter, chained
time-stamped records together with hashes so that changing an old entry breaks every
entry after it (and Ralph Merkle’s hash tree of 1979 lets one short value vouch for
a great many records); try it with five lines and a made-up sum, change line two,
and watch every number below it move. That makes a change visible. It doesn’t
make it cost. Proof-of-work, which Dwork and Naor proposed in 1992 to make junk
mail expensive and which Bitcoin later chained, is the one framing where a record
genuinely costs, and what it charges for is a search: how many tries it took to find a
lucky number. An empty block costs the same work as a full one. So the work prices
the search, not the moment anything becomes certified. Floyd and Hoare, in 1967 and
1969, attached claims to points in a program (“whenever you get here, this is true”),
and the claim is backed by a proof that’s paid for off the machine. And the certificates
of complexity theory, which go back to Stephen Cook’s 1971 work on NP, are strings
designed to be cheap to check: hand me the certificate and I can confirm the claim
quickly. Whether they’re also expensive to find is the famous open question of the
field, P versus NP, and nobody knows; what’s settled is only the cheap half. That’s the
opposite of a price on vouching: the whole design goal is that checking a claim costs
nearly nothing.

3.4 What they all agree on, and who they rule out
Lay them down, and this time what shows through is not one thing. It’s five different
jobs that the word “record” has been doing, and I’d been letting one word carry all
five. Each has a corpse next to it, and the corpses are different too.

Durability: the record can’t be silently undone. The bulla, the write-once disk, the
hash chain, Bennett’s card that has to be wiped. The corpse is the editable log, and
the company that kept its debts off the books: Enron hid its debt in side entities and
its auditor shredded the paper, and those books recorded nothing. But notice this job


                                           71
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


doesn’t need a witness at all, only a copy: a hash chain nobody signed is still hard to
change quietly, so long as somebody else holds the latest link, because a chain with no
copy anywhere can be rewritten from end to end and recomputed, and nobody would
know.

Authenticity: the record came from who it says it came from. Seals, the signature
only a key-holder can make, the consul’s stamp. The corpse is the forged charter and
DigiNotar. This job is about custody of a stamp, and it’s a different job from durability;
a perfectly authentic entry can still be erased, and a perfectly durable one can still be
a forgery.

Evidence: enough independent people stand behind the claim that lying is expensive.
Two witnesses, seven seals, Boyle’s gentlemen. It rules out anonymous assertion, and
it rules out “the universe keeps the receipt,” which I mention because people say it:
information spread into the environment is not a record anyone can read or rely on.
This one is about numbers of people and their risk, not about paper.

Accounting: the record checks itself for slips. The two columns. And here’s a thing
it’s easy to get wrong: the second column is not an outside witness. It’s you, checking
you. It catches a dropped digit; it doesn’t catch a careful liar, as you saw. It belongs on
this list as its own job, not as a cousin of the seven seals.

Cheap checking: a record whose correctness can be confirmed for much less than it
cost to make. Cook’s certificates, the signature, the hash. This one isn’t universal either,
and I thought it was. Whether checking needs to be cheaper than making depends on
who you’re worried about and how much a wrong record costs you; plenty of records
are checked by redoing the whole thing, and that’s fine when the thing is small.

Now the thing they don’t agree on, because none of them says it. Not one of these
jobs is pricing the act of certifying. Bennett prices merging and erasing, which a
certifying step might or might not be. Proof-of-work prices a search the designer
chose. Bookkeeping prices a discipline. Witnesses and seals price showing up and
guarding the stamp. I looked, with everything I had, and that’s where it ran out. If
the bill exists, nobody in this lineage wrote it down, and that’s either because it isn’t
there or because the one person who did write it down is on a shelf I never found. So
I’m going to have to try it myself, on the smallest thing I can build, and let you watch.
And I’ll have to be honest about which of the five jobs the small thing even attempts,
because it’s not going to be all of them.

3.5 The smallest thing that could carry the bill
Take a sheet of paper. Draw two boxes and label them NO and YES. That’s the reading,
a single yes-or-no question asked of the state, and I’m going to be careful about what
the question is, because after five thousand years of seals and witnesses the word
“vouch” is carrying a lot and this toy carries almost none of it. The question is only:
“has the designated flag been set.” Not “is some claim about a grouping true.” Not


                                            72
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


“did anyone check.” There is no claim in this toy, no evidence, no checker, nobody
standing behind anything. There is a flag. Whether a flag can ever be made to mean
that something was checked and can be relied on is a real question, and it’s not this
section’s; I’ll build toward it later, and until then please read YES as “the flag is up”
and nothing more. Where the state is: which box you’re in. That’s the whole state,
one bit. Then draw a line under the boxes for tally marks. The marks are not part of
the state; they’re the running total you keep beside it as you play, the way you’d keep
score beside a board game.

Now give yourself three moves. STAY: you don’t move, no mark. WORK: you don’t
move either (it’s a stand-in for every ordinary step a machine takes), no mark. VOUCH:
from NO you move to YES; from YES you stay in YES; either way you make one tally
mark, because in this toy the price belongs to the move’s name and not to where you
were standing. Play. Start in NO, make any sequence of moves you like, and stop in
YES. Count the marks. Now try to reach YES with zero marks. You can’t, and you can
see exactly why: the only move that crosses from NO to YES is VOUCH, and VOUCH
makes a mark. Now erase the mark from VOUCH’s rule and play again. YES for free,
every time. That’s the entire content of what I’m about to call a rule, and I want you
to see how little it is before I dress it up: I’ve decided that the move which crosses the
line makes a mark, and nothing else about the machine forces that. It’s a choice. The
next section is about whether I had to make it.

Why tally marks, by the way? Because they’re about the oldest receipt there is. The
real ones, the English treasury’s notched sticks split down the middle, get their own
story in Part III (Section 6), fire and all. The tally on your paper is nothing like those.
Nobody holds the other half. You keep it, beside the board, and you could rub a mark
out and nobody would ever know. Hold on to that, because by the end of this section
it’s the reason the toy does none of the five jobs a record does.

Here is the same toy, stated once, carefully, because this is the one place in the book
where I state it and everything later points back here. The thing on your paper has
five parts.

A set of states. (Here: NO and YES, and nothing else.)

A set of move names. (STAY, WORK, VOUCH.)

A step: for each state and each move name, where you land.

A cost for each move name: a whole number of marks, zero or more. (Zero, zero, one.)

A reading: for each state, yes or no.

That’s it. Add the one rule below and I’ll call it a certification system; in the checked
record the rule is a sixth field, so nothing counts as one without it. And I want to be
exact about what’s not in it. There’s no counter stored inside the state that’s forbidden
from going down; the marks are the side tally from the board game, and the tally only

                                            73
The Thiele Machine                                                               Devon Thiele


ever grows because the costs are whole numbers, zero or more. (A machine could
keep the total inside its state too; that’s an extra part, not one of the five, and Section 6
builds it.) There’s no window, no observer who sees only part of the state; that’s a
later question and it gets its own section. And the cost depends only on the move’s
name, not on where you are when you make it, which is a real simplification and I’ll
say so when it matters.

One rule, which I’ll call the toll. For every state and every move: if the reading is
NO before the move and YES after it, the move’s cost is at least one mark. That’s all.
It says nothing about any other move. It says nothing about how big a mark is in
anything you could measure. One mark is one mark; what a mark is worth, and why
the smallest charge is one and not two or a half, and whether I had any right to decide
that, come next, and I’m not sure of all of it.

And one theorem, which is the only thing the toy actually proves, and you’ve already
proved it by playing. Take any run of moves that starts in a NO state and ends in a YES
state. Then the marks it made add up to at least one. Here’s the argument in words,
and it’s short enough that you can hold the whole thing. Walk the run move by move,
reading the box at each step. It read NO at the start and YES at the end, and every
move either leaves the reading alone or flips it, so at some move it went from NO to
YES. The toll says that move cost at least one. Every other move cost zero or more.
Add them up: at least one. Notice what the argument did not need. It didn’t need
the reading to stay YES afterward; if a later move flipped it back to NO and another
flipped it to YES again, that’s two tolls, not a problem. It didn’t need the machine to
be finite. It didn’t need to know what any move does besides what the reading says
