before and after. It needed exactly one thing: the toll.

That’s the whole theorem. Here it is once more in the exact form, because from here
on the book carries two layers side by side: what I mean, in words, and what’s stated
and checked, in symbols you can hold me to. The symbols are few. N is the whole
numbers 0, 1, 2, and so on. S and I are just names for “the set of states” and “the set
of move names.” Writing step : S × I → S means “hand it a state and a move name
and it hands back a state.” A run is a list of move names, t = [i1 , . . . , in ], played from
a start s0 , one after another. The double arrow =⇒ reads “then”: the thing on its left
forces the thing on its right. And “by induction on the run,” in the proof, is the formal
name for the way you’d check it by hand: settle the empty run, then show that one
more move at the front can’t break what you’ve settled.


Definition 3.1 (Certification system). A certification system consists of a set S of states,
a set I of move names, a step function step : S × I → S, a cost cost : I → N, and a
reading cert : S → {no, yes}, subject to one rule, the toll: for every state s and move i,

                cert(s) = no and cert(step(s, i )) = yes =⇒ cost(i ) ≥ 1.



                                             74
The Thiele Machine                                                                  Devon Thiele


The run of t = [i1 , . . . , in ] from s0 ends at run(t, s0 ), the result of applying the steps
in order, and its total cost is cost(t) = cost(i1 ) + · · · + cost(in ), with the empty run
costing 0.


Defined as the record CertificationSystem (UniversalCertificationCost.v).


Theorem 3.1 (The universal floor). In any certification system, every run that starts at a
state reading no and ends at a state reading yes has total cost at least 1: if cert(s0 ) = no and
cert(run(t, s0 )) = yes, then cost(t) ≥ 1.

Proof. By induction on the run. If t is empty, the run ends where it starts, at a state
reading no, so the hypothesis “ends at yes” can’t hold and there’s nothing to prove.
Otherwise t = i :: t′ (the first move, then the rest); let s1 = step(s0 , i ). If cert(s1 ) = yes,
the first move is a crossing, the toll gives cost(i ) ≥ 1, and the rest cost at least 0, so
cost(t) ≥ 1. If cert(s1 ) = no, the rest of the run starts at no and ends at yes, so by the
induction hypothesis cost(t′ ) ≥ 1, and cost(t) = cost(i ) + cost(t′ ) ≥ 1. Nothing else
is used: not finiteness, not that the reading stays yes, not what any move does beyond
the reading before and after.

Where to check it: the record’s six fields are cs_state, cs_instr, cs_step, cs_c
ost, cs_cert, and the toll cs_cert_costs; the theorem is universal_nfi_an
y_substrate, in the same file; and the checked proof is the induction above, step
for step. These names identify the companion formalization. The argument is the
induction on this page. One honest edge: the theorem does not assume that a YES
state exists. If no state ever reads YES, the theorem is true for no runs at all, which is a
mathematician’s way of saying it’s true and useless. The toy on your paper has a YES
box, so it isn’t useless there. It would be natural to assume the system has to have at
least one NO state and one YES state; the checked statement has no such clause, and
that’s on purpose, because a theorem that holds for no runs is still a theorem and the
toy is where you supply the runs.

And one more edge, because it’s the first thing to bite when you ask a machine to
stand behind more than one thing. The definition has one reading in it. One question,
one flag, one toll on its crossing. Once the flag is up, a second claim has nowhere to
go: raising a flag that’s already up doesn’t move anything. So a second claim needs a
reading of its own, and a third claim a third: one reading per claim, each with its own
toll. Part III builds that properly, as a family of flags, one per threshold, each charged
when it goes up (Theorem 10.10), and the same theorem sends the bill for finiteness: a
record held in k bits that only ever turns bits on can take at most k + 1 different values,
so it can go up at most k times. A finite machine can keep only so many things up for
good in its whole life. That’s the opening chapter’s “you can’t keep all of it,” turned
into a count.



                                               75
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


3.6 What this does and doesn’t buy
I want to be very plain about how small this is, because the temptation is to look at the
word “theorem” and feel something has been established about the world. Nothing
has. What’s been established is that if you adopt the toll, then the flag can’t be raised
for free, in any system with those five parts that obeys it, no matter what the states
and moves are. The “if” is doing all the work. I chose the rule. A reasonable person
could ask why, and the only honest answer right now is “because that’s the thing I
wanted to be true,” which is not a reason.

Notice also what it doesn’t ask about how strong the thing is, in either direction. A
system is Turing-complete when it can imitate a Turing machine, and no stronger than
one when a Turing machine can imitate it. The theorem asks neither. Stronger than a
Turing machine, weaker, dead even: none of it reaches the floor. Bring the five parts,
charge the toll on the crossing, and you’re in scope. The floor doesn’t check what you
can compute, because it was never about what you can compute. It’s about what a
move is allowed to do for free.

Which brings up the objection a theorist makes in about four seconds, so I’ll make it
first. The toll is a floor, and a floor is easy to meet. Charge one mark for every move,
whatever it does, and the toll holds for any reading you like, since every crossing is a
move and every move costs one. So any computer with a step counter beside it, and
any yes-or-no question at all about its state, is a certification system. A clock passes.
That isn’t a loophole; it’s what the definition says, and it means the definition, on its
own, doesn’t tie the marks to certifying anything. It only says a crossing can’t be free.
(It’s also why being Thiele-complete, a base that can compute anything plus a flag
that obeys the toll, is a cheap thing to be.) Two things later in the book do the tying.
One is a ceiling: demand that a run’s total never exceed the number of times the flag
went up, and together with the floor exactly one bill survives, one mark per raise and
nothing on any other step (Section 7); a clock fails that the first time it charges a step
that raised nothing. The other is order, on the smallest machine I build: there the flag
can’t go up unless a passing check of a claim came first, then a commitment to that
same claim, and a clock can’t fake that, because it’s about which moves happened, not
how many marks they made (Theorem 14.9).

And the other side of that: nothing is in scope just for being a computation. A Turing
machine’s run isn’t an instance of this theorem because it’s a run. It becomes one when
somebody supplies all five parts for it, says which states read yes, and proves the toll
for that cost. Until then the theorem says nothing about it, and I won’t pretend it does.

That’s also where the other axis from the Flatland night ended up, once I checked it. It
isn’t a direction an ordinary computer can’t reach. Hand a Turing machine a reading,
charge the toll on its crossing, and it’s in scope like anything else. What the usual rules
leave out is the price, not the possibility.

The same goes for a system with no reading at all. If nothing in it answers “is the flag

                                            76
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


up,” then nothing in it can say, from the inside, that anything is entitled to be relied on.
Whatever entitlement it ends up with gets carried in from outside, by somebody who
signs their name to it, and nothing in the system priced it. Smuggled entitlement isn’t
entitlement, no matter whose name is on it, not for the system. Be careful which way
that cuts, though. Whoever reads the signature can be perfectly entitled on their own
account; that’s what an auditor has, and it’s honest as long as it’s called the auditor’s
and not the system’s. On the smallest machine I build later, the reason to believe its
checker says yes only when the claim is true is exactly that kind: a proof, checked
outside any record the machine keeps, and I’ll say so when I get there (Section 14).
What outside entitlement never is, is something the system itself earned.

And here’s a question I can only half answer: bolt two certification systems together,
and do you get one? Run them side by side, each move being a move of one or the
other, and add up the marks. It depends on the reading you give the pair. Take a
reading that can only go up when one of the parts’ readings goes up, like “either flag
is up” or “both are”: then any crossing of the pair is a crossing of a part, that part’s
toll charged it, and the pair obeys the toll. Take “the first flag is up and the second is
down,” and it doesn’t: that reading turns on when the second flag falls, and nothing
charges a fall. That’s an argument on this page, not a checked theorem. One product
of this kind is checked later, a host machine running a guest, read through “the host’s
own flag or its copy of the guest’s” (Theorem 14.22). Whether the class is closed under
composition or simulation in general, I don’t know. It’s open.

So why bother with the toy at all? Not because the lineage was looking for it. The
bulla was after durability, the seven seals after evidence, the consul’s stamp after
authenticity, the two columns after catching slips; none of them was trying to put a
price on the moment a flag goes up, and I shouldn’t pretend they were. The reason
is narrower. Everywhere in that lineage where somebody did locate a cost, it sat on a
step next to the flag and not on the flag: Szilard on the measurement, Bennett on the
wiping, proof-of-work on the search, Boyle on the instrument and the room. The toy
is the first thing I could build where the cost sits on the crossing itself, and it proves
that if you price that step, the floor follows everywhere, for any machine with the five
parts. That’s not an answer. It’s the question made exact enough to be wrong. And
of the five jobs a record does, the toy attempts none of them. Not even durability:
the flag can be lowered by any move you care to write, and the marks that don’t go
away are kept by you, the scorekeeper, beside the board, not by the machine. What the
toy has is a scorekeeper’s receipt for the crossing. Whether the machine can be made
to keep that receipt itself, where a step could reach in and change it, is Section 6’s
question. Authenticity, evidence, accounting, cheap checking: none of them is in here,
and I’ll say so again when it’s tempting to forget.

And here’s what I’ll owe you by the end. Whether the toll is a choice or a necessity:
the next section, and I’ll tell you now that the answer surprised me. What a mark is
worth in anything physical: later, and only partly. What an observer who sees only a


                                            77
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


window can and cannot recover, including whether they can even tell which step paid:
its own section. And whether a full-size machine, the kind you could actually run a
program on, can be made to obey the toll without cheating, and what that machine
looks like, and what it costs to vouch for structure in it: that waits for Part IV, on
purpose, and takes most of the rest of the book, and I’m still not sure I pulled it off.

For now you have a sheet of paper with two boxes, three moves, one rule you were
handed without a reason, and one theorem you proved yourself in about a minute.
Don’t let go of it. It’s the smallest version of everything that follows, and if it’s wrong
here, it’s wrong everywhere.

4 Why the toll isn’t arbitrary
I handed you a rule without a reason. The move that raises the flag makes a mark,
because I said so. If that’s all it is, this book is a long way of describing a preference,
and you should treat it the way you’d treat someone telling you their favourite colour
is a law of nature. So this section is me trying to find out whether I had to pick it.
I’ll tell you the shape of the answer up front, because I don’t want you reading forty
paragraphs to find out whether there’s a point: on a machine with a finite memory,
where the flag once raised stays up, the step that raises it has to forget something, and
forgetting is the one step Landauer’s principle puts a price on, when what’s forgotten
wasn’t already known (that last clause takes back more than it looks like, and I’ll show
you exactly how much). Three “ifs” in that sentence. Every one of them is a door you
can walk out of, and I’m going to show you each door, because the doors are where
the actual content is.

4.1 A closed room with no spare chair
Do this one with real objects, because the whole section rests on it and it’s about ninety
seconds of work. Draw a box on the table and call it the certified room. Put three
chairs inside the box and one chair outside, by the door. Four people, one per chair;
the people are the states your machine could be in, and the three inside are the ones
whose flag is already up. One move of the machine moves everybody at once: each
person stands up and goes to the chair the rule sends them to. Two rules. First: nobody
inside the room may end up outside, because the flag, once up, stays up. Second: the
person by the door must end up inside, because this move is the one that raises their
flag.

Now try to finish the move with one person in each chair.

You can’t. Three people start inside and have to stay inside, so they take the three
inside chairs between them, with nobody left out, because nobody may leave. The
person from the door has to come in. There is no fourth chair inside. Somebody shares.
Two of the machine’s possible states land on one state, and after the move you can no
longer tell, from where everyone is sitting, which of the two it was. The move forgot
something.


                                            78
The Thiele Machine                                                                Devon Thiele


That’s the whole argument, and I want to name the piece of mathematics that did
the work, because it’s old and it’s not mine. If you put more things into fewer boxes
than there are things, some box gets two. People call it the pigeonhole principle; it’s
the one from the opening chapter, where Jean Leurechon used it in 1622 to argue that
two people somewhere have the same number of hairs, and the name comes from
Dirichlet calling it the drawer principle in 1834. It’s the kind of fact a child accepts
and a mathematician spends a career finding new uses for. Here the use is: a step that
forgets nothing is a one-to-one shuffle, a one-to-one shuffle of a finite set of chairs hits
every chair, so the inside chairs are all taken by insiders, so there’s no room for the
newcomer. Finite. Permanent. Flip. Those three and nothing else, and the conclusion
is “two states became one.”

The checked version of the chairs is a theorem a few lines down, and it needs one
word first. “Injective” is the mathematician’s word for “forgets nothing”: a step is
injective when two different starts always give two different ends. The theorem says
exactly what the chairs said and takes exactly the three premises: a duplicate-free list
that names every state (finite), a reading that no step ever turns off (permanent), and
one state that reads NO before the step and YES after it (the flip). There is no price in
it anywhere. It is pure counting. I’ll come back to what counts as physics, but notice
that nothing so far has been.

Here are the words, exactly. For this whole section the setting is the five parts from
Section 3 without the toll: states S, move names I, a step, a reading, and (later) a cost.


Definition 4.1 (Finite, permanent, injective). The machine is finite when there is a list
of states with no repeats that contains every state. The reading is permanent when
no move ever turns it from yes back to no: for all s and i, cert(s) = yes implies
cert(step(s, i )) = yes. A move i is injective (forgets nothing) when different starts give
different ends: step( a, i ) = step(b, i ) implies a = b. A move that is not injective merges.


Defined as permanent and step_injective (PermanentCertification.v).


Theorem 4.1 (A permanent flip merges). On a finite machine with a permanent reading,
if cert(s) = no and cert(step(s, i )) = yes, then the move i merges.

Proof. Suppose i were injective. Let C be the list of states that read yes; it is finite
and has no repeats. By permanence, step(·, i ) sends every member of C into C. Being
injective, it sends the members of C to members of C with no two landing on the same
one, so its images are as many as C itself, and a list of that many distinct members of
C is all of C. So the yes-state step(s, i ) equals step(c, i ) for some c in C, and injectivity
gives s = c, so s reads yes. It reads no. That’s the contradiction, and it’s the chairs.

Checked as permanent_flip_is_not_injective (PermanentCertification.v).


                                              79
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


The proof there uses the standard-library fact that a duplicate-free list of n mem-
bers inside a list of n is the whole list, which is the pigeonhole in the form Leurechon
would recognise.

Is that new? As a theorem about flags, yes. The idea underneath, no, and a physicist
will recognise it on sight, so here’s where it comes from. In 1876 Josef Loschmidt
pointed out, against Ludwig Boltzmann’s account of how a gas settles down, that
the laws of mechanics run just as well backwards: reverse every molecule’s velocity
and the gas retraces its steps, so mechanics alone can’t make entropy only ever climb.
Twenty years on, in 1896, a young assistant of Max Planck’s in Berlin pushed harder.
He took Henri Poincaré’s recurrence theorem of 1890, which says a bounded mechani-
cal system comes back as close as you like to wherever it started, again and again, and
used it to argue that nothing in such a system can climb forever: give it time and it
comes back down. The assistant was Ernst Zermelo, the same Zermelo who’d patch
Frege’s floor twelve years later. Boltzmann answered the same year, not very politely,
that the times you’d have to wait for a return are so enormous that nobody would
ever see one.

Now look at the chairs again. A step that forgets nothing, on a finite set, is a reshuffle:
it moves everybody around in loops, and every loop comes back to where it started. A
flag that goes up and stays up is exactly a quantity that climbs and never comes back
down. So a reshuffle can’t carry one, which is Zermelo’s objection with the infinities
taken out. On a finite set you don’t need Poincaré’s theorem, only the loops, and you
don’t wait an enormous time, only as many steps as there are chairs. So what I can
claim here is narrower than the idea, and I’d rather say so: the merge-or-revoke split,
the exact match between “forced to be priced” and “merges,” the squeeze and entropy
forms of the bill, a built machine walking out of each door, and all of it checked. The
core move is older than the computer, and Zermelo was aiming it at the second law,
not at a flag.

4.2 Now charge for forgetting, and the toll falls out
Here’s the step I’d been circling since the kindergarten buckets. In the last section I
told you Bennett’s rule as he states it: what has to cost is erasing a bit or merging two
paths a computation could have taken. I didn’t ask you to believe it. I’m not going
to ask you now either. I’m going to write it down as a rule you can accept or refuse,
in the smallest form that does any work: any move that forgets something costs at least
one mark. Any move that is not injective has cost at least one. That’s it. Note what it
does not say. It says nothing about certifying. It says nothing about flags. It’s a price
on forgetting and only on forgetting.

Put the two together. The room says: on a finite machine with a permanent flag,
the move that raises the flag forgets something. The price says: a move that forgets
something costs at least one. So the move that raises the flag costs at least one. That
is the toll, the rule I handed you without a reason, and now it has one. The proof is


                                            80
The Thiele Machine                                                                     Devon Thiele


two lines: the first theorem says the flipping move merges, the premise says merges
are priced, done. I’ll keep saying “premise,” because that’s what it is, and because the
next section of this book is about what happened to some very smart people who put
a price where a premise goes and then treated it as a law of nature, and about half of
this one is me trying not to do that.


Premise 4.2 (Merge pricing). Every move that merges costs at least one: for all i, if i is
not injective then cost(i ) ≥ 1. (Checked name: merging_steps_priced.)


Theorem 4.2 (The toll from finiteness, permanence, and merge pricing). On a finite
machine with a permanent reading whose cost satisfies merge pricing, every move that turns
the reading from no to yes costs at least one. That is, the machine with that cost is a certification
system in the sense of Definition 3.1, and the universal floor (Theorem 3.1) applies to it.

Proof. A move that flips the reading merges, by Theorem 4.1; merge pricing charges it
at least one.

Checked as a2_from_merging_price_and_permanence; the packaging of such
a machine as a certification system is certification_system_from_merging_p
rice, and the run-level floor for it is permanent_certification_trace_floor
(PermanentCertification.v).

One more way to see the same thing, because it answers a rival I’d otherwise owe
you. The rival says: don’t price certification, price erasure, and keep an honest flag
that reports when something was erased. Fine; but a system can set its certificate at
cost zero with its erasure flag reporting nothing, exactly because the certifying move
merged two states and the flag didn’t say so (commit_without_erasure_syst
em_is_not_honest). Make the erasure flag honest, so that it reports every move
that forgets, and on a finite machine with a flag that stays up the erasure law sends
the same bill the toll does (honest_erasure_accounting_implies_a2). The toll
isn’t a rival to honest erasure accounting. It’s what honest erasure accounting says
about the certifying move.

So, is the toll arbitrary? Here’s the honest version. The toll is a consequence of three
things: a finite memory, a flag that stays up, and a charge on forgetting. If you accept
all three, you don’t get to refuse the toll; it’s forced. If you refuse any one of them,
the toll goes back to being my preference. So the question “did I have to pick it” has
turned into three smaller questions, which is what progress usually looks like: not an
answer, but a better set of things to argue about. Let me take the three doors in order,
and for each one, build the thing that walks out through it, because a premise you
can’t see the counterexample to is a premise you’re taking on faith.




                                                 81
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


4.3 Door one: keep everything, and nothing ever has to merge
Take a strip of paper that never runs out of boxes. The machine’s whole state is the
strip. Each move writes a 1 in the next empty box, and the flag is up as soon as any
box has a 1 in it. Check the three premises. Permanent: once there’s a 1, there’s always
a 1. Flip: the empty strip reads NO, and after one move it reads YES. Forgets nothing:
every move can be undone by erasing the last 1, so two different strips never become
the same strip. So here is a machine that raises a flag, keeps it up, and never merges
anything. The room argument has no grip on it, and the toll doesn’t follow. The
checked version is unbounded_history_escapes, and its state is a list of bits of
any length, which is the formal way of saying the strip has no end.

If the endless strip feels like a cheat, it’s a famous one. David Hilbert, in a lecture in
January 1924, told a story about a hotel with infinitely many rooms, every one of them
taken, where a new guest still gets a room: everybody moves from room n to room
n + 1, and room 1 comes free. That’s the chairs argument losing its grip, told as a joke
about a front desk. And here’s the part worth checking: Hilbert never published it.
The hotel became famous because George Gamow put it in a popular book in 1947,
and for a long time it wasn’t clear Hilbert had told it at all, until the historian Helge
Kragh traced it, in 2014, back to that 1924 lecture. A story everybody repeated, and it
turned out to be true, which is rarer than it should be. Bring it back to the table. In
the room, the person from the door had nowhere to sit because the chairs ran out. In
Hilbert’s hotel they never do, so everybody shifts one over and nobody has to share.
The strip machine is that hotel. It doesn’t change the argument; it shows you the
argument was about running out of chairs all along.

What walked out the door is the finiteness premise. Now cut the strip to eight boxes
and run it for real: eight boxes, nine moves. On the ninth move there’s nowhere
to write. To keep going you have to reuse a box, and the moment you reuse a box
two different histories end on the same strip, and you’re back in the room with a
shared chair. This is exactly the move Bennett made in 1973, when he showed that any
computation can be done without forgetting if you let it keep a copy of everything it
did; Landauer, back in 1961, had already written that for a program that doesn’t stop,
the space to hold every intermediate result “cannot be there.” The history escape is
real. It costs you a memory that never fills. Every machine you can buy has a memory
that fills.

One thing I have to say plainly, because the file is more careful than I’d like to be. The
theorem shows the strip machine has the other two properties and forgets nothing.
It does not contain a sentence saying “and this machine is infinite”; that’s something
you and I can see about a list of unbounded length, but no Coq statement says it. And
it contains no cost at all, so “certifies for free” is an inference I’m drawing (a move
that forgets nothing is allowed to cost zero under the price premise), not something
written in the theorem. I’d rather mark where the words outrun the file than let them
run.

                                           82
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


4.4 Door two: let the flag come back down
Take one coin. The rule is: turn it over. Heads is YES, tails is NO. Every move is
undoable (turn it over again), so nothing is forgotten. Tails goes to heads: that’s a
flip, NO to YES. And heads goes to tails: the same move takes the flag back down
somewhere else. Two states, finite as it gets, and the move that raises the flag forgets
nothing, so a schedule that charges only for forgetting is allowed to charge it nothing.
The file states the one move’s bijection and its on-then-off behaviour (revocable_
certificate_escapes); that the coin is finite and that the price may be zero are
read off the picture, not written in the theorem. The thing that walked out the door is
permanence.

Now here’s a fact that I think is sharper than the premise it replaces, and it was the
thing in this section that surprised me. Drop permanence entirely. Keep only finiteness.
Take any move that raises the flag anywhere. Then one of two things is true: the move
forgets something, or the same move lowers the flag somewhere else. There’s no
third option, and the proof below is a search: go through the finitely many YES states
looking for one this move turns to NO. Find one, and that’s the revocation; find none,
and the move is permanent at least for itself, which is all the room argument needs. So
a flag that goes up for free is a flag the same move can take back. A flag that nothing
takes back is paid for. You can’t have a free raise that stays raised, not on any finite
machine, not with any price schedule that charges for forgetting. That’s a narrower
sentence than “every certificate costs,” and I’ll take narrow and true over broad and
mine.


Theorem 4.3 (Merge or revoke). On a finite machine (no permanence assumed), if
cert(s) = no and cert(step(s, i )) = yes, then either i merges, or there is a state t with
cert(t) = yes and cert(step(t, i )) = no.

Proof. Check every yes-state on the finite list for one that i sends to no. If there is
one, that is the second alternative. If there is none, then i keeps every yes-state at
yes, which is permanence for the single move i; the argument of Theorem 4.1 uses
permanence only for the move it is about, so it applies, and i merges.

Checked as flip_merges_or_revokes, with the single-move form of the room
argument as permanent_at_flip_is_not_injective (PermanentRecordPric-
ing.v).

I’ll give you the three-card version too, because it shows the converse fails and I don’t
want you to think the picture is tidier than it is. Three cards, T0, T1, T2, with a star
on T1. The rule: T0 goes to T1, T1 goes to T2, T2 goes to T1. T0 gains the star (a
flip). T1 loses it (a revocation). T0 and T2 both land on T1 (a merge). So this move is
priced, by the forgetting rule, and yet it writes nothing permanent; it takes a star away
in the same breath. “The priced moves are exactly the permanent records” is false,


                                           83
The Thiele Machine                                                                   Devon Thiele


and the file proves it false with these three cards. What’s true is one direction: every
permanent raise is a priced move. The other direction has the three cards standing
in it. And “priced” here has an exact meaning worth one sentence: a move is forced
to be priced when every schedule that charges for forgetting charges it, and that holds
exactly when the move forgets something, with no finiteness needed at all, only a way
to tell two move names apart.


Definition 4.3 (Forced to be priced). A move i is forced to be priced when every cost
function satisfying merge pricing (Premise 4.2) charges i at least one.


Defined as forced_priced (PermanentRecordPricing.v).


Theorem 4.4 (Forced price is merging). If any two move names can be decided equal or
different, then a move is forced to be priced exactly when it merges. No finiteness is needed.

Proof. If i merges, merge pricing charges it at least one, whatever the cost function. If i
does not merge, define the cost that is 0 on i and 1 on every other move (this is where
telling move names apart is used). It satisfies merge pricing, since every merging
move is some move other than i and costs one, and it charges i nothing, so i is not
forced.

Checked as forced_priced_iff_merges (PermanentRecordPricing.v).


Corollary 4.5 (Permanent records are forced). On a finite machine, a move that never
turns the reading off and turns it on somewhere is forced to be priced. (By Theorem 4.3 it
merges; by Theorem 4.4 it is forced.) The converse fails: the three cards are forced, because they
merge, and they revoke.


Checked as forced_priced_iff_merges, permanent_record_write_is_fo
rced_priced, and the three-card counterexample forced_price_without_per
manent_record (PermanentRecordPricing.v).

4.5 Door three: forget for free
The third door is the easiest to describe and the hardest to argue about, so I’ll describe
it and then spend the rest of the section on the argument. Take two sheets of paper,
one blank and one stamped. One move: stamp whatever you’re handed. Finite, two
states. Permanent: stamped stays stamped. Flip: blank goes to stamped. Forgets: both
sheets end up as the same stamped sheet. Everything the room argument needs is
here, and the move merges. Now set the price of that move to zero. The toll fails, and
you can watch it fail: the flag went up for nothing. That’s free_merge_escapes,
and what walked out the door is the charge on forgetting. (The same file shows that
a price of one on that move satisfies all three premises, priced_reset_satisfie


                                               84
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


s_premises, so the premises can hold together; door three is about whether they
must.) Nothing in counting stops you from setting that price to zero. Only a claim
about the world does. The nearest such claim is Landauer’s, and I have to be exact
about the gap between the two: the premise as written charges every forgetting move,
whether or not you knew which state you were in, and Landauer’s own heat, as the
coin under the cup below will show, is owed only for what you didn’t know. So the
premise is Landauer’s claim taken in its worst case over what the machine might be
holding, and that’s the version the counting needs.

Here is what Landauer said, in 1961, as exactly as I can put it after reading the paper
rather than the summaries. A logical operation with no single-valued inverse (a step
that forgets, in this book’s words) must produce heat, “typically of the order of kT”
per operation, where k is Boltzmann’s constant and T is the temperature; and for the
specific case of resetting one bit whose value you don’t know, the minimum is kT
times the natural log of 2, about 0.69 kT. I want you to hear two things in that. First,
“of the order of”: he was not handing out a number to three decimals. Second, and this
surprised me, he did not measure anything. The paper is argument, with models. He
writes that he can “show, or at least very strongly suggest” the conclusion, and that
his reasoning gives “no guarantee that this minimum is in fact achievable.” That’s the
founding paper of the whole subject, and it’s a careful man saying “I think this is right
and here’s why.” I like him more for it.

Was it measured, eventually? Yes, and only recently. In 2012 a group at the École
Normale Supérieure in Lyon, Antoine Bérut and Sergio Ciliberto’s lab working with
Eric Lutz, trapped a single glass bead, two millionths of a metre across, in a double
well made of laser light, and used the two wells as the two values of a bit. Then they
erased the bit, by lowering the barrier, tilting the trap, and raising it again, many times
over, slower and slower, and measured the heat each time. The average heat came
down toward Landauer’s kT ln 2 and sat there as the erasure got slower. On average.
Single runs went under it; the bound is about the average, not any one erasure, and if
you only succeed in erasing half the time you owe nothing, which the paper’s formula
shows and which I think is the most honest line in it. Others have done it since with
different devices. So: predicted in 1961 by argument, seen in a laboratory fifty-one
years later.

And is it settled? No, and I’d be lying by omission if I left that out, because the people
who doubt it are not cranks. John Norton, a philosopher of physics, has argued since
2005 that the usual proofs of the principle quietly assume what they’re trying to prove,
and that the kinds of process they assume, combined, could be made to break the very
law the principle is supposed to guard. Charles Bennett, who did more than anyone
to build the subject, rated Earman and Norton’s 1999 form of this objection the one
of “greatest merit,” and then disagreed with it. Others replied to Norton; Norton
replied back. The Stanford Encyclopedia entry on the topic, written by a philosopher
of physics who works on exactly this, ends without a verdict. I’ve read what I could


                                            85
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


of both sides and I’m not qualified to referee them, and I’m not going to pretend
the laboratory settles a question about what the principle means in general, because
measuring one bead doesn’t do that.

So here’s what I did with it, and I think it’s the only honest thing to do. The charge
on forgetting is written into the checked work as a named premise. It’s a definition the
theorems take as an assumption, and nowhere is it proved as a general fact, because
it isn’t provable from counting; for particular machines with particular price lists it’s
checked (the stamp at cost one, above), which is a different thing. If Norton turns
out to be right, every theorem in this section still holds; they just have one premise
fewer that the world agrees to. If Landauer’s side turns out to be right, the premise is
physics. Either way, nothing in this section says a device does anything until someone
measures the device. The counting is mine to prove. The physics is a door I’ve labelled
and left open.

One question a physicist asks before any of that, and it’s a good one: the laws un-
derneath never merge anything. Classical mechanics carries each exact state forward
to exactly one next state and could carry it back again, and Liouville’s theorem adds
that a patch of states keeps its size as it moves; quantum mechanics is unitary, which
is one-to-one too. So when this section says a step merged two states, where did
the difference go? Out of the machine. The merge is in the machine’s own descrip-
tion, the states its reading is about. The machine together with everything around
it still runs one-to-one, and the distinction the machine forgot doesn’t vanish; it gets
pushed out into the surroundings, mostly as heat. The surroundings are door one’s
endless strip. That door is always open for the universe as a whole and shut for the
machine, because the machine isn’t the universe and its memory fills. Read that way,
Landauer’s premise is the claim that pushing a distinction out of a finite machine into
its surroundings costs heat, and that’s all it claims. Which also means the bill is heat
handed over, not heat wasted. Takahiro Sagawa showed in 2014 that a step that forgets
can, in principle, be run slowly enough that no entropy is produced overall: the heat
leaves the machine, the room’s entropy goes up by what the machine’s went down,
and nothing is lost that didn’t have to be. So on the premise the forgetting step can’t
be free, but it doesn’t have to be wasteful. When I call it a cost, I mean a transfer you
can’t avoid, not a loss you could have engineered away.

4.6 How much: the price grows with the squeeze
The toll says “at least one mark.” That’s a floor for raising one flag. The room argument
says more if you let it. Say there are m people already inside and k more come in
through the door in one move. (That’s a different k from the one in Landauer’s kT;
when the two meet, below, Boltzmann’s constant gets a little B hung under it, k B , so
you can tell it from a head count.) All m plus k of them end up in m chairs. That’s a
squeeze, by a factor of (m + k) over m, and if you accept a slightly stronger version
of the forgetting price, that each mark pays for at most one halving of the number
of distinguishable states, then the move costs at least the number of halvings in that

                                           86
The Thiele Machine                                                              Devon Thiele


squeeze, which is the base-two logarithm of (m + k)/m.

Back to door three’s stamp, with four sheets this time: three blank, one stamped, and
the stamp-everything move. Four states go to one. Before the move, to say which
sheet you had took two yes-or-no questions (is it one of the first two? then which of
those two?); after the move, it takes none. Two bits gone. Two halvings. So that move
costs at least two marks, and two marks is enough: a cost of exactly two satisfies the
halving rule (both facts are checked for these four sheets, quad_stamp_needs_two
and quad_stamp_cost_two_is_priced). The general statement is m + k at most
2 to the cost times m, and next to it in the file sits a logarithm form that rounds both
logarithms up and is weaker for it (three states and one newcomer round to the same
two bits on both sides, and the rounded form says nothing). The halving premise, like
the one before it, is a definition used as an assumption. The units are halvings, not
joules. To turn a halving into heat you multiply by k B T ln 2, and that multiplication is
the physics, not the counting.

That little k B deserves a short trip of its own, because it sits exactly where counting
turns into physics, and its name is a small history lesson. Ludwig Boltzmann’s grave
in Vienna has S = k log W carved on it (that k is the same k B , before anyone hung a B
under it): entropy is a constant times the logarithm of the number of ways the parts
could be arranged. The idea is his. The constant, and the equation written that way,
came from Max Planck, in his work on radiation around 1900. Planck named k after
Boltzmann, and in his Nobel lecture in 1920 he said that, as far as he knew, Boltzmann
had never introduced it himself, because Boltzmann never thought anyone would try
to measure it exactly. So the most famous constant in this corner of physics wears the
name of a man who didn’t write it down, as a gift from the man who did. Does that
change the bill? No. But look at the job the constant does in that equation. Take it
away and what’s left is the logarithm of a count, which is a number of halvings, which
is what the squeeze bound hands you. The constant is the exchange rate, and whether
the world honours that rate for a merge is the premise, not a theorem.

Exactly, with one new piece of notation: for a list D of states, write | D | for how many
it has, and imgi ( D ) for the number of different states the move i sends them to.


Premise 4.4 (Halving price). Each mark pays for at most one halving: for every move
i and every list D of states with no repeats, | D | ≤ 2cost(i) · imgi ( D ). (Checked name: c
ompression_priced. It implies merge pricing, since a merge sends two different
states to one and so needs cost(i ) ≥ 1.)


There’s a plainer way to read that premise, and it’s worth having because it says what
the premise is about. Look at one landing spot of move i and count how many states
land there; call the biggest such count the move’s worst pile-up. The premise holds
exactly when every pile-up has at most 2cost(i) states in it, which is to say the cost is



                                             87
The Thiele Machine                                                                 Devon Thiele


at least the base-two logarithm of the worst pile-up. One direction: take D to be one
whole pile, which lands on a single spot, and the premise says the pile has at most
2cost(i) members. The other: any list D splits by where its members land, each part fits
inside one pile, so | D | is at most the number of landing spots times the worst pile-up,
which is the premise. So the halving price asks a move to pay for the worst it could
ever do, whichever state it’s actually handed. That’s worst case on purpose, and it
has a home in physics. In the branch of thermodynamics that prices one run that
has to succeed every time, rather than an average over many, Philippe Faist, Frédéric
Dupuis, Jonathan Oppenheim and Renato Renner worked out in 2015 the least work
any logical process needs, and when every input might occur and no error is allowed,
their bound comes to k B T ln 2 times exactly that logarithm. Take an AND gate as the
example: three inputs land on 0, so it needs at least log2 3, about 1.6, halvings’ worth
of work (two marks, in whole numbers). The premise asks for that bound, counted in
marks instead of joules, of a device that has to work whatever it’s handed.


Theorem 4.6 (The squeeze bound). On a finite machine with a permanent reading and a
cost satisfying the halving price, let m be the number of states that read yes, and let a move i
turn k different no-states to yes. Then

                                                                            m+k
            m + k ≤ 2cost(i) · m,       equivalently      cost(i ) ≥ log2       .
                                                                             m

Proof. Put the m yes-states and the k newcomers in one list; it has m + k different
members. By permanence every yes-state lands on a yes-state, and by hypothesis
every newcomer does too, so all m + k land among the m yes-states: imgi ≤ m. The
halving price gives m + k ≤ 2cost(i) · imgi ≤ 2cost(i) · m.

The four sheets are the case m = 1, k = 3, where the bound is reached. With k = 1
the bound says cost(i ) ≥ 1, which is the toll again (a2_from_compression_price
_and_permanence). Checked as permanent_flips_compression_bound, with
the rounded-logarithm form permanent_flips_log_bound and the counting-only
cousin permanent_flips_collapse_at_least (at least k states collapse, with no
price premise at all).

4.7 The same bill, written in bits, and when it’s zero
There’s one more way to say all this, and I include it because it’s the way physicists
say it and because it hands you the one case where the bill is exactly zero, which I find
more instructive than any case where it isn’t.

Claude Shannon, in 1948, gave a number to “how much you don’t know”: if something
could be in any of n states and you have no idea which, your uncertainty is log base
two of n bits, and that’s the most it can be for n states. If you push your uncertainty
through a step that forgets nothing, it stays the same; through a step that merges
two states you might have been in, it drops. Now run the room. Before the move,


                                              88
The Thiele Machine                                                                Devon Thiele


you might be in any of the m + k states in play. After it, you’re in one of m. So
your uncertainty afterward is at most log2 of m, whatever you believed before. If you
started with no idea at all, every one of the m + k states equally likely, your uncertainty
was exactly log2 of (m + k), and the move removed at least log2 of (m + k)/m bits: the
same number as the halving count, now in Shannon’s units. Landauer’s principle, in
the form physicists write it, then says a step that removes that many bits from the state
gives off at least k B T ln 2 of heat per bit. Put the two together and the flip gives off
heat, and the exact statements below say how much and under which side conditions,
one of which (the temperature has to be taken as zero or above) is easy to skip and
shouldn’t be.

Why does Shannon’s number share a name with the physicists’ entropy at all? There’s
a story everybody tells. Shannon, the story goes, wanted to call it uncertainty, and
John von Neumann told him to call it entropy instead, for two reasons: the same
formula already lived in statistical mechanics under that name, and nobody really
knows what entropy is, so in an argument he’d always have the upper hand. It’s a
great story. It comes from Myron Tribus, who said Shannon told it to him in 1961, and
who printed it in Scientific American in 1971. Then in 1982 an interviewer, Robert Price,
asked Shannon about it, and Shannon said he didn’t think von Neumann had told him
any such thing. So it’s a legend with one witness, and the person the witness quoted
doesn’t remember saying it. What doesn’t hang on the story: the two formulas really
do have the same shape, and it still takes Landauer’s premise, a named assumption,
to turn a count of bits into heat.

Exactly, with the notation built first. A spread (probabilists say distribution) is a way
of giving each state a chance p( x ) ≥ 0, with the chances adding to 1. Its Shannon
entropy, in bits, is
                          H ( p) = − ∑ p( x ) log2 p( x ),
                                         x: p( x )>0

where the big sigma means “add up, over every state x with a chance above zero,”
and each term is a state’s chance times the bits it would take to single that state out.
That comes to log2 n when n states share the chance evenly and less when the chance
is lopsided. Pushing a spread through a move i gives the spread of where you land:
q(y) = ∑ x: step(x,i)=y p( x ). The bits the move removes are H ( p) − H (q).

Start with the half of the claim that costs nothing, Bennett’s half. A move that forgets
nothing sends each state somewhere different, so the chances just get carried to new
addresses, one for one. Nothing piles up and nothing spreads out. The uncertainty is
the same number before and after.


Theorem 4.7 (A move that forgets nothing removes no bits). Let the states be finite,
listed once each, and let f send states to states with f ( a) = f (b) only when a = b. Then for
every assignment of chances p, the pushed spread q has H (q) = H ( p).



                                               89
The Thiele Machine                                                                   Devon Thiele


Proof. An injective map on a finite list of distinct states is a reshuffle of that list: every
state is hit exactly once. So q( f ( x )) = p( x ) for every x, and the sum defining H (q) is
the sum defining H ( p) with its terms in a different order.

Checked as step_entropy_invariant_if_injective (PermanentCertificatio-
nEntropy.v). That’s why a price on removed bits can leave every reversible move free,
which is the shape the toll needs: the bill lands only where something was forgotten.


Theorem 4.8 (Entropy after a permanent flip). On a finite machine with a permanent
reading, let a move i turn k ≥ 1 different no-states yes, beside m yes-states. For any spread p
whose chance lies on those m + k states, the spread after the move has H (q) ≤ log2 m. For the
even spread on the m + k states, the move removes at least log2 mm+k bits.

Proof. After the move, all the chance sits on the m yes-states (permanence for the old
ones, the hypothesis for the new). There is at least one yes-state: the image of a state
that flips. Thus m ≥ 1. Write q1 , . . . , qr for the positive output probabilities, where
r ≤ m and their sum is 1.

For y > 0, ln y ≤ y − 1: the derivative of y − 1 − ln y is 1 − 1/y, so its minimum is 0 at
y = 1. Apply this with y = 1/(mq j ), multiply by q j , and add:

                             r               r
                 − ln m − ∑ q j ln q j ≤ ∑ (1/m − q j ) = r/m − 1 ≤ 0.
                            j =1            j =1


Dividing by ln 2 > 0 gives H (q) ≤ log2 m. The even input spread has m + k probabili-
ties each 1/(m + k ), hence H ( p) = log2 (m + k ). Subtracting the output bound gives
the claimed loss log2 ((m + k)/m).

Checked as permanent_step_entropy_ceiling and, for the even spread, perm
anent_flip_uniform_entropy_drop (PermanentCertificationEntropy.v).


Premise 4.5 (Landauer’s principle, as a premise). A step that lowers the entropy of
the machine’s state by ∆H bits, at temperature T, gives off heat Q ≥ k B T ln 2 · ∆H,
where k B is Boltzmann’s constant. (Checked name: landauer_heat, with k B T as
one variable.)


Corollary 4.9 (Heat floor of a permanent flip). Under Premise 4.5, with k B T ≥ 0, the
flip of Theorem 4.8 from the even spread gives off at least k B T ln mm+k ; with k B T > 0 that is
strictly positive.

Proof. Theorem 4.8 gives an entropy loss of at least log2 ((m + k )/m) bits. Multiply
by the nonnegative factor k B T ln 2 and use Premise 4.5. The identity ln 2 log2 x = ln x




                                                   90
The Thiele Machine                                                                 Devon Thiele


gives the displayed floor. Here m > 0 and k > 0, so (m + k )/m > 1 and its logarithm
is positive; if k B T > 0, the heat floor is strictly positive too.

Checked as permanent_step_entropy_ceiling, permanent_flip_uniform
_entropy_drop, entropy_le_log_support, permanent_flip_heat_floor,
and permanent_flip_heat_positive (PermanentCertificationEntropy.v).

How big is that? Take the case where the squeeze is two, one state flipping in beside
one that was already yes, so m = k = 1 and the floor is k B T ln 2. At room temperature,
about 300 kelvin, that’s roughly three zeptojoules: three thousandths of a billionth of
a billionth of a joule. And that’s the biggest bill a single flip gets from this corollary,
not the smallest. With k = 1 the floor is k B T ln mm+1 , and it shrinks as more states
already read yes: with a thousand of them it’s about a thousandth of k B T, some seven
hundred times less than the case of two. So one mark is not one halving. It’s one
halving exactly when the squeeze is two; for any thinner squeeze the physics asks
for less than a halving, and the toll still charges a whole mark, because marks come
in whole numbers (that’s the rounding the entropy road to the toll leans on, a little
further down). Whatever the size, it’s a bill only if you grant the premise; nothing on
this page measured anything. And even granted, it’s a bill nobody will ever see on a
meter: real logic gates spend many thousands of times more than this on every switch,
even the frugal ones. The point of the number isn’t that certifying is expensive. It’s
that, on the premise, it isn’t zero.

The even spread is the easy case, and you might worry the heat depends on picking it.
It doesn’t. Any spread that gives a real chance to every yes-state and to the state that
flips will do.


Corollary 4.10 (Positive heat for any full spread). On a finite machine with a permanent
reading, let move i turn a no-state s yes. Take any spread p that gives positive chance to s and
to every yes-state. Under Premise 4.5 with k B T > 0, the heat the move gives off is strictly
positive.

Proof. After the move, s and the yes-states all land among the yes-states, and there is
one more of them than there are yes-states, so two distinct states with positive chance
land on the same state. That merge removes a positive number of bits (Theorem 4.13
below), and a positive temperature times a positive number of bits is positive heat.

Checked as permanent_flip_full_support_entropy_drop_positive and
permanent_flip_full_support_heat_positive (PermanentCertificationEn-
tropy.v).

There’s a third road to the toll here too, and it’s the same shape as the merge road,
with bits in place of marks for forgetting.



                                              91
The Thiele Machine                                                                Devon Thiele


Definition 4.6 (Entropy-priced). On a finite machine, a cost is entropy-priced when, for
every move i and every spread p, the cost of i is at least the bits the move removes:
cost(i ) ≥ H ( p) − H (q), where q is p pushed through i.


Theorem 4.11 (The toll from entropy pricing). On a finite machine with a permanent
reading and an entropy-priced cost, every move that turns the reading from no to yes costs at
least one. So the machine with that cost is a certification system (Definition 3.1), and every
run from a no-state to a yes-state costs at least one.

Proof. Let move i turn s yes, and let m be the number of yes-states; m ≥ 1, since
step(s, i ) is one. Take the even spread on the m yes-states and s. By Theorem 4.8
with k = 1, the move removes at least log2 mm+1 > 0 bits, so the cost of i is a whole
number above a positive number, which makes it at least one. The run-level floor is
the universal floor (Theorem 3.1) applied to that system.

Checked as a2_from_entropy_price_and_permanence, with the packaging ce
rtification_system_from_entropy_price and the run-level floor entropy_
priced_trace_floor (PermanentCertificationEntropy.v).

Now the zero. Put a coin under a cup without looking. Rule: set it heads up. You
might have had tails; now you have heads; one bit of what you didn’t know is gone,
and that’s the bit the principle charges for. Now lift the cup, see heads, put the cup
back, and apply the rule again. Nothing you didn’t know changed. No bit was lost.
And the principle, applied to a state you already knew, demands nothing: the premise
holds exactly when the heat is zero or more, which is to say it sets no floor at all.
The principle charges for uncertainty removed, not for the shape of the move. This is
the generalized form of Landauer’s principle, worked out by Maroney in 2009 and
Sagawa in 2014, and Landauer himself had the seed of it in 1961: a row of bits all
known to be one can be reset with no entropy change and no heat.


Theorem 4.12 (A known state owes nothing). On a finite machine, if the spread puts all
its chance on one state s, then any move removes zero bits, and Premise 4.5 for that move holds
exactly when Q ≥ 0.

Proof. A spread on one state has entropy 0, and so does its image, which is again on
one state. So ∆H = 0 and the premise reads Q ≥ 0.

Checked as known_state_step_removes_no_entropy and known_state_fli
p_forces_no_heat (PermanentCertificationEntropy.v).

Be careful with that one, because it’s easy to overread. “A known state owes nothing”
does not mean a stamping machine run on a known-blank sheet gives off no heat.
A fixed device that merges states dissipates on known input too; Bennett calls that


                                              92
The Thiele Machine                                                                            Devon Thiele


wasteful, because entropy goes out into the room with nothing taken from the data.
What the theorem says is only that the premise sets no floor there. The floor comes
from what you didn’t know. That’s a sentence about the bill, not about the device.
And notice that the toll still charges the known-state stamp one mark, because the toll
is a rule about the move, and the move doesn’t know what the observer knows. That’s
the worst-case gap from door three showing up again, and it’s the price of having a
rule a machine can follow without asking who’s watching.

Now follow that all the way down, because it reaches further than one stamp. A
machine that runs a fixed rulebook from a start it knows is in a known state at every
step: no coin under any cup, ever. So on the premise as Maroney and Sagawa state it,
the step where such a run raises its flag owes no heat at all. Not “might owe nothing.”
Owes nothing. And spreading the start out over many inputs doesn’t rescue much.
The merge the chairs guarantee is between the state that flips and some state already
reading yes. Run the step only when it’s known that the flag is down, which is the
ordinary first raise, and the spread puts no chance on any state already reading yes,
so that particular merge removes nothing: Theorem 4.13’s strict term needs both states
to carry chance, and the heat for a full spread (Corollary 4.10) needs chance on every
yes-state, which is exactly what knowing the flag is down rules out. Whether the step
also merges states that do carry chance depends on the step, and nothing here forces
it to.

So here’s the sentence this section actually earns, and it’s smaller than the one I’d like.
A device that has to raise a flag and keep it up correctly from every state it might be in,
including states where it can’t tell whether the flag is already up, can’t do it for free, on
Landauer’s premise; that’s the design envelope, the worst case. A particular run from
a start it knows can, on the same premise. What stays forced in every case is the toll as
a rule about the move, because the rule can’t ask what the run knows. Wherever this
book says that settling something for good can’t be free if Landauer’s right, it means
the device sentence, not the run sentence.

Here’s the general case, and it’s the one that shows you where the bits go. Split
the bill state by state. Each state x you might be in carries its chance p( x ) along to
where it lands, step( x, i ), and finds whatever other chance landed there too. If nobody
else landed there, it owes nothing. If others did, it owes the difference between how
crowded its landing spot is and how much of the crowd it brought.


Theorem 4.13 (The bits removed, one term per state). On a finite machine, for any move
i and any chances p( x ) ≥ 0, with q the pushed spread,

                                     ∑
                                                                                         
              H ( p) − H (q) =                  p( x ) log2 q(step( x, i )) − log2 p( x ) .
                                  x: p( x )>0


Every term is zero or more, so a move never adds bits. If two different states x ̸= x ′ , both with



                                                     93
The Thiele Machine                                                                 Devon Thiele


positive chance, land on the same state, the sum is strictly positive.

Proof. Group the sum for H (q) by where things land: the chance q(y) at a landing spot
is the sum of the p( x ) that land there, so H (q) = − ∑ x: p(x)>0 p( x ) log2 q(step( x, i )).
Subtract from H ( p) term by term. Each term is non-negative because the landing spot
holds at least what x brought, q(step( x, i )) ≥ p( x ), and the logarithm keeps order. If
x and x ′ share a landing spot, that spot holds at least p( x ) + p( x ′ ) > p( x ), so the term
for x is strictly positive.

Checked as entropy_drop_as_point_sum, entropy_drop_nonneg, and entr
opy_drop_pos_of_support_merge (PermanentCertificationEntropy.v).

4.8 What you’re entitled to, and what you’re not
Let me total it: what have you earned the right to conclude, and what is still a door?

You’ve earned this: on any machine with finitely many states, a move that raises a
flag either forgets something or takes a flag down somewhere else. Pure counting, no
physics, no premise beyond finiteness, and the half of it where nothing comes down
is the four chairs. You’ve earned this: on a finite machine, if a flag, once up, stays up,
then raising it forgets something, and a move that raises k states collapses at least k
of them. Counting again. And you’ve earned this: if forgetting is charged for, the toll
follows, and if forgetting is charged per halving, the size of the toll follows too; each
of those derivations hands back a system with the five parts and the toll, so Section 3’s
floor applies to it as it stands. That’s the rule from Section 3, derived rather than
declared, with every premise named, for any finite machine with a flag that stays up.

Here’s what you haven’t earned, and I’d rather list it than have you assume it. You
haven’t earned that forgetting costs anything in the world; that’s Landauer, it’s mea-
sured for beads and argued over for the general case, and in the checked work it’s an
assumption with a name. And even granting it, Landauer charges a run that knows
where it is nothing at all (the lifted cup), so what the physics forces is a floor on a
device that has to work whatever it’s holding, not on any one run. You haven’t earned
that any machine you’d actually want to build is of this kind, either, and there are
two easy ways to miss. A machine that keeps its running total inside its own state, as
a number with no ceiling, has infinitely many states, so the finite premise fails for it
as a whole. And you can’t patch that by giving the total a ceiling. A total that only
climbs, held in finite memory, eventually either stops at its top, and then two different
histories leave the same top value, which is a merge, or rolls back over to zero, and
then it doesn’t only climb. So any running total a finite machine keeps for itself has
a horizon: it’s honest up to its width and not past it. And a price list that charges the
step that raises the flag, but lets some other step merge two states for nothing, raises
the flag honestly and still doesn’t charge for forgetting in general, so the merge-pricing
premise fails for it. Either one puts a machine outside these theorems as stated, though
a finite piece of it can still sit inside. Both machines I build later miss in both ways.


                                               94
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


The full-size one keeps its running total with no ceiling and lets an ordinary jump
land two states on one for nothing, and Part IV says exactly which finite piece of it is
a machine of this kind (Section 23). The smallest one (Section 14) keeps counters with
no ceiling, so it’s infinite outright, and some of its ordinary steps, counting a counter
down among them, can land two different states on one for free. So for both of them
the toll is a rule I chose; the chairs force it only on finite machines that price every
merge, and neither build is one. And you haven’t earned anything about what the flag
means. Four chairs don’t know what they’re certifying. The bill is for raising a flag
that stays up. Whether raising that flag ever amounts to standing behind a structural
fact, the “vouching” I keep promising and keep not delivering, is still the same open
question it was in Section 3, and it has moved exactly this far: if that flag stays up, it
was paid for.

One last thing, because it should nag at you. The toll is forced by the premises, but
the premises were chosen, and “permanent” in particular was chosen by me. Why
should a certificate stay up? Why not let it come down, pay nothing, and be honest
about it? That’s a fair question, and the three-card machine is the start of an answer:
a flag that comes down for free is a flag the same move takes back, and a record that
can be silently taken back is the thing the bulla and the hash chain and the write-once
disk were all built against. “Permanent” here is exactly that: the flag can’t be lowered.
The toy in Section 3 didn’t have it; the lineage in Section 3 was built around it; I chose
it. Whether that was the right job to pick out of the five is something you can argue
with me about, and I’d want you to.

And “permanent” is an idealization, which I should say before a physicist does. No
physical record lasts forever. A bit held behind an energy barrier leaks over it at some
rate, however slow, and a closed finite system comes back around, which is Zermelo’s
point from the chairs. The theorems in this section need permanence on every state,
including states the machine never visits, forever. Weaken that to “the flag stays up on
the states that actually turn up, for as long as anyone cares,” and merge-or-revoke tells
you what goes wrong: the move could take the flag down somewhere nobody ever
looks, and then it isn’t forced to merge at all. A version of the toll stated in chances
and time spans would be a different theorem, and I don’t have it.

One piece of it I can hand you, argued here on the page and not in the checked files.
Take one move and repeat it from one start, forever. The states that run passes through
are finitely many, so it falls into a loop. If the move forgot nothing on those states, it
would be a reshuffle of them, and a reshuffle brings every one of them back around,
the start included, where the flag was down. So if the flag goes up along that run
and stays up from some point on, the move merges two states the run itself visits. The
shared chair is one the machine actually sits in. For runs that mix different moves, I
don’t know; that’s open. And it doesn’t touch the known-state point above: a merge
among states the run visits still costs Landauer nothing if the run knew where it was.



                                           95
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


The next section is about a different door entirely: not whether forgetting costs, but
whether finding out does, because the demon’s whole trick was that it knew which
way the molecule was going, and I owe you a straight answer on whether knowing is
free.

5 Learning is free, committing is not
I ended the last section owing you an answer about knowing. The bill so far sits on
forgetting: a flag that stays up was paid for because raising it merged two states. But
there’s a thing that looks like the opposite of forgetting and feels like it ought to cost
more, not less. Finding out. Every time a machine rules out a possibility, it knows
more than it did. If forgetting a bit costs, does learning one cost too? There’s a strong
feeling about this, and the feeling is wrong, and the way it’s wrong is the content of
this section, so here’s the feeling first: learning is the expensive part. It’s a common
feeling, and most physicists had it too. It’s why the demon took a hundred and fifteen
years to exorcise. Or didn’t. “Exorcise” is the word the people who think it worked
like to use. John Earman and John Norton, the doubters from the last section, called
their two-part paper on it “Exorcist XIV: The Wrath of Maxwell’s Demon,” and I read
that Roman numeral as a joke about how many times the demon has been declared
gone. So hold the word loosely. I’m going to tell you the version where the exorcism
worked, because it’s the version that says where the bill goes, and the door from the
last section stays open behind it.

5.1 A small being at a small door
You met Maxwell’s demon in Section 3, in one paragraph. It gets a whole section here,
because the step it seemed to pay for and the step it actually pays for are what this
section is about.

In December 1867 James Clerk Maxwell, who had published his equations for elec-
tricity and magnetism two years before and had as good a claim as anyone to being
the most important physicist alive, wrote a letter to his friend Peter Tait describing a
problem he couldn’t get rid of. Take a box of gas at one temperature, with a wall down
the middle and a tiny door in the wall. Now imagine, he said, a “very observant and
neat-fingered being” sitting at the door, who can see individual molecules coming.
When a fast one approaches from the left, it opens the door and lets it through. When
a slow one approaches from the right, same. Otherwise it keeps the door shut. It
never pushes anything; it only opens and closes a frictionless door at the right mo-
ments. After a while the right side is hot and the left side is cold, and you’ve got a
temperature difference you could run an engine off, made out of nothing but looking.
That’s supposed to be impossible. It’s the thing the second law of thermodynamics
says can’t happen, and the second law is the law physicists are least willing to give up;
Eddington said that a theory found to contradict it has nothing for it but to collapse in
deepest humiliation, and nobody has had to test that yet.



                                           96
The Thiele Machine                                                         Devon Thiele


Maxwell put it in his textbook in 1871, and it got named Maxwell’s demon, though not
by Maxwell. William Thomson, later Lord Kelvin, called it a demon in Nature in 1874,
and Maxwell, in an undated note to Tait headed “Concerning demons,” tried to take
the name back: “Call him no more a demon but a valve.” Nobody listened, which is
probably for the best, because “Maxwell’s valve” would not have lasted a century. But
keep his correction, because it’s exactly right and it’s the whole problem: the being
does no work. It opens and shuts a door. So physicists spent the next century trying to
find where the being was cheating. I want you to feel the pull of the obvious answer,
because I felt it and so did most of them: the being has to see the molecules. Seeing
costs. Case closed. In 1929 Leo Szilard built a one-molecule version of the box and did
the arithmetic, and said the second law survives if finding out which side the molecule
is on costs at least as much entropy as the being gains. In 1951 Léon Brillouin made
it concrete: to see a molecule you have to bounce light off it, and bouncing a photon
costs at least kT ln 2, Landauer’s number before Landauer, and there was your toll
on looking. For thirty years that was the answer. Information costs because getting it
costs.

That’s a price on one way of looking, and it doesn’t show that every possible way of
making a record has to pay it. A device can burn energy without that being a law.

Szilard is worth one more minute, for a reason that has nothing to do with the demon.
Four years after the one-molecule engine, in September 1933, by his own later telling,
he was waiting at a traffic light on Southampton Row in London, having just read a
newspaper report in which Rutherford called the hope of getting power out of atoms
moonshine, and as the light changed it occurred to him that an element which gave
off two neutrons when it swallowed one could keep a reaction going by itself. That’s
the nuclear chain reaction, thought up crossing a street. It’s his memory of himself,
and Richard Rhodes’s history of the bomb is where most people meet it, so hold it
as the man’s own story and not as a timestamp. Does it change anything about the
demon? Nothing at all. It changes the picture: the same mind looked at one molecule
in 1929 and one neutron in 1933, and both times the question was what a single small
step forces downstream.

5.2 Bennett moves the bill
In 1982 Charles Bennett, who’d already shown in 1973 that computation can be done
without forgetting, took the demon apart one step at a time. The being looks at a
molecule and writes down which side it’s on. Is writing that down a merge? Picture
the being’s notepad, which starts blank. After looking, the notepad says “left” or
“right.” Two possible worlds before (molecule left, pad blank; molecule right, pad
blank). Two possible worlds after (left, “left”; right, “right”). Nothing merged. Two
in, two out, and you can read the before off the after. Copying what you see onto a
blank page forgets nothing, and a step that forgets nothing is a step Landauer doesn’t
charge for. Brillouin had priced one particular way of looking (bouncing light) and
then said all looking costs. Bennett showed a way of looking that doesn’t.

                                          97
The Thiele Machine                                                               Devon Thiele


So where is the bill? The being has one notepad and a lot of molecules. After the first
molecule the page is full. To do the next one it has to wipe the page. And wiping takes
two possible worlds (pad says “left”; pad says “right”) to one (pad blank). That’s the
merge. That’s the step with no way back. The demon pays, every cycle, not for seeing
but for making room to see again, and the amount it pays is at least what it gained,
and the second law sleeps soundly. That’s the rule from his 2003 notes I quoted in
Section 3: erasing and merging cost, and copying onto a blank place to write doesn’t.

Section 3 separated making a record from resetting it. Now you can see exactly which
step and why it was tempting, because looking feels like the active part. It’s the thing
the being does. Wiping feels like housekeeping. The housekeeping is where the money
goes. If there’s a sentence in this section I’d want you to carry out of it, that’s the one,
and I didn’t write it, Bennett did.

5.3 Two different things called “narrowing”
Here is what I had to get straight in my own head before any of this made sense, and
I’ll give it to you as a picture because that’s how I eventually got it.

Draw the machine’s possible states as a row of dots. Now draw a second row above it:
the dots that you, standing outside, still think it might be in. Those are two different
rows. The first is a fact about the machine. The second is a fact about you, about
what you’ve seen and what you’ve ruled out. Both rows can shrink. They shrink for
different reasons, and only one of them costs.

The machine’s row shrinks when two of its states land on the same state. That’s a
merge. That’s what the price charges. Under the halving rule from Section 4, a run
can’t shrink the machine’s own row by more halvings than it paid for. That’s the
theorem just below, and it’s the Section 4 squeeze bound run forward along a whole
program instead of one step. No new idea; the same chairs.

Exactly. Write ⌈log2 n⌉ for “log base two of n, rounded up,” the number of yes-or-no
questions it takes to pick one of n things. For a run t and a list D of starting states, let
imgt ( D ) be the set of states the run can end in, starting from somewhere in D, and
write |imgt ( D )| for how many there are (in Section 4 the symbol for one move already
meant the count; here I need the set and its size both). Let cost(t) be the run’s total
cost.


Theorem 5.1 (The machine’s own narrowing is priced). If the cost satisfies the halving
price (Premise 4.4), then for every run t and every list D of starting states with no repeats,

                        ⌈log2 | D |⌉ ≤ cost(t) + ⌈log2 |imgt ( D )|⌉.

Proof. By induction on the run. A single move of cost c shrinks a list with no repeats
by at most a factor 2c (that’s the halving price), which costs at most c in rounded



                                             98
The Thiele Machine                                                              Devon Thiele


logarithms; the states reachable after the rest of the run from the shrunk set are exactly
those reachable after the whole run from the original. Add the costs.

Checked as run_narrowing_priced_log (KnowledgeNarrowing.v). The run itself
is the witness; nothing else is handed in. That will matter in Section 8, and I’ll say why
at the end of this section.

Your row shrinks when you see something that some of your candidates couldn’t have
shown you. You cross those candidates off. Nothing happened to the machine. It
didn’t merge anything; it didn’t know you were watching; it would have done the
same thing with nobody in the room. The physicist Edwin Jaynes had a name for
mixing these up, and I think it’s one of the most useful names in all of science: the
mind projection fallacy, treating what you know about a thing as if it were a property
of the thing. Your list of candidates is in your head. The machine’s row is in the
machine. The halving price is about the machine’s row, and crossing a candidate off
yours doesn’t move it.

And here I have to be fair to Jaynes, because he’d argue with where I just took his
phrase. In a 1965 paper on Gibbs’s and Boltzmann’s entropies he wrote that entropy
is “an anthropomorphic concept” (a phrase he credited to Eugene Wigner): a property
not of the physical system but of the particular experiments you or I choose to do on
it. So for Jaynes the second law is about what’s known too, and the line I’d have liked
to draw, that the second law has opinions about the machine and none about you, is
exactly the line he’d refuse. Who’s right is one of the oldest fights in statistical physics,
Jaynes’s reading against Boltzmann’s, and I can’t settle it. I don’t have to. The spreads
in Section 4’s entropy theorems are spreads over the states the device might be in
when the step runs, and every theorem there holds whether you read those chances
as ignorance or as physics; “the floor comes from what you didn’t know” is the same
sentence in either reading, with “you” being whoever built the spread. What I need
from the fallacy is smaller than either side: the two rows are different rows, and only
one of them is the machine’s.

5.4 The demon on a sheet of paper
Build it, because the whole claim is four dots and two arrows and you should see it
merge or not merge with your own eyes.
