The machine has a hidden bit (think of it as the molecule’s side) and a display (the
notepad). Four states: write them as pairs, hidden then display. 00, 01, 10, 11. Two
moves.

MEASURE copies the hidden bit onto the display, by adding it in the way that a light
switch adds: if the hidden bit is 1, flip the display; if it’s 0, leave it. Draw the arrows.
00 goes to 00. 01 goes to 01. 10 goes to 11. 11 goes to 10. Look at the arrowheads:
every state has exactly one arrow landing on it. Nothing merged. MEASURE forgets
nothing.

                                             99
The Thiele Machine                                                                    Devon Thiele


WIPE sets the display to 0 whatever it held. 00 goes to 00; 01 goes to 00 as well. 10
goes to 10; 11 goes to 10 as well. Two arrows land on 00 and two on 10. That’s a
merge, twice over. Under any price that charges per halving, WIPE costs at least one.
MEASURE is allowed to cost zero.

Now be the observer. You can see the display and not the hidden bit. What you’re
shown, the display here, is what I’ll call a window: the part of the state an outside
observer gets to see. Section 7 is about windows in general; here the window is
just the display. The display starts blank, so your list of candidates is {00, 10}: two
possibilities, one bit you don’t know. The machine runs MEASURE. You look at the
display. If it shows 1, the only candidate that could have produced it is 10. If it shows
0, only 00. Your list went from two to one. You learned the hidden bit. The machine’s
price for that move: zero. Its own row of possible states went from {00, 10} to {00, 11},
still two; nothing it could have been got merged with anything else. You narrowed.
It didn’t. That’s the measuring half of Bennett’s argument on four dots, and WIPE’s
charge is the wiping half. So the demon just broke something: one bit gained, nothing
charged. Here’s the thing it broke, written out so you can see exactly where the crack
runs: for every list of starting candidates, every run, and every actual start in the list,
the index bits the observer gains (log2 of the candidates before, rounded up, minus
log2 of the candidates after) are at most what the run was charged. Four dots, and
that sentence is false.


Definition 5.1 (What an observer knows). Fix a window w from states to what can be
seen. Given a list Ω of candidate starting states, a run t, and the actual start s0 ∈ Ω,
the observer’s knowledge K (Ω, t, s0 ) is the list of candidates s ∈ Ω whose run shows
the same thing through the window at every step as the actual run does.


Defined as knowledge (KnowledgeNarrowing.v).

If that definition looks familiar, it should. It’s the standard way logicians of knowledge
set it up: what you know is whatever holds of every case you can’t tell apart from
the actual one, given everything you’ve seen (Fagin, Halpern, Moses and Vardi’s
Reasoning About Knowledge, 1995, builds a whole subject on it, runs and observations
included). And it’s the logically omniscient kind from the opening chapter, the kind
where knowing some facts means knowing everything that follows from them, for
free. I’m using it on purpose, flaw and all. This section is about learning, and learning
in that sense is exactly the thing that’s allowed to be free. Settling is the separate act
with a price, and nothing in this definition settles anything.


Theorem 5.2 (An observer can learn for free). There is a four-state machine (the demon),
a cost satisfying the halving price, a run of cost 0, and candidates with |Ω| = 2, for which
|K (Ω, t, s0 )| = 1. So the claim “for all Ω, t, s0 : ⌈log2 |Ω|⌉ − ⌈log2 |K (Ω, t, s0 )|⌉ ≤ cost(t)”
is false for that machine and that cost. In the same machine, every cost satisfying the halving


                                               100
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


price charges WIPE at least one.

Proof. The machine and run are the four dots above: MEASURE is a bijection, so cost 0
satisfies the halving price; the observer’s two candidates show different displays after
MEASURE; WIPE sends two pairs of states to one each, so the halving price needs its
cost ≥ 1.

Checked as observer_narrowing_can_be_free, demon_observer_learns,
demon_machine_spread_kept, measure_forgets_nothing, wipe_merges,
and wipe_costs_at_least_one (KnowledgeNarrowing.v).

I have to be exact about one thing the file is exact about. The halving rule is a floor. It
says merges cost at least this much; it does not say anything costs zero. So what the
theorem exhibits is one price schedule that meets the halving rule and charges MEA-
SURE nothing. A different schedule could meet the rule and still charge MEASURE;
nothing in counting forbids overcharging. The claim is “learning is not forced to cost,”
not “learning is free on every machine.” That’s weaker than the section title, and the
section title is what the strong feeling says before you check, so the title stays and this
paragraph stays next to it.

And the doubter from the last section cuts this side too, so I owe it to you, since I
leaned on him there. In 2013 John Norton argued for a no-go result: at the scale of
molecules, thermal jiggling keeps any process that’s supposed to be thermodynami-
cally reversible from ever actually finishing, and finishing it takes more entropy than
Landauer’s amount. If he’s right, Bennett’s free measurement isn’t free in practice
either, because it’s one of those processes. The theorem above survives that, because
it’s about price lists: a schedule that meets the halving rule isn’t forced to charge the
copy, whatever a real device spends. What wouldn’t survive is the physics I’ve been
hanging on it, that a real demon can look for nothing. If Norton is right, the line
between learning and committing keeps its counting and loses its physics. I can’t
referee that one either.

5.5 Who holds the pen changes the bill
Now the part that I think is the most beautiful fact in here, and the way to find it isn’t
by thinking; it’s by playing with the four dots. Run MEASURE twice. The first copies
the hidden bit onto the display. The second adds the hidden bit in again, and adding
a bit twice with a light-switch add gets you back where you were: the display is blank
again. Check the arrows: 10 to 11 to 10. The display went full and then blank, and
nothing merged, and the price was zero both times. So a display that was blank before
the first MEASURE can be put back to blank for free, by a second MEASURE. Just not
by WIPE.

What’s the difference? MEASURE consults the hidden bit when it clears the display. It
knows what’s written there, because it has access to the thing it was copied from, and


                                           101
The Thiele Machine                                                                    Devon Thiele


so it can undo the copy instead of erasing it. WIPE doesn’t look. It sets the display to 0
regardless, and “regardless” is exactly the many-to-one. Bennett has the general form
of this in the 2003 notes: erasing one of two copies that you know match is reversible,
because you’re not destroying information, you’re removing a duplicate. And it goes
further than Bennett in work that came after him: del Rio and colleagues in 2011
showed that the cost of erasing a system depends on how much the eraser already
knows about it, down to zero and in the quantum case past zero. The bill for clearing
a record is sent to whoever clears it, and it’s smaller the more they know. Try it with a
card under a cup and a sticky note: write the colour on the note, then erase the note
without lifting the cup (two possible notes become one blank: a merge) versus lift the
cup, check the note matches, and then erase (nothing unknown was destroyed). Same
blank note. Different bill.

5.6 The smallest machine that teaches for free, and the one that can’t
Two more small facts, and then the point. The demon measures what you learn by
comparing the start to the end, but an observer’s very first look already rules things
out before any step runs, so the fairer question is: after that first look, can a step teach
you more, for free? Yes, and the demon still does it. And the smallest machine that
can is three states in a ring: U goes to V, V goes to W, W goes to U, and the window
shows “true” only at W. Start with candidates {U, V}; both show false. Take one step.
From U you now see false; from V you now see true. One step told them apart, and a
ring forgets nothing, so a zero price meets the halving rule, and the file takes it.

Two states can’t do it, ever, with any arrows, and this is the one that needs no price
premise at all. If a machine has only two states and you can’t tell them apart at the
first look, then the window shows the same thing on both, and those two are all the
states there are, so the window shows the same thing everywhere, forever, and you
never learn anything. Try to draw a counterexample. You’ll draw the same two dots a
few times and give up, and the giving up is the proof. Three is the smallest number
of states on which two states that look alike at the first look can come apart at a later
look, and that’s what teaching is.


Theorem 5.3 (Three states are the minimum for free teaching). Call a machine a free
teacher when it has a cost satisfying the halving price, a list of candidates with no repeats
containing the actual start, and a run of cost 0 after which the observer knows strictly more
than after the first look, |K (Ω, t, s0 )| < |K (Ω, [ ], s0 )|. There is a free teacher with exactly
three states, and there is none with two or fewer.

Proof. Three: the ring U → V → W → U with the window true only at W, candidates
{U, V }, one step, cost 0 (a ring is a bijection, so cost 0 satisfies the halving price). Two
or fewer: two candidates that agree at the first look are, on a two-state machine, all
the states there are, so the window takes one value everywhere and no later look can
separate them. This half never uses the price at all.


                                                102
The Thiele Machine                                                              Devon Thiele


Checked as free_incremental_narrowing_with_three and no_free_incr
emental_narrowing_below_three (KnowledgeNarrowingMinimal.v), and the
demon-against-the-first-look form as demon_refutes_incremental.

5.7 What the toll prices, said at last
Now I can say, more precisely than I could two sections ago, what the mark in Section 3
is a mark for. Not for learning. What you know can be narrowed at no cost, with
nothing merged, on some machines under some honest price lists, and the demon is
one. Not for looking, not for copying, not for finding out. The mark is for the one
thing in Section 4 that couldn’t be done without merging, on a machine with finitely
many states: raising a flag that stays up. Learning is the demon writing on a blank
pad, which merges nothing. What the demon pays for is the wipe, a step with a shared
chair. The mark in Section 3 is paid for the same reason, because raising a flag that
stays up also has a shared chair, but it’s a different step: the demon machine has no
flag, and its file prices merges, not commitments. Same chair. Different room.

This is also where I settle up with Rovelli, my closest neighbour from the opening
chapter, because I put him and Bennett on opposite sides of one door, and I owe you
how much of that is mine. All of the reconciliation is mine. Rovelli’s paper doesn’t
make it, and in four places his own framing points somewhere else. He reserves
“choice” for an outcome that is stable and not predictable, and he rules out a thermostat
because it runs on a predictable mechanism; the commit in this book is a step a rule
fixes in advance, so by his own definition his result doesn’t cover it. His choice
is a branching, one possibility splitting into two, and he calls choosing in a sense
the inverse of erasing, because branching is the inverse of merging; the toll comes
from a merge, the opposite shape. His stability is for a while: he says stabilization
means something only on times that aren’t too long next to the time it takes things to
thermalize, and past that nothing stays chosen; my permanence is forever (and the last
section owned up that forever is an idealization). And he doesn’t stand beside Bennett
at all: he holds that any measurement is dissipative, credits the point to Reichenbach,
and doesn’t cite Bennett. So what Rovelli and I share is a sentence, that a choice that
sticks costs something like Landauer’s bill, and not a mechanism. Push on it and his
coin hitting the ground, a fact gained from something nobody could predict, sits closer
to what this section calls learning than to committing. I still think it’s the same instinct.
That’s my reading, not his, and you now have everything you need to disagree with
it.

So “No Free Insight,” the name I gave the toll before I understood it, is narrower than
it sounds, and I’d rather tell you the narrowness than let the name do work it hasn’t
earned. Insight in the sense of finding out can be free. The insight the toll prices is
the kind you’ve committed to, written into a record the machine can’t silently revise.
Whether that narrower thing deserves the name is a fair thing to argue about; I kept
the name because it’s the question I started with, and because the narrowing is the
finding, not a retreat.

                                            103
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


It also tells you how to read a bound that’s coming. Section 8 counts what it takes to
narrow a list of candidates down to a shorter one: at least as many yes-or-no questions
as it takes to point at the survivors among their rivals, a counting fact that holds for
anything with a list in it. Turning that count into a bill, saying a run actually paid that
many marks, is a different claim, and when the book makes it, for any system with a
counter in Section 8 and on the machine I build later in Section 22, the payment goes
in as a hypothesis: a decision tree (a branching chart of yes-or-no questions, which
Section 8 builds) no deeper than the number of paid steps the run took is handed in,
along with the lists themselves. This section is the reason it has to go in that way. The
narrowing alone doesn’t force anyone to pay; the demon just showed you a narrowing
that cost nothing. So wherever narrowing gets a price in this book, the payment is a
premise, and I’ll keep calling it one.

And one more boundary. This whole section is about a machine that’s finite and
deterministic and a watcher who crosses candidates off a list. There’s no quantum
anything in it. People sometimes reach for “observation collapses the state” when they
hear “watching narrows things down,” and I want to head that off: the narrowing here
is bookkeeping in the watcher’s list, the machine never notices, and the result would
be the same if the watcher were a filing cabinet. In 2010 a group in Tokyo (Toyabe,
Sagawa, Ueda, Muneyuki and Sano) did run a real demon, a tiny particle walked up
a staircase of potential by feedback on what a camera saw, and the energy it gained
was paid for by the information the camera took, with no violation of anything. The
demon is real, it works, and it pays. Where it pays is the part that took a century.

What I still owe: everything so far says “at least one mark” and I’ve been keeping
the marks on the side of the page, a running total you tally as you go. What happens
when the machine keeps that total itself, inside its own state, where a step could in
principle reach in and change it? That’s the counter, and it’s the next thing I have to
build.



Part III

The logic

6 The counter
Everything so far has kept the marks on the side of the page. You played the toy, you
made a tally as you went, and the tally lived in your hand and not in the machine.
That’s fine for a toy. For anything that’s going to run on its own, with nobody tallying,
the total has to live somewhere the machine can reach, which means the machine can,
in principle, reach it. So this section is about what a counter has to be before you’re
allowed to call it a receipt. Not the counter of some particular machine: the counter of


                                           104
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


any machine whose state carries a running total that every step bumps by whatever
a price list says that step costs. Section 3’s five parts don’t need one (there the total
was a sum you did on the side), so this is one piece added to the five, and the facts
below are about anything that has it. I’ll give you the answer first, because it’s short,
and then spend the section on why each word is there: a receipt is a total that lives in
the state, that only climbs, that equals the sum of what was charged, and that nothing
else could have been.

6.1 A stick, split down the middle
The oldest receipt I could find that you can still hold is a piece of wood. From about
1100, under Henry the First, until 1826, the English treasury recorded what it was
owed on tally sticks: a strip of hazel, notched across with cuts of set widths (a thumb’s
width for a hundred pounds, a swollen barleycorn for a pound, a bare cut for a penny),
then split lengthwise so that each half carried the same notches. The payer kept
one half, called the stock, which is one story for where the word stockholder comes
from. The treasury kept the other. When the time came to settle, you laid the two
halves together, and only the two original halves fit, because wood splits along a grain
nobody can copy. Add a notch to your half and the other half shows a gap where
the partner should be. Try to remove a notch and you find that wood can’t be uncut.
When they finally stopped using them, the clerks burned centuries of old tallies in the
furnaces under the House of Lords, overheated the flue, and burned down the Palace
of Westminster, which I mention because it’s the best fact I picked up for this book
and because it tells you how many of them there were.

Do it: notch a strip of card once for every coin you hand a friend, split it, keep half
each. Try to cheat, either direction. The three things you’ll find are the three things I
want. The total is the notches, added up, and nothing else (I’ll call that conservation).
You can add a notch but you can’t take one away (it only climbs). And two halves
that were notched together must agree; a half that disagrees is a forgery, and the wood
says which one (there is only one honest count). The treasury didn’t have the words.
They had the stick.

6.2 Why it has to climb
Start with the second property, because it’s the one that does the most work and the
one people fight hardest. Why can’t the counter ever go down?

Because of what the toll is for. The floor it buys, back in Section 3, says a run from
NO to YES costs at least one. That sentence is a floor: it says the run paid at least this
much. If the counter could come back down, a run could pay the toll, get its flag, and
then take the payment back, and the floor would be a floor on nothing; “this run cost
at least one” would be true of a run that ended having cost nothing. So a counter
that can fall is an accountant you can lean on to revise the books, and a floor stated in
terms of it isn’t a floor. The counter only climbing is not a flourish. It’s what makes
“at least” mean something. (In Section 3’s abstract theorem the total is a sum of whole


                                           105
The Thiele Machine                                                              Devon Thiele


numbers and climbing comes for free; this paragraph is about why a total stored in the
state, where a step could in principle write it, has to be designed so that no step ever
lowers it.)

The same rule turns up in two places that have nothing to do with each other, pointing
in opposite directions, and that’s a big part of why I trust it. In 1978 Leslie Lamport
asked how a set of computers that pass each other messages, with no shared clock,
could ever agree on what happened before what. His answer is a counter per machine
with two rules: add one before you do anything, and when a message arrives carrying
the sender’s count, jump your own counter above it (never below your own). Those
counters, he showed, respect cause and effect: if this caused that, this has the smaller
number. And they do it “with no actual timing mechanism,” his words; they’re not
clocks at all. Try it with three people passing notes and you’ll see it work in two
minutes, and then let one of them reset their counter to zero after reading a note, and
watch a reply come out numbered before the note it replies to. A counter that goes
down can’t be leaned on for order.

Where did Lamport get it? In the notes he keeps on his own papers, he says the
timestamps came from an earlier note by Paul Johnson and Bob Thomas on keeping
copies of a database in step, whose algorithm wasn’t quite right: it let things happen
in an order that broke cause and effect. What let him see the fix, he says, was special
relativity, which teaches that there’s no one order of events everybody agrees on, only
the order of what could have caused what. And he passes on a line from Jim Gray, the
same Gray as the commit at the start of the book: Gray had heard two opinions of the
paper, that it was trivial and that it was brilliant. Lamport’s answer is that he can’t
argue with the first and isn’t inclined to argue with the second. And what’s under the
relativity? His account stops there, so the chase does too. What it changes is only the
picture, and the picture is a good one: a number that’s allowed to climb and never to
fall is enough to write “this came after that” with no clock anywhere.

Now the other direction. In 1949 Alan Turing, and in 1967 Robert Floyd, each asked
how you prove a program stops. The answer, both times: find a quantity that goes
down on every step and can’t go down forever (a whole number that can’t go below
zero, say). If every step lowers it and it can’t fall forever, the steps can’t go on forever.
Up-only gives you order. Down-only gives you stopping. They’re not the same rule
(one needs the jump-above-the-message step, the other needs a floor it can’t fall below),
but they’re the same shape seen from the two ends: a one-way quantity is something
you can build on, and a two-way quantity is a number that happens to be written
down somewhere.

And the real-world case where a counter was allowed to go down, and got gamed
exactly there: Ethereum, one of the largest blockchains, charges “gas” for every step
of a program, and for years it refunded gas when a program freed up storage. Someone
noticed you could fill storage when gas was cheap, hold it, and cash the refunds when


                                            106
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


gas was dear, and a token was built to do exactly that, and the real work in a block
could reach nearly twice the block’s stated limit. In 2021 a change called EIP-3529
cut the refunds sharply (none for self-destruct, a smaller one for clearing storage, and
a cap of one fifth of the gas used). The written reasons are the gas token and those
overfull blocks. I read both as the same lesson: a counter that goes down was being
leaned on at the place where it went down. Ethereum comes back in Section 12 as one
of five small models of systems people actually run, and it’s the only one of the five
that prices a write at all, and it’s instructive that the part they had to fix was the part
that could fall.

6.3 Conservation: the total is the charges and nothing else
The first property sounds too obvious to state. The counter after a step is the counter
before plus what that step was charged. Add up a whole run and the middle values
cancel out, the way a sum of differences collapses to last minus first, and the total is
the sum of the per-step charges. Why state it?

Because it’s the property that fails quietly. Say a machine charges one for raising a
flag, and also, somewhere in its error handling, forgets to add the charge when the
step fails halfway through. Or charges two in one code path and one in another for
the same move. Or has one step that writes the counter directly. Then the counter is
mostly the sum of the charges, and “mostly” is the whole gap between a receipt and
a note that says “trust me, about this much.” Conservation is the sentence that there
is no “mostly”: every step, every outcome, every error, adds exactly its charge, and
a step that fails is charged the same as one that succeeds, because the charge is on
the attempt. For a machine built the way I’m describing, that sentence is the rule the
counter is updated by, so it can’t fail by definition. What can fail is the claim that a
real machine is built that way, and checking that means going through every move it
has, the failure branches included, one at a time, which is dull and is the whole job.
The run-long form, counter at the end equals counter at the start plus the sum of the
charges, then follows from the one-step rule by the cancelling sum; it’s below. It’s the
kind of theorem that looks boring and is the one you’d most want if you were going
to rely on the number. One thing it doesn’t say: that every mark bought something.
The ledger is exact about what was spent, not about what the spending was worth;
whether a mark bought a real narrowing is Section 8’s question, and it needs a witness
on top of the ledger entry.

6.4 Only one honest count
Here’s the property that surprised me by being provable at all. Suppose you fixed
the schedule: this move costs one, that move costs zero, and so on, for every move.
And suppose someone else keeps their own books: their own function from states to
totals, which starts at zero and, on every step, goes up by exactly what the schedule
says. Could their books disagree with the machine’s counter, somewhere, on some
state you can actually get to?



                                           107
The Thiele Machine                                                                 Devon Thiele


No. And the proof is the tally stick. Both totals start at zero. On every step both
go up by the same amount. So on every state you can reach by steps from the start,
they’re equal. That’s it; it’s an induction, the one-step-at-a-time argument from Sec-
tion 3’s floor. The mathematician’s word for this is initiality: the counter is the one
bookkeeping that all the others, if they’re honest about the schedule, turn out to be.
Given the schedule, the count is forced. Two things about that sentence I had to be
careful with, and they’re worth saying before the symbols. It doesn’t assume the other
books climb: climbing follows from the schedule, since the schedule never charges a
negative amount, so “only one honest count” and “it only climbs” aren’t two separate
demands on the other bookkeeper. And it holds on reachable states only. A state you
can’t get to from the start is one where it says nothing about whether the other books
agree, which is the right thing for a receipt to say.

Here are the properties exactly. First the piece being added to Section 3’s five, a counter
and a price list, and then the two facts about it. The counter gets the Greek letter µ
(mu), which is what the checked work calls it.


Definition 6.1 (A counter kept by a price list). A counter machine has a set of states,
a set of moves, a step function apply that takes a state and a move, a start state sinit ,
a schedule c giving each move a cost in N, and a counter µ from states to N, such
that µ(sinit ) = 0 and µ(apply(s, i )) = µ(s) + c(i ) for every state s and move i, with no
exceptions. A run of a list t of moves from s applies them in order, and c(t) is the sum
of their costs. A state is reachable when it is the start or is apply(s, i ) for a reachable s
and some i.


Theorem 6.1 (Conservation). In a counter machine, for every state s and every list t, µ at
the end of the run of t from s equals µ(s) + c(t). In particular µ never decreases along a run.

Proof. Induction on t. For the empty list both sides are µ(s). For a list i followed by
t′ , the one-step rule gives µ(apply(s, i )) = µ(s) + c(i ), and the induction hypothesis
from apply(s, i ) adds c(t′ ). Since every c(i ) ≥ 0, the counter never falls.


Theorem 6.2 (Only one honest count). In a counter machine, let B (for “books”) be any
function from states to N with B(sinit ) = 0 and B(apply(s, i )) = B(s) + c(i ) for all s and i.
Then B(s) = µ(s) for every reachable state s.

Proof. By induction on why s is reachable. At the start both are 0. If s = apply(s′ , i )
with B(s′ ) = µ(s′ ), then B(s) = B(s′ ) + c(i ) = µ(s′ ) + c(i ) = µ(s), the last step by the
counter’s rule.

Those two proofs are the whole of it, and they’re about any counter machine. There’s
no Coq statement of them over arbitrary states, so here they’re argued, on the page,
where you can check every line. The checked statements are about the machine I build

                                              108
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


later, which is one of these: Section 16 goes through every move it has and checks the
one-step rule on every branch, and Section 23 gives the run form and the uniqueness
under their checked names.

I want to flag what initiality does not do, because the word sounds grander than the
fact. It doesn’t pick the prices. The schedule is an input: somebody decided that
raising the flag costs one and adding two numbers costs zero, and nothing here says
that decision was right (Section 4 is where I argued the floor isn’t arbitrary; the rest
of a schedule has to be defended by whoever writes it). It doesn’t turn marks into
anything physical. And it isn’t the category theorist’s “initial object,” though the word
is borrowed for a related reason.

There is a universal property nearby, and I’ll say exactly how far it reaches so the
borrowed word doesn’t reach further. Take any other machine that understands the
same moves (call it the target), and pick a state of it to start from. Walking a list of
moves through it, one at a time, is the one and only way to send lists to its states that
starts where you said and keeps in step as the list grows by one. Programmers call
that walk down a list, one item at a time, a fold, and I’ll borrow the word. That’s an
induction on the list from its end, the same shape as the proof just above, and it never
looks at the other machine’s reading or its prices, which tells you how much the toll is
doing here: nothing. It’s a fact about lists of moves, not about states.

Coming down from lists to the states of the machine running them is where it gets
interesting, and where the borrowed word stops. Two different lists can leave a
machine in the same state. If they leave the target in two different states, there’s no
single place to send that state. That’s the whole obstruction, and it’s exact: the map
from states exists on the reachable ones precisely when equal states always come
from lists that agree on the other side (and the readings agree). Call that the descent
condition, because it’s what lets the fold come down from lists to states. A toll plus a
reading that agrees doesn’t force it to happen. A machine that keeps its whole history
as its state obeys any toll you like and still never comes down. So the fold is unique on
lists, and that’s what the word “initial” earns. It doesn’t make anybody’s states initial
among everything that obeys the toll, and I won’t say it does. The checked statements
(the fold, the descent condition, and three example targets that show where its edges
are) are written for the machine I build later, so they’re Section 23’s.

6.5 The toll is an old trick with a new name
Now a thing that sounds like a let-down and isn’t. It would be nice to have a new
kind of cost argument. This isn’t one. The toll is a case of a technique that algorithm
people have used since 1985 and that physicists had, in a different costume, in 1892,
and I’d rather tell you it’s old than let you think I invented it.

The trick is called the potential method, and here’s the whole of it. Give every state
a number, call it the potential, that measures how much “owing” is stored up in that
state. Then look at each step and ask: does the cost of the step, plus the change in

                                          109
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


potential it causes, ever come out negative? If it never does, you’ve got a bound: any
run costs at least the amount the potential dropped from start to finish, because the
drop had to be paid for by the steps along the way. Robert Tarjan and Daniel Sleator
used it in 1985, going the other way (potential as prepaid credit, to bound a run from
above), to analyse data structures that are occasionally expensive and usually cheap;
and the decreasing-function idea underneath it is the one Aleksandr Lyapunov used in
1892 to prove that a system settles down. Do the coin version: a stack of coins, PUSH
adds one and costs one, POP-ALL removes them all and costs as many as it removed,
potential equals the number of coins. PUSH costs one plus one potential; POP-ALL of
k coins costs k and drops the potential by k, net zero. So any sequence from an empty
stack costs at most twice the number of pushes, however many expensive pops are in
it. That’s the method. Three lines.

Push on that 1892 for a second, because a date like that hides a lot. Lyapunov wrote the
idea up as his doctoral thesis, in Russian. A French translation came out in 1907. The
English one came out in 1992, a hundred years after the original, and it was translated
from the French: a translation of a translation. So for most of the twentieth century
a reader with only English met the idea secondhand or not at all. Did the algorithm
people of 1985 get it from him? I can’t tell you, and nothing here needs them to have.
Whether anybody walked from one to the other on purpose is a question I’d like
answered. What it changes is the picture: the same idea, a number that only goes one
way along a run, turned up in a thesis about whether a moving system settles down
and in a paper about data structures, close to a century apart.

Now point it at the flag. Potential: one if the flag is down, zero if it’s up. A step from
down to up drops the potential by one, so for the step’s cost plus potential change
to be non-negative, the step has to cost at least one. That’s the toll, exactly, and the
two are the same statement: the toll holds for a machine if and only if every step
has non-negative amortized cost under the flag potential (“amortized cost” is just
that sum, the step’s cost plus the change in potential). Then the universal floor from
Section 3, “any run from NO to YES paid at least one,” is just the potential method’s
standard conclusion, the drop in potential from one to zero, and every system with
the five parts that obeys the toll is an instance (the checked record carries the toll
as a field, so that’s every certification system). Two more facts fall out of the same
picture. Under the toll, a run raises the flag at most as many times as its total cost; each
raise uses up a unit and a unit isn’t used twice. And if you demand the upper-bound
version too, that the potential before a step covers its cost plus the potential after, then
the two together hold exactly when raising the flag costs exactly one, everything else
costs zero, and the flag never comes down; that’s the sharpest version of the schedule,
and notice that Section 3’s toy doesn’t meet it: the toy’s VOUCH move, played from
YES, makes a mark although it raises nothing, which the floor allows and the exact
version forbids. (These two theorems let the price depend on the state as well as the
move’s name, which is wider than Section 3’s per-name cost; a per-name cost is a



                                            110
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


special case.) Two older tools sit beside these, named for completeness: running a list
of moves in a “writer” that accumulates a number returns the final state and the run’s
cost (run_writer_is_run_and_cost), and a per-move schedule is a “grade” fixed
before the run (run_graded_is_run); neither embeds those frameworks’ full type
systems, and the files say so. The writer is the move Danner and Licata make in their
cost semantics, a translation that carries a cost alongside a program’s result (Danner,
Licata and Ramyaa, ICFP 2015; Danner and Licata, Journal of Functional Programming,
2022). The grade is Katsumata’s: a computation carries its resource as a grade, and the
grades compose as the computations do (“Parametric effect monads and semantics
of effect systems,” POPL 2014). Orchard, Liepelt and Eades put grades into the types
of a working language (“Quantitative program reasoning with graded modal types,”
ICFP 2019). Read against them, the counter is a grade carried in the state by the step
rule, not in a type. And what does that difference even mean? A cost that lives in a
type gets checked before the program runs, by whoever checks the types; a cost that
lives in the state gets written during the run, by the step itself. Same number, different
moment of truth. Whether mine is an embedding of their frameworks or something
weaker is a question this book leaves open, and I’d love for someone who knows those
frameworks better than I do to settle it.

There’s one more neighbour, closer than any of those, and I’d rather name it than wait
for somebody to name it at me. A number the step keeps up to date and nothing
else ever reads is what program-proof people call an auxiliary variable, or ghost state.
Susan Owicki and David Gries added auxiliary variables to parallel programs in 1976,
because some true facts about such a program can’t be proved without one, under
the rule that an auxiliary variable never steers the program. Jean-Christophe Filliâtre,
Léon Gondelman and Andrei Paskevich, in 2014, worked out when ghost code can
be erased without changing what the program computes. By that test this section’s
counter is ghost whenever no step consults it, and Section 10’s honest extensions are
built exactly that way: the base moves the same whatever the ledger and the record say.
So what does putting it in the step buy, if the number is ghost anyway? Two things,
as far as I can see. The number is there while the machine runs, where a window can
show it (Section 7), and not only inside a proof somebody wrote afterwards. And the
rule that keeps it is one rule for every run of every program, not an annotation on the
one program somebody happened to prove. Whether a record stays ghost depends
on what else the step does with it; the machines in Part IV have parts that aren’t ghost,
and that’s where I’ll say which. One last relative, from the graph side: Section 3’s floor
is a cheapest-path bound in a system with weights on its moves. Every path from the
no-states to the yes-states crosses the line between them, and every edge across that
line weighs at least one. Weighted automata go back to Marcel-Paul Schützenberger
in 1961, and priced timed automata, which add clocks, were set out in 2001. The floor
is about the smallest case of what they compute.

Exactly, for any certification system with states S, moves I, step, per-name cost, and



                                           111
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


reading:


Definition 6.2 (Potential, amortized cost). A potential is a function Φ : S → N. A step
has non-negative amortized cost under Φ when cost(i ) + Φ(step(s, i )) ≥ Φ(s). The flag
potential is Φcert (s) = 1 if cert(s) = no and 0 if it reads yes.


Defined as amortized_nonneg and cert_potential (CostSemanticsCompari-
son.v).


Theorem 6.3 (The toll is the potential method). (1) The toll holds exactly when every step
has non-negative amortized cost under Φcert . (2) For any Φ with non-negative amortized cost
and any run t from s, cost(t) + Φ(run(t, s)) ≥ Φ(s). (3) Hence, under the toll, a run from a
no-state to a yes-state costs at least 1 − 0 = 1.

Proof. (1) Check the four combinations of the reading before and after: only no-to-yes
has Φcert dropping, by one, so the inequality there is exactly cost(i ) ≥ 1; in the other
three it holds for any cost. (2) Induction on the run, adding the per-step inequalities
so that the middle potentials cancel. (3) Apply (2) with Φcert , which is 1 at the start
and 0 at the end.

Checked as a2_iff_nonnegative_amortized_cost, potential_telescopi
ng, nfi_by_potential, and certification_system_is_potential_metho
d (CostSemanticsComparison.v), with the state-dependent-cost results flips_le_c
ost and a2_and_aara_iff_exact (CostFrameworks.v).

So what’s new, if the method isn’t? Only where it’s pointed. The potential method
is a way of proving things about costs. What this book adds is a claim about which
potential, the flag, and about what happens to that claim when you can only see a
window of the state. The method is Tarjan’s. The reading is mine, and I’m about to
find out what it can and can’t survive.

6.6 What the counter is, said once
A receipt is a total that lives in the state, only climbs, equals the sum of the charges
on every path including the failures, and is the only such total for its schedule. Each
of those four, counting “lives in the state” as the one the others are about, had a
home before this book: the stick, Lamport’s clocks and Floyd’s ranking functions, the
telescoping sum, the induction. None of them is physics. None of them says what
the charges should be. What they say is that once you’ve chosen the charges, the
counter isn’t a second opinion; it’s the arithmetic. And the toll on top of it is the
potential method with the flag as potential, which is to say a trick from 1985 wearing
the question from Section 2.

Here’s one thing the counter can’t do just by existing: if you can only see part of the


                                            112
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


state, can you tell what the counter is? Can you even tell, from outside, which step
paid? The stick works because you can lay the two halves together. What if you’re only
ever shown one half, through a window, and the window doesn’t show the notches?

One piece of that has a short answer, and I’ll give it now so the next section can
start from it. A window, for now, is just the part of the state an outside observer is
shown (Section 5’s display was one, and Section 7 is about windows in general). Call a
window counter-complete when some rule, applied to what the window shows, returns
the counter on every state; flag-complete likewise for the flag. Say a window forgets the
counter when changing the counter and nothing else never changes what the window
shows, and likewise for the flag.

The short answer: a window that forgets the counter is never counter-complete, what-
ever else it shows, and a window that forgets the flag is never flag-complete. Take any
state and make two copies of it, one with the counter set to 1 and one with it set to
2, everything else held still. The window shows the same thing for both, so any rule
gives the same answer for both, and one of the two answers is wrong. The flag is the
same argument with yes and no. On the stick: a window that shows you the wood’s
colour and its length but not the notches can’t tell you what’s owed, and staring harder
at the colour won’t help. (The argument needs a state space where the counter can
be changed on its own, the rest held still; that’s what “forgets” quietly assumes. The
machine I build later is such a space, and Section 23 has its checked version, with the
machine’s own full window.)

Be careful what that doesn’t say. It says neither part can be dropped. It doesn’t say
a window showing both is the smallest window that works, because nothing here
orders windows, so there’s nothing for it to be smallest in. And it’s about reading the
counter back, not about which step paid. That second question is harder, and it’s the
next section’s.

7 Windows and shadows
I left you with the stick split in half and asked what happens if you can only ever see
one half through a window that doesn’t show the notches, and with a harder question
under that one: can you tell, from outside, which step paid? This section is about
windows. It’s a section where the mathematics is so small that I’m going to state it in
full and then spend most of the pages on what it’s not, because the smallness is the
trap: the fact is a one-liner and people keep trying to climb over it with cleverness,
and you can’t, and seeing why you can’t is the content.

7.1 A cave, and the people who got good at it
You’ve probably heard a version of this, so let me tell it carefully, because the version
that usually gets told is the wrong half. In the seventh book of the Republic, Plato has
Socrates describe prisoners chained in a cave since childhood, facing a wall, with a fire
behind them and people carrying objects along a walkway between the fire and their


                                          113
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


backs. All the prisoners have ever seen is the shadows on the wall. To them, Socrates
says, the truth would be nothing but those shadows. That’s the part people remember,
and it usually gets used to say “the real world is hidden from us,” which is a thing
Plato did believe and which is not what I need from the story.

Here’s the half that matters for this book, and it’s one line further on. The prisoners,
Socrates says, hand out honours to whoever is quickest at spotting the shadows as
they pass and best at guessing which comes next. Read that again. The prisoners
get good at it. They build a whole science of shadows, with experts and prizes, and
it works, on shadows. What they can’t do is say anything about a carried object that
leaves no mark on the wall. Not because they’re stupid. Because the information
isn’t on the wall. Skill inside a window doesn’t reach past the window, no matter
how much skill. That’s the fact. Plato dressed it as a lesson about education, and it is
one, but strip the dressing and it’s a sentence about functions, and it’s going to be the
whole section.

7.2 The shadow of a cube
Do this one tonight with a lamp. Hold a cube face-on to the light: its shadow is a
square. Now hold up a square of card the same size: same shadow. A person who
sees only the wall can’t tell you whether what’s casting the shadow has any thickness
at all. Ask them, and they’ll tell you, truthfully, that they can’t know, and if they’re
honest they’ll also tell you that no amount of staring at that square will change it.

Now turn both a quarter turn. The card’s shadow collapses to a line. The cube’s stays
a square. Now the wall-watcher knows. What changed? Not their cleverness. The
window. A second look from a different angle is a bigger window than one look, and it
was bought with a turn and a second look. Edwin Abbott told this as a novel in 1884,
Flatland: a sphere visits a world of flat shapes and the only thing the flat shapes can
see is a circle that grows and shrinks as the sphere moves through their plane; from
one slice they can’t reconstruct a sphere, and from the sequence of slices over time,
they can start to. The escape from a window is never “think harder.” It’s always “a
different window,” and a different window always costs something: a turn, a second
look, time.

Who was Edwin Abbott? Not a mathematician by trade. He was headmaster of the
City of London School for twenty-four years, a clergyman, and the author of more
than forty books, a Shakespeare grammar among them. He put Flatland out under
the name “A Square.” His full name was Edwin Abbott Abbott, two A’s, and people
like to read the pen name as a joke on that, A squared; nice if true, but take it as a
lead. Here’s the part I like best, from a sketch of his life on the geometer Thomas
Banchoff’s pages: Flatland, by far the most read thing he wrote, isn’t mentioned at
all in his obituary in the London Times or in his entry in the Dictionary of National
Biography. The official record of the man was a window too: it showed the headmaster
and the grammarian and left out the one book people still read. That changes nothing


                                          114
The Thiele Machine                                                                Devon Thiele


in the argument. It’s the argument, acted out by an obituary. (Flatland already turned
up once in this book, in Section 1.)

7.3 The whole fact, in one paragraph
Here’s the mathematics, and I promise it’s all of it. You have a set of states, the real
things. You have a window, which is a function that takes a state and gives you what
you can see of it: the shadow, the slice, the half-stick without notches. And you have a
question about the state, which is also a function: it takes a state and gives an answer.
The thing you want is a decoder: a rule that takes what you can see and gives the right
answer to the question, every time. When does one exist?

Think about two states that cast the same shadow. The decoder sees the same shadow
for both, so it gives the same answer for both. So if the question has different answers
on those two states, the decoder is wrong on at least one of them, and there’s nothing it
can do about it, because it never saw the difference. That’s the whole fact. If a decoder
exists, then the question must already give the same answer on every pair of states
that look the same through the window. Mathematicians call the set of states that cast
one particular shadow the fibre over that shadow (think of the shadow as a point on
the wall and the fibre as the bundle of all the things that could have cast it), and the
sentence is: a decoder exists only if the question is constant on every fibre. That’s the
theorem just below, and the “only if” is the direction that bites. The other direction,
“if the question is constant on fibres then a decoder exists,” is true too, but it needs you
to be handed, for every possible shadow, one actual state that casts it, so you can look
up the answer there, and the handing is not free either, since someone has to supply
a representative for every shadow. (You can always fill a gap with a default answer.
The default doesn’t recover what was really there.)

Exactly. Let S be any set of states, V any set of views, w : S → V a window, and
q : S → A a question with answers in any set A. A decoder is a function d : V → A with
d(w(s)) = q(s) for every state s. The question is constant on fibres when w(s) = w(s′ )
implies q(s) = q(s′ ).


Theorem 7.1 (Decoders need constant fibres). If a decoder exists, the question is constant
on fibres. Conversely, if the question is constant on fibres and you are handed, for every view
v, a state r (v) with w(r (v)) = v, then d(v) = q(r (v)) is a decoder.

Proof. If w(s) = w(s′ ) then q(s) = d(w(s)) = d(w(s′ )) = q(s′ ). Conversely, d(w(s)) =
q(r (w(s))), and r (w(s)) has the same view as s, so by constancy its answer is q(s).

Checked as decoding_requires_fiber_constancy and selected_represen
tatives_give_decoder (ObservationPolicy.v), for arbitrary types.

Try the smallest case, by hand, because it’ll keep coming back. A state is a pair: a
position, 0 or 1, and a hidden flag, up or down. The window shows the position only.


                                             115
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


Two moves from (0, down): one sets the position to 1 and raises the flag; the other sets
the position to 1 and leaves the flag alone. Both land on position 1. Now write down
every possible decoder from “what I see” to “is the flag up”: there are exactly four
functions from two positions to two answers. Check each against both results. None
of the four gets both right, because both results show position 1 and one has the flag
up and one doesn’t. That exhaustive check is the theorem on this example; the general
statement is the one-line argument above, and that’s what’s checked. There’s no fifth
function hiding somewhere.

7.4 People who found this on their own
The fact is so plain that it got discovered separately in every field that has to deal with
seeing part of something, and I want to lay them beside each other, because that’s the
kind of evidence I trust: not that one smart person said it, but that people who’d never
met kept walking into the same wall.

In 1956 Edward Moore, working on the small switching machines that became com-
puter hardware, asked when an experimenter who can only feed a machine inputs and
watch its outputs can tell two of its internal states apart. His answer gave a precise
meaning to “indistinguishable from outside,” and a theorem with a sting in it: even
when every pair of states can be told apart by some experiment, there are machines
where no single experiment tells you which state you started in. What you can always
do is run an experiment after which you know which state you’re in now. In 1960
Rudolf Kalman, whose filter is in the navigation of aeroplanes and phones, asked the
same question for continuous systems, called it observability, and gave a test (a matrix
rank, which you can compute) for whether watching the output over time pins down
the internal state. His unobservable states are exactly a fibre: states whose difference
never reaches the output, and, this is the part people miss, never will, however long
you watch. More samples of the same window only repeat the same fibre. Try it on a
car: if your only instrument is the speedometer, two cars driving side by side at the
same speed read the same forever, and nothing on that dial will ever tell you which
mile marker either one started at. Swap the speedometer for an odometer and you
can recover both. Same car, different window.

Where did Kalman’s filter go first, before aeroplanes and phones? Toward the Moon.
In the autumn of 1960 Kalman called an acquaintance, Stanley Schmidt, at NASA’s
Ames Research Center, and came to visit, not knowing what Schmidt’s group was
working on. The group, a branch with eight people doing the analysis, was stuck on
how a spacecraft going around the Moon and back could work out where it was from
what its crew could measure through an optical sight: a few angles to the Earth and
the Moon. That’s a window problem with a capsule in it. The state is position and
velocity, the view is a handful of angles, and the job is to keep a running best guess
at the state from a sequence of views. Kalman presented his new filtering paper to
them, and with real work (their problem wasn’t linear and his theory was) it fit, and it
went into the feasibility studies for navigating Apollo. Schmidt and Leonard McGee,

                                           116
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


telling the story in 1985, call it a fortunate sequence of events and say the solution
might have gone undiscovered but for that meeting. What it changes: it shows the
limit from the useful side. The filter didn’t make the angles show more. It made a
sequence of views, over time, pin down the state, and it can only do that when the
state is observable from those views, which is Kalman’s own condition. The odometer,
not a cleverer speedometer.

In 1977 Patrick and Radhia Cousot built a whole discipline of program analysis, called
abstract interpretation, on throwing information away on purpose: run the program
over coarse descriptions of its values instead of the values, and accept that the answer
you get has to be true of every real value the coarse description could stand for. That
last clause is fibre constancy as a design rule. And in 1970 Ted Codd, inventing the
relational database, made programs independent of how the data is stored, and the
relational systems that followed gave users views, deliberately partial windows onto
the stored data. A decade after Codd, Bancilhon and Spyratos set out the view-update
problem: if a user changes what they see through a view, which of the many underly-
ing states that cast that view should the database move to? Several are legitimate. The
fibre, from the writing side.

And Parnas, from Section 2, hid things on purpose: a module is characterised by the
design decision it hides from its callers. Hiding is a window. The caller can’t later read
back what was hidden, including the things it later wishes it could check, and that’s
the price side of the coin whose benefit side Parnas was selling. None of these people
were doing philosophy. They were trying to build filters, databases, compilers, and
modules, and the wall is the same wall in each.

7.5 The clerk with two photographs
Now point it at the counter, because that’s why this section is here. Suppose you want
to bill for raising the flag, exactly: at least one mark for every step that raises it, and
nothing for a step that doesn’t. And suppose the person doing the billing is a clerk
who sees only a window on the state, a photograph before the step and a photograph
after. The clerk’s bill is a function of the two photographs. Can the clerk bill exactly?

Not if the window has the wrong kind of blind spot. Here’s why, and it’s the cube
again. Suppose there are two steps that give the clerk the same before-photo and the
same after-photo, and one of them raised the flag and the other didn’t. (The two-move
toy above is exactly such a pair; so are “a stamp goes onto a document inside a closed
drawer” and “someone opens and closes the drawer.”) The clerk has one bill for that
pair of photographs. If the bill is at least one, it overcharges the step that didn’t raise
the flag. If it’s zero, it undercharges the step that did. Any bill that never misses a
raise bills something that wasn’t a raise, and no bill from those photographs is exact.
The fix is the plain one: put the flag in the photograph. If the window shows the
reading, then “one when the reading goes from down to up, zero otherwise” is exact,
and such a window has no pair like the one above. That’s enough. It isn’t the only


                                           117
The Thiele Machine                                                                  Devon Thiele


way: a window can hide the flag and still have no colliding pair, in which case a bill
from the photographs can be exact; what the file proves the other way is only that a
colliding pair rules exact pricing out. And “exact” here has a definition: at least one on
every step that raises the flag, nothing on any step that doesn’t. That’s all the clerk’s
problem needs, and the bill “one for a raise, zero otherwise” meets it (step_pric
e_is_exact). So it’s exact about which steps get charged. It isn’t exact about how
much, and it doesn’t pick out one bill: “two for a raise, zero otherwise” meets it too.
Pinning the bill down takes one more demand, a ceiling: over any run, the total never
exceeds the number of raises. With the floor and that ceiling there’s exactly one bill
left, one per raise and zero otherwise; that’s an if and only if, proved for any system
whose bill is decided step by step (exact_commitment_pricing_characteriza
tion, CommitmentPredicateAdequacy.v). These are stated for any states, any steps,
any window; they’re the cube theorem with a price in place of a decoder.

Same clerk, now in symbols, so you can check every word I just used. Take the five
parts of Section 3 with a window w : S → V, and say a step (s, i ) raises the flag
when cert(s) = no and cert(step(s, i )) = yes. A price is any function of a state and
a move. It meets the floor when every raise costs at least one, and never overcharges
when every non-raise costs zero; together, it is exact (about which steps are charged;
the amount is pinned only by the whole-run ceiling above). A window price is one
computed from the two photographs only: price(s, i ) = b(w(s), w(step(s, i ))) for some
bill b : V × V → N. A collision is two steps (s1 , i1 ) and (s2 , i2 ) with w(s1 ) = w(s2 ) and
w(step(s1 , i1 )) = w(step(s2 , i2 )), the first a raise and the second not.


Theorem 7.2 (No exact window price across a collision). If the window has a collision,
every window price that meets the floor charges at least one on some step that is not a raise; so
no window price is exact. If instead the reading is a function of the view, cert(s) = r (w(s))
for some r, then the window price “one when r goes from no to yes, zero otherwise” is exact,
and the window has no collision.

Proof. Across a collision both steps get the same bill b(v, v′ ). The floor makes it at least
one because the first step is a raise; the second step, not a raise, pays it. If the reading
is r of the view, the window price reads the raise directly, and two steps with the same
photographs either both raise or both don’t, so there’s no collision.

Checked as shadow_floor_overcharges, shadow_cannot_price_exactly, w
indow_showing_reading_prices_exactly, and window_showing_reading
_has_no_collision (ShadowPricing.v), for arbitrary types.

So the exact price of raising the flag lives in the step itself, or in a window that shows
the flag. A window that contains a pair like that one can’t carry it. Whether a particular
machine has such a pair, for a particular window, has to be checked machine by
machine and window by window; the theorem only tells you what a pair does once



                                              118
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


you’ve found one.

Why can’t the clerk just watch the step itself? A clerk who does, who sees the whole
state before and the move, bills exactly with no trouble at all: “one for a raise” is a
function of exactly those two things, and it’s the step price above. So the collision bites
an observer who doesn’t see the step, or who’s handed an account of the step and can’t
trust the account. That second kind is the opening chapter’s trace problem come back.
If the names of the moves arrive in a log the program wrote, the program can write
whatever names it likes, and a clerk reading that log is reading one more window, one
the program painted. Seeing the move means being underneath the program, where
the step is.

7.6 The three escapes, and what each one costs
Suppose you’re the person outside, and you want to be convinced that a run paid. The
window you’ve got doesn’t show the counter. Here’s how bad that is, in the smallest
setting I can build. Take a counter machine from Section 6, give its states a position
and a flag as well, and give it a window that shows the position and nothing else.
Now take two runs from the same start, with the position at 0, the flag down and
the counter at 0. Run A makes one move that raises the flag, costs one, and lands at
position 1; its counter reads 1. Run B makes one move that does nothing but step to
position 1, at cost zero; its counter reads 0. Call the pair of photographs, position 0
then position 1, the transcript. Both runs leave exactly that transcript. A verifier is a
rule that takes a transcript and says accept or reject. It is sound when every transcript
it accepts comes only from states where the claim holds, and complete when every
transcript from a state where the claim holds is accepted. The claim is “the counter is
1.”

No verifier on these transcripts is both, and the proof is three lines. Suppose one were
both. Run A ends with the counter at 1 and leaves the transcript, so completeness
says the verifier accepts it. Now soundness, on that same accepted transcript: every
state that leaves it satisfies the claim, and run B’s does. So run B’s counter is 1. It
is 0. That’s the cube again, with a verdict in place of an answer: a verifier sees only
what the window kept, and two states that the window can’t tell apart get one verdict
between them.

Now dress the transcript up. Take any richer kind of transcript, with a way to squash
one down to its bare photographs, and say a verifier on the rich ones only looks at the
bare part when two rich transcripts that squash to the same photographs always get
the same verdict. If some rich transcript left by run A and some rich transcript left by
run B squash to the same photographs, then no verifier that only looks at the bare part
is sound and complete either: it gives those two the same verdict, completeness makes
that verdict accept, and soundness then lies about run B. Notice what that needs. The
pair has to survive into the richer kind of transcript; a design whose extra part tells
A from B doesn’t meet the premise, and the argument says nothing about it. So it


                                           119
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


doesn’t classify every transcript design. What it says is that a verifier that only reads
what the bare window keeps fails on that pair.

What can you do? Here are three things that work, and nothing says they’re the only
ones; as far as I can tell, cryptography uses all three. Each rests on something you
have to trust, and I’ll say what, because “a price” in the counter’s sense is not what
any of them costs.

You can be shown the whole state. Then there’s nothing to decode; you read the counter
off the state. The price is trust: you have to believe the state you were shown is the
state there was.

You can be shown a commitment: the ordinary window plus one extra bit that is set
when, and only when, the claim holds (here, that the counter reads exactly one).
Reading that bit gives a verifier that is sound and complete for that claim, if the
bit is binding (set only when the claim holds) and honest (set whenever it holds).
The trust is in those two “ifs,” which are a contract about who can set the bit. The
contract can be met, and a bit anyone can set breaks it, which is the one-line version of
why an unsigned log is just another window. Nothing in that picture has a hardness
assumption in it; whether a real commitment scheme meets the contract is a question
for cryptography, not for this book. (A clash of words I should own: “commitment”
here is the cryptographers’ word, something bound to a claim, which in their schemes
also hides the claim until it’s opened, and this bit doesn’t bother hiding anything. The
opening chapter’s commit is a different act, the closing of a question. Same word, two
jobs.) In 1999 Bruce Schneier and John Kelsey worked out how to make a log that an
intruder who takes over the machine can’t quietly rewrite, and the honest scope in
their paper is the honest scope here: it protects what was written before the break-in,
through keys, and nothing after.

Or you can ask. Interaction: the outside party gets to put a question and gets an answer
that pins the thing down. The price is the honesty of the answerer; a liar’s answer
is another shadow. Moore’s experimenter chose inputs; the zero-knowledge proofs
of Goldwasser, Micali and Rackoff in 1985 are the refined form, where a verifier is
convinced by a conversation designed to cut exactly the line between true and false
and nothing else, with a mathematical guarantee against a cheating prover. I mention
zero-knowledge to say what I’m not claiming: the asking in this section is one round,
with one fixed question (“tell me your counter”), and nothing in it models a cheating
prover; the honesty is assumed, not enforced. That’s a toy of the real thing, and I’m
not going to let the real thing’s reputation stand behind the toy.

The real thing even has a cave in it, which after Plato I can’t resist. In a paper for
the 1989 CRYPTO conference called “How to Explain Zero-Knowledge Protocols to
Your Children,” Jean-Jacques Quisquater and Louis Guillou, with their families on
the byline and Tom Berson, told it as Ali Baba’s cave: a ring-shaped tunnel with a
magic door at the back that opens only for a secret word. Peggy goes in down one


                                          120
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


side while Victor waits outside; then Victor walks to the fork and shouts which side
she should come out of. If she knows the word, she always can. If she doesn’t, she
gets away with it only when Victor happens to call the side she went in. Play it at
the table with a coin for Victor’s shout: one round, a cheat gets through half the time;
twenty rounds, about one time in a million. And here’s the part that belongs in this
section. In the way the story is usually told, Victor ends up convinced, but a video of
the whole thing convinces nobody else, because a staged run, where the two agreed
beforehand which sides he’d shout, makes exactly the same recording. The recording
is a window, and the real run and the fake one cast the same shadow. That’s the cube
in the cryptographers’ favourite bedtime story, and it’s why the real thing has to ask
live, many times, against a prover who might be lying: everything my one round
leaves out.

Each escape is a window with something added: the whole state, a bound bit, an
honest answer. None of them is “a smarter verifier on the old window.” Cleverness
lives on the wrong side of the projection. What’s true of any machine is the cube. The
machine I build later has pairs like these, and checked versions of all three escapes;
they’re stated on it, so they’re Section 23’s.

Now point the three escapes back at the record this book is about, because that’s
where they bite hardest. A record kept in a machine’s state is bits too. Hand someone
outside a copy of those bits with a note saying “the flag is up,” and they’re reading
a window: the run that really raised the flag and a box built to print that it did cast
the same shadow. So putting the record in the step answers “was this earned?” for
whoever can see the state and trusts the step that wrote it. For anybody else it moves
the question, from “did it run?” to “do I trust the box that says it ran?” Crossing that
line takes one of the escapes: the whole state, from a box you already trust; a bound
bit, which in practice means a signature over the record or a quote from measured
hardware (and Section 12 shows a quote vouches only for what was measured); or
asking, against a box that might lie, which is the cryptographers’ business. One more
relative deserves its name here, verifiable computation: the box hands back its answer
with a short proof that the answer is right, which a checker can verify without redoing
the work (Bryan Parno, Jon Howell, Craig Gentry and Mariana Raykova’s Pinocchio,
2013), and proof-carrying data passes proofs like that along a whole chain of parties
who don’t trust each other (Alessandro Chiesa and Eran Tromer, 2010). That’s the
strongest export there is, and notice what it exports: the claim, not the history. The
proof shows the answer is right for that input. It doesn’t show which machine did
the work, or when, and any box with the input can make one. Nothing in this book
supplies any of these escapes. The model’s record is local to the machine that keeps it,
and the hardware later in the book reports its record with no signature on it at all.

7.7 What this isn’t
Three things people reach for, and I’d rather take them off the table now.



                                          121
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


It isn’t mysticism. Nothing here says the window is false or the state is unknowable.
The wall is a function, the objects are its inputs, and the only claim is that the function
isn’t one-to-one on the thing you asked about. A richer window recovers it. Plato’s
prisoners could have turned around.

Somebody always says Rice’s theorem at this point, so let me say it first. It isn’t Rice’s
theorem, though it rhymes with it. The logician Henry Rice, in 1953, proved that
no program can decide any interesting property of what another program does from
its code, and a cousin of the fact here is that a run which hasn’t halted yet looks, so
far, exactly like one that never will. But Rice is about what’s computable. The cube is
about what’s there. The cube theorem holds for a toy with two states and nothing to
compute; the obstruction is missing information, not missing cleverness, and I’d be
overclaiming if I let the famous theorem lend its weight to the small one.

And it isn’t “with enough data you can recover anything.” Kalman’s unobservable
states stay unobservable for all time. The question is never how much of the window
you’ve got. It’s which window.

So: the counter lives in the state, and whether anyone outside can read it depends
entirely on what they’re shown, and a window with a pair like that in it can’t price
the flag exactly, not with any rule, ever. Which raises the question I’ve been pushing
in front of me since the buckets. Fine, the flag went up and was paid for and I can see
it in the right window. What does that entitle me to? A paid flag is a paid flag. What’s
the claim behind it, and when am I allowed to lean on it?

8 Structural entitlement
I keep writing the word “vouch” and then taking it back. Let me stop doing that and
say what it would take. A reading went from NO to YES, the toll charged the move
that did it (Section 3), maybe the reading stays up (Section 4 says what it costs to make
it stay), and the right window shows it (Section 7). Now: what is a later step allowed
to do because of that? That’s a different question from “is the thing true,” and the gap
between those two is the subject of this section, and I’d argue it’s the subject of most
of the arguments people have about evidence, so give me the long way round.

8.1 The coin that moved
Here’s an experiment you can run on a friend, and I’d ask you to actually run it,
because the feeling of it is the point. Put a coin under one of three cups while they
watch. Say, cup one. Send them out of the room. Move the coin to cup three. Then,
and this is the trick, put a second coin under cup one. Bring them back and ask: “Is
there a coin under cup one?”

They say yes. They’re right; there is. And they have a reason: they watched you put
it there. True, and believed, and justified by what they saw. And it’s not knowledge,
and you can feel that it isn’t, because their reason points at a coin that left. The coin


                                           122
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


that makes them right is not the coin they’re thinking of.

That’s a three-page paper from 1963 by Edmund Gettier, “Is Justified True Belief
Knowledge?”, which broke a definition people had leaned on since Plato, in about the
time it takes to read it. The definition, which people read into Plato’s Theaetetus, was
that you know something when it’s true, you believe it, and you’ve got good reasons.
Gettier’s two cases, and the cups, show a belief that passes all three tests and still isn’t
knowledge, because the reasons and the fact aren’t connected; they just happen to
agree. Bertrand Russell had a related case in 1948: somebody looks at a stopped clock
at the one moment it happens to be right, and they’re right about the time, and they
know nothing.

Is 1963 the bottom? Not even close, and 1948 isn’t either. The Stanford Encyclopedia’s
entry on the analysis of knowledge, which is where I’d send you to check me, gives a
case from the eighth-century Buddhist philosopher Dharmottara: you’re looking for
water on a hot day, you see water ahead, it’s a mirage, and when you get there you
happen to find water under a rock. And one from Peter of Mantua, in the fourteenth
century: Plato is running right next to you, you take him for Socrates, so you believe
Socrates is running, and Socrates is in fact running, in Rome, where you can’t see him.
Older still? Maybe. This is where the trail goes cold, which isn’t the same as where
it ends. What it changes is how much I trust the shape. People in different centuries,
languages and traditions kept building the same trap by hand: a reason that points at
one thing, and a truth that happens to be sitting on another.

What’s missing is a wire from the reason to the fact. Ask your friend what they’d need,
to be entitled to “there’s a coin under cup one,” and they’ll tell you: lift the cup. Not
“remember putting it there.” Lift it, now, and look. That lifting is an event, it happens
on the record, and after it the reason and the fact are the same object.

8.2 Plato nearly had it
Who was Theaetetus, though? The dialogue is named for a real person, and that side
of it usually gets left out. He was a mathematician. In the dialogue he’s a teenager,
and he tells Socrates that his teacher Theodorus had been showing them, one case at a
time, that the side of a square of area three, or five, and so on up to seventeen, can’t be
named by any fraction: the Pythagoreans’ diagonal from Section 2, done again case
by case. The young man’s idea was to stop going one case at a time and find one
word for all of them. Euclid’s tenth book, on lengths that share no common measure,
is thought to be largely his work, and he’s credited with being the first to study the
eight-faced and twenty-faced solids, two of the four Plato built air and water from.
The dialogue opens with him being carried home to Athens from the army at Corinth,
badly wounded and sick with the dysentery going round the camp, barely alive; the
usual date is 369 BC. And the conversation itself has come down as a record. Euclid
of Megara (not the geometer) says he took notes as soon as he got home, filled them
out later, and had Socrates correct them whenever he came to Athens, and he has


                                            123
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


the result read aloud. So the dialogue about what turns a true belief into knowledge
survives as a checked record of what was said. That changes nothing in the argument.
I just like that the book about knowledge is named for the man who took the diagonal
and made it general.

I want to be fair to the Theaetetus here, because it’s easy to be quick with the ancients
and they deserve better. Socrates, in that dialogue, doesn’t just say “true belief plus
reasons.” He tries three different senses of what the “account” behind a true belief
could be: a statement you can say aloud; a list of the thing’s parts; and, third, the
mark that sets this thing apart from everything else it could be confused with. He tries
each, and each fails, and the dialogue ends with nobody knowing what knowledge
is, which is one of the more honest endings in philosophy. But the third sense is the
one I’d underline. An account as the thing that distinguishes: the test that gives the real
case a value no rival gives. He couldn’t make it work because he had no way to say
what the account had to be attached to. Two and a half thousand years later, here’s
this book’s guess: the thing it has to be attached to is a state, and the account is an
object sitting in it. I’m not claiming that settles Plato. I’m claiming he was pointing at
