the right thing, and that’s my reading of the dialogue, which you can check against it
in an afternoon.

Push on that once more, because Socrates gives his own reason for dropping the third
account, and it isn’t the one I just gave. If the account means knowing the mark that
sets the thing apart, then knowledge has been defined as true belief plus knowledge
of something, and the word you were trying to define is back inside its own definition.
A circle. Does a check get out of it? It gets the word out: a test that ran and found the
mark isn’t defined in terms of knowing. Whether the test was any good is still a real
question, and it’s the question the rest of this section puts a price on. So I’d say the
circle moves rather than vanishes. It moves somewhere you can look at it, which is
the most I’d claim.

8.3 The shape, said once
So here’s what I mean by entitlement, and it has three parts, and I’ll try to earn each.

A run is entitled to a claim when three things are present. First, an object, carried in the
state: a grouping, a relation between groups, a counter, a package of constraints. Not
a belief; a thing you could print. Second, a checked relation between that object and the
claim: a test that was actually run, with its result on hand, not “a test exists.” Third,
an event on the record that says this object was put there and paid for, so that anyone
auditing the run can point back at the moment the claim was marked.

Said as a definition, so the rest of the section has something to point at:


Definition 8.1 (Entitlement). A run is entitled to a claim when three things are on hand:
an object carried in the run’s states; a checked relation between that object and the claim,


                                            124
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


meaning a test whose result is on the record, not a test that merely exists; and a paid
event, a move of the run at which the object was put in place and which the price list
charged at least one. In a certification system (Definition 3.1) a move that takes the
reading from no to yes is such a move, because the toll charges it. This is the book’s
word, not a Coq definition.


Without the third part, the object may be sitting right there and the claim may be true,
and the run still hasn’t earned it. That’s the cups: the coin is under cup one; the reason
is disconnected from it; nobody lifted the cup. Put it on Section 3’s sheet of paper,
the one with the NO box, the YES box and the tally line, and grow the toy by one
thing: the state is now the box you’re in plus whatever is written on the sheet beside
it. Next to the boxes, write a note: “coin under cup one, checked.” Writing the note is
a WORK move, and WORK costs nothing. The note is an object, it’s on the paper, and
it might even be true. What it doesn’t have is a crossing on the record: no move took
the reading from NO to YES when the note went down, and there’s no mark under
the line for it. The note is raw data, forged in one write, and any system with the five
parts lets you write one, because nothing in the five parts says what an ordinary move
may put in the state. A note put down by the move that crosses has a receipt, and
the receipt is the event. One limit on that word “receipt”: the crossing records that
something was paid for at that moment. What the crossing move actually looked at
before it crossed is up to whatever the move does, and the five parts don’t say.

And here’s the part to hold on to. Nothing in the five parts makes a later move read the
reading. The step function is handed the state and a move name, and it’s allowed to
ignore the YES box completely; plenty of systems will. So when I say a run is entitled, I
mean what someone auditing the run may conclude from the reading and the receipt.
The system doesn’t have to enforce it, and unless somebody builds it to, it won’t.

This is a good place to line up the three things the word established has had to mean so
far, because they blur easily, and a blur here would make the book look like it proves
more than it does. The yardstick is the opening chapter’s four conditions for a check
being about this very claim: the same property, the same thing, the same edition, and
an honest check.

The first column is Section 3’s bare toll: a paid crossing, and nothing says a check
happened at all (Section 9 has a remark saying exactly that). The second is this section’s
entitlement. The third is the small machine of Part IV, whose step won’t let a commit
through without a passing check of the same property, on the same thing, at the same
edition, for every program from a clean start (Theorem 14.9), whose checker comes
with a proof that it says what it means (Lemma 14.1, Theorem 14.11), and whose
certified runs cost at least three (Theorem 14.16). Even there two things are missing,
and I want them in the table and not in a footnote. The step doesn’t police whether a
check could have failed: a property every value has is a perfectly legal check, sound
and useless. And in all three columns the status belongs to whoever reads the record.
The machine doesn’t know anything. What its flag means is assigned from outside, by
whoever says what each property means.

Why does the honest check carry so much? Linda Zagzebski argued in 1994 that any
account of knowledge whose justification leaves even a small gap between having
good reasons and being right lets a Gettier case through: take a case where bad luck
makes the reasons point the wrong way, then add a stroke of good luck that makes the
belief true anyway. The first three conditions plus an honest check close that gap by
construction, and only one half of honesty is needed for it, the half that says no when
the property is false. Saying yes whenever it’s true is extra. A check that can be wrong,
a test suite that sometimes passes broken code, puts you straight back in her gap, and
then the record certifies something smaller and still true: this procedure said yes.

And who certifies that the check is honest? Not the record. Honesty is a fact about
what the check does on every input, and the opening chapter already said a finished
state can’t hold that kind of fact. It has to be carried by a proof about the checker,
done once, outside every run, and nothing on the record pays for it. So an established
claim is two things stuck together: a run property the record carries and a program
property a proof carries, and the proof is entitlement for the auditor, not for the
machine. Section 14 shows where that chain of reasons stops on a real machine.

The engineering version of this was already built, in 1997. George Necula’s proof-
carrying code: when you ship a program to a host that doesn’t trust you, you ship a proof
with it that the program obeys the host’s safety rules, and the host checks the proof that
arrived before running anything. Not your reputation. Not “a proof exists somewhere.”
The one in the box. A quarter century earlier Stephen Cook’s certificates had the same

                                           126
The Thiele Machine                                                                Devon Thiele


bones, from Section 3: a claim comes with a witness that’s cheap to check, and the
checker checks that witness. And David Hume, in 1748, arguing about miracles, laid
out the thing the receipt replaces: he weighed testimony against evidence, and said
a wise person believes in proportion to the evidence, and the whole of his argument
is a method for how much to trust a witness when you have no receipt. The move
in this book is to stop weighing. A claim on the record is either backed by its object
and its paid event, or it’s testimony from outside, and a run that leans on testimony
hasn’t earned it itself. It can inherit it, but only as far as the copy it leans on is genuine,
which is Section 7’s problem of a record shown from outside.

The philosopher who built the most on these two words is Robert Brandom, and his
Making It Explicit (1994) is where I’d send anyone who suspects I invented the pair. In
his picture, people talking keep score on each other: what each speaker is committed
to, what they’ve put themselves on the hook for, and what each is entitled to, what
they’re licensed to claim. You can be committed without being entitled (a reckless
assertion), many claims count as entitled by default until someone challenges them,
and entitlement can be borrowed: I can claim a thing on your say-so and defer to
you when I’m challenged. Lay mine beside his and the differences are the content.
His score is kept by the other people in the room; here it’s a reading in the state.
His entitlement often comes by default; here it’s an event that has to happen and
is charged. And his deferral is my testimony, which I’ve just let back in on a leash:
borrowed entitlement is only as good as the copy is genuine. Same two words, and
his came first.

And the logicians the opening chapter named in passing, the ones who taught the
logic of knowing to count. Here they are properly. Ho Ngoc Duc, in 1997, gave the
logic of knowing an operator for “true after some train of thought”: an agent doesn’t
know every consequence of what it knows now, but it can come to know any of them
by taking steps of reasoning. Steps. And Sergei Artemov and Roman Kuznets, in
2014, turned logical omniscience into a question of cost: a logic escapes it when every
valid claim that something is known comes with a proof whose size is bounded by
a polynomial in the size of the claim. The usual modal logics of knowledge can’t
pass that test unless NP equals coNP, which most people would bet against, and
justification logic passes it for knowledge stated together with its justification, because
the size of the justification pays for the search. A price, of a sort. So steps and a price
are both there, in their own form. What I still don’t find in them is the one I care about:
a single act that closes a question for good and is charged as that act. Their steps are
steps of reasoning, and their price is on finding a proof, not on settling.

Three things entitlement is not, which people reach for. It isn’t permission: an access
control system says who may write to what, and that’s granted from outside and
says nothing about truth; a process with permission to write the note still has no
entitlement. It isn’t “true, therefore usable”: that’s the cups. And it isn’t “sound by
luck”: a shortcut that gives the right answer because the inputs happened to cooperate


                                             127
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


is the stopped clock. The count below has one condition aimed at it, and I’ll tell you
what the condition says and how much it actually catches.

8.4 What narrowing costs: count the rivals
Now the number, because a book about a bill has to say how much. Here’s the idea in
a form you can do with three playing cards. Shuffle cards marked 1, 2, 3 face down.
Sort them using only questions of the form “is this one bigger than that one?”, and
count the questions. There are six orders the cards could be in. Each question has two
answers, so after one question you’ve split the six into at most two piles, after two
questions at most four, and you need to get down to one. Four is less than six, so two
questions can’t always do it, and three can, and you can draw the tree of questions on
paper and see it: six leaves, three deep. The number of questions you need is at least
the base-two logarithm of the number of possibilities you started with, rounded up:
that’s log2 of 6, which is a bit under 3, rounded to 3. Donald Knuth, in the volume
on sorting of The Art of Computer Programming, gives this as the lower bound for all
comparison sorting, and the shape of the argument is just: a tree f questions deep has
at most 2 to the f leaves, so it can’t tell apart more than 2 to the f cases.

And then the obvious next question: is the floor always the price? Try five cards.
There are 120 orders, log2 of 120 is a bit under 7, so you need at least seven ques-
tions, and seven is enough, though not by the obvious method. Finding the way is
a good evening with a deck of cards (Knuth has it, under the name merge insertion,
from Lester Ford and Selmer Johnson in 1959). Now twelve cards. They can be in
479,001,600 orders, log2 of that is about 28.8, so the count says at least 29. Ford and
Johnson’s method takes 30, and in 1965 Mark Wells showed that nothing does better:
twelve cards need 30. The floor was 29. The price is 30. So the count is a floor and only
a floor; it never promises the floor can be reached, and the bound later in this section
has to be read exactly the same way.

Ralph Hartley in 1928, before Shannon, measured information exactly this way: the
logarithm of the number of possibilities, no probabilities, just a count. That’s the mea-
sure here, and I’ll say plainly it’s Hartley’s and not Shannon’s: there’s no distribution
over the list, only the list’s length.

Now put it on a run. Say a run comes with a list of states that are “still on the table,”
the candidates, and a shorter list, with some ruled out. Call the first the prior and the
second the posterior, and I want you to hear those as a list you could print, not “the
space of possible worlds.” Picture the ruling-out as observations, each observation
that ruled something out being one branch point in a tree like the card tree. And here’s
the claim: if that tree is no deeper than the number of paid steps the run took, and
the tree has enough leaves to cover the narrowing in a way I’ll spell out in a moment,
then the counter rose by at least log2 of the prior’s length minus log2 of the posterior’s
length. At least as many marks as index bits the list lost, where the index bits of a list
are the yes/no questions it takes to point at one entry of it, the card count again. That’s


                                           128
The Thiele Machine                                                                Devon Thiele


the bound.

“Paid step” needs its own sentence. It means a step the price list charges at least one for.
In a certification system the toll guarantees that every crossing of the reading is one; a
price list is free to put a floor under more steps than that (a look, a send, a check), and
the count takes every paid step there is. The tree is a bare shape, branches and leaves
with nothing written on them, and “no deeper than the number of paid steps” is a
count along the run that happened. It isn’t a walk down the tree. A paid step doesn’t
have to have asked any question at all.

Notice, too, what the bound does and doesn’t say about the run. It takes the two lists,
the tree and the covering as given. It doesn’t say the run produced the posterior from
the prior; nothing in it reads the lists off the run. What it says is that, given lists, a tree
and a covering that someone supplies, the paid steps of the run cover the rounded
drop in list length. That’s Section 5’s warning come due: watching can narrow for free,
so the payment can’t be dug out of the narrowing. It goes in as a premise, the tree’s
depth against the paid steps, and I’ll keep calling it one.

8.5 What “narrower” buys: a stronger test
Before the count, one link that’s pure logic, and Plato’s third account is the whole
of it. Take a list of candidates and an observation, a function that says what each
candidate looks like from outside. The list’s membership test accepts an observation
when some candidate on the list shows it. Shrink the list, and the test can only get
pickier: anything the short list’s test accepts, the long list’s accepts too. The word for
that, and it runs backward from English, is stronger: the stronger test is the one that
lets fewer things through.

Pickier, though, isn’t the same as strictly pickier, and the cards show the gap. Take
all six orders as the prior, and as the posterior the three where card 1 sits left of card
2: 1-2-3, 1-3-2 and 3-1-2. First observation: “is 1 left of 2?” Every survivor says yes,
and the removed 2-1-3 says no, so the prior’s test accepts yes and no, the posterior’s
only yes. Strictly stronger. Second observation, same two lists: “is the first card a
3?” Now 3-1-2 says yes and the other two survivors say no, and among the removed
orders 3-2-1 says yes and 2-1-3 says no. Both tests accept yes and no. Same strength,
even though three orders are gone. What made the difference is a removed candidate
whose observation no survivor shares. That’s Plato’s mark, the thing that sets this case
apart from everything it could be confused with, turned into a function. Narrow the
list and keep one distinguishing removed candidate, and the test is strictly stronger;
narrow it without one, and the test may not have moved at all.

8.6 The count, exactly
Here are the words and the count, for any system with Section 6’s counter. A list is
a finite list of candidates, repeats allowed, and |Ω| is the length of the list Ω, repeats
counted. ⌈log2 x ⌉ is the base-two logarithm of x rounded up: the smallest k ∈ N


                                             129
The Thiele Machine                                                                    Devon Thiele


with 2k ≥ x. At x = 0 this index-bit count is defined to be 0 as well; the notation
⌈log2 0⌉ = 0 here is a convention for empty lists, not the real logarithm of zero. And
a −̇ b is subtraction on whole numbers that stops at zero, so 3 −̇ 5 = 0.


Definition 8.2 (Decision tree). A decision tree is a leaf, or a branch with two subtrees.
Its depth is 0 for a leaf and one more than the deeper subtree for a branch; its leaf count
L( T ) is 1 for a leaf and the sum of the two counts for a branch. Nothing is written on
a tree: no question, no answer, no candidate.


Lemma 8.1 (A tree is no wider than two to its depth). For every decision tree T, L( T ) ≤
2depth(T ) , and so ⌈log2 L( T )⌉ ≤ depth( T ).

Proof. Induction on the tree. A leaf has one leaf and depth 0, and 1 ≤ 20 . A branch
with subtrees of depths d1 , d2 has at most 2d1 + 2d2 ≤ 2 · 2max(d1 ,d2 ) leaves, which is 2 to
its own depth. The second half: L( T ) ≤ 2depth(T ) means depth( T ) is one of the k with
2k ≥ L( T ), and the rounded-up logarithm is the smallest of them.

Checked as decision_tree_leaves_le_pow2_depth and decision_tree_lo
g2_up_leaf_bound (MuShannonBridge.v). Both are stated over the tree type alone,
a leaf or a branch, with nothing about any machine in them.


Theorem 8.2 (Paid narrowing, counted). Take a system with a counter µ and a price list
c that obey conservation (Theorem 6.1): each step raises µ by exactly its charge. Let Ω and
Ω′ be lists with |Ω′ | > 0, let T be a decision tree with |Ω| ≤ L( T ) · |Ω′ | (the tree covers the
narrowing), and let t be a run from s ending at s′ in which at least depth( T ) steps are charged
at least one each. Then

                          ⌈log2 |Ω|⌉ −̇ ⌈log2 |Ω′ |⌉ ≤ µ(s′ ) − µ(s).

Proof. The rounded-up logarithm respects order, so the covering gives ⌈log2 |Ω|⌉ ≤
⌈log2 ( L( T ) · |Ω′ |)⌉. It is also subadditive on products of positive numbers, ⌈log2 ab⌉ ≤
⌈log2 a⌉ + ⌈log2 b⌉, because 2⌈log2 a⌉ · 2⌈log2 b⌉ ≥ ab. So

                  ⌈log2 |Ω|⌉ −̇ ⌈log2 |Ω′ |⌉ ≤ ⌈log2 L( T )⌉ ≤ depth( T ),

the last step by Lemma 8.1. By hypothesis at least depth( T ) steps of the run were
charged at least one, and no step is charged less than zero, so the sum of the charges
is at least depth( T ). By conservation that sum is µ(s′ ) − µ(s).

Argued here for any system with a counter that obeys conservation. The tree half is the
checked lemma above; the rest is arithmetic on three whole numbers, the two lengths
and the leaf count, and on the counter. Notice what’s missing from the hypotheses:
anything tying the lists to the run. That’s the honest shape of the bound.


                                               130
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


Three honest small prints, all of them visible in the statement. Both logarithms round
up separately, and the subtraction stops at zero, so when the prior and the posterior
round up to the same number of index bits (four candidates narrowed to three, say)
the bound says nothing. The lists are plain lists, not sets, so “index bits” is a difference
of rounded list lengths with repeats counted; a list can get shorter by dropping a
duplicate without losing a single candidate, and “a candidate was ruled out” and
“the list got shorter” are two different claims. And the difference isn’t the number of
questions anyone asked.

The covering condition, |Ω| ≤ L( T ) · |Ω′ |, is the nearest thing the count has to an anti-
stopped-clock clause, and I have to be exact about how near. Picture each survivor
standing for a little crowd of the candidates that were dropped, a crowd no bigger
than the tree has leaves. Then the condition says every candidate in the prior fits in
some survivor’s crowd. That limits how much can be deleted per leaf you paid for. It
doesn’t say why anything was deleted. So the condition rules out deleting too much
for the tree you’ve paid for. It doesn’t rule out deleting for no reason. A run can satisfy
every hypothesis of the count and have ruled nothing out on purpose; the count prices
the size of the drop, not the honesty of it.

8.7 What you’ve got
A paid flag is not a true claim; Section 7 left it at “a paid flag is a paid flag,” and
Section 9 will say it flatly. What a paid flag with an object and a checked relation
behind it gives you is entitlement: anyone auditing the run may treat the claim as
established, and can point at the event where that became legitimate. (Nothing in the
five parts makes the system itself read the flag; I said that above and I’m saying it
again because it’s the sentence most likely to get lost.) Entitlement costs at least the
index bits of narrowing it commits to, given lists, a tree and a covering somebody
supplies, and given a run that paid for the tree’s depth. The cups say why entitlement
and truth are different. Plato says what the checked relation has to do: distinguish.
Necula says how to build it. Hartley says what to count.

The machine I build later has all of these pieces at once, and Section 22 puts this whole
section on it, every hypothesis written out, with one worked member you can count
by hand. Before any of that, I owe you the word the toll is named after, the “insight”
in “No Free Insight” (Section 5), because I’ve been using it as if it meant one thing.

9 What insight is
I named the rule in this book “No Free Insight,” and the name ran ahead of any careful
account of what insight is. The book has been narrowing it ever since: not learning
(Section 5), not looking, not copying. It’s time to say what’s left, and to say it in a way
that someone who studies actual insight, in actual heads, wouldn’t laugh at. So who
are those people, and what did they find? Here’s what I ran into, pushed on as I go,
because the founding stories of a field get retold like any other stories, and a retold


                                            131
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


story is a lead to check.

9.1 Sultan and the sticks
In 1913 the psychologist Wolfgang Köhler went to Tenerife to run a research station
with a colony of chimpanzees, and the First World War then kept him there until 1920
with nothing to do but watch them. The famous one is Sultan. Food is outside the
cage, out of reach; two sticks are inside, each too short, but one fits into the end of the
other. Sultan tries each stick, fails, sulks, plays with the sticks, and then, by Köhler’s
account, at a moment you can see, joins them and reaches the food. Köhler’s word was
einsichtig, which came into English as “insight,” and the whole school of psychology
he belonged to, the Gestalt school, said that’s what thinking is: not stacking up tries
until one works, but a restructuring, the moment two sticks stop being two sticks and
become one tool. Karl Duncker gave the human version, in German in 1935 and
in English in 1945, five years after he died at thirty-seven; he’d spent his last years
working with Köhler at Swarthmore. You can set it up yourself: a candle, a box of
tacks, matches, and the task of fixing the candle to the wall. Almost nobody sees that
the box is a shelf, until they do. And then he found that if you hand people the box
empty, with the tacks poured out beside it, they solve it far more readily. Same objects.
What changed was which relation among them was on the table.

I like both of these for the same reason: the insight didn’t add an object. Sultan had
both sticks the whole time. The box was there the whole time. What arrived was a
relation, which is to say a piece of structure in Section 2’s sense, and the arrival was
sudden. Hold that, because it’s going to turn out that the thing the toll prices also
arrives in one step, and at its best it’s also a relation.

9.2 It isn’t a feeling
But here’s the finding I’d hand anyone who thinks insight is a feeling, and it comes
from someone who measured it. In the 1980s the psychologist Janet Metcalfe asked
people to solve problems while rating, every fifteen seconds, how “warm” they felt,
how close to the answer. On ordinary problems, algebra for instance, the warmth
climbs steadily and peaks at the answer, which is what you’d expect. On insight
problems, riddles of the candle-box kind, the warmth stays flat, flat, flat, and then the
answer arrives, and if anything the people who felt warmest beforehand were more
likely to be wrong. The feeling of being close is not a gauge of being close. Try it
yourself: write a number from one to seven every fifteen seconds while doing a long
sum, then while doing a riddle, and compare the curves.

And the most famous insight story there is fits Metcalfe uncomfortably well.
Archimedes, asked whether a goldsmith had cheated the king on a crown, gets into
a bath, sees the water rise, and runs home naked shouting “eureka,” I’ve found it.
That comes from Vitruvius, writing about two centuries later. Is it true? Galileo, at
twenty-two, in 1586, thought the method as Vitruvius tells it was too crude to catch a
clever goldsmith, and wrote a little tract, La Bilancetta, proposing a balance weighed


                                           132
The Thiele Machine                                                          Devon Thiele


in air and in water instead, which he thought was probably what Archimedes actually
did, since it rests on Archimedes’s own results. So the eureka is a legend, wrapped
around a real man and probably a real problem. Notice what the legend kept: the
bath, the shout, the running home naked. The feeling. What it got shaky is the part
that would count as the check, the test that could have caught the goldsmith. The bit
everybody remembers is the bit that tells you least.

So any account of insight that keys on the sensation, the “aha,” is keyed to something
that the data says is unreliable. Whatever insight is, it isn’t the feeling of having it.
That’s a relief, because a system of states and moves doesn’t have feelings, and a word
that only meant a feeling would be cheating if I hung it on one. The version this book
can price has to be keyed to an event, and the question is which.

9.3 What happens when a computation learns
Here’s the split, and I’ll say what the toll does with each part, and then I’ll say who
decided the split, because it wasn’t me. Keep Section 3’s sheet of paper in front of
you: the NO box, the YES box, the tally line, and the three moves STAY, WORK and
VOUCH.

The first thing: raw observation. Something comes in and gets written down. A counter
ticks. Nothing is claimed about what it means, nothing is marked as resting on it,
and the reading doesn’t move because of it. Later moves can read what it wrote, but
that reading is a move of its own. This is the demon’s pad in Section 5, and it’s what
the statistician Dennis Lindley measured in 1956 as “the information an experiment
provides,” the expected drop in your uncertainty: a real quantity, and a quantity about
what was seen. It can be free. The toll says nothing at all about a move that doesn’t
cross from NO to YES, so a price list may charge it zero: on the paper, STAY and
WORK cost nothing, and Section 5’s watcher narrowed a whole row of candidates
without paying a mark. “Can be” is the honest word. A price list is allowed to charge
for looking anyway, and whether looking costs anything in the physical world is a
different question that this sheet of paper doesn’t touch.

Lindley’s measure has a back story, and it runs through Bletchley Park. I. J. Good,
who was Alan Turing’s main statistical assistant at Bletchley Park in 1941, wrote in
1979 that Turing had worked out the expected weight of evidence an experiment
would give, to judge one of the codebreaking procedures before running it, and so
partly anticipated Lindley by about fifteen years, in work that stayed secret. Turing
measured evidence in bans, logarithms to base ten, with a tenth of one called a deciban,
and the name came from the town of Banbury, where tens of thousands of the sheets
used in that procedure were printed. It’s the same base-ten unit other people call the
hartley, after the Hartley from the last section. And Good adds that Turing didn’t
know the logarithm he was using had already appeared in 1878, in a paper by Charles
Sanders Peirce, the same Peirce from the opening chapter, who’d called it the weight
of evidence. Peirce is as far back as Good takes it. What it changes: nothing in the


                                          133
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


argument, but it shows how well trodden this first kind of thing is. For a century and
a half careful people have measured what an observation tells you, and every one of
those measures is about what was seen. That’s the side of the line the toll leaves alone.

The second thing: certified insight. Some move turns the reading from NO to YES.
Here is where the toll lives. In any system with the five parts that obeys the toll, that
move costs at least one mark, and every run that starts at NO and ends at YES pays at
least one somewhere along the way, which is Section 3’s universal floor. What’s being
charged for, at its best, is exactly the Gestalt thing: a relation, committed to. Not two
sticks; one tool, claimed. “At its best,” because Section 3 was careful about what YES
means: the flag is up, and nothing more. A crossing that writes down which relation
it’s committing to carries Sultan’s tool with it. A bare crossing, VOUCH on the paper,
commits to no relation at all, and it pays exactly the same.

The third thing isn’t a kind of event. It’s an observation about the price: it’s flat,
whatever is certified. Say the YES state also shows something striking, a deep relation,
a result nobody could have guessed, Sultan’s two sticks become one tool. The toll
charges the crossing at least one. It doesn’t charge the striking crossing more, because
the floor’s proof never looks at anything but the reading before and after. On the
paper: VOUCH from NO makes one mark whether you were thinking of Duncker’s
box or of lunch. Meaning is not cost. The depth of what’s certified adds meaning. It
doesn’t add a mark.

The candle box has a footnote that says the same thing from the other side. In 1962
Sam Glucksberg ran Duncker’s problem with money on it: some people were told
they could win five or twenty dollars depending on how fast they solved it. With
the tacks in the box, the people chasing the money did worse than the people who
weren’t. With the box empty, the money made no clear difference. Paying more didn’t
buy the insight, and on the hard version it got in the way. That’s a fact about heads,
not about records, and I won’t push it further than that. But it’s a nice mirror for the
paper. On the paper a deeper crossing isn’t charged more, and in Glucksberg’s room a
bigger prize didn’t bring the crossing sooner. In neither place does the price measure
the depth.

Here they are, exactly, for any certification system (Definition 3.1). Runs are written
as lists, the way Section 3’s proof wrote them: [ ] is the empty run, and i :: t is the run
that starts with move i and carries on with the run t.


Definition 9.1 (Certified insight event, raw observation). In a certification system, a
step from state s by move i is a certified insight event when it turns the reading on:
cert(s) = no and cert(step(s, i )) = yes. A move i is raw observation when no step by it,
from any state, is a certified insight event.


Remark 9.1 (What the toll prices, and what it doesn’t). Read off Definition 3.1 and


                                           134
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


Theorem 3.1; there is no further Coq theorem at this generality. (1) The toll puts no
bound on the cost of a raw-observation move; on Section 3’s board STAY and WORK
are raw observation and cost 0. (2) Every certified insight event is charged at least 1,
by the toll, and every run from a state reading no to one reading yes has total cost at
least 1, by the universal floor. (3) The price is flat: the floor’s proof uses nothing about
the end state but its reading, so adding any hypothesis about what else the end state
shows leaves the bound at 1 and cannot raise it. A system that wants to charge more
for a deeper certification has to write that into its price list, move by move; the toll
doesn’t do it for anyone.


So the account comes down to two facts and a warning. Looking can be free. Turning
the reading on can’t. And putting something remarkable behind the reading doesn’t
make it cost any more.

Who decided the split? Not the costs alone. The toll prices exactly one thing, the
crossing. A price list is free to put a floor under more moves than that (a look, a send,
a check) and free to leave other moves at zero, so the sorting into raw observation and
certified insight is by whether the reading moves, and that sorting is this book’s. The
part that’s forced is the floor under the crossing, and Section 4 is the argument for it;
anything a price list charges beyond that is a choice, and any concrete machine owes
you its whole table so you can see which choices it made.

9.4 Test, then commit, and nothing forces the second to follow the first
The philosopher Karl Popper said a theory earns its standing by being exposed: you
make a conjecture, you try to kill it, and what survives a real attempt counts for
something, where “real” means the test could have failed. His word for that earned
credit is corroboration. I’ve leaned on that idea through this whole book, and here’s
where a certification system has a version of it, and here’s where the version is weaker
than Popper and I have to say so.

Add a fourth move to the paper: CHECK. It looks at something (a sum, a coin under a
cup, a formula against a row of values), and it can come out pass or fail, and it doesn’t
move the box. Charge it whatever you like; charging it on the attempt, pass or fail,
fits Popper, because what made his test count was that it was really run and could
have failed. That’s the test. It’s raw observation in the sense above, because it never
turns the reading on. VOUCH is the commit. So the honest protocol is two moves:
test, then commit, and the costs are separate, one for the checking work and one for
the crossing.

But nothing in the five parts makes the second move wait for the first. The step is
handed the current state and a move name; the toll looks only at whether the reading
crossed. Play VOUCH from NO with no CHECK anywhere before it, and you land in
YES and make one mark, the same box and the same mark as the player who checked
first. The two tally lines differ by exactly what the CHECK was charged, and if you


                                            135
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


charged it nothing they don’t differ at all. The mark for the crossing is the same mark
either way. The receipt says a commitment was paid for. It does not say it was earned.
Popper’s corroboration needs the test; the toll doesn’t.

You can build a system that makes the commit wait. Let CHECK leave a mark in the
state when it passes, and write the step so VOUCH only crosses when that mark is
there. That’s a design, written into the step function, and it’s a perfectly good one.
Nothing in the five parts or the toll asks for it. That’s a real gap between the word
and the bare system, and the only honest thing is to leave it visible: the toll prices the
commit, and whether the commit was preceded by a test is a fact about the run, or
about a design somebody chose, not a guarantee of the five parts.


Remark 9.2 (Nothing makes the crossing wait). Read off Definition 3.1; there is no
Coq theorem. The toll constrains cost(i ) for moves that cross, and nothing else; the
step function is any function of the current state and the move. So a certification
system may have a move that crosses from a state no check has touched, and the toll
still holds. On Section 3’s board extended with CHECK, the run [VOUCH] from NO
crosses with one mark, and so does [CHECK, VOUCH]. Making a crossing depend
on an earlier check is a condition on the step function, which a particular system can
impose and the definition does not.


9.5 What the word means
So: insight, in the sense this book prices, is a relation committed to, in a move that
flips a reading from off to on, and that move costs at least one mark, in any system
with the toll, for any relation, whatever its depth. (And one edge from the paper: a
bare crossing that commits to nothing pays the same mark, so “a relation committed
to” is what the crossing is at its best, not what the toll guarantees.) Three boundaries,
each from a different place. From Metcalfe: it isn’t a feeling, and a system’s version
has to be an event. From the proof: the price is flat; a shallow commit and a deep
one both cost at least one, and cost is not depth. A system can pay heavily to check
a claim that turns out trivial, and Duncker’s box is one small commit. And from the
two-move protocol: a paid flag proves nothing on its own. Price and correctness are
separate books.

Which leaves a suspicion I’d have in your place. Everything so far has been one
reading on one sheet of paper, with a rule I chose and a count I bolted on. Is the shape
of that record something I picked, or is it what any honest record has to look like, on
any machine at all? That’s the next section: take any machine that steps, bolt a record
onto it, and see what shape it’s forced into. How a concrete machine hangs actual
claims on its parts, formulas and labels and where they sit in the state, comes in Part
IV.




                                           136
The Thiele Machine                                                                Devon Thiele



10 Records over any base: the latch
For the whole book so far I’ve been building up a thing with a flag and a counter,
and a fair reader is entitled to suspect that the whole apparatus is special pleading for
one machine, the one I keep promising to build. So here’s the section that answers
the suspicion with no particular machine in it at all, and sees what’s left. Take any
machine that steps deterministically: a Turing machine, a register machine (a few
numbered boxes that each hold a whole number, and a program that adds, subtracts
and jumps), a lambda calculus (Alonzo Church’s way of computing by nothing but
plugging expressions into expressions; Section 11 builds one), anything. Call it the
base. Now bolt a record onto it, under rules I’ll state, and ask: what can the record be?

The answer is one shape, and I’ll show you the shape first because it’s a thing you can
build from a cup and a die.

10.1 A cup and a die
Put a cup upside down on the table. The rule: the first time a coin lands in front of it,
turn it right side up. There is no rule for turning it back over. Now roll a die, and put
a coin down on every six. Roll twenty times. The cup turns over on the first six and
stays turned over. Write down which roll did it. That number, the roll that turned the
cup, is where the record happened, and the cup afterward is the record.

That’s a latch. Electrical engineers have had the circuit since 1918, when William
Eccles and Frank Jordan applied for a patent on a two-valve arrangement that holds
whichever state you last put it in; it became the flip-flop, and the registers and caches
in the device you’re reading this on descend from it. The simplest version has one
input, “set,” and the rule new state = old state or set: once set, it stays set, and there’s no
reset wire. The cup is that circuit: a flip-flop with its reset wire cut off.

(Eccles and Jordan didn’t call it a flip-flop. Their 1919 paper calls it a trigger relay.
Where the newer, sillier name came from I can’t source, so I’ll leave it at that.)

Is a flip-flop with its reset wire cut off only a picture, or did anybody ever build one on
purpose? Somebody did, and for a reason that’s very close to this book’s. In the mid-
1950s Wen Tsing Chow, an engineer at the Arma division of the American Bosch Arma
Corporation in Garden City, New York, was asked by the United States Air Force for a
more flexible and secure way to hold the fixed numbers, the targeting constants, inside
the guidance computer of the Atlas missile. What he and William Henrich patented
(filed in 1957, granted in 1962, under the plain title “Storage matrix”) was a grid with a
connection at every crossing, where you set the numbers by taking out the connections
you didn’t want, physically or by burning them out with too much current. The word
burn is right there in the patent, and people still say they burn a chip. The descendants
are called programmable read-only memories, PROMs, and a fuse blown in one stays
blown: there’s no current you can send to grow it back. A whole memory built out of
cups with no reset wire, because somebody wanted numbers nobody could quietly


                                             137
The Thiele Machine                                                                Devon Thiele


change later. Does that prove anything here? No. The theorem below doesn’t care
what a cup is made of. But it’s good to know the shape wasn’t invented for a sheet of
paper. Somebody needed it, for stakes a good deal higher than a die.

Now the claim, stated loosely and then exactly: every honest record over any base is a cup
with no reset wire, turned by some event the base passes through.

10.2 What “honest” has to mean
Here’s where the content is, and I’ll give you the five rules, because the theorem is
only as strong as they are.

A machine extends a base when there’s a map from the big machine’s states down to
the base’s, and that map starts in the base’s start states, reaches every one of them,
moves in step with the base (one step up top is one step down below, through the
map), and agrees about halting. The big machine may carry as much hidden state as
it likes beyond the base. That’s the “any base” part: the base doesn’t get to see the
extension, and the extension doesn’t get to change what the base does.

The extension carries a record, a yes/no reading, and a ledger, a counter. It’s an honest
extension when five things hold. One: the record’s next value depends only on the
base’s current state and the record’s current value. (I’ll call this driven by the computation.
It says the record answers to what the machine is doing, not to a clock on the wall
or someone’s hand.) Two: the ledger never goes down (Section 6). Three: the step
that turns the record on costs at least one; that’s the toll (Section 3). Four: once on,
the record stays on; that’s permanence (Section 4). Five: some run from a start state
actually reaches a step that turns the record on; otherwise the record is decoration.

Here are the words exactly. On/off is true/false, ∨ is “or” (on when either side is on),
and nextk is k steps.


Definition 10.1 (Base, record-carrying machine, cover). A base B is a set of states with
a step function nextB , a set of starting states, and a halting predicate. A record-carrying
machine M is a set of states with a step function next M , a set of starting states, a record
rec from states to Booleans, a ledger µ from states to whole numbers, and a halting
predicate. The cost of a step is cost(m) = µ(next M (m)) −̇ µ(m). A cover of B by M is a
map π from states of M to states of B that sends starting states to starting states, has
every starting state of B as the image of some starting state of M, commutes with the
steps, π (next M (m)) = nextB (π (m)), and agrees about halting: m halts exactly when
π (m) does.


Definition 10.2 (Honest extension, latch). M with cover π is an honest extension of
B when, for every state m: (R1, driven by the computation) there is one function f
with rec(next M (m)) = f (π (m), rec(m)); (R2, ledger) µ(m) ≤ µ(next M (m)); (R3, toll)
if rec(m) is off and rec(next M (m)) is on, then cost(m) ≥ 1; (R4, permanence) if rec(m)


                                             138
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


is on, so is rec(next M (m)); and (R5, a reachable write) some starting state m0 and some
k have rec(nextkM (m0 )) off and rec(nextkM+1 (m0 )) on. An event is a function h from base
states to Booleans, and its latch is the step (b, r ) 7→ (nextB (b), r ∨ h(b)). M factors as
the latch of h when, for every state m (reachable or not),

        (π (next M (m)), rec(next M (m))) = (nextB (π (m)), rec(m) ∨ h(π (m))).


Now the theorem. Under those rules, the base state and the record move exactly as a
latch: the record switches on at the first base state where some event holds, and never
off, and the event is read off the extension’s own rule by asking it what it does when
the record is off (stated exactly below). Everything else the extension carries, all the
hidden state, shows up only in its ledger; it can’t leak into the record’s behaviour.

I promised the content was in the definition, and here’s what that means: the proof is
a short case split on whether the record is already on, and it uses only two of the five
rules, “driven by the computation” and “permanent.” The ledger, the toll, and the
reachable-write clauses play no part in it. A latch is what you get from “answers only
to the base” plus “never comes back down,” full stop. The other three rules matter
for the converse: for any base and any event the base can reach, the latch of that event,
priced at one unit per write, is an honest extension. Put the two together and you’ve
got: honest records are exactly latches. One shape, no others, over any base.


Theorem 10.1 (The record is a latch). Let B be any base and M an honest extension of
it through π, with f the function of (R1). Then M factors as the latch of the event h(b) =
 f (b, off).

Proof. The base half of the equation is the cover’s step clause. For the record, split on
rec(m). If it is on, permanence (R4) makes the next value on, and on ∨ h(π (m)) is on.
If it is off, (R1) makes the next value f (π (m), off) = h(π (m)) = off ∨ h(π (m)). Only
(R1), (R4) and the cover are used; (R2), (R3) and (R5) are discarded.

Checked as record_axis_is_latch_holds (StructuralRecordAxis.v), with the
definitions BaseMachine, BaseCover, computation_driven, HonestBaseExt
ension and latch_factorization (StructuralCoreAnyBase.v), and the clauses
(R2) to (R5) as ledger_carried, rc_a2 (StructuralCore.v), record_permanent
and reachable_record_write (StructuralCoreCover.v).

One thing about that proof deserves a second look, because it cuts both ways. It never
asks what the base is. The cover decides that: whatever the map sends down is base,
and the record’s rule is allowed to read all of it; whatever stays up top is extension,
and (R1) keeps the record’s rule from reading it. Draw the line low, so the base is only
the computation’s own working state, and (R1) is a real demand. Draw it high, put
every table and every refusal bit into the base, and (R1) is easy to meet, and the latch


                                            139
The Thiele Machine                                                                    Devon Thiele


shape comes out exactly the same. So the theorem holds wherever you draw the line,
and that’s exactly why it can’t tell you where a record’s meaning lives. The meaning
lives in what the event h reads, and that’s in the base by construction. The pieces
above the line, the record and the ledger, are the ones that never steer anything; the
pieces that make a flag mean something sit below it, where this theorem doesn’t look.
So when the machines in Part IV arrive, ask them first which parts they put above the
line.


Theorem 10.2 (Every reachable latch is an honest record). Let B be any base and h any
event. Let Latchh have states (b, r, x ), starting states (b, off, 0) with b starting in B, step
(b, r, x ) 7→ (nextB (b), r ∨ h(b), x + δ) with δ = 1 when r is off and h(b) is on and δ = 0
otherwise, record r, ledger x, halting as b halts, and cover (b, r, x ) 7→ b. Suppose some starting
b0 and some k bring Latchh from (b0 , off, 0), in k steps, to a state whose record is still off and
whose base state satisfies h. Then Latchh is an honest extension of B.

Proof. (R1) holds with f (b, r ) = r ∨ h(b). (R2): each step adds 0 or 1. (R3): a step that
turns the record on has r off and h(b) on, so it adds 1. (R4): on ∨ h(b) is on. (R5) is
the supposition. The supposition asks for the first time h holds on some run; any run
from a start that reaches an h-state has such a first time, though the file states only the
first-time form.

Checked as latch_core_honest (RecordAxisDiscrimination.v).

A reversible base needs one more thing to carry a record, and the files say exactly
what. If the base never merges two states, keep every earlier record value in a growing
history beside the latch, and the whole step merges nothing either; but on a finite state
space a permanent record can’t be written by a step that merges nothing at all. A step
that merges nothing is called injective: no two states go to the same next state. And
r :: H is the history H with r put on the front, as in Section 9.


Theorem 10.3 (Records on reversible machines). (1) Let B be a base whose step is injective.
The machine with states (b, r, H, x ), step (b, r, H, x ) 7→ (nextB (b), r ∨ h(b), r :: H, x + δ)
(δ as in Theorem 10.2), starting states with r off, H empty and x = 0, has an injective step,
and under the supposition of Theorem 10.2 it is an honest extension of B. (2) On a finite state
space, a single injective step with a permanent reading never turns that reading from off to on.

Proof. (1) Equal images have equal base parts, so equal base states by injectivity; equal
histories r :: H, so equal records and histories; and equal ledgers once the equal δ is
subtracted. Honesty is the proof of Theorem 10.2 with the history carried along. (2) is
Theorem 4.1 of Section 4 with a single move.

Checked as history_latch_injective, history_latch_honest and finite
_reversible_cannot_write (RecordAxisDiscrimination.v), the last from perma


                                               140
The Thiele Machine                                                              Devon Thiele


nent_flip_is_not_injective (PermanentCertification.v).

So a base that never merges can still carry a record, if it’s allowed to grow a history
that never ends. A finite one can’t. On a finite machine the record’s first write is a
merge, and Section 4 already put the price on that.

10.3 Both rules do work: the toggle and the clock
A theorem with two hypotheses should have two counterexamples, one for each
hypothesis dropped, and it does, and they’re the two ways a record goes wrong in the
world.

Drop permanence. Take a base that just counts, and a record that flips at every step:
on, off, on, off. It’s driven by the computation; it’s not permanent; and it’s not a latch
of any event. This is a toggle, a piece of working state. A record you can revoke is
working state wearing a record’s clothes, and if a revocation has to stick, that’s a second
latch (“revoked”), which is how certificate revocation lists actually work: you add an
entry; you never delete the certificate. The pair theorem (stated below) covers two
latches that can each read the other; do it with two cups where the second only turns
over on an even roll if the first is already up, and you’ll see the second can never turn
before the first.

Drop “driven by the computation.” Take a base that counts, and a record that switches
on at the fifth tick of a hidden clock, whatever the base is doing. It’s permanent; it’s not
driven by the computation. This is a timestamp. A timestamp is not evidence; it says
when, not what happened, and a record switched by an outside party or a clock records
the party or the clock, not the computation. Try it with the die: play twenty rolls with
the rule “turn the cup after roll seven no matter what,” and notice you’ve recorded
nothing about the dice.

The file proves exactly the facts I named for each: the toggle is driven, not permanent
and not a latch; the clock is permanent and not driven. That each also keeps the other
rules (the ledger is the step count, the first switch-on costs one, a run reaches it) is true
by inspection, and isn’t a separate theorem.

So: permanent but undriven is a clock, driven but impermanent is a toggle, and a
record is the thing that’s both. That’s the whole discrimination, and I think it’s the
most useful three-sentence thing in this book for looking at systems other than the one
I build, which is why it’s here.

The pair theorem and the two counterexamples, exactly. The base for both counterex-
amples is the counter: states are whole numbers, the step adds one, every state is a
starting state, and nothing halts. Two more bits of shorthand: ¬r is r flipped, and a
statement in square brackets, like [k = 5], reads on when it’s true and off when it isn’t.


Lemma 10.4 (Two records are two latches). Let c1 , c2 be two records on M, with cover


                                            141
The Thiele Machine                                                                     Devon Thiele


π onto a base B, such that: there is one function F with (c1 (next M (m)), c2 (next M (m))) =
F (π (m), c1 (m), c2 (m)); the ledger never goes down; a step that turns either record on costs
at least one; and each record is permanent. Then there are h1 , h2 with c1 (next M (m)) =
c1 (m) ∨ h1 (π (m), c2 (m)) and c2 (next M (m)) = c2 (m) ∨ h2 (π (m), c1 (m)) for every m.

Proof. Take h1 (b, r2 ) to be the first part of F (b, off, r2 ) and h2 (b, r1 ) the second part of
F (b, r1 , off), then split on each record as in Theorem 10.1.

Checked as record_pair_is_two_latches_holds (StructuralRecordAxis.v).


Lemma 10.5 (The toggle). Let the toggle have states (n, r ), step (n, r ) 7→ (n + 1, ¬r ),
every state starting, record r, ledger n, cover (n, r ) 7→ n onto the counter. It is driven by the
computation, with f (b, r ) = ¬r; it is not permanent; and it factors as the latch of no event.

Proof. At (0, on) the next record is off, which breaks permanence; and any latch gives
on ∨ h(0) = on there.

Checked as toggle_not_permanent and toggle_not_latch (StructuralRecor-
dAxis.v).


Lemma 10.6 (The clock). Let the clock have states (b, k, r ), step (b, k, r ) 7→ (b + 1, k +
1, r ∨ [k = 5]), every state starting, record r, ledger b, cover (b, k, r ) 7→ b onto the counter. It
is permanent and not driven by the computation.

Proof. Permanence: on ∨ x is on. Not driven: the states (0, 5, off) and (0, 0, off) have
the same base state and the same record, and their next records are on and off, so no f
of the base state and the record can give both.

Checked as toggle_computation_driven, toggle_not_permanent, toggl
e_not_latch, clock_record_permanent and clock_record_not_driven
(StructuralRecordAxis.v). “Driven” is a condition on every state, reachable or not, and
that is what the clock’s proof uses.

10.4 Is there only one such machine? No. One structure, two free choices.
Here’s a sentence that’s tempting and wrong, and the way it’s wrong is more interest-
ing than the sentence: “there’s only one honest way to carry a record.” Three different
things get squeezed into that breath, and I’ll pull them apart.

First claim: given the toll and a fixed price list, is there one way to keep the books?
Yes; that’s Section 6’s initiality, and it assumes the price list.

Second claim: is every honest extension of a base the same machine, charges and all? No,
and the counterexample is embarrassing in its simplicity. Take any honest extension
and add one more coin to the bill on every step, whatever the step is. Now walk the

                                                142
The Thiele Machine                                                                 Devon Thiele


five rules. The record still answers only to the base and its own value (R1); the bill
never touches it. The ledger still never goes down (R2); it climbs faster, if anything.
The step that turns the record on still costs at least one (R3), because the toll is a floor
and a surcharge only raises the price. Once on, the record stays on (R4), and the same
run still reaches the write (R5). So the billed machine is honest, and it isn’t the machine
you started with: wherever the original sat still for free, the billed one pays a coin a
tick for sitting still. Do it with the cup and the die. Charge a coin for every roll, six
or not. The cup turns over on the same roll as before. You’ve changed the bill and
nothing about the record. A machine that charges for CPU time is honest and isn’t the
one that doesn’t.

But the billed machine isn’t a different structure. It’s the same machine with a different
price list. So the claim worth keeping is sameness up to the price schedule: compare two
machines by their record, their halting and their steps, through their maps down to
the base, and don’t compare charges. Fix which event the record is, and the bill stops
mattering; a flat surcharge, or any surcharge that depends on the current state, sits on
the same structure. That’s the first free choice. The walk above is the whole argument,
and it’s argued here, not checked over an arbitrary base: the checked statements, the
exact uniqueness refuted and the uniqueness up to schedule proved, are written for
the machine I build later, with its own certification reading as the record, and they’re
Section 23’s.

And then the second free choice, and this one still surprises me. Which event is the
record? Nothing in the five rules picks it. The converse above already says so, if you
read it twice: for any event the base can reach, the latch of that event, priced at one unit
per write, is an honest record. Do it with the die. One cup turns over on the first six.
Another turns over on the first one. Both are cups with no reset wire; both are honest.
Roll a one first, and until a six turns up the two cups disagree about whether anything
has been recorded. So which permanent reading counts as the record is a second thing
nobody forces on you. The price list is one free choice. The event is the other. That
second choice is the question Section 13 is about: what, if anything, makes certification
the event worth recording, rather than “the ledger passed one” or anything else.


Corollary 10.7 (The event is a free choice). Let B be any base and h1 , h2 two events, each
meeting the supposition of Theorem 10.2. Then Latchh1 and Latchh2 are both honest extensions
of B. If some starting base state b has h1 (b) on and h2 (b) off, then one step from (b, off, 0)
leaves the first record on and the second off.

Proof. Honesty is Theorem 10.2 applied twice. The step is the latch’s own rule: off ∨
h1 (b) is on and off ∨ h2 (b) is off.

Argued from latch_core_honest (RecordAxisDiscrimination.v) applied to each
event; the corollary itself is not a separate Coq statement.



                                              143
The Thiele Machine                                                                Devon Thiele


Now let the cup wobble. Say whatever turns it over sometimes does and sometimes
doesn’t, with odds you could write on a card. Does fixing the price list fix the odds?
No, and the counterexample is two cups with the same price tag and differently
loaded coins. Here’s the setup, said carefully. Let a record be a single bit that moves at
random: from each value, a list of weighted next values, every weight positive, never
empty, never leaving on once on, and with the write from off to on charged at least
one. Call two such records the same schedule when the same moves are possible and
every move is charged the same, and the same in probability when the weighted lists
are equal.


Theorem 10.8 (The schedule doesn’t fix the probabilities). (1) There are two honest
probabilistic records with the same schedule that are not the same in probability. (2) There is
an honest probabilistic record that no deterministic latch on its current value describes.

Proof. (1) From off, one record moves to off or on with weights 1 and 1, the other with
weights 1 and 2; from on, both stay on with weight 1; both charge 1 for the write. Same
possible moves, same charges, different weights. (2) The first record moves from off
both to off and to on, while a latch r ∨ h(r ) gives one value.

Checked as schedule_determines_probabilities_refuted and determin
istic_latch_handles_branching_refuted (ProbabilisticRecord.v), with the
definitions in ProbabilisticRecordCore.v. These are finite-weight models on one bit
with no base underneath; they say nothing about any particular machine.

Third claim: is there one state space, up to renaming, that every honest record-carrier
has to have? I don’t claim it. Nothing needs it.

10.5 Bases from outside, and a relation I have to be honest about
The theorem is stated for any base, and the checked work instantiates it on three
models of computation that other people built: a small Turing machine (any program);
a register machine of the kind Cook and Reckhow described in 1973, with unit-cost
indirect addressing (any program); and a lambda calculus (call-by-value, meaning an
argument is worked out before it’s plugged in, and made deterministic by letting a
term with no step left to take step to itself). On each, the latch form holds, by the one
generic theorem applied to that base (the checked names are listed with the formal
statement below). So a register machine with an honest record is a register machine
plus a cup. So is a lambda calculus. (There are two more instances, both machines I
build later: the small one, where the flag is shown to be a latch directly, in Section 14,
and the big one, in Section 23.)

Here are the three bases explicitly. A base needs a state, a next-state function, a set of
starting states and a halting predicate; the latch theorem asks for nothing else about
its instruction vocabulary.



                                             144
The Thiele Machine                                                                Devon Thiele


Definition 10.3 (Three concrete bases). The tape base has a finite Boolean list t, a head
index h, a program counter q and a natural-number cost field. Reading beyond the list
returns false. Writing at h extends the list with false cells if needed, then changes that
cell. Moving right increments h and extends the list through the new head position.
Moving left decrements a positive h; at h = 0, it prepends a false cell and keeps the
head at zero. A fixed finite program contains these instructions:

Instruction                                   Next state
Write a bit                                   Perform the write and advance q by one.
Move left or right                            Perform the move and advance q by one.
Branch to j                                   Set q := j if the current cell is true; otherwise
                                              advance q by one.
Halt                                          Leave the entire state unchanged.
ClaimTapeIsZero with parameter δ              Advance q by one and do nothing else.



An out-of-range program fetch is Halt. Every state is allowed as a starting state, and
halting means the fetched instruction is Halt. The cost field is preserved by every
instruction in this base. In particular, its ClaimTapeIsZero instruction neither erases
the tape nor charges the cost field; the name supplies no extra semantics.

The random-access base has a register function X : N → N and a program counter q.
For a fixed finite program its instructions are:

Instruction                                   Next state
Constant (i, c)                               Set X (i ) := c.
Add (i, j, k )                                Set X (i ) := X ( j) + X (k ).
Subtract (i, j, k )                           Set X (i ) := max(0, X ( j) − X (k)).
Indirect load (i, j)                          Set X (i ) := X ( X ( j)).
Indirect store (i, j)                         Set X ( X (i )) := X ( j).
Positive branch ( j, a)                       Set q := a if X ( j) > 0; otherwise advance q
                                              by one.
Jump to a                                     Set q := a.
Halt                                          Leave the entire state unchanged.



Each register-writing instruction advances q by one; its operands are evaluated in the
old state, and all other registers are preserved. A fetch outside the program also leaves
the state unchanged. Starting states have q = 0 and arbitrary register contents. A
state is halted when it fetches Halt or is outside the program. Unit cost here concerns
instruction counting, not the certification ledger.

The lambda base uses the terms and weak call-by-value rule defined in Definition 11.3.
To compute its next state, first try to reduce the function part of an application. If that
part cannot step and is an abstraction, either substitute an argument that is already
an abstraction or take a step in the argument. If neither applies, the term cannot

                                           145
The Thiele Machine                                                              Devon Thiele


step. Variables and abstractions cannot step by themselves, and there is no reduction
under an abstraction. The base leaves a term unchanged when it cannot step and calls
precisely those terms halted. Every term is allowed as a starting state, including open
terms.


These definitions make the examples instances of the base record. Applying the latch
theorem to them does not assert universality, an execution-time bound, or a simulation
between the three bases.

There’s also a relation defined between bases, weak base equivalence: two bases are
equivalent when some correspondence covers their start states both ways, related
states agree on an observation and on halting, and one step on one side is matched by
some number of steps, possibly zero, on the other. That “some number of steps” is the
stuttering idea Leslie Lamport (the same Lamport as Section 6’s message counters) put
forward in 1983: a fine-grained machine and a coarse one shouldn’t count as different
because one takes three ticks to do what the other does in one. The relation carries no
cost; a machine that multiplies huge numbers in one step and a Turing machine differ
in price, not in records. It’s proved to be an equivalence relation, and the latch form is
preserved across it.

There is a limit to that statement. The “preserved across it” proof throws away its
equivalence hypothesis; the latch holds on every base regardless, so the preservation
is true for a boring reason. And nowhere in the checked work are two of the bases
actually related by this relation. The relation is defined, it’s an equivalence, and it is
not used to connect the Turing machine to the register machine to the lambda calculus,
or any of them to the machines in Part IV. It would be easy to read that list as if it did.
What’s proved is that each base, separately, carries a latch. That’s the honest sentence.


Definition 10.4 (Weak base equivalence). Bases B1 and B2 , with observations o1 and
o2 into one common set, are weakly equivalent when some relation R relates every
starting state of each to some starting state of the other, and any related x, y have
o1 ( x ) = o2 (y), the same halting, some n ≥ 0 with R(nextB1 ( x ), nextnB2 (y)), and some
n ≥ 0 with R(nextnB1 ( x ), nextB2 (y)).


Theorem 10.9 (Outside bases, and the relation). (1) Weak base equivalence is reflexive,
symmetric and transitive. (2) If two bases are weakly equivalent, Theorem 10.1 holds over one
exactly when it holds over the other. (3) Theorem 10.1 holds over each of the three bases in
Definition 10.3, for every fixed program where the base has one.

Proof. (1) Reflexive with equality as R and one step against one. Symmetric by revers-
ing R. Transitive by composing the two relations; a step on the first base is matched by
n steps on the second, and those n steps by some number on the third, by induction
on n. (2) and (3) apply Theorem 10.1 directly. In (2) the equivalence hypothesis is


                                            146
The Thiele Machine                                                                  Devon Thiele


discarded.

Checked as weak_base_equiv_refl_holds, weak_base_equiv_sym_holds, w
eak_base_equiv_trans_holds (through weak_match_left_runs and weak_
match_right_runs), weak_equiv_preserves_record_latch_holds and re
cord_axis_is_latch_on_tm_holds (CrossBaseGranularity.v), record_axis_
is_latch_on_ram_holds (CrossBaseGranularityRAM.v) and record_axis_is_
latch_on_l_holds (CrossBaseGranularityL.v), with the definitions in CrossBaseG-
ranularityCore.v.

10.6 Records with more than two values
A cup has two positions. Some records have more: a counter of how many checks
passed, a level that only rises. The same reasoning goes through one threshold at a
time. For each value a, “the record has reached a” is a yes/no reading, and each of
those readings is a latch. What doesn’t go through is squeezing the whole record into
one cup. “Rises” needs one word: the values come with an order ≤, “is at or below,”
which needn’t compare every pair (that’s what makes it a partial order), and [ a ≤ x ] is
the yes/no reading “x has reached a.”


Definition 10.5 (A growing record). Let the record take values in a set A with a
partial order ≤ decided by a Boolean test. A record ρ on M, with cover π onto a
base B, is an honest growing record when: there is one function f with ρ(next M (m)) =
f (π (m), ρ(m)); it grows, ρ(m) ≤ ρ(next M (m)); the ledger never goes down and every
step that changes ρ costs at least one; and some run from a starting state reaches a step
that changes it.


Theorem 10.10 (Growing records are families of latches). (1) For every honest growing
record there is an h with

                     [ a ≤ ρ(next M (m))] = [ a ≤ ρ(m)] ∨ h( a, π (m), ρ(m))

for every value a and state m: each threshold is a latch, whose event may read the current value.
(2) The thresholds determine the value: if [ a ≤ x ] = [ a ≤ y] for every a, then x = y. (3) For a
growing record, charging every change is the same as charging every threshold that switches
on. (4) One latch is not enough: a three-valued record that climbs 0 → 1 → 2 over a one-state
base, each climb charged one, is honest, and no single Boolean latch with a decoding from the
base state and the latch reproduces it. (5) A chain of distinct k-bit words, each word’s set bits
contained in the next one’s, has at most k + 1 members.

Proof. (1) Take h( a, b, x ) = [ a ̸≤ x ] ∧ [ a ≤ f (b, x )]. If a ≤ ρ(m) already, growth and
transitivity give a ≤ ρ(next M (m)); otherwise the equation is the definition of h. (2)
Antisymmetry, with a = x and a = y. (3) Growth plus antisymmetry turn “the value
changed” into “some threshold switched on,” and back. (4) Over one base state, a


                                               147
The Thiele Machine                                                               Devon Thiele


latch and a decoding can produce at most two values, and the record takes three. (5)
Each strict step up the chain adds at least one set bit, and there are only k bits.

Checked as growing_record_decomposes_holds, thresholds_determine_
record_holds, record_price_iff_threshold_price_holds, one_latch_
refuted and chain_needs_bits_holds (GrowingRecord.v), with the definitions
in GrowingRecordCore.v. The order need not be finite; (5) is the finite-memory bound.

10.7 What the base being free buys you
The reason this section exists is to answer the suspicion I started with. The record isn’t
special pleading for one machine. Over any base, under rules you can read, a record
that answers to the computation and never comes down is a latch on an event, and
the proof doesn’t care what the base is. What a particular machine adds is not the
latch; it’s a choice of event and a choice of price list, and both are choices. The surcharged
cup shows the first: the bill can change and the record not notice. The two cups on
one die show the second: the rules are happy with either event. Any machine I build
will have to make both choices, and whether its choice of event is the right one is an
open question, and I’ll get to it. Before that, the question every machine with a record
has to face, and that no amount of good design makes go away. A record is worth
keeping because something later leans on it instead of working the thing out again:
that’s Section 2’s glance, reading a block’s bucket off the table instead of applying the
rule from scratch. Call any move like that a shortcut, and call it sound when it gives the
answer the long way would have given. (That gloss is about cost, leaning instead of
redoing, and the wall I’m about to show you doesn’t look at cost at all; the next section
says exactly what it does look at.) So: can a machine decide, from inside, whether its
own shortcuts are sound? That’s a wall, and it’s the same wall Gödel and Turing hit,
and I have to show you that it’s there before I show you anything that pretends to be
on the other side of it.

11 The diagonal
In Section 2 I said you’d watch the same move get made again and again as the book
went on: somebody says “everything is X,” it’s true enough to do real work with,
and then somebody draws the diagonal. I owe you the diagonal itself now, because
Section 10 just handed a record to any system that steps, and the next thing anyone
wants from a system with a record is for it to tell sound shortcuts from unsound ones
by itself. Before I let anything claim that, I have to show you the wall every such claim
runs into, and then show you exactly where a system with a record stands relative to
the wall. Not on the far side. Nobody’s on the far side.

11.1 Five names and a table
Do this first, with a pencil, because the whole family of arguments is this one trick
and you should own it. Write five friends’ names down the left of a page. Next to
each name, write a five-digit string of zeros and ones, anything you like. Now build a


                                             148
The Thiele Machine                                                                 Devon Thiele


new string: its first digit is the opposite of the first digit of the first row; its second digit
is the opposite of the second digit of the second row; and so on down the diagonal.
Look at what you’ve made. It differs from row one in position one, from row two in
position two, from every row at that row’s own position. So it’s nobody’s string. Your
table of five missed something.

With five rows and five digits that’s a cute fact. Georg Cantor’s point, in 1891, was
that it works for any list, however long, even infinite: hand me a complete list of all
infinite strings of two symbols, I’ll walk the diagonal flipping as I go, and I’ll hand
you back a string that’s on no row. So there is no complete list. There are more such
strings than there are places on any list, and that’s where “some infinities are bigger
than others” comes from. (He wrote the two symbols as m and w, not 0 and 1, and that
paper wasn’t even his first proof of the fact; the 1874 one was harder. The diagonal
was him finding the easy way.)

Now look at what the argument did, because it’s going to do the same thing again
and again, in new clothes, and I want you to recognise it each time. (Not every name
below is a flipped diagonal in the table sense. Kleene’s theorem is the tool that makes
the diagonal buildable, Rice’s is the general form, and Thompson’s is an attack that
uses the same trick.) There was a table: rows are the things being listed, columns are
questions, each cell says “does row i do column j.” There was the diagonal: the cells
where a thing is asked about itself. There was a flip: something with no fixed point,
like turning yes into no, applied along the diagonal. And the thing that got refuted
was the assumed object, the complete list. Nothing outside the assumption was touched.
Table, diagonal, flip, and the assumption eats itself. Hold those four.

11.2 The same move, again and again
Russell, 1902, from Section 2: the collection of all collections that don’t contain them-
selves. That’s Cantor’s flipped diagonal with “contains” as the table, and Russell
said as much; he got there by running Cantor’s argument on a supposed collection
of everything. What got refuted was the assumed object, the collection of everything,
and Zermelo’s fix was to stop assuming it.

Jules Richard, 1905: some English phrases define real numbers (“the ratio of a circle’s
circumference to its diameter”); there are only countably many phrases, so list the
numbers they define in order; run Cantor’s diagonal down their decimal expansions
and you get a real number no phrase defines, except that you just defined it, in the
phrase that describes the diagonal. The lesson that came out of that one is the lesson
this whole section turns on: keep apart the language a system talks in and the language
you use to talk about it. Mix them and the diagonal bites you.

Richard’s paradox has a cousin small enough to do at the table, and it comes with a
footnote I can’t resist. Russell, the first to put it in print, in 1906, credited it to G. G.
Berry, a junior librarian at the Bodleian Library in Oxford. A paradox that has outlived
empires, and it came from the library desk. In the version in Principia Mathematica it’s

                                              149
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


about syllables. Take the phrase “the least integer not nameable in fewer than nineteen
syllables.” There are only so many phrases shorter than nineteen syllables, so they
name only so many numbers, so some least number is left over, and the phrase picks
it out. Now count the phrase: the, least, in-te-ger, not, name-a-ble, in, few-er, than,
nine-teen, syl-la-bles. Eighteen. In eighteen syllables it has named the number that
can’t be named in fewer than nineteen. Same lesson as Richard’s, in a smaller coat:
“nameable” is a word about the language, used inside the language, and that’s where
the bite is.
