deployed system takes evidence from that system, and no row shows that certification
is the one event every model has to price.

So the thing my toy charges for, the moment the record is written, is charged for in
one of five real systems, and in that one the designers had to patch the place where
the charge could be clawed back. I find that neither a vindication nor a refutation. It’s
a fact about what people built, and what they built was mostly walls (hash chains,


                                             172
The Thiele Machine                                                               Devon Thiele


signatures) and penalties for contradiction, not tolls on commitment. Whether a toll
on commitment is a better design than a wall is not something I can prove, and I won’t
pretend the five say so. What I read in them, and it’s a reading of five fragments I
chose, is that the record axis is real in each of them (each has a bit that goes one way)
and that the price axis is mostly empty.

That leaves the question Section 10 raised and Section 13 has to face. Five systems,
five different events chosen as “the record”: finalized, committed, attested, logged,
checked. Is there anything that picks out one event as the one worth recording, or is
it a free choice every time? I have a guess. It’s a conjecture, and I’ll show you how to
kill it.

13 The pointer conjecture
Here’s where I am. A record over any base is a latch on an event (Section 10), and the
event is a free choice (Section 10 again, the two cups on one die). Five real systems
each picked a different event (Section 12). The toll in this book sits on certification.
Why that one? I don’t have a proof. I have a conjecture, and the honest shape of
a conjecture is: here’s the claim, here’s where I got the idea, here’s what’s checked,
here’s what isn’t, and here’s how to kill it. In that order.

13.1 The claim
Of all the events a machine could put on its meter, the ones its price list charges for
and its counter adds up, certification is the one whose records get copied: checked,
stored, and relied on across independent places that share no other state. Rival events
leave no such trail. If that’s true, certification isn’t a free choice; it’s the one event the
world around the machine keeps redundant copies of, and that’s a reason to price it
and not the others.

There’s a second handle on the same question, and it comes from Section 4. The
permanent-certificate theorem never uses the word certification for anything special:
given Section 4’s rule that forgetting is charged, it prices any yes-or-no reading that,
once on, stays on, on a machine with finite memory. So it points at a narrower candi-
date: the events to price are the ones that write a record no later step can take back.
Certification is one of them. As an exact answer that candidate is false, because a
merging step can also revoke (Section 4’s three cards). Whether the records that prolif-
erate are the permanent ones, and whether proliferation picks out anything the merge
criterion doesn’t, is what the two handles have to settle between them.

Two holes in that, which I can see from here, so you don’t have to find them for me.
The first is a missing premise. Even if the world copies certification records more than
any other kind, “copied” doesn’t give you “priced” on its own. Something has to
connect them, and the best candidate I have is a premise about incentives: a record
that many independent parties copy and lean on is exactly the record worth forging,
so it’s the one where a price buys the most protection. That’s a reasonable premise.


                                             173
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


It’s also a premise, and as I’ve stated the conjecture, it’s missing. The second hole is a
circle. If “certification” just means “the record other people rely on,” then of course it’s
the one that gets relied on and copied, and the claim says nothing. So the event has to
be picked out without mentioning reliance: here it’s a reading going up for good right
after a check of the same claim passed, which you can find in a run without asking
who reads it. Whether the world copies that event more than its rivals is then a real
question, and it could come out no.

That’s the whole conjecture. Now the rest of what a conjecture owes you.

13.2 Where the shape comes from, and how much of it survived
The shape is from physics, and I want to tell you where exactly, because I borrowed a
word and I didn’t get to keep the whole thing.

Quantum mechanics has a famous problem: a system can be in a blend of states,
and when you measure it you find one definite state, and nobody agrees on what
“measuring” did. In 1981 Wojciech Zurek asked a sharper question: of all the ways
a measuring device could end up, why does it end up recording one particular kind
of quantity (the position of a pointer on a dial, say) and not some blend? His answer,
developed over twenty years and summarised in a 2009 paper called “Quantum
Darwinism,” is that the environment decides. The air, the light, the table, everything
the device touches, is constantly interacting with it, and only certain states of the
device survive that interaction; those are the pointer states. And more: the environment
doesn’t just select them, it copies them. The light bouncing off a dial carries the dial’s
reading to every corner of the room, redundantly, so that a thousand observers can
each read a different scrap of the environment and all agree on where the pointer
is, without touching the dial. Objectivity, on this view, is redundancy: a property is
objective when many independent fragments of the world each carry it.

That’s the shape I borrowed. Certification is to a machine’s ecosystem (the machine
plus everything around it that reads, stores and relies on its records) what the pointer
reading is to the room: the thing that gets copied everywhere. It’s a good shape and
I think it’s the right intuition. Here’s what survived into the checked work, and I’m
going to be exact because the word “redundant” is doing less than it does for Zurek.

Zurek’s redundancy is graded (each fragment carries almost all the information, with
some small loss) and it requires the fragments to be disjoint: different observers reading
different parts of the environment. The checked definition is the zero-loss case with no
disjointness at all. An ecosystem is a state type, some number of observers, and one bit
per observer; an observer records an event when its bit is true exactly when the event
holds; an event proliferates when every observer records it. Nothing in that says two
observers draw on separate parts of the state. They could all be reading the same bit.
The file says so itself. So I kept the word and not the independence that makes Zurek’s
version mean “objective.” That’s a gap between the conjecture’s prose and its formal
object, and the prose is where the conjecture lives.

                                            174
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


There’s a deeper mismatch in the borrowing, and it runs against the book, so it goes
here. In Zurek’s picture the whole thing, system and device and environment together,
evolves by quantum mechanics’ rule for closed systems, and that rule never sends
two states to one; every step can be run backwards. So, seen from the whole, the
environment’s copying is just that, copying: the dial’s reading gets written onto fresh
light, nothing anywhere is forgotten, and it’s Door one of Section 4 with the rest of
the universe as the endless strip. That’s the operation this book says is free, Bennett
writing on a blank page. The forgetting shows up only when you look at the dial alone
and ignore what the light carried off. Then a blend of pointer readings decays into a
plain either-or, and two different blends can decay into the same either-or: two states,
one result, a merge in the coarse picture. So the opening chapter’s “every settling
forgets” fits the dial’s own view and not the view from the whole, and the thing the
conjecture leans on, proliferation, is the free half of the story. What that does to the
conjecture: if there’s a price, it isn’t on the copying. It’s on whatever makes the copy
final from the dial’s side, and the claim above, as written, points at the copy.

Which leaves the question to ask of any borrowed shape: has anybody checked the
original? For a long time quantum Darwinism was a theory without a lab. Then, in
2018 and 2019, three groups working separately, in Italy, China and Germany, went
looking for its fingerprint. The German one, at Ulm, with Zurek among the authors,
watched the spin of a single defect inside a diamond and the carbon atoms around it,
and saw the redundancy the theory predicts: the defect’s state turned up copied in
its surroundings, and it didn’t take much of the surroundings before more of them
told you nothing new. The other two did it with photons. Is that the bottom? Not
by a long way, and the people involved said so. Zurek himself pointed out that the
photon experiments make their copies artificially and that the diamond’s environment
is small, and others noted that all three are schematic versions of a real environment
and don’t rule out rival accounts. So the shape I borrowed has passed some first tests
in a lab, at the scale of a handful of atoms or photons, with the caveats written on it.
None of that touches the conjecture here, which is about machines and never rested
on quantum physics. It changes the picture: what I borrowed is a lead somebody is
checking, not a settled fact I get to lean on.

13.3 What’s checked
Definitions, a toy, a survey, and two refutations of things that would have been
stronger.

The definitions above, plus “unique pointer among rivals”: the event proliferates and
none of a listed set of rival events does. Uniqueness is relative to the list, necessarily,
since any event that holds on exactly the same states as a proliferating event prolifer-
ates whenever it does: the same fact under another name, so someone has to say which
names count as rivals. And the conjecture itself, as a schema: for every ecosystem in
some class, its metered event is the unique pointer among its rivals. The class and the
rivals are inputs. Nothing about them is proved.

                                           175
The Thiele Machine                                                                  Devon Thiele


Here’s the formal object, small enough to hold in one hand.


Definition 13.1 (Ecosystem, records, proliferates, pointer). An ecosystem is a type of
states, a number N of observers, and for each observer i a Boolean fragment Fi on
states. Observer i records an event E (a property of states) when, for every state s, E(s)
holds exactly when Fi (s) is true. E proliferates when every observer i < N records it. E
is the unique pointer among a list of rival events when E proliferates and no rival in the
list does. Given a class C of ecosystems, and for each member a designated metered
event and a list of rivals, the pointer criterion holds for C when every member’s metered
event is the unique pointer among its rivals.


Nothing in the definition makes two fragments read different parts of the state, and
“metered” is only a label: the definition has no metering in it.


Conjecture 13.1 (The pointer conjecture). Let C be the class of ecosystems that faithfully
model deployed record-keeping disciplines, observed through independent carriers (separate
parts of the world, each holding its own copy), with each discipline’s certification event as its
metered event and the other events a step rule could meter as rivals. Then the pointer criterion
holds for C.


The conjecture leans on four notions left without precise mathematical definitions:
what it is to “faithfully model” a system, which systems count as “deployed,” what
makes carriers “independent,” and which events “a step rule could meter.” That’s
why it’s a conjecture and not a theorem with a missing proof.

A toy: three observers on a replicated ledger, where certification proliferates and
“work done” doesn’t. The file labels it a sanity check, and it is one, not evidence.


Theorem 13.2 (The toy). Let the toy have states (a certified bit, a work count), three observers,
and every fragment equal to the certified bit. Then “certified” is the unique pointer among the
one rival “work at least 1”.

Proof. Every fragment is the certified bit, so every observer records “certified” by
definition. For the rival, take the state with the bit false and work 1: the event holds
and observer 0’s fragment is false, so observer 0 does not record it.

Checked as toy_cert_unique_pointer and toy_work_not_proliferating
(PointerObservable.v).

A survey of twelve events, one checked theorem: for each of the five systems in
Section 12, the designated event (finalized, committed, attested, logged, checked)
proliferates in the observer map I wrote for that system, and a rival (proposer work,

The Thiele Machine                                                                   Devon Thiele


a scratch counter, measurement noise, submission latency, prover steps) doesn’t. The

which does not proliferate, and a digital signature, which does. Twelve rows. And a
thirteenth that I think is the most important one: swap which bit every observer copies,

Theorem 13.3 (The survey, and the swap). (1) In each of the five observer models (proof-
 of-stake, gas, attestation, transparency, proof-carrying), the designated event proliferates and
 the designated rival does not; in the symmetric-MAC model the authentic-tag event does not

 pairs of bits (first, second), with three observers whose fragments all equal the second bit. Then
“second is true” is the unique pointer among the one rival “first is true”.

Proof. Each confirmation holds by definition: each observer’s fragment is true exactly
when the event holds. Each refutation exhibits one state where the event holds and
some observer’s bit is down. In (2) that state is (true, false).

Checked as twelve_candidate_measurements_checked and swapped_event
_is_pointer_checked (RecordProliferationSurvey.v, statements in RecordProlifer-
ationSurveyTarget.v); the five designated models together are five_labeled_mode
ls_have_selected_pointer (PointerObservableReductions.v), an instance of the
indexed form of the criterion, pointer_criterion_holds_indexed.

Two stronger claims, both refuted, and I’d ask you not to merge them because they
fail for different reasons.

The first stronger claim: every forgery-resistant commitment proliferates. If that were true,
certification would be the pointer because it’s the commitment. It’s refuted in three
observer models (deniable authentication, where only the designated verifier’s bit
tracks the event; a symmetric MAC, where the key holders share a secret and nobody
else can check; an object capability, an unforgeable token that grants access to whoever
holds it) and confirmed in two (a public log; a digital signature). Build the first with
three observers: give one a copy of the event’s bit and the other two a constant false.
The one records it; it doesn’t proliferate. The checked half is the map computation.
Whether my maps are fair to the real designs is argued in prose, and you should argue
back.


Theorem 13.4 (One blind observer is enough). (1) In any ecosystem, if some observer
i < N has Fi (s0 ) false at a state s0 where E holds, then E does not proliferate. (2) Let the


                                               177
The Thiele Machine                                                                 Devon Thiele


deniable model have states (authentic, verifier-accepts), three observers, observer 0’s fragment
the authentic bit and observers 1 and 2 constantly false. Then observer 0 records “authentic”,
and “authentic” does not proliferate. The symmetric-MAC and object-capability models also
fail to proliferate their events; the public-log and signature models proliferate theirs.

Proof. (1) Recording would require E(s0 ) ⇐⇒ Fi (s0 ), and the left side is true while
the right is false. (2) Observer 0’s fragment is true exactly when the event holds. Apply
(1) with observer 1 and the state (true, true). The other three refutations apply (1) to a
blind observer of their own model, and the two confirmations hold by definition.

Checked as blind_observer_blocks_proliferation and labeled_model_v
erdicts (PointerObservableCounterexamples.v). The theorem is about the observer
maps. That a third party in deniable authentication really cannot be convinced is the
modelling claim, and the model has no transcript, key or verifier in it to check that
against.

The second stronger claim: agreement plus accuracy plus locality imply permanence. That
is, if all observers agree, each sees the event exactly, and each updates by the same
local rule with no coordinator, then the recorded event can’t be undone. Refuted by
the smallest thing imaginable: one bit, two observers who both see it, and the rule
“flip.” All three conditions hold and true becomes false in one step (toggle_game_r
efutes_strong_pointer_necessity). Do it on paper; it takes a minute and it’s
humbling. What does give permanence is durability, “an observer’s true view stays
true,” added as a premise, and then it follows in a few lines (durable_consensus_
implies_permanence). So durability is the premise doing the work, and durability
is Section 4’s permanence wearing a different coat. Agreement doesn’t buy it. Do
the paper version again with one change: the rule is “stay true once true” instead of
“flip,” and the bit can’t fall, because the rule won’t let it, not because the observers
agree. (The machine I build later has a reading that’s durable in exactly this sense;
that instance is Section 23’s.) None of this rules out a narrower theorem with real
assumptions about the network, the adversary or durability; it rules out these two
strong forms.


Definition 13.2 (Observation game). A game has states, a number N of observers, a
Boolean event e, a Boolean view Vi for each observer, and a step map. For i, j < N it
has consensus when Vi = Vj on every state; authenticity when Vi (s) = e(s) for every
state and every i < N; coordinator-free update when one function ℓ on Booleans has
Vi (step(s)) = ℓ(Vi (s)) for every state and every i < N; durable views when Vi (s) true
gives Vi (step(s)) true for every i < N; and a permanent event when e(s) true gives
e(step(s)) true.


Theorem 13.5 (Agreement does not buy permanence; durability does). (1) It is false that
every game with N > 0, consensus, authenticity and coordinator-free update has a permanent


                                              178
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


event. (2) Every game with N > 0, authenticity and durable views has a permanent event.

Proof. (1) The toggle game: states are Booleans, two observers, event and both views
the identity, step “flip”. Consensus and authenticity hold trivially, the local rule is
“flip”, and the state true steps to false. (2) If e(s) is true, observer 0’s view is true by
authenticity, stays true by durability, and authenticity turns it back into e(step(s)).

Checked as toggle_game_refutes_strong_pointer_necessity and durab
le_consensus_implies_permanence (EcosystemGame.v, definitions in Ecosys-
temGameTarget.v).

13.4 What isn’t checked, and must stay that way on the page
That certification in deployed systems is singled out by redundant proliferation across
independent carriers. The proposed criterion has no precise definition of “independent”
or “deployed,” and no cost law connecting proliferation to price. Every correspon-
dence between a Coq observer map and a real system is a sentence I wrote. The
conjecture is a conjecture, and anyone who says the formal object proves it is reading
more than is there.

13.5 How to kill it
Three ways, in the order I’d try them.

One: find a deployed discipline that prices a non-proliferating event. A real system
with a toll on something nobody copies. That breaks “the priced event is the copied
one.”

Two: find a rival event that proliferates as well as certification in a real ecosystem. Then
certification isn’t unique and the conjecture’s “the one” is wrong. Or do it in a model:
show that something like a multiplication count or a head reversal proliferates by
the same standard I used, so the criterion picks out more than one event and decides
nothing.

Three: formalise an ecosystem honestly, with independence defined, where certifica-
tion fails the test. The symmetric-MAC row is already most of the way there for a
different claim; push it.

The checked work has already refuted two stronger forms of its own claim, which I
take as a sign the method works and as a warning about the main claim.

13.6 The end of the logic
That’s Part III, and the end of the logic that started in Part II. Here’s what it earned. A
toll on raising a flag is forced by three premises (Section 4). Learning is free, commit-
ting isn’t (Section 5). The counter is arithmetic once the schedule is fixed (Section 6).
A window with a colliding pair in it can’t price the flag exactly (Section 7). Entitle-
ment is an object, a check, and a paid event, and, given lists, a tree and a covering


                                            179
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


that someone supplies, it costs the index bits it commits to (Section 8). Insight is a
committed relation, not a feeling (Section 9). Over any base a record is a latch, with
two free choices, the price list and the event (Section 10). No inside procedure whose
flip a substrate can represent decides a shortcut property, given a recursion theorem,
which the nat family has by construction and L has by proof; on the machine Part IV
builds, a small guest gets one by proof too, and the whole machine can’t have one for
every map; a record carries the commitment instead (Section 11). Of five specifications,
read through my transcriptions, one prices the write (Section 12). And which event to
record is a conjecture with a borrowed shape and a listed set of refutations (Section 13).

What none of that is: a machine. Every theorem so far quantifies over “any states,
any steps,” or is about a small copy of somebody else’s system, or points forward at a
thing I keep promising. That’s the abstract part of the book, and it’s done. From the
next page on I stop saying “any machine” and build two, mine. A small one first, the
least I can make that still shows the whole model, and then a big one with every part
named and every price written down, so that everything above finally has something
to bump into. If a statement up there doesn’t mean what I think it means, that’s where
it’ll show. Part IV is the thing. Let’s see if it holds weight.



Part IV

The machine
14 The smallest honest machine
Parts I to III never built anything. They said “any states, any steps,” and whenever a
picture was needed, a board or some chairs or a cup stood in. Now I have to build a
machine, and the first worry I have about that is a slightly embarrassing one. Say I
build a big machine, with dozens of instructions, some picked for reasons and some
picked because I had to pick something, and every theorem holds of it. What did that
show? That the model works, or that I’m good at stacking instructions until the proofs
go through? A big machine is a wonderful place to hide a mistake. It’s a garage so full
of stuff that you could lose a car in it.

So before the big one, the small one. The least I can build that still shows the whole
model, every piece of it, with nothing waved at. If the idea only stands up with dozens
of instructions holding it, it’s their idea and not the model’s. If it stands up on six, the
six are the idea, and you can hold all of them in your head at once, which is more than
I can say for most things I’ve built.

The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


14.1 What the model actually asks for
Here’s what Parts II and III say the model adds to a machine. A record: a flag that
reads no or yes, “certified” or not. A toll: the step that raises the flag costs something
(Section 3). A ledger: the running total of those costs, a whole number that only climbs
(Section 6). And Section 10 proved a thing that turns out to make this whole chapter
possible: over any base at all, an honest record is a latch, a bit that switches on at an
event the base decides and never switches off (Theorem 10.1). The record watches the
base. It doesn’t compute anything the base couldn’t compute without it.

Push on that for a second, because it cuts the job in half. If the record adds no comput-
ing power, then all the computing power comes from the base, and the question “how
small can the machine be” splits into two questions that don’t touch each other. For
the base: what’s the smallest thing that can compute everything there is to compute?
For the record: what’s the smallest set of pieces that makes the flag mean something?

One honest asterisk on “don’t touch,” because the machine below makes it matter.
What’s blind is the flag and the ledger: the base never reads either of them. But
the pieces that make the flag mean something (a table of checked facts, a slot for a
commitment, a trap that stops a refused run) have to sit where the step can read them,
which is in the base, and they do steer the run: a failed check stops a program dead.
The latch theorem holds wherever you draw the line between base and record, which
is exactly why it can’t tell you where the meaning lives. On this machine the meaning
lives on the base side of the line, in the bookkeeping, and the flag on top reports it.

The record question, the second of those two, is the one Part III left open, and it’s open
on purpose. Section 9 said that testing a claim and committing to it are two different
acts, and that nothing in the five parts of the model makes the second wait for the first.
Read Section 3’s definition again with that in mind: a machine where you pay one
unit and raise the flag over nothing in particular obeys every rule in it. That machine
is honest about the price and silent about what was bought. A receipt for nothing. The
toll alone can’t fix that, because the toll is a rule about cost, and “was this earned” is a
question about order: did a check happen, of this claim, before the commitment, with
nothing changing underneath in between?

This machine is my attempt to make the order part of the machine, in the smallest
place I could find to do it. I’ll show you the pieces, then the proofs, then the places it
falls short, which there are, and which I’d rather you hear from me.

14.2 Where the counters come from
The base first, and the base isn’t mine. It’s Marvin Minsky’s. In a 1961 paper in
the Annals of Mathematics, and then in his 1967 book Computation: Finite and Infinite
Machines, Minsky studied a machine so bare it’s almost a joke. Picture a few bins of
pebbles and a numbered list of instructions. There are only two kinds of instruction:
put a pebble in bin c and go to the next line; or, if bin c has a pebble, take one out


                                            181
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


and jump to line j, and if it’s empty, just go to the next line. That’s it. No memory, no
tape, no arithmetic beyond plus one and minus one. When the line you’re on has no
instruction, the machine stops.

What Minsky showed is that two bins are enough to compute anything a Turing
machine can compute, as long as you’re willing to pack the input in a strange way.
The trick is to keep many numbers inside one number, as the powers of different
primes (2x 3y 5z holds three numbers in one), and to do arithmetic on the exponents
by multiplying and dividing with the second bin as scratch space. It is as slow as it
sounds. Exponentially slow. A two-counter machine doing your taxes would finish
sometime after the sun doesn’t. But “universal” is a claim about what’s possible, not
about what’s pleasant, and on that claim two bins of pebbles are as strong as anything.

Who cares? Minsky did, because the question then was where the edge of computation
sits and how little machinery reaches it. You should, because it means the base of this
chapter’s machine hides nothing: if it can compute everything with plus one, minus
one and a jump, then nothing about the record can be smuggling computing power in
through some instruction I made fancy. And I care because it’s the smallest universal
base I know of that is already in a Coq library, so the hard part (proving that its halting
question is undecidable) is someone else’s checked work and not my say-so.

And the pebbles aren’t only my picture. They were somebody’s actual machine, the
same year. In one issue of the Canadian Mathematical Bulletin, September 1961, Z. A.
Melzak described a computer made of distinguishable holes and an unlimited supply
of pebbles, with one three-place operation, and a few pages later Joachim Lambek
trimmed it to two moves: put a pebble in hole X; take one out of hole X if there’s one
to take. He called it an infinite abacus, and early on he writes “Our method is probably
not new,” which is a hard sentence to beat. He also tells anybody who distrusts infinity
not to worry about all those holes, since any one computation only ever uses finitely
many of them. Is that two inventions or one? Lambek says his was a modification
of Melzak’s, so call it one and a half, with Minsky’s as a separate find the same year.
And then Lambek went somewhere you wouldn’t guess: in 1986, with Philip Scott,
he wrote a book showing that typed lambda calculi and a certain kind of category are
essentially the same thing. Pebbles to category theory in one career, which is the trip
this Part takes too, in four sections instead of twenty-five years. Does any of it change
the argument? No. The library and I use Minsky’s version and Minsky’s name. But a
bare machine that several people reach for in the same year looks less like anybody’s
invention and more like a shape that was sitting there.

One word clash, before it bites. Minsky’s machine is usually called a counter machine,
and its bins are counters. Section 6 also had a counter: the ledger µ, the number that
only climbs. Same word, two completely different things, and I’d love to say I set that
up on purpose. In this chapter, counter means one of Minsky’s two bins, called A and
B, and the climbing total is always the ledger µ.


                                           182
The Thiele Machine                                                          Devon Thiele


14.3 The machine
Here’s the whole state. I’ll say each piece in words first.

   • Two counters, A and B. Each holds a whole number, with no upper limit.
   • A version for each counter, also a whole number with no limit. It starts at 0 and
     goes up by one every time its counter is written. Think of it as the counter’s
     edition number: a new value is a new edition.
   • A line number, which instruction comes next, counting from 1 the way Minsky
     does.
   • A fact table: a list of facts. A fact is three things stuck together: a property, a
     counter, and a version. “A is even, as of edition 3” is a fact. The table has room
     for sixteen. Why sixteen? It’s a pick, with no derivation behind it, and what the
     pick costs is in the last subsection of this chapter, the one on what the machine
     doesn’t do.
   • A channel: either empty, or holding one fact. This is where a commitment sits.
   • A trap: one bit, down at the start. When it goes up, the machine has refused
     something, and it stays up.

Everything above is the core, the part the base moves. Outside the core sit the two
pieces from the model: the ledger µ and the flag. The machine never reads either of
them to decide what to do next. That’s not a promise, it’s how the step is written, and
it shows up as a theorem below.

The properties a fact can name come from a tiny fixed language with three words: is
zero; is even; and is at least n, for any whole number n you like. Each one comes in two
forms. There’s the checker, a little program that computes yes or no: compare with
0, look at the last bit, compare with n. And there’s the meaning, the plain arithmetic
statement the checker is supposed to be checking: the number is 0; the number is two
times something; n is less than or equal to the number. Why both? Because a checker
is code, and code can be wrong in ways that look right, and “the checker says yes” is
only worth anything once somebody has proved it says yes exactly when the meaning
is true. That proof is one line per property, and it’s the first block below.

Now the six instructions.

Instruction             What it does, when the trap is     Cost
                        down
INC c                   Adds one to counter c, adds one    0
                        to its version, goes to the next
                        line.

The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele



Instruction              What it does, when the trap is           Cost
                         down

CHECK p c                Runs the checker for p on c’s            1

The first three are Minsky’s machine, plus a HALT so a program can say it’s done.
The last three are the record’s. Read them as a chain: you can only certify with a
commitment in the channel, you can only commit to a fact in the table, and the only
way into the table is a check that passed. Three links, and each one costs.

One of what? One unit of µ, the same unit as Section 3’s toll. Why one and not
ten? Because one is the smallest positive whole number, which is honestly the whole
defence, and Section 4 is the section where I tried to do better than that for the flag.
That argument doesn’t reach this machine, though (the end of the chapter says why),
so here the one is a choice, full stop. The zeros matter just as much: computing is free
on this ledger. Plus one, minus one and jumping around cost nothing at all. Only the
three acts that make a claim cost, and each of them costs whether it passes or traps.
Failing is not a discount.

The version rule. Here’s why versions exist, with numbers. Start with A = 4, version
0. CHECK is even A passes, and the table gets the fact (even, A, 0). Now INC A: A
becomes 5, and its version becomes 1. Now COMMIT is even A. The machine looks
for (even, A, 1), the claim about the current edition. The table only has (even, A, 0).
No match. Trap. The old fact is still sitting in the table, still true about edition 0, and
completely useless for committing to anything about edition 1. A fact is about one
edition of one counter, and an edition never comes back, because versions only go
up and never wrap. That’s the whole trick against stale evidence: you can’t check a

                                               184
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


number, change it, and then commit to the check.

That’s the opening chapter’s time-of-check-to-time-of-use bug, the file checked and
then swapped, and the database answer to it is Kung and Robinson’s: at commit time,
check that nothing you read was written in the meantime, and back out if something
was. The version rule is that check, done by the step, on one counter. It also shows
where the guarantee ends. It works because one step does every write and every
write bumps a version. A second writer that changed a counter without bumping its
version, a second processor or a device writing memory on its own, would walk right
around it, and none of the theorems below are about a machine with one of those.

Notice what isn’t a write. DEC on a counter that’s already 0 doesn’t change the counter,
so it doesn’t change the version. It’s a test that happens to move the line number.

The fact table. Facts go in and never come out. Nothing erases them and nothing
overwrites them. When the table is full, a seventeenth CHECK doesn’t push an old
fact out to make room; it traps. That’s a choice with a bill attached, and I’ll put the bill
in the section on what this machine doesn’t do.

Traps. Any failure puts the trap up and changes nothing else. Once it’s up, every
instruction leaves the core alone. A stored program stops at a trap. But I also prove
things about any list of instructions, not just programs, because an adversary doesn’t
have to run my programs; they can feed the machine whatever they want. For those
lists, an instruction after a trap is still charged its cost, and still changes nothing.

Now the exact version.


Definition 14.1 (Properties, checker, meaning). A property is one of: Zero, Even, or
Ge(n) for a whole number n. The checker eval( p, v) computes yes or no: v = 0 by equal-
ity, evenness by the parity function, n ≤ v by comparison. The meaning holds( p, v) is
the arithmetic statement: v = 0; there is an m with v = 2m; n ≤ v.


Lemma 14.1 (The checker says what it means). For every property p and every whole
number v, eval( p, v) = yes if and only if holds( p, v).

Proof. Split on the three properties. Equality with zero returns yes exactly at zero;
comparison with n returns yes exactly when n ≤ v. For evenness, the parity checker
returns yes at 0, no at 1, and the same answer at v + 2 as at v. Induction in steps
of two gives yes exactly at 0, 2, 4, . . ., the numbers 2m. Those are precisely the three
meanings.

Checked as eval_iff (EarnedCore.v).


Definition 14.2 (Core, state, claim, start). A core k holds two counters A, B and their


                                            185
The Thiele Machine                                                               Devon Thiele


versions (whole numbers), a line number, a fact table (a list of facts, a fact being a
triple of a property, a counter and a version), a channel (empty or one fact), and a
trap bit. Write val(k, c) and ver(k, c) for counter c’s value and version. A state s is a
core, written core(s), with a ledger µ(s) and a flag cert(s). The claim p of c in k is the
fact ( p, c, ver(k, c)). The table’s room is 16. The start start( a, b) has counters a and b,
versions 0, line 1, an empty table, an empty channel, the trap down, µ = 0 and the flag
down. A state is clean when its table and channel are empty and its flag is down.


Definition 14.3 (Instructions, costs, the step). The instructions are INC c, DEC c j,
HALT, CHECK p c, COMMIT p c and CERTIFY, with effects on a core with the trap
down as in the table above. Passing any check, commitment or certification requires
the trap to be down. With that condition, CHECK passes when eval( p, val(k, c)) = yes
and the table holds fewer than 16 facts, COMMIT passes when the claim p of c is in
the table, and CERTIFY passes when the channel holds a fact; a failing one sets the
trap and changes nothing else. On a core with the trap up, every instruction changes
nothing. Costs: CHECK, COMMIT and CERTIFY cost 1, the rest 0. One step on a state
is
                                                                                     
      exec(s, i ) = cexec(core(s), i ), µ(s) + cost(i ), cert(s) ∨ fires(core(s), i ) ,

where cexec is the core’s step and fires(k, i ) is yes exactly when i is CERTIFY and
passes at k. For any list t of instructions (a trace), run(t, s) applies them in order and
cost(t) adds their costs. A program is a list of instructions numbered from 1; a program
run fetches the instruction at the line number and executes it, and stops when the trap
is up, the line holds HALT, or the line holds nothing.


Defined as cexec, exec, run, total_cost, run_prog, start and Minimal.Ear
nedCore.clean_start (EarnedCore.v).

Read the step line slowly, because the rest of the chapter leans on its shape. The core
moves by its own rule and nothing else. The ledger adds the cost. The flag becomes
“it was up, or this is a CERTIFY that passed.” The core’s move doesn’t mention µ or
the flag anywhere. The base is blind to the record by construction.

A worked run, the shortest one there is. The program: CHECK is zero A; COMMIT is
zero A; CERTIFY. Start at start(0, b), for any b. Line 1: A is 0, the checker says yes, the
table is empty so there’s room, and the fact (zero, A, 0) goes in. µ = 1. Line 2: the claim
about A’s current edition is (zero, A, 0), and it’s right there. Into the channel. µ = 2.
Line 3: the channel holds a fact, the flag goes up. µ = 3. Line 4 has no instruction, so
the program stops. Three paid acts, in order, a flag that’s up, and a channel that names
the last earned commitment, which here is (zero, A, 0).

Now start the same program at start(5, b). Line 1: A is 5, the checker says no, the trap
goes up, µ = 1, and the program stops right there. The flag is down, and you can run


                                            186
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


it as long as you like: it stays down. That second run is the point of the first. The same
three instructions certify from some starts and refuse from others, because the check
could have failed, and from most starts it does. A check like that has a no pile, which
is the only kind the opening chapter counts as establishing anything.

Could I have picked an even dumber claim? Sure, and the machine would have let me.
CHECK at least 0 A passes on every number there is, so CHECK, COMMIT, CERTIFY
on it raises the flag for 3 from every start (stop the presses: a number is at least zero).
The step doesn’t police that. It checks order, aboutness and that the checker tells the
truth; whether the question was worth asking isn’t something it looks at. A check that
can’t fail establishes nothing, and this machine will charge you three and raise the flag
for it anyway. Spotting that is the reader’s job, with the property in hand, and it’s on
the list at the end of the chapter.

14.4 It computes everything two counters can
First the base, because if the base can’t compute, nothing else here matters.


Definition 14.4 (Two-counter program, compile, window). A two-counter program M
is a list of instructions, each either MINC c or MDEC c j. A configuration is a triple
(line, a, b). One step of M: if the line holds no instruction, M has stopped; MINC adds
one to c and goes to the next line; MDEC subtracts one from c and goes to line j if c is
above 0, and goes to the next line if c is 0. mrun(n, M, x ) is n steps from x, staying put
once stopped. The compile of M replaces each MINC c by INC c and each MDEC c j by
DEC c j. The window of a core k is the triple (line number, val(k, A), val(k, B)).


Theorem 14.2 (Step for step). For every two-counter program M and every core k with the
trap down: M has stopped at window(k ) if and only if the program compile( M ) has halted
at k; and if M steps from window(k ) to y, then one program step of compile( M ) from k
lands on a core with window y and the trap still down. So for every n, n program steps of
compile( M ) from k land on a core whose window is mrun(n, M, window(k )), with the trap
down.

Proof. Look up the instruction at the line. If there is none, both sides stop. If it’s
MINC c, the compiled INC c adds one to c and goes to the next line, which is exactly
the window’s move (the version also moves, but the window doesn’t show versions).
If it’s MDEC c j, split on whether c is 0, and both sides do the same thing in each
case. Neither instruction can trap. The run statement is induction on n, one step at a
time.

Checked as simulation_step and simulation_run (EarnedCore.v).


Theorem 14.3 (Halting matches). For every two-counter program M and whole numbers a,
b: M stops after some number of steps from (1, a, b) if and only if the program compile( M)


                                           187
The Thiele Machine                                                                Devon Thiele


halts after some number of program steps from start( a, b).

Proof. The start has window (1, a, b) and its trap is down. Apply Theorem 14.2 after
any number n of steps: the two configurations still have the same window, the trap is
still down, and one is stopped exactly when the other is halted. The same n witnesses
termination in either direction.

Checked as halting_correspondence (EarnedCore.v).

Now the part that isn’t mine. Proving that halting is undecidable for two-counter
machines is real work, and it’s already done, checked, in a shared Coq project called
the Coq Library of Undecidability Proofs (presented by Yannick Forster, Dominique
Larchey-Wendling and coauthors at CoqPL 2020). The two-counter result in it is
Larchey-Wendling’s, reached from his and Forster’s work on Minsky machines (CPP
2019) by way of FRACTRAN. Their two-counter machine has the same two instruc-
tions as Minsky’s, with the same rule for zero. So the only thing I have to prove is that
their machine and my INC/DEC fragment are the same machine, step for step, and
then borrow their theorem.

One honest wrinkle about what “undecidable” means in that library, because it isn’t
the textbook sentence. Every function you can write in Coq is a program, so “decidable”
there means “some Coq function answers it.” Coq by itself can’t prove that no Coq
function answers a question without an extra assumption about what programs are.
So the library says the strongest thing it can without one: if anything decided this,
then the questions on which a single-tape Turing machine doesn’t halt could be listed
by a program, which is the classic thing that can’t be done. That’s their convention,
and the theorem below inherits it exactly.


Theorem 14.4 (Halting is undecidable for this machine). The library’s two-counter ma-
chine agrees with the INC/DEC fragment: its step, its stop, and its termination match those of
the compiled program, so a library problem ( P, a, b) halts if and only if the compiled program
halts from start( a, b). Consequently, the question “does program P halt from start( a, b)?” is
undecidable in the library’s sense: a decider for it would make the complement of single-tape
binary Turing machine halting enumerable.

Proof. The agreement is a case split on the library’s instruction at the current line,
and then induction along the run, ending in Theorem 14.3. The compile map is
then a reduction from the library’s two-counter halting problem, which the library
proves undecidable, and the library’s own lemma carries undecidability across a
reduction.

Checked as mm2_step_iff, mm2_stop_iff, mm2_terminates_iff, mm2_halti
ng_iff and earned_core_halting_undecidable (EarnedCoreLinks.v), the last
applying the library’s MM2_HALTING_undec.

                                             188
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


What that buys, and what it doesn’t. It buys: the base of this machine is a universal
machine in Minsky’s sense, and nobody (in the library’s sense) can predict in general
what it’ll do. What it doesn’t buy is a fast machine, or one where your input arrives
conveniently. The counters start holding a and b, given directly; there’s no encoding
layer in my files. Minsky’s prime-power packing is how you’d get from “any Tur-
ing machine” to “two counters,” and that construction is his and the library’s, not
something I re-proved.

Is “given directly” just a convenience, or does it bite? It bites, and somebody found
exactly where. In 1972 Rich Schroeppel, in a short memo from the MIT AI Lab, proved
that a two-counter machine started with n in one counter and zero in the other can’t
compute 2n . So the packing Minsky needs is precisely the thing two plain counters
can’t do for themselves. Hand the small machine its inputs straight and there are
functions of them it can’t compute; hand it the inputs already packed and it computes
anything a Turing machine can. That’s no contradiction with the undecidability above,
which ranges over every program and every starting pair, packed ones included. The
base hides nothing. It just needs its input pre-chewed, and the chewing is somebody
else’s.

14.5 It’s a certification system, and the flag is a latch
Now the record. Three facts first, all of them read straight off the step line.


Theorem 14.5 (Ledger, toll, permanence). For every state s and instruction i,
µ(exec(s, i )) = µ(s) + cost(i ), and for every trace t, µ(run(t, s)) = µ(s) + cost(t). If
cert(s) is down and cert(exec(s, i )) is up, then i is CERTIFY, it passes at core(s), and
cost(i ) ≥ 1. If cert(s) is up, so is cert(exec(s, i )).

Proof. Read the ledger component of Definition 14.3: it adds exactly cost(i ). Repeated
substitution along a trace gives the sum of its costs, or, equivalently, induction on the
length of the trace does. The flag’s new value is its old value or fires(core(s), i ). A
false-to-true change therefore requires that event, whose definition requires a passing
CERTIFY. CERTIFY costs 1. An already true flag stays true under the same disjunction.



Checked as mu_conservation, mu_conservation_trace, only_certify_cer
tifies, a2 and cert_permanent (EarnedCore.v).

That third clause in the middle is Section 3’s toll, for this machine. Which means this
machine is one of the things Section 3 was about, and Section 3’s theorem applies to it
without my lifting a finger.


Theorem 14.6 (An instance of the certification system). The states, the instructions, the
step exec, the cost and the flag, with the toll of Theorem 14.5, form a certification system



                                            189
The Thiele Machine                                                                 Devon Thiele


(Definition 3.1). So the universal floor (Theorem 3.1) holds here: if cert(s0 ) is down and
cert(run(t, s0 )) is up, then cost(t) ≥ 1.

Proof. Take the state and instruction sets of Definitions 14.2 and 14.3, their step and
cost, and the flag as the reading. These provide the five data fields of Definition 3.1.
Theorem 14.5 supplies its one required rule. Applying Theorem 3.1 gives the claimed
bound.

Checked as earned_cs and earned_core_floor (EarnedCoreLinks.v); earned_
core_floor is universal_nfi_any_substrate, the checked name of Section 3’s
theorem, applied to earned_cs. The same floor is proved directly, without the link,
as nfi_floor (EarnedCore.v).

Then Section 10. Section 10 said: take any base, and any record that answers only
to the base and never comes back down, and the record is a latch. This machine has
a base: a program together with a core, stepping by the program step. And it has a
record, the flag, with the ledger riding along. So the question is whether it’s an honest
extension in Section 10’s five-rule sense (Definition 10.2), and if it is, Section 10 does
the rest.


Theorem 14.7 (The flag is a latch of the base). Let the base have states (program, core),
stepping by the program step, starting at start( a, b)’s core for any a, b, and halting when the
program has halted. Map each (program, state) to (program, core). Then the machine, run as a
closed machine on (program, state), is an honest extension of that base, and so its flag factors
as the latch (Theorem 10.1) of the event “the next instruction is a CERTIFY that passes.”

Proof. The rules of Definition 10.2 one at a time. Driven by the computation: the next
flag is the old flag or “the next instruction is a passing CERTIFY,” which is a function
of the base state and the old flag (that’s the step line). Ledger: µ only adds. Toll:
Theorem 14.5. Permanence: Theorem 14.5. A reachable write: the three-line program
of the worked run raises the flag from a start. Section 10’s theorem then gives the
factorization.

Checked as earned_core_honest and earned_core_is_latch (EarnedCore-
Links.v), the latter by record_axis_is_latch_holds; the step-level facts are cer
t_latch and base_blind (EarnedCore.v).

So far, nothing new. The toll, the floor and the latch are things Part III already promised
about any machine of this kind. The next subsection is the part Part III couldn’t give.

14.6 Commitments are earned
Here’s the shape before the words. Pick any run from a clean start, any list of instruc-
tions at all, chosen by somebody who’d love to cheat. Look at the moment a COMMIT
would pass. Then, somewhere earlier in that run, there’s a CHECK of exactly the


                                              190
The Thiele Machine                                                               Devon Thiele


same claim that passed and paid, at the same edition of the counter, and between
that CHECK and now, nothing touched the counter. Not “probably.” Not “on the
programs I wrote.” On every list of instructions anybody can write.

To say “nothing touched it” exactly, one word.


Definition 14.5 (Untouched). A list of instructions mid, run from a state s, leaves
counter c untouched when, for every way of splitting mid as t1 , then i, then t2 , executing
i at the core reached by running t1 from s leaves both ver(·, c) and val(·, c) as they
were.


Defined as untouched (EarnedCore.v).


Theorem 14.8 (A commitment was checked first). Let s0 be clean and pre any trace after
which COMMIT p c would pass. Then pre splits as pre1 , then CHECK p c, then mid, where:
the CHECK passes at the core reached by pre1 ; CHECK p c and COMMIT p c each cost at
least 1; c’s version after pre1 equals its version after pre; and mid, run from just after the
CHECK, leaves c untouched.

Proof. COMMIT passes, so the claim ( p, c, ver(c)) for the current version is in the table.
By the no-forging invariant (Theorem 14.12 below), that fact was written by a passing
CHECK p c at some point pre1 , with the version c had then; since it’s the current
version too, the two versions are equal. Versions never go down, and any instruction
that changes a counter’s value also raises its version, so an instruction in mid that
touched c would have left c’s version higher at the end than at the CHECK. It isn’t. So
nothing in mid touched c.

Checked as earned_commitment_provenance (EarnedCore.v).


Theorem 14.9 (A raised flag was checked, then committed, then certified). Let s0 be
clean and t any trace with cert(run(t, s0 )) up. Then for some p and c, t is

           pre1 , CHECK p c, mid1 , COMMIT p c, mid2 , CERTIFY, post,

where the CHECK passes at its state, the COMMIT passes at its state, the CERTIFY passes
at its state, c has the same version at the CHECK as at the COMMIT, and mid1 leaves c
untouched.

Proof. The flag starts down, so some first instruction raised it, and by Theorem 14.5
it’s a passing CERTIFY. A CERTIFY passes only with a fact in the channel, the channel
starts empty, and only a passing COMMIT puts a fact there, so some earlier COMMIT
p c passed. Theorem 14.8 at that COMMIT gives the CHECK, the equal version, and
the untouched stretch.


                                             191
The Thiele Machine                                                                    Devon Thiele


Checked as earned_certification_provenance (EarnedCore.v).

And the failure side, so you can see the refusals are clean and not half-done:


Theorem 14.10 (Unearned steps trap and change no claim). If COMMIT p c would not
pass at a core k, executing it puts the trap up and leaves the channel and the table as they were.
If CERTIFY would not pass at a state s, executing it puts the trap up and leaves the flag as it
was.

Proof. If the trap is already up, the core is unchanged and its trap remains up. Oth-
erwise, the failed COMMIT takes the failure branch of the instruction table: set the
trap, leave every other core field alone. A failed CERTIFY takes the same branch, and
its fires value is false. The flag update is then its old value or false, which leaves it
unchanged. The instruction’s charge still applies to the ledger.

Checked as unearned_commit_traps and uncommitted_certify_traps
(EarnedCore.v).

Read Theorem 14.9 once more for what it doesn’t say. Between the CHECK and the
COMMIT, the counter is untouched. Between the COMMIT and the CERTIFY, it isn’t
promised anything. You can check A is even, commit to it, add one to A, and then
certify. The flag goes up, and what it stands on is a commitment about the edition that
was current when you committed. The certificate is historical: “this was checked and
committed about this edition,” not “this is still true.” I think that’s the right meaning
for a certificate (a birth certificate doesn’t expire when the baby grows), but it’s a
meaning, and you should know which one you’re getting.

14.7 What a passing check means
Provenance says a CHECK happened. It doesn’t yet say the CHECK was right, and
that’s a separate question with a separate proof. A machine could have a perfectly
ordered chain of check, commit, certify, all standing on a checker that says yes to
everything. So: what does a fact in the table actually tell you about the counter?


Theorem 14.11 (Checker soundness). Let s0 be clean and t any trace, and let k be the core
of run(t, s0 ). For every fact ( p, c, v) in k’s table with v = ver(k, c), the property holds of the
counter’s current value: holds( p, val(k, c)). In particular, if COMMIT p c would pass at k,
then holds( p, val(k, c)).

Proof. Carry one sentence through every instruction: every fact in the table has a
version no higher than its counter’s, and if its version equals its counter’s, its property
holds of its counter’s value. A clean start has an empty table, so the sentence holds
there. A passing CHECK adds a fact at the current version, and the checker said yes, so
by Lemma 14.1 the property holds. A write raises one counter’s version, so every old



                                               192
The Thiele Machine                                                                   Devon Thiele


fact about that counter falls strictly behind and the second half no longer applies to it.
Nothing else changes a value or a version. The sentence holds after every instruction,
so it holds at the end. The part about COMMIT is the case where the claim is in the
table at the current version.

Checked as checker_soundness and committed_claim_holds (EarnedCore.v),
through the invariant sound and its one-step form sound_step.

So a live fact means exactly this: one of three arithmetic properties holds of one
counter’s current value. Not “the program is correct.” Not “the number is interesting.”
The property, of the value, now. That’s all “checked” means on this machine, and it’s
enough to be true.

So who checked the checker? Nothing on the record did. The record carries the run’s
half of the story: a CHECK, then a COMMIT of the same claim about the same edition,
then a CERTIFY. The other half, that the checker says yes exactly when the property
holds, isn’t in any run. It’s Lemma 14.1, a proof about the little program the step calls,
checked once by Coq and priced by nothing on the ledger. So a claim established here
stands on two legs: a fact about this run, carried by the record, and a fact about the
checker, carried by a proof that whoever reads the record has to accept. That’s the
Münchhausen trilemma from the opening chapter taking its third horn on purpose:
the chain of reasons stops at a proof, named and on the page, where you can decide
whether you’d have stopped there too. And the entitlement it gives is the reader’s.
The machine doesn’t know anything; it keeps the order.

Soundness rules out a lying checker, not a pointless question: at least 0 has a perfectly
sound checker and an empty no pile, as the worked run showed.

14.8 Nothing gets forged
The proof of Theorem 14.8 leaned on an invariant I promised to show you. Here it
is. The fear it answers: could some clever sequence of instructions get a fact into the
table without a CHECK writing it? A DEC with a funny jump target, a COMMIT after
a trap, something I didn’t think of? The answer is checked one instruction at a time,
which is the only way I trust myself to answer it.


Definition 14.6 (Earned fact; no forgery). After a trace t from s0 , a fact f = ( p, c, v) is
earned when t is pre, then CHECK p c, then mid, where the CHECK passes at the core
reached by pre, f is exactly the claim p of c at that core, and, if f is live at the end (v
equals c’s version after t), mid leaves c untouched. The trace has no forgery when every
fact in the table after it is earned.


Theorem 14.12 (No forging). For every core k, instruction i and fact f in the table after
executing i at k: either f was already in k’s table, or i is CHECK of f ’s property and counter,
it passes at k, and f is the claim it writes. Consequently, if a trace has no forgery, so does that


                                               193
The Thiele Machine                                                                      Devon Thiele


trace followed by any one instruction; and from every clean start, every trace has no forgery.

Proof. The first part is a case for each of the six instructions: only a passing CHECK
adds anything, and it adds exactly its claim. For the second, a new fact is earned by
the CHECK that just wrote it; an old fact stays earned, and if it’s still live after the new
instruction, its counter’s version didn’t move, so the new instruction didn’t touch the
counter and the untouched stretch grows by one. A clean start has an empty table,
which has no forgery, and the step carries it along any trace.

Checked as facts_step, no_forging_step and no_forging (EarnedCore.v).

14.9 A full table traps
Sixteen facts of room, and no eviction. Two halves to prove: nothing ever leaves, and
nothing ever overflows.


Theorem 14.13 (Bounded table, no eviction). Every instruction keeps every fact already
in the table. If the table holds 16 or more facts, CHECK p c puts the trap up and leaves the
table as it was. If the table holds at most 16 facts, it still holds at most 16 after any instruction.

Proof. With a raised trap no instruction changes the table. With the trap down, only
CHECK can change it, and a successful CHECK adds one fact without removing an
entry. Success requires a previous length strictly below 16, so the new length is at
most 16. At length 16 or greater that branch is unavailable: CHECK raises the trap
and preserves the table. Every other instruction preserves it as well.

Checked as facts_keep, full_table_traps and facts_bounded_step
(EarnedCore.v).

Why trap instead of making room? Because “making room” means deciding which
fact dies, and a fact that can die is a fact whose absence you have to explain later. A
table that only grows is a history you can read back, and the provenance proofs above
lean on exactly that. The bill for it is real, though, and it’s in the last subsection of this
chapter, the one on what the machine doesn’t do.

14.10 The window can’t see the record
Section 7 was about windows: a view of a state that shows some of it, and the theorem
that a window which can’t tell two states apart can’t price the step between them
exactly (Theorem 7.2). Here’s the smallest pair I could build where the window is
Minsky’s view of the machine (line number and the two counters) and the record is
everything else.

Run two traces from start(0, 0). The earned run is CHECK is zero A; COMMIT is zero
A; CERTIFY. The idle run is DEC A 0, three times. In the idle run, A is 0 every time,
so each DEC just goes to the next line and writes nothing. Both runs end on line 4,


                                                194
The Thiele Machine                                                                Devon Thiele


with A = 0 and B = 0, both versions 0. Through the window, identical. One of them
has paid 3, holds a fact, could commit again, and has its flag up. The other has paid
nothing, holds nothing, can’t commit, and its flag is down. Two photographs, same
picture, different people.


Theorem 14.14 (Same window, different record). The earned run and the idle run from
start(0, 0) end at cores with the same window and the same versions of A and B, and with
different ledgers, different flags, different tables, and different answers to “would COMMIT is
zero A pass.”

Proof. In the earned run, CHECK adds (Zero, A, 0), COMMIT puts that fact in the
channel, and CERTIFY raises the flag. The ledger is 1 + 1 + 1 = 3. No counter is
written. In the idle run each DEC sees zero, so it advances the line without writing a
counter or raising a version. Its three costs are zero and it adds no fact or commitment.
Thus both final windows are (4, 0, 0) with versions (0, 0). The earned table contains the
current zero claim and the idle table is empty, giving the stated difference in whether
another COMMIT would pass, as well as in the ledger and flag.

Checked as receipt_separation (EarnedCore.v).


Theorem 14.15 (No window oracle). There is no function g from windows to whole num-
bers with g(window) = µ at the end of every trace from start(0, 0). Likewise there is no
function from windows to yes or no that gives the flag at the end of every such trace, and none
that gives whether COMMIT is zero A would pass.

Proof. Such a g would have to give both 3 and 0 on the one window the two runs of
Theorem 14.14 share. The same for the flag and the commit right.

Checked as no_mu_oracle, no_cert_oracle and no_commit_oracle (Earned-
Core.v).

This is Section 7’s shape, made of pebbles: the record lives off the window. Anybody
who only watches the counters and the line number, which is everything Minsky’s
machine is, can’t tell you what was paid, what was committed, or whether the flag is
up. Not because they looked carelessly. Because it isn’t there to see.

14.11 The exact price is three
Section 3 said a raised flag costs at least one. On this machine that’s true and too
modest. A raised flag needs a CERTIFY, a CERTIFY needs a COMMIT, a COMMIT
needs a CHECK, and each of those is its own instruction costing one. So at least three.
One of what: three units of µ, one per paid act, each one the “one” I picked back in
the table. And three isn’t a guess that happens to hold; it’s the number of links in the
chain.


                                             195
The Thiele Machine                                                                 Devon Thiele


Theorem 14.16 (The minimum price of a certificate). If s0 is clean and cert(run(t, s0 ))
is up, then cost(t) ≥ 3 and µ(run(t, s0 )) ≥ µ(s0 ) + 3. For programs: if the flag is up after n
program steps from start( a, b), then µ ≥ 3 there.

Proof. Theorem 14.9 finds a CHECK, a COMMIT and a CERTIFY at three different
places in t, each costing 1, and every other instruction costs at least 0. The ledger
statement is Theorem 14.5. A program run is the run of the instructions it actually
executes, so the program form follows.

Checked as certified_run_min_cost and program_certified_min_cost
(EarnedCore.v).


Theorem 14.17 (Three is tight). For all whole numbers a and b, run the program CHECK
is zero A; COMMIT is zero A; CERTIFY for 4 program steps from start( a, b). If a = 0, it
ends with the flag up and µ = 3 exactly. If a ̸= 0, it ends with the flag down and the trap up,
and for every n, n program steps from start( a, b) leave the flag down.

Proof. If a = 0, the checker for Zero says yes at 0, so the first instruction adds
(Zero, A, 0) to the empty table and charges 1. No counter changes, so the second
instruction finds that same fact, puts it in the channel and charges 1. The third finds
the channel occupied, raises the flag and charges 1. The line is now 4, beyond the
three-instruction program, and the fourth program step adds no charge. The final
ledger is exactly 3. If a ̸= 0, the checker says no, so the first instruction sets the trap
and leaves the flag down. A program run takes no step once the trap is up, so every
later program step leaves the state, flag included, exactly where it is.

Checked as earned_run_check_can_fail and earned_run_refused_forev
er (EarnedCore.v), with the program named earned_run, and the lemma run_p
rog_trapped for a trapped run standing still. The version whose check can’t fail,
CHECK at least 0 A; COMMIT at least 0 A; CERTIFY, certifies from every start for
exactly 3 (min_cost_tight, with that program named witness). So the floor of
three is reachable from any start at all, and that’s the machine not policing trivial
checks, not the machine establishing something.

That’s the worked run from the start of the chapter, now as a theorem. The floor is 3,
and a run whose check could have failed pays exactly 3, so 3 is the price, not a bound
with slack in it.

And that’s every piece of the model, standing on six instructions: a base that computes
everything two counters can, a ledger that’s exact, a toll the universal floor applies to,
a flag that’s a latch of the base, a window that can’t see the record, and a commitment
that can’t happen unless a check of the same claim, on the same edition, came first
and was right. Every result above is closed: Coq reports no assumptions for any of
them. That isn’t my say-so. The file ends by asking Coq to print the assumptions of

                                              196
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


each headline theorem, and the book’s test suite compiles it and fails unless every one
comes back closed. (The project-wide audit behind the crosswalk doesn’t list these
files, which is why its rows mark them differently.) The base file uses nothing but
Coq’s standard library, so you can check it with nothing else installed; the link file
adds only the book’s own abstract records and the library of undecidability proofs.

14.12 One machine that runs them all
The small machine raises its flag only by checking, committing and certifying, and it
pays for that. The next question is whether one machine can stand in for all of them,
the way Turing’s universal machine stands in for every Turing machine. Here’s what
I mean by that. A universal Thiele machine is one fixed machine that runs any machine
of a stated class as a guest, with the guest’s record kept and the guest’s toll collected
by its own step, not by a convention some program running on it has to keep.

So I built a host. It carries a guest inside its own state: the guest’s program as data,
the guest’s counters, its table, its ledger, its flag. The host has one extra move, run one
guest step. In that one move it looks at the guest’s flag, takes the step, looks again,
and if the flag went from down to up, the host’s own copy of that flag goes up in the
same move, and the host pays for it.


Definition 14.7 (The host). A guest is a program P of this chapter’s machine to-
gether with a state g of it (Definition 14.3). A host state h has six parts: its own
core core(h), its ledger µ(h), its own flag own(h), the guest program P(h) held as
a list of instructions, the guest state g(h), and the mirror m(h), a yes/no copy of
the guest’s flag. The host has two kinds of move. OWN i runs the instruction i
on the host’s own core, costs what this chapter’s machine charges for i, and raises
own exactly when that machine’s flag would rise. GSTEP b costs b. If the host’s
core is trapped it does nothing else. Otherwise it moves the host to its next line
and, if the guest’s next instruction costs at most b, runs that instruction on g(h); in
the same move the mirror becomes m(h) ∨ (¬cert( g(h)) ∧ cert( g′ )), where g′ is the
new guest state. The host’s reading is own(h) ∨ m(h). The universal program is
U = [GSTEP 1; OWN (INC A); OWN (DEC A 1)]: one guest step, then two moves
that bring the host back to its first line.


Every instruction of the small machine costs at most one, so GSTEP 1 runs every guest
instruction there is. Why charge the budget b, and not the cost of whatever instruction
got fetched? Because charging the budget keeps the price a function of the move alone,
which is what the certification system of Part II asks for: you read the price of a host
move off the move, the way you read the small machine’s prices off its table, without
peeking inside the guest. The bill for that is easy to see. A host that steps a free guest
instruction, an INC say, still pays one for the move.

So the host’s ledger is closer to a clock than to a receipt for its guests: one unit per


                                           197
The Thiele Machine                                                                   Devon Thiele


guest step, whatever the step was. It never falls behind the guest’s own bill (part (3)
of Theorem 14.20 below), and it matches that bill only when every guest step happens
to cost one. Could a cleverer host charge exactly? Not with a price read off the move
alone. GSTEP 1 is the same move whether the guest’s next instruction is a free INC or
a paid CHECK, so one price can’t match both. A host that charges exactly would have
to peek, and I haven’t built one. That’s open, even for this chapter’s own programs.

And one thing about the definition before the theorems, so you know which of them
carry weight. GSTEP runs the guest’s instruction by calling the small machine’s own
step on the guest’s state: the guest’s step is a primitive of the host. So “the host runs
any guest” (Theorem 14.18) is true by construction. The host was built to do exactly
that, and the proof is mostly unfolding. The theorems with something in them come
after it. The mirror always equals the guest’s flag (Theorem 14.19). Nothing raises
the mirror unless the guest itself passes a CERTIFY inside a guest step the host paid
for (Theorem 14.21). No OWN move, in any host program at all, touches the guest’s
state or the mirror (the second sentence of that same theorem), and no host move of
either kind rewrites the guest’s program (hexec_gprog, UniversalThiele.v). And the
mirror is tied to the guest’s earned chain: if it’s up, the guest’s own run contains a
passing CHECK, then a COMMIT of the same claim, then a CERTIFY (host_mirror
_earned, UniversalThiele.v). That’s what “universal” means here, and it’s narrower
than it sounds: it runs any guest by construction, and it keeps the guest’s record by
theorem.

The isolation part is the oldest idea in this neighbourhood: it’s the reference monitor
from the opening chapter, Anderson’s 1972 move, one mechanism everything has to
pass through. Guarding one bit with a step rule is that same move, made very small.
What’s put together here is a priced, earned record under that move. The move itself
is Anderson’s.


Theorem 14.18 (The host runs any guest). (1) If the host’s core is not trapped, then after
n moves GSTEP 1 the guest state is the guest program’s own run of n steps from g(h), the
guest program is unchanged, and the host is still not trapped. (2) If the host’s core is at line 1
and not trapped, then 3n steps of the program U leave the guest exactly where n steps of its
own program put it. (3) For every two-counter program M and inputs a, b: M halts from
(1, ( a, b)) exactly when the host program made of OWN moves of the compiled M halts, from
a host whose core starts at ( a, b), whatever guest that host carries.

Proof. (1) Induction on n: a host that isn’t trapped stays untrapped through a guest
step, and with budget 1 the guest step is the guest’s own step. (2) One pass of U
is a guest step, then INC A and DEC A back to line 1, so it is (1) once per pass. (3)
A host program made only of OWN moves is the small machine, core for core, and
Theorem 14.3 does the rest.




                                               198
The Thiele Machine                                                                  Devon Thiele


Checked as universal_simulation, universal_program_simulation and h
ost_thiele_complete (UniversalThiele.v).


Theorem 14.19 (The copy is the record). Say a host state h agrees when m(h) =
cert( g(h)). Every host move takes an agreeing state to an agreeing state, so every host
trace and every stored host program does too, and a freshly loaded host agrees. In particular, if
h agrees and is not trapped, the mirror after n moves GSTEP 1 is the guest’s flag after n steps
of its own program.

Proof. One move at a time. An OWN move touches neither the mirror nor the guest. A
trapped GSTEP touches neither. An untrapped one sets the mirror to the old mirror or
the crossing, and the guest’s flag is a latch (Theorem 14.5), so if the old mirror equalled
the old flag, the new mirror equals the new flag. The last sentence is this together with
Theorem 14.18.

Checked as record_agreement_step, record_agreement, record_agreemen
t_program, hload_agrees and simulated_record (UniversalThiele.v).


Theorem 14.20 (The host’s step collects the guest’s toll). (1) If h agrees, is not trapped,
and the guest step that budget b allows takes the guest’s flag from down to up, then the mirror
is down before GSTEP b and up after it, the host’s ledger rose by exactly b, and b ≥ 1. (2) In
the run of (1) of Theorem 14.18, if the guest’s flag goes up between its steps n and n + 1, the
mirror goes up between the host’s moves n and n + 1, and that move costs 1. (3) For every
host trace t, µ( g(run(t, h))) + µ(h) ≤ µ(run(t, h)) + µ( g(h)): the host’s ledger grows at
least as fast as the guest’s.

Proof. (1) The guest’s flag rises only on a passing CERTIFY (Theorem 14.5), which costs
1, and the budget let it run, so b ≥ 1; the mirror was the guest’s flag, so it was down,
and the move sets it to the crossing. (2) is (1) at the matching move. (3) Induction on
t: a guest step that runs costs the guest at most the budget the host paid, and every
other move leaves the guest’s ledger alone.

Checked as toll_enforced_by_host_step, every_guest_crossing_is_a_
host_crossing, host_pays_for_guest, host_cost_covers_guest and sim
ulated_cost (UniversalThiele.v).


Theorem 14.21 (No free host certification). If the mirror is down at h and up after a host
move i, then i is GSTEP b with b ≥ 1, the host was not trapped, the guest’s next instruction
was CERTIFY, and the guest’s flag went from down to up in that move. A trace made only
of OWN moves leaves the mirror and the guest state exactly where they were. And the host’s
own flag rises only by an OWN CERTIFY that passes on the host’s core.




                                              199
The Thiele Machine                                                                Devon Thiele


Proof. An OWN move copies the mirror unchanged, and a trapped GSTEP does too,
so the rise is an untrapped GSTEP b whose guest step crossed; a crossing is a passing
CERTIFY, which costs 1 and needed the budget. The own flag moves by this chapter’s
step line.

Checked as no_free_host_certification_step, no_free_host_certific
ation, no_free_host_certification_program, guestless_runs_leave_
mirror and own_record_only_by_certify (UniversalThiele.v).


Theorem 14.22 (The host is a Thiele machine). For every host state and move, if the host’s
reading goes from no to yes, the move costs at least 1; the same holds for the mirror alone and
for the own flag alone. So the host read through own ∨ m, the host read through m alone, and
the guest class are certification systems (Definition 3.1), and any host trace that raises the
host’s reading costs at least 1.

Proof. The mirror’s half is Theorem 14.21; the own flag’s half is the small machine’s
toll on the host’s core. The trace form is Section 3’s universal floor.

Checked as host_toll, host_own_toll and host_mirror_toll (UniversalTh-
