iele.v), and host_cs, host_mirror_cs, guest_cs and host_nfi (UniversalTh-
ieleLinks.v).


Remark 14.1 (Two guests, run). Load the guest CHECK is zero A; COMMIT is zero
A; CERTIFY; HALT with both counters at 0. After two moves GSTEP 1 the mirror is
down; after three it is up, the guest’s flag is up, the host’s own flag is still down, and
the host has paid 3. Under the program U the mirror is down at host step 6 and up
at step 7, with 3 paid. The guest CERTIFY; CERTIFY traps on its first step: after five
moves GSTEP 1 the mirror is down, the guest is trapped, and the host has paid 5 for
nothing.


Checked as demo_certifies, demo_program_certifies and demo_forgery_
fails (UniversalThiele.v).

That copy can’t be faked. The proof walks every host move there is, and the copy
only rises in a guest step where the guest itself ran CERTIFY and passed. A host
program that never touches the guest leaves the copy exactly where it was. The copy
always equals the guest’s flag, the host’s ledger always grows at least as fast as the
guest’s, and a three-instruction loop runs any small-machine program one guest step
per pass. Since the small machine already runs every two-counter program, the host
runs every computation, and every guest’s toll is collected by the host’s own step, not
by a convention someone has to keep.

Why make such a fuss about a proof that walks every host move? Because the first


                                             200
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


universal machine had bugs. It’s the machine in Turing’s 1936 paper that reads another
machine’s description off its tape and does what that machine would do, and nobody
gets to call Turing careless. In 1947 Emil Post, in an appendix to a paper on a problem
of Thue, pointed out that the construction leaned on a convention it hadn’t earned,
and he patched a small defect in how the universal machine writes out each complete
configuration. Around the same time Donald Davies, who joined the National Physical
Laboratory in 1947, where Turing was designing a computer, worked through the
universal machine’s tables and found more mistakes. (It’s the same Davies who later
named the packet in packet switching.) His corrections were finally printed in Jack
Copeland’s collection The Essential Turing in 2004. People like to call them some of the
first bugs ever written, in a program for a computer that didn’t exist yet, which is a
lovely claim and a hard one to check, so take it as a lead and not a fact. What it changes
here: a universal machine is exactly the kind of construction where a careful person
leaves a hole, and the host’s theorems are checked by Coq one move at a time, which
is the kind of check that catches Davies’s kind of slip. It doesn’t catch a definition that
says the wrong thing. That’s why the definition is on the page, for you.

Here’s what that covers, said plainly, a sentence at a time. The guests are this chapter’s
programs, every one of them, from every state. That’s the stated class. It’s the same
kind of class Turing’s universal machine has: a fixed instruction set, and a finite
program held as data. The guest program sits in the host’s state as a list of instructions,
not packed into one number; packing it would add bookkeeping and nothing to the
record argument. A Thiele machine from somewhere else comes in through the two-
counter encoding. It keeps its computation. Its record and its event don’t come along
by any theorem: the toll I can promise it is its own flag’s, which still costs at least one
to raise, and whether that flag means what the foreign machine’s flag meant depends
on the encoding, which I’ve proved nothing about. It doesn’t keep its own price list
either. As a guest it pays one for each CHECK, COMMIT and CERTIFY and nothing
for counting, and the foreign machine’s reading has to be computed into a counter and
checked with this machine’s three properties. Picture a clerk who’ll stamp anybody’s
receipt, as long as it’s copied onto his forms and billed at his rates. A compilation that
keeps every foreign price exactly is not proved. And here’s why the extra move is the
point. A plain two-counter host could interpret guests too. But then the guest’s record
would be data the host’s program updates by convention, which is exactly the position
of the ordinary programmable computer from the front matter. That’s a fact about
how such a host is built, not about what interpreters can do: a fixed interpreter whose
own table was written to mirror the guest’s flag and charge for its crossing would sit
right where this host sits, and this host is one way to build it. Here the mirror, the
crossing test and the charge are in the host’s step rule, so Theorems 14.20 and 14.21
hold for every sequence of host moves, including ones that never run a guest.




                                           201
The Thiele Machine                                                          Devon Thiele


14.13 What it doesn’t do
Here’s where it falls short, in plain words, because a small machine is only honest if
its edges are as visible as its middle.

   • The check price is flat. CHECK costs 1 whether it’s asking “is this 0” or “is
     this at least a billion.” The property language is fixed and each property is one
     evaluation, so “pays for its work” here means that flat price, not a price that
     grows with how hard the question was. A machine that charged by the difficulty
     of the check would be a different machine, and I haven’t built it.
   • DEC on zero isn’t a write. It doesn’t change the counter, so it doesn’t change the
     version. That’s the right call for versions (nothing changed), but it means DEC
     on zero is a free way to move the line number without leaving any mark. The
     idle run in the window section uses exactly that.
   • After a trap, a trace still pays. On programs, a trap stops the run. On arbitrary
     traces, instructions after a trap are each charged their cost and none of them
     changes the core. I chose to keep charging so that the ledger stays the plain sum
     of what was issued (Theorem 14.5 has no exceptions); the price of that choice is
     that a trapped machine can still be billed for nothing.
   • “Checked” means what the property language can say. On this machine that’s
     is zero, is even and is at least n, and a live fact means one of those holds of one
     counter’s current value. It doesn’t mean the program is correct, or that anything
     follows from the property, or that the property was worth checking. So can a
     proved machine of this kind check “sorted,” the claim the opening chapter’s
     table runs on? Yes, through an encoding. A copy of this machine, instruction
     for instruction, with its property language left open, has provenance, checker
     soundness, no forging and the floor of three proved once for every property
     language that comes with an exact equality test and a checker proved equal to
     its meaning. Give it “the list this counter encodes is sorted” as a property and
     it certifies a sorted list for three and refuses an unsorted one forever (sorted_
     run_certifies, sorted_run_certifies_iff and sorted_run_refus
     ed_forever, EarnedGeneric.v). The copy is written out again in its own file,
     not derived from this one by a theorem; putting the two side by side is how you
     check they’re the same machine. What makes that a check of the list, and not of
     a number, is the proof that the checker means sortedness. Without that proof,
     “sorted” would be a number some unconstrained code wrote into a counter, and
     the record would be honest about the counter and silent about the list.
   • The certificate is historical. Between the COMMIT and the CERTIFY, the counter
     can change, and the flag still goes up. The flag says a claim was checked and
     committed about an edition, not that the claim is still true.
   • One latch, and a channel that moves on. The flag records that an earned chain
     happened, once. After that it stays up, and later CERTIFYs change nothing.


                                          202
The Thiele Machine                                                              Devon Thiele


      The channel is the part that names a fact: with the flag up from a clean start, it
      names a fact that some earlier passing COMMIT committed (certified_ch
      annel_earned and channel_names_last_commit, EarnedCore.v). But a
      later commitment replaces it, so at the end it names the last earned commitment,
      which needn’t be the one the flag rose on. Several claims need a latch each.
   • Sixteen checks per run, ever. Facts never leave and the table holds sixteen, so a
     run gets at most sixteen passing CHECKs in its whole life, and the seventeenth
     traps. A certificate needs only one, so this costs nothing for the theorems, but
     it’s a hard wall for any program that wants to keep checking forever, and this
     machine’s small version of the opening chapter’s “you can’t keep all of it.”
   • The clean start matters. Provenance, soundness, no forging and the price of
     three are all stated from a clean start. Hand the machine a table pre-loaded with
     facts nobody checked, and of course none of that follows. The theorems are
     about what the machine produces, not about what you smuggle in at the door.
     Spell the door out once: the theorems cover any list of instructions anybody can
     issue, from a clean start, on a step that runs as written, with nothing else writing
     to the machine. They say nothing about whoever sets or restores the start, about
     a reset, about hardware that misbehaves, or about whoever carries the flag’s
     value to you.
   • The host keeps a guest’s toll, not its prices, and its ledger is a clock. The
     universal host of the last subsection runs this machine’s programs and pays one
     per guest step whatever the step was, so its ledger is at least the guest’s and
     usually more. A host that charges exactly is open, even for this machine’s own
     programs. A machine from elsewhere gets in through the two-counter encoding
     with its computation intact; that its record, its event and its prices carry over is
     not proved. What I can promise it is that its flag, as a guest, still costs at least
     one to raise.
   • Slow, and fed directly. Universality is Minsky’s, with the inputs placed straight
     in the counters. Getting from an arbitrary Turing machine to two counters goes
     through his exponential packing, which is not in my files.
   • The step doesn’t police trivial checks. CHECK at least 0 passes on every value,
     so CHECK, COMMIT, CERTIFY on it raises the flag for three from any start
     (the note after Theorem 14.17). A check that can’t fail establishes nothing, and
     the machine raises the flag for it anyway. The step checks order, aboutness and
     an honest checker, and it leaves “was that worth asking” to whoever reads the
     record.
   • The toll is chosen here, not forced. Section 4’s argument forces a toll on a finite
     machine that pays for every merge. This machine is neither. Its counters have no
     ceiling, so it’s infinite. And its free instructions merge states: take a core at line ℓ
     with c at 1 and version w, and a core at line j − 1 with c at 0 and version w + 1,
     everything else alike, and DEC c j sends both to line j with c at 0 and version


                                            203
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


      w + 1, for nothing. So for this machine, as for the big one, the price of one is a
      design choice the chairs don’t force.

14.14 What comes next
The next section opens a much bigger build. It carries far more than this one: memory
and registers, modules and the arrows between them, a two-player game and its check,
and eventually hardware. I’ll introduce all of it there, from scratch, and I won’t lean
on any of it before then.

But I want one thing said plainly before you meet it, so it doesn’t surprise you later.
The big build prices commitments. Its toll on the flag is there and proved, and every
paid step is on its ledger. What it doesn’t do is enforce that a commitment was earned: in
it, the act that checks a claim commits to nothing, and the act that commits doesn’t
look for a passing check (Section 22 shows exactly where). Theorem 14.9, the one that
says a raised flag was checked, then committed, then certified, on the same edition
with nothing in between, is a theorem about this machine, the small one. The earned
version lives here.

So Part IV has two machines, and neither of them is the model. Both are Thiele
machines in the front matter’s sense, instances of the certification system with the toll
proved: this one as earned_cs (Theorem 14.6), the big one as thiele_cert_addr
_system (UniversalCertificationCost.v), whose toll is Theorem 17.8. This one is also
Thiele-complete. Its base is a two-counter machine, so it computes whatever a Turing
machine can while it carries the record and pays the toll (Theorems 14.2 and 14.3). And
a host built on it is a universal Thiele machine for its programs: it runs any of them as
a guest, by construction, and collects the guest’s toll in its own step, with the mirror,
the isolation and the no-free-certification theorems as the part that’s proved rather
than built in (Section 14.12). Whether the big one is Thiele-complete I haven’t proved,
and nothing in this book leans on it. Here’s why that’s open and not just unchecked.
Everything a program of the big build computes with and reads back goes through
sixteen registers and a hundred and twenty-eight memory words, and every write to
those is cut to sixty-four bits (Section 16). A machine like that looks finite-state, and
then the honest answer would be no, not “unproved.” But the build also has fields
with no ceiling (the ledger, the program counter, the tensor entries, the game’s counts
and the assertion channel), and the game’s counts, for one, are read back by its check.
I haven’t traced every way a program could use one of those as working storage, so
I can’t say no either. Its natural-number sibling, the step that keeps every number
whole, is a different story: it hosts every two-counter program (Section 24) and its
flag pays the floor (Theorem 26.6), so the pieces of Thiele-completeness are proved for
it, though no single theorem packages them. The small one shows the model whole,
with earned commitments, on the least I could build. The big one shows how much a
single build can carry while the toll still holds, and where it stops short. If you ever
find yourself wondering whether a property of the big one is the model’s or just the


                                           204
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


build’s, this chapter is the one to hold it up against. Six instructions. If the model
needs more than that, the big one is where it’ll show.

15 One machine, built three times
That was the small machine: six instructions, the whole model, earned commitments
and all, on the least I could build. Now the big one, which I’ll call the big build, and
which is the test bench where I find out how much a single machine can carry while
the toll still holds. From here on, through the hardware, everything is about it. When I
say “my machine” or “the machine” from now on, I mean exactly one thing: that build,
with its state record, its fifty-one instructions and the price of each, written down in
Coq and then turned into a hardware design. The six-instruction one keeps its own
name, the small machine. Not a toy, not “any system.” This one, warts included. I
want to say three things about it before I show you a single field, because the way
people misread a concrete machine is to mistake it for the idea.

First: this is one try. The theorems of Part III quantify over any states and any steps; the
thing in Part IV is one particular choice of states and steps, with sixteen registers and a
hundred and twenty-eight words of memory and fifty-one instructions, and every one
of those numbers was a decision I made, some of them for reasons and some of them
because I had to pick something. Because those theorems are stated for any states and
any steps, none of them mentions these numbers. If you built a different machine that
obeyed the toll, it would be a different try at the same idea, and the latch theorem
in Section 10 says its record would have the same shape underneath. Section 14 is
exactly that: a different try, much smaller, and its record is a latch. One difference I’ll
keep saying out loud: this build prices commitments but doesn’t enforce that they
were earned. That guarantee is the small machine’s (Section 14), and Section 22 shows
where this one stops short of it. The plainest sign is a name the two machines share.
CERTIFY in the small machine traps unless a commitment is waiting; CERTIFY here
(Section 17) raises the flag with nothing required before it. It’s still a Thiele machine,
an instance of the certification system with its toll proved (thiele_cert_addr_sy
stem, UniversalCertificationCost.v, with Theorem 17.8 as the toll). And the hardware
at the end isn’t a second one. It implements this one, inside bounds Section 27 states.
Why this one and not the small machine? History, plainly: the hardware was built for
this build first, and the small machine came last. A chip for the small machine is open
(Section 27).

Second: why build one at all, if the abstract theorems are the point? Because an ab-
stract theorem about “any machine” is checked against nothing until there’s a machine
to check it against, and an abstract statement can be wrong in ways nobody notices
until it meets one. The concrete machine is where the abstract claims get instantiated,
and each one meets it in a place I can name now. Section 3’s universal floor becomes
a theorem about these fifty-one instructions (Section 17, and its whole ladder in Sec-
tion 23). Section 6’s counter rule becomes a statement about one field of the state


                                            205
The Thiele Machine                                                              Devon Thiele


(Section 16, with the run forms in Section 23). Section 7’s windows become two states
that look the same and aren’t (Section 20), and the clerk’s collisions and the verifier’s
escapes become named pairs (Section 23). Section 8’s entitlement and Section 9’s in-
sight land in Section 22, after Section 19 has shown what a claim on this machine
physically is. Section 4’s finite-room merge argument becomes a statement about a
finite window onto this machine, because the whole record is not finite (Section 16
says why, Section 23 builds the window). Section 5, Section 10, Section 12 and Sec-
tion 13 land in Section 23 too, and Section 11’s diagonal comes home in Section 24.
Each of those places names the Part III claim it instantiates and points back to it rather
than arguing it again. When an instantiation goes through, it’s evidence the abstract
statement means what I think. When one doesn’t, the abstract statement is the thing
under suspicion, not the machine. A machine is how a person who thinks in shapes
checks that the shapes close.

Third: I built it three times, in three materials. Once as a mathematical object in Coq,
a step relation on a record of twelve fields, where every theorem about the machine
lives; I’ll call that version the kernel, because it’s the reference definition the other two
are held up against. Once as a hardware model in a language called Kami, which
is Coq again but shaped like a circuit, with a proof, instruction by instruction and
under stated side conditions on the hardware’s state, that the hardware’s step, read
back through an abstraction function, lands on the same state as the kernel’s step.
And once as the thing that falls out the far end of that model: Verilog, the language
chips are described in, which a tool chain turned into a file that would configure a real
programmable chip, if I owned one, which I don’t. Aristotle’s bronze from Section 2:
the statue in three materials, and the promise that it’s the same statue is a promise I
have to keep in Section 27, not assert here.

How hard is a promise like that to keep? There’s a machine that answers better than
I can, and it’s older than any of this. Between 1846 and 1848 Charles Babbage drew
a calculating engine, his Difference Engine No. 2, and never built it. The drawings
sat for about a hundred and forty years, until the historian Allan Bromley proposed
building it and the Science Museum in London did, with its curator of computing,
Doron Swade, running the project. The first thing they had to decide was what “build
it” meant. The drawings had dimensions that disagreed from one view to the next,
mechanisms left out, a whole assembly that did nothing, and one error in the carrying
of tens that would have stopped the engine from working at all. Swade’s own account
is blunt about it: built exactly as drawn, they didn’t expect it to work. So they set two
rules. Every change had to be a solution Babbage had used somewhere else in his own
designs, and every change had to come back off, so the machine could be returned
to exactly what the drawings show. The calculating section did its first full error-free
table, the seventh powers, on 29 November 1991, twenty-seven days before Babbage’s
two hundredth birthday, and the printer was finished in 2002. Eight thousand parts,
five tons.



                                            206
The Thiele Machine                                                          Devon Thiele


You’ll find it said that the errors were planted on purpose, to trip up anybody who
stole the plans. It’s a good story, and good stories are the ones to check. Swade’s
account lists the errors one by one and gives them no such motive; he calls the gap one
of engineering completeness, not of principle. So it goes on the shelf next to Hippasus
until somebody shows the letter where Babbage says so.

What does that change here? Swade had to answer the question Section 27 has to
answer: when the thing in the new material had to differ from the drawing, in what
sense is it the same machine? His answer was to write down every difference and
keep each one reversible. Mine is a proof, step by step, under side conditions that are
written down. Different tools, same promise, and it breaks the same way, through a
difference nobody wrote down.

What the next eleven sections are, in the order you’ll meet them, after the small
machine in Section 14. Section 16 is the state: the twelve fields and what each promises.
Section 17 is the instruction set and the cost schedule, all fifty-one, in a table, with
the twelve that are never free picked out. Those two are the reference chapters: every
name the rest of the machine’s story uses is handed over there first. Section 18 is
the category, built from scratch, with the two laws I made you wait for in Section 2.
Section 19 is about the claims a module can carry: a formula, a label, and the step
that checks one against the other. Section 20 is two states that look the same and
aren’t. Section 21 is a receipt, worked through in four acts. Section 22 puts Section 8’s
entitlement and Section 9’s insight on the machine. Section 23 is the machine as the
witness for the rest of Parts II and III, where the remaining forward pointers land on
named theorems. Section 24 is the interpreter and the guest, where the diagonal from
Section 11 comes home. Section 25 is the two-player game and its check, built from
zero. Section 26 is the accounting against physics and the hierarchy of what costs more.
Then the machine leaves the page: Section 27, in Part V, is the third material, the proof
turned into a chip, and the place where the same-statue promise gets kept or broken.

And one rule for all of them: no sentence about what the machine does stays on the
page unless I’ve read the step rule it describes. Where I’ve simplified, I say so. Where
a comment in the source and the rule next to it disagree, I follow the rule. The machine
is the one thing in this book I can be exactly right about, because it’s written down,
and being exactly right about it is the only way the abstract parts earn their keep.

16 The state record
A state of the machine is a record with twelve fields. I’m going to give you all twelve,
because the whole of Part III was about “the state” as an abstract thing and you’ve
earned the right to see what one looks like when it’s written down. Then I’ll tell
you what isn’t in it, which turns out to be as informative, and then the one piece of
structure that the rest of the book hangs on, the partition graph.




                                          207
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


16.1 The twelve fields
Here they are, in the order they appear in the source, with what each one is for. A few
instructions get named in passing, by the names the source gives them (the ones in
capitals). All fifty-one are in Section 17’s table with exactly what they do; here each
one gets a few words the first time it shows up, enough to follow the field it touches.

The partition graph: the modules (the groups from Section 2, each owning a range of
addresses), the arrows between them, and two counters that hand out fresh identifiers
and only ever go up. Its own record is below.

Four control and status words, held together in a small sub-record: the assertion channel
(the record calls this field the certification address, csr_cert_addr, and the rest of
the book just says assertion channel), one of the machine’s two certification readings,
holding the checksum (the sum of the character codes) of the most recent property
asserted on an arrow (the name says address and the contents say fingerprint; it’s
nonzero after an assertion unless that property’s checksum is zero, and each assertion
overwrites it rather than adding to it, so a later one can put it back to zero); a general
status word, which no step writes; an error code, which every fault in the kernel sets
to one (the hardware has a richer set of codes, and the kernel’s comment lists them,
but the kernel writes one and lets the hardware tell faults apart); and a heap base, used
by two instructions that address memory relative to it, which no step writes either.

The registers: a list of sixteen natural numbers, read and written through an index
taken modulo sixteen, so an out-of-range register name wraps rather than faults.

The data memory: a list of a hundred and twenty-eight natural numbers, addressed
modulo a hundred and twenty-eight, same wrapping rule.

The program counter: a natural number.

The counter from Section 6, which the source calls mu: a natural number, no upper
bound in the type. It starts at zero, and every step raises it by exactly the instruction’s
cost (Section 17), so no step lowers it. This is the field the whole book is about, and it
has no ceiling, which matters for Section 23 and I’ll flag it there.

A mu tensor: sixteen numbers, a flattened four-by-four grid, which one instruction
adds into. I’ll tell you what it’s for in Section 26, and I’ll tell you now that only one
instruction ever writes it. Don’t confuse it with the little tensors the modules carry
inside the graph (below): the one in the record is global and REVEAL (an instruction
that discloses a count of bits and pays for them) adds into it, while each module’s own
is written by a different instruction, TENSOR_SET.

The error flag: a bit that, once set, stays set; no step ever writes it back to false. The
faults that step on pass through a function that ors the new value with the old, and
the faults that jump to the trap address set it to true outright, so either way there’s
no path back. A latch, in Section 10’s sense (Definition 10.2), on the event “something


                                           208
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


went wrong.”

A logic accumulator and a mode word, which I include because they’re in the record and
not because they do anything: no step of the machine changes either. They mirror two
registers in the hardware, which gives them starting values (the mode word boots at
one; the kernel’s starts at zero), lets you read them back, and never writes them either.
The mode word’s comment says zero is “Turing mode” and one is “Thiele mode,” and
there’s a constant defined that the comment says unlocks operations, and no step rule
reads it. Two fields and a constant that are scaffolding, honestly labelled.

The witness counts: eight counters for the two-player game of Section 25, two for each
of the four ways the referee can ask the question, one for “the players agreed” and one
for “they didn’t.” Exactly one instruction writes them, CHSH_TRIAL, one round of
the game (the five instructions that run the game’s check, the CHSH_LASSERT family,
read them).

And the certified flag: the top-level yes/no reading of Section 3’s certification system
(Definition 3.1), the other of the two readings, set by exactly one instruction (CERTIFY)
and never cleared by any.

That’s the state. Every value written into a register or a memory word is truncated
to sixty-four bits on the way in; the kernel’s word is sixty-four bits wide. (The one
exception is XOR_SWAP, which swaps two registers and so only moves values already
in the register file.) The other numeric fields, the counter, the program counter, the
tensor entries, the witness counts and the assertion channel, are plain natural numbers
with no truncation. (The hardware’s datapath word is thirty-two. That’s a difference
I’ll have to account for in Section 27.)

Here is the record written out, with the two sizes and the word.


Definition 16.1 (The state record). A state s is a record with twelve fields, in this
order: the partition graph graph(s) (Definition 16.3); the control and status words,
a record of four natural numbers (certaddr, status, errcode, heapbase); the registers
regs(s) and the data memory mem(s), each a list of natural numbers; the program
counter pc(s) ∈ N; the counter µ(s) ∈ N; the global tensor, a list of natural numbers;
the error flag err(s), a boolean; the logic accumulator and the mode word, both in
N; the witness counts, eight natural numbers samexy and diffxy for x, y ∈ {0, 1}; and
the certified flag cert(s), a boolean. No field’s type bounds a number or fixes a list’s
length.


Definition 16.2 (Registers, memory, and the word). The sizes are the literals R = 16
and M = 128. Write w( x ) = x mod 264 for the 64-bit truncation. Reading register
r returns entry r mod R of the register list, or 0 when the list is too short. Writing v
to register r puts w(v) at position r mod R; on a list of length R it changes that entry



                                          209
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


and no other. Memory reads and writes are the same with M in place of R. Every
register and memory write in the step rules goes through these two writers, with one
exception: XOR_SWAP exchanges two register entries as they are, without truncating.


Checked as REG_COUNT, MEM_SIZE, word64, read_reg, write_reg, read_mem,
write_mem, and swap_regs (VMState.v); word64 is written as a bitwise and with
sixty-four ones, which is the remainder mod 264 .

Here’s the width difference in one sum. Add 232 − 1 and 1: the kernel stores w(232 ) =
232 , since that’s below 264 , and a thirty-two-bit word wraps the same sum to 0. The
counter is the sharper case. In the kernel it has no width at all; in the hardware
it’s a thirty-two-bit word. So the step-by-step hardware correspondence carries a
premise that the old counter plus the step’s cost is below 232 (the refinement lemmas in
ChshRetire.v and CouplingFaults.v, for example), and a run whose counter outgrows
that is outside what’s proved there (Section 27).

How much can a difference in width matter? There’s a famous answer, and it’s worth
the detour. On 4 June 1996 the first Ariane 5 rocket lifted off and broke apart about
forty seconds after its engines lit. The inquiry board, chaired by the mathematician
Jacques-Louis Lions, traced it to one conversion in the inertial reference software:
a sixty-four-bit floating-point number, an alignment value called BH that’s tied to
horizontal speed, squeezed into a sixteen-bit signed integer. On Ariane 4, where the
software came from, that value could never get big enough to overflow, because of
how that rocket flew in its first forty seconds. Ariane 5 flew differently. The value got
too big, the backup unit failed on it, the main unit failed the same way about seventy
milliseconds later, and the function doing the converting didn’t even serve a purpose
on Ariane 5; it was kept for commonality with the old rocket. The board’s report says
the assumption that made the conversion safe had been agreed on and never exposed
to outside review.

Push on what that changes for a counter that’s a natural number in one material and
thirty-two bits in another. A width premise that holds on one machine is a fact about
how that machine gets used, not about the code, and it travels with the code without
anybody noticing. The only defence I know is the dull one: write the premise into
every statement that needs it, where the next person will trip over it. That’s what
“below 232 ” in each hardware lemma is for, and it’s why a run that outgrows it is said,
out loud, to be outside what’s proved.

The counter’s rule, which Section 6 stated for any machine whose counter is kept by a
price list (Theorem 6.1), holds on this one exactly.


Theorem 16.1 (Conservation on this machine). For every state s and every instruction i,




                                          210
The Thiele Machine                                                                Devon Thiele




                              µ(apply(s, i )) = µ(s) + cost(i ),

where apply is the step function and cost is the schedule of Section 17 (Definition 17.4). No
premise is needed: it holds on every state, reachable or not, and on every branch, the faulting
ones included.

Proof. Coq’s proof is a case split over the fifty-one instructions and, inside each, over
the branches of the step (success, latch, trap). In every branch the new counter is
written as the old counter plus the instruction’s cost, either through one of the shared
state builders or, for PNEW, PSPLIT, PMERGE and CERTIFY (the steps that create a
module, split one, merge two, and raise the certified flag), written out in the rule. Each
case closes by computation. This is the one-step rule of Section 6’s Definition 6.1 with
the concrete schedule.

Checked as vm_apply_mu (MuLedgerConservation.v).


Remark 16.1 (The error flag latches, argued from the rules). If err(s) is true then
err(apply(s, i )) is true for every i. The argument is a reading of the rules, not a named
theorem: every rule either copies the flag, sets it to err(s) ∨ true through latch_err
(VMStep.v), or, on a trap, sets it to true. No rule writes false.


16.2 What isn’t in it
Three things people assume are in a machine state and aren’t in this one, each on
purpose.

There’s no program in the state. The step relation takes the instruction as an argument;
the program lives outside, and a runner fetches from it by program counter. So “the
state” never knows what it’s about to do, which is the right design for a thing whose
theorems quantify over all instruction sequences.

There’s no output in the state. The one instruction that emits a payload to the outside
world, EMIT, leaves the payload outside the Coq state entirely; what the state keeps
is the charge, at eight marks per character plus one more (the floor, which Section 17
explains), added into the counter with every other charge, and only as part of that
total. It can’t tell you that anything was sent, let alone what it said, because the same
total can come from other instructions.

And there’s no heap as a separate thing. Heap access is the base word plus an offset
into the same hundred and twenty-eight words of data memory. One memory.

Also absent, and this one is subtle: the record doesn’t fix the lengths of the register and
memory lists. They’re plain lists in the type. That the register list has sixteen entries
and the memory a hundred and twenty-eight is proved as a separate invariant, not


                                             211
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


enforced by the record. I mention it because “sixteen registers” is a theorem about
reachable states, and the type would let you write a state with three. (The invariant is
eg_size_permanent: every step keeps both lengths, from a state that has them.)


Lemma 16.2 (The two lengths are kept). Let s be a state with |regs(s)| = 16
and |mem(s)| = 128. Then for every instruction i, |regs(apply(s, i ))| = 16 and
|mem(apply(s, i ))| = 128.

Proof. Case split over the instructions and their branches. A step either keeps the two
lists as they are or writes them through the register writer, the memory writer, or the
swap. Each of those rebuilds the list as the part before position k, one new entry, and
the part after it, with k = r mod 16 or a mod 128; since k is below the length, the result
has the same length.

Checked as eg_size_permanent (EventGeneralization.v), stated there as “the size
reading is permanent”: if the reading holds before a step, it holds after.

One scope note on all of this. Everything the book proves about the kernel machine is
a statement about this record and the step rules, nothing more. What a real run has
beyond them, the program text, the stream an EMIT sends, the files a runner writes,
lives in the runner, the trace and the hardware’s test harness, not in the state.

16.3 The partition graph
This is the field that carries Section 2’s buckets.

The graph has four parts: a next-module counter, the list of modules, a next-arrow
counter, and the list of arrows. The two counters only go up (where they start is a
few paragraphs down); an identifier is never reused, so a deleted module’s number
is dead forever. A module has three parts. A region, the list of addresses it owns. A
list of strings the source calls axioms, which are labels no step reads (Section 19 shows
what the steps do with them); no step writes a nonempty list into one either, so every
module on a reachable state carries the empty list. And its own four-by-four tensor,
sixteen numbers, zero by default (the comment says “flat space”; Section 26). An arrow
is a source module, a target module, a coupling (a list of pairs of cells, one from each
side, plus a label), a bit that marks it as an identity arrow, and a cost field the comment
says records what was paid to certify it, which under the step rules is always zero
because the asserting step never writes it. That last one is a field with a promise in its
comment that the rules don’t keep. The module layer and the arrow layer are separate
things: two states can agree on every module and differ in their arrows, which is
exactly what Section 20 builds.


Definition 16.3 (Partition graph, module, arrow). A partition graph G is a record
(nG , modsG , aG , arrowsG ): a next-module number nG ∈ N, a list modsG of pairs (iden-


                                            212
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


tifier, module), a next-arrow number aG ∈ N, and a list arrowsG of pairs (identifier,
arrow). A module is a triple (region, axioms, tensor): a list of natural numbers, a list of
strings, and a list of natural numbers, sixteen zeros by default. An arrow is a record
(source, target, coupling, identity, certcost): two module identifiers, a coupling made
of a list of pairs of natural numbers and a label string, a boolean, and a natural number.
Adding a module to G gives it identifier nG , puts it at the front of the list, and raises
the counter to nG + 1; the arrow list is copied unchanged.


Checked as PartitionGraph, ModuleState, MorphismState, CouplingData,
and graph_add_module (VMState.v).

Now the regions, and here’s the design decision, because there’s a cheaper one. The
cheap way to give modules regions is to let every module own the prefix of memory
from zero up to its size, so two modules of size four own the same four cells; that’s
enough for every theorem about the counter and useless for anything about locality,
and it isn’t what Section 2’s buckets said. The kernel says what the buckets said:
nothing in two buckets. A region is a run of consecutive addresses, a base and a length,
and it lies inside the hundred and twenty-eight words that exist; the regions of distinct
modules are pairwise disjoint; and the step that creates a module, PNEW, traps (jumps
to a fixed error address and raises the error flag; Section 17 has the details) if the range
it asks for overlaps a range some other module owns (unless it’s exactly a range a
module already owns, in which case nothing changes and nothing’s charged beyond
the declared cost), or runs past the end of memory. Splitting a module, PSPLIT, gives
its first half to one child and the rest to the other, in place. Merging two modules,
PMERGE, requires their ranges to touch end to end, and traps otherwise. And all
three trap when the machine is out of module numbers, which is a story of its own
below. Every step preserves the properties, so from a state with no modules, every
reachable state has disjoint, contiguous regions (vm_reachable_regions_disjoi
nt, with the preservation theorems under it), each inside memory (vm_reachable_
partition_in_bounds). Those are invariants proved about reachable states; they
aren’t part of the record type, the same way the list lengths aren’t.

Two properties and a theorem, then, with nothing left to the imagination. Write
[b, b + n) for the list b, b + 1, . . . , b + n − 1, and reg(m) for a module’s region.


Definition 16.4 (Disjoint and contiguous regions). A graph G has disjoint regions when,
for any two entries of modsG at different positions in the list, no address lies in both
regions. A list r is contiguous when r = [hd(r ), hd(r ) + |r |), where hd(r ) is its first
element (0 for the empty list); the empty list is contiguous. G has contiguous regions
when every module’s region is contiguous. A state s′ is reachable from s when it arises
from s by zero or more steps of the step relation.


Theorem 16.3 (The regions stay a partition of addresses). (1) If graph(s) has disjoint


                                            213
The Thiele Machine                                                                 Devon Thiele


regions and s steps to s′ on any instruction, then graph(s′ ) has disjoint regions. (2) The same
holds for contiguous regions. (3) If graph(s) has no modules and s′ is reachable from s, then
graph(s′ ) has disjoint and contiguous regions.

Proof. (1) and (2) are a case split over the step relation. Steps that leave the module list
alone (every instruction other than PNEW, PSPLIT and PMERGE; TENSOR_SET does
change a module, but only its tensor) keep both properties trivially; so does every trap,
since a trap keeps the old graph. A successful PNEW has passed the conflict test, so
the new range meets no existing region except one it equals, and in that case the graph
is unchanged; the new range is [b, b + n) by construction. PSPLIT removes one module
and adds its first half and its rest, two disjoint subsets of the removed region, and on
a range [b, b + n) they are [b, b + ⌊n/2⌋) and [b + ⌊n/2⌋, b + n). PMERGE removes
two modules and adds one region inside their union, so disjointness survives without
any test; contiguity of the joined region is exactly what the adjacency test checks, and
without it the step traps. (3) is induction on the number of steps, starting from the fact
that a graph with no modules has both properties.

Checked as vm_step_preserves_regions_disjoint, vm_step_preserves
_regions_contiguous, and vm_reachable_regions_disjoint (VMStep.v),
with the per-operation lemmas graph_pnew_preserves_regions_disjoint, g
raph_hw_psplit_preserves_regions_disjoint, graph_hw_pmerge_pres
erves_regions_disjoint, graph_hw_pmerge_preserves_regions_conti
guous and psplit_halves_of_range under them. Nothing in these statements
mentions the hundred and twenty-eight words of memory; staying inside them is a
separate theorem, which needs the well-formedness condition below and comes right
after it.

Now an honest limit on the word “owns.” Nothing in the kernel enforces ownership.
LOAD, STORE, HEAP_LOAD and HEAP_STORE take an address and read or write
that cell without looking at any module’s region. The regions are read by the instruc-
tions that make and reshape modules (PNEW, PSPLIT, PMERGE) and by the two that
build arrows from regions (MORPH keeps only the coupling pairs whose ends lie
inside the two ranges; MORPH_TENSOR compares ranges), and no other step rule
reads one. Locality, a program touching only its own module’s cells, is a check the
hardware’s partition table makes, and the kernel doesn’t (Section 27).

A few edge cases the definitions settle that no theorem names, since you’ll find them
if you play: splitting a module that doesn’t exist (after its number is taken modulo
sixty-four) adds two empty modules, using up two module numbers; merging two that
don’t exist passes the adjacency check (the empty list is a run) and adds one empty
module, using up one; and the creating step reads its region as “first listed address,
then the count of distinct addresses,” so asking for cells 5 and 3 gets you 5 and 6, not
3 and 5. The hardware’s encoding carries base and length, and the kernel reads lists
that way to match.

                                              214
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


The well-formedness condition is three clauses: every module identifier is below the
next counter, every arrow identifier is below its counter, and every arrow’s two ends
name modules that exist. Every step preserves it, and so does a whole run (vm_step
_preserves_well_formed_graph, run_vm_preserves_well_formed_grap
h). That’s the reason PSPLIT and PMERGE delete every arrow that touches a module
they remove: an arrow left behind would name a module that’s gone, and the third
clause would fail.


Definition 16.5 (Well-formed graph). A graph G is well formed when three things hold:
every identifier in modsG is less than nG ; every identifier in arrowsG is less than aG ;
and for every arrow in arrowsG , its source and its target each appear as an identifier
in modsG .


Theorem 16.4 (Well-formedness is kept). (1) If graph(s) is well formed and s steps to s′
on any instruction, then graph(s′ ) is well formed. (2) If graph(s) is well formed, then for
any fuel k and any program P, the graph of the state reached by running P from s for at most
k steps, fetching each instruction by program counter and stopping when the counter leaves
the program, is well formed.

Proof. (1) is a case split over the step relation. Adding a module uses the counter as
the new identifier and then raises it, so every identifier stays below the counter; the
same holds for arrows. The steps that add an arrow (MORPH, COMPOSE, MORPH_
ID, MORPH_TENSOR) take its ends either from modules they have just looked up or
from arrows already in the graph, whose ends exist by the third clause; when a lookup
fails they latch an error and keep the graph. MORPH_DELETE only removes. PSPLIT
and PMERGE first delete every arrow whose source or target is a module about to
be removed, then remove it, so the third clause cannot break; a PMERGE that traps
keeps the old graph. (2) is induction on the fuel, using the function form of (1) at each
step.

Checked as vm_step_preserves_well_formed_graph (VMStep.v) for (1), and v
m_apply_preserves_well_formed_graph with run_vm_preserves_well_f
ormed_graph (SimulationProof.v) for (2). Both are proved for the partition rules of
this chapter: ranges, the overlap trap, the adjacency trap, and the two traps of the next
part.

16.4 Inside memory, and sixty-four numbers
Two more promises about the buckets, and both are about running out.

The first is memory. There are a hundred and twenty-eight words, numbered 0 to 127,
and a module that owns cell 200 owns a cell the machine doesn’t have. So PNEW
looks at every address in the range it’s about to claim and traps if any of them is 128
or more. Ask for cells 120 to 127 from the initial state and you get a module of eight


                                            215
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


cells, the last eight words of memory. Ask for cells 126, 127 and 128 and the step traps:
the error flag goes up, the program counter jumps to the trap address, the counter is
charged the declared cost anyway, and the graph is exactly what it was. Ask for the
empty range and there’s nothing to check, so the empty range is never past memory.

The second is module numbers, and it’s the one I find a little funny, because sixty-four
turns out to be a lifetime allowance and not a parking lot. Every module number
comes from the graph’s counter nG , which only goes up, and no number is ever
handed out twice: PSPLIT gives its two halves two fresh numbers and retires the old
one, and PMERGE gives the joined module a fresh number and retires both. So nG
counts every module number the run has ever issued, and a split followed by a merge
that puts the cells back exactly where they started has still spent three. The hardware’s
partition table has sixty-four slots, so the kernel’s rule is: a step that needs k fresh
numbers runs only when nG + k ≤ 64, and traps otherwise. PNEW needs one (and
asks for it even when the range is one a module already owns, so on a spent budget
every PNEW traps), PSPLIT needs two, PMERGE needs one. A run from the initial
state can make sixty-four module numbers in its whole life. The extracted runner
starts its counter at one (next part), so it gets sixty-three.

That has a nice side effect. PSPLIT and PMERGE read their module operands modulo
sixty-four, which is how the hardware’s six-bit slot field reads them. If a module
numbered sixty-four could exist, the operand 64 would land on module 0 and module
64 couldn’t be named at all. No such module exists: every number issued is below
sixty-four, so reading a live module’s number modulo sixty-four gives the number
back, and every module can be named by its own number. An operand of 64 or more
still names the module whose number is the remainder, so PSPLIT of 64 splits module
0. That’s arithmetic on the operand, not a module hiding behind another one.

Try the budget with a pencil, because the arithmetic is the point. Start from the initial
state, module counter at zero. PNEW on cells 0 and 1: one module, counter at one.
Then split it and merge the two halves straight back, again and again, so the same
two cells end up exactly where they started every time. Each round trip spends three
numbers, two for the split and one for the merge. Write the counter down after each
trip: 4, 7, 10, and on. How many trips before something traps? The split needs the
counter plus two to be at most sixty-four, and the merge needs the counter plus one.
After twenty trips the counter reads sixty-one. The twenty-first split asks for sixty-
three and gets it; the twenty-first merge asks for sixty-four and gets it; the counter
sits at exactly sixty-four. The twenty-second split would need sixty-six, and traps.
Twenty-one round trips, the same two cells the whole time, and that run can never
make another module. Not even with PNEW, which needs one more number too.


Definition 16.6 (A partition in bounds). A graph G is in bounds when it is well formed
(Definition 16.5), every address in every module’s region is less than 128, nG ≤ 64,
and no identifier appears twice in modsG .


                                          216
The Thiele Machine                                                               Devon Thiele


Checked as the definitions partition_in_bounds, regions_in_memory and mo
dule_ids_distinct (VMStep.v).


Theorem 16.5 (The partition stays in bounds). (1) If graph(s) is in bounds and s steps
to s′ on any instruction, then graph(s′ ) is in bounds. (2) If graph(s) is well formed, has no
modules and has n ≤ 64, and s′ is reachable from s, then graph(s′ ) has disjoint, contiguous
regions, every address in every region is less than 128, its next module number is at most 64,
it has at most 64 modules, and every module identifier m in it satisfies m mod 64 = m. (3)
The same holds for the step function, and for a bounded run of a program from such a state.

Proof. (1) A case split over the step relation, one part at a time; a trap keeps the old
graph, so only successful steps need an argument. Memory: a successful PNEW passed
the memory test; PSPLIT’s two halves are pieces of a region already inside memory;
PMERGE’s joined region is the two old regions laid end to end. The counter: each
step that takes fresh numbers checked that it had room for them, and no other step
touches the counter. Distinct numbers: a new module gets the counter as its number,
and well-formedness says every existing number is below the counter, so the new one
is different from all of them; removing modules can’t create a repeat. Well-formedness
itself is Theorem 16.4. (2) graph(s) is in bounds (no modules, so nothing to check but
the counter), and induction on the steps with (1) carries it to s′ . Then s′ has distinct
module numbers, all below n ≤ 64, so there are at most sixty-four of them, and
each one is below sixty-four, so taking it modulo sixty-four changes nothing. The
disjoint, contiguous regions are part (3) of Theorem 16.3. (3) The same case split, on
the function.

Checked as vm_step_preserves_partition_in_bounds for (1), with its parts
vm_step_preserves_regions_in_memory, vm_step_preserves_modules_
bounded and vm_step_preserves_module_ids_distinct, and vm_reacha
ble_partition_in_bounds for (2), using modules_count_bounded and mod
ule_id_mod_64, with the two tests module_room and region_in_memory (all
VMStep.v). For (3), vm_apply_preserves_partition_in_bounds and run_vm
_partition_in_bounds (SimulationProof.v). The chip makes the same two tests
and traps the same way (Section 27).

16.5 Where a run starts
I’ve been saying “reachable,” so here’s the starting state, the kernel’s init_state:
every register and memory word zero, program counter zero, counter zero, the tensor
zeros, the error flag down, the certified flag down, the assertion channel zero, the
witness counts zero, and a graph with no modules and no arrows. The module counter
starts at zero and the arrow counter at one. These are conventions of this initialization.
The theorems about reachable states start from this state, or from any state with no
modules. Three other initialization conventions used by the implementations differ
from this one: the library’s empty_graph starts both counters at one; the extracted


                                             217
The Thiele Machine                                                                 Devon Thiele


runner starts both at one (Coq can turn its definitions into an ordinary program, here
in the language OCaml, a step called extraction, and the runner is that program, the
one the demonstration in Section 21 drives); and the standalone copy of the kernel
starts both at zero. That copy is one long file, ThieleMachineComplete.v, that carries
its own copy of the machine so the whole build can be read top to bottom; a test checks
that its definitions match the kernel’s text, which is a test and not a proof. When I say
“initial” below I mean the kernel’s.

Four starting conventions that disagree about counting from zero or from one sounds
like carelessness, and maybe some of it is. It’s also one of the oldest arguments in
programming, and it has a famous referee. In 1982 Edsger Dijkstra wrote one of the
numbered notes he circulated to colleagues, EWD 831, titled “Why numbering should
start at zero.” His case goes through ranges first. Of the four ways to write “2 up to
12” with less-than signs, he picks the one that takes the bottom in and leaves the top
out, 2 ≤ i < 13: two ranges that meet end to end then share one number written once,
and the length is just the top minus the bottom. Start a sequence of N things at zero
and it’s 0 ≤ i < N, and each thing’s number is how many things came before it. He
reports that programmers on the language Mesa, which allowed all four conventions,
found the other three a steady source of clumsiness and mistakes, and he points out
that FORTRAN starts at one.

Does that settle it? It settles which convention is tidier, by an argument you can check.
It doesn’t settle which convention somebody else’s code used, and that’s the trap:
Minsky numbers lines from 1 and the small machine follows him, the big machine’s
program counter starts at 0, and the four initializations above split between 0 and
1. And look where the book already took his side without saying so. The regions
are written [b, b + n), bottom in, top out, and that’s why PSPLIT’s two halves, [b, b +
⌊n/2⌋) and [b + ⌊n/2⌋, b + n), meet at a number written once, with no plus one
or minus one anywhere. Is zero the right place to start counting? I can’t tell you.
Dijkstra’s note doesn’t claim to either; it shows which way makes fewer mistakes,
which is a different and more useful thing.


Definition 16.7 (The initial state). The initial state s0 has graph (n, mods, a, arrows) =
(0, [ ], 1, [ ]); all four control and status words 0; registers sixteen zeros and memory a
hundred and twenty-eight zeros; pc = 0; µ = 0; the global tensor sixteen zeros; the
error flag false; the logic accumulator and the mode word 0; all eight witness counts 0;
and the certified flag false.


Corollary 16.6 (What every run from the start keeps). For every state s′ reachable from
s0 : the graph of s′ has disjoint, contiguous regions, each inside memory; it is well formed; it
has at most sixty-four modules, each numbered below sixty-four; and |regs(s′ )| = 16 and
|mem(s′ )| = 128.



                                              218
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


Proof. s0 has no modules, so part (3) of Theorem 16.3 gives the regions. The graph of
s0 is well formed because all three clauses are about empty lists, and Theorem 16.4
carries it along every step. Its module counter is 0 ≤ 64, so part (2) of Theorem 16.5
gives memory, the count and the numbers. The lengths hold at s0 ; each step of the
relation lands on the value of the step function (the bridge between the two, which
Section 17 states as Lemma 17.1), so Lemma 16.2 carries them.

Checked as init_state (MuInitiality.v) for the values. The corollary is the four
theorems instantiated at s0 ; no single Coq name packages it, and the step “the empty
graph is well formed” is checked for the library’s empty_graph (empty_graph_
well_formed, VMState.v) rather than for this graph, whose counter starts at zero
instead of one.

16.6 The size constants
Sixteen registers, a hundred and twenty-eight words, sixty-four module slots, a region
size of sixteen. All four are definitions with literal values, and it’s easy to read the
first two as parameters. They aren’t: the proofs unfold the literal and compute with it
(unfold REG_COUNT; lia and its cousins appear throughout), no file binds either
as a variable or hypothesis, and no theorem is stated for other values. The proofs
are about sixteen and a hundred and twenty-eight. Retargeting means editing one
definition and every tactic that computes on the literal, which the hardware side’s own
comment admits for its table sizes. The sixty-four is the module-number budget of the
last part, the one the partition rules check, and the same number the hardware’s table
has slots for; the split and merge rules still write their operand reduction as “mod 64”
with the literal. The region-size constant is used nowhere at all.


Remark 16.2 (The four constants). The kernel defines R = 16 (REG_COUNT), M = 128
(MEM_SIZE), 64 (NUM_MODULES) and 16 (REGION_SIZE), each as a literal in VM-
State.v. R and M enter the semantics through r mod R and a mod M (Definition 16.2),
the initial lists (Definition 16.7), and one cap: MORPH reads at most M/2 = 64 cou-
pling pairs from memory. M also enters through PNEW’s memory test, and NUM_
MODULES through the module-number test of PNEW, PSPLIT and PMERGE (Defi-
nition 16.6 and Section 17). The operand reduction of PSPLIT and PMERGE writes
m mod 64 with the literal, not the constant, and REGION_SIZE appears nowhere else.
Every theorem in this chapter that mentions a size is about these values and no others.


16.7 What the record promises, and what it doesn’t
It promises: a counter that’s a natural number, a flag that’s a bit, an error that latches,
a graph whose regions don’t overlap and stay inside memory on any reachable state,
at most sixty-four module numbers per run, and sixty-four-bit truncation on every
register and memory write. It doesn’t promise: what the program is, what was emitted,
that the lists have their intended lengths (that’s a separate invariant), that the axiom


                                           219
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


strings mean anything, or that the per-arrow cost field records anything. And it’s one
choice of record. The abstract theorems needed only “a state, a step, a reading, a cost,”
and this is one way to fill those in, with twelve fields, two of which are scaffolding.

Next: what you can do to one of these. Fifty-one things.

17 The instruction set and the cost schedule
Fifty-one instructions. I’m going to give you all of them, because a reader who’s been
told “the machine charges for certification” deserves to see the whole price list and
check that nothing else is charged for in secret, and because the table is the thing that
makes Section 4’s argument (Theorem 4.2: finiteness, permanence and merge pricing
force the toll) checkable on this machine: here are the steps, here are the prices, go and
see which ones merge. Three things to know before the tables.

Every instruction carries a declared cost, which I’ll write d, chosen by whoever writes
the program; it can be zero. So read the counter as a receipt with that in mind: the
floor and the payload charges are the machine’s, and every other unit on it is a number
the program chose to write. (The kernel’s counter is a natural number with no ceiling.
The chip’s is a register of fixed width, and a big enough declared cost wraps it, which
Section 27 deals with.) The counter rises by exactly the instruction’s cost on every
path, success or failure, because the cost is on the attempt (Section 6’s conservation,
Theorem 6.1, checked on this machine as Section 16’s Theorem 16.1, vm_apply_mu).
(A housekeeping fact about every theorem name below: the rows are step relations,
but the theorems are stated on vm_apply, the function that computes a step, and v
m_step_vm_apply is the bridge. If the relation says one state steps to another on
an instruction, the function returns exactly that state.) Thirty-nine instructions cost
exactly d. Twelve cost at least one more than d, and those twelve are the cost-positive
class; the predicate that picks them out is called is_cert_setterb, and its own
comment says it is not the literal “sets csr_cert_addr” predicate (csr_cert_addr is the
source’s name for the assertion channel): it marks the positive-cost policy. In the step
rules only two instructions actually flip a certification reading (one sets the assertion
channel, one sets the flag), and I’ll point at them. For the channel, the fact is morph
_assert_step_sets_supra_cert_iff: from a clear channel, one step leaves it
nonzero exactly when that step is a MORPH_ASSERT on an arrow that exists, with a
property whose checksum isn’t zero. For the flag it’s the one line in CERTIFY’s rule.
The class is wider than the flippers, which is a design choice I’ll defend after the tables.

Register names wrap modulo sixteen and memory addresses modulo one hundred
and twenty-eight, and every value written to a register or a memory word is truncated
to sixty-four bits (Section 16).

And how to read the tables. In the cost column, S d means d plus one: S is Coq’s name
for “the next number,” which is the most Coq way possible of saying plus one, and
that plus one is the floor. The fault column says what a failure does. TRAP jumps to


                                            220
The Thiele Machine                                                                 Devon Thiele


a fixed trap address, 3840 (0xF00 in hexadecimal; it’s the chosen trap vector, a design
pick that nothing derives), and sets the error code and the error flag. LATCH steps on
to the next instruction, sets the error code and the flag, and changes nothing else. The
last column says whether the instruction is in the cost-positive class.

Where does that S come from? It’s older than Coq by about a century. In 1888 Richard
Dedekind published a little book whose title asks what numbers are and what they’re
for, and in 1889 Giuseppe Peano published a booklet, written in Latin, which is usually
counted as the first statement of the axioms for the whole numbers that people still
teach: there’s a first number, and every number has a next one, and a few rules about
how “next” behaves. The two were worked out independently, and the axioms often
go by both names. (Peano’s booklet is also where the sign ∈ that you met in Section 2
is usually said to come from.) Coq builds its whole numbers exactly that way, out of
zero and “the next one” and nothing else, so inside Coq the number three really is S
(S (S O)), the next of the next of the next of zero. What that changes here is small and
I like it: the floor on the twelve positive instructions isn’t a “plus one” slapped on a
price list. It’s one application of the smallest step the number system has. You can’t
charge less than one S and still charge something.

Here is the shape of a step, exactly, before the tables fill it in.


Definition 17.1 (Instructions, step relation, step function). An instruction is one of
fifty-one constructors, each with its operands and a declared cost d ∈ N. The step

an instruction to a state. A run from s on a program P (a list of instructions) with fuel
k fetches the instruction at position pc of P, applies it, and repeats, stopping after k
steps or when pc falls outside P. The program is never part of the state.

The table is a diet version, so here’s what it left on the plate. PNEW claims the range
from the first listed address for as many cells as there are distinct addresses, and traps
if any cell of that range is past the hundred and twenty-eight words of memory. If some
module owns exactly that range, nothing changes; otherwise a fresh module with no
axioms is added; and a PNEW that traps leaves the graph unchanged. All three take
fresh module numbers from a budget of sixty-four per run that is never refunded
(Section 16 tells that story): PNEW asks for one, PSPLIT for two, PMERGE for one,
and each traps when the budget can’t cover it. PSPLIT and PMERGE remove every
arrow touching a module they remove. Both take their module operands modulo
64 first, which always names the module itself (Theorem 16.5); the odd corner, an
operand of 64 or more, is in Section 16. PSPLIT accepts its left and right operands and
ignores them, and a missing module splits into two empty ones. PMERGE’s joined
range starts from the lower base.

The three rules that reshape modules, exactly. They use the region notions of Section 16
(Definition 16.4).

Definition 17.2 (PNEW, PSPLIT, PMERGE). For a list r, let r̄ be r with repeats removed
(first occurrences kept) and q(r ) = [hd(r̄ ), hd(r̄ ) + |r̄ |). A range q conflicts with G
when some module’s region shares an address with q without having the same set
of addresses. Write nG for the graph’s next module number; G has room for k when
nG + k ≤ 64. A trap keeps the graph, sets the error code to 1, sets the error flag, and
sets pc to 3840. Every branch below adds the instruction’s cost to µ, and every branch
that does not trap sets pc to pc + 1.

PNEW r: if G has no room for 1, or some address of q(r ) is 128 or more, or q(r ) conflicts
with the graph, trap. Otherwise, if some module’s region has the same addresses as
q(r ), keep the graph; if not, add a module with region q(r ), no axioms, and a zero
tensor.

PSPLIT m: if G has no room for 2, trap. Otherwise let m′ = m mod 64 and ρ the region
of m′ (empty if m′ is absent). Delete every arrow whose source or target is m′ , remove
m′ if present, then add a module with the first ⌊|ρ|/2⌋ addresses of ρ and another with
the rest. Its two region operands are not read.

PMERGE m1 , m2 : let m′j = m j mod 64 and ρ j their regions (empty if absent). If G has
no room for 1, or neither ρ1 ρ2 nor ρ2 ρ1 (concatenation) is contiguous, trap. Otherwise
delete every arrow touching m1′ or m2′ , remove both, and add one module whose
region is ρ1 ρ2 if that is contiguous and ρ2 ρ1 if not.

About LASSERT’s price: the declared length has to equal the length word in memory,
so declaring a smaller formula only gets you trapped (lassert_honest_cost; its
corollary lassert_honest_mu_cost says a successful LASSERT is charged the
length actually read, times eight, plus the floor). The eight is a pricing convention.
Nothing says each unit is a byte or that the charge counts physical information. So a


                                              224
The Thiele Machine                                                                   Devon Thiele


formula whose header says two units, checked with declared cost zero, costs 2 × 8 +
1 = 17, and a declaration of zero units for the same formula costs 1 and traps.

Theorem 17.2 (A successful LASSERT pays for what it read). Let s −            → s′ with i =
LASSERT with operands f , c, kind k, declared length ℓ and declared cost d. Let h(s, f ) be
the length word the checker reads from the formula header at the address held in register f . If
pc(s′ ) ̸= 3840, then ℓ = h(s, f ) and


                              µ(s′ ) = µ(s) + 8 h(s, f ) + d + 1.

Proof. The rule’s success test is the conjunction of “h(s, f ) = ℓ” and the satisfying
and falsifying checks; when the test fails the rule sets pc to 3840. So a step that lands
elsewhere passed the test, which gives ℓ = h(s, f ). The counter equation is then
conservation (Theorem 16.1) with cost(i ) = 8ℓ + d + 1.

Checked as lassert_honest_cost and lassert_honest_mu_cost (StateSpace-
Counting.v). The premise is about the landing address: a success whose next address
happens to be 3840 is outside the statement. Two more names sit nearby and are about
a different object. lassert_cost_from_component_floors and lassert_cos
t_is_its_formula (MuCostDerivation.v) concern a separate model of a constraint,
with a state count before and after and a description length: its total is defined as
log2 Ω − log2 Ω′ + bits, and the two theorems say that this total is that sum and that
any charge paying at least each term pays at least the total. Both hold by unfolding
the definition; neither is about the machine’s schedule.

MDLACC’s name is short for minimum description length, Rissanen’s idea from
Section 2, the one you worked on a row of thirty-two digits: a model’s bill is the bits to
write the model down plus the bits to write the data given the model. The step doesn’t
know any of that. It charges its declared d and steps on, with no graph change and
no register read. If a program uses it to enter a description-length bill, the number is
whatever the program declared, and nothing checks it against a description.

17.3 Group 3: compute and data transfer (14)
All fourteen step on; thirteen write one register and XOR_SWAP writes two; none
touches the graph or the status words; none faults. Cost d for every one; none is in
the positive class. None can move the assertion channel either: over any run of the
instructions the source calls classical, which includes all fourteen, the assertion channel
ends where it started (classical_trace_preserves_cert_addr). Arithmetic
doesn’t mint certified structure.

The payload prices in numbers, at declared cost zero: an EMIT of one character costs
8 + 1 = 9 and of ten characters 80 + 1 = 81 (the payload’s bit length is defined as eight
times its character count, payload_bit_length_ascii); a REVEAL of zero bits
costs 1 and of thirty-two bits costs 33. Revealing more costs more, one mark per bit,
and the cert operand that comes with it is never read, so what’s priced is the disclosure,
not anything it proves.

What the cells leave out. CHSH_TRIAL, given four bits, bumps the “same” or the
“different” counter for the setting pair x y, and that’s all it records: the witness counters
keep only same and different per setting pair, so no marginals are recorded, and
the inequality is not checked here. CERTIFY run again on a certified state still costs.
REVEAL adds its bits to entry (operand mod 16) of the global mu tensor in the record;
the operand is called module but acts as a direction index, not a module slot, and the
cert operand is not checked. Each supplied moment of the last three checks comes in
the instruction as a same/different pair of counts.

On success every CHSH_LASSERT variant only steps on: neither certification reading
changes. Success is visible only as “no trap.” The check happened, and nothing was
committed; Section 22 puts that next to Section 9’s test and commit. (The source
defines a marker word for a passed check, and no step writes it.) CHSH_TRIAL,
in the same group, never moves a certification reading from any state and costs its
declared d, which may be zero; Section 22 sorts it as raw observation in Section 9’s
sense (Definition 9.1), with the theorem. Because no marginals are kept, the checks are
zero-marginal conditions (the bridge to the physics, zero_marginal_column_con
tractive, is Section 25’s).

What the G345 variant checks: the base column check on the eight counters; each
supplied moment γ3 , γ4 , γ5 , given as a same/different pair, strictly between −1 and 1;
and a list of strict positivity tests on integer polynomials in the counts and the supplied
pairs, three for a two-by-two block and four for the leading minors of a four-by-four
matrix (Sylvester’s test for positive definiteness). All of it is integer arithmetic.

Sylvester’s name on a test about matrices fits in a way I enjoy, because the word matrix
is his. In 1850 James Joseph Sylvester used it for an “oblong arrangement of terms” out
of which you cut square blocks and take their determinants, and matrix was already
an old word for the place something grows from. That’s exactly what the test does:


                                            229
The Thiele Machine                                                                Devon Thiele


it cuts the top-left square blocks out of the big grid, one row deep, two, three, four
(the leading minors), and asks each one’s determinant to be positive. Was he the first
to state the test? The name doesn’t settle that; names stick to people for all kinds of
reasons, and I’d treat this one as a lead.

And notice the tests are strict: positive, not “at least zero.” That’s not fussiness, and
you can see why at the table. Take the two-by-two grid with 0 and 0 on the top row
and 0 and −1 on the bottom. Its top-left block is 0 and its whole determinant is 0:
both at least zero. But the grid isn’t positive semidefinite, because pushing on the
second direction alone gives −1. With “at least zero,” looking at only the top-left
blocks misses that; you’d have to check every square block on the diagonal. With
strict signs the top-left blocks are enough, and they certify strictly positive (definite)
blocks, which is the version of the shortcut that’s sound. How those blocks add up
to the nine-by-nine conclusion in the remark below is Section 25’s and Appendix F’s
argument, not this table’s.


Remark 17.1 (What a passing G345 step gives). Let s have err(s) false, let i be CHSH_
LASSERT_1AB_G345 with declared cost d and pairs ( a3 , b3 ), ( a4 , b4 ), ( a5 , b5 ), and let
s′ = apply(s, i ). If pc(s′ ) = pc(s) + 1 and err(s′ ) = err(s), then the nine-by-nine level
1+AB moment matrix built from the four correlators of s’s counters, with γ1 = γ2 = 0
and γ j = ( a j − b j )/( a j + b j ) for j = 3, 4, 5, is symmetric and positive semidefinite.
Section 25 and Appendix F carry the matrix and the argument; the check itself is q1ab
_g345_full_integer_check_kernel (VMStep.v) and the implication is chsh_l
assert_1ab_g345_no_trap_implies_npa_psd_q1ab (QuantumPartitionPSD_
1AB.v).
