And the leftovers from this table. MORPH reads a coupling block from memory (a
count, then pairs, then a label) and keeps only the pairs whose ends lie in the two
modules’ regions. MORPH_ID’s arrow has an empty coupling and the identity flag
set, and every call makes a fresh one. MORPH_ASSERT’s checksum is the sum of the
property string’s character codes, and it overwrites whatever the channel held; the
cert operand is never read. A sum of codes forgets order, and more: “ab” and “ba”
sum to the same number, and so do plenty of labels that have nothing to do with each
other. So the channel binds nothing beyond “some label with this sum was asserted
last.” MORPH_TENSOR adds its arrow only when both arrows and all four of their
end modules exist, both source regions are disjoint, both target regions are disjoint,
and modules owning exactly each union exist.

MORPH_GET reads the graph, and so does TENSOR_GET in group 5 (it reads a

                                            231
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


module’s tensor). The source still files both under the classical instructions, because
neither writes the graph, a channel, the certified flag or the witness counters. Keep
that in mind in Section 20.


Definition 17.3 (Classical instructions). The classical instructions are twenty-nine of
the fifty-one: the fourteen of Group 3; the eight of Group 4; and MDLACC, READ_
PORT, WRITE_PORT, HEAP_LOAD, HEAP_STORE, TENSOR_GET and MORPH_
GET. The other twenty-two are not classical: PNEW, PSPLIT, PMERGE, PDISCOVER,
LASSERT, LJOIN, EMIT, REVEAL, TENSOR_SET, CHSH_TRIAL, CERTIFY, the five
CHSH_LASSERT variants, and MORPH, COMPOSE, MORPH_ID, MORPH_DELETE,
MORPH_ASSERT and MORPH_TENSOR. For a list t of instructions, run(t, s) applies
them to s in order with the step function, with no fetching by program counter.


Theorem 17.3 (Classical runs move nothing that certifies). Let t be a list of classical
instructions and s any state. Then graph(run(t, s)) = graph(s), certaddr(run(t, s)) =
certaddr(s), and cert(run(t, s)) = cert(s).

Proof. First one step: for each classical instruction, every branch of its rule copies the
graph, the control and status words’ address field, and the certified flag from the old
state. The three with two branches (JNEZ, TENSOR_GET, MORPH_GET) copy them
in both. Coq checks this by a case split that closes by computation. Then induction on
t.

Checked as is_classical_opcode, classical_trace_preserves_graph, cl
assical_trace_preserves_cert_addr and classical_trace_preserves
_certified (ClassicalConservativity.v). The class is a choice of the file, not a closure
property: PDISCOVER is left out although its step changes nothing, and READ_PORT
is in although it costs at least one. The same three equalities hold when the program
runs by program counter, jumps and all (classical_opcodes_preserve_struc
ture_run_vm); Section 23 states that form.

The classical view can’t recover the flag either. Take the four fields a classical observer
sees, the program counter, the counter, the registers and the memory, and map a list of
states to the list of those four-field snapshots. No function on the snapshot lists gives
back the certified flag of the last state, for every list: no_classical_certificati
on_decider (WitnessPreservationImpossibility.v). The proof is two hand-built states
that agree on all four fields and differ in the flag; they’re records the type allows, not
states shown reachable from the start. Section 20 does the same with the graph.

Four plus three plus fourteen plus eight plus seven plus eight plus seven: fifty-one.

17.8 The schedule, read as a whole
Four cost shapes. Thirty-nine instructions cost exactly their declared d, which may
be zero. Eight cost d plus one, the floor: LJOIN, CERTIFY, MORPH_ASSERT, and
the five CHSH_LASSERT variants. Three cost a payload plus the floor: EMIT (eight
per character), READ_PORT and REVEAL (their bit count). And LASSERT costs the
formula length times eight plus the floor. The twelve with a floor are exactly the
positive class; that much is read off the definitions, and the theorems are one line each:
cert_setter_cost_pos, if the predicate holds, the cost is at least one; cert_se
tter_cost_above_declared, it’s at least one more than declared; and non_cer
t_setter_cost_is_declared, if the predicate fails, the cost is exactly what was
declared.


Definition 17.4 (The schedule). For an instruction i with declared cost d, the cost
cost(i ) is: 8ℓ + d + 1 for LASSERT with declared length ℓ; 8| p| + d + 1 for EMIT with
payload p of | p| characters; b + d + 1 for READ_PORT and REVEAL with bit count b;
d + 1 for LJOIN, CERTIFY, MORPH_ASSERT and the five CHSH_LASSERT variants;
and d for each of the other thirty-nine.


Definition 17.5 (The positive class and the setter class). The positive class is the twelve
instructions in the first four cases of Definition 17.4: LASSERT, EMIT, READ_PORT,
REVEAL, LJOIN, CERTIFY, MORPH_ASSERT and the five CHSH_LASSERT vari-
ants. The setter class is five of them: LASSERT, LJOIN, EMIT, REVEAL and MORPH_
ASSERT.


Theorem 17.4 (The floor). If i is in the positive class, then cost(i ) ≥ d + 1 ≥ 1. If i is
outside it, then cost(i ) = d, and with d = 0 the instruction is free.

Proof. Case split on i. Each of the twelve has a +1 in its cost, so the cost is at least one
whatever d is. The other thirty-nine cost d by definition.

Checked as instruction_cost, is_cert_setterb, cert_setter_cost_pos
and cert_setter_cost_above_declared for the first sentence and non_cert_
setter_cost_is_declared for the second, with declared_mu_delta reading
the declared cost d off any instruction (all VMStep.v), the setter class cert_addr_
setterb (AbstractNoFI.v) and the payload length payload_bit_length_ascii
(VMStep.v). Examples of the second sentence at work: morph_can_be_free, morp
h_compose_cost_zero, and the PNEW, PSPLIT and PMERGE cases inside parti
tion_free_but_certification_nonfree. One example runs a whole program
at zero: blind_program (StructuralAdvantage.v) is a ten-instruction search loop of
LOAD_IMM, ADD, SUB, JNEZ and JUMP, every one at declared cost zero, and blin
d_program_total_cost_is_zero says its costs sum to zero.



                                            233
The Thiele Machine                                                                   Devon Thiele


Now the design choice. Only two of the twelve flip a reading: CERTIFY sets the flag
and MORPH_ASSERT sets the assertion channel. The other ten are in the class because
they’re checks or emissions: LASSERT and the CHSH family check and charge for the
checking (Section 9’s Popper point: charge the attempt, pass or fail); EMIT, REVEAL
and READ_PORT move information across the machine’s boundary and charge per
bit; LJOIN is a join of certificates that does nothing yet and charges the floor anyway.
The toll of Section 3 (Definition 3.1) needs only the two flippers to be priced. The
schedule prices more. That’s allowed, Section 10’s billed machine says so (the toll is a
floor, and a surcharge only raises the price), and it’s a choice I’d defend this way: the
things that cost at least one are the things that claim to have looked at or sent something,
and I’d rather the machine never let a look or a send be free than argue about which
looks matter. You can disagree. The flippers are two; the floor is on twelve; both
numbers are in the table.

And more things to watch doesn’t mean a bigger floor. If an instruction triggers several
of the events you want priced, one mark covers all of them; the floors don’t add unless
you write a rule that makes them add.


Theorem 17.5 (The joint floor is the least). Let E1 , . . . , En be yes/no tests on instructions,
and let J (i ) = 1 if some Ej (i ) holds and J (i ) = 0 otherwise. For any cost function c from
instructions to N: c(i ) ≥ 1 for every j and every i with Ej (i ) if and only if J (i ) ≤ c(i ) for
every i. So J is the least cost meeting all the unit floors at once.

Proof. If c meets every floor and some Ej (i ) holds, then c(i ) ≥ 1 = J (i ); if none holds,
J (i ) = 0 ≤ c(i ). Conversely, if J ≤ c and Ej (i ) holds, then J (i ) = 1, so c(i ) ≥ 1.

Checked as joint_floor_is_least (ObservationPolicy.v). It’s stated for any in-
struction type, not only this machine’s.

A second thing you’ll notice: the arrow-building instructions are free at d equals zero.
MORPH, COMPOSE, MORPH_ID, MORPH_DELETE, MORPH_TENSOR, MORPH_
GET all cost d (morph_compose_cost_zero and its siblings), and so does PNEW.
Building structure is free. Asserting it is not. In Section 9’s terms (Definition 9.1),
building never turns a reading on, so it sorts with raw observation, and asserting
is certified insight; Section 22 lays the tiers out on the machine. Notice what that
does to a tempting sentence: a zero-cost PNEW changes the graph, so “every change
to the structure costs something” is false for this machine. What costs something is
vouching.

And here’s what the table makes checkable, all on this machine, all over the fifty-one
cases, one sentence per fact. One step that takes the assertion channel from zero to
nonzero costs at least one (no_free_certification). The same holds for the flag
(no_free_certification_certified). Either one raises the counter by at least
one (certification_requires_positive_mu). And over a whole run, a start


                                               234
The Thiele Machine                                                                   Devon Thiele


with the channel clear and an end with it set means the run contained a positive-cost
instruction and the counter rose by at least one (no_free_certified_insight).
One detail in that last one: the instruction it finds comes from a narrower list than
the twelve, a five-member predicate called cert_addr_setterb (LASSERT, LJOIN,
EMIT, REVEAL and MORPH_ASSERT), of which only MORPH_ASSERT writes the
channel. So the theorem says which kind of instruction was in the run, and morph
_assert_step_sets_supra_cert_iff is the finer fact about which one moved
the channel. Those are Section 3’s universal floor (Theorem 3.1), landed on fifty-one
constructors; Section 23 lines up the whole ladder of its instances.

Here are those facts exactly. Write certaddr(s) for the assertion channel, cert(s) for the
certified flag, and Σ( p) for the sum of the character codes of a string p.


Theorem 17.6 (Only CERTIFY touches the flag, and it stays set). For every state s
and instruction i: cert(apply(s, i )) is true if i is CERTIFY, and equals cert(s) otherwise.
Hence (1) if cert(s) is true, so is cert(apply(s, i )) for every i; and (2) if cert(s) is false and
cert(apply(s, i )) is true, then i is CERTIFY, cost(i ) ≥ 1, and µ(apply(s, i )) ≥ µ(s) + 1.

Proof. Case split over the fifty-one instructions and their branches: CERTIFY’s rule
writes true, and every other rule copies the flag. (1) follows because both cases give
true when the old value is true. (2): the old value is false and the new one true, so
the second case is impossible and i is CERTIFY with cost d + 1; the counter claim is
conservation.

Checked as step_certify (VMStep.v), vm_apply_certified (PrimeAxiom.v), c
ertification_reading_permanent (EventSwapTheorem.v) for (1), and no_fre
e_certification_certified with no_free_certification_certified_m
u (AbstractNoFI.v) for (2). The run form is kernel_certified_implies_positi
ve_mu (PrimeAxiom.v): if a run fetched by program counter starts with the flag down
and the counter at zero and ends with the flag up, the counter at the end is positive.


Theorem 17.7 (Only MORPH_ASSERT touches the channel). For every state s: (1) if i is
not a MORPH_ASSERT, then certaddr(apply(s, i )) = certaddr(s). (2) For i = MORPH_
ASSERT with arrow k, property p, certificate c and declared cost d: if arrow k is in the graph,
the step sets certaddr to Σ( p) and changes nothing else but pc and µ; if it is not, the step
leaves certaddr alone, sets the error code to 1 and the error flag to true, and changes nothing
else but pc and µ. In both cases c is not read and µ(apply(s, i )) = µ(s) + d + 1. (3) If
certaddr(s) = 0, then certaddr(apply(s, i )) ̸= 0 if and only if i is a MORPH_ASSERT
whose arrow is in the graph of s and whose property has Σ( p) ̸= 0.

Proof. (1) is a case split over the other fifty instructions and their branches; each copies
the address field, including the faulting branches, whose error writer changes only the
error code. (2) is the two rules read off. (3): if i is not a MORPH_ASSERT, (1) keeps the


                                               235
The Thiele Machine                                                                  Devon Thiele


channel at 0; if it is and the arrow is missing, (2) keeps it at 0; if the arrow is present,
the new value is Σ( p), which is nonzero exactly when the right side says so.

Checked as non_morph_assert_preserves_cert_addr and morph_assert_s
tep_sets_supra_cert_iff (RevelationRequirement.v), step_morph_assert_
ok and step_morph_assert_bad (VMStep.v), and ascii_checksum (VMState.v).
The channel is overwritten, not added to: a later MORPH_ASSERT with Σ( p) = 0 on
an existing arrow puts it back to zero. No step rule reads the channel or the flag.

There’s no gap between paying and flipping. The rule that writes the flag or the
channel is the same rule that adds the cost; it’s one step, and there is no state in
between where the reading has moved and the charge hasn’t landed. A simulator that
did these as two separate operations could get the order wrong; this machine has no
order to get wrong.


Theorem 17.8 (No free certification on this machine). (1) If certaddr(s) = 0 and
certaddr(apply(s, i )) ̸= 0, then cost(i ) ≥ 1. (2) If cert(s) is false and cert(apply(s, i )) is
true, then cost(i ) ≥ 1. (3) In either case, µ(apply(s, i )) ≥ µ(s) + 1. (4) If certaddr(s) = 0
and certaddr(run(t, s)) ̸= 0, then some i in t is in the setter class with cost(i ) ≥ 1, and
µ(run(t, s)) ≥ µ(s) + 1.

Proof. (1): every instruction outside the setter class leaves the channel alone, so i is
in the setter class, and each of its five members has a +1 in its cost. (2) is part (2) of
Theorem 17.6. (3) is conservation with (1) or (2). (4): the channel is 0 at the start and
nonzero at the end, so some step of the run takes it from 0 to nonzero; by (1) that step’s
instruction is a setter with cost at least one, and since the counter never falls, the end
counter is at least one above the start.

Checked as no_free_certification, no_free_certification_certifie
d and certification_requires_positive_mu (AbstractNoFI.v), and no_fr
ee_certified_insight (InsightTaxonomy.v). Here run applies the list in order,
as in Definition 17.3. Three neighbours say the same thing in other shapes. thiel
e_nfi_pc_indexed (AbstractNoFI.v) is the setter half of (4) for a run fetched by
program counter with fuel: if such a run ends with the channel set from a clear start,
the program contains a setter. partition_refinement_nonfree (PartitionRefine-
mentNoFI.v) is (4) under a name that says what it is for: going from no certified claim
to one is a strict refinement, and it isn’t free. And partition_free_but_certifi
cation_nonfree (same file) packages the contrast of this section in one statement:
PNEW, PSPLIT and PMERGE each cost zero at declared cost zero, none of the three
is in the setter class, and any run that takes the channel from clear to set raises the
counter by at least one.

One more fact the theorems lean on, about the per-arrow cost field of Section 16: there

is a function that writes a value into that field of one arrow, and graph_certif

17.9 What the chip has
The hardware encodes forty-seven of the fifty-one. The four it doesn’t are the four
CHSH_LASSERT_1AB variants: they exist in the kernel and in the hardware-side
abstraction function, but the hardware assigns them no opcode byte and the CPU has
no reference to them. (The Python side does number them, 47 to 50, which is 0x2F
to 0x32 in hexadecimal: the generated opcode table thielecpu/generated/generated_
core.py and the assembler script scripts/forge.py. Neither Coq nor the hardware gives
them a byte.) The test that checks kernel-against-hardware parity, which compares the
OCaml extraction’s opcode names with the ones defined in the hardware’s type file,
allows at most four missing, with a comment naming these four; it does not check that
it’s exactly these four. I’d rather you know the test’s shape than assume it’s tighter
than it is. Everything else in the table has a byte, and the bytes are Section 27’s.

One rule for reading everything above: where a comment in the step file and the step
rule next to it disagree, the book follows the rule, because the rule is what the proofs
are about.

That’s what you can do. Next: the arrows, which the table has treated as seven opcodes
and which are, underneath, a piece of mathematics I didn’t know existed when I built
them.

18 What a morphism is
Category theory, from scratch. I didn’t know what it was when I started this project;
Section 2 and Section 1 have the story of building it by feel, as “digital DNA,” and
finding out after the thing already ran that it had a name and a founding paper. So
this section is me explaining the mathematics I accidentally used, with the two laws I
made you wait for in Section 2, and then holding my own machine up against those
laws on the arrows it actually stores, including the one case where the obvious rule
for identities breaks them. That case is the most useful paragraph in here, and it’s near
the end.

18.1 Objects, arrows, and a quiet promotion
A category is the part of mathematics that takes the relationships between things as
seriously as the things, and then quietly decides the relationships matter more. Two
ingredients. Objects: the things. Arrows: the relationships between them. That’s the
entire inventory, and it looks thin until you notice what got promoted. In most of
mathematics the objects are the citizens and the maps between them are second-class
traffic. A category turns that around. The arrows are first-class, and nearly everything

                                            237
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


you can say inside a category you say by pointing at arrows, not by reaching inside
objects. That’s the Eilenberg and Mac Lane move from Section 2 (1945, “a continuation
of Klein”): stop asking what a thing is, ask how it’s carried.

And where did they get the word? Not from mathematics. They borrowed category
from the philosophers, from Aristotle and Kant, and functor (a map from one whole
category to another, which turns up much later in this book) from the philosopher
Rudolf Carnap, and then gave both words exact meanings none of those philosophers
had in mind. So Aristotle walks back into this book without being asked: the man
who put the form inside the bronze lent his word to the field that keeps track of forms
by their arrows. Does that change the laws? No. It’s a reminder that a word can start
in philosophy and arrive in mathematics with a precise meaning bolted on, which is
the thing I’ve been trying to do with established since the first page.

The objects can be anything, which is both why the theory reaches so far and why it
feels slippery the first time through. Sets. Vector spaces. Shapes. The theory doesn’t
care what the objects are made of; it cares how they connect. Here, the objects are
modules, the named pieces a partition cut the state into (Section 16), and the arrows are
claims about how two pieces relate. Why modules and not cells or registers? Because
a claim about a relationship has to attach to something the machine can name and
keep, and a module is the one thing in the state an arrow’s two ends can be: you can
read an arrow’s source and target back (MORPH_GET), and with selector two, the
number of pairs in its coupling.

Arrows also go by the name morphisms, and the words are interchangeable; I’ll use both.
An arrow runs from one object to another, written f from A to B. The thing everyone
imports from school and has to set down is the assumption that an arrow is a function.
It needn’t be. An arrow is whatever the category accepts as a structure-respecting way
to get from A to B, and here it’s something more pointed than a function: a morphism
is a claim, “these two modules are related, and here is the kind of relation,” with the
evidence stapled on.

18.2 The two laws, and why each
Section 2 gave you the definition in one breath. Here it is slowed down: two ingredi-
ents first, then the two rules Section 2 said you’d watch me have to prove. Together
they’re the whole definition, and the rules are the part people skip.

Composition. If there’s an arrow f from A to B and an arrow g from B to C, there must
be a composite arrow from A to C, written g after f. Why? Because relationships have
to chain. A to B, B to C, therefore A to C. Picture three dots in a row, A, B and C: f
hops from the first to the second, g from the second to the third, and the composite
takes the whole stride from A to C in one. Without that, every multi-hop path has to
be named individually, and the structure collapses into a pile of unconnected pairs.
A category without composition is a phone book without a search function. In the
machine, COMPOSE builds the long arrow.

                                          238
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


Identity. Every object has a do-nothing arrow to itself. Why bother? Because every
object needs a self-loop, even the boring ones: a module with no connections still has
to exist somewhere in the framework, and “the arrow that does nothing” is how you
say “this thing, unchanged” in a language that only speaks in arrows. On the drawing
it’s a small loop on A, leaving A and arriving back at A. MORPH_ID builds the loop.

And the two rules that make following arrows dependable, the ones Section 2 named
in a sentence and left for here. Associativity: following three arrows in a row gives the
same result whether you pair up the first two or the last two. Why? Because paren-
thesisation shouldn’t matter. Both spell the same three-hop path. If they came out
different, two programs that built the same chain in different orders would produce
two different morphisms, and that’s a bug: the chain is the thing, how you assembled
it is not. Identity laws: tacking the do-nothing arrow onto either end of an arrow gives
back the arrow. If the self-loop changed things, it wouldn’t be the self-loop.

That’s a category. Objects, arrows, composition, identities, associativity, identity laws.
Six words and you’ve got the whole of Eilenberg and Mac Lane’s definition.


Definition 18.1 (Category). A category has a collection of objects; for each pair of
objects A, B a collection of arrows f : A → B; for each f : A → B and g : B → C a
composite g ◦ f : A → C; and for each object A an identity id A : A → A. These satisfy
associativity, h ◦ ( g ◦ f ) = (h ◦ g) ◦ f whenever the composites are defined, and the
identity laws, f ◦ id A = f = idB ◦ f for every f : A → B.


This is the textbook definition. No Coq file in the tree states it as a structure and proves
the machine is an instance; what Coq checks is the list of laws below, each on its own.

18.3 What a coupling is
Now the evidence stapled to the claim. In the machine, a morphism carries coupling
data: a list of pairs of cells, one from the source module’s region and one from the
target’s, plus a label. A pair (a, c) says: cell a in the source is related to cell c in the
target. That’s the relational content of the arrow, the actual record of which parts of
one module correspond to which parts of another. What the pairs mean is up to the
programmer: “B refines A, and here’s which cells map to which”; “A is correlated with
B at these pairs”; “A simulates B, these transitions correspond.” The kernel enforces
the composition rule on the pairs. The interpretation is yours.

Composition on couplings is relational composition, the thing you learned without a
name when you learned that “a is a parent of b” and “b is a parent of c” gives “a is a
grandparent of c”: a pair (a, c) is in the composite exactly when there’s some middle
cell b with (a, b) in the first coupling and (b, c) in the second. That’s relational_co
mpose_spec, and the machine’s kernel function is proved to be that function (kern
el_relational_compose_same).



                                            239
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


Who put a name on that move first? People older than you’d guess. Augustus De
Morgan, writing on the logic of relations around 1860, took the “is” out of the old
syllogism, put a general relation in its place, and composed two relations to get the
conclusion. The example that gets quoted from that tradition is “x is the lover of a
servant of y,” which is relational composition with better gossip. When exactly he
read that paper to the Cambridge Philosophical Society, and on which pages it was
printed, the sources disagree, which is a small reminder that history is where you
start digging. Then in 1870 Charles Sanders Peirce, the same Peirce from the opening
chapter, carried Boole’s algebra of logic over to relations, with composition as one of
its basic operations, and he’s usually counted as the real founder of the theory. So
COMPOSE’s rule is older than computers, older than categories, older than Turing’s
clerk: a nineteenth-century logician’s product of relations, run on lists of cell numbers.
Does that change the proof? No. It changes how old the move is, not whether it holds
on this machine. That’s what Coq is for.

And here’s a thing I’d never have seen without the laws. The identity arrow in this
machine doesn’t carry its identity in its coupling. The cheap guess for an identity
coupling is the empty list, and the empty relation annihilates under composition: com-
pose anything with “no pairs” and you get “no pairs” back, not the thing you started
with (relational_compose_empty_l, relational_compose_empty_r). The
coupling that would act as an identity is the diagonal, every cell of the region paired
with itself, and that’s proved to work on both sides (morph_id_left_coupling,
morph_id_right_coupling); but storing a diagonal means listing every cell of
the region in every identity arrow, so the machine stores a flag on the record instead,
and COMPOSE honours the flag: if both arrows are flagged, the composite is flagged
too, and stored exactly the way MORPH_ID stores an identity; if only the first is
flagged, the composite’s pairs are the second’s; if only the second, the first’s; else the
relational composition (graph_compose_morphisms_coupling, four cases). The
flag is load-bearing. That’s why MORPH_ID stores an empty coupling and sets the
flag, and why MORPH_GET has a selector for the flag. (The lemma that says the
identity arrow is an identity, graph_add_identity_coupling, proves only the
flag. It doesn’t prove the coupling is diagonal, because it isn’t.)

Here are the objects exactly.


Definition 18.2 (Coupling, relational composition, diagonal). A coupling is a finite list
of pairs of natural numbers. Its relational composition with a coupling S is

                     R; S = [ ( a, c) | ( a, b) ∈ R, (b′ , c) ∈ S, b = b′ ],

listed in the order the pairs of R and then S are visited. The diagonal of a list X of cells
is [( x, x ) | x ∈ X ]. Two couplings are equivalent, R ≡ S, when they contain the same
pairs: ( a, c) ∈ R ⇐⇒ ( a, c) ∈ S for all a, c.



                                              240
The Thiele Machine                                                                 Devon Thiele


Definition 18.3 (Stored arrow and the composition rule). A stored arrow has a source
module, a target module, a coupling with a label, an identity flag, and a cost field.
Storing an arrow removes duplicate pairs from its coupling and sets its cost field to 0.
MORPH_ID on an existing module A stores the arrow from A to A with the empty
coupling (no pairs, label “empty”) and the flag on. COMPOSE of stored arrows f and
h, when the target of f equals the source of h, stores a new arrow from the source of
f to the target of h. If both are flagged, the new arrow is flagged and has the empty
coupling, the same record MORPH_ID stores. Otherwise its flag is off, its label is the
label of f , a semicolon, and the label of h, and its pairs are
                      
                      
                      
                       pairs of h                  if only f is flagged,
                      
                        pairs of f                  if only h is flagged,
                      
                      
                      pairs of f ; pairs of h
                      
                                                    if neither is.

If either arrow is missing or the target and source differ, COMPOSE builds nothing.


Checked as the definitions relational_compose, diagonal, coupling_equi
v (CategoryLaws.v), and empty_coupling_data, graph_add_morphism, grap
h_add_identity, graph_compose_morphisms (VMState.v); kernel_relati
onal_compose_same says the kernel’s copy of relational composition is the same
function, and graph_compose_morphisms_coupling (CategoryBridge.v) says the
stored composite’s flag is the two flags anded together and its pairs are equivalent to
the four-case rule (equivalent rather than equal because storing removes duplicates).

Here’s why “equivalent” and not “equal,” at the table. Let R be two pairs, (1, 2) and
(1, 3): cell 1 is related to cell 2 and to cell 3. Let S be (2, 5) and (3, 5): both of those are
related to cell 5. Compose by the definition, walking R’s pairs in order and matching
each against S. (1, 2) meets (2, 5) and gives (1, 5). (1, 3) meets (3, 5) and gives (1, 5)
again. The list is (1, 5), (1, 5): two copies of one fact, because there were two middles,
2 and 3, on the way from 1 to 5. Store it and the duplicate goes, leaving (1, 5) once.
Same pairs, different lists. So the book compares couplings by which pairs they hold,
and two routes to one place count as one place.

18.4 What Coq checks, exactly
I promised in Section 2 you’d watch me prove the two rules. Here’s what’s proved,
with the hypotheses, and you can decide whether it’s enough.

On coupling lists, with “the same” meaning “hold the same pairs, order and repeats
ignored” (coupling_equiv): composition is associative (relational_compose
_assoc, with nothing assumed; the kernel-record forms coupling_data_compos
e_assoc, morph_compose_assoc_coupling, morph_graph_compose_assoc,
which are stated on the pair lists stored in the records, and none of which mentions
the identity flag or the composite a COMPOSE actually builds). The diagonal is a


                                              241
The Thiele Machine                                                                    Devon Thiele


left identity when every pair’s source lies in the region, and a right identity when
every target does. Composition respects the equivalence on both sides. The empty
list absorbs. And on the tensor side (two arrows side by side, pairs appended), there’s
an interchange law when the cross terms vanish, and append is associative with the
empty list as unit (tensor_bifunctor, monoidal_coherence).

On the stored records: what COMPOSE builds is the four-case rule above; what
MORPH_ID builds is flagged identity; a new arrow gets the next identifier and old
ones are untouched; a composite’s certification-cost field is zero. Associativity and
both identity laws hold on the stored arrows themselves, flag and all, which is the
next part’s whole job. And the hardware’s COMPOSE step produces exactly the state
the kernel’s does, whole state, coupling and label included (driven_step_compo
se, under the hardware well-formedness invariant). That last one is closed, with no
axiom behind it; the whole-machine version, every opcode under its side conditions
(driven_step_wf), uses one standard extensionality axiom at the hardware layer,
which Section 28 will account for.

The laws on couplings, exactly.


Theorem 18.1 (Laws of relational composition). For all couplings R, S, T, R′ , S′ and
every list of cells X: (1) ( a, c) ∈ R; S if and only if there is b with ( a, b) ∈ R and (b, c) ∈ S.
(2) ( R; S); T ≡ R; (S; T ). (3) If every pair ( a, b) of R has a ∈ X, then diag( X ); R ≡ R; if
every pair has b ∈ X, then R; diag( X ) ≡ R. (4) If R ≡ R′ and S ≡ S′ , then R; S ≡ R′ ; S′ .
(5) [ ]; R ≡ [ ] and R; [ ] ≡ [ ].

Proof. (1) Unfold the definition: a pair of the output comes from some ( a, b) in R and
some (b′ , c) in S that passed the test b = b′ , and every such match produces one. (2) By
(1) on both sides, each says there are b and b′ with ( a, b) ∈ R, (b, b′ ) ∈ S and (b′ , c) ∈ T.
(3) By (1), ( a, c) ∈ diag( X ); R means a ∈ X and ( a, c) ∈ R, and the hypothesis makes
the first part automatic; the right case is the mirror. (4) and (5) are (1) again.

Checked as relational_compose_spec (item (1), an if and only if), relational
_compose_assoc, relational_compose_diagonal_left, relational_com
pose_diagonal_right, relational_compose_compat, relational_compo

Theorem 18.2 (Tensor on couplings). Let R ⊗ S be the list R followed by S. Then ( R ⊗
S) ⊗ T = R ⊗ (S ⊗ T ), [ ] ⊗ R = R and R ⊗ [ ] = R, as lists. And if F; G ′ ≡ [ ] and
G; F ′ ≡ [ ], then ( F ⊗ G ); ( F ′ ⊗ G ′ ) ≡ ( F; F ′ ) ⊗ ( G; G ′ ).

Proof. The first three are facts about appending lists. For the last, by (1) of Theo-
rem 18.1 a pair of the left side comes from one of four combinations, and the two cross
