18.5 Where the laws meet the stored arrows
Now the paragraph I said was the most useful. The associativity theorem above is
about coupling lists. The question that matters is whether the laws hold for the arrows
COMPOSE actually stores, flag and all, and the flag hides a trap you can walk into
with three arrows. Take two identity arrows on module A (two calls to MORPH_ID
give two arrows, each flagged), call them i1 and i2, and an arrow f from A to B with a
nonempty coupling P.

Here’s the wrong neighbour first, because the border is drawn by both sides. The
obvious rule for the flag is “a composite is never an identity; if the first arrow is
flagged, take the second’s pairs.” Under that rule, i1 composed with i2 takes i2’s
pairs, the empty list, and gets built with the flag off. Compose that with f: neither is
flagged now, so it’s the relational composition of the empty list with P, which is empty.
Compose the other way, i1 with (i2 with f): i2 with f gives P, then i1 with that gives P
again. Empty on one side, P on the other. Under the obvious rule associativity breaks
the moment two identities meet, the mirror case breaks too (an arrow g from B to A
with pairs Q, followed by the composite of i1 and i2, gives the empty list instead of
Q), and the composite of two identities is an arrow from A to A that is an identity for
nothing. A book that proved the laws on pair lists and let that stand on the records
would be proving the laws somewhere the machine doesn’t live.

The machine’s rule passes the flag along (Definition 18.3): two flagged arrows compose
to a flagged one. Run the same three arrows through it. i1 composed with i2 is a
flagged identity on A. That composed with f: only the first is flagged, so take f’s pairs,
P. i1 with (i2 with f): i2 with f has pairs P and the flag off, i1 is flagged, so P. Same both
ways. And g followed by the composite of i1 and i2 gives Q, and so does g followed
by i1, then i2. The flag is the whole difference.

“Same” needs pinning down, further than feels necessary, because a stored arrow
carries more than the laws care about. COMPOSE always stores a new arrow under a
fresh identifier, so “i1 followed by f equals f” can’t mean the same identifier; it means
a new arrow that is f in every way the machine can act on. Its labels don’t match
either: the two bracketings above store “empty;” in front of f’s label once and twice.


                                             243
The Thiele Machine                                                                        Devon Thiele


Labels are names for a person reading the graph, and MORPH_GET has no selector
for one. And a flagged arrow’s pairs are never read by COMPOSE, so there’s nothing
to compare there. So two stored arrows are the same arrow when they have the same
source, the same target, the same flag, and, when the flag is off, the same pairs. With
that, the laws hold on the stored arrows, with two side conditions that carry weight:
the graph has to be well formed (so the arrows being composed are still where they
were after each COMPOSE adds one), and an identity arrow has to go from an object
to itself. MORPH_ID only builds those, and a separate invariant says nothing else
ever gets the flag.


Definition 18.4 (The same stored arrow). Two stored arrows x and y are the same arrow,
x∼= y, when they have the same source, the same target and the same flag, and, if the
flag of x is off, their pairs are equivalent (Definition 18.2). Labels, identifiers and cost
fields are not compared.


Checked as the definition stored_arrow_equiv (CategoryBridge.v).


Theorem 18.3 (The category laws on stored arrows). Write xy for the arrow COMPOSE
stores from stored arrows x followed by y, each COMPOSE run in the graph the previous one
left. (1) If i and j are flagged and the target of i is the source of j, then COMPOSE of i and j
succeeds and stores the arrow from the source of i to the target of j with the flag on, the empty
coupling and cost field 0. (2) If the graph is well formed and f , k, h are stored arrows with the
target of f the source of k and the target of k the source of h, then the four COMPOSEs that
build ( f k)h and f (kh) all succeed, and ( f k)h ∼ = f (kh). (3) If i is flagged, its source equals its
target, and its target is the source of a stored arrow f , then COMPOSE of i and f succeeds
and i f ∼= f . (4) If i is flagged, its source equals its target, and the target of a stored arrow f is
the source of i, then COMPOSE of f and i succeeds and f i ∼         = f.

Proof. COMPOSE of two stored arrows whose ends match always succeeds, stores the
composite under the next arrow identifier, and leaves every other identifier where it
was. (1) is the first case of the rule. (2) Well-formedness says every stored identifier
is below the next one, so f and h are still found after the first COMPOSE on each
side. Both composites go from the source of f to the target of h, and both carry the
flag exactly when all three of f , k, h do. If the flag is off, at least one of the three
is unflagged, and there are seven cases, one per pattern of flags; in each, item (1)
of Theorem 18.1 turns both sides into the same membership condition. With none
flagged it’s associativity on pairs; with only k flagged both sides are the pairs of f
composed with the pairs of h; with two flagged both sides are the third arrow’s pairs.
(3) If f is flagged, so is i f , and both go from the source of f to its target, so there is
nothing more to compare. If not, i f has the pairs of f with repeats removed, which
the equivalence ignores. (4) is the mirror.



                                                  244
The Thiele Machine                                                                   Devon Thiele


Checked as graph_compose_identities_is_identity for (1), graph_compos
e_assoc_stored for (2), graph_compose_left_identity_stored for (3) and
graph_compose_right_identity_stored for (4) (CategoryBridge.v), with gra
ph_compose_stored and composite_record underneath.


Theorem 18.4 (Every stored identity is the identity of its object). Call a graph’s identity
arrows canonical when every flagged arrow in it has its source equal to its target and no pairs.
(1) If a state’s identity arrows are canonical and it steps on any instruction, the new state’s are
canonical. (2) If graph(s) has no arrows and s′ is reachable from s, then the identity arrows of
graph(s′ ) are canonical.

Proof. (1) A case split over the step relation. MORPH_ID stores an arrow from a
module to itself with no pairs. COMPOSE stores a flagged arrow only when both
inputs are flagged, and then from the source of the first to the target of the second,
with no pairs; when both inputs are canonical, those four ends are one object. MORPH
and MORPH_TENSOR store the flag off. Deleting an arrow, or the cascade when
PSPLIT or PMERGE removes a module, only removes arrows. Every other step leaves
the arrow list alone. (2) A graph with no arrows has nothing to check, and (1) carries
it along each step.

Checked as identity_arrows_canonical (the definition), vm_step_preserve
s_identity_arrows_canonical for (1), and vm_reachable_preserves_ide
ntity_arrows_canonical with vm_reachable_identity_arrows_canonic
al for (2) (CategoryBridge.v). The initial state has no arrows, so on every reachable
state every flagged arrow meets the side condition of (3) and (4) in Theorem 18.3,
and the identity laws hold for every identity arrow a program can build. The chip’s
COMPOSE follows the same rule: two flagged arrows give a flagged arrow whose
coupling descriptor holds no pairs and the label “empty” (Section 27 has the chip).

So the stored arrows obey associativity and both identity laws, up to the sameness
of Definition 18.4. Calling the whole thing a category in the full sense would still
take more: a Coq structure that packages the objects, the arrows and that sameness
and proves the laws once as an instance, and an account of a category whose objects
and arrows come and go as modules are split and merged. Neither is in the tree, and
nothing above claims either. The laws are each a theorem on their own.

Three more things Coq doesn’t say, smaller. Nothing proves composition is defined
on exactly the right pairs beyond “the first’s target equals the second’s source” by
number; a mismatch gives the error branch. Nothing in the law files mentions that
splitting or merging a module deletes every arrow touching it, so an arrow’s lifetime
is bounded by its modules’; that’s in the step rules (Section 16) and not in the laws.
And the per-arrow field the comment says records what was paid to certify it is never
written (Section 16 again), so “a composite’s cost field is zero” is a theorem about a



                                               245
The Thiele Machine                                                                 Devon Thiele


field that’s always zero.

18.6 Why this isn’t just extra state
Here’s the question I chewed on longest. If you can bolt extra registers onto an
ordinary machine and stash arrow identifiers in them, why does the arrow layer
matter?

Because extra registers have no provenance. You can write 42 into register 5 and call
it an arrow. The machine checks: does arrow 42 exist in the graph, put there by a
MORPH or a COMPOSE that actually ran? MORPH_ASSERT looks the arrow up and
fails, setting the error flag, if it isn’t there. Existence is all it checks; it doesn’t compare
the source and target against anything (you can read those back with MORPH_GET),
it stores a checksum of the property string, overwriting whatever the channel held,
and doesn’t check what the property says, and it never reads the certificate operand
you hand it. And it costs at least one even when it fails. Building the chain, by MORPH
and COMPOSE and MORPH_ID, is free at zero declared cost. Asserting it into the
assertion channel never is. You can build for nothing; you can’t vouch for nothing.
The graph is structure the machine holds outright, and Section 20 shows two states
that differ in nothing but that graph.

18.7 Two small facts that matter later
Failing arrow instructions still charge; the cost is on the attempt, like everything else.
And MORPH reads its coupling from memory: a count word (capped at sixty-four, half
the memory size, so a garbage count can’t send the reader past the end of memory),
then pairs, then a label, and it drops every pair whose ends don’t lie in the two regions.
With zeroed memory the count is zero and the coupling is empty, which matters for
Section 21.


Definition 18.5 (Loading a coupling from memory). For a MORPH whose cou-
pling block starts at word b, between modules with regions X and Y: let
k = min(mem[b], 64), read the pairs (mem[b + 1], mem[b + 2]), . . . , (mem[b + 2k −
1], mem[b + 2k ]), read a length-prefixed label starting at word b + 1 + 2k, and keep
only the pairs ( a, c) with a ∈ X and c ∈ Y.


Checked as the definition load_coupling_from_mem (VMState.v), with the cap
serialized_coupling_pair_count (64 is half the memory size). Two Python
tests outside Coq exercise it with real data. One is the Python test test_morph_
loads_nonempty_coupling_from_memory (tests/test_categorical_opcodes.py),
which drives the extracted runner of Section 16. Its program writes the count 1 and
the pair (0, 1) into words 80 to 82, runs PNEW twice, once on cell 0 and once on
cell 1, and then a MORPH from module 1 to module 2 with its coupling block at
word 80; the test asserts that the error flag is down, that the first arrow’s identifier
is 1, and that its stored coupling is exactly [(0, 1)]. The other, test_morph_read


                                              246
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


s_upper_half_memory (tests/test_rtl_morph_opcodes.py), runs the hardware in
co-simulation, puts the pair (1, 2) at word 80, in the upper half of memory, makes
modules on cells 1 and 2, and expects [(1, 2)]. These are tests, not theorems. The laws
of Theorem 18.1 hold for every list, so they cover nonempty couplings like these; that
the hardware’s MORPH produces the same state as the kernel’s is driven_step_m
orph (GraphReconstructionBridge.v), under the hardware invariant and with both
modules present and nonempty.

So the machine has modules, arrows between them, and pairs of cells stapled to the
arrows, and Coq has checked the laws those pairs obey, on the lists and on the stored
arrows, with the identity flag carried through the one case where the obvious rule
would break them. What none of it has yet is anything a module can be said to claim.
A coupling says which cells correspond. It doesn’t say anything is true about them.
That’s next.

19 Claims a module can carry
Here’s the gap Section 18 left open. Back in Part III, Section 7 ended by asking what
the claim behind a paid flag even is, and Section 9 answered that insight, at its best,
is a relation committed to in one priced step (Definition 9.1 and the remark after it),
talking about the claim as if it were a thing. On a sheet of paper it can’t be; the paper
has a NO box and a YES box and nothing to hang a claim on. The machine has plenty.
Section 16 gave it a state record with a graph of modules in it, each owning a range of
cells; Section 17 gave it fifty-one instructions, two of which turn a certification reading
on; Section 18 gave it the arrows. Time to make the claim a thing. The buckets in
Section 2 were a sorting of a pile into groups, and I promised the sorting would cost
something, and then the whole middle of this book turned out to be about raising a
flag, and you’d be within your rights to ask what the flag has to do with the buckets.
Here’s the link, and it’s the oldest link in this book: a group is a thing you can say
something about. “Everything in this bucket is red.” “This region of memory holds a
sorted list.” A group with nothing said about it is a label, and labels are cheap because
labels promise nothing. Calling a group “module A” commits you to exactly zero
about what’s inside it. Structure that earns the name starts one step later, when you
hang a claim on a group and make the group answer for it.

19.1 A question with a definite answer
Two words, so I can say that cleanly, and both are in every logic textbook; I’m giving
them to you because the book promised no unexplained jargon, not because they’re
hard.

A predicate states a precise condition on a thing. That gives the claim a meaning; it
does not, by itself, give an algorithm for deciding it. “Is this number bigger than five”
is a predicate about a number. “Does this region hold a sorted list” is a predicate about
a region of memory. A predicate is the shape a claim takes once its truth conditions


                                           247
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


are precise. The finite formulas used here can be checked by the procedures below;
that is an additional fact about these formulas. Notice what that rules out: “this code
is well written” isn’t a predicate until you say what you’d check.

A formula is a predicate built out of smaller yes-or-no pieces wired together with “and,”
“or,” and “not.” Take three switches, call them x1, x2, x3, each up (true) or down
(false), and the formula “(x1 or x2) and (not x1 or x3).” It comes out true exactly when
at least one of the first pair is up and, at the same time, at least one of the second
pair is. George Boole worked out in 1847 that you can do arithmetic on claims this
way, treating “and” like multiplication and “or” like a kind of addition, and that’s the
whole reason a machine can check a claim at all: a formula is something you evaluate,
by plugging in switch positions and turning the crank.

Why multiplication? Try it at the table. Write 1 for up and 0 for down, and multiply:
one times one is one, and anything times zero is zero. That’s “and” to the letter: the
product is up only when both are. Then the stranger thing Boole noticed. Say “x and x”
about one switch and you’ve said nothing new; it’s just x. In numbers that’s x × x = x,
and he made it a law of his system, and it’s a law ordinary numbers mostly break.
Which numbers equal their own square? Try a few. Two times two is four, no. A half
times a half is a quarter, no. Zero, yes. One, yes. That’s the whole list. So when Boole
wrote his bigger book in 1854, The Laws of Thought, he asked you to imagine an algebra
whose letters take the values 0 and 1 and nothing else. Every switch in this section
lives in that algebra.

And the 1847 book has a backstory worth a detour. Boole was largely self-taught and
spent about fifteen years as a schoolmaster, and what pulled him back to logic, early
in 1847, was a loud public quarrel between Augustus De Morgan and the Scottish
philosopher Sir William Hamilton over who had first thought of a small technical
idea in the old logic of syllogisms. Two well-known men fighting over credit, and a
schoolmaster watching from the side picks up the subject and writes the little book
this paragraph is about. Few people remember what the quarrel was over. Every
switch in this section runs on what the bystander wrote.

Then push on it, because Boole’s “or” isn’t quite the switches’ “or.” His plus only
made sense for things that can’t both hold at once, so “x or y” with both of them up
had no meaning in his system. In 1864 William Stanley Jevons, in a book called Pure
Logic, read “or” as “either or both,” which gives “x or x is x,” the same trick as before,
and he wrote to Boole saying plus ought to work that way. Boole wouldn’t have it,
since it broke the tie to ordinary algebra his whole system stood on. The switches
above use Jevons’s “or”: the first clause is true when x1 and x2 are both up. Does
that change anything about the checker? No; the crank turns the same way on every
formula in this book. It changes the picture: the “or” the switches use is the one the
man who invented the algebra turned down.

Do it. Set x1 up, x2 down, x3 up. First clause: x1 is up, so true. Second clause: not x1


                                           248
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


is false, but x3 is up, so true. Both true, so the formula is true: that choice of switch
positions is called a satisfying assignment, and you just found one. Now set x3 down
instead. Second clause: not x1 is false, x3 is false, so the clause is false, so the formula
is false. That’s a falsifying assignment. You’ve now done everything a checker does.
The checker has no cleverness in it; it has a formula, a row of switch positions, and a
crank.

19.2 Hang it on a group
Now take a group of memory cells and say: “the values in this group make this
formula true.” That’s a constraint hung on a group, and the formula can carry real
content: every value here sits between zero and a hundred; this region encodes a
satisfying assignment to the formula sitting over in that other region; this region is
sorted. Tony Hoare, in 1969, built a whole way of reasoning about programs out
of exactly this move: attach a claim to a point in a program (“whenever execution
reaches here, this is true”), and reason forward from claim to claim. Robert Floyd
had done it two years earlier on flowcharts. Their claims were checked on paper by
the person writing the proof. The machine’s version is a formula and two rows in
memory, checked by a step while it runs, and I’ll be straight about it: the check names
no module and no region. The machine has the pieces. It doesn’t join them.

And is two years earlier the bottom? Not even close, and the next step down is a paper
this book already leaned on. In June 1949, at a Cambridge conference held for the new
EDSAC computer, Alan Turing gave a talk three pages long, “Checking a large routine,”
the same note the counter chapter used for stopping (Section 6). Stopping was the
second half of it. The first half is this section’s move, twenty years before Hoare: the
programmer should make “definite assertions which can be checked individually,”
and the correctness of the whole should follow from them. His example program
computes a factorial using nothing but addition, and his picture for why you’d bother
is one you can do on the back of an envelope. Add up a long column of four-digit
numbers and hand someone only the total, and they have to redo the whole sum at
one sitting, because the carries tie every column to the one before it. Hand them the
total of each column as well, and the job falls apart into small checks they can do one
at a time. That’s a claim hung on a point in the middle of the work, so the person
checking never has to hold all of it at once. The paper got its due mostly later: in 1984
F. L. Morris and C. B. Jones republished it, with its misprints corrected, as an early
program proof by Alan Turing. Does any of that change the machine? No. It changes
the date on the idea, and it tells you something I like: the first person to ask how you’d
check a program put the claims in the middle of it, not at the end.

And here’s the thing I most want you to see, because it’s where “structure” and “cost”
finally touch. A claim hung on a group rules things out. Before the constraint, the cells
could hold anything. After it, they can only hold values that make the formula true.
That’s the fifth item on Section 2’s list, “adding structure rules possibilities out,” made
concrete: a formula on a region is a partition of all the ways the region could be filled

                                            249
The Thiele Machine                                                               Devon Thiele


into “allowed” and “not,” and the checked assignment is the proof that the allowed
side isn’t empty.

19.3 A label is not a check
Now the part I’m going to belabour, because it’s the single most common way to fool
yourself with a machine like this.

Section 16’s state record stores, next to each module, a list of strings it calls axioms.
You’d think you could write “sorted” in a list like that and see what happens. Go
looking for the step that reads that list and tests memory against it, and there isn’t one.
Nor does any step write it: every module the steps create starts with an empty list and
keeps it, and a merge or a split removes the modules it acts on, lists and all, and makes
its new modules with empty lists. A function that appends to the list exists in the Coq
model, and no step calls it. So the list is a field the machine carries and nothing more.
It’s a label, and one a program can’t even write. Whatever you put in it would cost
nothing and prove nothing, and you should hear that from the person who built the
thing. Try it with a card: write 5, 2, 9 on it, and underneath write “sorted.” Hand it to
someone and have them check each neighbouring pair. The second check fails. The
label sat there the whole time.


Remark 19.1 (What the steps do with the label lists). Each module in the state carries
a list of strings, its axiom list. Read off the definition of the step function: no rule reads
any axiom list. A step that makes a new module gives it the empty list, and one asked
for a range that is already a module’s returns that module unchanged. The steps that
split and merge modules delete the modules they act on and create their new modules
with empty lists. Every other rule leaves the lists of existing modules as they were.
The helper that appends to a list (graph_add_axiom, with graph_record_disc
overy built on it, both in VMState.v) is called by no rule. So along any run, every
module’s list is either the list it had at the start or empty. This is an inspection of the
definitions (vm_apply in SimulationProof.v, graph_pnew in VMState.v, graph_hw_
psplit and graph_hw_pmerge in VMStep.v), not a named theorem.


A check is different. The machine has one step whose whole job is to read a formula
from memory, read two rows of switch positions from memory, and turn the crank.
Section 17’s table lists it as LASSERT, in one row; here’s what the row leaves out.
The formula is stored in a fixed layout: a word saying how long it is, a word for the
number of switches, a word for the number of clauses, and then the clauses, each a
list of signed numbers (plus for the switch, minus for “not the switch,” zero to end
the clause). The two rows sit back to back with each other, at a separate address that
a second register holds: first a row that’s supposed to satisfy the formula, then a row
that’s supposed to falsify it. (The step also carries a flag for which kind of certificate
it’s checking, and one setting of that flag always traps. I’m describing the setting that
does the work.) The step checks both. If the first row doesn’t satisfy, or the second


                                             250
The Thiele Machine                                                                  Devon Thiele


row doesn’t falsify, or the length written in the instruction doesn’t match the length
written in memory, the step traps: it jumps to a fixed error address, sets an error flag,
and leaves memory, registers, and the modules exactly as they were. If both rows
check, it goes on to the next instruction.

Two things about that step that I think are the right design and want to defend. First,
it charges whether it passes or fails: the formula’s length times eight, plus its declared
cost, plus one, every time. You pay to check, not to be right; Popper again. (The
eight is a pricing convention, not a byte count; the file says so.) Second, and this is
why there are two rows: a formula that every assignment satisfies rules nothing out,
so a satisfying row alone proves nothing about structure, and the falsifying row is
the cheap proof that the formula isn’t that kind of formula, that it’s a real constraint
with a real “not allowed” side. The source’s name for what the second row stops
is “tautology inflation.” Try “x1 or not x1”: write out both rows and you’ll find no
falsifying one exists, so the step would refuse it. And the empty formula, with no
clauses at all, is the simplest tautology, and it’s refused too.

Here is the check, exactly as the step runs it. In the symbols, ∨ is “or,” ∧ is “and,” and
¬ is “not,” the same three words the switches used.


Definition 19.1 (The formula check). Let m be data memory, f the value of the instruc-
tion’s first register and b the value of its second. The formula words are w j = m( f + j)
for 0 ≤ j < 3 + m( f ): w0 is the length written in memory, w1 = v the number of
switches, w2 = q the number of clauses, and from w3 on come the literals, each read
as a signed 32-bit number, with 0 closing a clause. An assignment a maps switch
numbers to words, and switch x is up when a( x ) ̸= 0. Sat(w, a) scans the literals
in order, keeping a count of closed clauses: it is true as soon as the count reaches q;
it is false if a clause closes with no literal made true by a (a positive literal x is true
when x is up, a negative literal − x when x is down), or if the words run out first. The
satisfying row is a1 ( x ) = m(b + x ) and the falsifying row is a2 ( x ) = m(b + v + x ). For
the checking step with kind flag k and declared length ℓ, the check passes, written ok,
when m( f ) = ℓ, k is the satisfiable kind, Sat(w, a1 ) is true, and Sat(w, a2 ) is false.


Theorem 19.1 (What the check step does). Let i be the checking step with kind k, declared
length ℓ and declared cost c0 , and let s′ = apply(s, i ). Then s′ has the same graph, registers,
memory, certified flag and assertion channel as s, and µ(s′ ) = µ(s) + 8ℓ + c0 + 1. If ok, the
program counter advances by one and the error flag is unchanged. If not, the program counter
becomes the fixed trap address 3840 and the error flag is set.

Proof. This is the checking step’s case of the step function, read field by field: ok
is a pure function of s, and each field of s′ is written as stated. The counter line is
conservation for this instruction, whose price is 8ℓ + c0 + 1.




                                              251
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


Checked as the checking step’s case of vm_apply (SimulationProof.v) and the rule
step_lassert (VMStep.v), with the check as lassert_exec_ok and lassert
_check_ok (VMStep.v) over check_model_binary_fn and check_countermo
del_binary_fn (CertCheck.v). The pieces are named in vm_apply_lassert_p
c (DagRestriction.v) and vm_apply_mu (MuLedgerConservation.v); on a step that
doesn’t trap, the declared length equals the one in memory, lassert_honest_cos
t (StateSpaceCounting.v).


Remark 19.2 (Why a tautology cannot pass). Argued from Definition 19.1; there is no
separate Coq theorem. If the check passes, the scan with a1 reaches q closing zeros,
so the words hold q complete clauses. The scan with a2 sees the same words and
the same closing zeros, so it can only fail at a clause that closes with no true literal:
a2 makes some clause false. Hence a formula that every assignment satisfies, such
as x1 ∨ ¬ x1 , never passes, and neither does the formula with q = 0, which the scan
accepts for every row.


And third, which is subtle and easy to get wrong: this step doesn’t turn either reading on.
It checks, and it changes nothing it checked. Its evidence is in the run: the program
counter kept going and the error flag stayed off. Turning a reading on is a different
step, MORPH_ASSERT, which puts a property on an arrow (Section 9’s “commit”), or
CERTIFY, the bare step that raises the certified flag (Section 17 has both), and nothing
forces either to be adjacent to the check. A flag raised by the bare step carries no check
at all. Check and commit are two acts with two prices, and the machine, correctly I
think, refuses to pretend they’re one. What that does to Section 9’s test-then-commit
protocol on this machine is Section 22’s to show.

19.4 Who checks the checker
A fast checker that might be wrong just moves the trust somewhere else, and in 2005
Henk Barendregt and Freek Wiedijk gave this worry a name, the de Bruijn criterion,
after the logician who insisted on it: a proof system is trustworthy when its proofs can
be checked by a checker small enough that a person can audit it, independent of whatever
clever tool produced the proof. Euclid had the instinct: five postulates you can hold
in your head, and everything else meant to follow from them. The machine’s checker
is of that kind. In the chip I build at the end of the book it’s a controller with three
phases (idle, read the formula’s header, scan) that walks the formula word by word.
The proofs hold it up against the kernel (Section 15’s name for the machine’s reference
definition in Coq, the step function every proof in this part is about), and they show
its word-by-word scan returns the same answer as the kernel’s two checks, as long
as the formula declares at least one clause, its words hold an end-of-clause zero for
every clause it declares, and every word fits in thirty-two bits. It also proves that the
hardware step and the kernel step agree on the counter always, and on the program
counter whenever the check passes. “The hardware step” there is Coq’s model of it,


                                           252
The Thiele Machine                                                                  Devon Thiele


which keeps every field as a whole number with no thirty-two-bit bound; on the chip’s
own registers the agreement needs the counter to stay below 232 , and Section 27 states
it with that premise (Theorem 27.3). The same theorem pins the kernel’s error flag to
the check’s outcome, unchanged on a pass and set on a fail. That’s a fact about the
hardware and it’s Section 27’s to show; I mention it here so you know the checker isn’t
a black box, and so you know where to find the trusted base, which is short and listed
in Section 28.

The question in this subsection’s title is older than any checker, and its most famous
wording isn’t about what you’d guess. “Who will guard the guardians?” gets quoted
about governments and police and, lately, proof assistants, and it often gets pinned on
Plato. Push on that. Plato’s Republic has the worry, sort of: in Book III, Glaucon says it
would be absurd for a guardian to need a guardian, which is close in words and op-
posite in mood, a man calling the question silly. The Latin, quis custodiet ipsos custodes,
is from the Roman satirist Juvenal’s sixth satire, and it’s a joke about a husband. His
friends tell him to bolt his wife in and set guards on her; the line asks who’ll watch
the guards, since she’ll start with them. And it gets better. In 1899 an Oxford under-
graduate, E. O. Winstedt, found extra lines of that satire in a medieval manuscript in
the Bodleian Library, lines the other copies lack, partly overlapping the familiar ones,
and the famous question sits in that tangle. Scholars have argued ever since about
whether those lines are Juvenal’s at all. So the most quoted sentence about trusting
the checker comes with a doubtful source of its own. Does that change anything here?
No. De Bruijn’s answer is still the only one I know that works: you never get rid of
the last guard, you make the last guard small enough to watch yourself.

The two hardware facts, stated so their premises are in view. Two words first: a
hardware snapshot is the chip’s whole state at one tick of its clock, written the way
Coq’s hardware model keeps it, with whole numbers and no thirty-two-bit bound,
and α reads off which kernel state that snapshot stands for. Section 27 builds both,
and nothing else in this part of the book leans on them. (Yes, these are theorems about
a chip I have never held in my hand. Section 27 is very upfront about that.)


Theorem 19.2 (The chip’s scan is the kernel’s check). (1) Let the formula words be
w0 , w1 , q followed by literal words u, and let g1 , g2 be the two rows. If 1 ≤ q, u con-
tains at least q zeros, and every word of u is below 232 , then the hardware scan of u returns
Sat(w, g1 ) ∧ ¬Sat(w, g2 ). (2) For every hardware snapshot h and every checking instruction
i, write α(h) for the kernel state the snapshot stands for. There is a kernel state s′ that the
kernel’s step relation reaches from α(h) under i such that: µ(s′ ) equals the hardware counter
after the model’s step, with no bound on its size; if ok holds at α(h), the hardware program
counter after the step equals that of s′ ; and the error flag of s′ is unchanged when ok holds and
set otherwise.

Proof. (1) Induction on the literal words, with an invariant that ties the scanner’s three


                                               253
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


bits (current clause met by the first row, current clause met by the second row, some
earlier clause already missed by the second row) and its clause countdown to where
the two kernel scans stand. (2) Composes three lemmas about the hardware model:
the kernel step exists, the two counters agree, and the program counters agree on a
pass. Section 27 goes through both.

Checked as hw_scan_certcheck (LassertSpec.v), from hw_scan_spec, and logi
c_engine_equivalent_lassert (LogicEngineEquivalence.v).

So the little checker in the chip and the check the proofs talk about give the same
verdict, as long as the formula meets those three conditions, and the model of the
chip’s counter moves the way the kernel’s does, which on the chip itself holds below
232 .

19.5 Where, not just how much
Last piece, and it’s the one that the counter in Section 6 can’t give you. The counter is
a total. Two different runs can end at the same total having checked different things in
different places. “Did this run check the sorting constraint before it used the sorted list”
is not a question the total can answer, any more than a grocery total of twenty-three
dollars and forty cents can tell you whether you bought milk. The itemised receipt
can. The run gives you the itemised receipt: which step ran, what it charged (the
checked work reads a ledger off the run, one entry per step, and the entries add up to
the counter’s rise), and whether the error flag came on. A run somebody else hands
you needs its own evidence before you trust that receipt.

The itemised receipt has a history, and it’s the history of exactly this gap. James Ritty
ran a saloon in Dayton, Ohio, and believed some of his staff were pocketing money.
On a steamboat trip to Europe in 1878 he watched a mechanism that counted the
turns of the ship’s propeller, and wondered whether something like it could count
the money instead. In 1879 he and his brother John patented a “Cash Register and
Indicator,” and they sold a version under the wonderful name Ritty’s Incorruptible
Cashier. The first model was this book’s counter (Section 6) with brass on it: press
a key, the amount goes onto a dial showing the day’s running total. No drawer, no
paper. At closing time you hold the dial up against the cash. And that’s all a total can
do. It tells you that the money is short, never which sale went missing or who rang it
up. The paper came later. The patents passed to other owners and in 1884 to John H.
Patterson’s National Cash Register Company, and the story told about that company
is that it added a paper roll: one copy kept for the shop’s own books, one handed
to the customer. That last part I only have from histories of the company and of the
machine, so hold it the way you’d hold any company’s story about itself. The order is
right either way: first a total that can tell you something’s wrong, then a list that tells
you where. A run gives you the second kind.

And the rule I named No Free Insight back in Section 5 has a where. “Structural gain”


                                            254
The Thiele Machine                                                                 Devon Thiele


is what I call it when some step of a run takes the assertion channel from clear to
set, the machine-wide reading that says some label was asserted on some arrow. The
shallow question is whether the channel was clear at the start and is set at the end,
and you settle it by holding the first state next to the last. The machine isn’t built for
the shallow question. It’s built for which step. Walk the run and find a step where the
assertion channel went from clear to set; there’s always at least one such step when the
channel is set at the end and was clear at the start, and that step cost at least one, and
the cost can sit nowhere else. In the checked work the located version is a predicate
on runs, structure_addition_in_run, which says some step is such a step. The
gain has a location. The location has a price. That’s No Free Insight, said with the
claim behind it finally in view: a formula in memory, checked by a small auditable
checker, and a label asserted on an arrow by a step you can point at.

The located gain, exactly, with run(n, p, s) the run of program p from s with fuel n (Def-
inition 17.1) and addr(s) the assertion channel, which Section 17 writes certaddr(s).


Definition 19.2 (Structural gain, located). The run run(n, p, s) has a structural gain
when some step it executes goes from a state with addr = 0 to a state with addr ̸= 0.


Theorem 19.3 (The gain has a place and a price). (1) If addr(s) = 0 and
addr(run(n, p, s)) ̸= 0, the run has a structural gain. (2) The run has a structural gain
exactly when, at some step it executes from a state whose channel is 0, the instruction at the
program counter is an assertion step that names an arrow in the current graph and carries a
label of nonzero checksum. (3) Each such step costs at least one. (4) If p contains no assertion
step, no run of p has a structural gain.

Proof. (1) Induction on the fuel. At each executed step either the channel turns nonzero,
which is a structural gain, or it is still zero and the rest of the run starts again from a
clear channel; a run that stops with the channel still zero ends at zero, which contra-
dicts the end. (2) From a state with channel 0, one step makes the channel nonzero
exactly in the stated case, by part (3) of Theorem 17.7; then induction on the fuel. (3)
The assertion step is priced at its declared cost plus one (Definition 17.4), and any step
that takes the channel from 0 to nonzero costs at least one (Theorem 17.8). (4) follows
from (2).

Checked as supra_cert_implies_structure_addition_in_run, structur
e_addition_in_run_iff_morph_assert_bridge_pattern, morph_assert
_step_sets_supra_cert_iff and non_morph_assert_trace_has_no_str
ucture_addition (RevelationRequirement.v), with the price from no_free_cert
ification (AbstractNoFI.v).


Remark 19.3 (Clear at the start and set at the end is the stronger reading). The converse
of (1) fails, argued from part (2) of Theorem 17.7 and not checked as a theorem: a run

                                              255
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


can set the channel and later run an assertion whose label has checksum 0, which
writes 0 back. That run has a structural gain and ends with the channel clear. So the
shallow question (first state against last) and the located one (which step) can come
apart, and the files answer the located one.


One more boundary and then I’ll stop. A satisfying row and a falsifying row prove
that the formula can be met and isn’t trivial. They don’t prove the formula means what
the label next to it says. “sorted” in the axiom list and a checked formula in memory
are two things with no wire between them, and wiring them is a job for a proved
encoding, which is a separate piece of work. The step checks the formula. The label is
still a label.

So: what a flag could stand for is a formula, which the machine can check in one step
and which a different step can mark with a label. Nothing in the machine joins the
two, or either to a module. The check is separate from the commit, and the commit
has a place in the run.

Notice where everything in this section lives. The formula and its two rows sit in
memory, the labels sit on the modules, the arrows that get asserted sit in the graph.
Memory an ordinary computer has. The graph it doesn’t. Which raises a question I
can’t dodge: if somebody looks at this machine the way they’d look at an ordinary
computer, reading registers, memory, the counter, the program counter, the error flag
and the certified flag, and nothing else, can they even tell whether the graph is there?
Two states that look the same to that reader and differ in exactly the part that carries
the claims: that’s Section 20.

20 Two states that look the same
Section 7 said: a window that doesn’t show a thing can’t recover it, because two states
that look the same through it have to get the same answer (Theorem 7.1, decoders
need constant fibres). Section 7’s own pairs were about the flag and its price, and
they’re Section 23’s to show. This section’s pair is about the graph. Here it is, and it’s
smaller than you’d think, and then a caveat that has to go with it, and then a second
pair, built on a step, whose caveat is smaller.

Said without the word “fibre”: anything that only looks through a window has to give
the same answer to two states the window shows the same. Think of identical twins
and one passport photo. A border guard who goes only by the photo waves both of
them through or neither, and no amount of staring at the photo changes that. If the
two need different answers, the photo was the wrong thing to be looking at.

20.1 The pair
Take two states. Both have an empty register file and empty memory, program counter
zero, counter zero, error flag down, certified flag down, all eight witness counters zero,
a sixteen-zero tensor, and no modules at all. They agree on every one of those. Both

                                           256
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


have the fresh-identifier counters at one. In the first state, the arrow list holds one
arrow: source module zero, target module zero, empty coupling, identity flag on, cost
field zero, and its own number is zero. In the second state, the arrow list is empty.

That’s it. Six fields an ordinary observer reads (registers, memory, counter, program
counter, error, certified): identical. The rest of the record: identical. One list with one
entry versus one list with none. The theorem is categorical_separation: there
exist two states that are computationally equivalent (agree on those six) and categorically
distinct (different arrow lists). The proof is reflexivity six times and one discrimina
te on a list with an entry against a list without. It’s as short as a Coq proof gets.

Two things the same in everything you look at and still two things: philosophy has an
old fight about exactly that, and it’s worth a detour, because it tells you which side of
the fight this theorem stands on. Leibniz said it can’t happen, not for real things. There
are no two individuals indiscernible from each other, he wrote to Samuel Clarke in
1716, and he told a story to go with it. A clever gentleman of his acquaintance, talking
with him in front of the Electress Sophia in the garden at Herrenhausen, thought he
could find two leaves perfectly alike. She dared him to. He “ran all over the Garden a
long time” looking, and it was “to no purpose.” You can run his search tonight with a
handful of anything, leaves or coins or grains of rice: look hard enough and every pair
differs somewhere. Then in 1952 Max Black pushed back with a universe you can’t
build at the table. Nothing in it but two iron spheres, the same size, the same colour,
the same everything, some distance apart. Name a difference between them. There
isn’t one, and there are still two of them. People have argued about Black’s spheres
ever since, and I’m not going to settle it.

Here’s why I don’t have to. Leibniz’s claim is about every property a thing has. The
theorem above is about six. The two states aren’t indiscernible in his sense at all: one
has an arrow and the other doesn’t, and Coq tells them apart with a single discri
minate. They’re indiscernible to a window, which is a much cheaper thing, and it’s
the thing that matters for a machine, because an observer of a machine only ever gets
a window. Leibniz’s gentleman would always find his difference if he could look at
everything. It doesn’t help him if all he’s allowed to look at is six things about each
leaf.


Definition 20.1 (Equivalent and distinct). Machine states s1 and s2 are computationally
equivalent when they have equal registers, memory, counter µ, program counter, error
flag and certified flag. They are categorically distinct when their arrow lists differ.


Definition 20.2 (The separation pair). Let s A and s B both have empty registers and
memory, program counter 0, µ = 0, error and certified flags false, all four control and
status words 0, logic accumulator and mode word 0, all eight witness counters 0, the
tensor of sixteen zeros, and a graph with no modules, next module number 1 and next



                                           257
The Thiele Machine                                                                    Devon Thiele


arrow number 1. The arrow list of s A is the single entry numbered 0: source 0, target
0, empty coupling with empty label, identity flag on, cost field 0. The arrow list of s B
is empty.


Theorem 20.1 (Categorical separation). There are states s1 and s2 that are computationally
equivalent and categorically distinct; s A and s B are such a pair.

Proof. The six fields are equal field by field, by construction. The arrow lists are a list
with one entry and the empty list, which are different constructors.

Checked as categorical_separation (PartitionSeparation.v), with the definitions
computationally_equivalent and categorically_distinct from the same
file; the named copies of the two states are separation_A and separation_B
(ShadowProjection.v).

From it, the corollaries you’d expect. Any observer whose verdict depends only on
the six fields gives the same verdict on both (classical_observer_cannot_sep
arate); any yes/no test of that kind can’t tell them apart; any function that factors
through the six-field projection is constant on the pair (no_classical_separatio
n); and the difference survives a probe step, an ADD of nothing to nothing: after it the
arrow lists still differ (shadow_separation_theorem, shadow_strictly_loss
y). ADD is a classical instruction, one that writes a register and nothing in the graph,
which is why it makes a boring probe. And the plain statement that two distinct
states can have equal shadow is the last of the four parts of the degenerate-projection
theorem; its parts two to four are the quotient theorem just below, and Section 23 says
what its first part is.


Definition 20.3 (The shadow). The shadow of a machine state s is the six-field record
sh(s) = (registers, memory, program counter, µ, error flag, certified flag). It drops the
graph, the control and status words, the witness counters, the mode word, the logic
accumulator and the tensor.


Theorem 20.2 (The shadow separation theorem). There are states s1 , s2 and an instruction
p with (1) sh(s1 ) = sh(s2 ), (2) the arrow lists of s1 and s2 differ, and (3) the arrow lists of
the states after one step by p from s1 and from s2 differ. Moreover, for every type T and every
function f from states to T such that sh(s) = sh(s′ ) implies f (s) = f (s′ ), f (s A ) = f (s B ).

Proof. Take s A , s B and p = ADD into register 0 from registers 0 and 0 at cost 0. (1) and
(2) are Theorem 20.1. For (3), ADD changes registers, program counter and µ and
leaves the graph as it was, so each graph after the step equals the graph before. The
last part applies the hypothesis on f to (1).

Checked as shadow_separation_theorem, shadow_strictly_lossy (the

                                               258
The Thiele Machine                                                                 Devon Thiele


same three facts with the shadow equality written out) and no_classical_sep
aration (ShadowProjection.v); the yes/no version is classical_bool_test_in
distinguishable and the observer version classical_observer_cannot_se
parate (PartitionSeparation.v).

20.2 The window is a quotient
Here’s another way to say what the pair shows. The shadow is a map that sorts every
state into a bin, one bin per six-field record. Two states share a bin exactly when they
agree on the six fields; that’s all a bin is. A window that reads only the shadow can
only ever answer “which bin,” so it’s blind to everything that varies inside a bin. The
pair says the graph varies inside a bin. That’s what “the window forgets the graph”
means, said precisely.


Theorem 20.3 (The shadow is a lossy quotient). (1) sh(s1 ) = sh(s2 ) exactly when s1 and
s2 agree on registers, memory, program counter, µ, error flag and certified flag. (2) Let s1 and
s2 have equal shadows, equal graphs and equal control and status words. Then for every list
of classical instructions run in order from each, the two final states have equal shadows. (3)
There are distinct states with equal shadows.

Proof. (1) Two records are equal exactly when their fields are. (2) By induction on
the list: each classical instruction computes the shadow, graph and control and status
words of its result from the shadow, graph and control and status words of its input,
so agreement on those three passes from step to step. (3) is s A and s B .

Checked as parts (2) to (4) of degenerate_projection_theorem (TuringClassi-
calEmbedding.v), which are shadow_proj_kernel_is_eq_on_classical_sha
dow, classical_run_preserves_shadow_compat and shadow_strictly_l
ossy. Part (2) needs the equal graphs and control and status words, and the file says
why: MORPH_GET and TENSOR_GET are classical but read the graph, and the heap
instructions read one of the control and status words, the heap base. So a classical run
is a function of the bin together with the graph and those words, not of the bin alone.

20.3 The caveat
Now the caveat. The first state has an arrow whose source and target are module zero,
and there is no module zero; the module list is empty. So the first state is not well-formed
by Section 16’s three clauses, and since every step preserves well-formedness, it’s not
reachable from the initial state. (There’s a second reason, independent of the first: both
states have an empty register file and an empty memory, and every reachable state
has sixteen registers and a hundred and twenty-eight words.) The theorem is about
the type of states, not about states a run can get to. The pair is as simple as a pair gets,
as a type-level pair. As a claim about what a running machine can do, it says nothing.


Remark 20.1 (Why neither state of the pair is reachable). Let Z (s) say that s has exactly


                                              259
The Thiele Machine                                                                    Devon Thiele


16 registers and exactly 128 memory words. No step turns Z from true to false, and
the initial state has Z true, so every state reachable from it has Z true. Both s A and s B
have empty registers and memory, so Z is false for both, and neither is reachable.


Checked as eg_size_permanent (EventGeneralization.v), with the initial state’s
sizes from its definition (MuInitiality.v). The other reason in the text, the arrow whose
ends name a module that doesn’t exist, rests on Section 16’s well-formedness clauses
and is not restated here.

Does that gut it? No, and here’s why not: the type-level pair is enough for the shape
of the claim (the projection is many-to-one on the type, full stop), and a second pair
exists below, built on a step from the initial state, with no caveat of that kind. But it’s
a real distinction and I’d rather you have it than find it.

20.4 A step the shadow can’t see
Here’s a pair built on a step, and it’s the strictness theorem. Start where every run
starts: the initial state of Definition 16.7, with no modules and the next module number
at zero. Take one step: create a module on address zero (PNEW on the single cell zero,
which is inside memory, owned by nobody, with module numbers to spare, so no trap).
The fresh-module counter goes from zero to one. Now consider every classical run
from the same start: any sequence of steps, each by one of the twenty-nine opcodes
the source calls classical (Section 17 lists them in Definition 17.3: arithmetic, loads,
stores, jumps, the heap, the ports, and MORPH_GET and TENSOR_GET, which read
the graph and write nothing), in any order the program’s jumps pick. None of them
touches the graph, so after any such run the fresh-module counter is still zero. One
structural step changed a thing no classical run can change.

And it isn’t a trick of the starting point. Stop a classical run anywhere, at any state
it reaches from the initial state, and the same PNEW is a step from there too, raising
the counter by one, while every classical run from there keeps it put. The state PNEW
lands in has a graph that no classical run from the initial state ever has. Nothing here
is hand-built: every state in the theorem is one the machine reaches.


Definition 20.4 (Classical reachability). A program is classical when each of its instruc-
tions is one of the twenty-nine classical opcodes. A state s′ is classically reachable from
s when a chain of zero or more steps leads from s to s′ and each step is by a classical
instruction; the steps can come in any order, so a run whose jumps revisit instruc-
tions counts. Running a list means applying the step to each instruction in order; the
program-counter runner with fuel F fetches the instruction at the program counter F
times, following jumps.


Theorem 20.4 (Strictness, and with it conservativity). Let p be PNEW on the region [0] at
cost 0. (1) For every state s classically reachable from the initial state s0 (with s = s0 allowed):


                                                260
The Thiele Machine                                                                Devon Thiele


s is reachable from s0 ; p is a step from s; that step raises the next module number by one and
leaves the error flag as it was; every state classically reachable from s has the next module
number of s, and so does the state the program-counter runner reaches from s on every classical
program with any fuel; and the graph after p differs from the graph of every state classically
reachable from s0 . (2) At s0 itself: after p the next module number is 1, and every classical
program run by the program-counter runner from s0 , with any fuel, ends with next module
number 0. (3) For every state s and every classical program, running it from s as a list, or
under the program-counter runner with any fuel, leaves the graph, the assertion channel and
the certified flag as they were in s; so does every classically reachable state.

Proof. (3) By induction on the list, on the fuel, or on the chain of steps: the program-
counter runner either stops or fetches an instruction of the program, which is classical,
and no classical instruction writes the graph, the assertion channel or the certified
flag. (1) A state classically reachable from s0 therefore has s0 ’s graph: no modules
and next module number 0. Memory has a hundred and twenty-eight words in every
reachable state, so cell 0 is inside it, no module overlaps it, and a module number is
free, so PNEW does not trap and adds a module, raising the next module number by
one. Reachability holds because each classical step is a step. Every state classically
reachable from s0 has next module number 0, and the graph after p has 1, so the graphs
differ. (2) is (1) at s = s0 with the program-counter half of (3).

Checked as pnew_step_separates_thiele_from_classical_reachable
(TuringStrictness.v; the step is separating_pnew_step), pnew_step_separa
tes_thiele_from_classical_at_init for (2), and pnew_step_separates_
thiele_from_classical, the existential form with the initial state as witness. For
(3): classical_opcodes_preserve_structure (lists), classical_opcodes_
preserve_structure_run_vm (the program-counter runner) and classical_re

with classical_reachable_vm_reachable for reachability. thiele_strictl

The standalone copy of the kernel has its own witness for the strictness shape, and
that one is on a hand-built base: the step is MORPH_ID on module zero and the probe
is MORPH_DELETE of arrow zero; after the identity arrow is built the probe succeeds,
and after any classical run it fails (morph_delete_probe_separates_thiele_

Same shape, different instruction, and the reachable version above is the one I lean on.

20.5 Three things the windows drop, each on its own
The graph isn’t the only thing riding along beside the ordinary fields. There are three:
the counter, the certified flag, and the graph. Each one can differ between two states
while everything else you’d look at holds still, including the other two. Five pairs of


                                             261
The Thiele Machine                                                                  Devon Thiele


states show it, one per claim. Four of them are one instruction away from a clean start,
with CERTIFY on at least one side. The fifth is the separation pair from the start of
this section.

Write Z0 for the clean start: everything empty or zero, no modules, no arrows. It is a
hand-built state, not the machine’s initial state.


Theorem 20.5 (Each of the three is independent of the others). None of the following
functions exists. (1) A function from (memory, registers, program counter) to µ, correct on
every state. (2) The same, to the certified flag. (3) A function from (memory, registers, program
counter, µ) to the certified flag. (4) A function from (memory, registers, program counter,
certified flag) to µ. (5) A function from (memory, registers, program counter, µ, certified flag)
to the graph.

Proof. Each is the same argument: two states with equal inputs and different outputs
would force the function to give two answers on one input. The pairs, all but the
last one step from Z0 : (1) and (2) CERTIFY at declared cost 0 (µ = 1, flag on) against
PNEW of the empty region at cost 0 (µ = 0, flag off), both at program counter 1 with
memory and registers untouched; (3) CERTIFY at declared cost 2 against PNEW of
the empty region at cost 3, both with µ = 3, flag on against flag off; (4) CERTIFY at
