20.6 What the pair doesn’t prove
The obvious move is to reach for more room: bolt on a register, a tape region, any extra
slot, and surely an ordinary machine wriggles out. By hand, with no Coq statement
behind it, it doesn’t: the same collision rebuilds one size up, with the added slot
dropped from what the observer reads. Bolt on another, then? Same collision, one
size up again. Is there a size where it stops? Only one that I can see: the window
that reads every slot. That isn’t a window any more, it’s the whole state, and the pair
has nothing to say about it. Any window that drops something the rest of the state
doesn’t already pin down has a pair hiding in what it drops, which is Section 7’s point
about windows, not a fact about my machine. That cuts both ways. The pair also says
nothing about whether an ordinary machine can hold the graph. It can, encoded on
tape. A projection that sends different graphs to the same place can’t give the graph


                                             263
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


back on every state, and that’s all it says. It doesn’t rule out an encoding that keeps the
whole state, and it doesn’t make these particular opcodes necessary in every model.
What a faithful simulation owes the counter is a question about the simulator’s own
step rule, and the next subsection is about that.

20.7 The machine versus the program it runs
One more theorem belongs here, because it says what the pair means for the rest of
the book. Section 3’s universal floor was stated for any certification system. Now take
any such system that simulates my machine: it has a decoding of its instructions into
mine, an embedding of its states into mine, its step commutes with mine through the
embedding, and its certification bit reads my certified flag through the embedding.
Then two things hold for any run of the base system from uncertified to certified: it
paid at least one (that’s just the universal floor), and the embedded run on my machine
ends certified (thiele_represents_simulating_cert_system). My machine
itself is such a system, with the identity as the embedding (thiele_self_simula
ting), and that’s the only such construction in the tree apart from some generalised
variants.

Why does that matter? Because it separates two things people run together: the machine
doing the stepping (what the machine is) and the program it runs (what runs on it). The
floor is a property of the machine doing the stepping, and it transfers to anything that
faithfully runs on that machine. The pair in this section is a fact about the machine’s
state space, not about any program.

Here’s the picture I keep for it. Play Monopoly on the counter of a real bank. The
game has a bank of its own, with its own rules, and one of them is printed in the
rules sheet: the Bank never goes broke, and if it runs out of money the Banker may
issue more by writing on any ordinary paper. Inside the game that’s fine; the players
agreed to it. The real bank’s teller, standing right there, has no opinion about any of it.
Push a thousand in Monopoly money across her counter and her ledger doesn’t move,
because her rules are about her money, not the game’s. The real bank is the machine
doing the stepping. The game is a program it happens to be hosting. A rule that lives
in the game holds as long as the players keep to it. A rule that lives in the bank holds
whatever the players do.

(And since the game is on the table: its box told an origin story for decades, that an
out-of-work salesman named Charles Darrow invented it during the Depression. The
board is older. Elizabeth Magie patented The Landlord’s Game in 1904, with a square
track, railroads and a square that sends you to jail, and described it as a practical
demonstration of the system of land-grabbing. Darrow sold his version to Parker
Brothers in 1935, and the company bought Magie’s patent for a few hundred dollars.
A story told by the company selling the product is a lead to check, every time. It
changes nothing about banks. It’s a good reminder of who writes the story on the
box.)


                                           264
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


A fixed machine can enforce an invariant in its own transition table, and that includes
a Turing machine. Give its tape a ledger track and a certification cell, and write a table
that never sets the cell without bumping the ledger: that machine obeys the toll in its
step relation. It’s an instance of the abstract certification system, not a counterexample
to it. What it doesn’t do, built the ordinary way, is enforce the toll on the programs
it runs. A universal machine whose table was written only to interpret carries the
simulated certification bit as plain data on its tape. If the host is programmable, so
that other code shares that tape with the guest, any of that code can flip the bit without
paying, because the host’s step has no opinion about it. So an ordinary programmable
computer, as built, doesn’t enforce the toll for its programs; it isn’t that it can’t. A
fixed interpreter whose own table was written to mirror the guest’s bit and charge for
its crossing would enforce it, and the universal host of Section 14.12 is built that way.
My machine is in the first position when it simulates something else. The kernel’s
theorems are about the designated reading of the machine doing the stepping. That’s a
statement about which reading a step rule prices. It isn’t a claim that Turing machines
can’t price one. (The floor for a certification system with no embedding into mine at
all is universal_nfi_any_substrate, and the assumption receipt for thiele_r
epresents_simulating_cert_system is empty.)

Computing ran into this exact gap in hardware, and how it got out is worth the detour.
In 1974 Gerald Popek and Robert Goldberg asked when a machine can run guests,
a whole operating system inside another, efficiently and safely. Their answer is one
sentence you could check against any instruction set. Call an instruction sensitive if it
reads or changes the machine’s own settings, the things the host has to keep for itself,
and privileged if running it outside the host’s own mode makes the machine stop and
hand control to the host, which is called a trap. For the kind of machine they modelled:
if every sensitive instruction is privileged, a host can be built. The guest runs at full
speed, and whenever it touches something that matters, the machine itself stops it and
lets the host decide. That’s a host whose step has an opinion.

Then the obvious next question: did the machines people actually bought pass the
test? The most common one didn’t. In 2000 John Scott Robin and Cynthia Irvine went
through every instruction of Intel’s Pentium and found seventeen that are sensitive
and not privileged; POPF, which loads the processor’s flags, is the one usually pointed
at. A guest could run them and the host would never hear about it. The fixes came
two ways: VMware rewrote the guest’s code on the fly so the troublesome instructions
never ran as written, and in the middle of the 2000s Intel and AMD added hardware
support so they’d trap. Does that change anything here? Not the theorem. Popek
and Goldberg were after speed and isolation, not a record and a price, so their result
isn’t mine and mine isn’t theirs. It changes the picture, though. The universal host of
Section 14.12 sits where they’d want a host to sit, for the small machine’s programs:
the host’s own step collects each guest’s toll. And an industry learned the same lesson
the expensive way: a rule binds the guest only if it lives in the step underneath.



                                           265
The Thiele Machine                                                                    Devon Thiele


The smallest checked version of “a ledger beside an ordinary machine” is a Turing
machine configuration with a counter next to it, where each step adds one, plus one
more if it writes a nonblank symbol. The counter doesn’t disturb the machine.


Theorem 20.7 (A counter beside a Turing machine changes nothing). Let a Turing
machine with transition table δ step a configuration c to tmn (δ, c) after at most n steps
(stopping when δ has no entry). Pair each configuration with a counter, and step the pair by
stepping the configuration and adding the step’s charge. Then for every n, δ and pair (c, m),
the configuration part after at most n steps of the pair is tmn (δ, c). In particular this holds
from (c, 0).

Proof. By induction on n. For n = 0 both sides are c. For n + 1, if δ has no entry at
c, both runs stop and both sides are c. Otherwise the pair steps to (c′ , m′ ) where c′ is
exactly the Turing machine’s next configuration, whatever m′ is, and the induction
hypothesis at (c′ , m′ ) finishes it.

Checked as thiele_simulates_turing_gen and thiele_simulates_turin
g (ProperSubsumption.v). The “Thiele” in those names is a local record, a Turing
configuration and a number; it is not the machine of this book, and the file says not to
cite it as the machine simulating Turing machines.

And one honesty: the simulating-system record has a cost-preservation field (the base
charges at least what my machine would), and the theorem never uses it. It’s there for
a stronger statement that hasn’t been made.

Here it is exactly. A certification system is Section 3’s, Definition 3.1: states, moves, a
step, a cost per move, a certified bit, and the toll as a field.


Definition 20.5 (A system that simulates the machine). A simulating system is a certi-
fication system B together with a decoding d from its moves to machine instructions
and an embedding e from its states to machine states, satisfying three premises: the
step commutes, e(stepB (s, i )) = apply(e(s), d(i )) for all s, i; cost is preserved upward,
costB (i ) ≥ cost(d(i )) for all i; and the certified bit is reflected, certB (s) = the certified
flag of e(s) for all s.


Theorem 20.8 (The machine represents any system that simulates it). Let (B , d, e) be
a simulating system, s0 a state of B and t a list of its moves. If s0 is uncertified and the run
of t from s0 ends certified, then the total cost of t in B is at least 1, and the machine run of the
decoded list d(t) from e(s0 ) ends with the certified flag on.

Proof. The first part is the universal floor (Theorem 3.1) applied to B by itself. For the
second, by induction on t using step commutation, the embedding of B ’s final state is



                                                266
The Thiele Machine                                                                Devon Thiele


the machine’s final state on d(t) from e(s0 ); reflection turns “B ’s final state is certified”
into “that machine state has the flag on”. Cost preservation is not used.

Checked as thiele_represents_simulating_cert_system (UniversalCertifi-
cationCost.v), with the record SimulatingCertificationSystem (its fields scs_
step_commutes, scs_cost_preserved, scs_cert_reflects), the run lemma
scs_run_embed, and the identity instance thiele_self_simulating. The floor
for a system with no embedding at all is universal_nfi_any_substrate.

One limit on all of this, so it isn’t read as more. Certification is one event. Other
kinds of observable a machine might carry would each need their own event, their
own evidence and their own cost law, and nothing here supplies those. And stacking
several such predicates side by side gives a list of bits and nothing more: no topology,
no metric, and no independence between them beyond what Theorem 20.5 proves for
its three named fields.

So: two states, same shadow, different graph, at the type level in two lines and from
the initial state in one step. The graph is the thing the ordinary windows drop. Next,
what a run that uses the graph looks like on a receipt, in four acts.

21 The receipt in four acts
Four short acts with one receipt. They show the difference between an arrow that lives
in the graph and a register that holds its number, and they show the trace recording
what an assertion attempt cost, even when it fails. None of this vouches for a receipt
somebody else hands you, and none of it makes a property label true. I’ll say what each
act costs, and under each act I’ll name what’s checked, because the four acts together
are a script that runs (a small Python demonstration that asserts its own numbers as it
goes, and a test that runs it end to end), and the individual facts are the theorems.

That’s the kind of demonstration I trust: it doesn’t just print numbers, it checks them,
so if one ever drifts the script fails out loud instead of quietly printing something else.
Fair warning: this is one of the most bookkeeping-flavoured stretches of the book, a
receipt read line by line. Keep a pencil handy. Every number in it can be added up by
hand.

21.1 Act 1: the attempt costs, even when it fails
Run the assertion step on an arrow number that doesn’t exist. The demonstration does
it on a machine that has built no arrows at all, asserting arrow ninety-nine with the
property “two-hop” and declared cost zero. Any arrow number at or above the arrow
counter is absent, because well-formedness (Section 16) puts every arrow’s number
below the counter. What happens: the error flag latches on, because the lookup failed;
the assertion channel stays at zero, because failure doesn’t activate it; and the counter
goes up by one anyway, because the declared cost was zero and the floor is one.



                                             267
The Thiele Machine                                                                Devon Thiele


What’s checked: the failing branch of the assertion rule sets the error code, latches
the flag, steps the program counter and charges the cost, and changes nothing else
(step_morph_assert_bad); the counter rises by at least one on any assertion, any
state, any argument (morph_assert_mu_pos); the exact cost is declared cost plus
one (morph_cost_morph_assert); and from a clear channel, the channel becomes
nonzero if and only if the instruction is an assertion, the arrow exists, and the checksum
is nonzero (morph_assert_step_sets_supra_cert_iff), so a missing arrow
leaves it clear. The machine charges for the failed existence check. That’s what the
assertion guarantees and all it guarantees: it checks the arrow exists, stores a checksum
of the property string, and leaves the certificate operand unread.

Exactly, with i = MORPH_ASSERT on arrow k with property p, certificate c and de-
clared cost d:


Theorem 21.1 (A failed assertion still pays). (1) If the graph of s has no arrow numbered
k, then apply(s, i ) agrees with s on every field except four: pc becomes pc(s) + 1, µ becomes
µ(s) + d + 1, the error code becomes 1, and the error flag becomes true. In particular certaddr
and the graph are unchanged. (2) For every state s, cost(i ) = d + 1 and µ(apply(s, i )) ≥
µ(s) + 1.

Proof. (1) is the failure rule of MORPH_ASSERT, read through the bridge
(Lemma 17.1): it builds the next state from s with the error writer, which changes
only the error code, and the latch, which sets the flag. (2): the cost is the defini-
tion (Definition 17.4), and the counter claim is conservation (Theorem 16.1) with that
cost.

Checked as step_morph_assert_bad (VMStep.v), morph_cost_morph_asser
t (CategoryBridge.v) and morph_assert_mu_pos (InsightTaxonomy.v). The if-and-
only-if is part (3) of Theorem 17.7, morph_assert_step_sets_supra_cert_if
f. That an arrow number at or above the counter is absent is read from the second
clause of well-formedness (Definition 16.5); no lemma states it on its own, and the
demonstration’s machine has no arrows at all, so its case needs nothing.

21.2 Act 2: build the chain
Run the demonstration’s program. Three PNEWs, each claiming a cell of its own (cells
one, two and three, declared cost one each), which make modules A, B and C. Under
Section 16’s rules overlapping ranges trap, and so do ranges past memory, so the three
claims have to be different ranges inside the hundred and twenty-eight words, and
they are. Then MORPH f from A to B and MORPH g from B to C, declared cost two
each. Then COMPOSE h from f and g, declared cost one. Then MORPH_GET into
register zero the source of h and into register one its target, declared cost zero each.
The modules are numbered one, two and three because the runner the demonstration
drives starts its module counter at one; in the kernel’s own initial state they would be


                                             268
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


zero, one and two (Section 16). The arrows are numbered one, two and three either
way, since both start the arrow counter at one.

When it finishes, register zero holds 1, which is A, and register one holds 3, which
is C. Registers ten, eleven and twelve hold the three arrow numbers, and h, arrow
three, from A to C, sits in the graph. The counter reads eight: 1 + 1 + 1 + 2 + 2 + 1,
and nothing for the two MORPH_GETs. The demonstration asserts all of that. Had
every declared cost been zero, the counter would read zero; each of these instructions
charges what it declares.

Do the sum yourself before you trust mine. Write the eight instructions down the left
side of a sheet, the declared cost of each beside it, and add the column. Then do what
Turing asked for in 1949 (Section 19) and write a running total after every line, so a
mistake can only hide in one line at a time. Eight instructions and a total of eight,
by the way, is a coincidence and not a clue: change one declared cost and they part
company.

One detail from Section 18 that matters here: MORPH reads its coupling from memory,
a count word then pairs. With zeroed memory the count is zero, so f and g have empty
couplings, and if you MORPH_GET the pair count of h you get zero. The chain is
built; the relational content is empty, because nobody wrote any. That’s the honest
state of Act 2 on a blank machine. If you want pairs, write a coupling block first.

What’s checked: the success branches of MORPH, COMPOSE, MORPH_GET and
their selector function; each costs its declared cost (the six cost lemmas in the bridge
file); arrow construction can be free at zero (morph_can_be_free, morph_compos
e_cost_zero); and a run that contains none of the five instructions in the setter class
(LASSERT, LJOIN, EMIT, REVEAL, MORPH_ASSERT) leaves the assertion channel
exactly where it was (structural_trace_preserves_cert_addr). No named
theorem gives the register values or the total for this exact program: the total is the
sum of per-step costs the lemmas fix, and the register values come from running it.

Here is the channel fact Act 2 rests on, exactly. Write run(t, s) for applying a list t of
instructions to s in order (Definition 17.3).


Theorem 21.2 (Building leaves the channel alone). Let t be a list of instructions none of
which is in the setter class (LASSERT, LJOIN, EMIT, REVEAL, MORPH_ASSERT), and s
any state. Then certaddr(run(t, s)) = certaddr(s).

Proof. For one step: every instruction outside the setter class copies the address field
on every branch, by a case split that closes by computation. Then induction on t.

Checked as structural_trace_preserves_cert_addr (InsightTaxonomy.v),
on top of thiele_non_cert_addr_setter_preserves (AbstractNoFI.v). Act 2’s
program uses PNEW, MORPH, COMPOSE and MORPH_GET, none of them setters.


                                           269
The Thiele Machine                                                                   Devon Thiele


The theorem is about applying a list in order; the demonstration’s runner fetches by
program counter, and for a straight-line program with no jump and no trap the two
orders are the same. That step is read from the program, not checked. The costs are
fixed one instruction at a time: MORPH, COMPOSE, MORPH_ID, MORPH_DELETE,
MORPH_TENSOR and MORPH_GET each cost exactly their declared d (morph_cost
_morph and its five siblings, CategoryBridge.v), and so does PNEW, by the definition
of the schedule.

21.3 Act 3: assert
Run the same program with one more instruction after the COMPOSE: the assertion
on h, with the property “A-to-C-two-hop”, a certificate string the step never reads, and
declared cost four. It succeeds, because h exists. The channel moves to the checksum
of the property, which is the sum of its character codes, nonzero. The counter goes up
by five, four declared plus the floor, and reads thirteen. The demonstration also runs
a smaller probe to show the floor on its own: one PNEW at cost one, a MORPH_ID at
cost zero, and an assertion at declared cost zero. The assertion still charges one, and
the counter reads two.

Why does the property string need a non-NUL byte? (NUL is the character whose
code is zero.) Because the channel stores a plain byte sum. The empty string sums to
zero, and so would an all-NUL string, leaving the channel at zero: the step succeeds
and nothing was activated. Any string with a non-NUL byte works. And because
the step writes the checksum unconditionally, an assertion whose property sums to
zero, made after a good one, writes the channel back to zero. The channel holds the
fingerprint of the latest assertion, not a running record of all of them. “A-to-C-two-
hop” is just a label, and I’d ask you to hear “just a label” with Section 19 in your ear:
the step doesn’t check that h is a two-hop path. It checks that h exists.

What’s checked: the success branch (step_morph_assert_ok); the if-and-only-if
above; and the machine’s form of Section 9’s point that certified insight isn’t free
(Remark 9.1): any flip of either reading (the channel or the flag) from off to on costs
at least one and raises the counter by at least one (certified_insight_nonfree;
parts (1) to (3) of Section 17’s Theorem 17.8, which Section 22 files under Section 9’s
tiers). And one thing it does not do, which the demonstration prints out so nobody
misses it: the assertion sets the assertion channel, not the certified flag. Those are two
different readings set by two different instructions (Section 17), and this act sets one
of them.


Theorem 21.3 (A successful assertion). (1) If the graph of s has an arrow numbered k,
then apply(s, i ) agrees with s on every field except three: pc becomes pc(s) + 1, µ becomes
µ(s) + d + 1, and certaddr becomes Σ( p), the sum of the character codes of p. The certified
flag is not touched. (2) For any state s and any instruction j: if certaddr goes from 0 to nonzero,
or the certified flag goes from false to true, across the step apply(s, j), then cost( j) ≥ 1 and



                                               270
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


µ(apply(s, j)) ≥ µ(s) + 1.

Proof. (1) is the success rule read through the bridge. (2) is parts (1) to (3) of Theo-
rem 17.8, put together as one statement about either reading.

Checked as step_morph_assert_ok (VMStep.v) and certified_insight
_nonfree (InsightTaxonomy.v). With Act 3’s numbers: 8 + 4 + 1 = 13, and
Σ(A-to-C-two-hop) is nonzero because the string has a non-NUL character.

The trace now records a successful existence check and what it cost. The counter
can’t go down. The total by itself doesn’t say which assertion happened or where; for
that you need the trace (Section 19’s grocery receipt). And keeping honest books is a
different job from catching an adversary who hands you a different history (Section 7’s
escapes).

21.4 Act 4: equal observations can hide different graphs
Two programs and one probe. Program A is Act 2’s program: the three PNEWs,
the two MORPHs, the COMPOSE and the two MORPH_GETs (the demonstration
appends a HALT, which the runner stops at). When it ends, register zero holds 1,
register one holds 3, the counter reads eight, the error flag is down, and the graph
holds three arrows.

Program B never runs MORPH or COMPOSE. It makes three modules the same way,
claiming the same three cells, but declares their costs as two each, six in all. Then
it loads the two values straight into registers with LOAD_IMM, register zero gets 1
and register one gets 3, at declared cost one each. Six and one and one make eight,
so the counter matches. B’s graph has three modules and no arrows, because PNEW
and LOAD_IMM never add an arrow. Its registers hold the numbers one and three, a
claimed source and a claimed target, and the numbers are tokens, not graph entries.

The demonstration compares four values: register zero, register one, the counter and
the error flag. For A they are 1, 3, 8, down. For B they are 1, 3, 8, down. Same. That’s a
fingerprint, and a weaker one than Section 20’s pair, which agrees on all six shadow
fields. B is a different program from A in other ways, and the demonstration doesn’t
look at them: registers ten, eleven and twelve hold the arrow numbers in A and zero
in B, and B is shorter, five instructions against A’s eight.

Now the probe. Append MORPH_DELETE of arrow one, declared cost zero, to each
program. In A, arrow one is f, the first MORPH built, so the delete succeeds. In B there
is no arrow one, and the delete fails and latches the error. The demonstration asserts
both outcomes. MORPH_DELETE reads the graph, and the graph is the one thing a
LOAD_IMM can’t forge.

There’s a horse in this act, if you squint. In Germany in the early 1900s a mathe-
matics teacher named Wilhelm von Osten showed off a horse called Clever Hans,


                                           271
The Thiele Machine                                                                       Devon Thiele


who answered arithmetic questions by tapping a hoof, and got them right, in front of
crowds. Same answers out as a horse that could count: that’s Program B’s matching
fingerprint. Then the psychologist Oskar Pfungst stopped looking at the answers and
started changing the conditions, and published what he found in 1907. Put blinders
on Hans, or have him asked by someone who didn’t know the answer, and the arith-
metic fell apart. Hans was reading the questioner: tiny, unintended movements of
the head and body as the hoof reached the right number. That’s the probe. Pfungst
didn’t argue with the answers. He asked a question the answers couldn’t fake, one
that needed the real thing to be there, the way MORPH_DELETE needs an arrow to
be in the graph. And the part of the story I like best: nobody was lying. Von Osten
was never persuaded by Pfungst and kept showing his horse. A matching fingerprint
doesn’t need a cheat behind it, which is why you want a probe and not an accusation.

What’s checked, and here I have to be careful, because it’s tempting to point at Sec-
tion 20’s separation theorem as if it covered these two programs, and it doesn’t: that
theorem is one abstract pair of states, not Program A and Program B, and the equal
fingerprint for these programs is pinned by the script, not by Coq. The conservativity
theorem doesn’t cover B either, because B uses PNEW, and PNEW isn’t a classical
instruction: it adds modules. What Coq proves is the general shape, and the probe’s
half of it lives in the standalone copy of the kernel (Section 16 says what that copy is).
From any state whose arrow list is empty, MORPH_DELETE finds nothing (graph
_empty_morphisms_delete_fails_tc), and when the delete finds nothing the
error flag goes up (morph_delete_no_morphism_err_tc). B ends with an empty
arrow list. For the classical case: in the standalone kernel’s base state, any classical
run followed by MORPH_DELETE of arrow zero ends with the error flag up (classi
cal_trace_fails_morph_delete_probe_tc), and after a MORPH_ID the same
probe ends with it down (morph_id_step_passes_morph_delete_probe_tc);
the pair is packaged as the strictness witness (morph_delete_probe_separates_
thiele_from_classical_tc). In the kernel proper, the classical half is classic
al_trace_preserves_graph, which says a run of classical instructions leaves the
graph exactly as it was. So Act 4’s point is a theorem. Act 4’s numbers are a script.

The probe’s half, exactly. Write del( G, k ) for removing arrow k from graph G; it fails
when no arrow in G has number k.


Lemma 21.4 (The probe fails on an empty arrow list). (1) If the arrow list of G is empty,
del( G, k ) fails for every k. (2) If del(graph(s), k ) fails, then for every declared cost d, the step
from s on MORPH_DELETE of arrow k at cost d ends with the error flag true.

Proof. (1): removal first asks whether some arrow has number k; on the empty list the
answer is no. (2): the step function’s failure branch sets the flag to its old value or true,
which is true.




                                                 272
The Thiele Machine                                                                   Devon Thiele


Checked as graph_empty_morphisms_delete_fails_tc and morph_delet
e_no_morphism_err_tc (ThieleMachineComplete.v, the standalone copy of the
kernel). In the kernel proper the same fact is the failure rule step_morph_delete_
bad (VMStep.v).


Theorem 21.5 (One step the classical instructions can’t match). There are a state s0 and
instructions u and q such that the error flag of apply(apply(s0 , u), q) is false, while for every
list t of classical instructions the error flag of apply(run(t, s0 ), q) is true.

Proof. Take s0 with one module, numbered 0, no arrows, the arrow counter at 0, the
error flag down; u = MORPH_ID on module 0 at declared cost 0; and q = MORPH_
DELETE of arrow 0 at declared cost 0. After u there is an arrow 0, so q succeeds; this
part Coq checks by computing. A classical run keeps the graph (Theorem 17.3, in the
standalone copy’s form), so the arrow list is still empty, and Lemma 21.4 gives the
flag.

Checked as morph_delete_probe_separates_thiele_from_classical_tc,
with its halves morph_id_step_passes_morph_delete_probe_tc and classi
cal_trace_fails_morph_delete_probe_tc (ThieleMachineComplete.v). The
classical class there is the standalone copy’s own predicate, with the same twenty-two
exclusions as the kernel’s. Program B uses PNEW, which is not classical, so B is outside
this theorem; what covers B is Lemma 21.4, because B ends with an empty arrow list.

21.5 What the receipt is
The counter is what the schedule added up to: with the demonstration’s declared
costs (one per PNEW, two per MORPH, one for COMPOSE, four plus the floor for
the assertion), thirteen, of which the assertion’s five is the only part that touched the
assertion channel, and the floor’s one is the only part the toll forced. The graph carries
the structure the shadow leaves out. The trace tells you where things came from, as
long as whoever reads it has a history they can trust, which is Section 7’s question, the
one its three escapes answer, and not this act’s to close.

Said plainly, in three sentences. The receipt tells you what was paid, and on which
line. It doesn’t tell you the lines happened the way it says unless you trust whoever
hands it to you. And it doesn’t make any label on it true.

And one rule the acts have to respect: MORPH_DELETE removes one arrow and
nothing else, but PSPLIT and PMERGE delete every arrow touching the modules they
remove. An arrow’s life is bounded by its modules’. In the four acts no module is split
or merged, so nothing cascades; in a longer program, it would.

That’s one receipt, read act by act, with the price of every line on it. What the receipt
doesn’t do on its own is tell you what anyone is entitled to conclude from it, or sort
what happened in it into the kinds of learning Section 9 separated. Those were Part


                                               273
The Thiele Machine                                                              Devon Thiele


III’s questions, asked about any system with the pieces. The next section asks them of
this one.

22 Insight and entitlement on the machine
Section 21 left a receipt on the table and two questions beside it: what does a receipt
like that entitle anyone to conclude, and which of the things on it were learning and
which were commitment? Those are Section 8’s and Section 9’s questions, and in Part
III they were about any system with the right pieces: a reading, a toll, a counter, a price
list. They got by with cups, three playing cards and a sheet of paper with two boxes
on it, because that’s all the claims needed. The machine of Section 16 to Section 21
has every one of those pieces at once, and more of each than the paper ever did: two
readings instead of one, fifty-one moves instead of three, a declared price on every
move, and a counter that lives inside the state. So this is where the two chapters meet
something that runs. Some of their claims land cleanly. Some land with conditions the
paper never had to mention, because the paper had nothing to hide them in, and I’ll
say which as they come. And the machine has one thing the paper couldn’t: a theorem
with a long name and a longer hypothesis list, which is what entitlement looks like
when somebody actually has to check it.

22.1 The two readings, and who writes them
Section 3’s paper had one reading. The machine keeps two that look alike, and I’m
going to use them by name. (I’ll call them readings and not marks: since Section 3 a
mark has been one tally on the bill, and I’m keeping it that way.) One is the certified flag.
Only CERTIFY sets it, nothing ever takes it down (that part is proved), and it carries
no object and no check; it’s a bit. The other is the assertion channel. Only MORPH_
ASSERT writes it, and what it writes is a number worked out from the property’s label,
the sum of its character codes. A later assertion writes over it, an assertion with an
empty label writes a zero, which is the same as clearing it, and nothing proves the
channel stays set. Each sentence from here on says which of the two it’s about.

And here’s the part to hold on to: no step of the machine reads either one. Every rule
that mentions them sets them or leaves them alone. Section 8 warned that nothing
in the five parts makes a later move read the reading; this machine is a case where
nothing does. So when I say a run is entitled, I mean what someone auditing the run
may conclude from the reading and the receipt. The machine doesn’t enforce it.

Section 8’s note on the paper (the one beside Definition 8.1) has a machine version, and
Section 18 already showed it: 42 written into a register and called an arrow is a note,
raw data forged in one write, and the machine’s assertion step looks the arrow up and
refuses one that isn’t there. For entitlement, what matters is what the assertion leaves
behind: a paid event, charged at least one, and one reading on the whole machine,
a number worked out from a label. (It doesn’t record which arrow it named.) An
asserted arrow has a receipt, and the receipt is the event. One limit on that word


                                            274
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


“arrow”: the assertion step checks only that the arrow exists. Whether the run built it
or started with it depends on where the run started.

Here are the two readings as symbols, and the one more bit that shows up below: the
error flag, which a step raises when it can’t do what it was asked, and which stays up
once raised (Remark 16.1).


Definition 22.1 (The two readings). A state s of the machine carries a Boolean cert(s),
the certified flag, and a whole number addr(s), the assertion channel (Section 16’s field,
which Section 17 writes certaddr(s)), and a Boolean err(s), the error flag. Write
apply(s, i ) for the state after instruction i (Definition 17.1). The checksum of a label
ℓ is Σ(ℓ) = ∑ x∈ℓ code( x ), the sum of its character codes; it is zero exactly when every
character has code zero, and in particular for the empty label.


Who writes them, Section 17 already proved, over every instruction and every branch,
and I won’t state it twice: Theorem 17.6 for the flag and Theorem 17.7 for the channel
are the home of every sentence above about who sets what. The one thing to add is
that the flag’s permanence also holds for the machine’s unbounded step, the one that
keeps every number exactly instead of cutting it to sixty-four bits (vm_apply_u_cer
tified_permanent, VMUnboundedLedger.v).

22.2 Insight on the machine
Section 9 sorted what happens when a computation learns into raw observation, which
can be free; certified insight, which the toll prices; and the observation that the price is
flat whatever is certified (Definition 9.1 and Remark 9.1, argued there for any certifi-
cation system). On the machine each of those gets a theorem, and the flat price gets
a tier of its own, because the machine has a thing to certify that’s striking enough to
tempt anyone into thinking it should cost more.

The first thing, raw observation, on the machine. Something comes in and gets written
down. A counter ticks. Neither certification reading moves because of it. Later steps
can read what it wrote, and one of the machine’s own checks does, but that reading is
a separate, paid step. In the checked work the free case is the trial step, CHSH_TRIAL
(one round of a two-player game I build in Section 25), and it’s charged whatever its
instruction declares, which can be zero. An input read isn’t free: READ_PORT is on
the cost floor. And “free” here is a fact about this machine’s price list, not a claim that
looking costs nothing in the physical world.

The second thing, certified structural insight. Some step turns a certification reading
from off to on: the certified flag raised, or the assertion channel set by a property as-
serted on an arrow. On this machine that’s a theorem over every one of its instructions
(stated exactly below: any step that takes either reading from off to on costs at least
one and raises the counter by at least one). Section 9’s Gestalt reading of what’s being
charged for, a relation committed to, fits the assertion channel, which stores a number

                                            275
The Thiele Machine                                                                      Devon Thiele


worked out from a property on an arrow. The certified flag by itself commits to no
relation at all, which is Section 9’s bare crossing, and I’ll come back to that.

The third thing, certified game-witness insight. The run is certified and what it certifies
is a result from that game, the one I haven’t built yet, a result that no single fixed
strategy can produce: a score above two, when I get there. (That’s a statement about
the tallies the machine kept: with those counts, no one fixed strategy gives them.
Ruling out every model where the answers were settled in advance by some shared
hidden plan, which physicists call hidden-variable models, would need a different
argument and enough trials, and that isn’t what’s checked.) It gets its own tier because
the thing certified is so striking, and I’ll tell you what the proof says about it, because
it’s humbling. The theorem for this tier takes the hypothesis that the end state shows
that score above two, and then its proof discards that hypothesis and uses only the
second thing’s fact: that the certified flag went from off to on somewhere in a run,
which costs at least one. (The run is taken in list order, from a state where the flag
starts off.) The price of a certified game witness is the price of a certified anything: at
least one. The game adds meaning. It doesn’t add cost. That’s Section 9’s flat price,
landed. The three things are collected as one theorem (its name is in the trail below),
and I’d rather you know that its third part is its second part lifted from one step to a
whole run, for the certified flag only, with the game hypothesis dropped.

Here are the three, exactly. The two readings are the certified flag cert and the assertion
channel addr of Definition 22.1; apply(s, i ) is one step, cost(i ) is the price list’s charge
for i (Definition 17.4), and µ is the counter. The step that raises the flag is CERTIFY
and the one that writes the channel is MORPH_ASSERT. For lists, [ ] is the empty list
and i :: t is the list that starts with i and carries on with the list t, as in Section 9.


Definition 22.2 (Certified insight event, and the three tiers). A step from state s by
instruction i is a certified insight event when it turns a reading on: either addr(s) =
0 and addr(apply(s, i )) ̸= 0, or cert(s) = false and cert(apply(s, i )) = true. An
instruction is raw observation when no step by it, from any state, is a certified insight
event. Certified structural insight is a certified insight event. For the third tier, runs are
taken in list order: runlist ([ ], s) = s and runlist (i :: t, s) = runlist (t, apply(s, i )), with no
program counter involved. Certified game-witness insight is such a run that starts with
cert = false and ends with cert = true and with S > 2, where S is the game statistic
computed from the trial tallies the machine keeps (Section 25).


Lemma 22.1 (A trial is raw observation). Every trial step of the game is raw observation.
Its charge is the cost written in the instruction, which may be zero.

Proof. A trial step is neither CERTIFY nor MORPH_ASSERT, so by Theorem 17.6 and
part (1) of Theorem 17.7 it leaves both readings as they were, from every state. The
charge is read off the price list.


                                                 276
The Thiele Machine                                                               Devon Thiele


Checked as chsh_trial_is_tier0 (WitnessInsightGeneral.v); the charge is the
trial step’s case of instruction_cost (VMStep.v).


Theorem 22.2 (Certified insight is not free). If the step from s by i is a certified insight
event, then cost(i ) ≥ 1 and µ(apply(s, i )) ≥ µ(s) + 1.

Proof. Two cases. If the channel turned on, i is one of the five steps that reveal, emit,
join, check a formula or assert, because every other instruction leaves the channel
alone (a case split over all instructions); each of those five is priced at its declared cost
plus at least one. (By Theorem 17.7 it is in fact MORPH_ASSERT, but the proof only
needs the wider class.) If the flag turned on, i is CERTIFY, priced at its declared cost
plus one. Either way cost(i ) ≥ 1, and conservation, µ(apply(s, i )) = µ(s) + cost(i ),
gives the second half.

Checked as certified_insight_nonfree (InsightTaxonomy.v), from no_free_
certification, no_free_certification_certified and their counter forms
(AbstractNoFI.v), packaged there as certification_requires_positive_mu;
conservation is vm_apply_mu (MuLedgerConservation.v). It’s parts (1) to (3) of
Section 17’s Theorem 17.8 said in one breath, and part (2) of Theorem 21.3 is the same
statement met in Act 3; it gets its own block here because the third tier leans on it.


Theorem 22.3 (The price of a game witness is flat). Let t be a list of instructions and s
a state with cert(s) = false. If s′ = runlist (t, s) has cert(s′ ) = true and S(s′ ) > 2, then
µ(s′ ) ≥ µ(s) + 1.

Proof. The hypothesis S(s′ ) > 2 is not used. Induction on t. The empty list leaves the
flag false, which contradicts the end. For i :: t: if the flag is on after i, that step is a
certified insight event, so it raises µ by at least one (Theorem 22.2), and the rest of the
run never lowers µ. If the flag is still off after i, the induction hypothesis covers the
rest, and the step by i didn’t lower µ.

Checked as witness_insight_nonfree_general, through no_free_certif
ication_certified_trace_mu (WitnessInsightGeneral.v). The same lift for the
assertion channel, with the extra fact that the list contains an instruction of the five-
member class, is no_free_certified_insight (InsightTaxonomy.v). The three
tiers are collected as witness_insight_complete_taxonomy (WitnessInsight-
General.v): Lemma 22.1, Theorem 22.2 and Theorem 22.3, joined by “and.”

So Section 9’s two facts and a warning hold here word for word. Looking can be free.
Turning a reading on can’t, and putting a game result behind it doesn’t make it cost
any more.




                                             277
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


Section 9 also asked who decided the split, and said any concrete machine owes you
its whole table. This one’s table is Section 17’s. The floor sits under the whole cost-floor
class, Section 17’s positive class of twelve (Definition 17.5), which is wider than the
two steps that turn a reading on, and every step outside that class costs whatever its
instruction declares, which can be zero. So the sorting into three things is by which
reading moves, as it was in Section 9. The part of the schedule that’s forced is the floor
under the flag-raisers, and Section 4 is the argument for it (Theorem 4.2); the rest is a
choice, and Section 17 defends it under the table.

22.3 Test, then commit, on the machine
Section 9 put a CHECK on the paper and found nothing in the five parts that makes
VOUCH wait for it (Remark 9.2), and said a particular system could close that gap by
writing it into its step. This machine doesn’t. Here’s its version, the same gap with
numbers on it.

The test is LASSERT, the formula check Section 19 took apart: it charges on the attempt,
pass or fail, and it raises neither certification reading. The commit is one of two other
steps: MORPH_ASSERT, which puts a property on an arrow and sets the assertion
channel, or CERTIFY, which raises the certified flag with no arrow and no property
behind it at all, the weakest commit there is. So the honest protocol is two steps, with
two separate charges, one for the checking work and one for the flip.

And nothing in the machine makes the second step follow the first. The assertion
step checks only that the arrow it names exists. It has no way to read whether a
test ran earlier in the run on the formula the property names. A program can assert
“validated constraint” on an arrow with no test anywhere in its history and get the
same stored value (the number worked out from the label) for the same charge on that
step. The two whole states can still differ by whatever else the two programs did; pad
the shorter program with a step that does nothing and costs the same, and they agree.
So Section 9’s sentence holds here exactly: the receipt says a commitment was paid
for, not that it was earned. On this machine the toll prices the commit, and whether
the commit was preceded by a test is a fact about the program, not a guarantee of the
machine.

The two facts under that, exactly.


Lemma 22.4 (The check commits nothing). For every state s and every formula-checking
instruction i, addr(apply(s, i )) = addr(s) and cert(apply(s, i )) = cert(s), whether the
check passes or fails.

Proof. The check is neither MORPH_ASSERT nor CERTIFY. Apply part (1) of Theo-
rem 17.7 and Theorem 17.6.

Checked as instances of non_morph_assert_preserves_cert_addr (Revelation-


                                            278
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


Requirement.v) and vm_apply_certified (PrimeAxiom.v); no theorem names the
formula check’s case by itself. The same two equalities sit inside Theorem 19.1, among
everything else the check leaves alone; here they stand by themselves because they’re
the test half of the protocol.


Remark 22.1 (The commit reads no test). The assertion step’s rule has one condi-
tion, that the arrow it names is in the current graph. When it is, the new channel
value is Σ(ℓ) for the instruction’s label ℓ, and the charge is the declared cost plus one.
Nothing in the rule depends on which instructions ran before. This is read off the
rule (step_morph_assert_ok in VMStep.v and the matching case of vm_apply in
SimulationProof.v); the files state no separate theorem for it.


A worked chain, so the two prices have numbers. Say a register holds the address
of a formula whose declared length is four words, and another holds the address of
the two rows of values it’s checked against (one meant to make it true, one meant to
make it false; Section 19 laid them out). The check, with declared cost 0, is charged
4 · 8 + (0 + 1) = 33, pass or fail, and moves neither reading. Then, if it passed, an
assertion with declared cost 0 and the label “validated_constraint” on an arrow that
exists is charged 0 + 1 = 1 and sets the channel to the label’s checksum, which isn’t
zero, since the label has characters with nonzero codes. The total is 34, and the channel
crossed from zero on the second step, not the first. Skip the check and the assertion
alone still costs 1 and writes the same number. These numbers are the price function
evaluated on the two instructions (instruction_cost, VMStep.v), not a separate
theorem.

One edge the paper didn’t have, because the paper’s VOUCH, played from NO,
always crossed: an assertion with an empty label pays and raises nothing, because the
number it stores is zero. Paid, and no reading moved. Section 9’s “a crossing costs at
least one” is untouched by it; it just isn’t a crossing.

22.4 Entitlement on the machine
Now Section 8’s count. Section 8 said a run is entitled to a claim when it has an object,
a checked relation and a paid event (Definition 8.1), and that the leaning costs at least
the index bits of the narrowing it commits to, given lists, a tree, a covering, and a run
that paid for the tree’s depth (Theorem 8.2). On this machine that is a theorem with a
long name, structural_entitlement_representation, and I want to give you
its hypotheses, all of them, because the theorem is only as good as what it’s handed,
and a list of hypotheses is the kind of thing that gets skimmed while the conclusion
gets quoted.

First, what “paid step” means here. Section 8 counted every step the price list charges
at least one for, and on this machine those are the cost-floor steps from a few para-
graphs back: the steps that reveal, emit, join, check a formula, read a port (take in a


                                           279
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


value from outside the machine), certify or assert, and the checks for the two-player
game of Section 25. Only two of them, CERTIFY and MORPH_ASSERT, turn a read-
ing on. The tree is a bare shape, as in Section 8, and “no deeper than the number of
cost-floor steps” is a count along the run that happened. It isn’t a walk down the tree.
In the example below, two of the counted steps emit, and emitting raises nothing.

The theorem is handed: a decoder that turns the run’s receipts into an observation (in
the files the receipts are the list of instructions the run was handed, not a log of the
steps it took); an exact equality test on observations; a posterior that’s a strict subset
of the prior; one eliminated state and an observation that gives it a value no surviving
state gives (the distinguishing test, which is Plato’s third account from Section 8, made
into a function); a start with the assertion channel at zero, and an end that’s certified,
a word the files use here for something that never looks at the certified flag. It means
three things at once: no error latched, the posterior’s membership test accepts the
decoded receipts, and the assertion channel is nonzero; a decision tree no deeper than
the number of cost-floor steps the run executed; a non-empty posterior; and a second
observation function, the representative one, with a family of fibres, one per surviving
state, such that every prior state sits in the fibre of some survivor that gives it the
same representative observation. The fibre sizes together have to add up to at least
the prior’s length, and no fibre may be larger than the tree has leaves.

That last clause is Section 8’s covering condition, carried by fibres, and it’s the nearest
thing the record has to an anti-stopped-clock clause. I have to be exact about how
near. It says every prior state is covered by some survivor, and no survivor stands for
more states than the tree has leaves. That limits how much can be deleted per leaf you
paid for. It doesn’t say why anything was deleted. The representative observation is a
function somebody supplies, and one that returns the same thing for every state makes
“same representative observation” true of every pair; the small two-state example
below does exactly that. So the clause rules out deleting too much for the tree you’ve
paid for. It doesn’t rule out deleting for no reason.

Given all that, the theorem concludes three things: the posterior’s predicate is strictly
stronger than the prior’s, an assertion event happened, and the counter rose by at least
the index bits lost. Section 8’s three small prints hold here unchanged: both logarithms
round up separately and the subtraction stops at zero, the lists are lists with repeats
counted, and the difference isn’t the number of questions anyone asked.

Picture that chain as three links you can hold one at a time, like three cups in a row:
narrow the list, find the step that paid, count the bill. Two of the links are their own
theorems and I’ll name them so you can find them. Narrowing a list, with a test that
distinguishes, makes the membership predicate strictly stronger: feasible_stri
ct_subset_implies_strict_predicates, Section 8’s card argument checked
on lists of this machine’s states. And on this machine, reaching a certified end from
a clear start means an assertion event fired somewhere in the run: strengthening


                                           280
The Thiele Machine                                                               Devon Thiele


_requires_structure_addition. On that second one, one more thing about its
proof: its “strictly stronger” hypothesis is taken in and split. The strict half is thrown
away, and the other half only builds a premise that the last step ignores. What does
the work is “the channel was clear at the start and set at the end,” and the flip follows
from zero-then-nonzero. The theorem is true. Its name promises a tighter link than its
proof uses.

Here is the whole chain exactly, one link at a time. First the words.


Definition 22.3 (Runs, state lists, observations, predicates). A program p is a list of
instructions. The run run(n, p, s) with fuel n from state s repeats, at most n times,
“fetch the instruction of p at the program counter and apply it,” and stops early if
the counter points past the end of p. A state list is a finite list Ω of states; |Ω| is its
length, repeats counted. Ω′ is a strict sublist of Ω when every member of Ω′ is in Ω
and some member of Ω is not in Ω′ . An observation is a function obs from states to
lists of instructions, and an equality test is a Boolean function eq on such lists with
eq(o1 , o2 ) = true exactly when o1 = o2 . A receipt predicate is a Boolean function on lists.
The membership predicate of Ω under obs is

                PΩ (o ) = true ⇐⇒ eq(obs(s), o ) = true for some s ∈ Ω.

P is stronger than Q when P(o ) = true implies Q(o ) = true for every o, and strictly
stronger when, in addition, some o has P(o ) = false and Q(o ) = true. A state w is
distinguished from Ω′ by obs when obs(w) ̸= obs(t) for every t ∈ Ω′ .


The run with fuel is Section 17’s (Definition 17.1), written out again here because every
block below is stated on it.


Theorem 22.5 (Narrowing becomes strengthening). Let eq be an equality test, let Ω′ be
a strict sublist of Ω, and let w ∈ Ω with w ∈
                                            / Ω′ be distinguished from Ω′ by obs. Then PΩ′
is strictly stronger than PΩ .

Proof. “Strictly stronger” has two parts. (a) If PΩ′ (o ) is true, some t ∈ Ω′ has obs(t) = o;
that t is in Ω, so PΩ (o ) is true. This part is only the inclusion. (b) Take o = obs(w).
Since w ∈ Ω, PΩ (o ) is true. No member of Ω′ has observation o, so PΩ′ (o ) is false.
The gap between the lists would not give (b) by itself: a removed state can share
its observation with a surviving one, and then the two predicates accept the same
observations. That is why the distinguished state is a hypothesis of its own. In the
Coq proof the gap witness that comes with “strict sublist” is not used at all; the
supplied w does the work.

Checked as feasible_strict_subset_implies_strict_predicates (In-
formationGainToStrengthening.v), with the predicate defined as omega_predic


                                             281
The Thiele Machine                                                                 Devon Thiele


ate; the form that only says some strictly ordered pair of predicates exists is b
4_information_reduction_derives_strict_predicates (HonestNoFI_
TheoremsWithoutAssumptions.v).

That’s the first link: narrow the list with a test that separates, and the predicate gets
stronger. The second link needs the word “certified” pinned down, along with the one
step it points at.


Definition 22.4 (Certified end, structure addition). Fix a decoder d, a function from
instruction lists to lists. The files call the program p of a run its receipts: what the
decoder reads is the list of instructions the run was handed. The end state of a run
of p is certified for a predicate P when err = false there (the error flag is down),
P(d( p)) = true, and addr ̸= 0 there. The run run(n, p, s) has a structure addition when
one of the steps it executes goes from a state with addr = 0 to a state with addr ̸= 0.
(This is Section 19’s structural gain, Definition 19.2, under the name the files use here.)


Theorem 22.6 (A certified end from a clear start has an assertion event). Let Pstrong be
strictly stronger than Pweak , let addr(s) = 0, and let the end of run(n, p, s) be certified for
Pstrong . Then the run has a structure addition.

Proof. Only the third clause of “certified” is used: the channel is zero at the start and
nonzero at the end. Walk the run (induction on the fuel). At each executed step either
the channel turns nonzero, which is a structure addition, or it is still zero and the rest
of the run starts again from a clear channel. A run that stops with the channel still
zero ends at zero, which contradicts the end. The strictness hypothesis is taken apart
and its pieces feed nothing the conclusion needs. By part (3) of Theorem 17.7, the
step found is a MORPH_ASSERT naming an arrow that exists, with a label of nonzero
checksum.

Checked as strengthening_requires_structure_addition (NoFreeIn-
sight.v), through supra_cert_implies_structure_addition_in_run; the
step is identified by structure_addition_in_run_iff_morph_assert_brid
ge_pattern (both RevelationRequirement.v).

So a certified end from a clear start always points at a step you can name. Now the
count. It needs a tree, the cost-floor steps, and the fibres.


Definition 22.5 (Decision tree, cost-floor count, fibres). Decision trees, their depth
and their leaf count L( T ) are as in Definition 8.2. The cost-floor instructions are the
ones that reveal, emit, join, check a formula, read a port, certify or assert, and the five
game checks; the price list charges each of them its declared cost plus at least one.
c(n, p, s) is the number of cost-floor instructions among the steps run(n, p, s) executes.
The tree T is realized by the run when depth( T ) ≤ c(n, p, s). A posterior-representative


                                              282
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


reduction of Ω to Ω′ for an observation r and a tree T is a function F from states to state
lists (the fibres) such that: every s ∈ Ω lies in F (t) for some t ∈ Ω′ with r (s) = r (t);
|Ω| ≤ ∑t∈Ω′ | F (t)|; and | F (t)| ≤ L( T ) for every t ∈ Ω′ .


Lemma 22.7 (Paid steps cover the counter). For every run, c(n, p, s) ≤ µ(run(n, p, s)) −
µ ( s ).

Proof. The rise of the counter over the run is exactly the sum of the charges of the
executed steps (Theorem 16.1). Every cost-floor step contributes at least one to that
sum, and no step contributes less than zero.

Checked as info_priced_cert_executions_bound (MuShannonBridge.v), rest-
ing on cert_setter_cost_pos (VMStep.v) and delta_mu_equals_ledger_su
m.


Lemma 22.8 (Index bits are paid for). If T is realized by run(n, p, s), |Ω′ | > 0, and there
is a posterior-representative reduction of Ω to Ω′ for some r and T, then

                     ⌈log2 |Ω|⌉ −̇ ⌈log2 |Ω′ |⌉ ≤ µ(run(n, p, s)) − µ(s),

where ⌈log2 ·⌉ is the base-two logarithm rounded up and −̇ is subtraction on whole numbers
that stops at zero.

Proof. The fibres give |Ω| ≤ ∑t∈Ω′ | F (t)| ≤ L( T ) · |Ω′ |: sort the prior states by the
survivor whose fibre holds them, and each of the |Ω′ | groups has at most L( T )
members. The rounded-up logarithm respects order and is subadditive on products,
⌈log2 ab⌉ ≤ ⌈log2 a⌉ + ⌈log2 b⌉, so

                          ⌈log2 |Ω|⌉ ≤ ⌈log2 L( T )⌉ + ⌈log2 |Ω′ |⌉.

A tree of depth d has at most 2d leaves (induction on the tree), so ⌈log2 L( T )⌉ ≤
depth( T ). Chain the rest:

    ⌈log2 |Ω|⌉ −̇ ⌈log2 |Ω′ |⌉ ≤ depth( T ) ≤ c(n, p, s) ≤ µ(run(n, p, s)) − µ(s),

the middle step being realization and the last Lemma 22.7. The first clause of the
reduction, the one about the representative observation, is discarded by the Coq proof;
only the two counting clauses are used.

(MuShannonBridge.v), which goes through posterior_representative_redu
