That’s the third link: given the tree and the fibres, the counter covers the index bits the
list lost. Put the three links on one hypothesis list and you have the theorem.


Theorem 22.9 (Structural entitlement, represented). Fix fuel n, a program p, a start state
s, a decoder d, two observations obs and r, an equality test eq, a prior Ω, a posterior Ω′ , and
a decision tree T. Assume: (H1) eq decides equality of observations; (H2) Ω′ is a strict sublist
of Ω; (H3) some w ∈ Ω with w ∈      / Ω′ is distinguished from Ω′ by obs; (H4) addr(s) = 0;
(H5) the end of run(n, p, s) is certified for PΩ′ , the membership predicate of the posterior under
obs; (H6) T is realized by the run; (H7) |Ω′ | > 0; (H8) there is a posterior-representative
reduction of Ω to Ω′ for r and T. Then (C1) PΩ′ is strictly stronger than PΩ ; (C2) the run has
a structure addition; and (C3) ⌈log2 |Ω|⌉ −̇ ⌈log2 |Ω′ |⌉ ≤ µ(run(n, p, s)) − µ(s).

Proof. (C1) is Theorem 22.5 from (H1) to (H3). (C2) is Theorem 22.6 from (C1), (H4) and
(H5). (C3) is Lemma 22.8 from (H6) to (H8). The three conclusions share a hypothesis
list and nothing else: the proof of (C3) never looks at a membership predicate or at the
channel.

Checked as structural_entitlement_representation (HonestNoFI_
TheoremsWithoutAssumptions.v). The version with the end only required to be error-
free and accepted, with no channel clause and so no (C2), is observational_stru
ctural_entitlement_representation (same file).

Hold it up against Section 8’s three parts of entitlement (Definition 8.1) and they’re all
in the hypothesis list. The object is a pair of state lists and a decision tree. The checked
relation is the membership test with its distinguishing observation. The paid event is
a step that sets the assertion channel. That’s as close as the checked work comes to the
word; the word itself stays the book’s.


Remark 22.2 (Why two observations). The distinguishing observation and the repre-
sentative one can’t be the same function. If w ∈ Ω is distinguished from Ω′ by obs,
the reduction’s first clause puts w in the fibre of some t ∈ Ω′ with obs(w) = obs(t),
which the distinction forbids. Checked as distinguishing_observation_not_
posterior_representable (HonestNoFI_TheoremsWithoutAssumptions.v).


Remark 22.3 (The complete-tree bound). For any two lists with |Ω′ | > 0, a complete
tree of depth d = ⌈log2 (⌊|Ω|/|Ω′ |⌋ + 1)⌉ satisfies the covering inequality (exists_c
overing_tree). So if a bounded run run(n, p, s) realizes the complete tree of depth d
(executes at least d cost-floor steps), then ⌈log2 |Ω|⌉ − ⌈log2 |Ω′ |⌉ ≤ µ(run(n, p, s)) −
µ(s) (complete_tree_realization_bound, MuShannonBridge.v). The tree is


                                               284
The Thiele Machine                                                          Devon Thiele


still a hypothesis, the complete one of the right depth; what the form drops is any
tie between the two lists and the run. The lists only pick which depth the run has to
realize. It shows how much of (C3) is arithmetic on lengths once the paid steps are
counted. The same bound holds for lists whose states carry whole-number weights,
with total weight in place of length, given a realized tree whose leaf count times the
posterior’s weight covers the prior’s weight (info_priced_weighted_feasibl
e_reduction_bound), and the natural fibres of an observation give a reduction
whenever they meet the counting clauses (observation_partition_reduction
_implies_posterior_representative_reduction).


22.5 Every sound shortcut lands here, and what that sentence is worth
The book’s big-sounding sentence in this neighbourhood is: every sound structural
shortcut lands in that bound. I want to tell you exactly what it’s worth, which is less
than it sounds and more than nothing.

What’s checked is a record with fifteen fields, and here “record” is Coq’s word for a
bundle of named slots, not the kind of record Section 3 is about: seven pieces of data
(the decoder, the observation function, a representative observation, the equality test,
the prior, the posterior, the tree) and eight proof obligations over them. “Every sound
shortcut lands here” is the theorem that unpacks that record and applies the bound,
and its proof is four short steps (introduce, take the record apart, simplify, apply the
bound), because the record was defined to carry exactly the bound’s hypotheses. It’s
true by packaging. The right word for it is “a checklist”: a checklist for being a sound
shortcut, not a discovery about shortcuts.

And a checklist isn’t nothing, which is the “more than nothing” half. On 30 October
1935, at Wright Field, northeast of Dayton, Ohio, the Army was evaluating Boeing’s
new four-engine bomber, the Model 299. It took off, pitched up, stalled and crashed,
and two men died of their injuries, the Army’s pilot, Major Ployer Hill, and Boeing’s
chief test pilot, Leslie Tower. The airplane was fine. The crew had left the gust locks
on, the clamps that hold the control surfaces still while the plane sits on the ground. A
newspaper, as the story is usually told, called it too much airplane for one man to fly.
The answer wasn’t more skill, it was a card: a list of things to check, in order, every
time, and the story usually told is that this is where the pilot’s checklist comes from.
The airplane went on to be the B-17. Nothing on that card was a discovery. Every
item on it was something the pilots already knew. What the card did was make sure
none of it got left out when it mattered. That’s what the fifteen-field record does for
the bound: it finds nothing new about shortcuts, and it makes the eight hypotheses
impossible to drop quietly.

The checklist, exactly:


Definition 22.6 (Sound structural shortcut). For fuel n, a program p and a start state


                                          285
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


s, a sound structural shortcut is a record of seven pieces of data, d, obs, r, eq, Ω, Ω′ and
T, together with proofs of the eight hypotheses (H1) to (H8) of Theorem 22.9 for that
data: fifteen fields in all.


Corollary 22.10 (Every sound shortcut lands in the bound). For every sound structural
shortcut, conclusions (C1), (C2) and (C3) of Theorem 22.9 hold for its data.

Proof. Take the record apart into its fifteen fields and apply the theorem. Nothing else
happens.

Checked as every_sound_structural_shortcut_lands_here (HonestNoFI_
TheoremsWithoutAssumptions.v); a record is assembled from its fifteen parts by sou
nd_shortcut_from_components (same file).

22.6 A search whose surviving candidates can be counted
Put three coins under three cups. Each coin is heads or tails, so there are eight possible
rows under the cups. Someone hands you two answers: heads under the first cup,
tails under the second. Lift the first cup and compare. A matching answer leaves four
possible rows. Lift the second and compare. A match leaves two. The last coin can still
be either way. The list really shrank: eight, four, two. Nothing in that count needed a
claim about which way the last coin faces.

This is a parlour game, and an old one. In A Christmas Carol, in 1843, Scrooge’s nephew
Fred plays a game called Yes and No at his Christmas party: he thinks of something,
and everybody else asks questions he may only answer yes or no. He’s thinking of
an animal, a disagreeable, savage one that growls and grunts and lives in London,
and the answer is Uncle Scrooge. Most people know the game as twenty questions,
and twenty is a good number for it: each yes-or-no answer can at best cut the field in
half, and twenty halvings take a million or so possibilities, 220 = 1,048,576, down to
one. Push on that, though. The halving only happens because Fred answers truthfully
about what’s actually in his head. Lie once and the count still shrinks; it shrinks
around the wrong animal. That’s the cups again: the four and the two are real because
you lifted the cup and compared, not because somebody told you what was under it.

Here is that search on the machine. A candidate is a start state with an n-bit value
in memory, one bit per word, and the prior contains all 2n such states. The program
carries k supplied answers. For each one it loads the corresponding memory bit,
records the supplied answer through READ_PORT, compares the two, and jumps to a
trap if they disagree. If all the answers match, it makes a module, gives it an identity
arrow and asserts that arrow. The answers are supplied, not discovered by an oracle
inside the instruction: the question is which possible memory states this particular
answer sequence accepts.

After j matching questions, the surviving candidates are exactly the values whose first


                                            286
The Thiele Machine                                                                 Devon Thiele


j bits match those answers. There are 2n− j of them. So the posterior is tied to what the
program actually checks: run the program on any candidate, and it ends without an
error exactly when that candidate is in the posterior.

The two observations have different jobs here. One looks at the asked bits and can
tell a rejected candidate from every survivor. The other looks at the unasked bits.
For any candidate, keep its unasked bits and replace its asked bits with the supplied
answers. That gives a survivor with the same unasked bits. Each survivor represents
2k candidates, one for every possible assignment of the asked bits. These are the fibres
the bound needs. For the three cups and two questions, the survivor with the last coin
heads represents four rows, and the survivor with the last coin tails represents the
other four.

Each READ_PORT step costs two marks with these operands. The final assertion costs
one. Everything else in this program costs zero on this ledger, so the total is 2k + 1.
The complete binary tree has depth k, and the run executes k + 1 cost-floor steps. That
satisfies the representation theorem’s realization condition, which counts paid steps;
it is not a separate claim that the program stores or traverses that tree.


Theorem 22.11 (A checked bit search supplies the entitlement data). Let 1 ≤ k ≤ n ≤
64. Let the hidden memory value have length n, and let the k supplied answers agree with
its first k bits. With the candidate start states, asked-bit observation, unasked-bit representa-
tive observation, complete tree of depth k, and program just described, all the hypotheses of
Theorem 22.9 hold. The posterior predicate is strictly stronger, the run contains a structure
addition, and
                         ⌈log2 2n ⌉ − ⌈log2 2n−k ⌉ = k ≤ ∆µ = 2k + 1.

For every candidate of length n, membership in the posterior is equivalent to the run ending
without an error. The execution budget is 5k + 5 steps.

Proof. Each successful question compares one more memory bit with its supplied an-
swer; a mismatch reaches the trap. Induction over the questions gives the acceptance
condition and the paid steps. Enumerating all assignments to the unasked bits gives
the posterior’s size. Keeping those bits and replacing the asked ones supplies a repre-
sentative for every prior candidate, with 2k candidates in each fibre. A candidate with
its first bit opposite to the first answer witnesses strictness. The honest hidden value
survives and the assertion suffix raises the channel. These facts fill the representation
theorem’s hypotheses; the instruction-cost sum is 2k + 1.

Checked as bit_search_entitlement, bit_search_bound_reads, poster
ior_is_what_the_run_certifies (posterior membership is equivalent to an
error-free run) and bit_search_shortcut (BitSearchEntitlement.v).

With the three cups, two answers cost five marks and remove two index bits. This is


                                              287
The Thiele Machine                                                                 Devon Thiele


an example of the accounting theorem with a real candidate filter. It is not a speedup
theorem, and its prices are the chosen instruction schedule. The relation between the
answers and the candidates is proved for this program. The assertion instruction itself
still accepts a label without requiring that proof; Section 14’s small machine is where
the check-to-commitment rule is enforced by the step.

22.7 A small two-state witness
There is also a smaller witness to inhabiting the record. There’s a concrete run: a
twenty-three instruction program, given a budget of thirty-three steps and ending
with the counter at nineteen. It’s a factored search (find one cell in an N-by-N grid by
searching the two coordinates separately instead of walking every cell), followed by
three instructions, the last of which asserts an arrow. It has a prior list of two states
and a posterior of one, a two-leaf tree (which I’d read as one leaf per factor), and that
run is a closed term of the record type, which is Coq for a finished value with every
one of the fifteen slots filled and nothing left open. The bound reads off it: stronger
predicate, assertion event, counter up by at least one index bit. So the class isn’t empty.
One thing is written down and type-checks.

Now the honest picture of that member, because it isn’t a picture of a search narrow-
ing a candidate set. The prior is the start state and the end state of the same run,
the observation asks whether the counter equals nineteen, and the representative ob-
servation is the constant empty one, so the covering clause asks for nothing. The
member shows the record can be inhabited. It doesn’t show a real search shrinking
a real list of candidates. And there’s a boundary on the other side of it: the same
factored search with only its two emitting steps and no assertion at the end certifies
the observation (no error, the posterior’s test passes, the bound’s arithmetic holds) but
never raises the assertion channel, so the assertion-event conclusion doesn’t apply to
it. The three-instruction suffix is what closes that gap.

Here’s the member laid open, all of it, because it’s small enough to count. Fifteen
fields: seven data, eight proofs. The decoder is the identity on instruction lists. The
program p is the twenty-instruction factored search for N = 1 followed by three steps
that make a new group, give it its identity arrow (Section 18’s do-nothing arrow from
a module to itself, MORPH_ID), and assert that arrow with the label “factorized”; the
start s is the machine’s initial state; the fuel is 33; the end state, call it s19 , has counter
19. The other ingredients are these.

   1. The prior is the two-element list [s, s19 ].
   2. The posterior is the one-element list [s19 ].
   3. Strict narrowing: s19 is in both lists, and s is in the prior and not the posterior.
   4. The distinguishing observation returns p when the counter is 19 and the empty
      list otherwise. It returns p at s19 and the empty list at s, whose counter is 0.
   5. The tree is one branch with two leaves, depth 1.

                                              288
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


   6. The tree is realized: the run executes three cost-floor steps (the two that emit and
      the assertion), and 1 ≤ 3. This is a count, not a walk down the tree.
   7. The representative observation is written as “if the counter equals itself then the
      empty list,” which is always the empty list, and every fibre is the whole prior.
   8. The certified posterior: no error at the end, the membership predicate of [s19 ]
      accepts p, and the channel holds the checksum of “factorized,” which is not zero.
   9. The start is clear: the initial state’s channel is 0.

The equality test is decided by receipt_list_eqb_spec, the posterior is non-
empty by sighted_n1_supra_posterior_nonempty, and the fibres are sighte
d_n1_supra_representatives.


Remark 22.4 (What the member computes). Feeding these into the corollary gives a
strictly stronger posterior predicate, a structure addition, and ⌈log2 2⌉ −̇ ⌈log2 1⌉ =
1 ≤ 19 − 0. Every obligation about the run is discharged by running it inside the proof
checker (Coq’s vm_compute tactic), so the member is a computation, not an argument.


Checked as factored_n1_shortcut and factored_n1_shortcut_lands_in
_representation (StructuralAdvantageCertifiedShortcut.v); the version without
the suffix is in StructuralAdvantageObservedShortcut.v.

What it doesn’t do, said flatly. It doesn’t check that the factorisation is right. The
assertion step certifies that an arrow was asserted with a property label; nothing ties
that label to a factorisation checker. The same goes for the formula check of Section 19:
when it passes, it shows a formula can be made true and can also be made false, and
nothing makes the way of making it false one of the states in the prior list. Tying
a check to a list takes a premise of its own, and here that premise is the lists and
observation functions somebody supplies. It’s a receipt for what the run paid, not
a proof of what the run claimed. The speedup in that example (searching the two
coordinates separately, 2N steps, instead of the whole N-by-N grid, N squared steps)
is divide-and-conquer, which is as old as computing and which nobody is selling here.
And here’s what’s checked about it: the iteration counts are results about the runs, for
every N. The blind search over the N-by-N grid runs N squared iterations and ends
with the counter at 0; the factored one runs 2N and ends with the counter at 18. At N
= 1 the factored program is the slower one, two iterations against one. The point of the
example is only that the shortcut’s admissibility is on the record, with a cost, separate
from its dividend. And it is not a result about P versus NP, and anyone who reads it
as one is reading their own ambition into the bytes. One more boundary: there is no
unconditional bound on a single run’s narrowing. A single execution path doesn’t
carry enough information for that; the bound needs the tree, or a per-branch account
of what was ruled out, and the code refuses to claim more.



                                             289
The Thiele Machine                                                                 Devon Thiele


The numbers, so you can check them. The blind program, the one that walks every cell,
has every declared cost set to zero and ends with the counter at 0. The factored one
pays for two emitting steps with a one-character payload, each charged its payload’s
eight bits plus one, so 18; the three-instruction suffix adds one more for the assertion,
so 19. Put a price on the counter: say one mark is worth λ iterations, so a run costs its
iterations plus λ times its counter. The factored run is the cheaper one exactly when
2N + 18λ < N 2 , and once N is at least 18λ + 3 it always is. That’s the time tax in one
line: the blind search pays in time, the factored one pays a fixed eighteen marks for
knowing the grid splits, and past a size you can compute, knowing wins. The pure
arithmetic around it is lopsided too: for N ≥ 6, N 2 > 2N + 18, and for every k ≥ 1
there is an N ≥ 2 with N 2 ≥ k · 2N, so the ratio of the two iteration counts has no
ceiling.


Remark 22.5 (What the speedup theorems state). Write Bt for the ten-instruction blind
search with target t and Sl,r for the twenty-instruction factored search with targets l
and r, s0 for the initial state, run( F, p, s0 ) for the program-counter runner with fuel
F, and r15 (s) for register 15, which counts loop iterations. (1) If t + 1 < 264 and
F ≥ 5t + 8, then run( F, Bt , s0 ) has r15 = t + 1, counter 0 and program counter 10. (2)
If l + r + 2 < 264 and F ≥ 5(l + r ) + 16, then run( F, Sl,r , s0 ) has r15 = (l + 1) + (r + 1),
counter 18 and program counter 20. (3) For every N ≥ 1 with N 2 < 264 , every whole
number λ, and fuel Fb ≥ 5N 2 + 3 and Fs ≥ 10N + 6, let b = run( Fb , BN 2 −1 , s0 ) and
c = run( Fs , S N −1,N −1 , s0 ). Then r15 (b) = N 2 , µ(b) = 0, r15 (c) = 2N, µ(c) = 18, and

                r15 (c) + λµ(c) < r15 (b) + λµ(b) ⇐⇒ 2N + 18λ < N 2 .

(4) With the hypotheses of (3) and N ≥ 18λ + 3 in place of N ≥ 1, r15 (c) + λµ(c) <
r15 (b) + λµ(b).

Proof. (1) and (2) by a loop invariant: each pass through a loop body is five steps,
adds one to register 15 and one to the loop index, and charges nothing, because every
arithmetic, load and jump in both programs declares cost zero; the index reaches its
target because the subtraction on sixty-four-bit words is zero exactly when the two
words are equal, and both are below 264 . The exits are a few more steps each, and
in the factored program each exit runs one EMIT of a one-character payload at nine
marks. Past the end of the program the runner stops, so extra fuel changes nothing.
(3) is (1) at t = N 2 − 1 and (2) at l = r = N − 1, then arithmetic. (4) is (3), since
N ≥ 18λ + 3 gives N 2 ≥ 18λN + 3N > 2N + 18λ.

Checked as blind_program_run, sighted_program_run, time_tax_theore
m and time_tax_sighted_wins (StructuralAdvantage.v), all closed, with the loop
lemmas loop_iteration and loop_iterations and the word fact word64_su
b_zero_iff. iteration_savings_dwarfs_mu_cost and advantage_facto
r_unbounded (same file) are the two inequalities above, proved by arithmetic alone.

The case N = 1 is also computed directly: blind_halts_in_n_squared (fuel 8,
register 15 holds 1, counter 0) and sighted_halts_in_two_n (fuel 20, register 15

22.8 What landed
So here’s Section 8 and Section 9 on something that runs. Looking can be free: CHSH_
TRIAL moves no reading and can cost zero. Turning a reading on can’t: every one of
the fifty-one instructions was checked, and any step that does it pays at least one. A
game result behind the flag adds meaning and not a mark. The check and the commit
are two steps, LASSERT and MORPH_ASSERT, priced separately, and nothing in the
machine joins them or makes the second wait for the first. A certified end from a clear
start points at an assertion you can name, and a run that supplies a narrowing, a tree,
fibres and the cost-floor steps to cover the tree pays at least the index bits it commits
to; the record that packages all that is a checklist with one member, and the member
is honest about being small. A paid flag is still not a true claim, and the machine still
never reads either reading. Those are the parts of Section 8 and Section 9 this machine
witnesses. The rest of Parts II and III, the subsumption of an ordinary machine, the
windows and their collisions, the floor on all fifty-one, the finite fragment that pays
for its merges, gets the same treatment next, in Section 23.

23 The machine as witness
Parts II and III made claims about any machine and kept saying “when the machine
exists on the page, I’ll show you.” The machine exists, and by that I mean the big one,
the fifty-one-instruction test bench from Section 15 on, not the six-instruction small
machine, which keeps its own chapter and its own name. Some of the showing has
happened already: Section 16 put Section 6’s counter rule on one field, Section 17
put Section 3’s floor on fifty-one instructions, Section 20 showed Section 7’s window
losing the graph, and Section 22 just did Section 8 and Section 9 whole. This section is
the rest: for each remaining claim, the theorem about this machine, with its hypotheses
and its witness, so that the abstract parts can be checked against something that runs.
I’ve grouped them by the section they pay off, and where an earlier chapter of this
part already stated a fact, I point there instead of saying it again.

Fair question before any of it: why bother? Those claims were already proved for
any machine with the named parts, so what does one more machine add? Here’s the
worry it answers. A theorem about every machine with some property is also true
when no machine has the property. “Every unicorn in this room is pink” is true, and
it says nothing. A witness is the cheap insurance against that: one actual thing, every
hypothesis met, that the theorem is about. And then the next question, which is what
most of this chapter turns out to be about: once a theorem lands on a real machine,
does it say what the abstract version seemed to say, or something smaller? Sometimes
it’s the same. A fair number of times below it’s something smaller, and I’d rather you
watch each one shrink than find out later.


                                          291
The Thiele Machine                                                                 Devon Thiele


23.1 What this machine is, relative to an ordinary one (Section 2, Section 11)
An ordinary machine has arithmetic, memory, jumps, calls, ports and a halt. Of the
fifty-one instructions, twenty-nine pass the machine’s own test for that (is_class
ical_opcode), and I’d rather you see the test’s answer than my description of it.
It’s the same line Section 17 drew, and the twenty-two that fail are listed by name in
Section 17’s Definition 17.3, so I won’t make you read them twice. Everything else
passes: the arithmetic, the memory and heap moves, the jumps, calls and returns,
the ports, HALT and CHECKPOINT, and three that aren’t plain arithmetic but pass
anyway, because they leave the structure alone: MDLACC, which only charges the
ledger, and the two readers MORPH_GET and TENSOR_GET, which look at the
structure without changing it. Call a run classical when every instruction in it is one of
the twenty-nine.

Two theorems say the machine contains an ordinary one without disturbing the struc-
ture. Faithfulness: the shadow is, by definition, six fields (registers, memory, counter,
program counter, error, certified), and a classical run leaves the graph, the assertion
channel, and the flag where they were (classical_run_shadow_faithful; its
first half is true by unfolding the definition, its second half is the next theorem). Con-
servativity: a classical run preserves the graph, the channel, and the flag (classical_
opcodes_preserve_structure, from single-step lemmas per field). Neither says
anything about the other fields (the witness counters, the tensor, the logic accumulator,
the mode word), and I won’t claim more than that. Conservativity holds both ways
a program can run: as an in-order fold of the step function over a list, and under the
program-counter runner, which follows the jumps. So a classical program that loops
is inside what’s proved, and Section 20’s strictness theorem starts from the initial state
for the same reason.

Here are the test and the theorem exactly. The theorem is Section 17’s Theorem 17.3
under the name the files give it; it’s restated here because this is where its partner,
faithfulness, lives. For a state s write graph(s) for its graph, chan(s) for the assertion
channel (Section 17 wrote it certaddr(s)), flag(s) for the certified flag (Section 17’s
cert(s)), and µ(s) for the counter. The shorter names are only for this section.


Definition 23.1 (Classical opcode, classical run). is_classical_opcode returns
false on exactly the twenty-two non-classical instructions of Definition 17.3 and true
on the other twenty-nine. A list of instructions t is classical when every member passes.
For a state s0 , run(t, s0 ) applies the step function apply to s0 and the members of t in
list order, first to last; the program counter is not consulted. For fuel F, run pc ( F, t, s0 )
is the program-counter runner: F times, fetch the member of t at the program counter
and apply it, stopping early when the program counter is past the end of t; jumps
move the counter.


Theorem 23.1 (Conservativity). For every classical list t, every state s0 and every fuel F,


                                              292
The Thiele Machine                                                                  Devon Thiele


with s either run(t, s0 ) or run pc ( F, t, s0 ): graph(s) = graph(s0 ), chan(s) = chan(s0 ), and
flag(s) = flag(s0 ).

Proof. Induction on t. The empty list changes nothing. For a list i followed by t′ , three
single-step lemmas, each a case split over the instruction type, say that a classical
instruction leaves the graph, the channel and the flag as they were, and the induction
hypothesis covers t′ . For the program-counter runner, induction on F: each round
either stops or fetches a member of t, which is classical, so the same single-step lemmas
apply.

Checked as classical_opcodes_preserve_structure (ClassicalConservativ-
ity.v), from classical_trace_preserves_graph, classical_trace_preser
ves_cert_addr and classical_trace_preserves_certified, and classic
al_opcodes_preserve_structure_run_vm for the program-counter runner. cl
assical_run_shadow_faithful (TuringClassicalEmbedding.v) repeats the three
equalities and adds that the shadow of the final state is the record of its registers,
memory, program counter, counter, error bit and flag, which holds by unfolding the
definition.

A third, which goes by the name “Thiele simulates Turing” in the files and which I’ll
state for exactly what it is: there’s a file-local pairing of a Turing machine’s config-
uration with a counter, where the lifted machine’s step tracks the Turing machine’s
step and adds one to the counter (two if it wrote a non-blank), and a theorem that
running the lifted machine on n units of fuel projects to running the Turing machine
on n units (thiele_simulates_turing_gen, and thiele_simulates_turin
g for a start with counter zero). The file’s own scope note says not to cite it as the
VM simulating Turing machines. It’s a small lifted model, not the twelve-field state.
The honest sentence is: the pattern “an ordinary machine plus a counter that only
climbs” is instantiated once in miniature and proved to track the ordinary machine;
the twelve-field machine’s relation to ordinary computation is the faithfulness and
conservativity pair.

The degenerate-projection theorem (degenerate_projection_theorem) pack-
ages four parts, and this small simulation is the first. The other three are Section 20’s
quotient theorem, Theorem 20.3: two states have equal shadow exactly when they
agree on the six fields, a classical run from states that agree on the shadow, the graph
and the control and status words ends at equal shadows, and two distinct states can
have equal shadow.

23.2 The counter on this machine (Section 6)
Section 6 argued its facts about the counter for any machine whose state carries a
counter kept by a price list (Definition 6.1), and said the checked versions are about
this machine. Here they are. The one-step rule, counter after equals counter before
plus the instruction’s cost, is Section 16’s Theorem 16.1, checked by going through


                                              293
The Thiele Machine                                                                   Devon Thiele


all fifty-one instructions, the failure branches included; everything in this subsection
stands on it. Write cost(t) for the sum of the costs of a list t, sinit for the initial state
(counter 0), and call a state reachable when it is sinit or apply(s, i ) for a reachable s.

One thing about the checked name of the uniqueness half, because it misleads: mu_

should promise.


Theorem 23.2 (The counter on this machine). (1) For every state s and list t,
µ(run(t, s)) = µ(s) + cost(t). (2) For every state s and instruction i, µ(s) ≤ µ(apply(s, i )).
(3) Let B be any function from states to N with B(apply(s, i )) = B(s) + cost(i ) for all s and
i. If B(sinit ) = 0, then B(s) = µ(s) for every reachable s. Without the start condition, there is
a nondecreasing f with B(s) = f (µ(s)) for every reachable s.

Proof. (1) Induction on t, one application of the one-step rule per instruction. (2) The
one-step rule, with cost(i ) ≥ 0. (3) Induction on why s is reachable, exactly as in
Theorem 6.2; for the last part take f (n) = B(sinit ) + n.

Checked as mu_accumulates_trace_cost and mu_is_initial_monotone
(MuInitiality.v), vm_mu_monotonic_single_step (MuLedgerConservation.v) and
monotone_factors_through_mu (MuInitiality.v), all resting on vm_apply_mu.

Section 6 also pointed at a universal property nearby and said exactly how far the
borrowed word “initial” reaches. Here’s the trace fold, because the word is going to
get leaned on and you should see how little is under it. A target is any machine M that
takes this machine’s instructions: a set of states, a step step M , a cost per instruction,
and a reading that obeys the toll. Pick a state b of M to start from. Write t · i for the list
t with one more instruction i on the end, and Fb (t) for the state M ends in when you
walk the list t through it from b.


Theorem 23.3 (Folding a run is the only way). For every target M and starting state
b: Fb ([ ]) = b, and Fb (t · i ) = step M ( Fb (t), i ) for every list t and instruction i. And any
function g from instruction lists to states of M with g([ ]) = b and g(t · i ) = step M ( g(t), i )
for all t and i equals Fb on every list.

Proof. The first two facts are what walking a list means. For uniqueness, induct on
the list from its end. On the empty list both give b. If g(t) = Fb (t), then g(t · i ) =
step M ( g(t), i ) = step M ( Fb (t), i ) = Fb (t · i ). The proof never looks at the target’s
reading or its cost.




                                               294
The Thiele Machine                                                                 Devon Thiele


Checked as thiele_trace_fold_initial (ThieleInitiality.v), which the file also
exports under the older name thiele_is_initial_a2_substrate; the file’s
own comment says that name does not assert the machine’s states are initial. The
statement is over lists of this machine’s instructions, which is why it lives here and
not in Section 6.

Coming down from lists to states is where the borrowed word stops. Write ev(t) for
the state this machine is in after running t from its start, and call v a descended value at
a reachable state s when some list t has ev(t) = s and Fb (t) = v.


Theorem 23.4 (When the fold comes down to states). Fix a target M and a starting state
b.

(1) Every reachable state has exactly one descended value if and only if, for all lists t and u,
ev(t) = ev(u) implies Fb (t) = Fb (u).

(2) Suppose some function picks, for every reachable state, a list that reaches it. Then a
map h from the machine’s states to M’s states with h(ev([ ])) = b, h(apply(ev(t), i )) =
step M (h(ev(t)), i ), and the machine’s reading at ev(t) equal to M’s reading at h(ev(t)),
for all t and i, exists if and only if two things hold: the condition in (1), and the machine’s
reading at ev(t) equals M’s reading at Fb (t) for every list t. Any two such maps agree on
every reachable state.

(3) A picking function as in (2) exists, so the equivalence in (2) holds with no premise about
picking.

Proof. (1) If equal machine states give equal target states, then Fb (t) is a descended
value at ev(t), and any other one, Fb (u) with ev(u) = ev(t), equals it. Conversely,
if ev(t) = ev(u), then Fb (t) and Fb (u) are both descended values at that state, so
they’re the same one. (2) Any such map sends ev(t) to Fb (t), by induction on t from
its end, exactly as in Theorem 23.3; so it gives both conditions, and any two such maps
agree on reachable states. For the other direction, send each state s to Fb of the list
picked for s. The first condition makes that equal to Fb (t) for every t reaching s, which
gives the start and the step; the second gives the reading. (3) Number every list of
instructions so that every list gets a number. For a state s, pick the list with the first
number whose run reaches s, or the empty list if none does. Equality of machine states
is decidable, so each number can be checked; asking whether some number works at
all is an unbounded search, settled by the choice principle that comes with Coq’s real
numbers. If s is ev(t), the number of t works, so the search finds a list reaching s.

Checked as trace_descent_unique_value_iff, reachable_simulation_
exists_iff, reachable_simulation_requires_compatibility, and re
achable_simulation_unique (TraceStateDescent.v); the uniqueness for maps
someone supplies is also thiele_morphism_unique_on_reachable (ThieleIni-


                                              295
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


tiality.v). For (3): reachable_trace_representative, reachable_trace_rep
resentative_correct and reachable_representative_exists (Reachable-
TraceRepresentative.v), and generalized_reachable_simulation_holds, the
equivalence of (2) for every reading, target and starting state with the picking premise
gone. Its one assumption is the principle the proof’s search leans on, sig_forall_d
ec, already in the standard-library set the rest of the tree uses. It’s the choice the proof
above makes when it picks, and the library’s own comment gives it its exact name,
the limited principle of omniscience: for any yes-or-no test on whole numbers that a
program can decide, it hands you either a number that fails the test or the news that
every number passes, which no program could find out by searching. What it is not:
a program that rebuilds a list from a state. The picking is a search that exists, not one
anybody would run.

Three targets show where the edges are. One target has a single state and a reading
that never says yes. It obeys the toll, because nothing ever crosses, and it gets no
reading-preserving map from the machine’s states at all, because the machine has
a state that reads yes (no_vm_state_morphism_to_never_certifies, Claim-
BoundaryRegression.v). Another keeps only one bit, whether the certified flag is up,
raises it on CERTIFY, and leaves it alone on everything else; that one comes down fine,
and it reaches both no and yes (certification_quotient_satisfies_desce
nt, TraceStateDescent.v). The third is the interesting failure. It keeps the whole list
of instructions it was handed, charges the machine’s own prices, and reads the flag
with the machine’s own evaluator, so its reading agrees exactly. It still doesn’t come
down, because the empty list and a single zero-cost JUMP back to where the machine
already is leave the machine in the same state and leave two different histories behind
(certification_agreement_does_not_imply_descent, TraceStateDescent.v;
it comes back as part (2) of Theorem 23.15 below). The toll plus a reading that agrees
doesn’t force a target to forget its history. So the fold is unique on lists, and that’s
what the word “initial” earns here. It doesn’t make this machine’s states initial among
everything that obeys the toll, and I won’t say it does.

Last, Section 6’s short answer about windows, on this machine. Its full window shows
the memory, the registers, the program counter, the counter and the certified flag.
A window is counter-complete when some rule applied to what it shows returns the
counter on every state, and flag-complete likewise; it forgets the counter when changing
the counter and nothing else never changes what it shows, and likewise for the flag.


Theorem 23.5 (Neither the counter nor the flag can be dropped). The full window is
both counter-complete and flag-complete. Every window on this machine’s states that forgets
the counter, whatever else it shows, is not counter-complete. Every window that forgets the
flag is not flag-complete.

Proof. The full window shows both, so the rule just reads them off. For a window that


                                            296
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


forgets the counter, take one state and set its counter to 1 and, separately, to 2. The
window shows the same thing for both, so any rule gives the same answer for both,
and one of the two answers is wrong. The flag is the same argument with yes and
no.

Checked as P_full_complete_neither_mu_nor_cert_droppable, with for
gets_mu_not_mu_complete and forgets_cert_not_cert_complete (Neces-

nothing for it to be smallest in.

23.3 What no window recovers (Section 7)
Two windows, named. forget keeps the program counter, the counter, the registers,
and the memory. bare_observable keeps the program counter, the registers, and
the memory, and drops the counter. Each is a function from the twelve-field state to a
smaller record.

This is where Section 7’s fibre fact (Theorem 7.1: a decoder has to give the same
answer on states the window can’t tell apart) lands on the machine’s own windows.
Section 20 already stated the three witness pairs, as Theorem 20.6; here they are again
under Section 7’s name, with the two windows named. Each is listed as closed, with
no axiom of any kind behind it, in the last assumption audit (the report the Linux
build writes of every axiom each theorem leans on; Section 28 says what it covers),
and together they are packaged as thiele_content_irrecoverable_from_bar
e_projection. And one fact Section 20 didn’t state: every four-field snapshot has
two distinct preimages, one certified and one not (fiber_has_two_preimages), so
the many-to-one isn’t a special pair; it’s everywhere.


Definition 23.2 (Two windows; a function of a window). For a state s, forget(s) =
(pc(s), µ(s), regs(s), mem(s)) and bare(s) = (pc(s), regs(s), mem(s)). A field f of the
state is a function of a window w when some φ has φ(w(s)) = f (s) for every state s.


Theorem 23.6 (Three fields no window recovers). (1) flag is not a function of forget. (2)
µ is not a function of bare. (3) chan is not a function of forget.

Proof. Each part is one pair of states written out as records. For (2) the two states
agree on every field except the counter, which is 0 in one and 1 in the other (both have
program counter 10, registers (42, 0, 0, 0) and four zero memory words). Their bare
images are equal, so a φ would have to return both 0 and 1 on the same input. Parts (1)
and (3) are the same argument with a pair whose forget images are equal and whose
flags, or channels, differ. Nothing in these three proofs runs the machine; the pairs are
records.


                                          297
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


Checked as cert_not_function_of_forget, mu_not_function_of_bare_
observable and cert_addr_not_function_of_forget (ProjectionNonExis-
tence.v, 190, 209), packaged as thiele_content_irrecoverable_from_bare_p
rojection.

A fourth, from the diagonal section (Section 11’s second wall): no decoder on the four-
field window agrees, on every state, with “the assertion channel is nonzero” (structu
ral_shortcut_not_function_of_classical). The two states that break every
decoder aren’t hand-built records this time; they’re reached from the initial state by
running programs. Both start with the same two instructions. Then one runs MORPH_
ASSERT, which overwrites the channel with the checksum of its property string, and
the other runs an MDLACC whose charge of one matches MORPH_ASSERT’s, so the
four fields agree and the channel doesn’t. Because the witnesses are reachable, the
impossibility isn’t about records nobody could ever produce.

Three small theorems sit beside that one, and they’re worth a sentence each because
they close off the reading a skeptic reaches for. Hand the decoder an oracle of any
kind, a halting oracle included, and it’s still a function of the four-field window, so the
same two states break it (structural_axis_survives_any_classical_oracl
e): information that isn’t in the input can’t be supplied by an oracle. The two axes are
independent in that same sense, each not a function of the other’s window (axes_mu
tually_independent). And the predicate itself is decidable from the full state (st
ructural_membership_decidable), so this is not a gap in computability degree.
It’s a gap in what the window holds. The file says as much itself, and I’d rather you
didn’t read the independence of the two axes as a Turing-degree result.

One thing I have to say about how these are proved, because Section 7 stated the
general fact (decoding_requires_fiber_constancy), and it’s natural to say the
pricing results “are” that fact with a price in place of a decoder. As mathematics, fair.
As a proof dependency, no: outside its own file the general fact is used once, in the
attestation fragment from Section 12, not in any of these. These are proved directly
from their witness pairs. The abstract theorem and the concrete ones agree; neither
cites the other.

23.4 The floor, on fifty-one instructions (Section 3, Section 9)
Section 3’s universal floor (Theorem 3.1) says: any system with the toll, any run from
uncertified to certified, paid at least one. Section 17 put the one-step form on this
machine (Theorem 17.8). Here’s the whole ladder of its instances, from the narrowest
to the one I’d cite if I could cite only one.

Two readings of “certified” run through all of this, the flag and the channel, and who
writes each is Section 17’s Theorems 17.6 and 17.7. One thing about the channel’s
floor to keep in mind: its proof doesn’t use the fact that only MORPH_ASSERT writes
the channel; it uses a wider class of five instructions that may touch the channel, and
shows every one of them pays.

                                           298
The Thiele Machine                                                                 Devon Thiele


One step, the assertion channel: a step that takes the channel from zero to nonzero
costs at least one (no_free_certification; proof: only the five instructions in
that class can change it, and each has the floor). One step, the flag: same (no_fre
e_certification_certified; only CERTIFY sets it). One step, either reading:
the counter rises by at least one (certification_requires_positive_mu, ce
rtified_insight_nonfree). Over a run, the channel: the counter ends at least
one above where it started (no_free_certification_trace_mu), and the run
contains a floor-cost instruction (no_free_certified_insight). Over a run, the
flag: the counter ends at least one above where it started (a lemma, no_free_certif
ication_certified_trace_mu; it doesn’t also hand you the instruction). And the
machine packaged as a certification system twice, once per reading, so that Section 3’s
theorem applies to it directly (thiele_universal_nfi_cert_addr, thiele_un
iversal_nfi_certified).

Which is strongest? universal_nfi_any_substrate, the abstract one, and the
two packagings are its instances. The per-step and counter forms are sharper (they
name the instruction, or the counter rather than the summed cost) but narrower. No
single theorem says “either reading, over a run” for this machine; what exists is the
one-step either-reading theorem plus the two run theorems separately. Together they
say it. There’s no one name for it.

Here is the ladder as one statement, with cost the machine’s schedule (an instruction’s
declared cost, plus one for CERTIFY, MORPH_ASSERT, LJOIN and the game checks,
plus more for LASSERT, EMIT, REVEAL and READ_PORT; Definition 17.4) and run
the in-order runner of Definition 23.1. Parts (1) to (3) and the channel half of (4) are
Section 17’s Theorem 17.8 again; the new piece is the flag half of (4).


Theorem 23.7 (The floor on this machine). Let s be a state, i an instruction and t a list of
instructions. (1) If chan(s) = 0 and chan(apply(s, i )) ̸= 0, then cost(i ) ≥ 1. (2) If flag(s)
is false and flag(apply(s, i )) is true, then cost(i ) ≥ 1. (3) In either case µ(apply(s, i )) ≥
µ(s) + 1. (4) If chan(s) = 0 and chan(run(t, s)) ̸= 0, then µ(run(t, s)) ≥ µ(s) + 1; the
same holds when flag(s) is false and flag(run(t, s)) is true.

Proof. (2) The step leaves the flag alone unless i is CERTIFY, and CERTIFY with de-
clared cost d costs d + 1. (1) An instruction outside the class REVEAL, EMIT, LJOIN,
LASSERT, MORPH_ASSERT leaves the channel unchanged, by a case split over the
instruction type, and every member of the class costs at least one. (3) is (1) or (2)
together with conservation, µ(apply(s, i )) = µ(s) + cost(i ). (4) For the channel: if no
member of t were in the class, the channel would stay 0, so some member is, and the
total charge of t is at least that member’s charge; conservation over the run turns the
total into the rise of µ. For the flag: induction on t, splitting on whether the flag is
already up after the first step.

The Thiele Machine                                                                 Devon Thiele


Checked as no_free_certification (AbstractNoFI.v), no_free_certificati
on_certified, certification_requires_positive_mu, no_free_certif
ication_trace_mu and the lemma no_free_certification_certified_tr
ace_mu (WitnessInsightGeneral.v).

23.5 The finite fragment that pays for its merges (Section 4)
Section 4’s room argument (Theorem 4.2: finiteness, permanence and merge pricing
force the toll) needs a finite state space, and Section 16 told you the counter has no
ceiling, so the twelve-field state space is infinite. Here’s how that’s faced rather than
hidden.

Build a finite machine: four slots times a flag, eight states. Three moves: stamp (set
the flag, go to the next slot, cost one), jump to slot a (cost two), next slot (cost zero).
On it, every one of Section 4’s premises is a theorem, not a hypothesis: finite (fin_f
inite), permanent (fin_permanent), the next-slot move forgets nothing (fnext_
injective), the stamp and the jump merge (fcertify_merges, fjump_merges),
merges are priced (fin_merging_priced), and per halving (fin_compression_
priced). So Section 4’s two conclusions hold on it outright (fin_a2_from_mergin
g_price, fin_a2_from_compression_price). The counting lemma underneath,
that a duplicate-free list with at most K preimages per image has at most K times as
many members as images, is proved generically (fiber_bound_compression).

Then the bridge. Take a window on the twelve-field machine: the program counter
modulo four as a slot, and the certified flag. Map the three moves to CERTIFY with
declared cost zero (the floor makes the charge one, which is what the finite machine
charges the stamp), JUMP with declared cost two, and a CHECKPOINT with declared
cost zero. Then for every state and every move, the window of the stepped state is the
finite machine’s step of the window (vm_runs_finite_machine), the counter rises
by exactly the finite machine’s cost (vm_pays_finite_price), both over runs (vm_
runs_finite_trace), and a run of that fragment from unflagged to flagged raises
the counter by at least one (vm_fragment_certification_paid). So Section 4’s
argument applies to this machine through a window onto a finite fragment. That’s the
honest form. One limit goes with it: the jump’s charge of two is a choice the program
makes when it writes the instruction. The machine’s schedule allows it and doesn’t
force it.


Theorem 23.8 (The machine runs the finite fragment). Let win(s) = (pc(s) mod
4, flag(s)), and send the finite moves stamp, jump to a, and next to CERTIFY with declared
cost 0, JUMP to a with declared cost 2, and CHECKPOINT with the empty label and declared
cost 0. Write run(t, s) for the machine run of the images of a list t of finite moves, and frun,
fcost for the finite machine’s run and total cost (stamp 1, jump 2, next 0). For every t and
every state s,

          win(run(t, s)) = frun(t, win(s)),         µ(run(t, s)) = µ(s) + fcost(t).

                                              300
The Thiele Machine                                                               Devon Thiele


If moreover flag(s) is false and flag(run(t, s)) is true, then µ(run(t, s)) ≥ µ(s) + 1.

Proof. One step at a time, by computation: CERTIFY 0 moves the program counter
on by one and sets the flag, JUMP sets the program counter to a and keeps the flag,
CHECKPOINT moves on by one and keeps the flag, which are the three finite moves
read through the window; conservation gives the rises 1, 2 and 0. Runs follow by
induction on t. For the last part, the window run goes from an unflagged to a flagged
finite state, and on the finite machine every move that raises the flag costs at least one,
which is Section 4’s toll proved there from finiteness, permanence and merge pricing
(all three theorems on eight states).

Checked as vm_runs_finite_machine, vm_pays_finite_price, vm_runs_f

265, 286, 302); the finite toll is fin_a2_from_merging_price.

And on the full machine, Section 4’s merge-or-revoke (Theorem 4.3), directly: any step
that turns the flag on is non-injective and costs at least one (vm_certifying_step_
is_priced_merge), and JUMP 0 0 is non-injective and costs zero (vm_jump_is_fr

free; it does not satisfy “every merge is priced” (vm_prices_certifying_merge_l

and it’s the one to carry: the machine’s schedule puts the floor on the flag, not on
forgetting in general, and Section 4’s physics premise, if you grant it, would charge
the jump too. The machine is honest about certification and silent about everything
else it forgets.

In the words of Section 4 (Definition 4.1 and Premise 4.2), on the full machine with
step apply and schedule cost:


Theorem 23.9 (The certifying merge is priced; a free merge exists). (1) For every declared
cost d, CERTIFY d merges. (2) For every state s and instruction i, if flag(s) is false and
flag(apply(s, i )) is true, then i merges and cost(i ) ≥ 1. (3) JUMP to 0 with declared cost 0
merges and cost of it is 0. (4) Hence the full machine does not satisfy merge pricing.

Proof. (1) Take the initial state with the flag down and the same state with the flag
up. CERTIFY sends both to the same state: its result does not read the old flag (Coq
closes this by computation). The two starts differ, so CERTIFY is not injective. (2) Only
CERTIFY turns the flag on, so i is CERTIFY d for some d; it merges by (1) and costs
d + 1. (3) The initial state with program counter 0 and with program counter 1 both
land at program counter 0, with nothing charged. (4) Merge pricing applied to the
jump of (3) would demand a cost of at least one.

Checked as vm_certify_merges (FiniteCertMachine.v), vm_certifying_step_
is_priced_merge, vm_jump_is_free_merge and vm_prices_certifying_

23.6 Learning for free (Section 5)
Section 5’s demon (Theorem 5.2: an observer can learn for free) on this machine: load
a hidden value x into register one, with the observer watching register two. For x zero
and x one the observer sees the same thing (register two is zero either way). Now run
XOR_ADD of register one into register two at declared cost zero: the observer sees x.
The instruction’s cost is zero, the counter is unchanged, both runs started at zero (vm
_observer_narrowing_at_zero_cost, proved by computing). One bit learned,
nothing paid. Unconditional, in the sense that no physics premise is involved. I’ll also
say what the theorem doesn’t say: the file’s small abstract demon never merges two
states, but I haven’t stated that for this machine’s step.

23.7 Exact-price collisions (Section 7)
Section 7’s clerk (Theorem 7.2: no exact window price across a collision), on this
machine. From the clean state (empty registers and memory, counter zero, uncertified),
CERTIFY with declared cost zero and JUMP to one with declared cost zero show the
same bare_observable before and the same after, and the first raises the flag (v
m_bare_observable_collision). The counters differ afterwards, one against
zero, because CERTIFY pays the floor, and bare_observable doesn’t look at the
counter. For forget, which keeps the counter, give the JUMP a declared cost of one
so the charges match: same before, same after, one flips (vm_forget_collision).
Notice that this pair leans on the program choosing a declared cost: the JUMP is billed
one because somebody wrote one. Take that freedom away, fix every declared cost
at zero, and as far as I can read the step rules the forget window still collides. LJOIN
at declared cost zero charges the floor, moves only the program counter, and raises
nothing, so through that window it looks exactly like CERTIFY. That’s my reading of
LJOIN’s rule, not a stated theorem. The bare pair needs no chosen cost at all. So no
price computed from either window both meets the floor and never overcharges (vm_
bare_shadow_cannot_price_exactly, vm_forget_shadow_cannot_price
_exactly). The exact price of certification on this machine lives in the step, or in a
window that shows the flag. And the characterisation: the floor and no-overcharge
hold together exactly when the charged predicate is the flip predicate at unit price (ex
act_commitment_pricing_characterization).

You can run that collision at the table with two scraps of paper. On each, write the
same before-picture: program counter 0, empty registers, empty memory. Under it, on
the first scrap write CERTIFY with declared cost 0, and on the second JUMP to 1 with
declared cost 0. Below that, write the after-picture each one leaves in the bare window:
program counter 1, nothing else changed, the same on both. Fold the instruction line
under, hand both scraps to someone, and ask them to set a price from what they can
see. Whatever they charge the first scrap, they have to charge the second, because



                                          302
The Thiele Machine                                                                        Devon Thiele


they’re looking at the same two pictures. Charge one and the jump is overcharged.
Charge zero and the certification goes through free. The only way out is to unfold the
line, or to put the flag in the picture, and that’s the window that shows the flag.

The words, and then the result. Write flips(s, i ) for “flag(s) is false and flag(apply(s, i ))
is true”.


Definition 23.3 (Shadow price, floor, no overcharge, collision). Fix a window w. A
shadow price is a cost of the form c(s, i ) = p(w(s), w(apply(s, i ))) for some function p of
the observed pair. A cost c meets the floor when flips(s, i ) implies c(s, i ) ≥ 1, and never
overcharges when c(s, i ) = 0 whenever flips(s, i ) fails. A collision for w is two steps
(s1 , i1 ) and (s2 , i2 ) with w(s1 ) = w(s2 ), w(apply(s1 , i1 )) = w(apply(s2 , i2 )), flips(s1 , i1 ),
and not flips(s2 , i2 ).


Theorem 23.10 (Neither window prices certification exactly). (1) bare has a collision:
from the clean state, CERTIFY with declared cost 0 against JUMP to 1 with declared cost 0.
(2) forget has a collision: from the clean state, CERTIFY with declared cost 0 against JUMP
to 1 with declared cost 1. (3) For any window with a collision and any p, the shadow price
from p does not both meet the floor and never overcharge. So no shadow price from bare, and
none from forget, is exact.

Proof. (1) and (2) are computed. The clean state has program counter 0, empty registers
and memory, counter 0, and the flag down. Both steps end at program counter 1 with
registers and memory untouched; CERTIFY raises the flag and charges 0 + 1, the jump
raises nothing. In (2) the jump charges 1, so the counters agree as well. (3) Meeting the
floor charges the certifying step at least one. The other step shows the same observed
pair, so the shadow price charges it the same amount, and not overcharging demands
zero for it.

Checked as vm_bare_observable_collision, vm_forget_collision (Shad-
owPricing.v, 154), the general shadow_cannot_price_exactly, and its two in-
stances vm_bare_shadow_cannot_price_exactly and vm_forget_shadow_c
annot_price_exactly. The other direction is Theorem 7.2: a window that shows
the flag has a shadow price that is exact (window_showing_reading_prices_ex
actly) and no collision (window_showing_reading_has_no_collision).

23.8 The verifier and its three escapes (Section 7)
Section 7 told the verifier argument with a toy: two runs that leave the same transcript,
one that paid and one that didn’t, and a verifier that has to give them one verdict.
Here is the pair on this machine, and the two theorems with it. Start the machine at its
clean state (empty registers and memory, counter zero, uncertified). State A is where it
lands after one CERTIFY with declared cost zero, which charges one; its counter reads
1. State B is where it lands after one PNEW with an empty region (a new module with


                                                  303
The Thiele Machine                                                                   Devon Thiele


no memory cells in it), declared at cost zero; its counter reads 0. The bare window
of Definition 23.2 shows the same thing on both runs: the same start, then the same
memory, the same registers, the same program counter. The bare transcript τ is that
pair of photographs. A verifier V takes a transcript and says accept or reject. It is sound
when every transcript it accepts comes only from states where the claim holds, and
complete when every transcript from a state where the claim holds is accepted. The
claim is “the counter is 1,” and τ is explained by exactly two states, A and B.


Theorem 23.11 (No sound and complete verifier on the bare window). For the claim
“the counter is 1,” with τ explained by A and by B and by nothing else, no verifier on bare
 transcripts is both sound and complete.

Proof. Suppose V were both. The counter at A is 1 and A explains τ, so completeness
says V accepts τ. Now soundness, on that same accepted τ: every state that explains
it satisfies the claim, and B explains it. So the counter at B is 1. It is 0.

Checked as bare_setting_no_sound_complete_verifier (VerifierImpossi-
bility.v), with the two states po1_state_A and po1_state_B from NecessityOf-
MuLedger.v; no axioms.

Now dress the transcript up. Let T be any richer kind of transcript, with a way
π to squash one down to its bare photographs, and a relation saying which states
explain which transcripts. A verifier V on T factors through π when it only looks at the
squashed part: V = V ′ ◦ π for some rule V ′ on bare transcripts (the small circle means
“squash first with π, then apply V ′ ”), or equivalently, two transcripts with the same π
always get the same answer.


Theorem 23.12 (A richer verifier that only looks at the bare part does no better). Sup-
pose there are two transcripts t A , t B in T with π (t A ) = π (t B ), t A explained by A, and t B
explained by B. Then no verifier on T that is sound and complete for “the counter is 1” factors
through π.

Proof. If V = V ′ ◦ π, then V (t A ) = V ′ (π (t A )) = V ′ (π (t B )) = V (t B ). Completeness at
t A , which A explains with counter 1, gives V (t A ) = accept. So V (t B ) = accept, and
soundness at t B , which B explains, says the counter at B is 1. It is 0.

Checked as V_does_not_factor_through_classical (VerifierExhaustive-
ness.v), with every premise an explicit hypothesis and the two states fixed to A and B.
The pair t A , t B is a premise, and it’s the whole condition: the collision has to survive
into the richer transcript type. A transcript type with no such pair doesn’t meet the
premise, and the theorem says nothing about it. So it doesn’t classify every transcript
design.



                                               304
The Thiele Machine                                                                 Devon Thiele


Here are the three constructions, with the relations written down. The relation matters:
it says which state a transcript is allowed to describe. If it quietly assumes a truthful
answer, the verifier has not earned the right to trust a liar.


Definition 23.4 (Three richer transcripts and their explanations). Keep the states A, B
and their shared bare transcript τ from above, with µ( A) = 1 and µ( B) = 0. Write
E0 (s, t) for t = τ ∧ (s = A ∨ s = B). The claim remains µ(s) = 1.

A full-state transcript is a finite list t of machine states. Define ES (s, t) to mean that t is
nonempty and its last entry is s. The verifier rejects the empty list; otherwise it accepts
exactly when the last entry’s counter is 1.

A commitment transcript is a pair (t, b) of a bare transcript and a Boolean. For any
chosen explanation relation EC , the commitment contract is the pair of implications, for
all s, t, b:
                       EC (s, (t, b)) ∧ b = true =⇒ µ(s) = 1,

                          EC (s, (t, b)) ∧ µ(s) = 1 =⇒ b = true.

These are binding and honesty, respectively. The verifier accepts exactly when b is
true. One relation meeting the contract is EH (s, (t, b)) ⇐⇒ E0 (s, t) ∧ (b = true ⇐⇒
µ ( s ) = 1).

A response transcript is a pair (t, r ) of a bare transcript and a natural number. Define
E I (s, (t, r )) ⇐⇒ µ(s) = r. The verifier accepts exactly when r = 1. This relation
imposes no condition on the bare component t; the response alone carries its entire
truth condition.

Each construction assigns verification the constant abstract cost 1.


Theorem 23.13 (Three conditional escapes). The full-state verifier is sound and complete
relative to ES . For every EC satisfying the commitment contract, the commitment verifier is
sound and complete relative to EC . The response verifier is sound and complete relative to
E I . Each has cost 1 under the stipulated cost assignment. The honest relation EH satisfies the
commitment contract; the unchecked relation EU (s, (t, b)) ⇐⇒ E0 (s, t) does not.

Proof. For the full-state verifier, an explaining state is precisely the last entry. Reading
that entry’s counter therefore accepts exactly when the explaining state’s counter is 1.
An empty transcript is rejected and has no explaining state.

For the commitment verifier, acceptance says b is true. Binding then gives the claim
for every explaining state, which is soundness. Conversely, honesty says that any
explaining state satisfying the claim has a true bit, which the verifier accepts. The
equivalence in EH gives both implications directly. Under EU , however, B explains
(τ, true) even though µ( B) = 0. That violates binding.


                                              305
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


For the response verifier, explanation gives µ(s) = r. Acceptance adds r = 1, so
µ(s) = 1. Conversely, µ(s) = 1 and explanation give r = 1, hence acceptance. The
three cost claims follow from the assigned constant.

Checked as substrate_escape_succeeds (VerifierEscape_Substrate.v), commit
ment_contract_verifier, honest_commitments_satisfy_contract, unc
hecked_bit_violates_contract (VerifierEscape_Hardness.v), and interacti
ve_escape_succeeds (VerifierEscape_Interaction.v).

The collision is gone, and no trick did it: the extra information pulls A and B apart.
The full-state transcript shows the counter outright. The honest commitment for A
carries a true bit and the one for B a false bit. The honest responses are 1 and 0. In
none of the three is the verifier asked to tell identical inputs apart, which was the
impossible job.

Now the limit, and I’d rather say it before you find it. A list of states has no authen-
tication built into it, so nothing in it stops a liar from handing over whatever the
verifier wants to see. The commitment contract is assumed, and the unchecked bit
above is what happens when the assumption is dropped. The response relation only
allows a truthful counter value, so asking a question here does not buy resistance to a
cheating prover. And the cost 1 is an abstract price I wrote down, not a measurement
of what it takes to authenticate a state, check a cryptographic proof or send a response.
What these three show is which extra distinctions a verifier can use. They are not an
adversary model, a security parameter or a hardness reduction.

So what would it take to make that commitment bit binding for real, against somebody
who wants to cheat? Cryptographers had to face that one in the open, and the place
I’d point is a short paper Manuel Blum presented at the CRYPTO meeting in 1981,
“Coin Flipping by Telephone.” His setup: Alice and Bob have just divorced, they live
in different cities, and they want to flip a coin over the phone for who gets the car,
with nobody they both trust to do the flipping. If Alice flips and announces, Bob has
to take her word. If Bob calls it first, Alice can lie about how it landed. Blum’s way out
is for one side to commit first: send something that fixes the choice without showing
it, and open it only after the other side has called. And what keeps that commitment
binding isn’t anybody’s promise. It’s a bet that a certain kind of big number is hard
to factor. Push on that and you’re standing on the honest edge of this subsection. In
Blum’s protocol, binding is earned, on the condition that factoring is hard. Here it’s
written into the contract and assumed outright, and the unchecked bit above shows
what’s left without it. That’s why I won’t say these escapes beat a cheater. Blum’s
paper is the kind of thing it would take, and nothing like it is in this chapter.

23.9 Records on this machine (Section 10)
Section 10 showed, over any base, that an honest record is a latch, and argued that
two things stay free: the price list and the event. Every checked statement of those


                                           306
The Thiele Machine                                                              Devon Thiele


two freedoms is about this machine, so here they are. First the latch itself: Section 10’s
Theorem 10.1 holds with this machine’s unbounded step as the base, for each program,
halting when the program counter is past the end (record_axis_is_latch_on_
vm_holds, CrossBaseGranularity.v). So this machine with an honest record is this
machine plus a cup, the same as the three outside bases.

Then the strong reading of uniqueness: is every honest extension of this machine the
same machine as this one? In the form the words suggest it’s false, and the counterex-
ample is Section 10’s surcharged cup, made real. Take this machine and add a step
counter to the ledger, so every step costs one more than it did. It’s honest: the toll is a
floor, and a surcharge only raises the price. It extends the base. And it is not the same
machine, because this machine with an empty program sits still and pays nothing
per step, and the billed one pays at least one per step for sitting still (adequate_
core_uniqueness_refuted, honest_vm_extension_uniqueness_refuted;
the counterexample is BilledCore). A machine that charges for CPU time is honest
and isn’t this one. One thing about how those two theorems are stated, so the five
rules don’t quietly change on you: neither is written with the five rules of Section 10
(Definition 10.2). The first uses a looser test of “honest” (a ledger that never falls,
the toll, a run that reaches the record being on, and a clause about halting: for every
two-counter machine, some start state has to halt exactly when that machine does).
That’s Minsky’s two-counter machine, the one Section 14’s small machine is built on,
with its halting problem borrowed there from the Coq undecidability library; here it
only has to be matched, and Section 24 runs one as an interpreter on this machine. The
second is written for machines that run this machine underneath, with a map onto its
states standing in for the “driven by the computation” rule. Slightly different lists, the
same spirit.

Here are both lists, and the sameness they’re tested against. One word in the first
definition needs saying: the machine has two step functions, and the unbounded one
keeps every number in its registers and memory exactly, instead of cutting it to a fixed
width the way a chip has to. The files use that one here. And “halts” gets a convention:
the program counter has run off the end of the program with register nine reading one,
which is the “guest halted” status the two-counter interpreter of Section 24 writes there,
so this machine’s halting lines up with the two-counter problems in the adequacy
clause. One letter, too: in this section M and N are record-carrying machines in
Section 10’s sense, not the trace fold’s target from earlier in the chapter.


Definition 23.5 (This machine as a record-carrying machine). The Thiele core has states
( p, s), a program and a machine state. Its step runs one instruction of p from s on
the unbounded machine, and leaves ( p, s) alone when the program counter points
past the end of p. Every state is a starting state. Its record is the certified flag cert(s),
its ledger is µ(s), and it halts when the program counter equals the length of p and
register 9 holds 1.


                                            307
The Thiele Machine                                                                           Devon Thiele


Definition 23.6 (Adequate; same core). A record-carrying machine M is adequate when
(R2) and (R3) hold, some run from a starting state reaches a state with the record on,
and for every two-counter machine problem P some starting state m P has: P halts
exactly when some nextkM (m P ) halts. That last clause is an existential match, one
problem at a time, not a simulation in either direction. M and N have the same core
when some relation R between their states relates every starting state of each to some
starting state of the other, and any related m, n have the same record, the same next-
step cost, and related next states. R need not be a function, so state one machine keeps
and the other doesn’t can be ignored.


Definition 23.7 (Honest extension of this machine; observed sameness). M is an honest
extension of this machine when there is a cover of the Thiele core by M (Definition 10.1,
with the Thiele core as the base) and (R2) to (R5) hold. M and N are observed the same
when some R relates starting states both ways as above, and any related m, n have the
same record, the same ledger value, the same halting, the same next-step cost, and
related next states.


Theorem 23.14 (Exact uniqueness is false). Let the billed core have states ( p, s, k ), step
( p, s, k) 7→ ( p, s′ , k + 1) where ( p, s′ ) is the Thiele core’s step from ( p, s), every state starting,
record cert(s), ledger µ(s) + k, and the Thiele core’s halting. It is adequate and it is an honest
extension of this machine, and it has neither the same core as the Thiele core nor is it observed
the same.

Proof. Every step of the billed core costs at least one. The Thiele core’s starting state
([ ], s0 ), empty program and initial machine state, never moves and costs 0 per step.
Any relation of either kind must relate it to some billed state, and the two must have
the same next-step cost: 0 against at least 1. Adequacy and honesty are checked clause
by clause, the halting clause by the two-counter interpreter that already runs on the
Thiele core.

Checked as billed_core_adequate, billed_core_honest_extension, bil
led_core_not_equiv, billed_core_not_observed_equiv, adequate_cor
e_uniqueness_refuted and honest_vm_extension_uniqueness_refuted
(StructuralUniqueness.v), with the definitions Adequate, core_equiv (Structural-

uiv (StructuralCoreCover.v), and the Thiele core’s own adequacy thiele_core_ad

Keeping more history doesn’t make a machine different under this sameness, and it’s
worth seeing why the relation has to be allowed to forget.


Theorem 23.15 (History is forgotten by the relation, and only by it). (1) The machine
that runs the Thiele core and keeps a list of every state it has passed through has the same core

                                                   308
The Thiele Machine                                                                    Devon Thiele


as the Thiele core. (2) Consider instead a target that is fed instruction lists one instruction at a
time, keeps the whole list it was fed, charges the price list, and reads certification by running
its list on this machine from the initial state. Its reading agrees with this machine’s on every
list, and the price list obeys the toll on it, yet it does not factor through this machine’s state:
the empty list and the list holding one free jump to address 0 leave this machine in the same

Proof. (1) Relate ( p, s, H ) to ( p, s); records, costs and steps match because the history
is never read. (2) Call the free jump to address 0 j. From the initial state it costs 0 and

Checked as history_core_equiv_thiele (StructuralCore.v) and certifica
tion_agreement_does_not_imply_descent (TraceStateDescent.v), the third

So agreeing with this machine on every certification reading doesn’t make a machine
a function of this machine’s state. When a history-keeper counts as the same as this
machine, it’s because the relation was allowed to drop the history, and for no other
reason.

Back to the billed machine. It isn’t a different structure; it’s the same machine with a
different price list. So the claim worth keeping is uniqueness up to the price schedule:
compare two machines by their record light, their halting, and their steps, through
their maps down to this machine, and don’t compare charges. Here I have to be plain
about how much that claim says. Every machine it covers runs this one underneath,
and “the same machine” means each state is related only to the state of this machine
that its own map assigns it. So the result says the extra bookkeeping and the price
list don’t matter. It doesn’t say unrelated machines coincide. With the record fixed
to this machine’s own certification reading (the certified flag: the bit only CERTIFY sets,
which carries no object and no check), uniqueness up to schedule holds (cert_rec
ord_schedule_uniqueness_holds): the billed machine is an instance, and so is
any machine that adds to the bill any amount that’s a function of the program and the
current state. (The flat one-per-step bill is the separate BilledCore.) One structure,
many price lists.


Definition 23.8 (The same up to the schedule). Let M cover the Thiele core through
π. M is priced when (R2) and (R3) hold. M is the same as the Thiele core up to the schedule
when both are priced and some relation R satisfies: R(m, t) only when t = π (m); every
starting state of each side is related to some starting state of the other; and related
states have the same record, the same halting, and related next states. Charges are
not compared. M is an honest certification extension when rec(m) = cert of π (m) for
every m, M is priced, and (R4) and (R5) hold. It is an honest tied extension when instead

rec(m) = g(π (m)) for some one function g, with the other clauses the same.

cation extension is the same as the Thiele core up to the schedule. In particular, so is the billed
core, and so is the machine that runs the Thiele core and adds e( p, s) to a side counter at every

Proof. Take R(m, t) to mean t = π (m). The cover gives the two start conditions,
halting, and the step clause; the record clause is the hypothesis rec(m) = cert of π (m).

Checked as cert_record_schedule_uniqueness_holds, billed_core_equ

And then the second free choice, Section 10’s two cups on one die, on this machine.

Theorem 23.17 (Not unique for a tied record). Let the meter core be the Thiele core with

record is only required to be some reading of the computation.

Proof. The record is g(π (m)) with g( p, s) = [µ(s) ≥ 1]. It is priced because the ledger
is the Thiele ledger and a step that turns it on raises µ from 0 to at least 1; permanent
because µ never falls; and written by the certifying step from the initial state. Now
take the starting state ([ ], s1 ) with s1 the initial machine state except µ = 1, flag off.
Any R must relate it to some starting state of the meter core, and only to itself, since
the cover is the identity. There the meter core’s record is on and the Thiele core’s is
off.
