23.10 Pricing and verifying on this machine (Section 12)
Section 12 read five real systems at three levels (specification, transcription, wrapper)
and said some of the wrappers are written for this machine. Here they are, together
with the one sentence about pricing this machine’s own flag.

First the gas wrapper’s class, on this machine. Price the certified flag at one per raise
and nothing otherwise, and both halves of Section 12’s gas-schedule exactness hold,
the floor and no overcharge (thiele_vm_commit_pricing_is_exact, GasMeter-
ing.v, through Theorem 12.4). That exact schedule isn’t this machine’s own counter,
which also bills computation that commits nothing; on every raise the unit price is
at most what the counter charges (thiele_unit_price_lower_bounds_mu). It’s
the same split the exact-price subsection above drew with collisions: the exact price of
certification lives in the step, and the counter is a bigger bill that contains it.

The attestation wrapper is a separate file, built on the verifier pair A and B of the
previous subsection. A report there is a bare transcript plus one measurement register,
and an honest report of a state carries a transcript that state explains and a register
equal to its µ.


Theorem 23.18 (Attestation cannot factor through the bare transcript). Let V be a
verifier on reports that is sound (it accepts only reports every honest explanation of which has
µ = 1) and complete (it accepts every honest report of a state with µ = 1). Then V is not a
function of the bare transcript: there are reports with equal transcripts on which V differs.

Proof. The pair A, B gives two reports with the same transcript, one honestly explain-
ing a state that paid (µ = 1) and one a state that did not (µ = 0). Completeness makes
V accept the first; soundness makes it reject the second.

Checked as attestation_cannot_factor_through_bare_transcript
(TEEAttestation.v), an instance of V_does_not_factor_through_classical
(Theorem 23.12); the same file has the pair itself (replay_is_a_two_preimage_
witness) and the positive side, a sound and complete verifier at unit cost once the
register is readable (measurement_enriched_attestation_succeeds). The
register’s faithfulness is a premise of the model, not a fact about hardware. Section 12’s
quote fragment has two more statements that lean on this machine’s transcript type:
quote_projection_faithful says the quote, written into the machine’s bare-
transcript format, loses nothing, and quote_runtime_verifier_separation
says no verifier correct for the platform’s runtime flag depends only on that encoding
(TPMQuoteGap.v; the separation is V_does_not_factor_through_classical
again, with the pair A, B as its fixed witnesses).

                                              311
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


The transparency wrapper is Section 7’s commitment escape in log vocabulary. Under
a disclosure contract (a premise: the inclusion bit is set on every honest transcript of a
run with µ = 1, and a set bit binds every explaining run to µ = 1), there is a verifier
that reads the log’s inclusion bit, is sound and complete for the claim µ = 1, and costs
one unit (abstract_log_bit_verifier, TransparencyLog.v). Delete the log and
no verifier on the bare transcript is sound and complete for that claim at any cost (a
bstract_bare_verifier_impossible, which is Theorem 23.11 under another
name), with the collision pair behind it exhibited as abstract_mu_collision_wi
tness. The pair has the shape of a split view, one transcript for two runs; it is not an
RFC split view, which is two inconsistent log histories: a log that shows one version
of its past to you and a different one to me, the move the certificate-transparency logs
of Section 12 are built to get caught making.

The proof-carrying wrapper is Section 7’s interaction escape. A transcript that carries
the certificate admits a checker, sound and complete for µ = 1 at unit cost (proof_r
ounds_escape, ProofCarryingVerifier.v); strip the certificate and no checker on the
bare transcript is sound and complete at any cost (bare_pcc_impossible). And
the prover’s side has a floor. A script is a program run from the initial state with a fixed
fuel, and it’s level k when it ends with the certified flag up and one of the CERTIFY
steps it executed was charged at least k. Then its counter rises by at least k, and for
every k ≥ 1 a single CERTIFY charged k does it at exactly k (level_k_verificati
on_floor, level_k_verification_floor_tight). The first is level_k_cert
ification_cost_floor (MuHierarchyTheorem.v) by exact application, which is
the lower half of Section 26’s mu-hierarchy, Theorem 26.7, so the formal statement and
proof live there. The floor prices the run’s certification events. It says nothing about
proof size, prover time, or the checker’s work.

In each of the three, the unit cost is stipulated, and none of them prices or verifies
the real system it borrows a name from. How to knock them down: for attestation,
a sound and complete verifier on the bare transcript; for transparency, a sound and
complete verifier that needs no log, for the same claim; for proof-carrying code, a
script of level k whose counter rises by less than k, or a sound and complete checker
with no certificate.

Theorem 23.19 (The certified flag is a permanent consensus). For any N > 0 and any

23.12 What landed
Every pointer from Parts II and III that said “on the machine” has a name in this
chapter. What’s not here, and stays not here: a single either-reading run theorem;
“every merge priced” on the full machine (false, by the free jump); a statement of
Section 6’s counter facts or Section 10’s two free choices over an arbitrary base (those
are argued in their chapters, checked only here); and any claim that the small lifted
model is the twelve-field machine. The machine is a witness. It’s not a bigger claim
than the theorems on it.

24 Interpreters and the guest machine
Section 11 left the diagonal standing on any substrate, on a little family built to fit it,
and on L, and said the machine is one more substrate of that kind, conditionally. The
machine is on the table now, so here it is, in three pieces. First the wall pointed at the
full machine, where it is conditional on a recursion premise that can’t be granted for
every map and can’t hold for any class containing a correct decider’s flip, and where a
decider standing outside exists and is checked. Then two interpreters, programs of the
machine that run a smaller machine handed to them as data. Then the guest, where
the recursion theorem is proved rather than assumed. I’ll say which interpreter the
recursion theorem lives on, because nobody can check a claim about “the interpreter”
if there are two.

24.1 The diagonal, pointed at the machine
Here’s Section 11’s question, asked of this machine. The machine carries a record; the
record is a latch on an event (Section 10); for my machine the event is a certification,
and Section 22 said a certification reading, with its receipt, is what lets an auditor
treat a shortcut as admissible. So: can the machine have, as one of its own programs,
a procedure that correctly decides, for every program, “does this program admit a
sound shortcut”? That would be autopilot. Hand it any program and it says yes or no,
and it’s always right.

That’s the question in plain words, and the checked statement is narrower, so here it
is before the proof. In the checked work “admits a shortcut” is a concrete property of
programs: its bounded run from the start state ends in the same state as the bounded
run of one fixed reference program, a three-instruction one that allocates a group,


                                           313
The Thiele Machine                                                               Devon Thiele


makes its identity arrow (Section 2’s do-nothing arrow from a thing to itself), and
asserts it. Two programs that behave alike agree on the property, and there’s one
program that has it and one that doesn’t. The diagonal doesn’t see soundness. For
that one reference program the checked work does show the property lining up with
a sound-shortcut record from Section 22. For other programs it says nothing of the
kind, and a procedure that returns soundness records for some programs, or only for
restricted inputs, or with outside evidence, is not what the wall rules out.

Here is that property exactly. Write sinit for the machine’s initial state and run1000 ( p, s)
for the state the machine reaches from s running p, cut off after a thousand steps.


Definition 24.1 (The machine’s shortcut property). Let r be the three-instruction pro-
gram that opens a group (a module) on cell 0, builds that module’s identity arrow,
and asserts the arrow just built; in Section 17’s table these are PNEW, MORPH_
ID and MORPH_ASSERT. A program p admits the shortcut when run1000 ( p, sinit ) =
run1000 (r, sinit ). The program r admits it; the empty program does not.


Checked as vm_admits_shortcut_extensional, with vm_admits_shortcut_
yes and vm_admits_shortcut_no for the two witnesses (StructuralUndecidabil-
ity.v; r is simple_morph_trace in SimpleMorphShortcut.v). The no-witness is a
computation: the empty program leaves sinit where it is, and r does not. The link
to Section 22’s record is vm_instantiation_target_witnessed: for r alone, a
sound-shortcut record exists.

Section 11’s wall (Theorem 11.1) is about any substrate: programs, a run, a counter, an
encoding of programs as data, a class of representable transformations, and a recursion
theorem for that class. The machine supplies most of that on its own. It doesn’t supply
the last piece. Here’s the honest form.

The concrete machine (vm_structural_shortcut_undecidable): the generic the-
orem applied to my machine’s bounded runs (no decider says yes exactly when a
program admits the shortcut), carrying as explicit hypotheses an encoding of pro-
grams as data, a class of representable transformations, and a recursion theorem for
that class. (A companion statement, vm_structural_shortcut_undecidable_
encoded, discharges the encoding with a proved round trip between programs and
numbers, leaving only the representable class and its recursion theorem as premises.)
Asked for every map on programs, that recursion premise is false, and the reason is
the cutoff, not the size of memory: equality after a thousand steps is something you
can check by running both programs, so the flip of that check has no fixed point. So
the corollary needs a class that leaves the flip of every correct decider out, and with
such a class it says exactly that: the flip of a correct decider has no program whose
thousand-step runs match its image’s from every state. The proved recursion theorem
further down is for the machine’s guest, a smaller machine it runs as data, and it



                                             314
The Thiele Machine                                                                 Devon Thiele


answers a different question.


Premise 24.2 (A recursion theorem for the full machine). A class Rep of maps on
machine programs such that every f in Rep has a program q with run1000 (q, s) =
run1000 ( f (q), s) for every state s. The class with only the identity map meets it (take
q empty), and so does any class of constant maps. The class of all maps doesn’t:
Theorem 24.3 names a map with no such q.


Theorem 24.1 (The wall on the machine, conditional). For every class Rep satisfying
Premise 24.2, there is no Boolean function d on machine programs such that the flip of d (the
empty program when d( p) is true, r when it is false) is in Rep and, for every p, d( p) =
true ⇐⇒ p admits the shortcut.

Proof. Build the substrate from the machine’s bounded run, with enc( p) the initial
state with the number of p stored in one of its number fields (the logic accumulator of
Section 16) and dec reading it back (the round trip between programs and numbers
is proved), the given Rep, and the premise as its recursion theorem. The predicate
of Definition 24.1 is a shortcut predicate with witnesses r and the empty program,
and it is extensional because it reads only the run from one state. Then Theorem 11.1
applies.

Checked as vm_structural_shortcut_undecidable (StructuralUndecidabil-
ity.v, encoding as hypotheses) and vm_structural_shortcut_undecidable_en
coded (VMSubstrateEncoded.v, encoding discharged by vm_encode_decode_con
crete). In both, the decider ruled out is one that says true exactly when a program
admits the shortcut. That the empty class meets the premise is logic, not a stated
theorem.

Now the honest part Section 11 did with a pencil on its little family: who counts as a
decider. The theorem rules out a decider whose flip the machine can itself represent.
It says nothing about a decider standing outside. And here’s a thing that surprised
me about my own machine: its bounded runs (a thousand steps, then stop) make the
shortcut predicate decidable from outside, by just running both programs and com-
paring. So an outside decider exists. What the theorem says is that such a decider’s
flip can’t be one of the machine’s own representable transformations, under the recur-
sion premise. Same boundary as on Section 11’s family, Richard’s lesson again: the
language you talk about the machine in is not the language it talks in.


Theorem 24.2 (Bounded runs are decidable from outside). Let dout ( p) be true exactly
when the two states run1000 ( p, sinit ) and run1000 (r, sinit ) are equal. Then dout is a total
Boolean function, and dout ( p) is true exactly when p admits the shortcut. Moreover, let Rep
be any class of maps on machine programs such that every f in Rep has a program q with



                                              315
The Thiele Machine                                                                  Devon Thiele


run1000 (q, s) = run1000 ( f (q), s) for every state s. Then the flip of dout (the empty program
when dout ( p) is true, r when it is false) is not in Rep.

Proof. Equality of machine states is decidable, since a state is a finite record of numbers,
lists of numbers, and flags; comparing the two bounded runs is therefore a total
function, and it is correct by its definition. If its flip were in Rep, then dout would be a
decider of exactly the kind Theorem 11.1 rules out, applied to the machine’s bounded
runs with that Rep (the instance is Theorem 24.1).

Checked as vm_bounded_shortcut_decide_correct and vm_bounded_decid
er_flip_not_representable (VMBoundedDecidability.v).

The same file says the two sentences I keep leaning on as theorems of their own, so
you don’t have to take my word for how they follow.


Theorem 24.3 (The full-machine recursion premise fails, and every correct flip has no
fixed point). (1) It is not the case that every map f on machine programs has a program q
with run1000 (q, s) = run1000 ( f (q), s) for every state s. (2) Let d be any Boolean function on
machine programs with d( p) = true ⇐⇒ p admits the shortcut, for every p, and let f d (q)
be the empty program when d(q) is true and r when it is false. Then there is no program q
with run1000 (q, s) = run1000 ( f d (q), s) for every state s.

Proof. (2) If such a q existed, the class whose only member is f d would satisfy
Premise 24.2 and contain the flip of a correct decider, which Theorem 24.1 rules out. (1)
If every map had such a q, the class of all maps would satisfy the premise and contain
the flip of dout , which is correct by Theorem 24.2; that theorem rules this out.

Checked as vm_full_recursion_premise_refuted and vm_correct_flip_
has_no_fixed_point (VMBoundedDecidability.v), both closed under the global
context. In Coq, (1) reads ~ (forall f, exists q, forall s, vm_run q
s = vm_run (f q) s), and (2) reads forall d, (forall p, d p = true
<-> vm_admits_shortcut_extensional p) -> ~ exists q, forall s,
vm_run q s = vm_run (if d q then [] else simple_morph_trace) s,
with vm_run the thousand-step run and simple_morph_trace the program r.

So the machine’s property is decidable from outside, and the wall on the machine
separates nothing from classical halting: it’s about bounded runs, and the premise
can’t be granted for every map (part (1) of Theorem 24.3), and no class can both meet
it and contain a correct decider’s flip (part (2)). So the machine’s version can’t be
knocked over that way, and it doesn’t say much either: it’s the diagonal applied to
a property I can decide. Put plainly: against a decider that’s actually correct, the
machine’s conditional wall has no bite at all, because no class it would need can hold
that decider’s flip.

The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


Take the thousand-step cutoff away and the question changes shape, so here’s the run
with no stopwatch on it. Unbounded halting is its own relation, and it has its own
facts.


Definition 24.3 (Halting without a cutoff). Program p halts at r from s when there is
some number k with runk ( p, s) = r and the program counter of r is at or past the end
of p.


Theorem 24.4 (A program halts at most once). If p halts at r1 from s and halts at r2 from
s, then r1 = r2 .

Proof. Let the witnesses be k1 ≤ k2 . Once the program counter is past the end, a step
changes nothing, so runk2 ( p, s) = runk1 ( p, s), and the two results are equal. The other
order is symmetric.

Checked as vm_halts_at and vm_halts_at_deterministic (VMUnbound-
edExec.v). This relation is not the bounded run of Definition 24.1: the bounded run
always returns a state, halted or not, and nothing identifies the two. The interpreters
in the rest of this chapter work with unbounded runs too (under a sibling step I’ll flag
below): programs of my machine that run a smaller machine handed to them as data.
I’ll call the smaller machine the guest.

24.2 Why an interpreter at all
An interpreter is a program that reads another program as data and does what it says.
It’s one of the oldest tricks in computing, and it’s the trick that makes the diagonal
bite: the Contrarian card in Section 11 needs “hand me to the Checker,” which means
a program has to be able to be handed, as a number, to another program. On this
machine, a program is a list of instructions, and there’s a proved round-trip encoding
of programs as natural numbers (program_to_nat and back; the wall above used
it). So programs can be data. What’s left is to show that a program on the machine
can run a program given as data, and to say exactly which programs.

How old is “one of the oldest”? Turing’s 1936 paper already has one: the universal
machine, which reads another machine’s rule table off its tape and does what the table
says. And the first one people actually used came in through the side door. John
McCarthy, writing up his new language Lisp around 1960, wanted to show it was
neater than Turing machines, so he wrote a universal function for it, eval, the language
describing how to evaluate itself, and showed it was shorter and easier to follow than
a universal Turing machine. In his own history of Lisp, that was for the paper, a thing
to read; the notation for writing programs as data was made up for the paper with
no thought of using it in practice. Then S. R. Russell, Steve Russell, noticed that eval
could serve as an interpreter and coded it by hand, and there was a running language
with an interpreter that nobody had planned. McCarthy adds that the surprise froze


                                           317
The Thiele Machine                                                                    Devon Thiele


some decisions he’d made “rather lightheartedly” for the paper. So the trick has a
habit: written to be read, it ends up being run. The interpreters below go the other
way round, on purpose. They’re written to run on the machine, and the proofs check
that what runs is what the page says.

A warning about what the round trip does and doesn’t give you. The decoder is
a Coq function, outside the machine. The encoding the wall above uses parks the
program’s number in the logic accumulator, a field no instruction ever reads, and
there’s a theorem that no fixed program can then report even the encoded program’s
certification bit through any observation that ignores that field (no_logic_acc_enc
oded_interpreter). It doesn’t rule out a different encoding. The two interpreters
below are different encodings: the code arrives as an ordinary number in an ordinary
register, which is something a program can read.

Here it is exactly. Write s[acc := n] for the state s with its logic accumulator replaced
by n, apply for the sixty-four-bit step, and run( F, q, s) for the program-counter runner:
F times, fetch the instruction of q at the program counter and apply it, stopping early
when the program counter is past the end of q.


Lemma 24.5 (The accumulator commutes with every step and every run). For ev-
ery state s, instruction i, number n, program q and fuel F: apply(s[acc := n], i ) =
apply(s, i )[acc := n] and run( F, q, s[acc := n]) = run( F, q, s)[acc := n].

Proof. The step form is a case split over every instruction: none reads the accumulator
and none writes it. The run form is induction on F, using the step form at each fetch;
the fetch reads only the program counter.

Checked as vm_apply_logic_acc_commutes and run_vm_logic_acc_commut
es (VMEncodedInputAccess.v).


Theorem 24.6 (No interpreter for the accumulator encoding). Say q halts from s showing
b under o, for a test o from states to booleans and a bit b, when for some F the state run( F, q, s)
has its program counter at or past the end of q and o of it is b. Let enc( p) be the initial
state with the accumulator set to the number of p. For every program I and every test o with
o (t[acc := n]) = o (t) for all t and n, it is not the case that for every program p and bit b, I
halts from enc( p) showing b under o exactly when p halts from the initial state showing b
under the certified flag.

Proof. Suppose I did. The program consisting of CERTIFY 0 halts from the initial state
with the flag up, so I halts from its encoding showing true. By Lemma 24.5 the run of I
from the encoding of the empty program is the same run with a different accumulator,
and o ignores the accumulator, so I also halts from the encoding of the empty program




                                                318
The Thiele Machine                                                              Devon Thiele


showing true. Then the empty program would halt from the initial state with the flag
up; it halts at once with the flag down.

Checked as vm_apply_logic_acc_commutes, run_vm_logic_acc_commutes,
halts_observes_logic and no_logic_acc_encoded_interpreter (VMEn-
codedInputAccess.v, 33, 47, 56).

Both interpreters below run under the machine’s natural-number sibling (vm_apply_
u, run_vm_u). That’s a second execution model and I’ll flag it: same instruction type,
same twelve-field record, but writes and arithmetic keep the exact value instead of
cutting it to sixty-four bits, and subtraction stops at zero instead of wrapping around.
The guest registers are unbounded because of it. The two steps are separate definitions,
and no theorem here ties the sixty-four-bit machine to its unbounded sibling.

24.3 The first interpreter: a two-counter machine as guest
A two-counter machine (Minsky’s, from the 1960s) has a program counter and two
counters that hold naturals; its instructions are: halt, increment one or the other, and
“decrement-or-jump” on one or the other (if the counter is zero, step on; otherwise
decrement and jump to a target). That’s all, and once the input is encoded as a number
it’s enough to compute anything a Turing machine can, which is why it’s the classic
small target for undecidability proofs.

The title of Minsky’s 1961 paper is the clue I can’t leave alone. It’s about “Post’s
problem of tag.” Who’s Post, and what’s tag? Emil Post, in 1921, on a fellowship at
Princeton, was playing with about the simplest rewriting game there is. Take a word
of 0s and 1s. Look at its first letter, chop the first three letters off the front, and stick
something on the end: 00 if the letter you looked at was 0, 1101 if it was 1. Repeat,
and stop when fewer than three letters are left. Try it at the table. Start from 1000: you
get 01101, then 0100, then 000, then 00, and it stops. Start from 100: you get 1101,
11101, 011101, 10100, 001101, and then 10100 again, and it goes round forever.
Post wanted a rule that tells you, for every starting word, which of those happens. He
worked at it for months and later called it hopeless, and as far as I can tell it still is: a
hundred years on, nobody knows whether that one little game, with that one rule, can
be decided. Minsky’s paper showed that tag games in general can compute anything,
which is why Post’s name is on it. It didn’t settle Post’s own game. And the chase
goes one step further. In 2008 Liesbeth De Mol turned the famous 3n + 1 problem
(halve an even number, triple an odd one and add one, and ask whether you always
get down to 1) into a small tag game of the same kind. So is Post’s game secretly as
hard as everything, or just stubborn? I can’t tell you, and as far as the published work
goes, nobody can yet.

None of that changes the interpreter below. It changes the picture. The two-counter
machine came out of a hunt for the smallest thing that can’t be predicted, and the
smallest things are exactly where the open questions are still sitting.


                                            319
The Thiele Machine                                                         Devon Thiele


The machine hosts one. Each guest instruction is packed into a word: opcode in the
low three bits, jump target in the rest, and the words are packed into one number
at a width chosen from the program. The host program is a fixed list of sixty of the
machine’s instructions, all at declared cost zero, with the terminal program counter at
sixty and a status register that reads one for “guest halted” and two for “malformed
guest word.” What’s proved, with none of it carrying an axiom in the last assumption
audit (Section 23): each guest step is simulated by a positive number of host steps
landing in a state that represents the new guest configuration (cm2_uniform_inter
preter_simulation_total); the guest halts with a given final configuration if and
only if some fuel brings the host to the halted status with that result (cm2_uniform
_interpreter_raw_correct_total); the canonical encoding never reaches the
malformed status (cm2_uniform_interpreter_raw_never_malformed); and
the guest diverges if and only if the host program counter never reaches sixty at any
fuel (cm2_uniform_interpreter_raw_divergence_total). Through that, the
two-counter halting problem maps onto “does this host run ever reach the halted
status” (mm2_halting_host_iff), and so, in the synthetic sense of the Saarland
library of undecidable problems that Section 11 met beside L (what “synthetic” buys
is spelled out in the Rice part below), “does this host run ever halt” is undecidable
(actual_unbounded_host_synthetic_undecidability). It’s a reduction, not
a self-interpreter: it shows the machine can host a universal-enough guest, and it
connects the machine’s halting to a known undecidable problem.

One detail here changes what counts as a guest. The two-counter machine this inter-
preter runs branches when a decrement succeeds and falls through when the counter is
zero. The convention is not cosmetic: the two-instruction program “increment counter
0, then decrement counter 0 and jump back” runs forever under that convention (cm
2_loop_diverges, and the interpreter running it never halts, cm2_loop_host_n
ever_halts), while the same pair under the zero-branching convention halts after
two steps (zero_branch_pair_terminates, VMUnboundedCM2Applicability.v).
That a zero-branching guest is a weaker machine overall is argued, not checked, and
no result depends on it; the zero-branching guest is simply not used as a witness of
universality.

24.4 The second interpreter: the machine running a piece of itself
Now the one the recursion theorem lives on. Take a twelve-instruction fragment
of the machine’s own instruction set: halt, load-immediate, transfer, add, subtract,
multiply, and, or, shift left, shift right, jump, jump-if-nonzero. Four guest registers
(numbers zero to three), unbounded values, a guest program counter, a guest ledger,
and “terminated” meaning the guest program counter has run off the end of the guest
program. A guest program is well-formed when every register name is below four and
every declared cost is below two hundred and fifty-six.

The literal host listings, complete encodings and block-by-block verification are in
Appendix I. In this guest, HALT advances the program counter; leaving the program

                                         320
The Thiele Machine                                                                    Devon Thiele


is what ends execution.

The host is a fixed list of a hundred and twenty-two of the machine’s instructions, at
declared cost zero. It keeps the guest’s four registers in its registers zero to three, a
status in register nine (running, terminated, malformed), the guest ledger in register
eleven, the guest program counter in register twelve, a width in thirteen, and the
packed guest code in fourteen. The host’s own counter never moves, since every host
instruction is at cost zero; the guest’s ledger is just a number sitting in register eleven.
Under the hypotheses that the guest program is well-formed and fits the width: a
terminating guest run gives a host run that reaches program counter one hundred
and twenty-two in the corresponding done state (self_interpreter_complete);
any host run that reaches one twenty-two from an encoded configuration decodes
to a terminal guest run (self_interpreter_sound); together, a biconditional on
the final guest configuration (self_interpreter_correct); the guest never termi-
nates if and only if no fuel reaches one twenty-two (self_interpreter_diverge
nce); and for arbitrary packed data, a fetched word whose low four bits are thirteen,
fourteen or fifteen sends the host to the end with the malformed status and the guest
registers, ledger and program counter as they were (self_interpreter_malform
ed; opcode zero is the sentinel for “no instruction here”, which is how a guest ends).
The guest step is proved to be the unbounded sibling’s own step on the guest fields (g
_step_is_vm_apply_u), the code round-trips (g_decode_guest_code_roundt
rip), and running the guest is actual machine execution (g_eval_is_actual_vm_
execution).

Here’s the same thing in the notation that makes it checkable and unreadable in equal
measure:


Definition 24.4 (Guest configurations and runs). A guest configuration c is a program
counter, a ledger and four registers, all natural numbers. A guest program p is a list
of the twelve guest instructions. gstep p (c) executes the instruction of p at c’s program
counter on unbounded values and leaves c alone when there is none; grun p (n, c) is n
such steps. c is terminal for p when its program counter is at least the length of p. p
is well-formed when every register field is below 4 and every declared cost below 256,
and p fits the width w when every packed instruction word of p is below 2w .


Theorem 24.7 (The self-interpreter is correct). Let p be well-formed and fit w, and let
U be the fixed host program of 122 instructions, run by the program-counter runner on the
unbounded step applyu ; write urun( F, s) for F steps. For a guest configuration c, let H (c) be
a host state at host program counter 0 whose registers 0 to 3 hold c’s registers, register 9 holds
0, registers 11 and 12 hold c’s ledger and program counter, register 13 holds w and register 14
holds the packed code of p; the seven scratch registers (4 to 8, 10 and 15), the host counter and
every other field are arbitrary. Say a host state is done for c′ when it has host program counter
122, registers 0 to 3, 11 and 12 holding c′ , register 9 holding 1, registers 13 and 14 as in H (c),


                                                321
The Thiele Machine                                                                   Devon Thiele


and the host counter and every field outside the registers as in H (c). Then for all c and c′ ,

     ∃n. grun p (n, c) = c′ and c′ is terminal            ∃ F. urun( F, H (c)) is done for c′ ,
                                                                                            
                                                     ⇐⇒

and the guest run from c never reaches a terminal configuration exactly when no F brings
urun( F, H (c)) to host program counter 122.

Proof. The core is a block lemma: from H (c) with c not terminal, a positive number
of host steps reaches H (gstep p (c)), with new scratch values. The block fetches the
packed word at the guest program counter (well-formedness and the width make the
fetch return exactly that instruction’s word), splits it into fields with shifts and masks,
dispatches on the opcode, and performs the guest instruction on registers 0 to 3, 11 and
12; each opcode’s block is checked by computing with the host’s own step. Induction
on n gives the forward direction, followed by the fixed terminal sequence that sees
the end sentinel and writes status 1. The backward direction is strong induction on F:
122 is past the end of U, so once reached the host stays there, and a block boundary
has host program counter 0, so a run that reaches 122 must pass through whole blocks.
Divergence is the contrapositive of the two directions.

Checked as self_interpreter_complete, self_interpreter_sound, self
_interpreter_correct and self_interpreter_divergence (VMSelfRun.v,
208, 244, 264), with h_block and h_simulation (VMSelfRun.v) and the done-state
definition h_done.

So the machine runs a fragment of itself, as data, with a proof that what it computes
is what the fragment computes. Twelve of fifty-one; four registers of sixteen; and the
“itself” is the unbounded sibling, with its saturating subtraction, not the sixty-four-bit
step. A fragment. “Self-interpreter” can sound as if it covered the whole instruction
set. It doesn’t, and I’d rather the numbers be in front of you.

24.5 Rice, on the guest
With the interpreter in hand, Section 11’s wall lands on the guest without any premise
about recursion. Say two guest programs behave the same when, for every input placed
in register zero, they terminate with the same final registers and the same guest ledger,
or both don’t (g_equiv; note it sees returned registers and ledger, not the final pro-
gram counter or the step count). A property of guest programs is extensional when
well-formed programs that behave the same agree on it. Then: for any extensional
property that holds of some well-formed program and fails of the program that jumps
to itself forever, the predicate “well-formed and has the property” is undecidable, in
the synthetic sense the Saarland library uses (the complement of two-counter halting
reduces to its complement) (self_rice). “Decided” has a stated meaning here (g
_decides): a well-formed guest program that, given any fixed way of numbering
programs, terminates on the number of every well-formed program and reports the
property by whether register zero ends at one. A guest program that decided such


                                                 322
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


a property would make the complement of halting for single-tape Turing machines
over a two-letter alphabet enumerable (the library calls these SBTM, single-tape bi-
nary Turing machines; the book just says single-tape) (self_rice_representab
le). “Halts on input zero” is a named instance. That “undecidable” is the library’s
synthetic notion, a reduction and an enumerability statement, and not a bare negation
of every decision procedure one could write in Coq.

One more word on that, because “undecidable” here is the Saarland library’s word
and it means something exact. Inside Coq, the library doesn’t say “no algorithm
decides this” outright. It says: if you could decide this, you could enumerate (list, one
after another, by a program) every Turing machine that never halts. Nobody can do
that: the machines that do halt can already be listed (run them all a little at a time
and write each one down when it stops), so with both lists you could decide halting
by waiting to see which list a machine turns up on, and that’s Turing’s wall. So it’s a
reduction, a promise that a decider here would be a decider there.

The words first, then the theorem.


Definition 24.5 (Behaviour, extensional, decides, undecidable). For a guest program
p and input x, beh p ( x, g, µ) holds when some grun p (n, c x ) is terminal with registers
g and ledger µ, where c x has program counter 0, ledger 0 and registers ( x, 0, 0, 0).
Programs p and q behave the same when beh p ( x, g, µ) ⇐⇒ behq ( x, g, µ) for all x, g, µ.
A property P of guest programs is extensional when P( p) implies P(q) for well-formed
p and q that behave the same. A guest program D decides P under a numbering e of
programs when D is well-formed and for every well-formed p there are g and µ with
behD (e( p), g, µ) and (g0 = 1 ⇐⇒ P( p)). A predicate Q is undecidable, in the library’s
sense, when a Coq function deciding Q would make the complement of single-tape
Turing-machine halting enumerable.


Theorem 24.8 (Rice on the guest). Let P be extensional, let w be a well-formed program with
P(w), and let P fail for the one-instruction program that jumps to itself. Then “well-formed
and P” is undecidable. If moreover some guest program decides P under some numbering, the
complement of single-tape Turing-machine halting is enumerable.

Proof. For the first part, send a two-counter machine m to a guest program that saves
its input in register 2, loads m’s two starting counters, runs a guest copy of m, puts
the input back in register 0 and clears the other three, and then runs w, with every
instruction before w at declared cost 0. If m halts, the program behaves like w, so it
has P; if m does not halt, it never terminates, behaves like the self-jump, and lacks
P. That reduces the complement of two-counter halting, undecidable in the library,
to the complement of “well-formed and P”, and a predicate whose complement is
undecidable is undecidable. For the second part, a guest decider gives a Coq decider:
for a well-formed p, search for the least fuel at which D on e( p) is terminal (it exists,


                                            323
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


so the constructive search over the naturals finds it) and read register 0.

24.6 The guest recursion theorem
Here’s the theorem the fragment exists for. Statement, in full, because which transfor-
mations the guest can compute is the condition that matters. For every transformation
F from guest programs to guest programs that maps well-formed programs to well-
formed programs, and every guest program D that represents F (D is well-formed, and
run on the code of any well-formed program p, D terminates with register zero hold-
ing the code of F applied to p), there is a well-formed guest program p that behaves
the same as F applied to p (vm_guest_recursion_theorem_closed). Kleene’s
second recursion theorem, for the twelve-instruction guest, with “the machine can
carry out the transformation” meaning “some guest program computes it on codes.”

The proof is a construction, which is Section 11’s point about Kleene’s little gem
(Moschovakis’s phrase): the content is the building, and the contradiction in Section 11
was just the last line. The shape: from the representing program D, build an evaluator
that reads a program’s code, specialises that program to its own code, runs D on the
specialised code, and runs the program D returns. The finite algorithm and its output
encoding are given below. Realise that evaluator as a guest program e; take the code
of e; and the witness is e specialised to its own code by a ten-instruction guest prefix
that pairs a fixed number with the input (g_pair_specialize). The prefix is the
specialising step made as guest instructions (logicians call this step s-m-n: fix one input
of a program and get a new program that needs one input fewer), and the theorem
that it specialises correctly (g_pair_smn, which says the specialised program on an
input and the original on the paired input finish the same way, in both directions) is
what makes the witness a guest program rather than a Coq-level construction. So: p is
e with its own code baked in; run on any input, it evaluates D on the code of p, gets
the code of F p, and runs that. It’s tempting to say the prefix pairs “p’s own code”;
more exactly it pairs the code of the evaluator e, and e builds p’s code from it. So
L is a tool on this route, not a source: the recursion theorem is proved on the guest
directly, and it isn’t pulled back from L’s own recursion theorem in Section 11. The
mathematical dependency is an effective translation from the computable evaluator
to a counter program and then to the guest. The checked implementation uses L
and counter-machine compilers for that translation; their role is to preserve the input-
output relation, not to supply the fixed-point argument.


                                           324
The Thiele Machine                                                                 Devon Thiele


Here is the statement with every word unfolded, using Definitions 24.4 and 24.5. Write
⌜ p⌝ for the code of a guest program: translate p into the machine’s own instructions,
then take the machine’s program number of that list.


Definition 24.6 (Represents, pairing prefix). A guest program D represents a map F
from guest programs to guest programs when D is well-formed and for every well-
formed p there are g and µ with behD (⌜ p⌝, g, µ) and g0 = ⌜ F ( p)⌝. The pairing is
⟨ x, y⟩ = (2y + 1) · 2x . For a number x and a guest program e, spec(e, x ) is a fixed
ten-instruction prefix, all at declared cost 0, followed by e with its jump targets moved
up by ten.


Here are the ten instructions themselves. Lines are numbered from zero, every instruc-
tion has declared cost zero, and the relocated program starts at line 10. The input is
(r0 , r1 , r2 , r3 ) = (y, 0, 0, 0).

Line                                            Operation
0                                               Set r2 := 1.
1                                               Set r0 := r0 + r0 .
2                                               Set r0 := r0 + r2 .
3                                               Set r1 := x.
4                                               If r1 is nonzero, jump to line 7; otherwise
                                                advance.
5                                               Set r2 := 0.
6                                               Jump to line 10, the start of the relocated
                                                program.
7                                               Set r0 := r0 + r0 .
8                                               Set r1 := r1 − r2 , with natural subtraction.
9                                               Jump to line 4.



At line 4 after j turns through the loop, the registers satisfy r0 = (2y + 1)2 j , r1 = x − j,
r2 = 1, r3 = 0, with 0 ≤ j ≤ x. A nonzero r1 doubles the first number and reduces the
second by one. At j = x the loop exits and clears r2 , leaving exactly the paired input
and three zero registers. Relocation adds 10 to every instruction address and jump
target of e; ordinary next-line steps and jumps therefore correspond in both directions.


Lemma 24.9 (The prefix pairs). For all e, x, y, g, µ: behspec(e,x) (y, g, µ)               ⇐⇒
behe (⟨ x, y⟩, g, µ).

Proof. The prefix doubles register 0 and adds one, then doubles it x more times by a
counted loop on register 1, then clears its scratch register and jumps to the start of
the moved copy of e. That takes 4x + 7 steps, charges nothing, and leaves registers
(⟨ x, y⟩, 0, 0, 0), which is where a run of e on ⟨ x, y⟩ starts. A moved program runs
exactly as the original with every program counter shifted.

Checked as g_pair_smn (VMGuestRecursion.v), both directions of the equivalence.

24.7 The evaluator, without a black box
There are two program encodings in this chapter. The interpreter appendix packs
words at a chosen fixed width for fast field selection. The recursion theorem instead
uses a self-delimiting syntax code. Mixing them would change the program being
constructed.

For the syntax code, encode a natural number n as n true bits followed by one false
bit. Encode an instruction by its numeric tag followed by its operands and cost, each
in that unary form. The tags are:

Instruction             Tag                               Following fields, in order
HALT                    24                                cost
LOAD_IMM                8                                 destination, immediate, cost
XFER                    7                                 destination, source, cost
ADD, SUB, MUL           11, 12, 35                        destination, first source, second
                                                          source, cost
AND, OR, SHL, SHR       31, 32, 33, 34                    destination, first source, second
                                                          source, cost
JUMP                    13                                target, cost
JNEZ                    14                                source, target, cost



Prefix the instruction sequence with its length, also in unary. Convert the resulting bit
list to a number by B([]) = 1 and B(b :: r ) = b + 2B(r ), treating false and true as 0
and 1. The final leading one distinguishes the end of the bit list. Decoding repeatedly
takes parity and divides by two until that leading one is reached, then parses the
unary fields and the specified number of instructions. Reject an unknown tag, an
unfinished field or leftover bits. Encoding then decoding a guest program returns that
program: induction on each unary field gives its boundary, followed by induction on
the instruction list. This is the number ⌜ p⌝ used in the recursion theorem.

Fix the representing program D. The following finite calculation ED (n, z) either re-
turns a number or reports that this trial has no result:

   1. Unpair z as ⟨c, y⟩. For a positive z, repeatedly divide by two until it is odd: the
      number of divisions is c, and the odd remainder is 2y + 1. Decode c as a guest
      program e′ ; a failed decode gives no result.
   2. Form the actual instruction list spec(e′ , c) using the ten-instruction prefix above
      and the relocated copy of e′ . Encode that list.
   3. Run D on that code for n guest steps. If it has not terminated, give no result.
      Otherwise decode register zero as a guest program q; reject a failed decode.
   4. Run q on y for n guest steps. If it terminates, return the packing of its four


                                           326
The Thiele Machine                                                                Devon Thiele


      registers and ledger given below. Otherwise give no result.

Only positive paired inputs are needed for the fixed point; the implementation’s
unpairing convention sends zero to (0, 0), whose program code fails to decode. Every
trial terminates. It uses finite list operations, arithmetic and two bounded runs. Now
try n = 0, 1, 2, . . . until a trial returns a result. This search need not terminate, which
is exactly what is needed to represent a partial computation. Once a trial returns
a result, every larger trial returns the same result: a terminated guest run stays at
its terminal configuration. If the two required runs terminate after n1 and n2 steps,
any n ≥ max(n1 , n2 ) succeeds. Conversely, a successful trial contains those two
terminating runs.

The output packing also matters because behaviour includes the ledger. For final
registers ( a, b, c, d) and ledger µ, put

                        v = b + 2s ( d + 2s c ),    P( a, b, c, d, µ) = 2((2v + 1)2s ) + 1 2µ .
                                                                                          
s = a + b + c + d,

To decode a valid packing, first count its trailing zero bits to recover µ, remove the
following odd factor’s low one bit, and divide the remainder by two. The result is
(2v + 1)2s . Repeat the trailing-zero operation to recover s and v. Since each register is
at most s < 2s , successive base-2s digits of v recover b, d, c, and a = s − b − c − d. This
works also at s = 0: all four registers are zero.

The evaluator’s search is a partial recursive calculation. The compilation fact used
here is that such a calculation can be realised by a finite counter program with its
input and output represented as natural numbers. The traditional universality con-
structions and the precise counter conventions are identified in Appendix J. The im-
plementation checks the translation through the weak call-by-value calculus and an
increment/decrement counter machine. This is a computability result; it supplies no
useful bound on the resulting program’s size or running time.

The counter program is then simulated in the four-register guest. Its administration
has declared cost zero. Its output epilogue unpacks P: the first trailing-zero loop
charges one per division, producing exactly µ ledger units; the second loop and the
register reconstruction charge zero. Thus the guest evaluator ends with the actual four
registers and ledger, rather than merely a code of them. The paired input’s construc-
tion and all work before that final charging loop cost zero. This is why including the
ledger in behavioural equality does not break the fixed-point construction.


Theorem 24.10 (Guest recursion theorem). For every map F from guest programs to guest
programs that sends well-formed programs to well-formed programs, and every guest program
D that represents F, there is a well-formed guest program p that behaves the same as F ( p).

Proof. Let R be the relation that holds of a number z and an output m when z =


                                              327
The Thiele Machine                                                              Devon Thiele


⟨c, y⟩ with c the code of some program e′ , the run of D on ⌜spec(e′ , c)⌝ terminates
with the code of a program q in register 0, and the run of q on y terminates with
registers and ledger that pack to m. The finite trials ED (n, z) above return exactly
those outputs. Their unbounded search, realised by the counter translation and the
cost-restoring epilogue, gives a well-formed guest evaluator e with exactly this input-
output behaviour. Put c = ⌜e⌝ and p = spec(e, c), well-formed because e is. By
Lemma 24.9, beh p (y, g, µ) ⇐⇒ behe (⟨c, y⟩, g, µ), and by the construction of e the
right side holds exactly when F (spec(e, c)) = F ( p) terminates on y with registers g
and ledger µ. That is p behaving the same as F ( p). The self-reference is the prefix
handing e its own code; the recursion theorem for L in Theorem 11.3 is not used.

Checked as vm_guest_recursion_theorem_closed (VMGuestRecursion.v),
a proof of the proposition vm_guest_recursion_theorem (VMRecursionTar-
get.v), with g_represents_transformer (VMRecursionTarget.v), g_pair_sm
n (VMGuestRecursion.v), hfun_sem and RD_MMA (VMGuestEvalL.v), and g_pipel

Two things it isn’t. It isn’t a recursion theorem for the full fifty-one-instruction machine,
and nothing can be one in the sense Premise 24.2 asks for every map: that premise is
false (part (1) of Theorem 24.3). The guest theorem answers a different question. It
gives fixed points for the guest’s representable transformations, under the unbounded
sibling’s runs, up to equal registers and ledger, and no correspondence theorem turns
that into equal thousand-step runs of the full machine from every state. And the
ledger: the pairing prefix, the evaluator and the compiled Minsky machine all run at
declared cost zero, and a last loop charges, one cost-one instruction per unit, exactly
the ledger of the program being imitated. So the witness ends with the same registers
and the same ledger as F applied to it, because the ledger is part of what “behaves the
same” means. What the theorem doesn’t speak to is efficiency, how many instructions
the witness executes to get there.

24.8 What this closes
The natural objection to a guest recursion theorem is that the evaluator and the spe-
cialiser aren’t things a guest program can call. Here they are: the specialiser is a guest
prefix and the evaluator is a compiled guest program. So the two ingredients of Sec-
tion 11’s diagonal hold on this machine’s guest by proof : Rice from the interpreter,
recursion from the construction. What I haven’t proved is the shortcut predicate itself
on the guest; the wall at the start of this chapter is about bounded-run equality with


                                            328
The Thiele Machine                                                              Devon Thiele


one reference program on the full machine (Definition 24.1), and the guest results are
about behaviour on registers and ledger. On the full machine the diagonal holds under
a premise that no class containing a correct decider’s flip can meet (Theorems 24.1
and 24.3). Both are true; they’re different sentences; and the fragment is where the
unconditional ingredients live.

Next: the one instruction family I’ve been pointing at since Section 16 without building,
the two-player game and the integer check the machine runs on it.

25 The CHSH check
I’ve pointed at a game since Section 16 without building it. Here it is, built from zero,
and then the one thing my machine actually does with it, which is smaller and more
exact than “it checks for quantum behaviour,” a sentence that’s tempting and wrong.
The short version, so you know where this is going: the machine never computes the
famous number and never writes down the famous bound. It tests seven facts about
integers in eight counters. If they pass, a certain five-by-five table has a property called
positive semidefinite, and that property forces the famous number under the famous
bound. The wall is a consequence, not an ingredient. Everything else is explaining
those sentences.

But first, why is a quantum game in a book about records at all? Not for the physics.
Nothing in this section tests nature, and the machine can’t tell honest play from a
made-up tally (the guarantee paragraph below says exactly how). It’s here for three
reasons, all about the machine. It’s a check whose content is striking enough to tempt
anyone into thinking that certifying it should cost more than certifying something dull,
and the three tiers of Section 22 show it doesn’t: certified is certified, at the same floor.
It sets free observation against a priced check: a round of the game is written down for
nothing, and judging the pile costs the floor. And it’s an integer test small enough to
live inside one instruction and be carried all the way down to a circuit, which makes
it a serious test of whether a check survives the trip to hardware. One more thing to
know before any of it: a passed CHSH check feeds no record. On success it steps on,
and neither the flag nor the assertion channel moves (Section 17). The check happened,
and nothing was committed.

25.1 The game
Two players, Alice and Bob, in separate rooms. A referee flips two coins and hands
Alice a question x, zero or one, and Bob a question y, zero or one. Alice answers
a, zero or one; Bob answers b. No talking during the game. They may agree on a
plan beforehand, as detailed as they like. They win a round when their answers differ
exactly when both questions were one. In words: if either question is zero, match; if both
are one, differ.

Try to win every time. A plan is a list: what Alice says to x equals zero, what she says
to x equals one, and the same two for Bob. Four bits. Now write the four requirements


                                            329
The Thiele Machine                                                                    Devon Thiele


the rounds impose: a0 equals b0 (both asked zero); a0 equals b1; a1 equals b0; a1 differs
from b1. Chain the first three: a0 equals b0 equals a1, and a0 equals b1, so b0 equals
b1. But the fourth says a1 differs from b1, and a1 equals b0 equals b1. Contradiction.
One of the four must break. So any plan loses at least one of the four question pairs,
and if the referee asks all four equally often, the best a plan can do is three out of
four. Seventy-five percent. Do it the long way too: there are sixteen plans (four bits),
and if you write them all out and count wins you’ll find eight win three rounds and
eight win one, and none wins four (the broken requirements always come in odd
numbers, which you can see by adding up the four equations: the left sides cancel
to zero and the right sides to one). Sharing a coin before the game to pick a plan at
random doesn’t help; a mixture of numbers no larger than three-quarters is no larger
than three-quarters. Arthur Fine proved in 1982 that the whole “pre-agreed answers,
no influence between rooms” story is exactly the mixtures of those sixteen lists, one
scoreboard for all four questions at once; the sixteen are the whole classical story.

The number. Recode answers zero and one as plus one and minus one. For each
question pair, let E be the average, over many rounds, of Alice’s answer times Bob’s.
The CHSH quantity is S equals E00 plus E01 plus E10 minus E11. For one fixed plan
each win adds one to S and each loss subtracts one, so S is wins minus losses: a three-
win plan has S equal to two, a one-win plan has minus two. With equal question
frequencies, the win rate is one half plus S over eight. So “seventy-five percent” and
“S at most two” are the same fact, and the second is the one that got the name.

The machine can play the three-out-of-four ceiling for free. One short program sets
up two modules and then runs four trials, one per question pair, with both players
answering zero every time. After the recoding every answer is plus one, so all four
correlators are one: the all-ones plan, which matches on every pair and so wins the
three pairs that ask for a match. Every instruction in it is declared at cost zero.


Theorem 25.1 (The classical ceiling, reached at zero cost). Let t be the list PNEW, PSPLIT,
and four CHSH_TRIAL instructions, one for each question pair ( x, y), each with both answers
0 and declared cost 0. The cost model’s total charge for t is 0, and running t in order from the
clean state (all registers zero, counter zero, no trials recorded) leaves trial counters whose score
S = E00 + E01 + E10 − E11 , computed in rationals from the counters, equals 2.

Proof. Computation: the charge is a sum of six zeros, and running the six steps leaves
one “same” round in each of the four pairs, so each correlator is 1 and S = 1 + 1 + 1 −
1 = 2.

Checked as classical_bound_achieved (ClassicalBound.v). Nothing in it says
the rounds were played; a program can tally anything at zero cost, and the theorem
only shows that the ceiling is reachable. The other side, that no finite mixture of plans
beats two, is Theorem F.2 in Appendix F, one direction of Fine’s result.



                                                330
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


25.2 Where it came from, and why anyone cared
So who started this, and why would anybody care whether two rooms can win a coin
game? The trail starts in 1935, with Einstein, Podolsky and Rosen asking whether
quantum mechanics describes everything that’s real about a pair of particles. Their
argument: if measuring one particle lets you predict the other’s result with certainty,
the result must already have been fixed, and the theory leaves that out. The wall they
had in mind was a pre-agreed list of answers, the plan above. And the first thing worth
checking is whether the paper even says what Einstein meant. By his own account,
not quite. Podolsky did the writing, and that June Einstein wrote to Schrödinger that
the essential thing had been “smothered by formalism.” The person who lays that
letter out is Arthur Fine, the same Fine whose theorem closed the sixteen plans above,
in his encyclopedia entry on the argument. So even the founding paper is a lead to
check, not a verdict.

For thirty years that was philosophy. In 1964 John Bell turned it into arithmetic: if each
particle carries pre-agreed answers and nothing travels between the rooms, certain
averages can’t exceed a fixed number, and quantum theory predicts they do. And
where does a paper like that get published? In a brand-new journal called Physics
Physique Fizika, which charged authors no page fees and in fact paid them by the word,
and which folded in 1968 after four volumes. The story told in Andrew Whitaker’s
biography of Bell is that the journal gave out no free copies, so Bell spent his payment
buying copies of his own paper to mail to other physicists. What his inequality rules
out is the pair of assumptions together, called local realism (answers exist before you
ask, and no influence across the gap), not either one alone. In 1969 Clauser, Horne,
Shimony and Holt rewrote it as the four-average form above, S at most two, which
could be tried in a lab with imperfect equipment.

Then the obvious next question: did anybody actually try it? Freedman and Clauser
tried it in 1972; Aspect’s group did it in 1982 with the measurement settings switched
while the photons were in flight. Before that, in 1975, Alain Aspect went to see Bell at
CERN to tell him what he planned, and by Aspect’s own account Bell heard him out in
silence and then asked, first thing, whether he had a permanent position. Aspect did.
Bell’s reason, as Aspect tells it, was that most physicists would take the experiment
for a waste of time, or take him for a crackpot. And in 2015 three groups (Hensen’s in
Delft with electrons a kilometre apart; Giustina’s; Shalm’s) closed the two main escape
routes at once. Clauser, Aspect and Zeilinger got the 2022 Nobel for it. So in under
fifty years the subject went from a question you needed a permanent job to risk to a
Nobel. The lab number sits above two. A remaining escape, that the referee’s coins
were secretly correlated with the particles, is a philosophical one and I’m not going to
pretend it’s closed.

What quantum play does: if the players share an entangled pair and choose what to
measure from their question, the best they can do is S equals two times the square root
of two, about 2.83, a win rate of about eighty-five percent. Boris Tsirelson showed in

                                           331
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


1980 that that’s a ceiling: quantum correlations violate Bell, but only up to there.

And the wall above that, which is the one I find most instructive. In 1994 Popescu
and Rohrlich asked: what if you only demand that nothing can be signalled, that
Alice’s answers on their own have the same odds whatever Bob is asked, and the
other way round? Then you can write down a “box” (the PR box, after their initials)
that wins every round (its answers differ exactly when both questions are one, by fiat,
each answer alone a fair coin), S equals four, and nothing about it lets either room
send a message. So relativity alone doesn’t explain the quantum ceiling; the PR box
obeys relativity and beats 2.83. The order is: two for plans, 2.83 for quantum, four for
no-signalling.

And the box has the same kind of history as everything else in this book: somebody
got there first. Popescu and Rohrlich’s initials stuck, but the big review of the field by
Nicolas Brunner and four coauthors credits boxes like it to Peter Rastall and, separately,
to Leonid Khalfin and Tsirelson himself, both in 1985, nine years before. Then the
question that really matters: if relativity isn’t what stops things at 2.83, what is? People
have tried candidates. In 2005 Wim van Dam showed that with enough PR boxes, Bob
could work out any yes-or-no function of both their inputs after Alice sends him a
single bit, which would make the whole question of how much two parties need to
talk collapse, and that’s a strong hint the boxes are too good to be real. In 2009 Marcin
Pawłowski and five coauthors proposed a principle they called information causality:
Bob can’t get more information about Alice’s data than the bits she actually sends him.
Ordinary and quantum physics both obey it, and any theory that beats 2.83 breaks it.
It recovers part of the quantum boundary, not all of it. Which principle fixes 2.83 is
still an open question, and this book won’t answer it. My machine’s check is a fence
at the middle step.

25.3 Wrong turns to take off the table
Every one of these gets said with a straight face, and every one is easy to say by
accident, so here they are, each with what’s actually true beside it.

“Faster than light.” Nothing travels. Each room alone sees fair coins; the correlation
shows up only when you lay the two columns side by side afterward. “Quantum
means random.” The average S is fixed by the state; what’s random is each single
answer; the plans are the less random side. “A Bell violation proves nonlocality.” It
rules out local realism, both assumptions together, and every real test has loopholes
with names. “A tally above two proves nonlocality.” No: S is a population average,
and one finite tally can land above two by luck. Four rounds, one per question pair,
with coin-flip answers, reach S equals four one time in sixteen. That gap between a
population bound and a finite sample is the problem Zhang, Glancy and Knill work
through for real Bell tests (Physical Review A, 2013), and the book doesn’t solve it.
The kernel proves only the narrow thing, that a tally above two is not explained by
one fixed plan replayed every round (chsh_violation_rules_out_locally_fact


                                            332
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


orizable_coupling), and that narrow thing is what the sentence has to stay. And
“the PSD test proves the data is quantum.” (PSD is short for positive semidefinite, the
property of the five-by-five table from the short version; the next part builds both.)
It doesn’t, and the direction matters. Passing implies the five-by-five table, pinned
in a way the next part explains, is PSD, and that implies S squared is at most eight;
both are proved. Whether the correlators of a PSD table like that are the correlators
of some quantum strategy is the cited Tsirelson, Landau and Masanes result, and I
haven’t proved it here. Failing says nothing: the check is sound and not complete, and
quantum behaviour can fail it. Every one of the sixteen plans fails it, and I’ll show you
why. What it guarantees is in the last part of this section.

25.4 The five-by-five, and what positive semidefinite means
Here’s the mathematics the check rests on, and it’s one idea: a table of numbers could be
a table of dot products. Take a two-by-two symmetric table with a and c on the diagonal
and b off it. It’s positive semidefinite (PSD) when a and c are at least zero and a times
c minus b squared is at least zero. Check two by hand: ones on the diagonal and one
half off, the determinant is three quarters, passes; ones on the diagonal and 1.2 off,
the determinant is negative, fails. The reading: PSD means the table could be the dot
products of some arrows, and 1.2 is too big a dot product for two arrows of length one.
That’s the whole idea, generalised to bigger tables.

Now the table. Rows and columns labelled I, A0, A1, B0, B1 (the identity, Alice’s
two questions, Bob’s two). Diagonal all ones. The I row and column all zero (that’s
“zero marginals”: the table takes each answer alone to average to zero, a fair coin;
the machine records no marginals and doesn’t test this). A0 with A1 zero, B0 with
B1 zero (no round asks Alice both questions, so no tally holds that average, and the
table sets it to zero). Those zeros are choices, they pin the table to one slice, and I’ll
come back to what they cost. And the four Alice-Bob cells hold the four correlators E.
That’s a five-by-five with four free numbers in it. It splits into the one in the corner
and a four-by-four block made of an identity and the two-by-two grid E of correlators,
and PSD of that block is the same as saying E shrinks every vector (E is a contraction),
which is three inequalities: one minus E00 squared minus E10 squared at least zero;
one minus E01 squared minus E11 squared at least zero; and their product at least the
square of (E00 E01 plus E10 E11).

Run it. All four correlators 0.6 except E11 at minus 0.6, S equals 2.4: the two diagonal
terms are 0.28 and 0.28, the cross term zero, passes; above two, below 2.83. All four
at one over root two (E11 negative): diagonals zero, cross term zero, passes with no
slack, S equals two root two exactly, the 2.83; nudge any entry’s size up and a diagonal
goes negative. The all-ones plan (one, one, one, one): first diagonal is one minus one
minus one, negative, fails, though S equals two and it’s a perfectly legal classical play.
The PR box (one, one, one, minus one): fails the same way. A fence at the middle step,
and a fence that keeps out every one of the sixteen plans: each has all four correlators
at plus or minus one, so the first diagonal is always one minus one minus one. Only

                                           333
The Thiele Machine                                                                  Devon Thiele


diluted mixtures of plans get through.

In 2007 Navascués, Pironio and Acín showed this is the first rung of a ladder: big-
ger tables of expected products, each PSD, each a necessary condition for quantum
behaviour when its entries are left free, each rung tighter, and (their 2008 paper) con-
verging to the quantum set (strictly, the set from commuting operators, which can
differ from the tensor-product set in general scenarios). The machine’s table is the first
rung with the marginals and the two within-party entries pinned to zero. Pinning is
a stronger demand than the rung makes, so passing puts you inside the first rung,
and a quantum point can still fail. Landau in 1988 and Masanes in 2003 found the
exact boundary for this two-questions-each case, and it’s not a straight line at 2.83
but a curved surface (the arc-sine form) touching it at one point. So the obvious next
question: if every rung is tighter than the last, does some rung finally land exactly on
the quantum set and stop? A 2026 paper by Chaturvedi says no: no finite rung of the
ladder captures the whole quantum set even in this simplest case, which is the caution
this book keeps about the ladder, confirmed from outside.

25.5 What the machine actually does
Eight counters (Section 16): for each of the four question pairs, one counting rounds
where the answers matched and one where they differed. One instruction, the trial,
bumps one counter per round, after checking all four inputs are bits; it checks no
inequality and records no marginals. Then one instruction, the check, reads the eight
and tests seven integer facts. For each pair, let N be same plus different and D be same
minus different (so E is D over N). The seven: the four N are strictly positive (every
pair was sampled; a pair with no rounds is rejected, not read as a correlator of zero);
A, which is N00 squared N10 squared minus D00 squared N10 squared minus D10
squared N00 squared, is at least zero; B, the same with the other column, is at least
zero; and with C equal to D00 D01 N10 N11 plus D10 D11 N00 N01, C squared is at
most A times B. Those are the three contraction inequalities with the denominators
cleared. No division, no reals, no square root, no S. Try it: counters (same, different) of
(4, 1), (4, 1), (4, 1), (1, 4) give E of 0.6, 0.6, 0.6, minus 0.6; N is five and D is three (minus
three for the last); A is 175, B is 175, C is zero; passes. That’s the first example above,
the S equals 2.4 one, in integers.

If the seven pass, the instruction steps on: the program counter advances and the
ledger rises by the charge, and nothing else changes, not the flag, not the channel;
success is visible only as “no trap.” If any fails, it traps to the fixed address with the
error code and flag. Either way it costs the declared cost plus one, the floor. The
theorem chain, in words: a passed check gives PSD of the five-by-five built from
the counters; contraction and PSD are equivalent, both directions; and PSD forces S
squared at most eight. The names are in the statements below. The underlying algebra
is one identity: four times the sum of the four correlators squared, minus S squared,
is a sum of six squares (chsh_gap_is_sum_of_squares), so if the row sums of
squares are at most one, S squared is at most eight (tsirelson_squared), and the

                                               334
The Thiele Machine                                                                 Devon Thiele


point one over root two reaches it (tsirelson_tight). That’s Tsirelson’s bound as
algebra, with no Hilbert space (the mathematical home of quantum states) in it.

Here is the chain as three statements. The derivations are in Appendix F; this is what
they prove.


Definition 25.1 (Correlators from the counters; the pinned matrix). For a state s and
a question pair xy, let Exy (s) = (samexy − diffxy )/(samexy + diffxy ) from its trial
counters, read as 0 when both are 0. For reals Exy , M( E) is the symmetric five-by-
five matrix on I, A0 , A1 , B0 , B1 with ones on the diagonal, Exy in the cells ( A x , By ) and
( By , A x ), and zero everywhere else (Definition F.5). M is PSD when vT Mv ≥ 0 for
every real vector v, and S( E) = E00 + E01 + E10 − E11 .


Theorem 25.2 (The gate implies the pinned matrix is PSD). Let s be a state whose error
flag is false, let d be a declared cost, and let s′ be the result of CHSH_LASSERT d on s. If the
error flag of s′ equals that of s, then M ( E(s)) is symmetric and PSD.

Proof. When the integer check fails the step sets the error flag, which the hypotheses
rule out, so the check passed. Its four positivity facts make every denominator positive,
so each Exy (s) is Dxy /Nxy , and dividing the other three facts by positive squares turns
them into the three contraction inequalities (Lemma F.15). Contraction is equivalent
to PSD of M( E) by a Schur complement on the four-by-four block (Corollary F.13).
Nothing about the program counter is needed: the error flag alone says which branch
ran.

Checked as chsh_lassert_no_trap_implies_npa_psd (QuantumParti-
tionPSD.v), through chsh_lassert_check_implies_npa_psd and npa_psd_
iff_column_contractive.


Theorem 25.3 (PSD forces the Tsirelson bound). For all real E00 , E01 , E10 , E11 : if M( E) is
symmetric and PSD, then S( E)2 ≤ 8.

Proof. A PSD matrix with unit diagonal has every three-by-three principal minor at
                                                    2 − E2 , and on rows A , B , B it is
least zero. On rows A0 , B0 , B1 that minor is 1 − E00   01                1  0   1
      2     2                                                              2      2
1 − E10 − E11 , so the four squares sum to at most 2. The identity 4 ∑ xy Exy − S = a
sum of six squares then gives S2 ≤ 4 · 2 = 8.

Checked as npa_psd_implies_tsirelson_bound (MuLedgerQuantumBridge.v),
with the row bounds npa_psd_zero_marginal_implies_row_bounds and the
identity chsh_gap_is_sum_of_squares (TsirelsonFromAlgebra.v); this is Theo-
rem F.14 in the appendix.

The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


Corollary 25.4 (A passed gate means the bound). Under the hypotheses of Theorem 25.2,
S( E(s))2 ≤ 8.

Proof. Theorem 25.2 supplies positive semidefiniteness of the pinned moment matrix
for these four correlators. Theorem F.14 in the derivation appendix applies to every
such matrix and gives S2 ≤ 8. Its quadratic form calculation is printed there; no
additional property of the machine is used.

Checked as the composition of chsh_lassert_no_trap_implies_npa_psd and
