Remark 25.1 (Sound, not complete). The pinned matrix is stricter than the quantum
question it is usually read against. PSD of M ( E) gives the correlators a PSD completion,
since the zeros are one choice of the two free entries (zero_marginal_implies_e
lliptope, ElliptopeCompletion.v). The converse fails. The all-ones plan has a PSD
completion (deterministic_strategy_elliptope), and every deterministic
plan is a quantum strategy, a standard fact cited and not proved here; yet its minor
on rows A0 , B0 , B1 is 1 − 1 − 1 = −1, so M( E) is not PSD there, and a tally of one
matching round per pair gives A = 1 − 1 − 1 = −1 in the integer check, so the gate
traps. Those two failures are my arithmetic, not named theorems. So a pass proves the
bound and a trap proves nothing about the tally. The zero-cost trace of Theorem 25.1
is exactly such a tally: it reaches S = 2 and the gate would throw it out.


One thing about that trap is worth saying on its own. The check traps to the same
fixed address that LASSERT uses when a formula’s certificate fails, with the same error
flag and the same rule for the charge: the attempt pays, declared cost plus one, and
LASSERT more for the formula’s length. One wall comes from the moment-matrix
mathematics (the table of expected products above), which I didn’t write. The other
is a logical constraint a program hands to LASSERT. The step treats them the same
way: the counter charges the attempt to narrow, and it never asks whether the wall
was found or built. And that’s a claim about the step, not about the chip. Four of the
check instructions below have no hardware encoding at all, and that doesn’t change a
word of the step theorems. The law lives in the transition, not in the gate count.

None of that algebra is new, and I don’t want it to read as if it were. Tsirelson’s bound
has been formalised before, in Isabelle/HOL by Echenim and Mhalla and in Lean’s
Mathlib, and Navascués, Pironio and Acín already analyse this very matrix by Schur
complement and discuss the level above it. What I think is mine here is smaller: an
integer decision procedure on the counters, living inside an instruction; a checked link



                                           336
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


from “the instruction didn’t trap” to PSD to the bound; and a circuit proved equal to
that check for thirty-two-bit counters.

So here, in one paragraph, is what the gate guarantees. If the machine steps past the
check without trapping, then every question pair was sampled, the four empirical
ratios satisfy three polynomial inequalities, hence the fixed five-by-five is PSD, hence
S squared is at most eight. It does not guarantee that the tally came from honest play
(a program chooses its own trial inputs and can tally whatever it likes at zero cost;
the kernel has a zero-cost trace with S equals four, TsirelsonUpperBound.v, to
make sure nobody forgets). It does not guarantee any marginal is zero (the machine
records no marginals and can’t test them). It does not guarantee any quantum state
exists, or that the correlators lie in the quantum set rather than a larger fence. And it
traps the tally of every single plan, honest classical play included. It has no margin for
sampling noise either. Honest play at Tsirelson’s point aims at correlators of plus or
minus one over root two, and there every pair of squared correlators the check adds
up comes to exactly one, the edge of what it accepts. So an honest tally aimed at that
point sits right on the line, and ordinary luck over a finite number of rounds pushes it
over a good share of the time, and the check traps. That’s my arithmetic about where
the point sits, not a theorem in the files. The check certifies a shape of the tally. What
the shape means is a question for whoever supplied the rounds.

And the tally isn’t a claim. Trials pile up for free; the counters are a record of what
a program said happened, and the ledger has no opinion about a record. The priced
step is the one that stands up and commits to something. On this machine the only
instruction that can move the assertion channel off zero is MORPH_ASSERT: a run
of a program with no MORPH_ASSERT in it, from channel zero, never reaches a
nonzero channel (non_morph_assert_trace_cannot_gain_supra_cert, Rev-
elationRequirement.v). A wider theorem with a misleading name, nonlocal_corr
elation_requires_revelation, says that if a run from channel zero ends with
it nonzero, the program contains a REVEAL, EMIT, LJOIN, LASSERT or MORPH_
ASSERT. Its “supra” predicate is just “the channel is nonzero”; it knows nothing about
CHSH, and asking for REVEAL in front of a super-quantum claim is runtime policy,
which the source says. What MORPH_ASSERT commits to is a label on an existing
arrow. Whether the label is true of the pile of tallies is a separate question, and CHSH_
LASSERT is the priced check that answers part of it. Statistics are free; the claim about
them is what costs.

In the chip, the check is a circuit, and the word-level circuit is proved to compute
the same seven facts as the kernel for every set of eight thirty-two-bit counters (the
intermediate products need 134 and 268 bits, which is why the circuit takes twenty-
nine firings, one hardware rule run twenty-nine times over (Section 27 says what a
rule is); chsh_check_word_correct, chsh_run_result, and, for the whole step
under its usual side conditions, chsh_lassert_refines). The kernel’s counters
are unbounded naturals and the chip’s are thirty-two bits, so the equivalence is for


                                           337
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


counters that fit. That’s Section 27’s.

25.6 A rational stand-in for an irrational number
One number you’ll see in the files: 5657 over 2000, which is 2.8285, and two root
two is 2.82842... It’s the four-decimal round-up, chosen so that rational code can test
“above the Tsirelson bound” without square roots, and it’s safe because 5657 squared
is 32,001,649 and eight times 2000 squared is 32,000,000, so the fraction sits above root
eight by about seven parts in a hundred thousand (rational_tsirelson_bound).
It’s used in a receipt-level predicate and a few rational theorems. It is not used in the
integer gate, and the real-number theorems use root eight. Nothing in the hardware
files mentions it either: the chip checks CHSH in integers.

25.7 Three more tests, and how far each one is in the machine
The second rung: a nine-by-nine table on I, the four questions, and the four Alice-Bob
products, with the correlators and five extra free numbers for three- and four-body
entries. Its PSD is again equivalent to a contraction-like condition (q1ab_psd_iff_c
olumn_contractive), and there are four more check instructions in the kernel for it,
taking the extra numbers as caller-supplied counters, with a cascade of two Schur steps
down to a four-by-four that Sylvester’s criterion closes (chsh_lassert_1ab_g12
345_no_trap_implies_npa_psd_q1ab). Soundness only; the interior predicates
demand strict positivity, so boundary points need another route. And a fact that’s
easy to list without noticing what it means: the variant with all five extra numbers
at zero certifies a strict subset of the classical set (the ball where the four correlators’
squares sum to at most one), forcing S at most two (q1ab_check_at_gzero_imp
lies_classical_bound); it can’t certify anything above the classical line. To get
a point above two you have to supply the extras (q1ab_certifies_a_supercla
ssical_chsh_point, S equals 2.4 with one extra at minus one half). Those four
instructions are the four with no hardware encoding (Section 17). In order: the one
with all five extra numbers at zero, then the one with only the four-body entry free,
then three free entries (the two three-body entries and the four-body one, closed by
a four-by-four Sylvester test), then all five. Each is proved sound on its own (chsh_
lassert_1ab_no_trap_implies_npa_psd_q1ab, chsh_lassert_1ab_g5_n
o_trap_implies_npa_psd_q1ab, chsh_lassert_1ab_g345_no_trap_impl
ies_npa_psd_q1ab, chsh_lassert_1ab_g12345_no_trap_implies_npa_p
sd_q1ab, QuantumPartitionPSD_1AB.v, 5076, 5104, 5156). Their parameter domains
grow in that order. That the sets they accept grow too is not proved, and I won’t say
it. The Python side (the assembler script and the generated opcode table, Section 17)
gives them the numbers 0x2F to 0x32; no Coq file and no hardware file uses those
bytes.

The two sizes are one test, not two. A single positive-semidefinite predicate takes the
size as a parameter, and the five-by-five and the nine-by-nine are it at two sizes.

The Thiele Machine                                                                  Devon Thiele


Definition 25.2 (The size-generic PSD test). A claim is a top index n and a ma-
trix M indexed by naturals. It is realizable when Mij = M ji for all i, j ≤ n and
∑i≤n ∑ j≤n vi Mij v j ≥ 0 for every real vector v. The CHSH claim of E is top index
4 with the matrix M( E) of Definition 25.1; the level-1+AB claim uses top index 8 and
the nine-by-nine matrix.


Corollary 25.5 (The level-1 test is the size-five case). For all real E00 , E01 , E10 , E11 : the
three contraction inequalities hold if and only if the CHSH claim of E is realizable. The same
holds at size nine for the level-1+AB contraction condition and its claim.

Proof. Realizability at top index 4 unfolds to symmetry and PSD of the five-by-five, by
computing the finite sums, and that is equivalent to contraction by Corollary F.13. At
size nine the same unfolding meets Theorem F.20. Nothing new is proved about the
matrices; the point is that one predicate covers both.

Checked as column_contractive_iff_general_realizable (GenRealizabil-

machine-step form vm_chsh_lassert_step_is_general_realizable, which
has the hypotheses of Theorem 25.2.

The third thing: the elliptope, the set of correlators for which some choice of the two
missing entries (A0 with A1, B0 with B1) makes the five-by-five PSD. Every one of the
sixteen plans is inside it (deterministic_strategy_elliptope), mixtures stay
inside (elliptope_convex), Tsirelson’s point is inside (elliptope_tsirelson),
the PR box is out (pr_box_not_elliptope), and it’s strictly bigger than the classical
set (beyond_classical_elliptope). There’s a decider for it with a soundness
proof, in two branches: a strict Sylvester check with the completion supplied, and a
rational factorisation certificate of the completed matrix, checked in integers. What’s
proved is that a pass puts the correlators inside the set and that no choice of inputs
gets the PR box through (elliptope_check_full_sound, elliptope_full_
gate_never_accepts_pr_box), and, by computation, that some named points
pass, the all-ones plan and a point that the cited arc-sine boundary puts exactly on
the quantum edge among them (gate_accepts_all_ones, gate_accepts_pyt
hagorean_boundary). The file’s header also argues that every point with a rational
PSD completion has such a certificate; that is a comment, not a theorem. It is not an
instruction. No step of the machine mentions it, and its file says the opcode and cost
schedule are not done. I may call it a decider with a soundness proof. I may not call it
part of the machine.

25.8 What isn’t proved
The arc-sine curve. That any of these sets equals what quantum mechanics can reach.
That any state or measurement achieves 2.83. Those are the cited external results, and
the files say so in their scope notes. Also: the finite-mixture theorem (fine_theo


                                              339
The Thiele Machine                                                              Devon Thiele


rem in the source) proves only one direction, that a finite local model satisfies the
bound; Fine’s actual theorem is an equivalence, so “Fine’s theorem is proved” would
be wrong and I haven’t said it. And one more thing the kernel says about itself, which
the guarantee paragraph above already used: a zero-cost trace is not thereby classical
(the S equals four trace). The correlators (one, one, one, minus one) are the PR box,
not a classical play; the classical vertex that fails the gate is (one, one, one, one).

That’s the game, the number, the two walls, and the check. Last of the machine
sections: what all this costs against physics, and the hierarchy of what costs more.

26 The counter against physics, and the mu-hierarchy
Section 4 did the physics argument once: on a finite machine a permanent flag merges
states, Landauer’s principle (a named premise) prices merges, and the toll follows.
I’m not going to do it again. This section is about what the machine’s counter has to
do with any of that, and the answer is: less than the word “Landauer” in a file name
suggests, and I’d rather you hear the exact amount from me.

26.1 A bookkeeping indicator, bounded by what it indicates
The machine has a function that, for each instruction, returns one if the instruction’s
cost is positive and zero otherwise. The source calls it irreversible_bits, and
the name is the problem, so let me say what it is before saying what it’s called. It’s
an indicator: it marks cost-positive instructions. Sum it over a run and you get the
count of cost-positive instructions executed. The theorem is that this count is at most
the run’s total cost (total_irreversible_bits_le_cost), and the proof is two
cases per instruction: if the cost is zero the indicator is zero; if the cost is positive the
indicator is one and one is at most the cost. A zero-one indicator bounded by what it
indicates. That’s all.

What it shares with Landauer: the shape, a lower-bound quantity attached to an event.
What it doesn’t share: everything else. It’s not an irreversibility theorem. There’s no
physics in the proof, no microscopic erasure model, no physical entropy, no Boltzmann
constant. The label “irreversible” on a cost-positive instruction is bookkeeping, not a
proof that the instruction erased anything or was physically irreversible. Section 23
showed you that the machine’s zero-cost JUMP does merge states and is charged
nothing. And several of the cost-positive instructions (the check, the join, the emit)
change only the program counter and the ledger when they succeed; by the step rule
they’re one-to-one on the state, which I get from reading the definition and not from a
stated theorem. The indicator counts charges. It doesn’t count erasures.


Definition 26.1 (The indicator). For an instruction i with schedule cost cost(i ), let
ind(i ) = 0 if cost(i ) = 0 and 1 otherwise. For a list t of instructions, ind(t) and cost(t)
are the sums over its members.




                                            340
The Thiele Machine                                                               Devon Thiele


Theorem 26.1 (The indicator is bounded by the cost). For every list of instructions t,
ind(t) ≤ cost(t).

Proof. Per instruction, two cases: cost zero gives 0 ≤ 0, positive cost gives 1 ≤ cost(i ).
Induction on t adds the cases up.

Checked as irreversible_bits_le_cost and total_irreversible_bits_l
e_cost (LandauerDerivation.v, 240). The source names the indicator irreversibl
e_bits.

26.2 The calibration is a unit conversion
There’s a function in the source that multiplies the counter by a chosen energy per
mark, and a theorem that a state with one mark, at the scale kT ln 2 per mark, carries
kT ln 2 of energy (calibrated_mu_landauer_energy, proving the predicate m
u_landauer_calibration for every k and T). Read that for exactly what it is: a
unit conversion, true by definition, with the scale as a free input. Nothing in it picks
the scale. The theorem would be just as true with the scale set to a dollar a mark,
and I’d rather say that than let the name “Landauer” in it do any work. What would
connect marks to joules is the premise in Section 4, landauer_heat, and that one is
an assumption with a name that nothing proves. And even as a scale, k B T ln 2 a mark
is the floor for one particular squeeze, a halving. Corollary 4.9’s floor for a flip that
brings k states into a room already holding m is k B T ln mm+k , and for one newcomer into
a big room that’s far below a halving, roughly k B T/m. Price every mark at k B T ln 2
and you can overstate the floor of a single narrow flip by a factor that grows with m.

Remember the constant from Boltzmann’s grave in Part II, the exchange rate between
a count and heat? It has a newer chapter, and it makes the point sharper than I can.
The k B in k B T ln 2 turns a temperature into an energy, and for most of its history it
was a measured number, with error bars, pinned down by careful experiments. Since
20 May 2019 it isn’t. That day the international system of units was redefined so
that Boltzmann’s constant is exactly 1.380649 × 10−23 joules per kelvin, by definition,
and the kelvin is whatever makes that true. So the conversion from temperature to
energy has been a convention since then, in the strictest sense: nobody can measure
it wrong any more. What’s still physics is everything around it, whether wiping a
bit at a temperature really sheds that much heat, which is what the Lyon bead was
measuring. The calibration theorem is the same kind of move as that redefinition. It
fixes a conversion, and the physics, if there is any, is somewhere else.


Definition 26.2 (Energy at a scale). For a real number c (joules per mark) and a state s,
the energy of s at scale c is µ(s) · c. The Landauer calibration at k B and T is the statement
that every state with µ(s) = 1 has energy k B T ln 2 at scale k B T ln 2.


Theorem 26.2 (The calibration is a unit conversion). (1) For all real k B and T, the


                                             341
The Thiele Machine                                                              Devon Thiele


Landauer calibration at k B and T holds. (2) There are two energy readings of the state, at
scales 1 and 2, that disagree on every state with one mark.

Proof. (1) Substitute µ(s) = 1: 1 · k B T ln 2 = k B T ln 2, by ring arithmetic, for any k B
and T, positive or not. (2) At µ(s) = 1 the two readings are 1 and 2.

Checked as calibrated_mu_landauer_energy (PricingPhysicsAudit.v), which
proves mu_landauer_calibration (PricingPhysicsTarget.v) for all k B and T, and
mu_has_no_intrinsic_joule_value (PricingPhysicsAudit.v). The physics is
the premise of Section 4, restated here once in the form the next theorems test. In
words first: a dissipation hands each instruction a whole number of heat units, each
unit worth kT ln 2. Landauer’s principle, in that currency, says an instruction that
takes at least one state where some yes-or-no property is false to a state where it’s true,
and never sends a true one back to false, dissipates at least one unit. The calibration
says no instruction dissipates more units than the counter charges it. One word about
that word: “dissipation” here means heat handed to the surroundings, not waste, in
the sense Section 4 took from Sagawa: a bill for where the forgotten bit goes, not a tax
on doing it badly. Two premises, nothing proved about either, and the only question
is whether they can sit in the same room:


Premise 26.3 (Landauer, in units of the counter). A dissipation is a function δ from
instructions to naturals, counted in units of k B T ln 2. Landauer’s principle, in this
vocabulary (Premise 4.5 of Section 4): every instruction that collapses a yes-or-no
property has δ(i ) ≥ 1, where i collapses P when some state with P false is sent to a
state with P true and every state with P true is sent to one with P true. The calibration:
δ(i ) ≤ cost(i ) for every instruction. Neither is proved anywhere; the theorems below
ask whether they can hold together.


26.3 The premises have to be able to hold together
Here’s the one piece of this section that I think is good physics discipline, and it’s a
consistency test. Suppose you want to claim the counter tracks dissipation. You need
two premises: that a positively charged step dissipates something positive, and an
upper calibration that bounds dissipation by the charge. Can those two hold at once?
There’s a theorem saying exactly when (calibrated_model_exists_iff_posi
tive_cost): a model satisfying both exists precisely when every operation you’ve
chosen to count (the statement below calls those eligible) costs at least one. I should
say how cheap that is. The model the proof builds takes the dissipation to be the cost
itself, so the theorem shows the two premises don’t contradict each other, not that the
counter tracks any dissipation. Still, it does bite on a schedule: if you count a zero-cost
step, no such model can exist. The one place the tree shows the premises holding
is a one-bit reset, where resetting costs one and idling costs nothing (bit_model
_has_satisfiable_calibration); for the machine’s certifying steps it follows


                                            342
The Thiele Machine                                                                     Devon Thiele


from that equivalence and the floor theorems of Section 23, and I haven’t stated it
as a separate theorem. The full machine fails the test, and there’s a theorem that
says so flatly: no dissipation function can both charge at least one for every step that
collapses two classes of states, for any yes-or-no property of states you care to pick,
and stay bounded by the machine’s cost, because JUMP to one at cost zero collapses
the classes of the property “the program counter is one” and costs nothing (landaue
r_dissipation_premises_inconsistent). The premise pair fails for the whole
instruction set. That’s the honest shape, and it’s the same shape as Section 23’s “prices
the certifying merge, leaves the jump free.”


Theorem 26.3 (When the premises can hold together). (1) For any set of operations, any
predicate “eligible” on them, and any cost, a dissipation with δ(i ) ≥ 1 on every eligible i and
δ(i ) ≤ cost(i ) on every i exists if and only if every eligible operation costs at least one. (2) On
a one-bit machine with a reset of cost 1 and an idle of cost 0, taking “eligible” to mean “sends
two different states to one”, such a dissipation exists. (3) On the full machine, no dissipation
satisfies Premise 26.3 for every yes-or-no property.

Proof. (1) If such a δ exists, 1 ≤ δ(i ) ≤ cost(i ). Conversely, take δ = cost. (2) The reset
is the only operation that sends two states to one, and it costs 1; apply (1). (3) Let P be
“the program counter is 1”. JUMP to 1 with declared cost 0 collapses P: it sends the
initial state, where P is false, to one where it is true, and every state lands at program
counter 1. So δ of that jump is at least 1 and at most its cost, which is 0.

Checked as calibrated_model_exists_iff_positive_cost (ObservationPol-
icy.v, with calibrated_positive_model at :83), bit_model_has_satisfia
ble_calibration and landauer_dissipation_premises_inconsistent
(LandauerDissipationStrongForm.v), with the definitions step_collapses_bool_
classes (LogicalErasureCertFlip.v) and cost_dissipation_calibrated (Lan-
dauerDissipationStrongForm.v).

But now the history escape from Section 4, pointed at the machine. Keep the previous
state in a history list (push it onto the front each step; below, s :: h is the list h with s
put on the front) and every fixed-instruction step becomes injective, while the step you
can see stays the same; the program counter can collapse to one place while the bigger
state keeps its past. That move applied to the zero-cost jump is a theorem (zero_cos
t_vm_jump_has_injective_history_lift): the free merge, lifted to a machine
with history, isn’t a merge. So “this step merged, therefore it dissipated” is not a
sentence about the visible step alone; it’s a sentence about the whole state including
whatever history is retained, and a physical model has to say what’s retained. The
permanent-certificate theorem in Section 4 supplies that for the certifying step on finite
memory. For the rest of the machine it’s unsaid.


Theorem 26.4 (Keeping history makes the free merge injective). Let the history step


                                                343
The Thiele Machine                                                                        Devon Thiele


send a pair (s, h), a state and a list of past states, to (apply(s, i ), s :: h). For any step function,
the history step with a fixed instruction is injective, and its first component is the original step.
In particular JUMP to 1 with declared cost 0 costs 0, takes the initial state with empty history
to program counter 1, and its history step is injective.

Proof. Undoing the history step, by popping the list, returns the old pair, so two pairs
with the same image are equal. The rest is computation.

Checked as retained_history_step_injective (ObservationPolicy.v) and zer
o_cost_vm_jump_has_injective_history_lift.

26.4 The calorimeter protocol: a specification, not a measurement
Here is how one would measure this, and it’s here because it makes the boundary exact.
Take a two-state register with energies zero and a gap, a population p in the excited
state, and the simplest possible rate equation for how p changes in one time step (a
rate for climbing into the excited state, a rate for falling out of it, and the length of the
step). For the canonical reset (population one half to zero, with the rates chosen so the
equation closes), the heat delivered to the bath is exactly half the gap (canonical_r
eset_heat_exact). Choose the gap to be twice kT ln 2 and that heat is exactly kT
ln 2 (selected_gap_gives_landauer_heat).

Read that twice, because the temptation is to read it as a derivation of Landauer’s
number and it’s the opposite. The gap was chosen to make the heat come out as
Landauer’s number. The same populations and rates with half that gap give half
the Landauer value, and there’s a theorem exhibiting identical population dynamics
with different heat (master_equation_does_not_fix_heat_scale). The rate
equation fixes the shape; the energy scale is a selected Hamiltonian (the physicist’s
name for the rule that says what energy each state has), and selecting it is not deriving
it.


Definition 26.4 (The two-state protocol). For a gap ∆, the register’s mean energy at
excited population p is ∆ · p. One step of the rate equation is

                                p′ = p + δt k01 (1 − p) − k10 p ,
                                                               


and the heat to the bath over a step from p to p′ is defined as ∆p − ∆p′ . The canonical
reset takes p = 21 , δt = 1, k01 = 0, k10 = 1, ending at p′ = 0, and counts one logical
event.


Theorem 26.5 (The heat is fixed by the chosen gap). (1) The canonical numbers satisfy
the rate equation. (2) For every ∆, the canonical reset’s heat is ∆/2. (3) For all k B , T, the
gap ∆ = 2k B T ln 2 gives heat k B T ln 2. (4) If k B > 0 and T > 0, the gap k B T ln 2 gives
heat strictly below k B T ln 2. (5) There are two different gaps for which the same canonical


                                                 344
The Thiele Machine                                                                  Devon Thiele


populations satisfy the rate equation and the heats differ.

Proof. All five are field arithmetic on the definitions: 12 + 1 · (0 − 12 ) = 0; ∆ · 12 − ∆ · 0 =
∆/2; and ln 2 > 0 for (4). For (5) take gaps 1 and 2.

Checked as canonical_reset_satisfies_master_equation, canonical_r
eset_heat_exact, selected_gap_gives_landauer_heat, smaller_gap_r
efutes_unconditional_landauer_floor (given k B > 0 and T > 0) and maste
r_equation_does_not_fix_heat_scale (CalorimeterProtocol.v, 19, 29, 41, 57),
with the definitions in CalorimeterProtocolTarget.v.

What ties it to the machine: the protocol counts one logical event (the file defines that
count as the constant one), and that equals what CERTIFY from the clean state charges,
and no step of the machine switches certification on for less (vm_minimal_certif
ication_charges_canonical_reset_mu, vm_certification_charges_at
_least_canonical_reset_mu, given a step that turns certification from off to on).
Both are stated for the unbounded sibling of the step from Section 24, not for the sixty-
four-bit one. There is no theorem mapping the protocol’s two register states to any
machine state. The file’s “heat to the bath” is the register’s mean energy before minus
after, so it also assumes the bath receives what the register loses, and no Coq says
that. So a device test would have to measure the gap, the populations, the rates, and
the bath heat independently; separately establish thermal admissibility and detailed
balance (that the up and down rates stand in the ratio the temperature dictates); and
separately establish that the device’s physical reset is the machine’s certify event. The
protocol is an executable experimental specification. It is not a measured device, and
it is not an unconditional conversion of marks to joules, and anyone who tells you
otherwise is reading a file name.


Theorem 26.6 (The protocol’s one event against the machine’s floor). Write applyu for
the unbounded step. (1) From the clean state, whose flag is down, CERTIFY with declared
cost 0 under applyu raises the flag and raises µ by exactly 1, the protocol’s count. (2) For
every state s with the flag down and every instruction i, if applyu (s, i ) has the flag up then
µ(applyu (s, i )) ≥ µ(s) + 1.

Proof. (1) is computation. (2) is the floor for the unbounded step, only CERTIFY sets
the flag and it costs its declared cost plus one, with conservation for applyu .

Checked as vm_minimal_certification_charges_canonical_reset_
mu and vm_certification_charges_at_least_canonical_reset_mu
(CalorimeterProtocol.v, 97). No theorem connects the protocol’s two register states to
any machine state.

The Thiele Machine                                                                 Devon Thiele


26.5 What permanence adds to Landauer: nothing new, said plainly
Here’s a fair question: is there a prediction the permanent-certificate theorems make
that Landauer’s principle alone doesn’t? No, and the reason is short. The smallest
case, one certified state and one flipping in, is “set a bit to one whatever it held,”
which is the reset Landauer described and Bérut measured; Landauer’s own name for
it is “restore to one.” The general bound, kT ln((m plus k) over m) for squeezing m
plus k equally likely states into m, is Landauer’s formula for that squeeze. What the
permanence theorems add is the derivation: which premises about a machine (finite,
permanent) make the certifying step a reset, so that Landauer applies to it. That’s a
result about the machine, not about physics, and it’s the right size.

26.6 The mu-hierarchy, and how small it is
Computer science has a famous result called the time-hierarchy theorem: more time
buys you problems you provably couldn’t solve with less. Whose is it? It’s from
1965, in a paper by Juris Hartmanis and Richard Stearns, “On the Computational
Complexity of Algorithms,” the paper people point to as the start of the whole study
of how much computing costs, and the one that gave the field its name. They got the
Turing Award for it in 1993. I mention it so you can see exactly whose shadow this
section is standing in. The silhouette is “more of the resource buys something you
couldn’t have had.” Here’s the machine’s version, and then how much smaller the
thing inside the silhouette is.

Call a run level-k certified when it ends with the flag up and its executed instructions
include a CERTIFY whose charge (declared cost plus one) is at least k. Then for every k
at least one: there’s a level-k certified run with total cost exactly k (the one-instruction
run CERTIFY with declared cost k minus one; its charge is k, it certifies, and that’s the
whole bill), and any level-k certified run costs at least k (the executed CERTIFY at level
k charged at least k, everything else at least zero, and Section 6’s conservation sums
them) (mu_hierarchy_theorem). Corollary: no fixed budget caps all certifications,
because for any budget B the level B plus one run exceeds it (mu_hierarchy_no_up
per_bound).


Definition 26.5 (Level-k certified). For fuel F and a program t, let exec( F, t) be the
instructions the program-counter runner actually executes from the initial state in F
steps, in order. The pair is level-k certified when the final state has the flag up and
exec( F, t) contains a CERTIFY with declared cost d and d + 1 ≥ k. The cost of the pair
is the final µ minus the initial µ, and the initial one is 0.


Theorem 26.7 (The mu-hierarchy). For every k ≥ 1: some pair has cost exactly k and is
level-k certified, and every level-k certified pair has cost at least k. Consequently, for every
budget B there is a k ≥ 1, namely B + 1, such that no pair with cost at most B is level-k
certified.



                                              346
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


Proof. Witness: the one-instruction program CERTIFY k − 1, run for one step, charges
k and sets the flag. Lower bound: the executed CERTIFY charged at least k, its charge
appears in the run’s ledger entries, every other entry is at least zero, and conservation
makes the final µ the sum of the entries. The budget statement is the lower bound at
k = B + 1.

Checked as mu_hierarchy_theorem (MuHierarchyTheorem.v), with level_k_c
ertified, mu_hierarchy_strict, mu_hierarchy_no_upper_bound and mu_
dimension_unbounded.

How small is that? Very. The time-hierarchy theorem is deep because it separates what
can be computed with more time. This separates what was charged: a run that declared
a bigger charge was charged more. It’s conservation plus the floor, and the “level” is
defined by the charge itself. I keep it because it’s true and because the silhouette is
instructive: the counter is a resource in the formal sense that more of it is strictly more,
and no budget is enough for everything. I don’t keep it because it’s surprising. It isn’t.

26.7 What this section is
A ledger that counts charges, bounded by cost; a calibration that’s a premise; a consis-
tency check the premises pass; a measurement protocol that’s a specification with a
selected scale; and a hierarchy that’s arithmetic. The physics in this book is in Section 4,
as a named premise with its critics named. Here there’s accounting, and I’ve tried to
call every line by its right name. That’s the end of the machine. The chip is next, and
after that, what it took to check any of this and where the checking stops.



Part V

The hardware
27 From the proof to the chip
Aristotle’s bronze, from Section 2: the same statue in three materials, and a promise
I made in Section 15 that I’d keep here. The materials are a step relation in Coq, a
hardware model in a language called Kami, and Verilog that a tool chain turns into
a configuration file for a programmable chip. This section walks the chain from the
top down and, at every link, says one of three words: proved, tested, or trusted. The
discipline is the seL4 paper’s, where a team that had just proved an operating-system
kernel correct spent a paragraph listing what they hadn’t proved (the compiler, the
assembly, the hardware), and I think that paragraph is the most important one in the
paper. So here’s mine, at length.

One thing about names first. The chip isn’t a Thiele machine. It’s hardware that


                                            347
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


implements one, the big build, inside stated bounds: forty-seven of the fifty-one
instructions have an encoding, and its words are thirty-two bits where the kernel’s are
sixty-four. A laptop implements a Turing machine the same way, with a finite memory
the model doesn’t have.

Why the big build and not the small machine, when the small machine is where a
raised flag is proved earned? History, not design. The hardware was built for the big
build first, and the small machine of Section 14 came last; a chip for it is open. So no
circuit in this book enforces that a commitment was earned. The chip’s certified bit is
the big build’s, which prices every commitment and doesn’t make the commit wait for
a check, so on this chip a raised flag can be the receipt for nothing from the opening
chapter. The theorem that a raised flag was checked, then committed, then certified,
and the universal host that carries it to any guest, live in Coq only.

27.1 Hardware as rules
First the idea that makes any of this possible, because it’s not obvious that a circuit
can be a thing you prove theorems about. In the early 2000s Arvind’s group at MIT
described hardware as a set of rules: each rule is a condition (when may I fire) and
a batch of register updates that happen all at once or not at all. The compiler’s job
is to build the arbitration logic so that rules which don’t conflict can fire in the same
clock cycle while the result still looks as if they fired one at a time. Bluespec is the
commercial language built on that idea; its compiler, bsc, went open source in 2020.
What the idea buys: a circuit whose behaviour is “as if one rule at a time,” which is a
thing you can reason about the way you reason about a program.

Then Kami, from Chlipala’s and Arvind’s groups in 2017: a Coq library for writing
Bluespec-style hardware inside Coq and proving things about it as transition systems;
their case study verified a family of multicore RISC-V processors (RISC-V is an open,
freely usable instruction set). What it buys: one Kami design refines another, checked
by Coq. What it leaves trusted is the path out of Coq: if the Bluespec compiler preserves
meaning, the circuits inherit the proofs. If.

27.2 The chain, top to bottom
The CPU as a Kami module. The processor is one Kami module, with registers (sixteen
general registers of thirty-two bits, a hundred and twenty-eight words of data mem-
ory, a hundred and twenty-eight instruction words of a hundred and twenty-eight
bits each, the partition table, the arrow tables, the tensor store, the eight counters)
and rules: a main step rule, and multi-cycle state machines for the checking step,
for the two arrow-building instructions that read memory, and for the game check
(twenty-nine firings, Section 25). Two methods (a method is an entry point the module
offers to whatever sits outside it) matter for what follows: loadInstr, which writes
one instruction word, and start, which clears the halted flag and sets the program
counter to zero and does nothing else. The CPU resets halted: it comes up stopped, so
a program can be loaded before anything runs. The arrow tables are six, of sixteen


                                          348
The Thiele Machine                                                               Devon Thiele


slots each: arrows, coupling descriptors, formula descriptors, certificate descriptors,
descriptor metadata, and coupling pairs. The checking step’s machine keeps two
buffers of sixty-four words for the formula and its certificate. And the ledger is writ-
ten by the same step rule that executes the instruction, not by a separate datapath.
(ThieleTypes.v and ThieleCPUCore.v give these numbers.)

Start from reset: proved. From the reset state, calling start produces exactly the state
every execution theorem begins from, calling no other method (start_from_rese
t), and that call is a legal step in Kami’s semantics (start_substep).

Each instruction refines the specification: proved, under premises. Three layers. A firing
of the real step rule, read through Kami’s semantics, updates the registers exactly
as a Gallina function step_next says (Gallina is the plain programming language
inside Coq, the one the kernel’s step is written in) (rule_next_correct, step_
next_correct). Then one theorem per opcode, forty-eight in all and every one
generated by a script: thirty-five in one file, three for the partition instructions in a file
of their own, and ten for the arrow instructions at both encodings: if the fetched word
is that opcode, the machine is live (not halted, no error, every multi-cycle machine
idle), the alarm is down (the alarm is a flag the chip raises when the ledger falls
below the tensor total), and the stated counters don’t overflow thirty-two bits, then
the hardware snapshot after the step equals the abstract kami_step of the decoded
instruction (step_add_refines and its siblings). The overflow premises are where
the two machines meet: the kernel’s registers are sixty-four-bit words and the chip’s
are thirty-two. Some of these theorems carry more premises (an address inside the
active module’s range, module ranges that don’t overlap, and others), so I’ll stay with
“under its stated side conditions.” The full admission catalogue, including the different
conditions on the two arrow encodings and on fault paths, is printed in Appendix G.
Then the multi-cycle ones: the game check retires through its twenty-nine firings to the
same place (chsh_lassert_refines, with chsh_only_rule_enabled saying
nothing else can fire meanwhile), the checking step through its header and scan firings
(lassert_sat_refines, lassert_unsat_refines; the scan’s premises include
that the formula’s clause count is at least one and at most the number of terminator
words it holds, and that the formula’s addresses and the charge fit in thirty-two bits;
the abstraction function agrees with the kernel on the ledger always, and on the
program counter when the check passes, logic_engine_equivalent_lassert),
and the memory-reading arrow instructions under their admission premises (table
room, modules present, pairs fit; morph_ext_retire, compose_ext_retire). A
master theorem gathers them: any instruction in an “admitted” list of fifty-five cases
(some opcodes at two encodings, plus fault paths) retires, meaning from a live state
the scheduler picks step, every later firing runs to an idle state, and that state matches
kami_step (admitted_retires). The word “admitted” there means “admitted
under premises,” not Coq’s Admitted, and no proof in the hardware tree ends in
Coq’s Admitted (the pun would have been unfortunate). Finally kami_step meets



                                             349
The Thiele Machine                                                                    Devon Thiele


the kernel’s own vm_apply through an abstraction function (embed_step_compu
te), whose file sorts the opcodes into unconditional, preconditioned, and covered
elsewhere.

The refinement theorems are equations between snapshots, field by field, which is the
stronger of the two contracts Appendix G tells apart, not a looser relation picked to
make the proofs go through. (The checking step against the kernel is weaker than
that, and says exactly where.) Here are the words and five of those theorems exactly:
one per-opcode refinement, two multi-cycle ones, the checking step against the kernel,
and the master theorem.


Definition 27.1 (Board state, snapshot, step firing). A board state b is the value of
every register of the Kami module. snap(b) reads off the fields the specification talks
about, as natural numbers, and kstep is the Gallina function kami_step that the
specification gives for one instruction on a snapshot. next(b) is the board state after
one firing of the step rule, the instruction word fetched(b) being the one at the fetch
address. b is live when it is not halted, has no error, and every multi-cycle machine
is idle; the alarm is up when the ledger is below the tensor total. The hardware word
width is 32 bits.


Theorem 27.1 (ADD refines). Let b be a board state whose fetched word is an ADD word
with destination d, sources r1 , r2 and declared cost c. Suppose the alarm is down, the error
flag is false, the halted flag is false, pc(b) + 1 < 232 , µ(b) + c < 232 , and the sum of the two
source registers is below 232 . Then snap(next(b)) = kstep(snap(b), ADD d r1 r2 c).

Proof. The step rule’s writes, read through Kami’s semantics, are given field by field
by generated lemmas, one per field of the snapshot: the program counter goes up
by one, the ledger by c, register d gets the 32-bit sum, everything else is unchanged.
With the three bounds, each 32-bit addition equals the natural-number addition the
specification uses, and the two snapshots agree field by field.

Checked as step_add_refines (StepRefine.v), on top of rule_next_correct
and step_next_correct (RuleStep.v, 66). The thirty-seven siblings have the same
shape with their own bounds (SUB, for instance, asks that the subtrahend not exceed
the minuend).


Theorem 27.2 (The game check refines). Let the fetched word of b be CHSH_LASSERT
with declared cost c, the alarm down, no error, not halted, pc(b) + 1 < 232 , µ(b) + c + 1 <
232 , and the trap vector equal to the kernel’s trap address. Then after the step firing and twenty-
nine firings of the check rule, the snapshot equals kstep(snap(b), CHSH_LASSERT c).

Proof. The step firing charges the ledger c + 1 and starts the check machine on the
eight counters. The twenty-nine firings compute the seven integer facts at the widths

                                               350
The Thiele Machine                                                                      Devon Thiele


of Section 25, and chsh_run_result gives the final program counter, error flag and
error code as functions of the word-level check, which chsh_check_word_correc
t equates with the kernel’s check for every eight 32-bit counters. Every other field is
untouched by the check firings.

Checked as chsh_lassert_refines (ChshRetire.v), with chsh_run_result
(ChshRun.v) and chsh_only_rule_enabled (ChshRetire.v).


Theorem 27.3 (The satisfiable LASSERT refines). Let the fetched word of b be LASSERT of
the satisfiable kind with formula register f , certificate register, length ℓ and declared cost c, and
let a be the value of register f . Suppose the alarm is down, no error, not halted, pc(b) + 1 < 232 ,
the trap vector is the kernel’s trap address, the memory word at a is ℓ, a + 3 + ℓ < 232 , the
clause count n stored at a + 2 satisfies 1 ≤ n ≤ z, where z is the number of zero (terminator)
words among the formula’s literal words, and µ(b) + 8ℓ + c + 1 < 232 . Then there is an m
with 1 ≤ m ≤ ℓ such that after the step firing, the header firing and m scan firings the check
machine is idle for the first time, and the snapshot there equals kstep(snap(b), LASSERT).


Checked as lassert_sat_refines (LassertRetire.v), through the scan lemma that
follows.


Lemma 27.4 (The hardware scan computes the kernel’s checks). For any two assign-
ments gm , gc , numbers a, v, n and a list of words w: if 1 ≤ n, n is at most the number of
zero words in w, and every word of w is below 232 , then the hardware scan of w for n clauses
returns the conjunction of the kernel’s model check of gm and countermodel check of gc on the
formula whose words are a, v, n followed by w.

Proof. Induction on w. A zero word closes a clause: if it was satisfied, the scan moves
to the next clause, and the last clause ends the scan; a nonzero word is a literal, read as
a signed 32-bit number, whose truth under the assignment is the kernel’s. The bound
n ≤ the number of terminators keeps the list from running out before the last clause.
For the theorem, memory words are 32-bit by construction, and the bounds on a and
ℓ keep every address in range.

Checked as lassert_sat_refines (LassertRetire.v), lassert_unsat_refines
for the other kind, and hw_scan_spec, hw_scan_certcheck (LassertSpec.v, 120).

The partition-only reading abs0 and the full reading abs are defined field by field in
Appendix G. The first comparison uses the partition-only reading; the later full-state
theorem uses the full reading.


Theorem 27.5 (The checking step against the kernel). For every snapshot h and every
LASSERT instruction i, there is a kernel state v′ with vm_step(abs0 (h), i, v′ ) such that


                                                 351
The Thiele Machine                                                                Devon Thiele


µ(v′ ) = µ(kstep(h, i )); if the kernel’s check of the formula in abs0 (h) passes, the program
counters agree too; and the error flag of v′ is that of abs0 (h) when the check passes and true
when it fails.

Proof. Choose v′ to be the kernel successor of abs0 (h) for this LASSERT. Both defini-
tions add 8ℓ + c + 1 to the ledger, independently of success, so their ledgers agree.
On a passing check each advances the program counter by one. The kernel’s success
branch preserves the old error flag and its failure branch sets it to true. These substi-
tutions give the three conclusions; equality of every state field is not asserted by this
theorem.

So the ledger always agrees, the program counter on a pass, and the error flag in both
cases. Checked as logic_engine_equivalent_lassert (LogicEngineEquiva-
lence.v).


Definition 27.2 (Retires; admitted). An instruction i retires from b to d when b is
live, the firings that follow the step firing (each chosen by the module’s own sched-
uler while some machine is busy) run from next(b) to d, d is idle, and snap(d) =
kstep(snap(b), i ). Admitted means that the fetched instruction and initial board state
satisfy one of the fifty-five cases in Appendix G. That catalogue gives the common
conditions, each case’s ledger increment and every additional premise.


Theorem 27.6 (Every admitted instruction retires). For every b and i, if (b, i ) is admitted
then i retires from b to some d.

Proof. A case split over the fifty-five constructors, each closed by its own retirement
lemma, which packages a refinement theorem above with the fact that the scheduler
picks step at a live state and that the multi-cycle firings run to idle.

Checked as admitted_retires (RetireMaster.v), with Retire and admitted.

And the whole-machine version, every opcode under its side conditions (driven
_step_wf), which, in the assumption audit (Section 23), uses one standard axiom,
functional extensionality on dependent functions. Most of the per-rule theorems above
use that one and a second, eq_rect_eq, the axiom form of uniqueness of identity
proofs; the audit lists which. Both are standard, and Section 28 accounts for them,
along with how to rerun the audit on the sources in front of you.

The whole-machine statement compares kami_step with the kernel’s step through
an abstraction function, under a per-opcode condition, and lifts to runs.


Theorem 27.7 (The specification step is the kernel step). Let abs be the full snapshot
reading and WF the per-instruction conditions printed in Appendix G. (1) For every snapshot

The Thiele Machine                                                                Devon Thiele


h and instruction i with WF(h, i ): abs(kstep(h, i )) = apply(abs(h), i ). (2) For every
fuel F, program t and snapshot h such that WF holds at every state the run visits, for the
instruction it fetches there: abs of the specification’s run of t for F steps from h equals the
kernel’s program-counter run of t for F steps from abs(h).

Proof. (1) A case split on the instruction: the opcodes with no condition go through
one shared lemma for the plain compute instructions, and each conditioned opcode
has its own. (2) Induction on F, using (1) at each fetched instruction; the condition is

Checked as driven_step_wf (GraphReconstructionBridge.v) and driven_trace

The condition is True for every opcode not named here. CALL and RET need a well-
formed snapshot, with a program-counter bound for CALL. CHSH_TRIAL needs
its four operands to be bits. LASSERT needs its length to agree with the memory
header. TENSOR_SET and TENSOR_GET need valid indices, and TENSOR_GET an
existing module. MORPH, COMPOSE, MORPH_TENSOR and MORPH_GET need
the extended table invariant; MORPH_ID needs the empty-descriptor invariant and
an existing nonempty module; MORPH_ASSERT and MORPH_DELETE need a well-
formed arrow table. PNEW needs a table counter of at most sixty-four, a nonempty
normalized region and a clear tensor slot; PSPLIT and PMERGE need a well-formed
partition table, live operands with nonempty ranges (at least two cells for PSPLIT, two
different modules for PMERGE) and clear fresh slots. None of the three needs room
in the table. When the module numbers run out, or a PNEW range runs past memory,
the chip traps the way the kernel does (Section 16), charges the counter and keeps
running, and the theorem covers that trap like any other branch. The chip’s error
word tells the partition faults apart, 0xBADF001D for a missing module number or a
range past memory and 0xBADF001E for an overlap or a merge whose ranges don’t
touch (ERR_PARTITION_VAL and ERR_PARTITION_OVERLAP_VAL, ThieleTypes.v);
the kernel writes 1 for every fault. Reset doesn’t make these true forever; a run has
to keep establishing them. This is a theorem about the Gallina specification, one level
above the clocked rules.

Underneath all of that sit four small files that check the floorboards: that every one
of the twelve CPU rules is something Kami’s evaluator can actually run; that a run
picked rule by rule (always the first rule that’s ready) really is a Kami run, with a
bound on firings, an early stop exactly when no rule is ready, and a ready rule at reset;
that no register ever changes its declared kind on any run from reset; and thirteen facts
about what the registers hold at reset. (In order, those are CoreRules, CoreExecu
tion, CoreTyping and DispatchReset.) What none of them pins down: fairness,
the allocation invariants along a reachable run, or meaning through the tools below
Kami. One more file is worth naming so nobody leans on it: rtl_inventory_arit
hmetic (RTLGapRegistry.v) is the equation 37 + 10 + 0 = 47, an inventory count of


                                             353
The Thiele Machine                                                                Devon Thiele


opcodes (not of the forty-eight refinement theorems above), and it would still hold if
every hardware proof were deleted.

The arrow-building instructions run through a coupling state machine, and the picture
is simple: it builds a list of cell pairs, then tidies it. Descriptor zero is reserved for the
empty coupling, with base 0 and count 0 (CouplingComposeKami.v); the pair table
holds sixteen entries; and a normalization loop runs over the newly built pair range
(CouplingFsmNorm.v). Their fault branches retire in the step firing alone with the
error set (step_morph_ext_fault_refines and its siblings, CouplingFaults.v),
and their success paths retire under the admission premises (morph_ext_retire,
compose_ext_retire). From kami_step down to the kernel they also need the
extended table invariant above.

The loader: proved for the receive, the hand-off and the report, its start discipline proved by
a solver, the rest tested. Here’s the part that answers a question worth asking in plain
words: what’s the point of a chip you can’t load? The answer is a second Kami module,
also extracted, not hand-written: a serial receiver. It samples one input pin through
two registers (the standard way to avoid reading a wire mid-change), reads each bit
at the middle of its period, and reassembles bytes in one of the oldest serial formats
still in use: one low start bit, eight data bits least-significant first, one high stop bit, at
115,200 bits per second. A twenty-megahertz clock gives 174 cycles per bit, which is
0.22 percent slow, within tolerance. On top of that a small assembler takes a two-byte
count N, then N instructions of sixteen bytes each, writes each through loadInstr,
and then calls start. And a reporter sends fifteen bytes back: a header byte, a status
byte, then the program counter, the counter, and the error code as four bytes each, and
a trailer byte. That’s the whole interface: one wire in, one wire out, four LEDs.

You can check that 0.22 percent at the table, and it’s worth doing once, because it’s
the whole trick of the format. Divide twenty million by 115,200 and you get about
173.6. A counter can only count whole cycles, so it counts 174, and twenty million
divided by 174 is about 114,943 bits per second: 0.22 percent slow. Then the obvious
next question: does that matter? The receiver lines itself up on the falling edge of the
start bit and reads each bit at what it thinks is the middle, and with every bit its idea of
the middle drifts a little later. By the middle of the stop bit, nine and a half bits in, it’s
about two percent of a bit late, give or take the cycle or two the two-register sampler
adds at the start. It would have to slip half a bit before it read the wrong one. And the
next start bit lines it up all over again, so the drift never gets to pile up past one byte.
That’s how two machines whose clocks don’t quite agree get to talk at all.

That trick is older than any chip, and it’s worth following back. Teleprinters had the
same problem: a machine at each end of a long wire, each turned by its own motor,
and keeping two motors in exact step over a long line was the hard part. The way out
was to start the receiver at the beginning of each character and let it come to rest at
the end, so it only had to keep in step for one character at a time. Howard Krum was


                                             354
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


granted a patent on a version of that in 1918, and the unit people use for signalling
speed, the baud, is named after Émile Baudot, whose telegraph code ran over lines
like those. Who had the start-stop idea first? I can’t tell you. Krum’s patent has a
date on it, and a patent is where somebody stakes a claim, not where the question gets
settled. None of it changes a theorem. It changes the picture: the one input pin on this
chip frames its bytes the way teleprinters framed their characters, a start, the data, a
stop, about a hundred years on.

What’s proved: take any program of one to a hundred and twenty-eight instructions,
start the receiver from reset, and play on the simulated pin the serial frames of the
count and of instructions zero through k. Then the loader holds instruction k ad-
dressed to slot k, its request flag has flipped once per instruction, and it asks for s
tart exactly when k is the last one (serial_program_load); every cycle of that
run is a call of the real sample method; the load rule passes exactly that address and
word to loadInstr (load_rule_hands_off); and loadInstr puts the word at
that address (load_instr_writes). A program of zero instructions is a separate,
smaller fact: fed straight to the assembler, with no serial pin in between, the count
bytes alone raise the start request (empty_program_starts).

And the way back out is proved too. Once the CPU is halted or in error, run the
loader’s report rule once per clock cycle. The pin sits high for one cycle, then carries
the serial frames of fifteen bytes: the header 0xDE, a status byte whose three low bits
are halted, error and certified, then the program counter, the counter and the CPU’s
error code as four bytes each, least significant first, and the trailer 0xAD. The values
are the kernel state’s, read through the same abstraction every execution theorem uses,
so the bytes on the wire are the machine’s state and not a separate story. A receiver
built the loader’s way, started idle, reads back exactly those fifteen bytes, and the pin
stays high from then on (serial_status_report). Before a halt or an error the
reporter does nothing (report_waits). Its premise is worth saying out loud: Kami’s
semantics don’t say when a rule fires, so the theorem takes one firing of the report rule
per clock cycle as given.

What’s tested only, as far as Coq goes: the rule that actually fires start and the LED
output. No Coq theorem names them. (The extracted circuit’s start discipline has a
separate solver proof, further down, and the LEDs have only the simulations.) And
one thing the loader file says about itself that I’ll repeat: Kami’s semantics let a rule
fire whenever its guard holds, and the file does not prove that the load rule takes each
word before the next replaces it. That’s a real gap between “the receiver assembles the
right word” and “the CPU got every word,” and only the simulations cover it, which
are finite. The solver properties don’t close it either: they say the loader never writes
after start, not that every word was taken.

Here’s the start, in the theorem’s own words:




                                          355
The Thiele Machine                                                                     Devon Thiele


Theorem 27.8 (Start from reset). From the reset register map, any execution of the start
method calls no other method, and its updates applied over the reset map give exactly the state
every execution theorem starts from: halted false and program counter 0, everything else at
reset.

Proof. The start operation makes two assignments: clear the halted bit and set the pro-
gram counter to zero. It performs no call and preserves all other registers. Applying
those assignments to the reset map gives exactly the stated map, field by field.

Checked as start_from_reset (CPUStart.v), with start_substep for the step of
the module.


Theorem 27.9 (Serial load). Let w0 , . . . , w N −1 be instruction words with 1 ≤ N ≤ 128,
and k < N. Run the receiver model from its reset state over the serial frames of the bytes N,
0, and then the sixteen bytes of each of w0 , . . . , wk . At the end, the loader holds address k and
word wk for the CPU, its request flag equals “k is even”, and its start request is set exactly
when k + 1 = N.

Proof. One frame, a start bit, eight data bits and a stop bit, takes the receiver from idle
back to idle having delivered exactly that byte once (one_frame, by computation).
Induction over the bytes then follows the assembler: two count bytes, then sixteen
bytes per word with the address counting up, the request flag toggling per word and
the start request raised after the last.

Checked as serial_program_load (LoaderSerial.v), with one_frame and step_
is_rxSample, which says each cycle of the model is a call of the real Kami sample
method. The zero-instruction case is empty_program_starts, in the same file.


Theorem 27.10 (Hand-off and write). (1) If the load rule (load_rule) runs from a
register map holding request r, acknowledge a, address x and word w, then r ̸= a, its only
method call is loadInstr with x and w, and its only update sets acknowledge to r. (2) If l
oadInstr runs with x and w, it calls no method and its only update writes w at address x
of instruction memory.

Proof. The load rule’s guard is r ̸= a. Once that guard holds, its action sends the
stored address and word to the instruction-memory write method and copies r into
the acknowledgement register. It has no other action. The called method updates the
instruction-memory array at the supplied address to the supplied word, preserving
every other array entry and every other register; it calls nothing. These are the two
local contracts. They do not by themselves prove that every serial request eventually
receives a matching call.




                                                356
The Thiele Machine                                                                    Devon Thiele


Checked as load_rule_hands_off and load_instr_writes (LoaderSerial.v,
695).


Theorem 27.11 (Status report). Let b be the CPU’s registers with the halted bit h or the
error bit set, and let s be the kernel state they abstract to. Let R be the fifteen bytes: 0xDE; the
status byte h + 2e + 4c, where e and c are the error and certified flags of s; the four bytes, least
significant first, of each of the program counter of s, the counter µ(s) and the CPU’s error code,
each taken modulo 232 ; and 0xAD. Start the transmitter neither active nor done, and run the
report rule once per cycle for 1 + 15 · 10 · 174 cycles, the status getters returning b in the first
cycle and anything afterwards. Then the pin reads high in the first cycle and then the serial
frames of R in order; the loader’s receiver, started idle, decodes that sequence to exactly R; and
for any further cycles the pin stays high and the transmitter does not change.

Proof. In the first cycle the guard sees halted or error, each status getter returns its
register of b, and the rule latches the fifteen bytes and starts sending. Each byte then
goes out as a low start bit, eight data bits least significant first and a high stop bit, 174
cycles per bit, by induction over bytes, bits and cycles. The fifteen latched bytes equal
R by computation on words. The loader’s receiver turns each frame back into its byte
(one_frame, above), so it reads R. After the last stop bit the transmitter is done, and
a done transmitter keeps the pin high whatever the rule sees.

Checked as serial_status_report (ReportSerial.v), from report_transmits,
report_bytes_kernel, report_bytes_fields, status_byte_value and re
port_done_stays, with report_step_is_rule (each modelled cycle is a firing
of the real Kami rule, its calls the CPU’s six getters), get_tx_is_tx_out (the pin is
the transmitter’s output) and report_waits (nothing happens before a halt or an
error). Assumptions: functional extensionality and the uniqueness of equality proofs,
the two Kami itself uses.

Composition: proved by reflexivity. The system is the CPU module followed by the
loader module. The loader’s calls to loadInstr, start, and the status getters are
the CPU’s own methods, so they close inside the design; what’s left over (sample,
transmit, LEDs) becomes the pins. A one-line theorem says the printer (the program,
below, that writes the design out as Bluespec text) receives the CPU’s syntax followed
by the loader’s.

A second extraction, to software: tested. Separately from the chip, Coq’s extraction also
turns the kernel’s step into OCaml, and a runner built on it executes programs. What
Coq proves about it is about the Coq side. For every state and instruction, the ob-
servable record taken after one kernel step satisfies the floor (a flag that goes from
down to up comes with the counter at least one higher) and never shows the counter
lower than before (ocaml_observable_nofi_and_monotone, OCamlExtraction-
Bridge.v). The lemma named ocaml_runner_observable_defined says only



                                                357
The Thiele Machine                                                               Devon Thiele


that the observable exists, which is true of any Coq function; it is not a cross-language
equivalence. That the built binary returns the same observable is checked by a parity
test suite, not proved. And the checked-in runner file (build/extracted_vm_runner.ml)
takes each step by calling the extracted Coq step, so the steps themselves follow the
current rules, but the code wrapped around them is its own and differs from the
kernel: it starts both graph counters at one, stops on an error, stops at HALT and
writes a status word, and steps over a CHECKPOINT written without a cost (and the
two port directives) without charging; a CHECKPOINT with a cost goes through the
kernel’s step like everything else. No theorem in this book is about that runner. The
board simulations do use it as the reference they compare against, which makes those
comparisons exactly as good as the runner is, and I’d rather say that than let “agrees
with the software machine” sound like it names the kernel. None of the seventeen
board programs uses CHECKPOINT.

Extraction: trusted. Coq’s extraction turns the Kami syntax tree for the system into
OCaml. The stock extraction command is an unverified translator (Letouzey’s 2003
design; later work proves erasure correct, but that’s not the command used here). And
the step just before it, turning Kami’s module syntax into Bluespec’s, is a Kami library
function in a file that contains no theorem at all. Two trusted links in a row, and I’m
naming them.

Printing, patching, compiling: trusted, tested. A vendored printer (about a thousand
lines of OCaml) prints Bluespec. A script then does things to the text that I’ll list
because “nothing hand-written but clock primitives” is a tempting sentence and it’s
not exact: it strips the printer’s wrapper module; rewrites one vector construction
into the form the 2024 bsc accepts; turns large vector registers into register-file cells;
runs bsc (2024.07) and deletes the date line bsc stamps, so the output depends only
on the input; and turns flattened registers into Verilog arrays. For the system it also
wraps the top module with an interface made of the outermost methods, a wrapper
that keeps the printed instantiation lines verbatim and, by its own docstring, writes
no expression, register, or rule. Each text transform is audited by a script that says
of itself that it is “not a compiler correctness proof.” And one Bluespec library cell, a
hundred-line register file in Verilog, is read by synthesis and comes from nobody’s
proof. These change storage shape, not logic, by their own account, and they’re tested,
not proved.

The gate that catches hand edits: tested. The nightly full run rebuilds the extraction, reruns
the whole pipeline, and fails unless the two Verilog files it produces are byte-for-byte
identical to the tracked ones. A hand edit to the generated Verilog fails the build. And
the CPU printed inside the system must compile byte-for-byte to the CPU printed
alone, else the script exits; that’s how I know the system wrapper didn’t touch the
CPU. Be clear about what this gate protects: that the tracked Verilog is exactly what
the extractor prints from the current sources. It doesn’t say those sources are the ones
the proofs were checked against; that’s the job of the proof build on the same commit.


                                             358
The Thiele Machine                                                                          Devon Thiele


Simulation: tested. The suite is seventeen programs: nine directed cases (the two
short serial tests, arithmetic-then-halt and a jump loop, are two of them) and eight
generated from a fixed random seed. The directed cases include memory reads and
writes on both sides of the sixty-four-word bank boundary, allocation past the memory
limit, overlapping partitions, splitting and merging, composition, and allocation-table
exhaustion. Each program goes in as serial frames on the board’s one input pin, and
the fifteen-byte report comes back on its output pin. Three things run it. One is the
netlist yosys mapped for the chip, written back out as Verilog and simulated with
yosys’s models of the chip’s cells. One is the extracted Verilog of the same board top.
One is the OCaml runner extracted from the Coq step. The netlist and the Verilog must
agree exactly on the report bytes, the LEDs and every probed state field. The Verilog
and the runner must agree on the program counter, the counter, the error flag, the
sixteen registers, the 128 data words, the certified flag, the module and arrow tables
and the witness counters. And each report must match the state it reports. Every
program also runs without pressing the reset button, the netlist from its initial values
and the Verilog from all zeros, so the board wrapper’s power-on reset has to do the
job alone. The formal property lines ride along in the Verilog run as checks, any failed
check fails the run, and fifteen named triggers from them must each be hit by some
program. All seventeen programs and all fifteen triggers passed in the recorded run.1
These are finite tests on zero-delay models. The netlist they simulate is the one before
place and route; the placed and routed design itself is not simulated. Three of the
chip’s cells (the input buffer, the clock synthesiser and the clock gate) are behavioural
stand-ins, and the block RAM is a functional model. So the simulations say nothing
about every program, about the analog behaviour of the clock, about physical timing,
or about a powered board. And since the runner is the reference, they are only as good
as the runner.

Seventeen programs sounds like a lot until you ask how many there could be. A
program here is up to a hundred and twenty-eight instructions of a hundred and
twenty-eight bits each, so the longest ones alone come in two to the power 16,384
different bit patterns, a number about 4,900 digits long, and seventeen of them ran.
Edsger Dijkstra had a sentence for this, and the version in his 1976 book starts by
admitting he’d already said it many times and written it in many places: program
testing “can be quite effective for showing the presence of bugs, but is hopelessly
inadequate for showing their absence.” (I’m quoting it as John Harrison quotes it,
from that book.) That’s why this paragraph says tested and not proved, and why the
solver checks below get paragraphs of their own: they’re the part that doesn’t count
programs one at a time.
   1 Board simulation record: CI Full run 37188435151, source revision 710fdaf912b0e3df1107f6a5

376df0b05adb9b1c, 4 October 2026, in which every job passed, including the solver and netlist jobs
described below. These identify the supporting record; the comparison and its limits are stated here. A
