                                                   359
The Thiele Machine                                                               Devon Thiele


Safety in the extracted circuit: proved by a separate solver. This is a different tool pointed
at the same Verilog, and it gets its own paragraph because it is the one place where
a proof reaches the circuit without going through Kami’s semantics. Yosys reads
the extracted files with extra property lines added to a copy (the tracked files aren’t
touched, and the added lines only watch registers, they never drive anything), and a
driver called SymbiYosys hands the questions to a solver. Each proof is an induction
over every state reachable from reset, with no bound on how long the run is. There
are three.

The partition table. The table never holds more than sixty-four slots, and the allocation
counter stays between one and sixty-four. Every slot at or above the counter is empty.
Every nonempty slot lies inside the 128-word memory, and nonempty slots never
overlap. A partition instruction that faults sends the program counter to the trap
vector and leaves the table as it was. And only PNEW, PSPLIT and PMERGE ever
write the table. The solver gets this as 321 separate obligations (a reset base, a frame
step saying nothing else touches the table, one step for each partition instruction, and
the pairwise cases for overlap), and a missing, failed or timed-out one fails the job. The
memory’s read signals are left arbitrary, so the result holds for whatever the memory
could return.

Control. The error flag never clears except by reset, and nothing executes while it is
set. The arrow-table counter stays between one and sixteen, and every valid arrow
slot sits below it. The counter register changes only when the main step rule or the
checking step’s scan rule fires. The halted flag clears only through start. This one
runs unbounded model checking (an engine called PDR, short for property-directed
reachability) over the whole state space, so the multi-cycle machines are inside it at
every phase and every interleaving. What the list doesn’t say is that the counter never
goes down. It is a thirty-two-bit register and a big enough charge wraps it, which is
exactly why the Coq theorems carry overflow premises. So what does the chip do
when the counter runs out of room? Nothing special. A declared cost is the low eight
bits of the instruction word, so one instruction declares at most 255, plus its floor of
one where it has one and any payload charge, and the counter adds modulo 232 : no
trap, no flag, and the sum after a wrap is just a small number. A run that pushes the
counter past 232 − 1 is outside every refinement theorem above, and on that run “only
climbs” is false. It’s an old point of this book turning up in silicon: a counter that only
climbs can’t live in a fixed number of bits forever, so it has to stop, stick, or wrap, and
this one wraps.

The loader. Five properties after reset: start is called only while halted; instruction
memory is never written after start; start occurs at most once; the report begins only
after start and after halt or error; and no second report begins after the first has been
sent. Six auxiliary invariants are proved with them. The induction depth of four
bounds the solver’s search, not the length of the run covered, and both the reset base
and the inductive step have to pass. The check keeps the complete extracted CPU in


                                             360
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


the system.

The two CPU proofs assume that start is called only while the CPU is halted. The
loader proof is the one that establishes that for the loader, and the loader is the only
caller, so the three fit. But they are three separate runs, and that they fit is my reading
of them, not a mechanical composition. Beside each proof sits a cover task: every
property has a named trigger event, and the task shows that a real transition of the
circuit reaches it within sixteen cycles from a state satisfying all the properties (the
CPU is not reset in those tasks). That keeps a property from being true only because
its trigger never happens. It says nothing about properties I never wrote.

What these are, and aren’t. They are statements about the extracted Verilog as Yosys
reads it, checked by Yosys and its solvers, not Coq proofs of the translators. They are
not the Coq theorems either: the partition-table list says the same kind of thing as
the well-formedness premises of the refinement theorems, but nothing links the two
statements formally. They don’t replace the premises of the Coq report theorem, and
they don’t prove the serial input was the program the user meant. And what they
read is the extracted Verilog, not the mapped netlist that becomes the bitstream. The
next check reaches part of that gap.

The board and loader against the mapped netlist: proved, conditional on the CPU. A second
solver check takes the netlist yosys mapped for the chip, the very file nextpnr is
handed (a digest check ties the jobs to it), and the extracted RTL of the same board
top. It proves by induction, a reset base and one arbitrary step, that the loader, the
reporter and the board wrapper’s reset logic behave the same on both sides: the same
serial transmit pin, the same four LEDs, the same start and load enables, the same
connected bits of the instruction and address bus. The CPU and its memories are
cut out of the comparison. Seven signals come back from the CPU (program counter,
counter, error flag, halted flag, certified flag, error code, and whether it can take an
instruction), both sides get the same values, and the values are otherwise arbitrary. So
the result reads: if the two CPUs answer alike, the two loaders act alike. It is not a
proof that the chip’s CPU matches the Verilog’s. The report is stamped as component
equivalence and not whole-chip equivalence, and the CPU and memories in the netlist
are checked only by the simulations above. The clock primitives are checked for their
types and divider ratio, and the model is synchronous and functional: no analog clock,
no delays.

Synthesis, place and route, bitstream: trusted, tested. yosys maps the Verilog to the chip’s
lookup tables and flip-flops; nextpnr-xilinx places and routes it; and Project X-Ray’s
tools turn the result into a bitstream, the file that fills a programmable chip’s configu-
ration memory and makes the blank grid into this circuit. None of those three carries a
proof; yosys (2013) is a free synthesis suite covering most of Verilog, nextpnr followed,
and X-Ray documented the chip’s bitstream format by building many designs with
the vendor’s tool and cross-correlating the bits. Two tests sit on this link. A timing


                                            361
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


gate reads the clock-synthesiser settings out of the board wrapper, computes the clock
it produces (twenty megahertz), and fails if nextpnr’s achieved frequency is lower;
the recorded run achieved 27.22 megahertz against the 20 required. And a round
trip decodes the bitstream two ways: the raw bits must equal the frames that were
encoded, and the bits decoded back to named features and re-encoded must match
too, so a bit the database can’t name shows up as a mismatch.

The board wrapper: the one hand-written logic file. It takes the board’s two-hundred-
megahertz clock, which arrives as a pair of wires with opposite voltages, and turns it
into one signal; feeds that to the chip’s clock synthesiser, which multiplies by five and
divides by fifty to get twenty megahertz and raises a LOCKED flag when it’s stable;
drives the clock onto the chip’s clock network only while locked, so the CPU never
sees a half-formed clock; and then instantiates the extracted system, ties three enables
high, and wires four LEDs. It also supplies power-on reset: a five-bit counter starts
at zero after configuration and counts the first sixteen CPU clock edges; a registered
reset keeps the system in reset until that count has completed and the reset button is
released. This matters because all-zero configuration state is not the machine’s reset
state. A pin file maps the clock pair, the reset button, the LEDs, and the two serial
pins to the connector names of a specific board, a Digilent Genesys 2 (its chip is the
Kintex-7 xc7k325tffg900-2, the part the synthesis script targets), per the file’s note. The
pin names match Digilent’s published master constraints file for that board.

27.3 Who all this is safe against
Every guarantee in this chain is about programs. Take the chip as built, from reset,
with its step doing what the proofs say, and any program the loader hands it, buggy
or hostile, gets the kernel’s rules, the counter’s charges and the flag’s latch. That’s the
threat model, and I’d rather say it out loud than let “every program” sound bigger
than it is. Outside it: whoever sets the start (a reset or a power cycle clears the flag,
and nothing on the board remembers it was ever up); the loader, which takes any
program at all and can’t tell you it’s the one you meant; the two wires, in and out;
anybody with a probe, a glitch or a laser who flips a register; and the tool chain the
table below marks trusted. The small machine’s theorems have the same shape on
paper: they start from a clean start, one step at a time, and say nothing about whoever
chose that start or about a second writer that changes a counter without bumping its
edition. None of that is a hole in a theorem. It’s where the theorems stop.

The report is the clearest case. Theorem 27.11 proves the fifteen bytes on the pin are
the machine’s state, read through the same abstraction as everything else. It doesn’t
prove who sent them. The frame is a header, a status byte, three numbers and a trailer:
no key, no fresh number from whoever’s reading, no digest of the program that ran.
Anybody with a serial cable can send the same fifteen bytes. So for someone who
wasn’t standing at the board, the record moves the question from “did it run?” to “do
I trust the box that says it ran?”, and crossing that takes something this book doesn’t
build: an attestation over measured state, which Section 12 shows vouches only for

                                           362
The Thiele Machine                                                                Devon Thiele

27.5 Why generated, and why it’s the stronger artifact
Someone will say “it’s just generated code.” Here’s why that’s backwards. The gener-
ated Verilog is the artifact the proofs are about, one translation removed; a hand-written
CPU would carry no proof at all. The CI gate makes any hand edit fail. So generated
code is the stronger artifact, with its translators named as trusted, which is a better
position than hand-written code whose translator is a person. And “it synthesized,
so it’s correct” is the wrong turn in the other direction: synthesis checks that the text
describes some circuit; a wrong circuit synthesises as happily as a right one. The evi-
dence of function is the co-simulation, the board simulations and the solver checks,
not that yosys finished.

27.6 Thompson’s knife, again
Every link marked “trusted” is a place where Ken Thompson’s compiler from Sec-
tion 11 could sit unseen: a translator that plants something and re-plants it when it
translates itself. Extraction, the printer, bsc, yosys, nextpnr, the X-Ray database. I
don’t believe any of them does. I can’t prove it, and the discipline of this section is to
say so rather than to let “formally verified” cover a chain whose bottom half is trust
and tests.

And a planted knife isn’t the only way a trusted link goes wrong. Sometimes nobody
plants anything and the bottom row of the table, the chip itself, is just wrong. In 1994
Thomas Nicely, a mathematics professor at Lynchburg College who was computing
with twin primes and their reciprocals, found that his new Intel Pentium got some divi-


                                              364
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


sions wrong. The example everybody passes around is 4,195,835 divided by 3,145,727,
which the bad chips got wrong in the fourth decimal place. Intel’s explanation was
missing entries in a table inside the divider: five of them, it said, dropped by a script.
Intel set aside about $475 million to cover it.

Push on the five, because that’s the part that got retold. In 2024 Ken Shirriff went to
die photographs of an affected chip, read the table’s layout off the silicon, and counted
sixteen missing entries, left out by a mistake in the table’s mathematical definition,
of which only five ever mattered. So the story that got repeated for thirty years had
the effect right and the cause off, and it took somebody reading the actual silicon to
say so. Floating-point arithmetic went on to become one of the places where formal
verification earned its keep in industry; John Harrison, who did that work at Intel,
brings up this very bug in a 2007 survey of it. Does any of that touch this book’s chain?
The chip here was never switched on, so no. But it’s why the last row of the table
says trusted, unchecked and not something kinder. This design runs on a chip made of
lookup tables, a few hundred thousand of them, and nobody here has read them off
the silicon either.

27.7 The numbers, true of one recorded run
Sixteen registers of thirty-two bits; a hundred and twenty-eight words of data and of
instructions; instructions a hundred and twenty-eight bits wide; sixty-four partition
slots, the same sixty-four module numbers the kernel hands out per run (Section 16),
each module in its own slot; forty-seven of fifty-one opcodes encoded (Section 17);
fifty-five retirement cases. From the full run 37188435151 at source revision 710fd
af9, 4 October 2026: 53,117 of 407,600 lookup-table sites (thirteen percent; nextpnr
counts each half of a six-input lookup table as a site, and the datasheet lists 203,800
six-input tables), 10,390 flip-flop sites, no DSP slices, two block RAMs, a bitstream of
11.4 megabytes whose round trip matched 2,887,071 bits by encoding and 2,887,590
by meaning, a placed and routed clock of 27.22 megahertz against the 20 required,
and every simulation and solver job in that run passing. Those numbers belong to
one run, and the gate above is what ties any run’s numbers to the sources it was built
from; when the sources change, the numbers do, and the gate says so. No hash of the
bitstream is printed here, and the run’s own files won’t be kept forever, so what lasts
is the revision: rebuild from it and compare.

27.8 What the chip is, and isn’t
The chip is the third material. The proofs reach from the kernel’s step relation to the
firing of Kami rules. Everything below that is translated by tools I trust and checked
by tests I’ve described in numbers. The bitstream is a wiring list, not evidence that the
wiring computes anything; the evidence is the simulations and the solver checks. And
no board was ever powered on: I don’t own one, the repository records no run on one,
and I’d rather end this section on that sentence than on a flourish. What I can say is
this. Any claim of the form “the proof says the chip does X” has to pass through this



                                           365
The Thiele Machine                                                          Devon Thiele


table, and the table says exactly where the proof stops. And it’s the big build’s chip,
so nothing on it enforces that a commitment was earned.



Part VI

Checking it, and its edge

28 What Coq is, and why
Coq is a proof assistant, which is a phrase I had to go and look up. Underneath the
phrase it’s a programming language, but one whose type system is strict enough to
do a thing ordinary languages can’t: you write a proof down as a program, and the
compiler refuses it unless the program genuinely matches the statement you claimed.
You can’t talk it into a maybe.

The name is a joke three ways at once, and it’s worth knowing before you say it out
loud in English. Coq is French for rooster. It’s also a nod to Thierry Coquand, who
worked out the logic it started from with Gérard Huet, and to that logic’s initials, CoC,
for the Calculus of Constructions; and there’s a French habit of naming research tools
after animals. The English slang reading did what you’d guess. By the development
team’s own account, some people, women students especially, ended up never learn-
ing the tool because of its name. So in March 2025 it got a new one, the Rocq Prover,
after Rocquencourt, the Inria site where it was first built, and after the Roc, the giant
bird of legend, so the bird stayed. Everything in this book was checked with Coq 8.18,
from before the rename, so that’s the name I use. The rooster changes nothing about
what got checked.

28.1 Types as claims
Here’s the idea, and it’s one idea. In a normal language a type says what kind of
value a variable holds: in Python, “x is an int” means x is a whole number. In Coq,
types are claims. The type “n is greater than zero” is the type of proofs that n is posi-
tive. A function from “n is greater than zero” to “n plus one is greater than zero” is a
proof that if n is positive, n plus one is too, and the compiler checks that the function
really has that type, the way it would check that a function from integers to strings
really returns strings. This correspondence between proofs and programs has a name,
Curry-Howard, after two people who noticed it separately decades apart, and Coq’s
foundation, the Calculus of Inductive Constructions, from Coquand, Huet and Paulin-
Mohring in the late 1980s, is a type system built to exploit it. The “inductive” part
means you define your own recursive types (numbers, lists, trees, machine states) in-
side the system instead of having them handed down as primitives, so the foundation
is explicit; nothing is smuggled.



                                          366
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


“Decades apart” undersells it, and the gap is worth a side trip. Haskell Curry noticed
in 1934 that the type of a function from A to B reads like the claim “A implies B,” and
that the types his functions could have lined up with the claims you can prove; he
and Robert Feys pushed it further in 1958. William Howard wrote the sharper version
in 1969, and then it went around as a photocopied manuscript until 1980, when it
was finally printed in a collection of essays for Curry. So the idea under the tool this
book is checked with spent its first eleven years as a stack of photocopies. Is that the
bottom? No. Reading a proof of “if A then B” as a method that turns any proof of A
into a proof of B is older still: the intuitionists had it in the 1920s and 1930s, Brouwer,
Heyting and Kolmogorov, which is why people also call it the BHK interpretation.
Where it really starts I can’t tell you. It changes nothing in what the checker checks.
It changes how I’d tell the story: nobody sat down one day and invented “proofs are
programs.” It kept getting noticed, by people coming from different directions, until
somebody wrote it down plainly.

The compiler checks whether the types line up. If your proof has a hole and you write
“trust me,” it rejects you. But here’s the part people skip, and it’s the part that matters:
the compiler checks that the proof matches the statement. It does not check that the
statement says what you meant. Hand it a statement that means nothing and it’ll prove
it for you, three characters, no complaint. So a proof being accepted is not the same as
the thing being true. It means this proof matches this statement, and whether that’s
the right statement is on me, not the machine. Section 3 said a short version of this and
I’m saying it again because every section since has leaned on it: the checked names in
this book are a promise that the proof is there, and the sentences around them are my
claim about what the statement says, and the second can be wrong while the first is
fine, which is why so many sections of this book stop to say exactly what a statement’s
hypotheses are.

28.2 Why I used it
Not to make anything true. I used it because I don’t trust my own eye to catch a gap
in an argument I want to believe. I spent months convinced by my own reasoning,
pushed the proof through, and watched a key step come apart in my hands. The
machine caught where I’d fooled myself. That’s what it’s for. And the same definitions
are the source the running machine is extracted from and the specification the chip’s
hardware model is proved to refine (Section 27), through an extraction step I trust
and side conditions I state, so the thing that checks the argument is, one trusted step
removed, the thing that becomes the artifact. Gap-catcher and extractor. Not the proof.
The proof is the argument, and an argument has to close in a way a person can follow,
or it hasn’t closed at all, which is why this book exists in prose and not as a list of
theorem names.

Two precedents show that a proof assistant is a serious tool and not a toy. CompCert,
Xavier Leroy’s C compiler, written and proved correct in Coq: the assembly it emits
behaves as the source does, for programs with defined behaviour. And Georges

                                            367
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


Gonthier’s 2005 proof of the four-colour theorem, a century-old problem whose first
proof (in 1976) needed a computer to check thousands of cases and was distrusted for
exactly that reason, redone in Coq so that the checker was the small, auditable thing
and the cases were the program. That’s de Bruijn’s criterion from Section 19 applied
to mathematics itself: the thing you have to trust is the small kernel, not the big proof.

The 1976 proof deserves its own side trip. Kenneth Appel and Wolfgang Haken did
it at the University of Illinois, and the mathematics department changed the slogan
on its postage meter to “Four colors suffice.” The slogan it replaced had been on the
department’s mail since the middle 1960s, and it said that 211213 − 1 is prime, a prime
Don Gillies, in the same university’s computer science department, had found. Think
about that for a second. For years on end a mathematics department stamped its mail
with results nobody could have checked by hand, first one and then the other, and
both were right. So was the distrust of the 1976 proof wrong? I don’t think so. The
worry was never that the computer lied. It was that nobody could read what had been
checked, and a check you can’t look at is hard to lean on. Gonthier’s answer was de
Bruijn’s: make the part you have to read small enough to read.

28.3 What “zero Admitted” means
“Zero Admitted” is literal. Nowhere in the proof tree did I write “trust me” and walk
on. Every step the checker could see, it saw, end to end, with no “and the rest is
obvious.” A hygiene fact about the gap-catcher, not a verdict on the argument: it says
I didn’t let myself skip a step where the machine was watching. It does not say the
statements are the right statements.

What it doesn’t mean, listed. It doesn’t mean the theorems prove physical reality;
they prove things about the machine as formalised, and whether that describes the
world is answered by experiments (Section 4, Section 26). It doesn’t mean Coq’s own
foundation is proved consistent; it’s believed consistent, and that can’t be proved from
inside, by Gödel (Section 11), so the foundation is trusted, and “trusted” has substance:
it’s the same kernel CompCert and the four-colour proof stand on, and a bug in it
would take all of them down together, which is a kind of safety in numbers. It doesn’t
mean the hardware correspondence is unconditional; Section 27’s table says where
the proof stops. And it doesn’t mean no axioms: the proofs use five standard-library
assumptions, and the assumption audit names them: functional extensionality on
dependent functions (two functions that agree everywhere are equal); uniqueness
of equality proofs, in the form the standard library calls eq_rect_eq (only in the
hardware proofs, through the Kami library); two decidability principles that come
with the standard library’s real numbers; and, in a little over a hundred theorems,
the law of excluded middle (every proposition is true or false). The count, from the
full audit: the full-corpus probe covers 14,589 named theorems across 511 files: 7,009
close under the global Coq context outright, and 7,580 use only Coq standard-library
assumptions. Zero project-local axioms appear in any of the 14,589 dependency trees.
Three files sit outside that probe: the small machine, its version for any property

                                           368
The Thiele Machine                                                          Devon Thiele


language, and its universal host (Section 14). Each ends by printing the assumptions
of every headline theorem in it, and the test suite compiles all three and fails unless
every one of those lines says the theorem is closed under Coq’s own rules, with no
axiom at all. A lemma a closed theorem uses is closed with it. So for those three files
“nothing assumed” means exactly that, and the evidence is the files’ own printout, not
the big audit. In plain words: about fourteen thousand theorems, a little under half
of them needing nothing at all, and the rest leaning only on those standard-library
assumptions, none of mine. Those numbers belong to the audit run that produced
them; the shape doesn’t move between runs, the counts do.

28.4 What you’re trusting, in one place
If you accept every checked theorem in this book, here is what you’re still taking on
trust, all of it, so you don’t have to collect it from five chapters.

   1. The statements. The checker confirms a proof proves its statement. It doesn’t
      confirm the statement says what my sentence about it says. That’s why the book
      prints the important ones in full, premises and all, and why Appendix E prints
      the Coq text of fifteen of them beside a line on whether my sentence says exactly
      that, more, or less. A machine check supplements that reading.
   2. Coq’s kernel and its foundation, and the five standard assumptions above.
   3. The path out of Coq. Programs pulled out of Coq as runnable code by its extrac-
      tion mechanism, and the circuit description handed to the Bluespec compiler,
      are trusted from that point on. The synthesis and layout tools, the chip, and the
      board are trusted too, and Section 27 lays the chain out link by link. This is the
      list Ken Thompson’s lecture from Section 11 was about. I didn’t write Coq, or
      OCaml, or the Bluespec compiler, or yosys, so by his moral I can’t fully trust any
      of them, and neither can you. What I can do is keep the list short and print it, so
      you know exactly which tools you’re being asked to believe have no spare key
      cut into them.
   4. The tested parts. The Python demonstrations and the test suite are evidence that
      the code does what’s claimed on the runs tried, not proof that it always does.
   5. The physics. Anywhere a theorem has Landauer’s principle or a calorimeter
      in it, the physical premise is named and assumed (Section 4, Section 26), never
      derived.
   6. The standalone copy. A few results are checked in ThieleMachineComplete.v,
      the one-file copy of the kernel kept so the build can be read top to bottom, and
      not in the kernel itself (the crosswalk shows which). A test, not a proof, checks
      that the copy’s definitions match the kernel’s text. The extracted runner and the
      hardware refinement both use the kernel, not the copy.
   7. Whoever sets the start and whoever reads the record. Every guarantee about
      the record is about programs run from a clean start on a step that does what


                                          369
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


      its definition says. The operator who chooses the start, a reset, the loader, the
      wires and anyone reading a report they didn’t watch being made are outside it
      (Section 27 says this for the chip).

28.5 The auditor on top
Beyond the type checker, the project has a custom proof auditor I called the Inquisitor,
because a thing that reads every proof looking for ways you’ve cheated deserves
a name you won’t forget. It runs on every commit, and its source names about a
hundred distinct rules. The main families: no holes (no Admitted, no admit, no
give-up, no unproved axiom or parameter in project code); vacuity heuristics (no
theorem whose conclusion is literally True or a tautology; no theorem of the shape “P
implies P”; existence claims backed by a constant witness get flagged, and a flag is a
reason to look, not a verdict, since some constructions like a fixed interpreter program
are supposed to be fixed and get judged on what they compute); physics-definition
heuristics (no physical quantity defined as a placeholder constant, no physics claim
without an invariance condition); scope enforcement (the proof tree is split into tiers,
the kernel tier may not import from research-side files, and every active file must
reach the cost or semantics foundation through its imports, or it doesn’t get to claim
the kernel’s pedigree); and comment hygiene (no unfinished or historical markers in
maintained source). Its rules are heuristics. They point at places to look. They don’t
prove a theorem means what it should, and they can’t promise every empty premise
got caught.

So none of this is foolproof, the checker and the auditor included, and I don’t treat
it as if it were. That’s the reason the thing also got built and run. The extracted
runner executes the kernel’s own definitions, the hardware’s gate-level netlist and
its source description run the same programs and their results get compared field by
field against the kernel’s, and the tests are written to fail when a result quietly stops
holding. A proof can be hollow in a way nobody spots. A machine that runs the same
program three ways and has to agree every time is much harder to fool, and when it
disagrees, it tells you where to look.

28.6 Checking the companion formalization
The mathematical claims are the statements printed in this book, with their stated
hypotheses and the arguments given here. Running software is an additional way to
check their formal counterparts. It isn’t a prerequisite for reading the argument.

A reproducible check needs a fixed copy of the proof sources, dependencies and
probes. Changing that copy changes the object being checked; a later software result
cannot silently revise a theorem in this edition. The procedure below describes the
companion proof build. With Python 3, GNU make, Coq 8.18 and its standard library,
OCaml, ocamlfind and CSDP installed, run this from the root of a checkout of the
sources at a fixed revision (the hardware numbers in Section 27 name the one they
came from):

                                          370
The Thiele Machine                                                              Devon Thiele


python3 scripts/reproduce_coq.py

That copies the sources into a fresh directory and works only from the copy: it builds
the two vendored libraries the hardware proofs use (bbv and Kami), regenerates the
build file, rebuilds every proof from source, runs the contract probes that re-check the
named theorems and their assumptions, and runs Coq’s independent checker over the
result. It reuses no compiled proof from the checkout, and it writes its pass file only
after every stage passes. A failed run resumes from the snapshot it captured, and a
change to the sources needs a fresh run:

python3 scripts/reproduce_coq.py --resume \
  --output artifacts/reproduction/RUN_DIRECTORY

The run has to pass. Don’t stop at the pass: read the theorem types and their global
dependencies, because a closed report doesn’t make a theorem’s own premises go
away. The hardware generation is a separate command needing the Bluespec compiler
(Section 27), and its outputs have to name the source they were built from; a passing
proof build doesn’t give you a fresh synthesis.

That’s the checker. What’s left is to tell you how to break what it checked.

29 How to break this
Every main claim in this book comes with the exact shape of the thing that would kill
it. I went to the trouble on purpose. A claim you can’t break is a claim that wasn’t
saying anything, and I’d rather hand you a loaded gun pointed at my own work than
a sentence too vague to aim at. So these are written as instructions: here is the trace to
find, the object to build, the theorem to exhibit. Build one and the proof tree falls, and
I mean that as an invitation.

The invitation is an old one, and people have put prices on it. Donald Knuth gives the
first person to find each error in his books one hexadecimal dollar, 0x$1.00, which is
$2.56, deposited these days at the Bank of San Serriffe, a bank that doesn’t exist, since
real checks turned out to be an open door for fraud. Why pay strangers to find your
mistakes? His own page says it plainly enough: a careful reader makes the book better
for everyone who reads it next. This chapter doesn’t come with a bank, real or made
up. What it comes with is, for every claim, a description of the exact object that would
make it fall, so you know before you start what counts as winning.

Before the list, the honest part about it. Most targets below are theorems Coq has
checked, and knocking one of those over head-on would take a bug in Coq’s kernel.
That can happen, but it isn’t where I’d put my money. The places a reader can actually
win are aimed at me, not at Coq, and there are four. A sentence of mine that says
more than the Coq statement it cites (Appendix E puts fifteen of them side by side to
make that easy). A Coq definition that doesn’t capture the English word it’s named
for: on the small machine, “is at least 0” is a check that can’t fail, and the step certifies


                                            371
The Thiele Machine                                                               Devon Thiele


it anyway, so “certified” there doesn’t mean “found something out” (Section 14 says
so, and that’s the kind of gap to hunt). A list of premises that only its own example
satisfies. And a result that holds in the standalone copy of the kernel and not in the
kernel itself (Section 16).

29.1 The abstract claims (Parts II and III)
The universal floor (Section 3). Build a certification system that satisfies the one-step toll
and give a run from uncertified to certified with total cost zero. universal_nfi_
any_substrate falls. If you instead drop the toll, you’ve built a free-certification
system, not a counterexample.

The toll from premises (Section 4). Exhibit a finite, duplicate-free list of every state, a
certificate no step revokes, and an injective step that switches it on. permanent_f
lip_is_not_injective falls, and the derivation of the toll with it. An infinite
state space, a revocable certificate, or an unpriced merge is not a counterexample; the
file already builds one of each. For the squeeze bound, a finite permanent machine
with a cost meeting the halving premise where one step switches k states on beside m
certified ones and two to the cost times m is less than m plus k; permanent_flips
_compression_bound falls. For merge-or-revoke, a finite machine and an injective
instruction that switches a reading on without switching it off anywhere; flip_merg
es_or_revokes falls. A move that merges and also revokes isn’t a counterexample
to anything; it’s the three cards.

The bill in bits (Section 4). Exhibit a finite machine with a permanent certificate, a
move that switches k states on beside m certified ones (k at least one), and a spread
of probability over those m plus k states whose image under the move has entropy
above log base two of m. permanent_step_entropy_ceiling falls. For the
general form, a step and a spread under which two different states, each with some
probability, land on the same state while the entropy doesn’t drop; entropy_drop
_pos_of_support_merge falls. A heat measurement on a real device below what
the bound asks doesn’t touch either theorem. It refutes the premise landauer_hea
t for that device, which is Landauer’s principle, and that’s a fight with physics, not
with the counting. And a certifying step from a state already known that gives off no
heat isn’t a counterexample: known_state_flip_forces_no_heat says that case
owes nothing.

Learning is free (Section 5). Show that the four-state demon’s measure step merges two
states, or that its observer’s candidate list doesn’t shrink. observer_narrowing_ca
n_be_free falls. A different price schedule that charges the measure step is allowed
and isn’t a counterexample; the claim is “not forced,” not “always free.”

The counter (Section 6; on this machine, Section 16 and Section 23). Find a state and an
instruction such that the counter after is anything other than the counter before plus
that instruction’s cost; the loud version is a counter that goes down. vm_apply_mu
falls. Or find two bookkeepings that both start at zero, both follow the schedule step

                                             372
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


by step, and disagree on a reachable state; mu_is_initial_monotone falls.

Windows (Section 7). Exhibit a window and a price computed from the observed before
and after that meets the floor and never overcharges, on a machine where two steps
share their before and after pictures and only one certifies. shadow_cannot_pri
ce_exactly falls. A window that shows certification is not a counterexample; the
theorem says exactly that such a window prices exactly.

Entitlement (Section 8; on this machine, Section 22). Produce a strict narrowing of a
candidate list, with a distinguishing observation, that does not yield a strictly stronger
membership predicate; feasible_strict_subset_implies_strict_predica
tes falls. Or exhibit a run meeting every hypothesis of the representation theorem
whose counter rose by less than the index bits lost; structural_entitlement_re
presentation falls.

The latch (Section 10). Exhibit an extension of a base whose record is driven by the
computation and never switches off, and which is not a latch on any event. record_
axis_is_latch_holds falls. A record that switches off, or one driven by a hidden
clock, is the file’s own pair of counterexamples, not yours.

The diagonal (Section 11, Section 24). Two routes. A decider for some substrate with a
shortcut predicate whose flip the substrate can represent and which answers correctly
on every program; the generic proof fails at a named step. For the nat family, a d that
correctly decides the predicate of the substrate built from d. (The concrete machine’s
version offers no third route: its recursion premise is false for the class of all maps,
and given a decider correct on every program, its flip has no fixed point with equal
thousand-step runs from every state; Section 24 proves both, as vm_full_recurs
ion_premise_refuted and vm_correct_flip_has_no_fixed_point.) The
guest has no premise to supply, so it gets two targets of its own: a map on well-formed
guest programs that some guest program represents, with no well-formed program
equivalent to its own image, and vm_guest_recursion_theorem_closed falls;
or a decider for a property of guest programs that respects equivalence, holds of some
well-formed program and fails for JUMP 0, and vm_guest_rice_holds falls.

The pointer conjecture (Section 13). It’s a conjecture, so the three routes are its own: a
deployed discipline pricing a non-proliferating event; a rival event proliferating as
well as certification in a real ecosystem; an honest formalisation with independence
defined where certification fails the test.

One concession goes with it, and I make it in full. The window results, the separation
of the two witness states, and the counter’s uniqueness don’t single out certification.
Their proofs use only that the step carries something the classical picture doesn’t
determine, so the same shape of result holds for any such field. Nothing in Parts II to
V proves that certification is the one event a model is forced to price; Section 4 forces
a price on every merge, certifying or not. That’s the conjecture, and Section 13 is the


                                           373
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


case I make for it.

29.2 The machine claims (Parts IV and V)
The small machine (Section 14). Four targets. From a clean start, a run that raises the
flag without an earlier passing CHECK, COMMIT and CERTIFY of the same claim,
with the counter’s version unchanged between the CHECK and the COMMIT; earne
d_certification_provenance falls, and earned_commitment_provenance
for a COMMIT alone. From a clean start, a trace that leaves a fact in the table nobody
checked; no_forging falls. From a clean start, a run that ends certified for a total
charge under three; certified_run_min_cost falls, and a run at exactly three is
not a counterexample: CHECK “A is 0”, COMMIT, CERTIFY from a start where A
is 0 is one, and the same program from any other start is refused forever (earned_
run_check_can_fail, earned_run_refused_forever). A check that can’t fail
certifying for three isn’t a counterexample either; the step doesn’t police trivial checks,
and the book says so. A two-counter machine and a program whose run on the small
machine disagrees with it step for step, or halts when it doesn’t; simulation_step
or halting_correspondence falls.

The partition (Section 16). From the initial state, run any program and land on a state
where two modules share a cell, a module owns a cell numbered 128 or more, the
module counter is past sixty-four, or two modules carry one number. vm_reachable
_partition_in_bounds falls (and with the first, vm_reachable_regions_disj
oint). A PNEW past memory or on a spent budget that traps isn’t a counterexample;
trapping is the rule doing its job.

The arrows (Section 18). Three stored arrows with matching ends in a well-formed
graph whose two bracketings, built by COMPOSE, differ in source, target, flag, or
(flag off) a pair; graph_compose_assoc_stored falls. An identity arrow from an
object to itself and an arrow out of that object whose composite isn’t the same arrow,
in that sense; graph_compose_left_identity_stored falls, and the mirror for
graph_compose_right_identity_stored. Or a run from the initial state that
stores a flagged arrow between two different modules, or one with pairs; vm_reacha
ble_identity_arrows_canonical falls. Two composites with different labels, or
different identifiers, aren’t counterexamples; the sameness ignores both on purpose,
and Section 18 says why.

Separation (Section 20). Show that the two witness states differ in one of the six shadow
fields, or that their arrow lists are the same. categorical_separation falls. Error
behaviour is not the target; the arrow list is.

Strictness (Section 20, Section 23). Exhibit a classical program (any list of the twenty-
nine classical opcodes, run as a list or by program counter with its jumps, for any
fuel) whose execution changes anything in the graph (the fresh-module counter, the
arrow list, any of it), the assertion channel or the certified flag. Or find a state some
classical run reaches from the initial state where PNEW on cell zero traps or leaves the

                                           374
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


fresh-module counter fixed, or where the graph it produces is one a classical run from
the initial state also produces. thiele_strictly_extends_classical falls, and
with it pnew_step_separates_thiele_from_classical_reachable. Both
start from the initial state, so there’s no hand-built base to argue with.

The floor on fifty-one (Section 23). Find a run starting with the flag down and the counter
at zero, ending with the flag up and the counter at zero. certification_require
s_positive_mu breaks at the step that prices the flip. Add the counterexample as a
theorem and the build refuses to compile on top of it.

The finite fragment (Section 23). Exhibit a state and one of CERTIFY at zero, JUMP at two,
CHECKPOINT at zero whose result, read as program counter modulo four and the
flag, differs from the finite machine’s step, or whose counter rise differs from one, two,
zero. vm_runs_finite_machine or vm_pays_finite_price falls. A program
using JUMP at cost zero is outside the fragment; the full machine leaves that merge
free on purpose.

The classical CHSH bound (Section 25). Exhibit four fixed bits and a tally consistent with
that one plan, every pair sampled, scoring above two. chsh_violation_rules_o
ut_locally_factorizable_coupling falls, and so does known mathematics. A
randomised plan landing past two by luck doesn’t count; the theorem is about one
fixed plan, and Section 25’s coin-flip example shows the luck.

The integer gate (Section 25). The game check has two walls, and here’s how to knock
each one over. A correlator that passes the three contraction inequalities whose five-
by-five is not PSD (forward), or a PSD five-by-five of that shape whose correlators
aren’t contractive (reverse); npa_psd_iff_column_contractive falls. A correla-
tor whose pinned five-by-five is PSD (contractive, by the equivalence) with S squared
above eight; npa_psd_implies_tsirelson_bound falls. The PR box and the clas-
sical mixture (1, 0, 1, 0) are not counterexamples to any of these. Both fail contraction
by plain arithmetic (the table in Appendix F.4), which is what the theorems need them
to do, not what would break them.

The four 1+AB instructions (Section 25). Four bigger checks, four targets, one per in-
struction. Each of the four instructions that checks the nine-by-nine matrix has its own
theorem: from a state with no error, if the instruction advances the program counter
by one and leaves the error flag alone, the nine-by-nine matrix at the state’s correlators
and the instruction’s moments (all zero for the plain one; for the other three, the free
ones read from the supplied counts and the rest zero) is positive semidefinite. Exhibit
such a run where the matrix isn’t, and the matching theorem falls: chsh_lassert
_1ab_no_trap_implies_npa_psd_q1ab, chsh_lassert_1ab_g5_no_trap_
implies_npa_psd_q1ab, chsh_lassert_1ab_g345_no_trap_implies_npa
_psd_q1ab, or chsh_lassert_1ab_g12345_no_trap_implies_npa_psd_q1
ab. A trap on a point inside the set isn’t a counterexample. The checks are sound,
not complete, and the full one traps wherever its matrix is semidefinite without being


                                           375
The Thiele Machine                                                               Devon Thiele


definite, because each of its tests is strict (Appendix F.6).

The elliptope completion (Section 25). This one’s a shape, not an instruction, so you’re
trying to push a point in or out of it. Three targets, one per theorem, plus the decider
beside it. Signs a0 , a1 , b0 , b1 , each squaring to one, and a vector on which the completed
matrix of that plan goes negative; deterministic_strategy_elliptope falls. A
correlator with some positive semidefinite completion and S squared above eight; e
lliptope_tsirelson falls, and with it the claim that one completion can’t stretch
both Cauchy-Schwarz budgets at once. Real numbers x and y that make the PR box’s
completed matrix positive semidefinite; pr_box_not_elliptope falls. And for the
decider that sits beside it: inputs on which it says yes while the correlators have no
PSD completion at all (S squared above eight is one way to show that); elliptope_
check_full_sound falls. The all-ones plan and (1, 0, 1, 0) aren’t counterexamples
here either, from the other side: the completion admits them (turing_point_elli
ptope for the second), which is what the theorems require.

The hardware (Section 27). A counterexample to the whole-machine refinement (dr
iven_step_wf) has to satisfy its precondition and break its stated equality. A co-
simulation mismatch on a valid input challenges the tested transfer for that revision;
then pull it apart link by link (encoding, observation timing, extraction, printing, bsc,
the harness). An input outside the theorem’s domain, or a toolchain mismatch, doesn’t
refute the conditional theorem. It refutes a trusted link, which is worse for me and
more useful for you. The solver checks have a target of their own: a run from reset on
the extracted circuit that breaks a partition-table, control or loader property, which the
property-carrying simulation prints as a failed assertion and the solver would hand
back as a counterexample. For the netlist comparison, an input stream on which the
loader’s outputs differ in the two models while the CPU responses agree.

The five models (Section 12; the wrappers stated on this machine, Section 23). Each fragment
has a theorem with a named falsifier: a finality fork with nobody slashable; a gas
schedule meeting floor and no-overcharge whose charging predicate differs from the
commit predicate on some step; a sound and complete attestation verifier that reads
only the bare transcript, or a function of the quote that recovers the unmeasured
runtime flag; one of the RFC’s own example proofs that the transcribed inclusion
check rejects, or an input with leaf index equal to tree size that it accepts; a program
the bounds checker accepts whose verification condition fails. Each kills one fragment.
None of them, and I want this clear, says anything about the real system beyond the
fragment.

The audit (Section 28). Run the assumption probe on any kernel-tier theorem and
find a project-local axiom or parameter in its dependencies, and the claim of zero of
them falls. For the small machine and its host, compile either file and find a printed
assumption line that isn’t closed. Run the Inquisitor and read what it says; it fails
on high and medium findings. A new finding means somebody looks. It doesn’t


                                             376
The Thiele Machine                                                                Devon Thiele


automatically mean a theorem is false.

29.3 What’s mine and what isn’t
This is not a claim to have been first. Appendix C does the sorting item by item, with
sources: what was known, what’s added, and what kind of addition it is. Here’s the
short form, and I’d welcome correction on any boundary.

Borrowed, with names. As the opening chapter warned, I usually had the hunch first
and found these names after, and that order doesn’t make any of it mine. Every-
thing in Part I (every source is cited where it’s used). The category theory (Eilenberg,
Mac Lane). Turing, Church, Kleene, Rice, Cantor, Gödel, the diagonal pattern, Law-
vere’s unification, and the mechanized versions of them in HOL4, Lean, and Coq
(Norrish, Carneiro, Forster, Kunze, Smolka). Bell, CHSH, Tsirelson, Wehner, NPA,
Landau, Masanes, Fine, the elliptope, and the machine-checked proofs of Tsirelson’s
bound that came before mine (Echenim and Mhalla in Isabelle, and Lean’s mathlib).
Landauer, Bennett, Szilard, Maxwell, and their critics. The potential method (Tarjan)
and its mechanizations (Nipkow, Charguéraud and Pottier), Lamport’s clocks, Floyd
and Hoare. Gettier, Necula, Cook, Hartley, Shannon, Rissanen. Zurek. The guar-
antee about every program: the reference monitor (Anderson), execution monitors
(Schneider), and monitors checked at every instruction and verified in Coq (Azevedo
de Amorim and coauthors). The counting under the permanence results: Poincaré’s
recurrence, as Zermelo used it. The seL4 and CompCert discipline. Kami, Bluespec,
yosys with SymbiYosys and the solvers under it, nextpnr, X-Ray. The facts under the
permanence results are Landauer’s own example and Shannon’s bounds, and “set a
bit to one whatever it held” is my way of saying his RESTORE TO ONE.

Formal reconstructions. The Coq development defines the state types, transition sys-
tems, real-matrix predicates, encodings, and proof terms this book uses. When I say a
theorem is checked, I mean the stated proposition has a kernel-checked proof under
its printed premises. That doesn’t make the underlying idea mine, and it doesn’t make
it new.

What this project proved, inside its stated interfaces. The abstract floor, which is the poten-
tial method with one particular potential. The derivation of the toll from finiteness,
permanence, and a named price, in counted states and in bits, with each premise’s
counterexample built. The fixed-schedule ledger identity and uniqueness. The named
projection witnesses. The conditional representation theorem for entitlement. The
latch form over any base, with its two counterexamples and converse, and the two
uniqueness results (held up to schedule, refuted for tied records). The small machine’s
earned record (checked, then committed, then certified, about the same edition, noth-
ing forged, three at least), its universality through Minsky, and the universal host’s
mirror, its isolation and its refusal to certify for free. The substrate diagonal, the L
results, and the guest recursion theorem by construction. The integer gate implying
the pinned matrix is PSD (a sufficient test, not a necessary one), the equivalence with


                                             377
The Thiele Machine                                                               Devon Thiele


contraction, and Tsirelson’s bound from PSD, which is known mathematics checked
again here and tied to an instruction. The per-opcode hardware refinement and the
loader theorems, and the solver-checked safety properties of the extracted circuit. All
of it with premises printed. Of that list, the toll derivation, the pricing form of the
window fact, and the latch form are the only pieces I’d call new statements, and only
in the sense that I didn’t find them stated where I looked. The fourth thing I’d name
is built and checked rather than new in idea: a record that’s priced, and on the small
machine earned, under the reference monitor’s every-program move, which is old
and isn’t mine. Appendix C names the same four the same way, with the prior work
beside each.

Interpretation, which is mine and not proved. That structure is what a computation
establishes and the toll is the right thing to price. That certification is the pointer event.
That the record axis “belongs in the step.” Those are proposals, with the arguments
I’ve given, and the proposals are where I’d aim first if I were you.

30 The claim ledger
Here’s everything this book claims, one line each: what kind of claim it is, and where it
lives. “Proved” means proved under the premises printed in that section, and nothing
more. If a line here ever says more than its section does, the section is right and the
line is wrong. “By unfolding” after it means the proof does little more than read the
answer off the definitions, a case split whose every branch is a line: true, checked, and
carrying almost nothing the definitions didn’t already say. If you’re counting results,
count those differently; I’d rather mark them than let them pad the list.

Ledger is a good word for it, and it’s older than bookkeeping. Around 1400 a ledger
was a book that lay permanently in one place, a big church breviary, say, from the old
verb leggen, to lay; the account-book sense turns up in the 1500s. A book that stays
put. That’s the job here too. The home sections are long and they wander, and this is
the one place where every claim lies still, so you can come back and find it where you
left it.

30.1 Claims about the model
First the model. Every line in this table is about any system that has the pieces the line
names: a state and a step, plus whatever the result asks for, a reading and the toll, a
counter and a price list, a window, programs. None of them is about my machine. The
table runs over several pages, in reading order.

Here’s one way to use it, and it takes five minutes. Pick the sentence in this book you
trust least. Find its line. Read the Kind column before anything else. Then go to the
home section and check that the line says no more than the section does. If it says
more, you’ve found my mistake, and the end of this section says what I’d like done
about it.
