30.3 What I propose and haven’t proved
And then there’s what I’m proposing. These are mine. They reach further than any
theorem in here, and nothing in the tables puts an unavoidable physical price on every
observable change.

   • That the axis belongs in the step (Section 31, Section 32).
   • That the usual account of a computation is a shadow of the step (Section 32).
   • That certification is the event worth recording, which is the pointer conjecture
     (Section 13).
   • That this is a structural account of computation and not just a cost model (Sec-
     tion 31).
   • That the toll is the right thing to price, against a wall or a penalty for contradic-
     tion (Section 12, Section 32).

                                               397
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


And four things left open: whether Landauer’s critics are right, which would leave
every theorem standing and one premise unowned by the world (Section 4); whether
certification really is the pointer event (Section 13); whether there’s a smaller start
than a partition, by a ruler someone can state (Section 2); and whether a universal
Thiele machine can keep a foreign machine’s own record and price list; the one built
in Section 14.12 keeps a foreign machine’s computation and makes it pay a toll, and
nothing more about its record or its prices is proved, not even an exact price for the
small machine’s own programs, since its guest step costs its budget whatever the guest
instruction cost.

That’s the whole ledger. If you find a claim in this book that isn’t on it, or a line that
says more than its home does, that’s my mistake, and I’d want to hear about it.

31 Scope
This is the line around what I’ve proved. Inside it: an accounting law for one event,
a derivation of that law from premises each with its own counterexample, a set of
windows that provably lose it, a record axis that’s a latch over any base, a diagonal
that holds by proof on a fragment of the machine, a six-instruction machine on which
commitments are earned and which computes what two counters can, an integer gate
that implies a bound by algebra, and a chain from the step relation to a wiring list
with each link labelled. Outside it: everything that follows. This is the fence. I built it
myself, so lean on it before you trust it.

G. K. Chesterton has a famous fence, in a 1929 book called The Thing. A reformer finds
a fence across a road, can’t see what it’s for, and wants it cleared away; the wiser one
tells him to go off and find out why it was put there, and only then come back and
argue for tearing it down. This section runs the other way round. Every post below
comes labelled with what it’s there for, the overclaim it stops, so you don’t have to go
off and find out first. Pull up any post you like. Just look at what walks through the
gap when you do.

Physical interpretation of the counter. The ledger is unique once the start and schedule
are chosen. That doesn’t make it entropy, and it doesn’t make it energy. A physical
bridge needs a model of which states carry information, premises that can all hold
at once, and a real argument tying the formal charge to dissipation. The permanent-
certificate theorems supply the first for an abstract finite machine with a permanent
reading. The two premises are shown able to hold together only for a one-bit reset; for
the machine’s certifying steps that isn’t stated as a theorem. The full machine’s jump
merges program counters and is charged nothing, which breaks the bridge outright
(Section 23, Section 26), and the calorimeter protocol shows that population dynamics
don’t fix the energy scale. No joule value attaches to one mark without thermal and
device premises (Section 4, Section 26). In short: once you pick the start and the price
list, the number is forced by arithmetic, and it isn’t energy. The rest of that paragraph
is the list of what I’d need before it could be.

                                           398
The Thiele Machine                                                                Devon Thiele


Class separation. The witnesses show specific windows losing specific fields. They
don’t stop a conventional simulator from keeping those fields in its encoding. No
separation of standard complexity classes follows from the collisions, or from the
charge levels climbing without bound (Section 7, Section 20, Section 23, Section 26).
I’ll be blunt about why I’m careful here. Whether P equals NP is one of the seven
problems the Clay Mathematics Institute put a million dollars on, at a meeting in Paris
in May 2000. One of the seven has been solved since, the Poincaré conjecture, by
Grigori Perelman. P versus NP hasn’t. If a two-state collision on my machine settled
it, somebody would be owed a million dollars, and it wouldn’t be me. A window that
loses a field is a fact about that window. A complexity class is a fact about what every
possible program can do within a budget, and nothing in these collisions reaches that
far.

Trace initiality, and what it doesn’t settle. The universal property of the trace fold is about
evaluating lists of instructions: pick where a target starts, and there’s exactly one way
to fold a list into it (thiele_trace_fold_initial, Section 23). The counter’s
uniqueness assumes a schedule. Exact pricing assumes an event, and a reference
count that says what charging too much means (Section 7). Those results make the
construction precise. None of them shows that the category I chose, or the event I
chose, is physically necessary.

Other observables. Certification is one worked example. A family of other observations
might turn up other structural laws, but each would need its own events, its own
evidence, and its own cost rules, justified on their own terms. The window and oracle
results are about what specific maps keep. They don’t show infinitely many indepen-
dent dimensions, zero mutual information, or a cost for changing coordinates, and
piling predicates on top of each other doesn’t give a topology, a metric, or indepen-
dence (Section 20).

Program predicates versus state observations. The state-level collision (Section 7’s wall)
and the program-level diagonal (Section 11’s wall) live in different domains. Linking
them would take a theorem of its own. The nat family (Section 11) and the bounded-
machine theorem (Section 24) keep their explicit quantifiers and representability
premises.

Entitlement bounds. The representation theorem is handed its tree and its representative
reduction, along with the covering and payment conditions. It doesn’t dig the tree out
of an arbitrary run, and it isn’t a Shannon bound on every trace (Section 22).

Quantum behaviour. The fixed-matrix equivalence is about one completion with zero
marginals and zero within-party moments. The elliptope lets the within-party mo-
ments move, at the level of correlators. Full behaviours with marginals, and operator
realisations, need identifications this book doesn’t make. A sound runtime check
isn’t complete for those bigger sets, and the elliptope decider is not an instruction
(Section 25).


                                             399
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


The record axis. The proved structural result is: a permanent record driven by a base
computation is a latch on an event; on finite hardware its write merges states; and
the machine’s named projections don’t recover it. Certification is one instance, not a
theorem selecting the unique event every system must record (Section 10, Section 13).
A finite monotone multi-valued record decomposes into threshold latches, not into
one Boolean latch. Revocation, including revocation priced from the other side as in
Casper, lies outside the permanent-record axis; a price on revocation doesn’t transfer
to a price on the write (Section 12). Probabilistic records don’t inherit the uniqueness
result either. Two honest random records can have the same branches and the same
charges and still give those branches different weights, one choosing evenly and one
two to one, so the schedule doesn’t fix the probabilities (schedule_determines_p
robabilities_refuted). And no single deterministic latch explains a record that
can branch both ways from the same observation (deterministic_latch_handl
es_branching_refuted). Weak base equivalence is defined and is an equivalence;
no two of the four bases are related by it in the checked work, and the latch form holds
on each separately, so it doesn’t tell them apart (Section 10, Section 23). In short: a
record that stays up is a latch, and on finite hardware its write merges states; which
event deserves the latch isn’t proved; records that can come back down lie outside all
of this, and random ones lose the uniqueness.

Who it’s safe against. Every guarantee about the record is about programs: any list of
instructions, run from a clean start on a step that does what its definition says, one
writer stepping at a time. That covers the buggy program and the hostile one. It
doesn’t cover whoever sets the start (a snapshot put back, a table loaded with facts
nobody checked), a reset or a power cycle, the loader that picks the program, the wire
that carries the report, someone who flips the flag with a probe, the tools that built the
step, or a second writer that changes a counter without bumping its edition. Those are
the operator, the hardware and the tool chain, and they’re outside this fence. A record
read by someone who didn’t watch it being made is only as good as their reason to
believe the box that shows it. The ways across that I know of, a quote over measured
state and a proof that travels on its own, are in Section 7 and Section 12, and this book
builds neither (Section 27).

The guest. The twelve-instruction guest has a direct Rice reduction, numeric decoding,
verified dispatch, a guest-callable specialiser, and a recursion theorem proved by
construction. For the full fifty-one-instruction machine the recursion premise is false
when asked for every map, because equality after the thousand-step cutoff can be
decided by running both programs; the machine’s wall is the diagonal applied to that
decidable property, and nothing more (vm_full_recursion_premise_refuted,
vm_correct_flip_has_no_fixed_point, Section 24).

The five models. Each is a fragment transcribed from a specification, with a named
theorem and a named limit: the Casper transcription has no deposits or fork choice;
the gas fragment omits the refund cap; the attestation fragment has no signatures; the


                                           400
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


transparency verifier covers control flow, not collision resistance; the proof-carrying
checker is a three-instruction role model. None is a claim about the real system beyond
its fragment (Section 12).

The two machines. Part IV has a small machine and a big build, and they prove different
things. The small machine of Section 14 (two counters, six instructions) is where
commitments are earned: a raised flag went through a passing check, a commitment
and a certification of the same claim, nothing is forged, and the cheapest certificate
costs exactly three, a price reached by a check that could have failed (the step doesn’t
police trivial checks: a check that can’t fail certifies for three too). It’s also where
universality is proved, by matching Minsky’s two-counter machines step for step and
borrowing their undecidable halting from the Coq library. The universal host built
on it runs any of its programs as a guest by construction, since the host’s guest step
runs the guest’s own step as a primitive. What’s proved beyond that is that the mirror
always equals the guest’s flag, that no host move raises it for free, that the host’s
own instructions never touch the guest, and that a raised mirror means the guest’s
own run checked, committed and certified the same claim (host_mirror_earne
d, UniversalThiele.v). The host’s ledger covers the guest’s and isn’t proved to equal
it, and a machine from somewhere else comes in through the two-counter encoding
with its computation kept and a toll still paid; its own record and prices aren’t proved
to carry over. Its check price is flat, its fact table holds sixteen, and its certificate
is historical (Section 14 lists the rest). The big build of fifty-one instructions prices
every commitment and doesn’t enforce that one was earned: its check and its commit
are separate steps, and nothing makes the second wait for the first (Section 22). So
“commitments are earned” is a theorem about the small machine, not the big one.

The comparison machines. The small machines I built to compare against are fragments
too. The random-access memory result covers an addressed list memory with load,
increment and decrement on cells (concrete_ram_write_reads_back and its
neighbours), and it’s about that machine. The register machine Section 10 puts the
latch on (record_axis_is_latch_on_ram_holds) is a different small machine,
the one with indirect addressing, and that theorem is about it. The reversible-machine
result covers arithmetic update cores: add and subtract, each undone by the other,
with or without wrapping at a modulus (janus_like_unbounded_inverse, ja
nus_like_bounded_inverse). Neither is a theorem about real memories or full
reversible languages. The cost-semantics results are local correspondences, not full
cost-framework embeddings: the trace’s cost is a writer cost and a grade, and the toll
is the potential method with one potential (Section 6). Nobody’s whole type system
gets embedded either.

Outward consequences. I looked for results about real systems that would need the
record axis. Five narrow ones are proved, each as a two-state countermodel: a
certificate-transparency client’s local tree head can’t decide whether the world’s log is
consistent (ct_local_view_insufficient); a quote check that matches only the


                                           401
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


composite digest accepts a mismatched selection (tpm_selection_binding_is_
necessary); a local suffix can’t decide a trusted anchor (weak_subjective_suff
ix_insufficient); an acknowledgement without a durable commit record can be
lost (wal_ack_requires_durability); and a current local log can’t decide what
happened before it (audit_local_snapshot_insufficient). Each reduces to a
known indistinguishability or durability argument. Five stronger candidates would
need protocol or hardware semantics I haven’t formalised, and I’ve proved nothing
about them. So none of this yields a new outside result that both needs the record axis
and is ready to use.

The hardware. The Coq refinement chain stops at Kami’s semantics. Below that: ex-
traction, printing, bsc, yosys, nextpnr, X-Ray, and the board primitives remain trusted,
with the checks named. Beside the chain, a separate solver proves by induction that
the extracted circuit keeps its partition-table, control and loader safety properties on
every run from reset, and that the loader and board wrapper match the mapped netlist
if the CPU answers alike on both sides; no proof compares the CPU and its memories.
Seventeen programs passed the board-specific simulation across the mapped netlist
(before place and route), the extracted Verilog and the runner, including reset and
power-on checks. The Coq status-report theorem retains its premise that the report
rule fires once per clock cycle. The solver checks are not Coq theorems, and neither
they nor the finite simulations prove the translation chain correct. No physical board
run is recorded (Section 27).

Where each result lives. Every system that follows the toll, whatever its states: the
floor, at most as many certifications as cost, and the potential-method reading. Every
finite machine whose price covers merges: the toll for permanent records, and which
instructions every such price must charge. Every finite machine paying per halving:
the machine’s own narrowing bound. Every machine extending a base with a driven,
permanent record: the latch. Every window through which a certifying and a non-
certifying step look alike: no exact price from the window. This build only: the
schedule and its numbers, the collisions of its own windows, the integer gate and
its PSD bridge, the hardware correspondence, the fifty-one instructions, the finite
fragment.

What I’m proposing beyond that. That the axis belongs in the step; that certification is the
event worth recording; that this is a structural account of computation and not just
a cost model. Those reach further than any theorem here, and no theorem here puts
an unavoidable physical price on every observable change. They’re the argument,
and the argument is what the rest of the book was. What kind of claim is that? A
proposal about which distinctions an account of computation ought to draw, and no
proof settles an “ought”. The proofs show the proposal hangs together, follows from
premises I’ve named, and costs little (six instructions on the small machine); whether
anyone should adopt it is argued, not proved. Here’s what would weaken it: if every
use people have for the record turned out to be recoverable from a log the program


                                            402
The Thiele Machine                                                               Devon Thiele


writes plus a correctness proof about the program, or if the real systems keep choosing
walls over tolls for good reasons, as the five in Section 12 mostly did.

32 Conclusion
I started with one word and a machine I couldn’t explain. Here’s where the word
ended up, and where the machine did.

Structure turned out to be relations among things, kept under chosen changes, carried
by whatever stuff, always relative to a frame. The start I chose, the smallest one by
the count of names, was a sorting of a pile, and the thing nobody I read had priced
was the moment you stand behind the sorting. That was Part I, and it ended with a
question.

The question got an exact form in Part II: five parts, one rule, one theorem you proved
at the table. Then the rule stopped being only my preference. On a finite machine
where the flag stays up, raising it forgets something, and if forgetting is charged
for, the way Landauer’s principle charges for it in its worst case, the toll follows.
That’s a derivation under three premises you can refuse one at a time, each with its
counterexample built, not a proof that every computation has to adopt the rule; and
the charge on forgetting is a named premise with its critics named. Learning can be
free; committing to a record that stays put can’t be, on those premises. That’s as far as
physics goes in this book, and I’ve tried to keep it exactly that far.

Part III was the logic, and here’s what it earned, in the order it was earned. The
counter is arithmetic once the schedule is chosen. A window in which a raising step
and a quiet one look the same can’t price the raise exactly, by a fact about functions
far older than the machine. Entitlement is defined as an object, a checked relation, and
a paid event; on the machine, under the hypotheses of the representation theorem,
one of which is that the run already paid a floor step for every level of a covering
tree, those payments cover the index bits it commits to (no run is shown to have to
pay them, and the bit search of Theorem 22.11 shows the hypotheses can be met);
and it is a license to lean on a claim, not a proof that the claim is true. Insight, in the
sense the toll prices, is a committed relation, not a feeling, and its floor is flat: at least
one, however deep. The claim behind the flag is a formula on a group, checked by a
small checker, and the check is a different step from the commit. Over any base, an
honest record is a latch, with two free choices, the event and the price list; “only one
substrate” is false and “one structure, many price lists” is true once the event is fixed.
No procedure the substrate itself can represent decides the shortcut predicate, given a
recursion theorem, by the same diagonal that broke Frege’s floor, and the machine’s
answer is to record the commitment rather than automate the judgement. Of five
record disciplines I modelled in fragments, one prices the write. And which event to
record is a conjecture, with its refutations listed.

Part IV built twice. The small machine comes first in the telling, though it was built last,


                                             403
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


two counters and six instructions, and on it the model stands whole: a raised flag was
checked, then committed, then certified, on the same edition of the same counter, noth-
ing gets forged, the cheapest certificate whose check could have failed costs exactly
three (the step doesn’t police trivial checks), and it computes everything Minsky’s
two-counter machines can, so its halting is undecidable. Earned commitments and
universality are proved there. So is a universal Thiele machine, with its scope said
plainly. One fixed host holds any small-machine program as data and runs it, and that
part is true by construction, since the host’s guest step runs the guest’s own step as a
primitive. The theorems are the rest: the host’s mirror always equals the guest’s flag,
no sequence of host moves raises it for free, the host’s own instructions never touch
the guest, and a raised mirror means the guest’s own run checked, committed and
certified (host_mirror_earned, UniversalThiele.v). An ordinary programmable
computer, as built, doesn’t do that for the programs it runs; a fixed interpreter built
to mirror and charge would. All of it is proved in Coq with nothing assumed: each of
the small machine’s three files prints the assumptions of every headline theorem, and
the test suite fails unless each comes back closed. Guests are small-machine programs,
which compute everything, and a machine from somewhere else comes in through the
two-counter encoding with its computation kept and a toll still paid; its own record
and its prices aren’t proved to carry over. Then the big build, one try, in three materials,
whose job was to be the witness: every “when the machine exists” from the earlier
parts landed on a theorem with a name. It prices every commitment on its fifty-one
instructions and doesn’t enforce that one was earned; the check and the commit stay
two separate steps there, on purpose and on the page. The places where the machine
came up short of the idea stayed on the page too: the free jump, which has its theorem,
and the four instructions with no hardware encoding. So did the near miss: the obvi-
ous rule for composing identity arrows breaks associativity the moment two of them
meet, and the machine’s rule passes the identity flag along, so the laws hold on the
arrows it stores, each one a theorem. Part V was the chain to the chip, with every link
labelled proved, tested, or trusted, and the sentence that no board was ever powered
on. Part VI was how to check it and how to break it. Every result carries the shape of
the thing that would kill it, gathered in one place (Section 29): a run from uncertified
to certified with the counter never rising; a contractive correlator whose pinned matrix
isn’t positive semidefinite; a certification system that follows the toll and certifies at
total cost zero; a function on numbers that correctly decides the shortcut predicate of
the substrate built from it. Any one of them brings down the theorem it matches. I
hunted. I came up empty. For a theorem Coq has checked, that’s no surprise: finding
one would take a bug in the checker. The places a reader can really win are where my
sentence says more than the statement does, or a definition doesn’t catch the word it’s
named for, and Section 29 starts with those.

If you asked what’s new here, I wouldn’t give you one thing, because there isn’t
one. There are four, and each comes with its fence and its neighbours. First, the
toll isn’t only my preference: on a finite machine a reading nothing turns off can


                                            404
The Thiele Machine                                                          Devon Thiele


only be turned on by a step that merges states, so if merges are priced, raising it
costs (Theorem 4.1, Theorem 4.2). The counting under it is the finite cousin of the
recurrence argument Zermelo threw at Boltzmann in 1896, and the price on a merge is
Landauer’s, as a premise. Second, a window that shows a raising step and a quiet one
the same can’t price the raise exactly (Theorem 7.2); that a price computed from what
a window shows can’t tell apart two steps the window shows the same is elementary,
and what’s here is the pricing form. Third, a record driven by the computation that
never switches off is a latch on one event, over any base (Theorem 10.1); latches and
history variables are old, and the theorem covers only records that never come down.
Fourth, a record that’s priced, and on the small machine earned (Theorem 14.9), under
the move of guaranteeing something about every program. That move isn’t mine at all.
It’s the reference monitor’s (Anderson, 1972), made precise for monitors that watch a
run (Schneider, 2000), and verified in Coq for monitors checked at every instruction
(Azevedo de Amorim and coauthors, 2015). What’s put together under it here, built
and checked rather than new in idea, is the check bound to the edition it looked at,
the toll paid on top, and a universal host that carries both to any program of the small
machine it runs as a guest. Appendix C sorts all four with sources.

And two things I’d point at if you asked how far the checking reaches. Neither is a
fifth new thing, and neither feeds the record: a game check that passes changes no
certification reading, it just doesn’t trap (Section 17).

In the build: an integer check on eight counters, run by one instruction, forces a five-
by-five matrix to be positive semidefinite, and from there the Tsirelson bound follows,
and the chain never once reaches for physics. No Hilbert space, no operators, no
observables. The route through the matrix isn’t mine; it’s the first rung of a ladder
Navascués, Pironio and Acín built in 2007, and the semidefinite road to Tsirelson’s
bound is older than that. What’s here is the check that runs in whole numbers inside
an instruction, and the checked link from “this instruction didn’t trap” to the bound.
It’s algebra you can follow line by line, and the assumption audit on that link finds
exactly three standard axioms from Coq’s own library (two that come with its real
numbers, and functional extensionality) and nothing of mine, which is how anyone
can see that no physics was smuggled in.

In the model: the diagonal rules out a correct decider whenever its flip can be ex-
pressed inside the substrate and the substrate supplies the fixed point; in L the fixed
point is proved from the reduction rules and the diagonal is Rice’s theorem; and on
my machine’s own guest the fixed point is proved by construction, so the wall stands
there by proof and not by premise. For the full machine the recursion premise is false
when asked for every map, because its cutoff property is decidable from outside, and
the flip of every correct decider has no fixed point; both are theorems. Those are
different sentences, and sharing a vocabulary doesn’t make them one.

What’s open, by my count. Whether the toll is the right thing to price, as against a


                                          405
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


wall or a penalty for contradiction, which is what the five real systems mostly built.
Whether certification is the pointer event. Whether a universal Thiele machine can
keep a foreign machine’s own record and price list; the host in Section 14.12 keeps
a foreign machine’s computation and makes it pay a toll, and nothing more about
its record or prices is proved, not even an exact price for the small machine’s own
programs. Whether a chip for the small machine can carry its earned record into silicon.
Whether Landauer’s critics are right, which would leave every theorem standing and
one premise unowned by the world. And the question I’d most like someone to take
from me: is there a smaller start than a partition, by a ruler they can state? I said in
Section 2 it would change this book. It would.

And the two computers from the first pages, the sorter and the copier, holding the
same bits. Walk the warehouse again. On an ordinary machine there’s still no lamp
for what the sorter did, and nothing in this book changes that. On the small machine
there is one: a flag and a counter you can read off the state, and a theorem that, from
a clean start, the flag can’t be up unless a check of that very claim, about that very
edition, passed first, where a claim can be any property whose checker is proved to
mean what it says, “this counter, read as a list, is sorted” among them (sorted_run_
certifies_iff and sorted_run_refused_forever, EarnedGeneric.v). That’s
the one lamp I set out to light. It’s a lamp for whoever can read this machine’s state. A
“tests passed” sheet fits it only when the test is a checker proved to mean what it says;
the sticker and the very sure AI from the first pages ask something else, whether to
believe a report you didn’t watch being made, and nothing in this book answers that
(Section 31). Whether every machine ought to have that lamp is the argument, not the
proof.

So that’s the Thiele Machine. An abstract model with five parts and one rule, an
argument made with it that the usual account of a computation is a shadow and the
axis it leaves out belongs in the step, and two builds of it to check the argument against,
a small one and a big one, the big one in three materials. The theorems are what they
are, with their premises printed. The interpretation is mine, and I’ve tried to say at
every turn which is which, because the first time through I was the only one checking,
and I’ve met me, and that’s not enough people. Now there’s you.

A Things I had to learn first
I had been around computers my whole life and paid attention to people like John
Carmack on how graphics actually get made, but I came in with none of the formal
fields this work turned out to need. By the time the proofs compiled I’d needed
enough of half a dozen of them that I had to put down somewhere what those fields
had words for. This appendix is that place. None of it is the argument. It’s what I
needed to be able to make it. Everything below is what I understood after I went and
read about it; I’m not claiming to teach you these subjects, and if you already know a
part, skip it.


                                           406
The Thiele Machine                                                                 Devon Thiele


A.1 Bits, bytes, and what a CPU sees
A bit is one digit that’s either zero or one, the smallest fact a machine can hold. Every-
thing else is bits stacked up. Eight of them make a byte, which lands you any number
from 0 to 255, and the first thing that genuinely surprised me is that the same byte is
also a letter: a convention called ASCII simply agrees to call 65 the letter A, 48 the digit
0, 32 a space. Nothing in the byte knows which it is. The meaning is a convention laid
on top.

You can see the convention’s seams with a pencil. Write 65 in binary: 1000001. Knock
off the first two digits and what’s left, 00001, is 1, and A is the first letter. B is 66, which
ends in 00010, two. Now lower case: a is 97, which is 1100001, the same pattern with
one more bit switched on, the one worth 32. Every capital and its small letter differ in
exactly that bit. That’s on purpose. The first version of the code, in 1963, had no lower
case at all; when lower case arrived, in the 1967 revision, it was placed so the two cases
differ by one bit, which made matching them, and building keyboards and printers,
simpler. Nothing in the byte knows it’s a letter, but somebody made the letters easy
for a circuit to tell apart.

Everything in this subsection is about real CPUs and about my machine, the big build
of Part IV. None of it belongs to the abstract model, which has a kind of state and a
step rule and nothing about widths or slots.

A word is a chunk of bits the CPU treats as one unit. My machine’s reference kernel
(its definition in Coq) uses 64-bit words (any number from 0 to about 18 quintillion);
the synthesised hardware uses 32-bit words (0 to about 4 billion). The abstract model
doesn’t care which width.

A register is a named storage slot inside the CPU that holds one word; my machine
has sixteen, r0 through r15, and they’re the fastest place to read or write. Memory is
a longer list of word-sized slots accessed by index, the address; my machine has 128
words of it, and that’s the entire address space. The program counter is one specific
register that tracks where in the program the machine is; after every instruction it
moves forward by one unless the instruction says jump. A stack pointer is a register
pointing at the top of a region used for nested calls: CALL pushes a return address
there, RET pops it, and r15 is the stack pointer by my convention. A port is a named
channel for talking to the outside world; the kernel doesn’t model the outside, it
charges for the communication and accepts the value the instruction declares.

Modular arithmetic means counting wraps at a maximum: with a maximum of 16,
17 wraps to 1. The machine wraps register indices modulo 16 and memory indices
modulo 128, so r17 is r1. Bitwise operations work on the bits of a value one position
at a time: AND is 1 only when both bits are, OR when either is, XOR (exclusive or)
exactly when they differ. A shift moves every bit left or right, which multiplies or
divides by a power of two. Popcount is the count of one-bits in a value. Hexadecimal
is base 16, digits 0 to 9 then A to F, written with a 0x prefix: 0xFF is 255.

                                              407
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


A trap means the machine routes execution to a fixed address instead of advancing, the
hardware’s “this went wrong, go to the handler.” An ISA, instruction set architecture,
is the list of every instruction a CPU recognises, each identified by an opcode, a
numeric tag the hardware decodes. My machine has fifty-one. The abstract model has
none; it has a step rule.

A.2 The notation the formal parts use
I don’t think in these symbols, and I had to learn to read them. The natural numbers
are 0, 1, 2, and so on, written with a double-struck N; the integers add the negatives;
the reals are the whole number line. A function from a set A to a set B is written
with an arrow. For a finite set, vertical bars around it mean its size; for a number, its
absolute value. A big sigma is a sum over every member of a set. A delta before a
quantity means the change in it. An upside-down A means “for every”; a backwards
E means “there exists.” A double arrow is implication; a double-headed one is “if and
only if.” A small circle between two functions is composition, apply the right one first.
Angle brackets around a random quantity mean its long-run average, which I picked
up from the Bell-test papers. In this book a circled plus is bitwise XOR and a circled
times has one meaning, the tensor instruction’s concatenation of two coupling lists;
the quantum sense of that symbol never appears, because the game section does its
work in plain integer arithmetic. A superscript T on a matrix is its transpose, rows
and columns swapped, and I with a subscript n is the identity matrix.

A.3 Coq, in just enough detail
Coq is a proof assistant: a programming language whose type system is expressive
enough that proofs are programs and the compiler checks them (Part VI has the long
version). A Theorem is a named statement followed by a proof; a Lemma is the
same thing used for an intermediate result; a Definition introduces a named value;
an Inductive type is one with a finite list of constructors, the only ways to build a
value of it (Coq’s natural numbers have two: zero, and successor of another natural).
A tactic is a step inside a proof: induction (base case, then step), destruct (split into
cases), reflexivity (prove a thing equals itself), simpl (compute), lia and lra and nra
(arithmetic solvers for integers, linear reals, and polynomial reals), psatz (a certificate
search for polynomial inequalities). Qed ends a proof and asks Coq to check the
whole chain. Admitted is the keyword for “I claim this without proof,” and it appears
nowhere in the active tree. A Hypothesis inside a Section is a named premise that
becomes an argument of every theorem that uses it when the Section closes; “closed
under the global context” doesn’t make it go away. Print Assumptions lists the global
axioms a theorem depends on; on the kernel tier it shows only standard-library ones.
A total function always returns a value, and Coq requires every function to be total;
the machine’s step function is, error cases included. “Parametric in K” means the
proof works for any K; the machine’s sizes are literal constants, and the proofs are
about those literals.



                                           408
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


A.4 Category theory beyond Part IV
Part IV builds objects, arrows, composition, identities, associativity, and the identity
laws from scratch. Beyond that: a functor is a structure-preserving map from one
category to another, sending objects to objects and arrows to arrows while respecting
composition and identities; think of it as a translation rule between two worlds of
structure. An embedding is a functor that throws nothing away, and faithful is the
precise version for arrows: two distinct arrows never land on one. Conservative is
the version for inverses: if the image of an arrow has an inverse, the arrow already
had one, so the functor can’t manufacture an isomorphism (an arrow with an inverse)
that wasn’t there. The two properties are different, and neither gives the other. Read
the natural numbers under addition as a category with one object and an arrow for
each number, and the same for the integers. The inclusion of the first into the second
is faithful, since distinct naturals stay distinct integers, but not conservative: 1 has no
inverse among the naturals, and its image has one, minus 1. The other way round, the
functor from the integers onto the trivial one-arrow group is conservative, since every
arrow of the integers already has an inverse, but not faithful: it sends every integer to
the same arrow. An embedding needs faithfulness specifically. A monoidal product
combines two objects or two arrows into one, with a unit and laws that make the
combining behave; the tensor instruction is tensor-shaped, and the checked laws for it
are the interchange law under a side condition and associativity with the empty list as
unit. An initial object has exactly one arrow into every object; the counter’s uniqueness
in this book is a uniqueness-on-reachable-states fact, not a category-theoretic initial
object. Yoneda’s lemma is where the categorical engine first clicked for me, the night I
stopped borrowing other people’s runtimes, and nothing in the formal development
uses it.

A.5 Bell-test vocabulary
A correlation between two outcomes is the average of their product; with outcomes
plus or minus one it lies between minus one and one, plus one meaning always match,
minus one always differ. A correlator is one such average in a labelled setting, E00 for
Alice’s setting 0 and Bob’s 0. The marginal of a joint distribution is the distribution of
one side alone with the other averaged out; zero-marginal means each side’s outcome
is plus or minus one equally often on average. A local hidden-variable model is one
where both outcomes are fixed by a shared random variable agreed before the game
plus each side’s own setting; Bell’s theorem says no such model produces certain
correlations quantum mechanics does. No-signalling means neither side’s marginal
depends on the other’s setting. Quantum-realisable means compatible with some
quantum state and measurements; the NPA hierarchy gives a ladder of necessary
tests, each a positive-semidefiniteness condition on a moment matrix, and no single
rung is sufficient in general. The PR box is the no-signalling correlation that wins the
game every time, stronger than quantum mechanics allows; nature doesn’t provide
it. Cauchy-Schwarz is the inequality that a dot product is bounded by the product
of the lengths. The Tsirelson bound is two root two, the largest game score quantum

                                           409
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


mechanics allows; the classical bound is two and the PR bound is four. (If you go
looking for Boris Tsirelson’s 1980 paper, look under Cirel’son, the spelling the journal
printed, or you may not find it.) The elliptope is the set of correlators that can be filled
out into a positive-semidefinite matrix.

A.6 Hardware and synthesis vocabulary
A hardware description language describes circuits as text; Bluespec is high-level
(rules, and the compiler builds the arbitration) and Verilog is low-level (registers and
wires). Register-transfer-level Verilog describes how data moves between registers
each clock cycle and is what synthesis tools consume. Synthesis compiles a description
down to logic gates; yosys is an open-source synthesis tool. Place-and-route assigns
gates to positions on a chip and wires them; nextpnr-xilinx does it for the chips this
design targets. A bitstream is the binary file an FPGA reads to configure itself, and the
X-Ray tools produce one from the routed design in two moves: fasm2frames packs
the routed design into configuration frames, then xc7frames2bit writes the frames
out as the bitstream. An FPGA is a chip you program after manufacturing: physical
gates, configurable connections. A LUT, look-up table, is the FPGA’s basic logic
primitive, a small memory programmed to implement any small Boolean function; a
flip-flop is a one-bit memory cell; a carry chain is wiring for fast addition; distributed
RAM is memory built out of LUTs; block RAM is dedicated memory; DSP slices are
dedicated arithmetic. This design doesn’t use the DSP slices. Synthesis runs with
yosys’s -nodsp option, so the multiplier inside the game check (one wide multiplier,
shared across the phases of a multi-cycle check) is built out of LUTs. With DSP slices
the design didn’t finish placing and routing inside the build’s time limit; the open-
source placer stalled and the routing came out congested. It computes the same
thing either way. The choice is about what the tools can place and route, not about
correctness. A netlist is the gate-level circuit written out; a VCD waveform is a record
of every signal at every time step in a simulation; iverilog and Verilator are open-
source Verilog simulators. A bisimulation is a precise notion of two systems behaving
the same under a chosen relation on their states; field-by-field equality of states is one
particular, stronger contract, and Part V says which the hardware proofs use. A parity
test is the empirical cousin: run two implementations on the same set of inputs and
check that they agree, a correspondence earned by testing rather than by proof.

How old is the idea of a chip you wire after you buy it? Younger than you might
guess. Ross Freeman, one of the founders of Xilinx, came up with it in 1984, and the
first one sold, the XC2064, came out in 1985 with sixty-four little logic blocks in an
eight-by-eight grid, each able to compute any function of four inputs. The chip this
design targets counts its lookup-table sites in the hundreds of thousands, and this
design uses about fifty-three thousand of them (Section 27 has the numbers). Same
idea, forty years on. The IEEE dedicated a milestone plaque to it in 2026.




                                            410
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


A.7 Other terms I use without rebuilding
Provenance is the recorded chain of where an object came from; on the small machine,
a commitment’s provenance is the passing check that came before it (Section 14). Simu-
lation, in computer science, is one system imitating another’s input-output behaviour;
a Turing machine simulates any system of the model, my machine included, by writ-
ing the whole state out on its tape, and the difference this book is about is what a
window on that tape shows. That’s real, and it’s exactly what people reach for when
they want to wave the whole question away: if a tape can stand in for the state, what
was the difference? The tape carries a picture of the state, not the state, the way a
photograph of a fire keeps you exactly as warm as any other photograph. The counter
and the toll live in the step rule, not in the bytes, and an encoding copies the bytes.
A Turing machine built with the toll in its own transition table is a different case: it’s
an instance of the model, not a simulation of it. What no machine can do is make a
simulated rule binding just by writing it down on tape.

Projection is a function that drops information on purpose. The bare window on my
machine keeps three things, the registers, the memory and the program counter, which
are what a Turing machine already has, and that’s why projecting lands you back in
ordinary computation. It drops everything else, including the three that were doing
the new work: the counter, the certification readings, and the arrow graph. Other
windows keep more: forget also keeps the counter, and shadow_proj keeps six
fields and drops the graph. Nothing is wrong with any of them. They’re perfectly
good functions. They just cost you what made the state more than a tape. A quotient
is the operation of declaring two things the same when they agree on what you chose
to look at and working with the classes instead. A projection does exactly that: it
doesn’t just drop fields one at a time, it glues together states that the dropped fields
kept apart. The fibre of a function over a value is everything the function sends to that
value. An injection sends no two inputs to the same output; a surjection covers every
output. Decidable means an algorithm always halts with a yes-or-no answer; keep the
claim and the algorithm apart, since the algorithm decides the claim only once there’s
a proof that its answer matches. Polynomial time means running time bounded by a
power of the input size; P is the problems solvable that way, NP the problems where a
candidate solution can be checked that way, and whether the two are the same is open.
The two budget predicates in the checked work, error_free_preservation_bud
get and positive_input_certification_budget, are not complexity classes.
Each lets the trace be chosen separately for every input, and the bounds they take are
plain functions with no requirement to be polynomial.

“Kernel” wears three hats in this book, and I’d rather point that out than let it ambush
you. First, mathematics: the kernel of a map is what it sends to the identity, and for
a projection the useful version is the relation “these two states project to the same
thing.” Second, the proofs, where the hat comes in two sizes: the kernel tier is the
part of the Coq development the main theorems live in (Section 28), holding both the


                                           411
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


model’s theorems and my machine’s definition, and the files are where the model is
written down, not the model itself; and Coq’s own kernel is the small checker that
accepts or rejects every proof. Third, the operating-system kernel, which I never use
and mention only so you know it isn’t meant. The sentence around the word always
says which one is.

A.8 Matrices
A matrix is positive semidefinite (PSD) when vT Mv ≥ 0 for every vector v; the game
check is all about one matrix being PSD. The determinant of a square matrix is a single
number that is zero exactly when the matrix squashes some direction flat. For a two-
by-two matrix with rows ( a, b) and (c, d) it’s ad − bc. For a bigger one, expand along
a row: for each entry, delete its row and column, take the determinant of what’s left,
multiply by the entry, alternate the signs, and add up; the recursion bottoms out at two
by two. A principal submatrix is what you get by choosing some of the indices and
keeping only those rows and the same columns; its determinant is a principal minor.
A symmetric matrix is PSD exactly when every principal submatrix is, every one of
them, and the game check uses the three-by-three ones (Appendix F.4). The Schur
complement turns a question about a block matrix into a question about a smaller one.
For a symmetric block matrix with corner block P, off-diagonal block Q and other
corner R, it’s R − QT P−1 Q, and when P is positive definite the whole matrix is PSD
exactly when that complement is (Lemma F.8). Positive definite matters; invertible
isn’t enough. Take P = −1 and every other entry zero: the complement is zero, which
is PSD, and the whole matrix isn’t.

A.9 Borrowed ideas the book pushes on
These get their full story in the chapter that uses them; here’s the one-line version for
when you’ve forgotten which one Landauer was.

The pigeonhole principle: put more pigeons than holes and some hole holds two. Sec-
tion 4’s room with too few chairs is that, and so is the proof that a permanent flag can
only be raised by a step that forgets something. Landauer’s principle (Rolf Landauer,
1961): a step that wipes information, lowering the entropy of what a machine holds
by some number of bits, gives off at least Boltzmann’s constant times the temperature
times the natural log of two in heat per bit. In this book it’s always a premise with
its name on it, never derived (Section 4, Section 26). Entropy, in Claude Shannon’s
sense: for a spread of chances over states, roughly the average number of yes-or-no
questions you’d need to pin the state down, so an even spread over n states has log2 n
bits. A spread, in this book, is just a list of chances that add up to one. Maxwell’s
demon (Section 5): a little creature that watches molecules and sorts fast from slow,
seemingly for free; Charles Bennett’s answer was that the measuring can be free and
the wiping of the demon’s notes is what costs. The potential method (Robert Tarjan,
1985): pay for a run with a quantity stored in the state, so a step’s bill plus the change
in the stored quantity is what you count; Section 6 reads the toll as that method with



                                           412
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


one particular potential.

The halting problem (Alan Turing, 1936): no program decides, for every program
and input, whether it stops. Kleene’s recursion theorem (Stephen Kleene, 1938): for
any transformation of programs that can itself be computed, some program behaves
exactly like its own transform. Rice’s theorem (Henry Rice, 1953): any property that
depends only on what a program does, and isn’t true of all programs or of none, can’t
be decided by a program. The diagonal is the move under all three: build the thing
that does the opposite of what the table says about it (Section 11). L is a small lambda
calculus, a language made of nothing but functions applied to functions, which Yan-
nick Forster and Gert Smolka built in Coq and which Section 11 and Section 24 use as
a tool. A hash is a short fingerprint of a longer piece of data, made so that finding two
inputs with the same fingerprint is supposed to be hard; a hash chain folds each new
record into the fingerprint of the last, and a Merkle tree folds them pairwise into one
root (Section 3, Section 12).

Extraction is Coq’s mechanism for turning definitions into runnable code in another
language; nothing it produces is checked by the proofs after it leaves Coq (Section 28).
Kami is a Coq library for writing hardware as rules and proving things about them,
from Choi and coauthors (Section 27). A refinement proof says a lower-level step
does what a higher-level one says, under stated side conditions; Section 27’s are per
instruction.

A.10 Words this book builds
These are mine, or mine in the sense that I pinned them down for this book. Each is
built properly in the chapter named; this is a reminder, not the build.

A few words first, because everything else hangs off them and each has exactly one
meaning. The model (or the abstract model) is a kind of state and a rule for stepping,
plus exactly the extra pieces a given theorem asks for: a certification reading and the
toll, or a counter and a price list, or a window, or programs written as states and a
recursion theorem. The name Thiele Machine belongs to the model. Parts I to III
live there, and every claim in them is about any system with the pieces it names. A
substrate is the model’s shape with whatever extension a theorem names, and nothing
else; the word never means my machine, and never the side of a simulation that does
the stepping (Let me be straight with you). My machine (also the machine I build, the
build, the big build) is the concrete machine that fills in many of those pieces at once:
its state record, its fifty-one instructions and their prices, the reference kernel in Coq,
the guest, the extracted runner, and the hardware. The small machine (the smallest
honest machine, Section 14) is the other piece of scaffolding, and it comes first in
Part IV. The scaffolding is both of them together. Parts IV and V live there. A Thiele
machine, lower case, is any system proved to be an instance of the certification system
(Definition 3.1), five parts and the toll; the paper toys are, and so are both builds.
Thiele-complete means a Thiele machine whose base is Turing-universal, so it computes


                                           413
The Thiele Machine                                                                Devon Thiele


anything a Turing machine can while carrying the record and paying the toll; the small
machine is proved Thiele-complete, and for the big build it’s open. That’s a low bar on
purpose: a Turing-complete base with a latch and the toll is enough, and a clock that
charges one for every move pays the toll. A universal Thiele machine runs any machine
of a stated class as a guest, with the guest’s record kept and its toll collected by its
own step; one is proved for the small machine’s programs (Section 14.12). Running
the guest is by construction there, since the host’s guest step runs the guest’s own
step as a primitive; the theorems are the mirror, no free host certification, the host’s
own instructions never touching the guest, and a raised mirror meaning the guest’s
own run was earned (host_mirror_earned, UniversalThiele.v). A machine from
elsewhere keeps its computation and pays a toll there; its own record and prices aren’t
proved to carry over. The chip isn’t a Thiele machine; it implements the big build
inside the bounds Section 27 states. When a word below belongs to only one of the
two layers, the entry says which.

A partition is a sorting of a pile into groups, nothing in two groups and nothing left
over (Section 2). A certification system is a state type, moves, a step, a cost per move,
and a yes-or-no reading, plus one rule, the toll: a move that turns the reading from
no to yes costs at least one (Section 3). The files call that rule A2 in one of their two
numbered lists (Appendix B). A move merges when two different starting states land
on the same end; one that never does is injective, it forgets nothing. A reading is
permanent when no move turns it from yes back to no (Section 4).

The counter, which I also call the ledger: in the model, a number carried in the state that
starts at zero and that every step raises by exactly that step’s charge (Section 6). My
machine has exactly one, and the source calls it mu (µ) (Section 16). Two other things
get called counters, and each chapter says which: Minsky’s two bins on the small ma-
chine, and the eight witness counters that tally the game’s rounds (Section 25). Neither
is the ledger. A price list (on my machine, the cost schedule) says what each move costs;
the model takes it as given, and my machine’s table of what each instruction costs is
in Section 17. A receipt is a total that lives in the state, only climbs, equals the sum of
the charges on every path including the failures, and is the only such total for its price
list (Section 6 gives the argument for any system with a counter and a price list; the
checked theorems are about my machine, Section 23).

These belong to my machine only, and none of them appears before Part IV. A module is
one group in my machine’s partition of its memory; its region is the run of consecutive
data-memory addresses it owns, a base and a length, inside the hundred and twenty-
eight words; no two modules’ regions overlap, and a run hands out at most sixty-four
module numbers (Section 16). An arrow (a morphism) goes from one module to another
and carries a coupling, a list of pairs of cells, one from each side, plus a label (Section 16,
Section 18); in Section 2, “arrow” means only the category theorist’s general word.
The certified flag is set by CERTIFY and nothing ever clears it; the assertion channel is
a separate number written by MORPH_ASSERT (Section 16, Section 17, Section 23).


                                             414
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


In the model there is just a certification reading, yes or no (Section 3). The guest is a
twelve-instruction fragment of my machine, run as data by an interpreter written in
my machine’s own instructions (Section 24). That’s the big build’s guest. The universal
host’s guest is a different thing: a program of the small machine, held as data by the
host and run one step at a time (Section 14.12). Each chapter says which one it means.

These belong to the small machine only (Section 14). A two-counter machine is Minsky’s:
two counters holding whole numbers with no upper limit, and two instructions: add
one, and subtract one and jump if the counter is above zero, or else go on to the next
line; already enough that nobody can decide in general whether one halts. The small
machine is a two-counter machine plus HALT and three instructions for the record,
six in all: INC, DEC, HALT, CHECK, COMMIT and CERTIFY. A counter’s version is
its edition number: it starts at 0 and goes up by one every time the counter is written,
so an edition never comes back. A fact is a property, a counter and a version together,
such as “A is even, as of edition 3”; the properties come from a fixed language of
three, is zero, is even and is at least n. The same theorems also hold for any property
language whose checker is proved to mean what it says, and one such language reads
a counter as a list and asks whether it’s sorted (sorted_run_certifies_iff and s
orted_run_refused_forever, EarnedGeneric.v). The fact table holds up to sixteen
facts, and the only way in is a CHECK that passed; nothing ever leaves it. The small
machine’s channel holds one committed fact or nothing, and COMMIT puts a fact
there only if the table has it about the counter’s current edition. It names the last
commitment earned that way, and a later COMMIT replaces it (certified_chann
el_earned and channel_names_last_commit, EarnedCore.v). The trap is a bit
that goes up when an instruction refuses, and then nothing in the core moves again.
A commitment is earned when a passing check put its fact in the table first, about the
same edition, with no write to that counter in between; on the small machine every
flag raised from a clean start is earned, and that’s a theorem there, not on my machine.
CHECK, COMMIT and CERTIFY cost one each and everything else costs nothing, so
the cheapest certificate costs exactly three, and a check that could have failed reaches it:
CHECK is zero on A, COMMIT, CERTIFY, from a start where A is 0. The step doesn’t
police trivial checks; is at least 0 passes every value and certifies for three too.

A window is any function that shows you part of a state (Section 7); a shadow, said
loosely, is what a window leaves you with, and the shadow, as a named window, is
my machine’s six-field one of Section 20 (registers, memory, program counter, counter,
error flag, certified flag). A collision is two steps that look the same through a window,
before and after, where one raises the flag and the other doesn’t (Section 7). Entitlement
is what a run has when it carries an object, a checked relation between that object and
a claim, and a paid event that put the object in place: a license to lean on the claim, not
a proof that it’s true (Section 8). A latch is a record that switches on the first time some
event holds and never switches off (Section 10). The diagonal’s substrate (Section 11)
is the model’s shape extended with programs, a run that may give nothing back, a



                                            415
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


counter that never falls, a way to write programs as states, the transformations the
substrate counts as its own, and its own recursion theorem for those; the proof of the
diagonal uses neither the counter nor the toll.

B Every assumption in one place
This book leans on a small number of rules that nothing proves, plus a handful of
record types that carry rules as fields. I’ve named each one where it’s used. Here they
are side by side, because a reader who wants to break this book should be able to see
every place where it says “suppose,” in one list, with what each “suppose” buys.

There’s one tangle to undo first, and it’s my fault. The checked work has two different
records with two different numbered lists of “axioms,” and both lists use the label A2
for different things. The book uses “the toll” for the rule that matters and avoids the
bare labels; this appendix maps the labels for anyone reading the files.

B.1 The records that carry a rule
Definition B.1 (Certification system). The record CertificationSystem (Univer-
salCertificationCost.v) has five data fields, a state type, a move type, a step function, a
cost per move in N, and a yes/no reading, and one proof field, cs_cert_costs: a
move that turns the reading from no to yes costs at least one. This proof field is the
toll of Section 3, and in this record’s numbering it is called A2. Every result stated “for
any certification system” assumes it, because the record cannot be built without it.


Definition B.2 (Abstract certification machine). The record AbstractCertMachine
(AbstractNoFI.v) is narrower: its moves are the fifty-one instructions of the machine in
Part IV, and it has a step, a reading, and one proof field, acm_preserve, saying that
an instruction outside a fixed list of five certification-address setters never turns the
reading from no to yes. In this record’s numbering, A1 is the reading itself, the field
acm_cert, a yes/no certification indicator on every state: the state has to include
one. Coq enforces A1 through the record type. A record with that field left out isn’t a
record of this type, so A1 is discharged when the record is built. The field acm_pres
erve is A3, the starting condition “the reading starts at no” is a theorem hypothesis
called A2, and “each of the five setters costs at least one” is a separate lemma called
A4 (cert_addr_setter_cost_pos). Its theorem abstract_nfi concludes that a
run from no to yes contains one of the five setters; it does not mention cost.


So the same idea, “the crossing costs,” is A2 in one list and A4 in the other. The book
means the first: the field cs_cert_costs.


Definition B.3 (Quantitative certification system). The record QuantitativeCerti
ficationSystem (QuantitativeNoFI.v) extends a certification system with a witness,
a function W from states to N, and a threshold N ∈ N, and adds two proof fields: (A3,


                                           416
The Thiele Machine                                                                 Devon Thiele


qcs_cost_bounds_witness) W (s) + cost(i ) ≥ W (step(s, i )), the witness grows by
at most what the move cost; and (A5, qcs_cert_threshold_witness) a state that
reads yes has W (s) ≥ N. An optional extension, QuantitativeCertificationSy
stem_full, adds (A4, qcsf_witness_nondecreasing) W (s) ≤ W (step(s, i )).


Theorem B.1 (The floor raised to a threshold). In a quantitative certification system, every
run from a state with witness 0 (this starting condition is called A6) to a state that reads yes
has total cost at least N.

Proof. Adding A3 along the run telescopes: the witness at the end is at most the
witness at the start plus the total cost, so at most the total cost. A5 says the end witness
is at least N. Neither A4 nor the toll is used.

Checked as universal_nfi_quantitative (QuantitativeNoFI.v). A3 and A4
bound opposite directions, and neither implies the other: witness 1, cost 0, witness
0 satisfies A3 and breaks A4, and witness 0, cost 0, witness 1 does the reverse. Two
instances are built: the machine’s assertion channel with threshold 1 (thiele_quan
titative_nfi_cert_addr), and a family for the game trials of Section 25, whose
cost counts valid trial instructions and whose threshold is any N: reaching N recorded
trials from none takes at least N valid trial instructions (chsh_trial_count_lowe
r_bound).
