Three remarks on the table. First, the recursion premise for the full machine is false
when asked for every map (its thousand-step cutoff property can be decided by run-
ning both programs), and holds for trivial classes such as the identity map and the
constant maps, and for no class containing the flip of a correct decider; for the twelve-
instruction guest, the corresponding statement is a theorem with no premise (vm_g
uest_recursion_theorem_closed, Section 24). Second, the class Substrate
(Substrate.v) carries a different rule from the toll, mu_monotone: the counter never
goes down on a step. Neither implies the other, the diagonal uses neither, and on
the machine both hold. Third, merge pricing is Landauer’s principle taken in its
worst case over what the machine might be holding: it charges every merging move,
while the principle in its general form charges only for uncertainty actually removed
(Theorem 4.12).

B.3 The axioms of the checker itself
Beyond the premises above, the checked proofs rest on Coq’s own foundation and on
five standard-library axioms, which the assumption audit lists theorem by theorem:
functional extensionality on dependent functions (the most used, across the kernel
and the hardware); uniqueness of equality proofs, eq_rect_eq (only in the hardware
proofs); two decidability principles for the real numbers (used wherever real analysis
is, for example in the game check of Section 25); and the law of excluded middle (in a
little over a hundred theorems). No axiom or parameter of the project’s own appears
in the audited theorems. Section 28 says what that does and doesn’t mean.

C What’s mine, and what isn’t
Every chapter of this book leans on somebody, and I’ve named them where I lean.
This appendix does a different job, and it’s the one where I’d most like to be caught
out early rather than late. For each thing the book could be accused of claiming as its
own, it says what was already known, what this work actually defines, builds, proves,
or connects, and what kind of contribution that is. Six kinds, and they aren’t the
same claim: a new result (a statement nobody had); a new proof of something known;
a mechanization (a known result checked by a machine, here Coq); an implementation
(something built that runs); a synthesis (known pieces put together under one question);
and a conjecture. Every kind can be worth doing. None of them is the others. And if
you read down the list and notice that “new result” hardly shows up, good. You’re
reading it right.

Two warnings about my own evidence before the list. First, “I didn’t find it” is a fact
about my searches, not about the literature. I searched with every tool I had, and some
tools will cheerfully invent a citation if you let them, so where it matters I say where I
looked, and you should assume it may well be sitting in a paper I’d need a few more
lifetimes of homework to read. Second, nothing below is inferred from how many
theorems there are, from the audit’s clean bill, or from a good story about who came
before. Those tell you the work was checked. They don’t tell you it’s new. Fourteen


                                           419
The Thiele Machine                                                          Devon Thiele


thousand checked theorems could, in principle, be fourteen thousand careful ways of
agreeing with Tarjan.

C.1 1. The universal floor and the potential method
Known: the potential method of amortized analysis, a function on states whose drop
bounds the cost of a run, is Tarjan’s (1985), and it has been mechanized more than once
(Nipkow in Isabelle/HOL, 2015 and 2019; Charguéraud and Pottier’s time credits in
Coq, 2019), built into type systems for automatic resource analysis (Hoffmann and
coauthors, 2011 onward), and recast in cost-aware type theories (Niu, Sterling, Grodin
and Harper, 2022). Mine: choosing the potential that is one when a designated reading
says no and zero when it says yes, so that “the crossing costs” (the toll) and “every
run that crosses paid” (the floor) are the potential method’s two halves (Section 6).
Kind: a mechanization of a known technique with a particular choice of potential. The
choice is the point: it makes “was certified” something the account must carry. The
theorem is not new mathematics. If it looks clever, that’s Tarjan’s cleverness; my part
was picking which number to plug in.

Go back to Tarjan’s paper and there’s a sentence that sits right on the line this book
draws. He opens with the dictionary (to amortize is to put money aside at intervals,
as in a sinking fund) and then gives two views of the method. In the banker’s view
the computer is coin-operated, and each operation is handed credits to spend or save;
in the physicist’s view, which he credits to Daniel Sleator, every state has a potential
and you count its changes. Then he stops to say that the credits are only an accounting
device: the programs that actually run contain no mention of credits or debits. That’s
exactly right for what he wanted, a bound proved about a program from outside. It’s
also exactly the gap. In his method the coins live in the proof. The one move I chose
was to put them in the step, where no program takes a step without it being counted.
Same arithmetic, different place.

C.2 2. The toll from finiteness, permanence, and a price on merges
Known: that steps which merge states (no single-valued inverse) are what Landauer’s
principle charges for is Landauer’s (1961), sharpened by Bennett (1973, 1982, 2003;
the words “the erasure of a bit or the merging of two computation paths” are from
the 2003 abstract); generalizations and the dependence on the input distribution are
Maroney’s (2009), Sagawa’s (2014), Wolpert’s; the critique is Earman and Norton’s
and Norton’s. Write-once memory is an old topic in coding theory (Rivest and Shamir,
1982), about reuse rather than price. And the counting under the theorem is older
than any of that: Theorem 4.1 is the finite, discrete cousin of the recurrence argument
Zermelo, using Poincaré’s theorem of 1890, turned on Boltzmann in 1896, aimed at a
reading instead of at entropy (Section 4 tells it). Mine: the short pigeonhole argument
that on a finite machine a reading nothing can turn off can only be turned on by a
merging step (Theorem 4.1), the merge-or-revoke dichotomy, the characterisation of
the moves every merge-pricing schedule must charge, the squeeze and entropy forms



                                          420
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


for a permanent flip, and a built counterexample for each premise (Section 4). Kind:
small new statements, I think, with mechanized proofs; the physics is a named premise
and is Landauer’s. Searches: I didn’t find this exact statement anywhere I looked, and
nobody’s search covers a whole field, mine least of all; I found no mechanization of
Landauer’s principle in Coq, Isabelle, or Lean.

C.3 3. Learning free, committing priced
Known: that measurement can be done at no fundamental cost and the cost sits
in erasing the record is Bennett’s resolution of Maxwell’s demon (1982), with the
quantitative trade-off by Sagawa and Ueda (2009). Mine: the four-state demon and the
three-state ring as checked models, and the two-state impossibility (Section 5). Kind:
mechanization and illustration of a known physical point inside my ledger. Not a new
physical claim. Bennett did the hard part in 1982; I built a toy with four dots on it and
got Coq to agree with him.

C.4 4. Windows that can’t price what they hide
Known: a function of an observation is constant on the observation’s fibres; that’s ele-
mentary, and the systems version of it is Moore’s distinguishing experiments (1956),
Kalman’s observability (1960), and the completeness question of abstract interpreta-
tion (Cousot and Cousot, 1977; Giacobazzi, Ranzato and Scozzari, 2000). Mine: stating
the pricing version (no window price is exact across a collision) and exhibiting collid-
ing pairs for the machine’s two named windows (Section 23). Kind: mechanization of
an elementary lemma, plus specific facts about this machine.

C.5 5. Structural entitlement and its bound
Known: decision-tree counting bounds (a tree that tells N cases apart has depth at
least log2 N); certifying algorithms that hand over checkable certificates (McConnell,
Mehlhorn, Näher and Schweitzer, 2011); proof-carrying code (Necula, 1997); the gap
between justified true belief and knowledge (Gettier, 1963). Mine: the definition of
entitlement as an object, a checked relation, and a paid event on the record, and
the assembled theorem that, under its listed hypotheses, a certified strengthening on
the machine pays at least the index bits it commits to (Section 8, Section 22). Kind:
synthesis plus mechanization; the counting idea is standard, the assembly and its
vocabulary are this work’s, and the pricing policy is assumed, not derived.

C.6 6. The record axis is a latch
Known: monotone, write-once state is old: the latch (Eccles and Jordan, 1918), sticky
bits (Plotkin, 1989), grow-only state in replicated data types (Shapiro and coauthors),
history variables and stuttering in refinement (Abadi and Lamport, 1991). Mine: the
exact statement that a record driven by the computation that never switches off is,
over any base, a latch on one event, with its converse and a counterexample for each
of the two conditions, and the uniqueness-up-to-price-list result with the refutation
of the stronger uniqueness (Section 10, Section 23). Kind: a small structural lemma, I



                                          421
The Thiele Machine                                                          Devon Thiele


think not stated before in this form (I found no prior statement in the searches I ran),
built from old notions, and mechanized.

C.7 7. The diagonal, L, and the guest’s recursion theorem
Known: Kleene’s recursion theorem and Rice’s theorem; Lawvere’s fixed-point form
(1969) and Yanofsky’s retelling (2003); mechanized recursion theorems and Rice (Nor-
rish in HOL4, 2011; Carneiro in Lean; Forster, Kunze, Smolka and coauthors in Coq,
including L itself, 2017, and the Coq Library of Undecidability). Mine: the diagonal
stated once over any substrate that supplies a recursion theorem; Rice and halting
proved again for L from its reduction rules; and a recursion theorem constructed for
the machine’s twelve-instruction guest, ledger included, with the evaluator compiled
into guest instructions through L and the library (Section 11 and Section 24). Kind:
checked instances, not new theorems of computability. The guest result is an instance
of a theorem that holds for any model with universality and s-m-n; the work is in
building that for this machine.

C.8 8. The game check
Known: that positive semidefiniteness of a correlation matrix gives the Tsirelson
bound is Tsirelson’s (1980) and Wehner’s semidefinite proof (2006); the moment-
matrix hierarchy, the Schur-complement analysis of this very level-one matrix, the
arcsine characterization, and the level 1 + AB are Navascués, Pironio and Acín’s (2007,
2008), with Landau (1988) and Masanes (2003); and Tsirelson’s bound has already
been checked by machine, in Isabelle/HOL (Echenim and Mhalla, 2023) and in Lean’s
mathlib. Rational sum-of-squares certificates are Peyrl and Parrilo’s (2008). Mine: a
decision procedure in integer arithmetic on outcome counters that runs inside one
instruction; a checked chain from “that instruction didn’t trap” to “the pinned level-
one matrix is positive semidefinite” to “S2 ≤ 8”; proofs of the contraction equivalence
by explicit test vectors; the level-1 + AB cascade and an elliptope gate in whole num-
bers, with a soundness proof and no step of the machine attached to it; and a circuit
proved to compute the same check on 32-bit counters (Section 25 and its derivation
appendix). Kind: implementation and mechanization, with a new proof of a known
equivalence in one slice. I found no prior formalization taking counters as input or
linking a machine instruction to the bound, and that’s a report on where I looked, not
on everything that exists.

C.9 9. The verified path to a chip
Known: Kami (Choi, Vijayaraghavan, Sherman, Chlipala and Arvind, 2017), Kôika
(Bourgeat, Pit-Claudel, Chlipala and Arvind, 2020), the end-to-end verified stack of
Erbsen and coauthors (2021), CakeML on the verified Silver processor (Lööw and
coauthors, 2019), and the discipline of naming what isn’t proved (CompCert, seL4).
Mine: an instruction-by-instruction Kami refinement for this machine, a proved serial
loader, solver-checked inductions on the extracted circuit’s partition-table, control and
loader safety, and a labelled chain to a bitstream (Section 27). Kind: implementation


                                          422
The Thiele Machine                                                          Devon Thiele


of an established method. No new verification method; extraction, synthesis, and the
chip are trusted, and no board was run.

C.10 10. Five record disciplines, one question
Known: each system and its guarantee belongs to its designers: Casper (Buterin and
Griffith, 2017), Ethereum’s storage gas and refunds (EIP-2200, EIP-3529), extend-only
TPM registers, Certificate Transparency (RFC 9162), proof-carrying code. Mine: asking
all five whether the write is priced, with a small checked fragment of each (Section 12).
Kind: synthesis and an organizing reading; the fragments are not verifications of those
systems.

C.11 11. The pointer conjecture
Known: Zurek’s quantum Darwinism (2009), with Ollivier, Poulin and Zurek (2004)
and Blume-Kohout and Zurek (2006): preferred states are the ones whose records
proliferate redundantly in the environment. Mine: borrowing that shape for the
question of which event deserves a record, with definitions, a toy, and refutations of
two stronger forms (Section 13). Kind: conjecture. No claim about quantum physics.

C.12 12. The counter as a receipt
Known: one-way counters that give order and termination are old: Turing’s 1949 note
on checking a large routine, Floyd’s ranking functions (1967), Lamport’s clocks (1978).
Carrying a run’s cost beside its result is the writer cost of Danner and Licata and
the graded effect semantics of Katsumata (2014), with a working-language version
in Orchard, Liepelt and Eades (2019). Mine: putting three properties side by side
(the total only climbs, it equals the sum of the charges on every path including the
failures, and it is the only such total for a given price list), the argument for any
system with a counter and a price list, and the checked versions on the machine
(Section 6, Section 23). Kind: synthesis, with mechanization on the machine; the
abstract statements are argued in the text and are not checked in Coq. Whether the
counter is an embedding of the graded frameworks or something weaker I haven’t
settled.

C.13 13. Couplings and the stored-arrow laws
Known: the category (Eilenberg and Mac Lane, 1945), and that relations compose
associatively with the diagonal as identity. Mine: the machine’s rule for composing
stored arrows, which passes the identity flag along so that associativity and both
identity laws hold on the arrows it stores, each a theorem, together with the checked
laws for relational composition and for the tensor on couplings (Section 18). The
obvious rule for composing identity arrows breaks associativity, and the book says so
where it matters. Kind: implementation and mechanization of known structure on
one machine. Not a result in category theory.




                                          423
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


C.14 14. The small machine
Known: two-counter machines are Minsky’s (1961, 1967), and the undecidability
of their halting is checked in the Coq Library of Undecidability (Forster, Larchey-
Wendling and coauthors, 2019, 2020). The guarantee about every program is older than
any of this, and it isn’t mine either. It’s the reference monitor (Anderson, 1972): a check
that sits in the path of every operation, so no program gets around it. Schneider (2000)
worked out what a monitor that watches a run can enforce: only safety properties, the
kind a bad run breaks at some finite moment, and “no CERTIFY without an earlier
earned COMMIT” is one of those. Azevedo de Amorim and coauthors (2015) verified,
in Coq, monitors that check tags at every instruction. Mine: a six-instruction machine
on two counters, with a version for each counter, a bounded fact table and a channel;
its theorems that a committed fact was checked first about the same edition, that
nothing is forged, that nothing is evicted, that the channel names the last earned
commitment (certified_channel_earned and channel_names_last_comm
it, EarnedCore.v), and that the cheapest certificate whose check could have failed
costs exactly three and no less (the step doesn’t police trivial checks, so one that can’t
fail costs three too); the same theorems for any property language whose checker is
proved to mean what it says, a sorted list read out of a counter included (sorted
_run_certifies_iff and sorted_run_refused_forever, EarnedGeneric.v);
and the step-for-step match with the library’s machine, so halting is undecidable for it
(Section 14). Kind: an instance of monitor enforcement, implemented and mechanized,
with two things on top that I didn’t find put together where I looked: the check is
bound to the edition of the thing it checked, and a toll is paid for the commitment.
The universality and the undecidability are borrowed, and the other properties are
short consequences of the step rule. Whether the design is new I can’t say, and I make
no claim beyond the proofs.

C.15 15. The universal host
Known: Turing’s universal machine (1936), which runs any machine given as data,
and the universal register machines that run two-counter programs. Keeping a guest
and the code running beside it out of each other’s state is what a virtual machine
monitor promises (Popek and Goldberg, 1974). Mine: a host that runs any program
of the small machine as a guest and has one extra move, a guest step that mirrors the
guest’s flag and charges in the same step. Running the guest is by construction: the
guest step runs the guest’s own step as a primitive, so “runs any guest” isn’t where the
work is. The theorems are that the mirror always equals the guest’s flag, that it rises
only in a guest step that passed CERTIFY, for every sequence of host moves, that the
host’s own instructions never touch the guest, that a raised mirror means the guest’s
own run checked, committed and certified the same claim (host_mirror_earned,
UniversalThiele.v), and that the host’s ledger covers the guest’s (Section 14.12). An
ordinary programmable computer, as built, doesn’t do this for the programs it runs,
because the code beside a program shares its memory and can flip anything; a fixed
interpreter built to mirror and charge would, and that’s the shape this host has. Kind:

                                           424
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


implementation and mechanization of a small design. The universality is borrowed
from the small machine and from Minsky. A foreign machine’s own record and prices
are not proved to carry over, and the host’s ledger only covers the guest’s; the book
says so where it states the result.

C.16 What that adds up to
Read straight down the list and the honest summary is this. The mathematics un-
derneath this book is mostly known, and some of it is very old. What’s mine is the
question (should an account of computation carry what was certified and what cer-
tifying cost, as part of how it steps), and the answer isn’t one result. It’s four, and I
name them the same way wherever they come up. The toll derived from finiteness,
permanence and a price on merges (item 2; the counting is the finite cousin of Zer-
melo’s recurrence objection, and the price is Landauer’s, as a premise). The pricing
form of the window fact (item 4; the fact itself is elementary). The latch form of a
record that never comes down (item 6; latches and history variables are old). And a
record that’s priced, and on the small machine earned, under the reference monitor’s
every-program move (items 14 and 15; the move is Anderson’s, Schneider’s and the
micro-policy authors’, and what’s added is the check bound to its edition, the toll on
top, and a universal host that carries both to any small-machine program it runs as a
guest). The first three are small exact statements I didn’t find stated where I looked;
the fourth is built and checked rather than new in idea. Under all four sits a large
body of mechanized proof that ties those statements to two machines that run, the
small one and the big build, and my best attempt at saying which is which, which
you should check as hard as anything else in here. If someone shows me item 2, the
pricing form in item 4, or item 6 stated earlier, I’ll move it up the list and be glad to,
and a little embarrassed, in that order.

D Every result and where it is checked
Every numbered result in this book is in the table below, in the order it appears, with
the Coq names that carry it, the file each lives in, and what the last full assumption
audit printed for it. “none” means the theorem is closed: its proof uses nothing
beyond Coq’s own rules. The other entries name the standard-library assumptions
it uses: FE is functional extensionality on dependent functions, UIP is uniqueness of
equality proofs (eq_rect_eq), RD is the pair of decidability principles that come with
the real numbers, and EM is excluded middle. “def” marks a definition, which has
nothing to assume. “closed (file)” marks a theorem of the small machine’s three files,
EarnedCore.v, EarnedGeneric.v and UniversalThiele.v, which the project-wide audit
doesn’t list: each file ends by printing the assumptions of every headline theorem,
the test suite compiles it and fails unless every one of those lines says closed, and a
lemma that a printed theorem uses is closed with it. “+N” after a file means N other
files in the tree define a name spelled the same way; the row gives the file this result
uses. A result whose only file is ThieleMachineComplete.v, with no “+N”, is checked
in the standalone copy of the kernel and not in the kernel itself (Section 16); a test, not

                                           425
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


a proof, ties that copy to the kernel. A premise or a conjecture has no Coq name on
purpose: it’s assumed or open, and the section that states it says so.

This table is an index of companion formalizations. The statements, hypotheses and
arguments are in the numbered sections it points to. An audit status reports the
recorded check; running a later version does not change a claim in this book.

E The exact words of fifteen theorems
This book states its theorems in its own words, and Section 28 says why that’s a risk:
the checker confirms a proof matches its statement, not that my sentence matches the
statement. So here are the statements themselves for fifteen of the results the argument
leans on hardest. Each is copied from its file with the comments taken out and nothing
else changed, and each comes with its file, a plain reading, and a line on whether the
book’s printed version says exactly that, more, or less. You don’t need to read Coq to
use this. Put the printed theorem next to the block and check that every premise in
the block turns up in the sentence. That’s the whole test. These are the statements this
book was checked against; if a file differs later, the book means the one printed here.

E.1 The universal floor
universal_nfi_any_substrate, coq/kernel/nfi/UniversalCertificationCost.v,
with the record it quantifies over.

Record CertificationSystem := mk_cert_system {
   cs_state : Type;
   cs_instr : Type;
   cs_step : cs_state -> cs_instr -> cs_state;
   cs_cost : cs_instr -> nat;
   cs_cert : cs_state -> bool;
   cs_cert_costs :
     forall (s : cs_state) (i : cs_instr),
       cs_cert s = false ->
       cs_cert (cs_step s i) = true ->
       cs_cost i >= 1;
}.




                                           464
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


Theorem universal_nfi_any_substrate :
  forall (CS : CertificationSystem)
         (trace : list (cs_instr CS))
         (s0 : cs_state CS),
    cs_cert CS s0 = false ->
    cs_cert CS (cs_run CS trace s0) = true ->
    cs_total_cost CS trace >= 1.

In plain words: a certification system is a record of a state type, a move type, a step,
a cost and a yes-or-no reading, plus one more field, cs_cert_costs, which is the
toll: a move that takes the reading from false to true costs at least one. Since the toll
is a field, every system the theorem talks about has it. The theorem: start at a state
reading false, run any list of moves (cs_run applies them in order, cs_total_co
st adds their costs), end at a state reading true, and the costs add up to at least one.
Theorem 3.1 says exactly this; the rule Definition 3.1 states as the toll is the record’s
last field here.

E.2 A permanent flip merges
permanent_flip_is_not_injective, coq/kernel/nfi/PermanentCertification.v,
inside a section that fixes the states, the moves, the step and the reading.

Variables (S I : Type).
Variable step : S -> I -> S.
Variable cert : S -> bool.

Definition finite_states (all : list S) : Prop :=
  NoDup all /\ forall s, In s all.

Definition permanent : Prop :=
  forall s i, cert s = true -> cert (step s i) = true.

Definition step_injective (i : I) : Prop :=
  forall a b, step a i = step b i -> a = b.

Theorem permanent_flip_is_not_injective :
  forall all s i,
    finite_states all ->
    permanent ->
    cert s = false ->
    cert (step s i) = true ->
    ~ step_injective i.

In plain words: finite_states all says the list all has no repeats and every state is
on it, so there are finitely many. permanent says once the reading is true, every move
keeps it true. step_injective i says move i never sends two different states to the
same one. The theorem: on a finite machine with a permanent reading, a move that
takes some state from false to true isn’t injective, so it merges two states. Theorem 4.1
says exactly this, with “merges” meaning “isn’t injective”.




                                          465
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


E.3 The toll from finiteness, permanence and merge pricing
a2_from_merging_price_and_permanence, the same file and section, with a
cost on moves added.

Variable cost : I -> nat.

Definition merging_steps_priced : Prop :=
  forall i, ~ step_injective i -> cost i >= 1.

Definition a2_holds : Prop :=
  forall s i, cert s = false -> cert (step s i) = true -> cost i >= 1.

Theorem a2_from_merging_price_and_permanence :
  forall all,
    finite_states all ->
    permanent ->
    merging_steps_priced ->
    a2_holds.

In plain words: merging_steps_priced says every move that isn’t injective costs
at least one, and a2_holds is the toll. The theorem: finite, permanent and merges
priced give the toll. Theorem 4.2 says this and one thing more, that the machine with
that cost is then a certification system the universal floor applies to. That second half
isn’t in this statement. It’s the definition right after it in the file (certification_s
ystem_from_merging_price), which fills the record’s toll field with this theorem,
so the printed form is true, and it leans on two Coq items, not one.

E.4 No exact window price across a collision
shadow_cannot_price_exactly, coq/kernel/nfi/ShadowPricing.v, inside a
section that fixes the states, moves, step, reading and a window obs.

Variables (S I O : Type).
Variable step : S -> I -> S.
Variable cert : S -> bool.
Variable obs : S -> O.

Definition flips (s : S) (i : I) : bool :=
  negb (cert s) && cert (step s i).

Definition shadow_cost (price : O -> O -> nat) (s : S) (i : I) : nat :=
  price (obs s) (obs (step s i)).

Definition meets_floor (cost : S -> I -> nat) : Prop :=
  forall s i, flips s i = true -> cost s i >= 1.

Definition never_overcharges (cost : S -> I -> nat) : Prop :=
  forall s i, flips s i = false -> cost s i = 0.

Definition shadow_collision : Prop :=
  exists s1 i1 s2 i2,



                                          466
The Thiele Machine                                                        Devon Thiele


     obs s1 = obs s2 /\
     obs (step s1 i1) = obs (step s2 i2) /\
     flips s1 i1 = true /\
     flips s2 i2 = false.

Theorem shadow_cannot_price_exactly :
  shadow_collision ->
  forall price,
    ~ (meets_floor (shadow_cost price) /\
       never_overcharges (shadow_cost price)).

In plain words: flips s i says move i takes s from false to true. A shadow price is
any function of what the window shows before and after a step. meets_floor says
every flip costs at least one, never_overcharges says every step that isn’t a flip
costs nothing, and a shadow_collision is two steps that look the same through
the window, before and after, one a flip and one not. The theorem: given a collision,
no shadow price does both. Theorem 7.2 bundles this with two neighbours from the
same file, that a price meeting the floor charges some non-flip at least one (shadow_
floor_overcharges) and that a window showing the reading prices exactly (win
dow_showing_reading_prices_exactly). This statement is the middle clause,
and the book says exactly what it says.

E.5 The record is a latch
record_axis_is_latch_holds, coq/kernel/foundation/StructuralRecordAxis.v;
the definitions come from StructuralCoreAnyBase.v and StructuralCoreCover.v.
Definition record_permanent (M : RCM) : Prop :=
  forall s, rc_cert M s = true -> rc_cert M (rc_next M s) = true.

Definition computation_driven (M : RCM) (B : BaseMachine) (C : BaseCover M B)
  : Prop :=
  exists f : b_state B -> bool -> bool,
    forall m, rc_cert M (rc_next M m) = f (base_state M B C m) (rc_cert M m).

Definition HonestBaseExtension (M : RCM) (B : BaseMachine) (C : BaseCover M B)
  : Prop :=
  computation_driven M B C /\ ledger_carried M /\ rc_a2 M /\
  record_permanent M /\ reachable_record_write M.

Definition latch_next (B : BaseMachine) (h : b_state B -> bool)
    (x : b_state B * bool) : b_state B * bool :=
  (b_next B (fst x), orb (snd x) (h (fst x))).

Definition latch_factorization (M : RCM) (B : BaseMachine) (C : BaseCover M B)
    (h : b_state B -> bool) : Prop :=
  forall m,
    (base_state M B C (rc_next M m), rc_cert M (rc_next M m)) =
    latch_next B h (base_state M B C m, rc_cert M m).

Definition record_axis_is_latch : Prop :=
  forall M B C, HonestBaseExtension M B C ->
    exists h, latch_factorization M B C h.

Theorem record_axis_is_latch_holds : record_axis_is_latch.



                                         467
The Thiele Machine                                                                            Devon Thiele


In plain words: here a machine M steps by itself (rc_next gives the one next state),
carries a reading rc_cert and a ledger, and sits over a base B through a cover C, a map
down to the base’s states that commutes with the step. computation_driven says
the reading’s next value is some function f of the base state and the reading’s current
value. Honest means driven, a ledger that never falls, the toll, a permanent reading,
and some reachable step that writes it. latch_next is the latch of an event h: the
base steps, and the record becomes “already on, or h holds now.” The theorem: every
honest extension evolves exactly as the latch of some event. Theorem 10.1 says a little
more than this statement: it names the event, h(b) = f (b, off), where the statement
only says one exists. The proof builds exactly that event (its first move is exists
(fun b => f b false)), so the printed form is what the proof shows, not only
what the statement says. And the proof uses two of the five honesty conditions,
driven and permanent; the other three are carried along and never used.

E.6 A raised flag was checked, then committed, then certified
earned_certification_provenance, minimal/EarnedCore.v.
Theorem earned_certification_provenance : forall s0 tr,
  clean_start s0 -> cert (run tr s0) = true ->
  exists pre1 p c mid1 mid2 post,
    tr = pre1 ++ CHECK p c :: mid1 ++ COMMIT p c :: mid2 ++ CERTIFY :: post /\
    check_ok (core_of (run pre1 s0)) p c = true /\
    commit_ok (core_of (run (pre1 ++ CHECK p c :: mid1) s0)) p c = true /\
    certify_ok (core_of (run (pre1 ++ CHECK p c :: mid1 ++ COMMIT p c :: mid2) s0))
      = true /\
    ver (core_of (run pre1 s0)) c = ver (core_of (run (pre1 ++ CHECK p c :: mid1) s0)) c /\
    untouched (run (pre1 ++ [CHECK p c]) s0) mid1 c.



In plain words: the clean-start premise on s0 says the fact table and the channel are
empty and the flag is down, and run tr s0 runs a list of instructions. The theorem:
from a clean start, if the flag is up at the end, the list splits as some start, CHECK
p c, a middle, COMMIT of the same p c, another middle, CERTIFY, and the rest;
the CHECK, the COMMIT and the CERTIFY each pass where they run; the counter’s
version at the CHECK equals its version at the COMMIT; and nothing in the first
middle touched that counter. Theorem 14.9 says exactly this.

E.7 Checker soundness
checker_soundness, minimal/EarnedCore.v.
Theorem checker_soundness : forall s0 tr f,
  clean_start s0 ->
  let k := core_of (run tr s0) in
  In f (facts k) -> f_ver f = ver k (f_ctr f) -> holds (f_prop f) (val k (f_ctr f)).


In plain words: from a clean start, after any list of instructions, every fact in the table
that’s about its counter’s current version is true of that counter’s current value, where
holds is the property’s meaning written without the checker. Theorem 14.11 says
exactly this in its first sentence; its “in particular” is the next corollary in the file, comm
itted_claim_holds.




                                                      468
The Thiele Machine                                                            Devon Thiele


E.8 No forging
no_forging, minimal/EarnedCore.v, with the two definitions it uses.
Definition earned (s0 : state) (tr : list instr) (f : fact) : Prop :=
  exists pre mid,
    tr = pre ++ CHECK (f_prop f) (f_ctr f) :: mid /\
    check_ok (core_of (run pre s0)) (f_prop f) (f_ctr f) = true /\
    f = claim (core_of (run pre s0)) (f_prop f) (f_ctr f) /\
    (f_ver f = ver (core_of (run tr s0)) (f_ctr f) ->
     untouched (run (pre ++ [CHECK (f_prop f) (f_ctr f)]) s0) mid (f_ctr f)).

Definition no_forgery (s0 : state) (tr : list instr) : Prop :=
  forall f, In f (facts (core_of (run tr s0))) -> earned s0 tr f.

Theorem no_forging : forall s0 tr, clean_start s0 -> no_forgery s0 tr.


In plain words: a fact is earned when a passing CHECK of exactly that property
and counter wrote it somewhere in the list, it is exactly the claim that CHECK made,
and, if it’s still about the counter’s current version, nothing touched the counter since.
no_forgery says every fact in the table at the end is earned. The theorem: from
every clean start, every list of instructions leaves no forgery. That’s the last clause of
Theorem 14.12, with Definition 14.6 saying the same as earned; the one-step clause
before it is facts_step.

E.9 The minimum price of a certificate
certified_run_min_cost, minimal/EarnedCore.v.

Theorem certified_run_min_cost : forall s0 tr,
  clean_start s0 -> cert (run tr s0) = true ->
  total_cost tr >= 3 /\ mu (run tr s0) >= mu s0 + 3.

In plain words: from a clean start, a list of instructions that ends with the flag up cost
at least three in total, and the ledger rose by at least three. Theorem 14.16 says exactly
this in its first sentence; its form for stored programs is program_certified_min_
cost.

E.10 Three, reached by a check that could have failed
earned_run_check_can_fail and earned_run_refused_forever,
minimal/EarnedCore.v, with the program they run.
Definition earned_run : list instr := [CHECK PZero CA; COMMIT PZero CA; CERTIFY].

Theorem earned_run_check_can_fail : forall a b,
  (a = 0 ->
     cert (run_prog 4 earned_run (start a b)) = true /\
     mu (run_prog 4 earned_run (start a b)) = 3) /\
  (a <> 0 ->
     cert (run_prog 4 earned_run (start a b)) = false /\
     err (core_of (run_prog 4 earned_run (start a b))) = true).

Theorem earned_run_refused_forever : forall n a b,
  a <> 0 -> cert (run_prog n earned_run (start a b)) = false.




                                           469
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


In plain words: earned_run is CHECK “A is 0”, COMMIT the same, CERTIFY, and
start a b puts a in A and b in B with an empty table. The first theorem: run it for
four program steps; if a is 0 the flag is up and the ledger is exactly 3, and if a isn’t 0
the flag is down and the trap is up. The second: if a isn’t 0, the flag is down after any
number of steps. So three is reached by a check that could have failed, and when it
fails nothing ever certifies. Theorem 14.17 says this. The older witness in the same file,
min_cost_tight, reaches three with “A is at least 0”, a check that can’t fail; the step
doesn’t police that, and Section 14 says so.

E.11 The copy is the record
record_agreement, minimal/UniversalThiele.v.

Definition agrees (h : hstate) : Prop := mrec h = E.cert (gst h).

Theorem record_agreement : forall tr h, agrees h -> agrees (hrun tr h).

In plain words: the host keeps a mirror bit mrec beside the guest’s state gst, and
agrees h says the mirror equals the guest’s own flag. The theorem: a host state that
agrees still agrees after any list of host moves, whatever they are. Theorem 14.19 says
this for lists of moves and adds stored programs and loading, which are record_ag
reement_program and hload_agrees.

E.12 No free host certification
no_free_host_certification, minimal/UniversalThiele.v, with the host’s
moves and their costs.
Inductive hinstr : Type :=
| OWN (i : E.instr)
| GSTEP (b : nat).

Definition hcost (i : hinstr) : nat :=
  match i with OWN j => E.cost j | GSTEP b => b end.

Definition crossing (g g’ : E.state) : bool := negb (E.cert g) && E.cert g’.

Theorem no_free_host_certification : forall tr h,
  mrec h = false -> mrec (hrun tr h) = true ->
  exists pre b post, tr = pre ++ GSTEP b :: post /\ b >= 1 /\
    crossing (gst (hrun pre h)) (gst (hexec (hrun pre h) (GSTEP b))) = true.


In plain words: a host move is either OWN i, one of the small machine’s own instruc-
tions on the host’s core, or GSTEP b, one guest step with budget b, which costs b
whatever the guest instruction cost. crossing g g’ says the guest’s flag went from
down to up. The theorem: if the mirror is down before a list of host moves and up
after it, then somewhere in the list there’s a GSTEP b with b at least one at which the
guest’s flag crossed. Theorem 14.21 prints the one-move form, no_free_host_ce
rtification_step, which also says the host wasn’t trapped and the guest’s next
instruction was CERTIFY; this is the form for whole lists that it lifts to. Neither says
what the guest did before its CERTIFY. That a raised mirror means the guest’s own


                                           470
The Thiele Machine                                                                                Devon Thiele


run checked and committed first is the next theorem.

E.13 A raised mirror stands on the guest’s own earned chain
host_mirror_earned, minimal/UniversalThiele.v.
Theorem host_mirror_earned : forall tr a b P x y,
  mrec (hrun tr (hload a b P x y)) = true ->
  exists n gtr pre1 p c mid1 mid2 post,
    gtr = E.trace_of n P (E.start x y) /\
    gst (hrun tr (hload a b P x y)) = E.run gtr (E.start x y) /\
    gtr = pre1 ++ E.CHECK p c :: mid1 ++ E.COMMIT p c :: mid2 ++ E.CERTIFY :: post /\
    E.check_ok (E.core_of (E.run pre1 (E.start x y))) p c = true /\
    E.commit_ok (E.core_of (E.run (pre1 ++ E.CHECK p c :: mid1) (E.start x y))) p c
      = true /\
    E.certify_ok (E.core_of (E.run (pre1 ++ E.CHECK p c :: mid1 ++ E.COMMIT p c :: mid2)
                               (E.start x y))) = true /\
    E.ver (E.core_of (E.run pre1 (E.start x y))) c
      = E.ver (E.core_of (E.run (pre1 ++ E.CHECK p c :: mid1) (E.start x y))) c /\
    E.untouched (E.run (pre1 ++ [E.CHECK p c]) (E.start x y)) mid1 c.



In plain words: load the host with a guest program P and a guest start (x, y) (hloa
d gives the guest a clean start), run any list of host moves, and suppose the mirror is up
at the end. Then for some number of steps n, the guest’s state is its own program’s run
of n steps, and the instructions that run executed split exactly the way Theorem 14.9
splits a trace: a passing CHECK, a COMMIT of the same claim at the same version
with the counter untouched between, then a passing CERTIFY. So the host’s mirror
can’t be up unless the guest’s own program earned it. The book’s sentences citing h
ost_mirror_earned say this in words; the Coq says a little more than they need,
since the chain sits inside the instructions the guest program itself executed and not
just in some list.

E.14 Structural entitlement, represented
structural_entitlement_representation,
coq/kernel/nfi/HonestNoFI_TheoremsWithoutAssumptions.v.
Theorem structural_entitlement_representation :
  forall (fuel : nat) (trace : list vm_instruction)
         (s_init : VMState)
         (decoder : NoFreeInsight.receipt_decoder vm_instruction)
         (obs_fn : VMState -> list vm_instruction)
         (repr_obs_fn : VMState -> list vm_instruction)
         (obs_eqb : list vm_instruction -> list vm_instruction -> bool)
         (omega_prior omega_posterior : list VMState)
         (tree : MuShannonBridge.DecisionTree),
    (forall o1 o2, obs_eqb o1 o2 = true <-> o1 = o2) ->
    InformationGainToStrengthening.is_strict_subset omega_posterior omega_prior ->
    (exists s_witness,
      In s_witness omega_prior /\
      ~ In s_witness omega_posterior /\
      InformationGainToStrengthening.observation_distinguishes obs_fn s_witness omega_posterior) ->
    s_init.(vm_csrs).(csr_cert_addr) = 0 ->
    NoFreeInsight.Certified
      (run_vm fuel trace s_init)
      decoder
      (InformationGainToStrengthening.omega_predicate
         obs_eqb omega_posterior obs_fn)
      trace ->
    MuShannonBridge.decision_tree_realized_by_trace fuel trace s_init tree ->
    MuShannonBridge.feasible_size omega_posterior > 0 ->
    MuShannonBridge.PosteriorRepresentativeReduction
      repr_obs_fn tree omega_prior omega_posterior ->
    let P_prior :=
      InformationGainToStrengthening.omega_predicate
        obs_eqb omega_prior obs_fn in
    let P_posterior :=
      InformationGainToStrengthening.omega_predicate
        obs_eqb omega_posterior obs_fn in




                                                      471
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


   NoFreeInsight.strictly_stronger P_posterior P_prior /\
   NoFreeInsight.has_structure_addition fuel trace s_init /\
   Nat.log2_up (MuShannonBridge.feasible_size omega_prior) -
     Nat.log2_up (MuShannonBridge.feasible_size omega_posterior) <=
     (run_vm fuel trace s_init).(vm_mu) - s_init.(vm_mu).



In plain words: on the big build, fix fuel, a list of instructions, a start, a decoder, two
observations, an equality test, a prior and a posterior list of states, and a decision tree.
The eight premises: the test decides equality; the posterior is a strict sublist of the
prior; some state in the prior and not the posterior is told apart by the observation;
the start’s assertion channel is zero; the run ends certified for the posterior’s member-
ship predicate; the tree is realized by the run; the posterior isn’t empty; and there’s
a posterior-representative reduction. The conclusions: the posterior’s predicate is
strictly stronger, the run has a structure addition, and the drop in index bits, rounded
up, is at most what the ledger rose. Theorem 22.9 says exactly this, (H1) to (H8) and
(C1) to (C3) in this order. Where shorter sentences in the book say that leaning on
a fact “costs at least the index bits,” this is all they mean: the sixth premise already
says the run paid a floor step for each level of the tree, and the theorem shows those
payments cover the bits. It doesn’t show that a run has to make them.

E.15 The game check implies a positive semidefinite matrix
chsh_lassert_no_trap_implies_npa_psd,
coq/kernel/quantum/QuantumPartitionPSD.v.

Theorem chsh_lassert_no_trap_implies_npa_psd :
  forall s mu_delta,
    let s’ := vm_apply s (instr_chsh_lassert mu_delta) in
    s’.(vm_err) = s.(vm_err) ->
    s.(vm_err) = false ->
    npa_psd (state_zero_marginal_npa s).

In plain words: on the big build, take a state with the error flag down and run CHSH_
LASSERT on it with any declared cost. If the error flag afterwards is what it was (the
check didn’t trap), then the five-by-five matrix built from the state’s witness counters,
with the marginals set to zero, is symmetric and positive semidefinite; npa_psd says
both. Theorem 25.2 says exactly this.

F The CHSH derivation, in full
This appendix supports Section 25. That section tells the story; this one does the
algebra. Each item gives the exact statement with all its hypotheses, the steps a reader
needs to check it, and the Coq name with its file. Nothing here identifies any matrix
with a quantum state. Where the reading “quantum” appears, it is a cited result from
outside the kernel.

F.1 A. Setting and notation
Definition F.1 (Settings, outcomes, correlators). Alice receives a setting x ∈ {0, 1} and
Bob a setting y ∈ {0, 1}. Each answers a bit, recoded as an outcome a, b ∈ {+1, −1}


                                                     472
The Thiele Machine                                                              Devon Thiele


(bit 0 becomes +1, bit 1 becomes −1). The correlator Exy is the average of the product
ab over the rounds with settings ( x, y). The CHSH quantity is

                                S = E00 + E01 + E10 − E11 .

I collect the four correlators into the 2 × 2 matrix
                                                    !
                                            E00 E01
                                     E=               ,
                                            E10 E11

whose rows are indexed by Alice’s setting and whose columns by Bob’s. The rows of
E are ( E00 , E01 ) and ( E10 , E11 ); the columns are ( E00 , E10 ) and ( E01 , E11 ).


The     same    polynomial   S   appears  under    three     names in  the
source:        CHSH     (kernel/quantum/TsirelsonGeneral.v),    CHSH_val

Definition F.2 (Counters). The machine keeps eight counters in the record WitnessC
ounts (kernel/foundation/VMState.v): for each setting pair, samexy counts rounds
whose two answer bits matched and diffxy counts rounds whose bits differed. recor
d_trial (kernel/foundation/VMStep.v) adds one to exactly one of the eight. Write

                                                                              Dxy
          Nxy = samexy + diffxy ,       Dxy = samexy − diffxy ,       Exy =       .
                                                                              Nxy


A matched round contributes ab = +1 and a differing round ab = −1, so Dxy is the
sum of the products and Dxy /Nxy is their average. Since | Dxy | ≤ Nxy , every correla-
tor from counters lies in [−1, 1]. In Coq the integers are chsh_n_z and chsh_d_z
(kernel/foundation/VMStep.v). When a bucket is empty, the real-valued correlator
state_bucket_correlation (kernel/nfi/MuLedgerQuantumBridge.v) and the
rational one chsh_correlator_q (kernel/quantum/CHSHStatisticalBridge.v) both
return 0 by convention. The CHSH score of a tally, chsh_stat_from_wc (CHSH-
StatisticalBridge.v), adds the first three correlators and obtains − E11 by swapping the
two counters of the last bucket.

F.2 B. The classical bound
Lemma F.1 (Deterministic strategies). Let a0 , a1 , b0 , b1 ∈ {+1, −1}. Then −2 ≤ a0 b0 +
a0 b1 + a1 b0 − a1 b1 ≤ 2.

Proof. Factor: a0 b0 + a0 b1 + a1 b0 − a1 b1 = a0 (b0 + b1 ) + a1 (b0 − b1 ). If b0 = b1 then
b0 + b1 = ±2 and b0 − b1 = 0; if b0 ̸= b1 the other way round. In both cases exactly
one of the two brackets is ±2 and the other is 0, so the expression is ±2 times a sign,
which is +2 or −2. There are sixteen sign choices, and every one of them gives exactly


                                            473
The Thiele Machine                                                                       Devon Thiele


±2, never 0 or ±4.

The Coq proofs do not factor; they split into the sixteen sign cases and compute. The
rational statement is local_S_2_deterministic (kernel/quantum/BoxCHSH.v):
for f A , f B : N → Q with every value ±1, the absolute value of f A (0) f B (0) +
f A (0) f B (1) + f A (1) f B (0) − f A (1) f B (1) is at most 2. The real statement is determi
nistic_strategy_chsh_bounded (kernel/quantum/MinorConstraints.v), with
conclusion −2 ≤ · · · ≤ 2.


Definition F.3 (Finite factorizable model, is_factorizable). A real-valued correla-
tion function E( a, b, x, y) is factorizable (kernel/quantum/MinorConstraints.v) when
there exist response functions A( x, λ), B(y, λ), weights p(λ) and a natural number
λmax such that: 0 ≤ p(λ) ≤ 1 for λ ≤ λmax ; ∑λλmax    =0 p ( λ ) = 1; every A ( x, λ ) and every
B(y, λ) is −1 or +1; and for all a, b, x, y, E( a, b, x, y) = ∑λλmax
                                                                  =0 p ( λ ) A ( x, λ ) B ( y, λ ). The
outcome arguments a, b are dummies; only correlations are modelled.


Theorem F.2 (fine_theorem, one direction only). If E is factorizable,
then −2 ≤ E(0, 0, 0, 0) + E(0, 0, 0, 1) + E(0, 0, 1, 0) − E(0, 0, 1, 1) ≤ 2 (ker-
nel/quantum/MinorConstraints.v; restated as factorizable_CHSH_classical
_bound).

Proof. Substitute the factorization: S = ∑λ p(λ)Sλ , where Sλ is the deterministic
expression of Lemma F.1 at the signs A(·, λ), B(·, λ). Each Sλ ∈ [−2, 2], the weights
are nonnegative and sum to 1, so −2 = ∑λ p(λ)(−2) ≤ S ≤ ∑λ p(λ) · 2 = 2.


Remark F.1 (What the name does and does not cover). Fine’s 1982 theorem is an
equivalence between several descriptions of local models and the Bell inequalities. f
ine_theorem proves one direction: a finite factorizable model obeys the bound. It
proves no converse, and it covers only finitely many hidden states (λ ≤ λmax ), not an
arbitrary probability space. The transfer to rational boxes is local_box_CHSH_bou
nd (kernel/quantum/MinorConstraints.v): if box_correlations B is factorizable
then the real image of |S( B)| is at most 2.


The finite-tally statement concerns one fixed strategy replayed on every recorded
round.


Definition F.4 (WCLocallyConsistent). For bits a0 , a1 , b0 , b1 ∈ {0, 1} and a counter
record w (kernel/quantum/CHSHStatisticalBridge.v), w is locally consistent with
( a0 , a1 , b0 , b1 ) when, for each setting pair ( x, y): if a x = by then diffxy = 0, otherwise
samexy = 0; and every bucket is sampled, N00 , N01 , N10 , N11 > 0.




                                                 474
The Thiele Machine                                                                       Devon Thiele


Theorem F.3 (A tally above 2 is not one replayed strategy). Let w be a counter
record whose rational score chsh_stat_from_wc w is greater than 2. Then
for all bits a0 , a1 , b0 , b1 , w is not locally consistent with ( a0 , a1 , b0 , b1 ). This is
chsh_violation_rules_out_locally_factorizable_coupling (ker-
nel/quantum/CHSHCouplingBridge.v). Its contrapositive form, locally_consisten
t_classical_bound, states that a locally consistent record has score of absolute value at
most 2.

Proof. Under local consistency each sampled bucket is pure: if a x = by every round
in the bucket matched, so Exy = Nxy /Nxy = +1; otherwise every round differed and
Exy = −1. In signs, Exy = α x β y with α x = (−1) ax and β y = (−1)by . The score is then
the deterministic expression of Lemma F.1, which is at most 2 in absolute value. A
score above 2 contradicts this.

The theorem rules out one explanation, a single four-bit plan used on every round. It
says nothing about a local model that redraws its hidden state every round; Section 25
gives a four-round coin-flip tally with score 4.

F.3 C. Tsirelson’s bound from algebra
Lemma F.4 (The six-square identity, chsh_gap_is_sum_of_squares). For all real
a, b, c, d,

          4( a2 + b2 + c2 + d2 ) − ( a + b + c − d )2
             = ( a − b )2 + ( a − c )2 + ( a + d )2 + ( b − c )2 + ( b + d )2 + ( c + d )2 .

(kernel/quantum/TsirelsonFromAlgebra.v, closed by ring.)

Proof. Expand the square on the left: ( a + b + c − d)2 = a2 + b2 + c2 + d2 + 2ab + 2ac −
2ad + 2bc − 2bd − 2cd. So the left side is

               3( a2 + b2 + c2 + d2 ) − 2ab − 2ac + 2ad − 2bc + 2bd + 2cd.

On the right, each variable appears in exactly three of the six brackets (a in a − b, a − c,
a + d; b in a − b, b − c, b + d; c in a − c, b − c, c + d; d in a + d, b + d, c + d), so the
squared terms add to 3( a2 + b2 + c2 + d2 ). The cross terms are −2ab from ( a − b)2 ,
−2ac from ( a − c)2 , +2ad from ( a + d)2 , −2bc from (b − c)2 , +2bd from (b + d)2 and
+2cd from (c + d)2 . Both sides agree term by term.

Since the right side is a sum of squares, S2 ≤ 4 ∑ xy Exy
                                                       2 for any four reals; this is cauc

hy_schwarz_chsh (TsirelsonFromAlgebra.v).

Lemma F.8 (Schur complement, the!standard form). Let P be symmetric positive definite.
                           P Q
The symmetric block matrix         is PSD if and only if R − QT P−1 Q is PSD.
                           QT R

Proof. For u, w of the right sizes,
        !T           !       !

The first term is never negative because P is positive definite, and it is zero at u =
− P−1 Qw. So the form is nonnegative for all (u, w) exactly when the second term is
nonnegative for all w.

Remark F.3 (What PSD of the pinned matrix means). M ( E) is the level-1 moment
matrix with the two within-party entries ⟨ A0 A1 ⟩ and ⟨ B0 B1 ⟩ pinned to zero. Its PSD is
sufficient for the correlators to admit some PSD completion (item G, zero_margina
l_implies_elliptope), and it is not necessary: the all-ones plan has a completion
but fails here. So a check built on M( E) is sound for the completion set and not
complete for it, and it rejects some honest classical tallies. That correlators with a
PSD completion are exactly those reachable by quantum measurements is Tsirelson’s
theorem, cited and not proved here (item H).

D = 3, 8, 8, −3: A = 25 · 100 − 9 · 100 − 64 · 25 = 0, B = 100 · 25 − 64 · 25 − 9 · 100 = 0
and C = 3 · 8 · 10 · 5 + 8 · (−3) · 5 · 10 = 0. It passes with no slack, at S = 2.8.

with Sij = h11 hij − h1i h1j for i, j ≥ 2 (here S is the Schur matrix, not the score),
                                                              2

                                                    j                 i,j≥2


So if h11 > 0 and the (n − 1) × (n − 1) matrix S gives a nonnegative form, then h does too.

Proof. Expand the square: h211 v21 + 2h11 v1 ∑ j≥2 h1j v j + (∑ j≥2 h1j v j )2 . The left side is

Dividing by h11 > 0 keeps the sign.

tally of item E with correlators (3/5, 4/5, 4/5, −3/5) has H11 = 1 − 9/25 − 16/25 = 0,
so the full 1+AB check traps on it for every choice of γ, though the level-1 check of
item E accepts it. The source proves soundness only; no converse is stated.

Theorem F.25 (Deterministic plans are inside, deterministic_strategy_ellip
tope). (ElliptopeCompletion.v) If a20 = a21 = b02 = b12 = 1, then ( a0 b0 , a0 b1 , a1 b0 , a1 b1 ) is
elliptope realizable, with x = a0 a1 and y = b0 b1 .

Proof. With these entries the form equals v20 + ( a0 v1 + a1 v2 + b0 v3 + b1 v4 )2 . Expanding
the second square gives a20 v21 + · · · on the diagonal, which is v21 + · · · by the unit
squares, and the cross terms 2a0 a1 v1 v2 = 2xv1 v2 , 2a0 b0 v1 v3 = 2E00 v1 v3 , and so on for
all six pairs. A sum of two squares is never negative.

The all-ones plan is the instance classical_tightness_witness_elliptope,
and the classical mixture (1, 0, 1, 0) is turing_point_elliptope, at x = 1, y = 0,
with form v20 + (v1 + v2 + v3 )2 + v24 .


Theorem F.26 (Convexity and finite mixtures). For 0 ≤ λ ≤ 1, if E and F are elliptope
realizable, so is λE + (1 − λ) F (elliptope_convex, ElliptopeCompletion.v). For finitely
many members with nonnegative weights summing to at most 1, the weighted sum is realizable
(elliptope_finite_mixture). Every finite mixture of deterministic plans is realizable
(lhv_mixture_elliptope).

Proof. The form is affine in ( E, x, y) for each fixed v. Take the completion (λx1 + (1 −
λ) x2 , λy1 + (1 − λ)y2 ); the form at the mixture is the same mixture of two nonnegative

                                                 488
The Thiele Machine                                                                        Devon Thiele


forms. The finite version is induction on the number of members, with the shortfall in
weight absorbed by the zero point (elliptope_zero). The last statement combines
this with Theorem F.25.


Theorem F.27 (Tsirelson inside the completion set, elliptope_tsirelson). (Ellip-
topeCompletion.v) If E is elliptope realizable then S2 ≤ 8.

Proof. For a symmetric PSD matrix the bilinear form obeys Cauchy-Schwarz,
B(u, w)2 ≤ Q(u) Q(w) (psd_cauchy_schwarz), because Q(u + tw) = Q(u) +
2t B(u, w) + t2 Q(w) ≥ 0 for all t and Lemma F.11 applies. Take u1 = e A0 and
w+ = e B0 + e B1 : B(u1 , w+ ) = E00 + E01 , Q(u1 ) = 1, Q(w+ ) = 2 + 2y. Take
u2 = e A1 and w− = e B0 − e B1 : B(u2 , w− ) = E10 − E11 , Q(w− ) = 2 − 2y. So
c21 ≤ 2 + 2y and c22 ≤ 2 − 2y with c1 = E00 + E01 , c2 = E10 − E11 , and both bud-
gets are nonnegative. Then c21 c22 ≤ (2 + 2y)(2 − 2y) = 4 − 4y2 ≤ 4, so c1 c2 ≤ 2, and
S2 = (c1 + c2 )2 = c21 + 2c1 c2 + c22 ≤ (2 + 2y) + 4 + (2 − 2y) = 8.

The completion can make a row of E longer than 1 (the all-ones plan has rows of
squared length 2), which is why this proof does not use the row bounds of item D.


Corollary F.28 (The PR box is outside, pr_box_not_elliptope). (ElliptopeComple-
tion.v) (1, 1, 1, −1) is not elliptope realizable, since its S2 = 16 > 8.

Theorem F.30 (Soundness of the gate, elliptope_check_full_sound). (Elliptope-
Gate.v) If elliptope_check_full returns true on a counter record, any completion
buckets and any certificate, then the four correlators of the record are elliptope realizable. And

The gate is not an instruction. Neither VMStep.v nor VMState.v mentions it, and the
file’s own header says that binding it into the step relation, a cost rule and a hardware
mirror is not done.

F.8 H. What is not proved
The following are cited results or open, and none of them is a Coq theorem in this
development.

The arcsine boundary. For two settings and two outcomes per side, the correlators
reachable by quantum measurements are characterized by | arcsin E00 + arcsin E01 +
arcsin E10 − arcsin E11 | ≤ π and its sign variants (Tsirelson, Landau 1988, Masanes
2003). No arcsine appears in any Coq statement; the only mentions are comments in
ElliptopeGate.v. The claim that (3/5, 4/5, 4/5, −3/5) lies on that boundary is such a
comment: arcsin 35 + arcsin 54 = π2 by the 3-4-5 triangle, so the sum is π. It is correct
arithmetic about a cited characterization.

Equality with the quantum set. That the completion set of item G is exactly the set
of quantum correlators is Tsirelson’s representation theorem, cited in the header of
ElliptopeCompletion.v and not proved. That PSD of any of these matrices is necessary
for quantum behaviour is the NPA reading, also cited.



                                               490
The Thiele Machine                                                          Devon Thiele


Achievability. No state and no pair of measurements is constructed. Theorem F.6 is a
point of R4 , not an experiment.

Completeness of the checks. Every check here is proved sound, never complete. The
1+AB cascade is strict and misses boundary points. The comment in ElliptopeGate.v
that the second branch accepts every point with a rational PSD completion is a math-
ematical remark about LDLT factorizations, not a theorem in the file; nor is there a
theorem that the four 1+AB checks accept nested sets.

Finite levels. For full behaviours, marginals included, the NPA levels are relaxations.
Chaturvedi (arXiv 2607.14569, 2026) shows that no finite NPA level characterizes the
complete quantum set even in this simplest Bell scenario.

Statistics and physics. Nothing here says how many rounds make a tally informative,
and nothing says the counters came from honest play; a program chooses its own trial
inputs.

F.9 I. Prior work
                                √
Tsirelson proved the bound 2 2 for quantum correlations in 1980 and showed that
quantum two-outcome correlators are inner products of real unit vectors. Landau
(1988) and Masanes (2003, arXiv quant-ph/0309137) gave the exact characterization
for two settings and two outcomes. Wehner (2006, arXiv quant-ph/0510076) proved
Tsirelson bounds, CHSH among them, by a semidefinite program on the 4 × 4 Gram
matrix of those vectors. Navascués, Pironio and Acín (2007, arXiv quant-ph/0607119;
2008, arXiv 0803.4290) built the hierarchy of moment-matrix tests; their 2008 paper
applies a Schur complement to this level-1 matrix, recovers the arcsine condition, and
discusses the 1+AB level. Formal proofs of Tsirelson’s bound already exist, by Echenim
and Mhalla in Isabelle/HOL (arXiv 2306.12535) and in Lean’s mathlib (tsirelson_
inequality in Mathlib.Algebra.Star.CHSH), and exact rational sum-of-squares certifi-
                                                                                      √
cates go back at least to Peyrl and Parrilo (2008). So the moment-matrix route to 2 2
is standard. What is specific here is narrower: an integer certificate computed from
outcome counters and checked inside one instruction, a mechanized chain from “the
instruction did not trap” to PSD of the pinned matrix and on to S2 ≤ 8, and a hardware
circuit proved equal to that integer check for every choice of 32-bit counters. I did not
find that chain elsewhere, and I make no claim beyond it.

G Hardware retirement: the assumptions in full
The word admitted in Section 27 names a set of inputs on which the retirement theorem
applies. It is not permission to hide the inputs. This appendix spells out that set. All
the conditions here are conditions on the state before the instruction starts. A bound
in one row is not automatically a hypothesis of another.




                                          491
The Thiele Machine                                                              Devon Thiele


G.1 Common notation and conditions
Write W = 232 . A hardware word denotes its unsigned value from 0 to W − 1; word ad-
dition and subtraction wrap modulo W. All inequalities below concern the unsigned
values as natural numbers, before any wrap. Write r j for register j, H for the heap base,
q for the program counter, and c for the declared cost decoded from the instruction.
Register indices are four bits, module indices six, and data-memory addresses seven.
Thus taking an address means reducing it modulo 128. The stack pointer is register
15.

Every case requires the fetched word to encode the indicated instruction and its
operands, the alarm to be down, the machine to be live, and q + 1 < W. Here live
means not halted, error false, and the logic, game-check and coupling state machines
all idle. The alarm tests whether the ledger is below the sum of the tensor entries. The
ledger requirement is µ + ∆ < W, with ∆ given in each row. Even a jump or a halting
instruction has the printed q + 1 < W premise: these are the sufficient conditions of
the theorem, not a claim that each one is necessary.

For a module m, write bm and sm for its stored base and size. An address x is in the active
range when bm ≤ x < bm + sm for the active module m. The trap agreement condition
says that the board’s trap-vector word equals the fixed LASSERT trap address in
Section 17. The partition-operation and MDL-operation counters are diagnostic fields;
call them P and D.

For the arrow tables, let NM , ND , NP be the next allocation indices for arrows, coupling
descriptors and coupling pairs. A descriptor records a base and count in the pair table,
together with a label length and label word. Each table also marks which entries are
valid. The following abbreviations state complete predicates:

Name                                          Condition
V                                             Every valid arrow index is less than NM .
R                                             Every valid arrow refers either to descriptor
                                              0, or to a valid descriptor whose index is less
                                              than ND .
Z                                             Descriptor 0 is marked invalid.
E                                             Descriptor 0 has base 0 and count 0.
B                                             For every valid descriptor, its base plus its
                                              count is at most NP .
Pairs                                         Every pair-table index below NP is marked
                                              valid.
Labels                                        Every valid descriptor has label length L
                                              with 1 ≤ L ≤ 32 and label word less than 2 L .
Disjoint                                      The regions of distinct modules in the
                                              snapshot graph are disjoint.



An invalid descriptor has effective label length 1 and effective label word 1. An arrow’s

                                           492
The Thiele Machine                                                               Devon Thiele


coupling list is the slice at its descriptor’s base and count. For composition, the output
list is empty if both arrows are identities, the other arrow’s list if exactly one is an
identity, and the relational join otherwise: enumerate a pair ( x, z) for each ( x, y) in
the first list and (y, z) in the second. Repeated pairs count as repeated entries when
measuring the room required.

The arbitrary operands are deliberate limitations of these correspondences. If a snap-
shot omits an abstract field, agreement of snapshots does not recover it. In particular,
a result for an arbitrary evidence list does not show that the board stored or checked
that list. Section 27 separates snapshot agreement from a statement about the entire
kernel state.

G.3 Memory-reading and checking cases
The remaining seven cases are the two extended MORPH paths, the two extended
COMPOSE paths, the two LASSERT kinds, and CHSH_LASSERT. They carry the
common conditions above and the following additional ones.

MORPH, missing-module path. The increment is c. Require NM < 16 and ND < 16,
and at least one of the selected source and target modules has size zero. This is a fault
retirement, not a successful arrow construction.

COMPOSE, invalid-input path. The increment is c. Require V and NM < 16, and
either one of the two arrow slots is marked invalid or the first arrow’s target differs
from the second arrow’s source. This too is a fault retirement.

                                          494
The Thiele Machine                                                          Devon Thiele


MORPH, pair-loading path. The increment is c. Require NM < 16, ND < 16, and both
selected modules to have nonzero size. Let a be the seven-bit address decoded for the
coupling buffer and let n be its first memory word. Require NP < 16, n + NP ≤ 16,
a + 2n ≤ 127, and a + 1 + 2n < 128. The word at a + 1 + 2n must be zero. The n pairs
stored in the next 2n words must each have their first coordinate in the source region
and their second coordinate in the target region. Thus neither a count nor an endpoint
is accepted merely because the buffer fits.

COMPOSE, pair-building path. The increment is c. Require NM < 16, ND < 16,
NP < 16, and V, R, Z, E, B, Pairs and Labels. Both input arrow slots must be valid and
their middle module must match. Their effective label lengths must sum to at most 32.
Finally, NP plus the length of the output coupling list defined above must be at most
16.

LASSERT, unsatisfiable kind. The increment is 8ℓ + c + 1. Require trap agreement
and the formula’s memory header to equal the declared length ℓ. This case retires
through the unsupported-unsatisfiability failure described in Section 17; it does not
establish an unsatisfiability checker.

LASSERT, satisfiable kind. The increment is 8ℓ + c + 1. Require trap agreement,
the memory header at the formula address a to equal ℓ, and a + 3 + ℓ < W. The
clause count stored at a + 2 must be at least one and at most the number of zero
terminator words in the literal sequence. These are the conditions of Theorem 27.3
and Lemma 27.4.

CHSH_LASSERT. The increment is c + 1. Require trap agreement. The arithmetic
check itself may pass or fail; retirement covers either result. Its complete integer
predicate and its mathematical consequence are in Appendix F.

G.4 What the catalogue establishes
These are fifty-five admission cases, counting the separately named encodings and
fault paths. They are sufficient hypotheses for the retirement theorem. They do not
assert that a program can never leave this set, that a failed premise makes the hardware
incorrect, or that all abstract instructions have an encoding.

The proof divides the cases by what can change. For an ordinary arithmetic or data-
moving instruction, evaluate the register writes and the program-counter and ledger
updates, then use the bounds to replace word arithmetic by the natural-number arith-
metic of the specified instruction. For memory and partition instructions, the active-
range and representation conditions make their guards and selected addresses agree.
For arrow operations, the validity, descriptor and capacity conditions make the table
lookup or update represent the stated graph operation. A fault path instead proves
agreement on its specified refusal.

A multi-cycle instruction also needs an invariant through its internal firings: the scan



                                          495
The Thiele Machine                                                             Devon Thiele


has processed exactly the prefix already visited, the partial arithmetic equals the corre-
sponding expression on the saved operands, and unrelated state fields are unchanged.
The scan and game-check arguments are given in Section 27. The coupling scan loads
the next pair, checks its two region memberships and advances its count; composition
enumerates the finite join defined above, with the identity cases separated. The room
and address conditions keep each write within its intended table. At completion, the
accumulated list is the specified one. This is how the per-instruction arguments enter
the master case split; a list of theorem names alone would not supply that explanation.

G.5 Reading a snapshot as a kernel state
Two readings occur in Section 27. They copy the same scalar state: program counter,
ledger, error flag, logic accumulator, status, certification flag, four control registers
and eight witness counters. They turn register entries 0–15, memory entries 0–127 and
tensor entries 0–15 into lists in increasing index order. The board’s halted flag and
diagnostic counters have no separate kernel-state fields.

The partition-only reading, abs0 , reconstructs modules by visiting indices N − 1, N −
2, . . . , 0, where N is the next module index. It omits a module whose size is zero. Each
remaining module gets the interval of addresses from its base through base plus size
minus one, an empty axiom list and a zero tensor. The graph’s next module index is
N, its arrow list is empty and its next arrow index is one. This is the reading used in
the checking-step comparison.

The full reading, abs, uses the same modules and intervals, but gives each module
its sixteen stored tensor entries. It visits arrow indices in descending order below
NM , omitting invalid slots. A valid entry supplies source, target and identity flag. Its
descriptor supplies the coupling label and the list of pairs in its stored range, read
in increasing offset order and skipping absent pairs. An absent descriptor supplies
an empty pair list and the default empty-coupling label. Each reconstructed arrow
has certification cost zero. The graph’s next arrow index is NM . This is the reading
in Theorem 27.7. The theorem compares the reconstructed state; it does not recover
evidence absent from the snapshot.

G.6 The full-state bridge conditions
The full-state bridge and clocked retirement have different hypotheses. The following
predicates complete the definition of WF in Theorem 27.7. They concern the snapshot’s
natural-number fields and optional table entries, before any extra bounds required by
the clocked board.

A well-formed partition table has 1 ≤ N ≤ 64. A well-formed arrow table has no valid
arrow at an index at least NM . The empty-descriptor condition says that descriptor zero is
absent. The extended invariant consists of these three conditions together with ND > 0
and all of the following: every valid arrow names a descriptor index below ND ; every
present descriptor’s base plus count is at most NP ; and every slot in every present


                                           496
The Thiele Machine                                                           Devon Thiele


descriptor’s range holds a pair. It does not require every index below ND to hold a
descriptor.

The stack condition is p < 128 and ( p − 1) mod 264 < 128, where p = r15 and the
subtraction in that second expression is subtraction modulo 264 . Since p < 128, this
is equivalent to 1 ≤ p < 128. A clear tensor slot has every stored tensor entry zero,
including entries beyond the sixteen that the reading retains.
